aspects.title: Information conveyed exclusively by a CSS background-image (no img element, no DOM text equivalent)
aspects.plain: A picture carrying real meaning (a price banner, a 'SOLD OUT' stamp) is painted via CSS background-image with no DOM text, so a screen-reader user never learns it.
aspects.description: An element carries meaning purely through a CSS background-image — set in a stylesheet rule, an inline style= attribute, or injected by script — and that same meaning exists nowhere as real text in the DOM. Because there is no img/svg/object/input element and no alt slot, every ACT 1.1.1 rule (which is scoped to elements that can hold an accessible name) returns Inapplicable; there is no target to evaluate. A human must look at the rendered page, recognize that a background image is carrying information (a price banner, a status/stock icon, a 'SOLD OUT' stamp, a required-field marker, a weather condition glyph, a logo), and then verify whether that exact information is ALSO available as text elsewhere on the page. This is a two-step semantic + visual judgment: (1) does this background image depict required information, and (2) is that information redundant in the DOM text?
aspects.scLimb: The core 'all non-text content that conveys information has a text alternative' requirement (G94 / 'serves the same purpose'), applied to the background-image mechanism that the SC covers but the ACT accessible-name rules structurally cannot reach.
aspects.whyUncovered: Every ACT 1.1.1 rule targets elements that can hold an accessible name (img, role=img, svg[role], object, input[type=image], a). A CSS background image is none of these, so all rules return Inapplicable and the corpus has zero background-image pages. Automated checkers cannot do this either: they cannot reliably enumerate which background images carry information vs decoration, and even if they could, deciding whether the info is 'already conveyed elsewhere on the page' is a meaning-comparison task between a rendered image and surrounding prose. Trusted Tester gives this its own dedicated manual test (7.C) precisely because it is not automatable.

references.quote: it is not possible to associate text alternatives with images that are included via CSS. Text alternatives are necessary for people who cannot see images that convey information that is required to understand the content of the page.

This failure would apply equally in a case where the background image was declared in the HTML style attribute, as well as in a case where the background image declaration was created dynamically in a client script
Test 7.C — `1.1.1-decorative-background-image` Test Condition: The background image is not the only means used to convey important information.

aspects.ttWhy: Meaning carried by a CSS background image is exactly what 7.C evaluates.

pages.scenario: Building-society loan card whose headline rate '19.3% APR Typical Variable' lives only as pixels in a stylesheet background-image SVG; the visible DOM prose says only 'Where else would you find a better interest rate?' (verbatim F3 example 1).
pages.mechanism: The load-bearing price (19.3% APR Typical Variable) is rendered exclusively by `p#bestinterest { background-image: url(svg) }`. A CSS background image generates no accessibility-tree node and cannot carry a text alternative, so a screen-reader user hears the unanswered question and never learns the rate; forced-colors/hide-backgrounds drops it for sighted users too.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: There is no img/svg/role=img/object/input[type=image] — nothing nameable — so every ACT 1.1.1 rule is Inapplicable and axe/WAVE/Lighthouse have no target. They cannot OCR the data-URI SVG to find '19.3% APR', cannot classify the flag as informative vs decorative, and cannot perform the meaning-comparison of whether the rate appears as text elsewhere.

citation.quote: In this example, the image TopRate.png is a 180 by 200 pixel image that contains the text, "19.3% APR Typical Variable."

pages.scenario: Record-shop catalogue table where each row's stock status (In stock / Last copy / Pre-order / Sold out) is shown ONLY by a CSS-class background-image glyph in a text-empty leading cell; row text is just artist/title/format/price (F3 example 2 mechanism).
pages.mechanism: Stock status lives only in `td.stock.in/.last/.pre/.sold` background-image glyphs on empty, unlabelled cells, contributing nothing to the accessibility tree. A screen-reader user hears the Sold-out row identically to the In-stock row and could try to buy an unavailable record; hide-backgrounds/forced-colors removes all glyphs.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The status carriers are <td> cells with a CSS background and no nameable element, so ACT 1.1.1 rules are Inapplicable and axe/WAVE/Lighthouse see only empty cells. They cannot OCR the four distinct glyphs, cannot tell they encode mutually exclusive inventory states, and cannot verify 'Sold out' appears nowhere as text.

citation.quote: A book distributor uses background images to provide icons against a list of book titles to indicate whether they are new, limited, in-stock, or out of stock.

pages.scenario: Volunteer sign-up form whose required-field markers are red-asterisk background images on empty <span> elements set via the HTML style= attribute, with no '*' character, no 'required' text, and no required/aria-required attribute anywhere (F3 style-attribute carrier).
pages.mechanism: Each `label .mark` is an empty span whose inline-style background-image asterisk is the only 'required' indicator; the span is empty in the accessibility tree and there is no required/aria-required state. A screen-reader user hears 'First name, edit text' with no hint it is mandatory and cannot distinguish required from optional fields.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every field has a proper <label for>, so no missing-label/missing-alt fires; because no required/aria-required is present, 'required not indicated programmatically' rules also do not trigger (nothing is technically missing). The marker is a background image on a <span>, so ACT 1.1.1 is Inapplicable. Only a human seeing the rendered asterisks can tell mandatory-ness is image-only.

citation.quote: This failure would apply equally in a case where the background image was declared in the HTML style attribute, as well as in a case where the background image declaration was created dynamically in a client script (see example 3 below).

pages.scenario: Restaurant menu where each dish's spice level (1/2/3 chillis) is shown only by chili-pepper background images that JavaScript injects onto empty <span class=heat> from a data-heat attribute; the menu text never says mild/medium/hot (F3 example 3 script-injected carrier).
pages.mechanism: A client script sets `span.heat { background-image }` (one chili tile repeated N times, width=N*16px) from data-heat; the count is a background image on an empty span and never enters the accessibility tree, and data-heat is not exposed as content. A screen-reader user cannot tell the 3-chili Phaal from the 1-chili Daal — a safety-relevant gap.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The glyphs are script-set background images on empty spans — no image-alt target, no accessibility node — so ACT 1.1.1 is Inapplicable. A scanner sees only empty spans (or an inline style url() it cannot interpret), cannot OCR the chili tiles, cannot infer the count encodes intensity, and cannot judge the heat level is missing from text.

pages.scenario: Weather widget where temperature and 'feels like' are real text but today's and each hour's CONDITION (rain/cloud/sun) is conveyed solely by a script-injected background-image glyph on empty span/div elements driven by data-cond; a 'half-labelled' trap.
pages.mechanism: `.wx .glyph` and `.hours .g` get their condition icon via `el.style.backgroundImage` from data-cond; the condition is a background image on an empty element with no accessibility-tree presence, while the sibling temperature IS text. A screen-reader user hears '12 degrees, feels like 9' but never that it is raining — the decision-relevant fact.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The widget has visible text (temperature) so text-presence and contrast checks pass and it 'looks labelled'; the condition carriers are background images on empty elements with no nameable target, so ACT 1.1.1 is Inapplicable. No tool can OCR the raincloud/sun SVGs or reason that condition is a separate datum from temperature and is the one missing as text.

citation.quote: Text alternatives are necessary for people who cannot see images that convey information that is required to understand the content of the page.

pages.scenario: Airline seat-map where exit-row seats (row 12) are flagged only by a green emergency-exit background-image glyph on seat buttons whose accessible names are just the seat numbers; a generic legend mentions exit rows but is not programmatically tied to specific seats.
pages.mechanism: `button.seat.exit` has accessible name = seat number ('12A'); the exit-row status is carried only by the `.exit` background-image glyph, which adds no accessibility node. A screen-reader user hears '12A, button' identically to a normal row, missing the legal/evacuation/cost consequences of an exit-row seat. The unlinked legend cannot be mapped to specific seats by AT.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every seat button has a non-empty accessible name, so button-name/accessible-name rules pass; the exit indicator is a background image (no image-alt target, no extra node), so the F3 carrier is not a nameable element and ACT 1.1.1 is Inapplicable. Tools cannot OCR the exit glyph, cannot tell exit-row status is missing from the name, nor detect that the legend fails to associate with seats.

citation.quote: For each background image, determine whether important information provided by it is available without it.

pages.scenario: PASS control: order-tracking timeline using the SAME CSS background-image status-badge carrier as the failing pages, but the meaning of every badge ('Order confirmed', 'Out for delivery', 'Delivered') is also written as real adjacent text and the badges are aria-hidden, so the image is redundant.
pages.mechanism: `.badge.done/.truck/.wait` are aria-hidden background-image glyphs; the equivalent status is a real text node in the sibling `.step .status` in the same logical order. A screen-reader user hears every status as text once, cleanly; hide-backgrounds/forced-colors loses nothing. The background images are decorative reinforcements of text, satisfying F3 step 2 / TT 7.C.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Automated tools cannot evaluate a background-image for 1.1.1 at all, so they neither flag nor clear it — and crucially cannot tell this PASS apart from the case-02/case-06 failures, which use the identical background-image status-glyph carrier. Only a human doing the two-step 7.C judgment (is the image informative? is the meaning redundant in adjacent text?) can establish that here the answer to step 2 is yes.

citation.quote: The meaning of the background image is also available without the background image.

aspects.title: A genuinely informative/functional image marked decorative (alt="" / role=presentation) so AT cannot reach it
aspects.plain: An image that carries needed information (a 'Verified seller' badge, a recipe-step diagram) is wrongly tagged decorative with empty alt, so a screen reader skips it.
aspects.description: An image that actually conveys needed information or function is declared decorative — alt="", role=presentation, or role=none — so it is correctly hidden from AT per the markup and the ACT name-presence/decorative rules all PASS (the markup is internally consistent). The real failure is that the image SHOULD have carried a text alternative: it is the sole carrier of a fact or function (a 'Verified seller' badge, a size chart, a signature image, the only diagram of a recipe step, a wizard progress meter, a severe-weather pictogram). Detecting this requires viewing the rendered image, judging that it carries information the user needs, and concluding the author's 'decorative' declaration is wrong. It is the exact inverse of the corpus's tested case (correctly-decorative) and is a pure intent/meaning judgment that no syntactic check can make.
aspects.scLimb: The boundary between the SC's 'conveys information ⇒ must have a text alternative' limb and its 'Decoration/Formatting/Invisible ⇒ ignored by AT' exception limb — specifically catching mis-classification where author fiat wrongly invokes the decorative exception (F38/F39 applied contextually).
aspects.whyUncovered: The synthetic corpus asserts decorative-vs-informative by MARKUP FIAT — the author pre-declares alt=""/role=presentation and the rule trusts it; the rule can never fail a 'decorative' image because it never asks whether the image is truly decorative. So a meaningful image with alt="" PASSES 23a2a8/46ca7f/e88epe by construction. Automated tools share this blind spot: an empty alt is syntactically valid, and no tool can know that THIS particular badge is the only verification signal or that THIS empty-alt image is the only copy of the diagram. Trusted Tester 7.B requires the human to first decide 'is the image the only means of conveying important information?'

references.quote: When an image is used for decoration, spacing or other purpose that is not part of the meaningful content in the page then the image has no meaning and should be ignored
Determine if the image is the only means of conveying important information on the page.

Sometimes there is non-text content that really is not meant to be seen or understood by the user. Transparent images used to move text over on a page; an invisible image that is used to track usage statistics; and a swirl in the corner that conveys no information but just fills up a blank space

aspects.ttWhy: 7.B checks an empty-name/decorative image is not the only carrier of important info.

pages.scenario: Marketplace listing whose 'Verified seller' green-check badge — the only per-listing signal that this seller passed identity verification — is an inline SVG suppressed from AT via role=presentation + aria-hidden. Unverified sellers render the same row without the check, so the badge's presence is the data; no text states this seller is verified.
pages.mechanism: Informative trust badge declared decorative: the wrapper span carries role=presentation and the SVG aria-hidden=true, so the verification fact is pruned from the accessibility tree though it is the sole per-listing carrier (Trusted Tester 7.B condition 1 fails; F38/F39 inverted).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: An aria-hidden/role=presentation graphic is exactly what ACT 46ca7f and e88epe PASS by construction, and 23a2a8 only applies to named images. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse treat an empty name as a correct decorative declaration and never ask whether the badge SHOULD have been informative; judging the green check is the lone trust signal requires seeing it and reasoning about marketplace context.

citation.quote: a swirl in the corner that conveys no information but just fills up a blank space to create an aesthetic effect are all examples of this... This type of non-text content, therefore, is marked or implemented in a way that assistive technologies (AT) will ignore it and not present anything to the user.

pages.scenario: Energy-switching page whose three-tariff price comparison (peak/off-peak unit rates and standing charge) is painted only onto a <canvas role="presentation"> with no table or text fallback, so screen-reader users get no prices.
pages.mechanism: The entire tariff comparison (peak / off-peak unit prices and standing charge for three energy plans) is painted onto `<canvas id="rateChart" role="presentation">`. A canvas exposes no DOM descendants to the accessibility tree and role=presentation confirms it is ignored; there is no <table>, <dl>, or text duplicate, so the pricing data is lost to AT (informative graphic declared decorative).
pages.selectorNote: Tariff prices live only in this canvas marked decorative; orig said svg but it is a canvas
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: role=presentation on an SVG is valid decorative markup ACT 46ca7f/e88epe PASS. No tool OCRs the SVG <text> nodes to discover a measurement table, and none can know the data appears nowhere else; recognizing this decoration is the sole carrier of the sizing data needs reading the rendered numbers and confirming no text equivalent.

citation.quote: The intent of this success criterion is to make information conveyed by non-text content accessible through the use of a text alternative. Text alternatives are a primary way for making information accessible because they can be rendered through any sensory modality (for example, visual, auditory or tactile) to match the needs of the user.

pages.scenario: Candle-shop product grid where the middle card's only 'SOLD OUT' signal is a diagonal red stamp composited over the photo as a CSS background-image (inline SVG data URI). The card's aria-label names the candle only, the button stays enabled and unmarked, and no 'sold out' text exists — so AT users perceive an in-stock product with a working buy button.
pages.mechanism: Essential state (availability) conveyed exclusively by a CSS background image, which by design cannot carry a text alternative and is not exposed in the accessibility tree; the information is not programmatically determinable anywhere (F3 failure condition: check #2 true, check #3 false).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: There is no element and no alt to evaluate — CSS background images are outside the inspection surface of axe/WAVE/Lighthouse, so they cannot flag a missing text alternative at all; the button has a valid name and is not disabled, so 4.1.2 passes. Detecting it requires seeing the stamp, noticing the button is still active, and reasoning the state lives only in an un-alt-able layer.

citation.quote: The CSS background-image property was designed for decorative purposes and it is not possible to associate text alternatives with images that are included via CSS. Text alternatives are necessary for people who cannot see images that convey information that is required to understand the content of the page. Therefore, it is a failure to use this property to add images to convey this required information.

pages.scenario: Pharmacy prescription page for Warfarin 5 mg whose dosing schedule (Morning 2 tablets, Midday 1, Night 1, take with food, do not crush) is conveyed only by an aria-hidden SVG pictogram; the caption restates only 'morning and midday doses as shown above'.
pages.mechanism: The safety-critical Warfarin 5 mg regimen — Morning 2 tablets, Midday 1 tablet, Night 1 tablet, TAKE WITH FOOD, DO NOT crush (swallow whole) — is drawn only in a pictogram marked `aria-hidden="true"`, which removes the SVG and all its <text> dose-count nodes from the accessibility tree. The caption ('Take your morning and midday doses as shown above. Do not skip doses.') is a pointer that omits the counts, the night dose, and both safety warnings.
pages.selectorNote: Dosing pictogram hidden from AT; orig role=none wrong, real suppressor is aria-hidden
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: role=none on an SVG is valid decorative markup ACT 46ca7f/e88epe PASS by construction. No tool OCRs the pictogram to recover the regimen, none knows the schedule appears nowhere else, and none can weigh that the lost content is medical dosing instructions; catching it requires recognizing the pictogram is the only dosing source and that the caption is an empty pointer for AT.

citation.quote: The image is **NOT** the only means of conveying important information.

pages.scenario: Transit authority weekend service advisory where the substantive content (B line suspended Bedford Ave-Church Ave, Q line rerouted via the N line skipping DeKalb/Atlantic, free shuttle buses) is conveyed only by a route diagram delivered as with a data-URI SVG source. The prose says only 'Service changes are in effect this weekend' and names no line or station.
pages.mechanism: The actual advisory rendered as a diagram and given a null alt: alt="" removes the img from the accessibility tree (screen readers skip it silently) while the prose is vague boilerplate naming nothing, so the specific advisory is unavailable non-visually (classic F38/F39 empty-alt form applied to substantive content).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: alt="" is the textbook null alternative (H67) and ACT 23a2a8 explicitly does not apply to empty-alt images while e88epe/46ca7f treat the empty name as a correct decorative declaration; axe/WAVE/Lighthouse pass empty-alt images by design and never OCR the data-URI SVG or notice the prose names no lines.

citation.quote: A text alternative for an image should convey the meaning of the image. When an image is used for decoration, spacing or other purpose that is not part of the meaningful content in the page then the image has no meaning and should be ignored by assistive technologies.

pages.scenario: Bank 2FA enrollment page where the authenticator QR code (encoding the otpauth secret) is an inline SVG marked role=presentation, with no 'enter setup key manually' text, no copyable secret, and no alternate enrollment path. AT users literally cannot turn on 2FA because the function lives entirely in an image they cannot reach.
pages.mechanism: A FUNCTIONAL image (the enrollment mechanism, not merely informative) declared decorative: role=presentation prunes the QR from the accessibility tree, and with no manual-key fallback the equivalent function is denied — SC 1.1.1's control/input limb requires a name and equivalent way to use it, neither of which exists.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: role=presentation on an SVG is valid decorative markup ACT 46ca7f/e88epe PASS; there is no alt to flag as missing. No tool decodes the QR to learn it is a functional otpauth secret or knows there is no manual-key fallback; recognizing it is the sole enrollment mechanism requires understanding the 2FA flow and inspecting for an alternative path.

citation.quote: For non-text content that is a control or accepts user input, such as images used as submit buttons, image maps or complex animations, a name is provided to describe the purpose of the non-text content so that the person at least knows what the non-text content is and why it is there.

pages.scenario: PASS control: an editorial coffee-brewing article with a purely aesthetic corner flourish correctly hidden via role=presentation + aria-hidden, where all meaning lives in the prose. The page also contains an INFORMATIVE brew-ratio diagram that is correctly exposed with a real aria-label AND duplicated in the text, so judges must distinguish true decoration from the mis-marked-information failures in cases 01-06.
pages.mechanism: Correct application of the decoration exception: the flourish conveys no information and has no function, so hiding it loses nothing; the informative ratio diagram is exposed via aria-label and duplicated in prose/caption, so no image is both informative and hidden — SC 1.1.1 is satisfied.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Tools would also pass this page, but only for the shallow reason that the decorative element has an empty name and the informative one has a non-empty name. The calibration value is human: a judge must verify the hidden image genuinely conveys no information rather than reflexively flagging every role=presentation image as a suppressed-meaning failure.

citation.quote: a swirl in the corner that conveys no information but just fills up a blank space to create an aesthetic effect... Putting alternative text on such items just distracts people using screen readers from the content on the page... This type of non-text content, therefore, is marked or implemented in a way that assistive technologies (AT) will ignore it and not present anything to the user.

aspects.title: Non-empty alt that is not actually an alternative: filename, placeholder, or auto-generated label (F30)
aspects.plain: An image's alt text is just a filename or junk placeholder like 'DSC_0481' or 'image', so it passes checks but tells a blind user nothing.
aspects.description: An image has a non-empty accessible name that LOOKS like content but is not a usable substitute for the image: a filename ('DSC_0481.jpg', 'hero-2.png', 'banner_final_v3'), a CMS auto-caption ('image', 'photo', 'picture'), a programming reference ('img_001', 'Intro#2'), or an upload artifact ('Screenshot 2024-03-11 at 14.22.png'). Because the string is non-empty, every ACT presence rule PASSES. The descriptive-name rule (qt1vmo) only catches this if the placeholder happens to name a DIFFERENT identifiable asset; a filename like 'IMG_4823.jpg' on a sunset photo names nothing identifiable, so qt1vmo cannot judge it wrong against the asset. A human recognizes 'this is a filename / generic placeholder, not a description' — a meaning/intent judgment about the STRING itself relative to what the image depicts.
aspects.scLimb: The core 'text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose' requirement — the equivalence/adequacy facet (G94 'serves the same purpose'), which the ACT presence rules deliberately do not assess and which qt1vmo only covers for identity mismatch.
aspects.whyUncovered: The corpus never uses filename-style or placeholder alt values; all informative pages use the genuinely-descriptive string 'W3C logo', so presence always passes and quality is out of scope by construction. qt1vmo's failures are IDENTITY mismatches (wrong logo named), not NON-ALTERNATIVE strings. A purely automated keyword blocklist ('image','photo','spacer') is brittle and the SC explicitly does not mandate one; deciding that 'sunset_beach_final.jpg' is a filename-not-alt, or that 'Banner' is too generic, requires reading the string AS a human and comparing it to what the image actually shows. F30 is defined as a manual 'is this actually a text alternative?' check.

references.quote: If the text in the "text alternative" cannot be used in place of the non-text content without losing information or function then it fails because it is not, in fact, an alternative to the non-text content.
filenames that are not valid text alternatives in their own right such as "Oct.jpg" or "Chart.jpg" or "sales\oct\top3.jpg"
placeholder text such as " " or "spacer" or "image" or "picture" etc that are put into the 'text alternative' location on images or pictures.

aspects.ttWhy: Non-empty name failing as an equivalent description is 7.A's name-quality judgment.

pages.scenario: Local-news article hero photo depicting a transit-fare protest (crowd marching past a domed City Hall, banners reading 'FAIR FARES'/'NO HIKE') whose alt is the raw DSLR camera filename alt="DSC_0481.JPG".
pages.mechanism: Image accessible name is computed from alt = 'DSC_0481.JPG'; a screen reader announces a camera filename instead of the protest scene, so the alternative cannot substitute for the photo (F30 filename non-alternative).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse only check alt is present and non-empty, which 'DSC_0481.JPG' satisfies; qt1vmo can only catch a name that names a DIFFERENT identifiable asset, and a camera filename names nothing identifiable, so judging it a filename-not-description requires a human reading the string against the depicted pixels.

citation.quote: filenames that are not valid text alternatives in their own right such as "Oct.jpg" or "Chart.jpg" or "sales\oct\top3.jpg"

pages.scenario: E-commerce product-card grid where each thumbnail depicts a visually distinct item (yellow rain jacket, green hiking boot, blue bottle, orange daypack) but every image's alt is its CMS storage slug, e.g. alt="prod-9921-thumb-2".
pages.mechanism: Each image's accessible name is the slug (prod-####-thumb-#), a programming reference that conveys none of the product's colour/shape/category; the descriptive product title lives only in a separate sibling heading/link, not the image's name.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every img has a non-empty alt so image-alt passes; the slug names no identifiable brand asset so qt1vmo finds no identity mismatch; distinguishing a storage slug from a real product description requires a human comparing the string to the rendered thumbnail.

citation.quote: programming references that do not convey the information or function of the non-text content such as "picture 1", "picture 2" or "0001", "0002" or "Intro#1", "Intro#2".

pages.scenario: Healthcare 'Our team' staff directory where four visibly distinct headshots (varying hair, skin tone, glasses, age) all carry the identical generic placeholder alt="photo".
pages.mechanism: Every informative portrait's accessible name is the placeholder 'photo'; a screen-reader user hears 'photo, photo, photo, photo' and cannot associate any face with any person — the alt serves no equivalent purpose for an informative image.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: 'photo' is a non-empty alt so image-alt passes on all four; a keyword blocklist is brittle and unmandated; 'photo' names no identifiable asset so qt1vmo finds no identity mismatch; recognising it as a generic placeholder on informative portraits is a human meaning judgment.

citation.quote: placeholder text such as " " or "spacer" or "image" or "picture" etc that are put into the 'text alternative' location on images or pictures.

pages.scenario: Investor-relations report embedding three DIFFERENT data charts (revenue bar chart 38/41/44/48, MAU line chart, regional pie chart) all carrying the export-default alt="Chart.jpg", with no adjacent data table.
pages.mechanism: All three charts' accessible name is the export filename 'Chart.jpg'; three distinct datasets collapse to one meaningless filename and no long description/table conveys the quantitative information non-visually.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: All three images have non-empty alt so image-alt passes; no 1.1.1 automated rule treats duplicate alt as a violation; 'Chart.jpg' names no identifiable asset for qt1vmo; recognising it as an export filename whose charts' data must be in text is the F30 manual check.

citation.quote: filenames that are not valid text alternatives in their own right such as "Oct.jpg" or "Chart.jpg" or "sales\oct\top3.jpg"

pages.scenario: Help-center 2FA tutorial whose step-2 screenshot shows a Security settings panel with a highlighted 'Two-factor authentication' row and a blue 'Turn on' button, but the alt is the macOS capture filename alt="Screenshot 2024-03-11 at 14.22.png".
pages.mechanism: The screenshot's accessible name is the macOS capture filename; the procedural/spatial information (which button to click, where it sits in the panel) is shown only in the pixels and is lost to AT, so the filename cannot substitute for the screenshot.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The image has a non-empty alt so image-alt passes; the timestamped capture filename contains no banned keyword token (defeating heuristics) and names no identifiable asset (defeating qt1vmo); recognising it as a capture filename and that the depicted button is the load-bearing step content is human visual/semantic judgment.

citation.quote: If the text in the "text alternative" cannot be used in place of the non-text content without losing information or function then it fails because it is not, in fact, an alternative to the non-text content.

pages.scenario: Spanish-language (lang=es) recipe blog whose hero photo depicts a specific dish (bowl of red pozole with hominy, radish, lime, oregano) but whose alt is a title-cased WhatsApp-export filename auto-derived by WordPress: alt="Img 20231104 Wa0006".
pages.mechanism: The image's accessible name is the CMS title-cased filename 'Img 20231104 Wa0006' (IMG + date 2023-11-04 + WA sequence); its capitalised word-like tokens identify nothing about the dish and cannot substitute for the photo, and being word-shaped it evades naive filename detection.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The image has a non-empty alt so image-alt passes; the string is title-cased with no banned token so keyword heuristics do not flag it; it names no identifiable asset so qt1vmo finds no identity mismatch; recognising it as a WhatsApp-export filename rather than a description of pozole requires a human reading a deliberately word-like string against the rendered dish.

citation.quote: filenames that are not valid text alternatives in their own right such as "Oct.jpg" or "Chart.jpg" or "sales\oct\top3.jpg"

pages.scenario: PASS control: a photo-essay 'photo of the day' showing the same kind of protest scene as case-01, but with a genuine descriptive alt='Crowd marching past the domed City Hall building, holding banners reading Fair fares and No hike'.
pages.mechanism: The image's accessible name is a full scene description that can substitute for the photo (G94): removing the image and leaving the alt loses no essential information, so the equivalence/descriptiveness facet passes alongside presence.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Automated tools pass this only because alt is non-empty — the same shallow signal that also wrongly passes the case-01..06 failures; they cannot tell THIS alt is a real alternative while 'DSC_0481.JPG' is not, so only the human-judgment layer confirms the genuine pass and isolates the string as the variable.

citation.quote: The text alternative should be able to substitute for the non-text content. If the non-text content were removed from the page and substituted with the text, the page would still provide the same function and information. The text alternative would be brief but as informative as possible.

aspects.title: Alt literally describes the image but is wrong for the image's purpose-in-context (link target or control function)
aspects.plain: An image's alt names what it depicts but ignores its job, so a printer-icon button reads 'inkjet printer' instead of 'Print', confusing a screen-reader user.
aspects.description: An image has an alt that correctly identifies the depicted thing — so it passes presence rules and even passes qt1vmo (it IS descriptive of the image in isolation) — but it is the WRONG alternative for the role the image plays on this page. The Understanding doc makes this explicit: the SAME globe image needs alt 'International Travel' on a travel site but 'International Campuses' on a university site; a newspaper-front-page thumbnail that links to a homepage needs the publication name, not a description of the masthead photo. The same applies to images used AS controls: a printer icon button needs 'Print this page' not 'inkjet printer'; a magnifying-glass submit button needs 'Search' not 'magnifying glass'; an image-map area / input type=image needs its destination/action. Judging equivalence requires understanding the image's FUNCTION and context (what it links to, what action it performs, what point it illustrates), not just what it literally depicts.
aspects.scLimb: Two intertwined limbs the corpus never exercises: (a) the core 'serves the SAME PURPOSE' equivalence requirement evaluated in CONTEXT (G94), and (b) the SC's distinct 'non-text content that is a control or accepts user input ⇒ name describes its PURPOSE' limb (functional images: links, buttons, input type=image, image-map areas).
aspects.whyUncovered: qt1vmo evaluates whether the name describes the IMAGE in isolation — every corpus page is one isolated img on a blank body with no link, no control, no surrounding prose — so it has no notion of the image's purpose-in-context. A literal-but-context-wrong alt ('globe') passes even when the globe is a link whose purpose is 'International Travel'. The functional/control limb is entirely absent from the corpus (no a/img, button/img, input[type=image], or area). Automated tools cannot infer an image's intended communicative purpose from page context or link destination; this is the SC's hardest judgment.

references.quote: An image of the world that is used on a travel site as a link to the International Travel section has the text alternative "International Travel". The same image is used as a link on a university website with the text alternative "International Campuses".
A thumbnail image of the front page of a newspaper links to the home page of the "Smallville Times". The text alternative says "Smallville Times".

For non-text content that is a control or accepts user input, such as images used as submit buttons, image maps or complex animations, a name is provided to describe the purpose of the non-text content

aspects.ttWhy: 7.A requires the name to describe the image's meaning/purpose in context, not literal depiction.

pages.scenario: News aggregator grid: a newspaper front-page thumbnail is the sole content of a link to the publication's homepage, but its alt accurately describes the cover PHOTO ('Front page photo of a flooded town square under grey skies') instead of naming the publication. A correctly-labelled card (alt='The Harbor Gazette') is included for contrast.
pages.mechanism: Because the is the only content of the , the image alt becomes the link's accessible name. The link to The Riverside Courier is therefore named for the cover photograph, not the publication, so the alternative does not serve the link's purpose-in-context (G94/H30 linked-thumbnail rule).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The img has a non-empty, genuinely descriptive alt so image-alt passes, and the link therefore has a non-empty accessible name so link-name passes. No tool resolves the destination (a newspaper homepage) or knows the convention that a linked front-page thumbnail must be named for the publication it opens; judging that 'a flooded town square' is the wrong name for a link to The Riverside Courier requires understanding the link's purpose — human semantic judgment.

citation.quote: A thumbnail image of the front page of a newspaper links to the home page of the "Smallville Times". The text alternative says "Smallville Times".

pages.scenario: Public-library catalogue search: the submit control is an icon button whose magnifying-glass image has alt='magnifying glass' (names the depicted icon, not the action 'Search'). A second submit (arrow, alt='Go') is correctly purpose-named for contrast.
pages.mechanism: For a button whose sole content is an image, the button's accessible name is the image alt. The search submit therefore announces 'magnifying glass, button' rather than 'Search'; the non-text content is a control, so its name must describe its purpose, not its glyph (the canonical G94 example).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A button/image-input with a non-empty accessible name satisfies axe/WAVE/Lighthouse name checks; 'magnifying glass' is a valid non-empty string. No tool understands that this control submits a search and that its name should be 'Search' rather than a description of the icon; recognising the mismatch requires reasoning about the control's function.

citation.quote: A search button uses an image of a magnifying glass.  The text alternative is "search" and not "magnifying glass".

pages.scenario: Hospital wayfinding image map: a floor-plan has one clickable per room, each navigating to that room's directions page, but each area's alt describes the region's APPEARANCE ('Large blue rectangle in the top-left corner', 'Grey block on the right') instead of the destination. One area (Pathology Lab, Room 115) is correctly labelled for contrast.
pages.mechanism: Each <area> alt is its accessible name and serves as that hotspot's link text. A screen-reader/keyboard user navigating the map hears shape/colour descriptions ('Large blue rectangle, link') with no idea each leads to Radiology/Phlebotomy/etc.; the alt does not serve the same purpose as the selectable region (H24).
pages.selectorNote: Image-map image is the visible target; orig <area> has no on-page box
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The only area rule a linter enforces is that alt is present and non-empty; 'Large blue rectangle in the top-left corner' satisfies it. Tools do not resolve each area's href to a room page nor judge that a shape/colour description is the wrong alternative for a navigation target; knowing the blue rectangle IS Radiology requires understanding the map's interactive purpose.

citation.quote: Check that the text alternative specified by the alt attribute serves the same purpose as the part of image map image referenced by the area element of the image map.

pages.scenario: Airline boarding-pass action bar: the print button (onclick=window.print()) has a printer image with alt='inkjet printer' (names the depicted device, not the action). Its visible 'Print' caption is aria-hidden so it does not reach the accessible name. Two sibling buttons ('Add to Apple Wallet', 'Email boarding pass') are correctly purpose-named.
pages.mechanism: The button's only name-contributing content is the child image (the caption is aria-hidden), so AccName(button)='inkjet printer'. A screen-reader user hears 'inkjet printer, button' with no indication it prints the boarding pass; the control's name describes the appliance, not its purpose.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse pass any button with a non-empty accessible name, and 'inkjet printer' is valid. They do not execute or interpret onclick=window.print() and cannot judge that 'inkjet printer' names the device rather than the print action; detecting that the name should be the control's purpose requires understanding what activating it does.

citation.quote: For non-text content that is a control or accepts user input, such as images used as submit buttons, image maps or complex animations, a name is provided to describe the purpose of the non-text content so that the person at least knows what the non-text content is and why it is there.

pages.scenario: SaaS footer language switcher built from flag-image links: each flag is the sole content of an that switches the UI language, but its alt literally names the depicted flag/country ('Flag of Japan', 'Flag of Germany', 'Flag of Brazil') rather than the language the link selects. The English link (alt='English') is correctly purpose-named for contrast.
pages.mechanism: Each flag img is the only content of its <a>, so the image alt becomes the link's accessible name. The language-switch control therefore announces 'Flag of Japan, link' — a country, not a language — so a user seeking their language hears a flag/country description; the alternative does not serve the link's purpose (selecting a language). hreflang carries the purpose programmatically but is not the accessible name.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every flag img has a non-empty accurate alt so image-alt passes, and each link has a non-empty accessible name so link-name passes. Tools do not interpret href='/?lang=ja'/hreflang to learn the link selects a language, and cannot judge that 'Flag of Japan' is the wrong alternative for a language-selection control (a flag being a poor proxy for a language) — contextual human judgment.

citation.quote: An image of the world that is used on a travel site as a link to the International Travel section has the text alternative "International Travel". The same image is used as a link on a university website with the text alternative "International Campuses".

pages.scenario: Food-delivery order-confirmation screen: the cancel-order control is a red stop-sign graphic rendered as an inline <svg role='img'> whose <title> accessible name is 'Red octagon' (names the depicted shape, not the action). Its visible 'Cancel' text is aria-hidden. A sibling 'Track driver' control is correctly purpose-named.
pages.mechanism: The button's only name-contributing content is the SVG, whose accessible name is its <title> 'Red octagon' via aria-labelledby (the visible caption is aria-hidden). So AccName(button)='Red octagon'. A screen-reader user hears 'Red octagon, button' with no hint it cancels the order; the control's name describes the geometry, not its purpose.
pages.selectorNote: Highlight the cancel button; orig SVG <title> has no box
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse see a focusable control with a non-empty accessible name ('Red octagon' via the SVG title) and report no violation. They do not interpret the data-action='cancel-order' handler and cannot judge that 'Red octagon' describes the shape rather than naming the cancel action; understanding the stop-sign metaphor means 'cancel' is human semantic judgment.

citation.quote: For non-text content that is a control or accepts user input, such as images used as submit buttons, image maps or complex animations, a name is provided to describe the purpose of the non-text content so that the person at least knows what the non-text content is and why it is there.

pages.scenario: PASS boundary on a travel site: a globe is the sole content of an and its alt is 'International Travel' (serves the link purpose, not the depiction 'globe'); a printer icon
pages.mechanism: The globe img is the only content of its link, so the image alt becomes the link's accessible name 'International Travel' — exactly the link's purpose; the printer button's accessible name is its child image alt 'Print this page' — exactly the action. In both, the alternative serves the same purpose as the non-text content even though it does not describe the depiction (G94/H30 ideal).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A tool sees the same surface signal as the failing pages — a non-empty alt/accessible name on a linked image and on an icon button — and would report 'no violation' here just as it (incorrectly) does on case-01..06. It cannot distinguish a purpose-correct alternative ('International Travel') from a purpose-wrong one ('globe'/'inkjet printer'); only a human comparing the alternative against the element's purpose-in-context can confirm this page is actually correct.

citation.quote: This text alternative should not necessarily describe the non-text content.  It should serve the same purpose and convey the same information.  This may sometimes result in a text alternative that looks like a description of the non-text content.  But this would only be true if that was the best way to serve the same purpose.

aspects.title: Complex image (chart/diagram/map) has a plausible alt/long description that drops information the image conveys (F67)
aspects.plain: A chart, map, or diagram has alt text that sounds descriptive but omits key data it shows (the trend, the addresses), so a blind user gets only part.
aspects.description: An informative complex image — a data chart, a diagram, a map, a schematic — has a non-empty, descriptive-sounding short alt and/or a long description, so it PASSES every presence rule and passes qt1vmo (the name correctly identifies the image in general). But the short alt is insufficient for a complex image, and/or the long description omits specific information the image actually conveys: a venue map whose description names the venues but gives no locations/addresses; a chart whose description gives totals but not the trend; a flow diagram whose prose lists boxes but not the connections. The SC requires the alternative to present the SAME information (G94 short + G73/G74 long descriptions). Catching this requires viewing the image, enumerating the information it conveys, and confirming each datum is or is not present in the text — a same-purpose/completeness comparison that is the inverse of a presence check.
aspects.scLimb: The core 'text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose / presents the same information' requirement applied to complex non-text content (charts/diagrams/maps) needing long descriptions — the adequacy/completeness facet the ACT presence rules explicitly disclaim and that the corpus never builds (no complex images at all).
aspects.whyUncovered: The corpus contains only single static raster /role=img divs and one trivial SVG — no charts, diagrams, maps, or any complex image needing a long description. The presence rules only check that some non-empty name exists; qt1vmo checks gross identity, not partial-equivalence, so an alt can correctly identify a chart yet drop its trend or specific data and qt1vmo PASSES it. Automated tools cannot read what a chart depicts nor verify a prose description against it. F67 is explicitly a manual 'does the long description serve the same purpose / present the same information?' check.

references.quote: the failure that occurs when the long description for non-text content does not serve the same purpose or does not present the same information as the non-text content

While this description provides useful information, it does not convey the same information as the image because it provides no specific location information such as the address or the distance of each location from some fixed point.

The longer description identifies the type of chart, provides a high-level summary of the data, trends and implications comparable to those available from the chart. Where possible and practical, the actual data is provided in a table.

aspects.ttWhy: 7.A judges whether the name/description gives an equivalent (complete) description of the image.

pages.scenario: Winter-Games spectator guide with an inline-SVG street map of five venues. The figcaption names each venue and its sport but states no addresses, streets, distances, or spatial relationships — the verbatim F67 Olympic-venue-map failure transposed to a self-contained page.
pages.mechanism: F67: the SVG has a valid accessible name (aria-labelledby) and a prose long description (figcaption), but the description omits all locational data the map's pixels encode (positions, streets, distances, side of river), so the text alternative does not present the same information as the map.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse only verify a non-empty name and an associated description exist (both true here) and qt1vmo passes on gross identity. No tool rasterizes the map, enumerates the spatial information it conveys, or diffs that against the prose — the same-purpose completeness comparison requires a human to view the map and confirm each datum is missing.

citation.quote: While this description provides useful information, it does not convey the same information as the image because it provides no specific location information such as the address or the distance of each location from some fixed point.

pages.scenario: Finance dashboard with a four-bar quarterly-revenue chart showing three quarters of growth then a sharp red-highlighted Q4 collapse annotated '↓ port strike'. The aria-describedby caption recites the four dollar figures but never states the trend, which bar is the outlier, or the on-chart cause.
pages.mechanism: F67/G92: the chart has aria-label + aria-describedby (both present), but the description gives only isolated data points and drops the trend (rise then collapse), the outlier (Q4, drawn red), and the annotated cause — so substituting the description for the image loses the chart's actual message.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Name and description presence both pass and qt1vmo passes; no checker reads the bar heights to compute the trend, recognises the red bar + annotation as flagging the outlier, or verifies the caption states either. 'Numbers present but message absent' is a human reasoning step over the rendered pixels.

citation.quote: The long description would read "Bar Chart showing sales for October. There are 6 salespersons. Maria is highest with 349 units. Frances is next with 301. ... The primary use of the chart is to show leaders, so the description is in sales order."

pages.scenario: Credit-union loan-decision flowchart (inline SVG) with two decision diamonds, three outcome boxes, and Yes/No arrows. The figcaption lists every box but states none of the connecting arrows or the branch conditions, so the reader learns the stages but not what leads to what.
pages.mechanism: F67: the SVG has a valid accessible name (aria-labelledby) and a descriptive figcaption, but the caption enumerates only nodes and omits the directed edges and Yes/No conditions that ARE a flowchart's content — score<660 to Decline, score>=660 & DTI>40% to Manual, score>=660 & DTI<=40% to Auto-approve — so it does not present the same information.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Name + description presence pass; no tool traces path marker-end arrow edges, associates them with the Yes/No text labels, or determines the caption fails to state any connection. Knowing a flowchart's meaning lives in its edges — and that the prose dropped them — is a semantic judgement.

citation.quote: Without a long description that provides complete information, a person may not be able to comprehend or interact with the web page.

pages.scenario: City metro network map as a raster (SVG via data: URI, true bitmap-style image with alt). Four interchange stations are marked with double-ring markers (Central, Kingsway, Riverbank, Eastfield). The aria-describedby 'Network description' names each line and its termini but never states a single interchange.
pages.mechanism: F67/G73: the img has a correctly-identifying alt and an associated long description (aria-describedby), but the description gives lines + endpoints and omits every interchange — the load-bearing fact for journey planning — so a rider can name lines yet cannot plan any trip requiring a line change; the text does not convey the same information as the map.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The alt is meaningful, the description is associated, and qt1vmo passes (correct identity). No tool rasterizes the data-URI map, recognises the double-ring markers as interchanges, infers which line pairs meet at each, and checks the description for those facts. Distinguishing 'names the lines' from 'lets you change lines' is human transit-map reasoning.

citation.quote: check that the long description conveys the same information as the non-text content

pages.scenario: Phase-II clinical-trial scatter plot (inline SVG) of drug exposure vs. clearance time for 60 participants, showing a strong positive correlation plus a contrasting-colour cluster of seven high outliers (slow metabolisers). The aria-labelledby name and figcaption restate the axes and N but state neither the correlation nor the outlier cluster.
pages.mechanism: F67/G95: the SVG has a valid accessible name and a caption, but the caption conveys only the chart's scaffolding (axis titles, units, sample size) and drops the two findings the plot is published to show — the positive correlation and the high-outlier subgroup — so the long alternative does not present the same information.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Name + description presence pass and qt1vmo passes; no tool fits a regression to the circle coordinates, detects the high-value cluster, or verifies the caption mentions either. 'Axes and N present but the result missing' is a human reading of the point cloud.

citation.quote: this technique is used to provide a short text alternative that briefly describes the non-text content. (A long text alternative is then provided using another technique such that the combination serves the same purpose and presents the same information as the original non-text content.)

pages.scenario: PASS control: a municipal open-data five-year water-use bar chart whose long description fully reconstructs the image — an associated data table giving every exact value plus a sentence stating the trend (steady decline, 26% total, largest drop 2027 to 2028). Boundary case proving presence of a description was never the question; completeness is.
pages.mechanism: G92 satisfied: the chart has aria-label + aria-describedby pointing to a <table> (exact values) and a trend paragraph; removing the image and substituting the table + trend sentence loses no information, so the text alternative serves the same purpose and presents the same information. F67 does not apply.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: An automated tool also reports no error here — but for the wrong reason: it passes on the identical name+description-presence signal that wrongly greenlights cases 01-05. This control demonstrates a checker cannot distinguish the complete description (06) from the incomplete ones (01-05); only a human comparing text to image can tell this one actually reconstructs the data.

citation.quote: If the non-text content were removed from the page and substituted with the short and long descriptions, the page would still provide the same function and information.

pages.scenario: Bilingual staff-intranet engineering org chart (inline SVG): VP, two directors, four leads joined by connecting reporting lines. The figcaption lists all seven name/title pairs as a flat roster but states none of the reporting relationships. An Arabic roster line is correctly marked lang="ar", masking the real defect.
pages.mechanism: F67: the SVG has a valid accessible name (aria-labelledby) and a descriptive caption, but the caption is a flat roster and drops the connecting-line hierarchy (Rivera & Tanaka report to Haddad; Nair & Kowalski to Rivera; Russo & Farouk to Tanaka) — the only information an org chart adds over a staff list — so it does not present the same information.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Name + description presence pass, and the foreign-language passage is even correctly tagged so language checks are clean too. No tool follows the path connectors to derive the hierarchy or checks the caption encodes it. Recognising that an org chart's content is its edges — and that a roster drops them — is a semantic judgement over the diagram.

citation.quote: Check that the long description serves the same purpose or presents the same information as the non-text content.

aspects.title: Image of meaningful text whose alt does not reproduce the same text
aspects.plain: An image whose content is really words (a quote graphic, a coupon banner) has alt that summarizes rather than repeating them, so a screen-reader user misses the text.
aspects.description: An image whose primary content IS text — a logo wordmark, a quote rendered as a graphic, a pull-quote image, a 'terms' graphic, a scanned notice, a price/coupon banner that is essentially words — has a non-empty alt that describes or summarizes the image instead of reproducing the words. Because the alt is non-empty it passes presence rules, and because it may correctly identify the image ('promotional banner') it can pass qt1vmo, yet a screen-reader user never receives the actual text the image displays. For an image of meaningful text the alternative must contain the SAME text. Distinguishing this requires reading the words in the image and confirming they appear in the alt — a transcription-equivalence judgment a checker cannot perform (it cannot OCR reliably, and the corpus has no text-in-image cases).
aspects.scLimb: The core 'serves the equivalent purpose' requirement for the specific case of images of text — Trusted Tester 7.A step 1.d: the accessible name must contain the SAME text the image displays. (Note: this is the 1.1.1 text-alternative facet, distinct from 1.4.5 Images of Text.)
aspects.whyUncovered: The corpus's informative images are logos described as 'W3C logo' — a label, never a case where the alt must REPRODUCE displayed words. Presence rules only require a non-empty name; qt1vmo checks whether the name identifies the image, not whether it transcribes text the image shows. No fully-automated checker reliably OCRs an image and compares the extracted text to the alt, and the SC does not mandate one. Trusted Tester carves out a specific manual step (7.A.1.d) for 'image of meaningful text', confirming it is a separate human judgment.

references.quote: If the image is of **meaningful text**, ANDI Output must contain the **same text**.

If the text in the "text alternative" cannot be used in place of the non-text content without losing information or function then it fails because it is not, in fact, an alternative to the non-text content.

Text alternatives are a primary way for making information accessible because they can be rendered through any sensory modality (for example, visual, auditory or tactile) to match the needs of the user.

aspects.ttWhy: 7.A step 1.d requires an image of meaningful text to contain the same text.

pages.scenario: Marketing-email promo banner rendered as a flattened image (inline-SVG data: URI). Pixels read 'SUMMER SALE / 20% OFF EVERYTHING / Use code SAVE20 at checkout / Ends Sunday, August 31'. alt='Summer sale promotional banner' truthfully labels the image but reproduces none of the load-bearing words; a screen-reader user can never enter SAVE20.
pages.mechanism: The image's accessible name is the alt ('Summer sale promotional banner'); the strings SAVE20 and 'August 31' exist only as SVG <text> glyphs in the image pixels and are absent from the DOM text and the accessibility tree (verified: DOM innerText contains SAVE20 = false; a11y image node name = alt only). For an image of meaningful text the alternative must contain the SAME text (TT 7.A.1.d); it does not, so the equivalent-purpose requirement is unmet.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse only verify alt is present and non-empty (it is), so image-alt passes; qt1vmo can also pass because the name is an accurate label of the image. No tool OCRs the banner to learn its pixels spell SAVE20 and then compares that to the alt. Deciding the alt must REPRODUCE the displayed code/deadline rather than merely label the image is the manual transcription-equivalence judgment carved out at TT 7.A.1.d.

citation.quote: If the image is of **meaningful text**, ANDI Output must contain the **same text**.

pages.scenario: Long-form news article drops in a stylised pull-quote baked into an image (inline-SVG data: URI): 'The future is already here — it's just not very evenly distributed.' — William Gibson, 1993. alt='Decorative pull-quote graphic in the article' labels the image; surrounding prose never restates the quote, so AT users lose both the quotation and its attribution.
pages.mechanism: Accessible name = the alt. The quotation words and 'Gibson' are absent from the DOM text and a11y tree (verified: 'Gibson' present in a11y tree = false). The token 'evenly' appears only because the page h1/title is 'What evenly distributed really means' — that is page chrome, not a restatement of the quote. Calling the image 'decorative' is also wrong since it carries information. For an image of meaningful text the alt must contain the same text; it does not.
pages.primarySelector: img.pullquote[alt="Decorative pull-quote graphic in the article"]
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: alt is present and non-empty so image-alt passes. No scanner OCRs the graphic to learn it spells a specific attributed quotation, nor checks the alt against those words, nor can it judge that the article prose fails to restate the quote. The word 'decorative' would make naive tools MORE confident it is fine. Recognising the omission is a human semantic/visual call.

citation.quote: When non-text content contains words that are important to understanding the content, the alt text should include those words.

pages.scenario: Internal recognition page shows an 'Employee of the Quarter' certificate built as inline <svg role="img"> named by a single <title>='Award badge'. The certificate's meaningful content (EMPLOYEE OF THE QUARTER / Awarded to Dana Okafor / Q2 2026 · Customer Success) is drawn with SVG <text> elements that the named-image collapse hides from AT.
pages.mechanism: With role="img" + a <title>, the accessible name is 'Award badge' and the SVG subtree is presented as one graphic; descendant <text> is not exposed (verified: a11y image node name = 'Award badge'; 'Dana Okafor' and 'QUARTER' absent from the accessibility tree). The recipient and quarter — meaningful text the image displays — never reach AT, and the name must contain that same text but does not.
pages.selectorNote: Highlight the SVG graphic; orig <title> child has no box
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe svg-img-alt and ACT 7d6734 only require the SVG to have A non-empty name; 'Award badge' satisfies that. No checker reads the inner <text> glyphs, recognises they are the meaningful content, and verifies the name reproduces them — and the named-img collapse removes those <text> nodes from the a11y tree, so even a tree-walking tool would not treat them as the alternative. Judging the name must include the recipient/date is a manual transcription-equivalence call.

citation.quote: If the image is of **meaningful text**, ANDI Output must contain the **same text**.

pages.scenario: SaaS marketing page renders its entire three-tier pricing comparison as one exported image (inline-SVG data: URI): Starter $0/mo, Team $29/mo (MOST POPULAR), Scale $99/mo, with seat counts and event limits. alt='Pricing plans comparison' labels the image but drops every plan name, price, and limit.
pages.mechanism: Accessible name = 'Pricing plans comparison'. The tier names, prices ($0/$29/$99), seat counts, and event limits exist only as SVG <text> glyphs and are absent from the DOM text and a11y tree (verified: '$29' and 'Scale' present in a11y tree = false). AT users learn a comparison exists but not its contents, so they cannot compare or choose a plan. For structured meaningful text the alternative must present the same information; G94 requires a long text alternative with the complete text when it exceeds a short alt — none is provided.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: image-alt passes on the non-empty alt. No scanner OCRs the graphic to recover '$29/mo', '50,000 events', 'Scale $99/mo', nor checks the alt enumerates the tiers, nor can it tell the picture IS a price table that should have been live HTML. Recognising the omission requires reading the rendered table and the alt and comparing — a human visual/contextual judgment.

citation.quote: If the text in the image is more than can fit in a short text alternative then it should be described in the short text alternative and a long text alternative should be provided as well with the complete text.

pages.scenario: Gulf-region fashion store (lang=ar, dir=rtl) Eid promo banner is a flattened image (inline-SVG data: URI) carrying the offer in Arabic plus a Latin code: عروض العيد / خصم 30% على كل الفساتين / استخدم الرمز EID30 / حتى 15 شوال. alt='seasonal sale graphic' is non-empty, generic, and in English on an Arabic page; it drops the discount, the category, the code EID30, and the deadline.
pages.mechanism: Accessible name = 'seasonal sale graphic'. The Arabic offer lines and the Latin code EID30 exist only as SVG <text> glyphs and are absent from the DOM text and a11y tree (verified: 'EID30' present in a11y tree = false). An Arabic AT user receives neither the offer terms nor the code, and the alternative is in a different human language than the content. For an image of meaningful text the alternative must contain the same text, in the content's language (Understanding note on matching the human language).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: image-alt passes on the non-empty alt. No scanner OCRs Arabic out of a raster, recognises the embedded Latin promo code, and verifies the alt reproduces those words in the page's language. A lang mismatch between an alt string and image content is not a check any automated tool performs. Transcription equivalence across a script/language boundary is a manual judgment.

citation.quote: Text alternatives and equivalents should match the human language of the original content (normally the default human language of the page).

pages.scenario: Municipal water-utility CMS posts a scanned 'Boil Water Advisory' as an image (inline-SVG data: URI styled like a scanned form): Affected Maple Ward zones 3 and 4 / Boil all tap water for 1 full minute / In effect until Thursday, June 25, 8:00 AM / Questions (555) 204-7781. alt='Public notice' names the document type but loses every safety-critical instruction, date, and the hotline.
pages.mechanism: Accessible name = 'Public notice'. The affected zones, boil duration, lift date/time, and phone number exist only as SVG <text> glyphs and are absent from the DOM text and a11y tree (verified: 'June 25' and '204-7781' present in a11y tree = false). AT conveys that a notice exists but not its life-safety content. For an image of meaningful text the alternative must contain the same text; a document-type label cannot substitute for the instructions and dates.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: image-alt passes on the non-empty alt; the name is a truthful document-type label so qt1vmo can pass too. No scanner OCRs the scanned notice to recover 'boil for 1 full minute' or 'until Thursday, June 25', nor checks the alt against that text, nor can it tell this image is a wall of safety instructions rather than a photo. Recognising the words must be transcribed is a human visual/contextual judgment.

citation.quote: it is not, in fact, an alternative to the non-text content.

pages.scenario: PASS control: a yoga-studio promo banner that is itself a flattened image of text (inline-SVG data: URI) with the same offer-copy family as the failing cases — 'NEW STUDENT OFFER / 5 classes for $15 / Use code FLEX15 online / Offer ends Friday, March 6' — but the alt transcribes every displayed word, including the code and deadline.
pages.mechanism: The accessible name is the full offer string and the a11y image node name includes 'FLEX15' and 'March 6' (verified: both present in a11y tree = true). Replacing the image with its alt loses no information — the code and deadline both survive. For an image of meaningful text the alternative must contain the same text, and here it does, so 1.1.1 is satisfied. Same component and domain-family as case-01 but opposite outcome, isolating that the defect is transcription-equivalence, not the existence of an image of text.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The same OCR-and-compare step automation cannot do to FAIL the other cases is the step needed to CONFIRM this one passes. image-alt and qt1vmo pass here exactly as on case-01, so a scanner cannot distinguish this correct page from the failing one — only a human reading the image and the alt can tell THIS alt reproduces the words (pass) while case-01's does not (fail). The pass/fail boundary is invisible to automated tools.

citation.quote: When non-text content contains words that are important to understanding the content, the alt text should include those words.

aspects.title: Text look-alike (homoglyph / Unicode confusable) glyphs representing text with no text alternative (F71)
aspects.plain: Visible 'text' is secretly built from look-alike letters of another alphabet, so it reads fine by eye but a screen reader announces garbled nonsense or silence.
aspects.description: Visible 'text' on the page is actually composed of characters from another script chosen because their glyphs LOOK like the intended letters/digits — Cyrillic 'о' for Latin 'o', Greek 'ϲ' for 'c', Cyrillic letter for '3'. Sighted users read the intended word; a screen reader reads garbled output or silence because the codepoints are not the letters they resemble. Per F71 this is effectively non-text content (the meaning rides on glyph shapes, not the actual characters) and it lacks the required text alternative. No img/svg/object element is involved, so all ACT 1.1.1 rules are Inapplicable. Catching it requires comparing the rendered glyphs against the actual codepoints / what a screen reader would announce in the page's language — a human reading judgment.
aspects.scLimb: The SC's 'all non-text content ... has a text alternative' requirement extended (per F71) to text-look-alike glyph substitution, where displayed meaning is carried by glyph shape rather than the encoded characters and no text alternative is provided.
aspects.whyUncovered: The corpus contains only img/role=img/SVG targets; there are no homoglyph/confusable text pages, and every ACT 1.1.1 rule is Inapplicable here because there is no name-bearing element. Reliable automated detection is brittle — confusables span thousands of codepoints across scripts, legitimate multilingual content mixes scripts, and the SC does not mandate a blocklist — so deciding that 'ϲоοk' is Latin 'cook' rendered in confusables (vs legitimate Greek/Cyrillic text) is a human reading-against-language judgment.

references.quote: The objective of this failure condition is to avoid substituting characters whose glyphs look similar to the intended character, for that intended character.

The following word looks, in browsers with appropriate font support, like the English word "cook", yet is composed of the string U+03f2 U+043E U+03BF U+006B, only one of which is a letter from the Western alphabet. This word will not be processed meaningfully, and a text alternative is not provided.
If look-alike glyphs are used, and there is not a text alternative for any range of text that uses look-alike glyphs, then the content does not meet the Success Criterion.

aspects.ttWhy: Homoglyph real text (no img/background/CAPTCHA element); F71 falls outside all four TT image tests.

pages.scenario: Recipe site marketing hero <h1> 'Anyone can cook tonight.' where the word 'cook' is the verbatim F71 example string (U+03F2 Greek lunate sigma, U+043E Cyrillic o, U+03BF Greek o, U+006B Latin k); only the final k is Latin, no text alternative.
pages.mechanism: The heading text node contains four mixed-script code points whose glyphs render as 'cook' but are not the Latin letters c-o-o-k; a screen reader announces the Greek/Cyrillic code points as garbled mixed-script output (or skips them), never the word 'cook', and no aria-label or visually-hidden Latin equivalent provides a text alternative (F71).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: No img/svg/object/role=img exists, so every ACT 1.1.1 rule is Inapplicable and axe-core/WAVE/Lighthouse report nothing; the <h1> is a valid, non-empty, high-contrast heading that passes naive checks. Deciding that 'ϲоοk' is Latin 'cook' rendered in confusables (vs legitimate Greek/Cyrillic text) requires reading the rendered glyphs against the page language (lang=en) and comparing them to the actual code points — a human reading judgment.

citation.quote: The following word looks, in browsers with appropriate font support, like the English word "cook", yet is composed of the string U+03f2 U+043E U+03BF U+006B, only one of which is a letter from the Western alphabet. This word will not be processed meaningfully, and a text alternative is not provided.

pages.scenario: Checkout trust copy 'You'll be redirected to PayPal to approve $2,040.00' where the brand name PayPal in a p.note span is encoded mostly in Cyrillic look-alikes, with no real-text brand label.
pages.mechanism: Checkout trust copy contains `p.note > span.brand` whose 'PayPal' is encoded as confusables: U+0420, U+0430, U+0443, U+0420, U+0430 (five Cyrillic look-alikes) plus a Latin l (U+006C). The brand name in body text is mostly Cyrillic with no aria-label or visually-hidden Latin equivalent, so a screen reader announces the Cyrillic code points instead of 'PayPal' (F71).
pages.selectorNote: Cyrillic-confusable PayPal wordmark in trust copy; brand span sits in p.note, not div.pay
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: No img/svg/role=img is involved, so all ACT 1.1.1 rules are Inapplicable and scanners find nothing; the paragraph and badge are valid, non-empty, high-contrast text. A scanner cannot tell that this 'PayPal' is six confusables impersonating a brand rather than a legitimate string — and the visible submit button 'Pay with PayPal' is in correct Latin, deepening the ambiguity. Recognizing the substitution requires reading the glyphs against lang=en.

citation.quote: While the glyphs for some of these characters may look like the glyphs for other characters in visual presentation, they are not processed the same by text-to-speech tools.

pages.scenario: Product-page primary CTA — an <a> styled as a button reading 'Buy Now' — whose characters are B u U+0443(Cyrillic у) [space] N U+043E(Cyrillic о) w, with no aria-label, so the link's accessible name is the mixed-script string.
pages.mechanism: The accessible name of the most important control on the page is computed from text containing two Cyrillic look-alikes, so a screen reader announces the link as a mixed-script jumble (e.g. 'B u <cyrillic-u> N <cyrillic-o> w, link'), not 'Buy Now, link'; a user navigating by links list or tab order cannot identify the purchase action, and no text alternative is provided (F71; 1.1.1 control situation).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The link HAS a non-empty accessible name, so axe-core link-name, WAVE, and Lighthouse PASS; there is no graphical name-bearing element, so all ACT 1.1.1 rules are Inapplicable. Scanners cannot tell the accessible name is a confusable spelling of 'Buy Now' rather than a legitimate odd string — that requires reading the glyphs against lang=en and recognizing the cross-script substitution.

citation.quote: The objective of this failure condition is to avoid substituting characters whose glyphs look similar to the intended character, for that intended character.

pages.scenario: Bank login form whose <h1> heading AND submit button both read 'Login', authored entirely as numeric character entities Lοgіn that decode to L + Greek o (U+03BF) + g + Cyrillic i (U+0456) + n — exercising F71's explicit character-entity branch, with no text alternative.
pages.mechanism: The browser decodes the entities before building the accessibility tree, so AT sees the Greek-o/Cyrillic-i code points (not the markup); a screen reader announces the heading and the submit button as a mixed-script string ('L <greek-o> g <cyrillic-i> n'), not 'Login', so a blind user cannot identify the form or confidently activate the correct submit control on a security-sensitive page, and no text alternative exists (F71 entity variant).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Two layers defeat scanners: after parsing, entities ARE characters so 'source uses entities' tells a tool nothing, and the resulting heading and button name are valid, non-empty, high-contrast (axe button-name passes). No img/svg/role=img exists, so all ACT 1.1.1 rules are Inapplicable. Catching it requires decoding the entities and comparing the resulting glyphs to the page language.

citation.quote: This failure also applies to the use of character entities. It is the incorrect character used because of its glyph representation that comprises a failure, not the mechanism by which that character is implemented.

pages.scenario: Clearance product page whose headline sale price '$300' uses Cyrillic capital letters chosen for their digit shapes ($ U+0024 + З U+0417 Cyrillic Ze + О U+041E + О U+041E Cyrillic O), with no aria-label; a deliberately ambiguous-but-correctly-encoded SKU 'RX-O0OO' (Latin O U+004F + digit 0 U+0030) is included as a near-miss distractor.
pages.mechanism: The load-bearing sale price is encoded as Cyrillic letters whose glyphs look like 3/0; a screen reader announces them as the Cyrillic letters (e.g. 'dollar Ze O O') rather than 'three hundred dollars', so a blind shopper cannot hear the actual price, and no text alternative is provided (F71, which explicitly covers numeral confusables). The SKU near-miss is genuinely encoded and conformant, so a judge must isolate the real defect.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: No img/svg/role=img, so axe-core/WAVE/Lighthouse report nothing for 1.1.1; the price node is valid, non-empty, high-contrast text. A scanner cannot distinguish '$300 written in Cyrillic confusables' from a genuine '$300', and the genuinely-encoded O/0 SKU on the same page shows not every odd-looking string is a defect. Telling them apart requires reading each code point against the page language.
