citation.quote: The characters U+0033 and U+04E0 both look like the number "3", yet the second is actually a letter from the Cyrillic alphabet.

pages.scenario: Long-tail variant: a portfolio hero displays the designer's name 'Sumi Tanaka' (Mathematical Sans-Serif Bold, U+1D5E6 etc.) and role 'Designer & Illustrator' (Mathematical Sans-Serif Italic) pasted from a social-bio 'fancy text' generator; these are Mathematical Alphanumeric Symbols whose glyphs only resemble Latin letters, with no plain-Latin text alternative.
pages.mechanism: Mathematical Alphanumeric Symbols are math-notation code points, not alphabet letters; most TTS engines either announce each glyph by its verbose Unicode name ('mathematical sans-serif bold capital S, ...') or skip them as unknown, so a screen reader never hears 'Sumi Tanaka, Designer and Illustrator' — the whole point of the profile — and no text alternative exists. Same SC limb as classic F71: meaning rides on glyph shape, not the encoded characters.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: No img/svg/role=img, so axe-core/WAVE/Lighthouse report nothing; the <h1> is valid, non-empty, high-contrast. Crucially these code points are letters by Unicode general category (Lu/Ll), so even a hypothetical 'heading contains non-letter characters' heuristic would not flag them. Recognizing that 𝗦𝘂𝗺𝗶 is 'Sumi' in math-bold requires reading the glyphs against the page language.

citation.quote: The objective of this failure condition is to avoid substituting characters whose glyphs look similar to the intended character, for that intended character. The Unicode character set defines thousands of characters, covering dozens of writing systems.

pages.scenario: Boundary/PASS control on a kitchen-knife page: (A) the hero heading visually reads 'Cook' using confusable glyphs (U+03F2 U+043E U+03BF + k) but marks them aria-hidden and supplies a visually-hidden real-Latin 'Cook' text alternative; (B) a recipe quotes legitimate, language-tagged Greek (τζατζίκι and Καλή όρεξη, lang=el); (C) plain-Latin brand and CTA controls.
pages.mechanism: The aria-hidden confusable glyphs are skipped by AT and the sr-only span exposes the real word, so the heading is announced as 'Cook well, eat well.'; the Greek spans are tagged lang=el and announced correctly as Greek. No range of text relies on look-alike glyphs without an alternative, so F71's failure condition ('there is not a text alternative for any range of text that uses look-alike glyphs') is not triggered.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Symmetry point: just as scanners cannot DETECT the F71 failures (no graphical element; valid non-empty text), they equally cannot CONFIRM this page is fine — axe-core/WAVE/Lighthouse have no model that the hidden sr-only 'Cook' rescues the decorative confusable heading, nor that the Greek is legitimate rather than abuse. Both verdicts require the same human reading judgment.

citation.quote: If look-alike glyphs are used, and there is not a text alternative for any range of text that uses look-alike glyphs, then the content does not meet the Success Criterion.

aspects.title: Visual-only headings: text styled to look like a heading but marked up as plain p/div/span (F2)
aspects.plain: Text styled to look like a section heading is coded as a plain paragraph or div, so a screen-reader user can't jump between sections or locate them.
aspects.description:
A block of text is visually presented as a section heading — larger, bold, distinct font/spacing, set off from surrounding paragraphs so a sighted reader unambiguously perceives it as the title of the section that follows — but it is marked up as a

,

, or (often with a class like 'title' or 'heading1') with no

-

and no role=heading. The relationship 'this text labels the following section' is conveyed entirely through presentation and is lost programmatically. Correctly judging this requires (a) recognizing visually that the text functions as a heading and (b) deciding that the content beneath is a distinct section it titles — neither is in the DOM. This is the canonical F2 failure and the Trusted Tester 10.B condition 'each visual heading is programmatically determinable.' Includes the mixed case where some sub-section labels are real headings and some are styled
s (partial failure).
aspects.scLimb: Programmatic determinability of heading/section structure: a visual heading's relationship to the content it titles must be exposed via heading markup, not styling alone (TT 10.B).
aspects.whyUncovered: The ACT 1.3.1 corpus tests headings ONLY through ARIA required-property mechanics (4e8ab6: role=heading must carry aria-level). Every heading fixture already has role=heading or an h1-h6; none presents text that LOOKS like a heading to the eye but carries no heading semantics. No fixture's correct verdict depends on comparing rendered visual weight against the absence of heading markup, and a static checker cannot decide that bold large text 'is' a heading.

references.quote: So they used CSS to style the P element to look like a heading and they called it a heading. But they failed to use the proper HTML heading element. Therefore, the Assistive Technology could not distinguish it as a heading.
Each programmatically determinable heading is a visual heading and each visual heading is programmatically determinable.
headings are often in a larger, bold font separated from paragraphs by blank lines

aspects.ttWhy: Canonical F2: each visual heading must be programmatically determinable.

pages.scenario:
SaaS/agency pricing page where the page title, three section labels ('Choose a plan', 'What's included in every plan', 'Frequently asked') and two tier names are all large bold styled

— full F2 failure with ZERO

-

and zero role=heading on the page (website-builder/designer persona).
pages.mechanism:
Every visual heading is a

with presentational CSS only; accessibility tree exposes them as role=paragraph/generic, never heading. Live AX snapshot returned 0 headings, so a screen reader builds no document outline and 'find next heading' reports nothing — the canonical F2 / inverse of TT 10.B (visual heading not programmatically determinable).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss:
No missing/empty attribute and well-formed markup. axe page-has-heading-one does not hard-fail a heading-free page; heading-order only evaluates existing heading elements (none here); WAVE raises only a 'No heading structure' alert. Deciding a styled

IS a section heading requires reading rendered visual weight + judging it titles the block beneath — visual/semantic judgment.

citation.quote: The author intended to make a heading but didn't want the look of the default HTML heading. So they used CSS to style the P element to look like a heading and they called it a heading. But they failed to use the proper HTML heading element. Therefore, the Assistive Technology could not distinguish it as a heading.

pages.scenario: Help-center 'Returns & Refunds' FAQ that has one real <h1> (page title) but renders all five questions as <div class="q"> styled at 150% bold — each obviously a sub-heading titling its answer, none a heading element (junior-dev hand-coded persona). The legitimate <h1> makes the partial-outline failure more deceptive.
pages.mechanism: The five div.q questions expose as role=generic static text; the live AX headings list contains only the single <h1>, so 'next heading' skips straight past all five FAQ questions. The Q&A's internal structure is visually obvious but not programmatically determinable (TT 10.B).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Because a valid <h1> exists, page-has-heading-one PASSES and heading-order finds one well-ordered heading with nothing to flag; WAVE reports '1 heading' with no error. No rule can infer the bold 150% <div> questions are headings that belong in the outline — that requires recognizing a Q&A pattern from rendered hierarchy.

citation.quote: If ANDI does not identify a visually apparent heading → not defined programmatically.

pages.scenario:
Institutional 'Open Data Policy' authored in a word processor and pasted into a CMS: each numbered section heading ('1. Scope', '2. Definitions', '2.1 Research data', '3. Data-Sharing Principles' ...) is a styled

with an inline-styled run — a two-level visual outline with no and no role=heading (Word-paste round-trip-loss persona; long-tail).
pages.mechanism: Every heading run resolves to static text inside a paragraph; live AX returned 0 headings. The numeric prefixes (2.1/2.2) and indentation encode a heading LEVEL hierarchy that is also lost — a screen reader cannot perceive the 1→2→2.1 nesting and must read linearly. F2 / TT 10.B.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss:
Markup is fully well-formed: valid

/ with valid inline font-size/font-weight, nothing empty. Inline styles look identical to ordinary emphasis, so a linter cannot distinguish an emphasized phrase from a section heading; axe has no rule turning a styled bold paragraph into 'should be a heading'. Interpreting the numbering + visual weight as a heading outline is human comprehension.

citation.quote: In other words, the elements are used according to their meaning, not because of the way they appear visually.

pages.scenario: Web-archived ('view in browser') HTML email newsletter built from nested <table role="presentation"> layout grids, where each story's section heading ('Top Story'/'Desktop CNC prices...', 'Quick Hits', 'Tool of the Week', 'Community Spotlight') is a bold 22px <span class="sectionhead"> inside a layout <td> — no <h*>, no role=heading (email-template developer persona; long-tail).
pages.mechanism: Each span.sectionhead exposes as inline role=generic text; live AX returned 0 headings, so heading navigation is impossible and the user must traverse the linearized table. The layout tables are correctly presentational (role=presentation, no <th>), so 14.x passes — the failure is isolated to 10.B (visual heading not programmatically determinable).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Document is well-formed: presentational tables (no 'data table missing headers' finding), valid styled <span>s, nothing absent. No rule promotes a bold styled <span> to 'should be a heading'; a heading-free page is at most a soft alert; email markup lacks any <h*> for a tool to order or compare. Recognizing 'Quick Hits' as a section heading requires reading the newsletter's visual rhythm.

citation.quote: This document describes a failure that occurs when a change in the appearance of text conveys meaning without using appropriate semantic markup.

pages.scenario: Food-blog recipe ('Brown-Butter Banana Bread') — PARTIAL-FAILURE MIX: real <h1> title plus a real <h2> 'Ingredients', but two visually identical peer subsection labels 'Method' and 'Notes & Substitutions' are <div class="step-head"> sharing the same CSS class with no heading semantics (agency-CMS-template persona).
pages.mechanism: 'Ingredients' exposes as heading level 2; 'Method' and 'Notes & Substitutions' expose as role=generic. Live AX returned only [h1 'Brown-Butter Banana Bread', h2 'Ingredients'] — the two most procedurally important sections are silently dropped from the outline despite being rank-equal visually. TT 10.B's 'each visual heading is programmatically determinable' is broken for 2 of 3.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The real <h1>/<h2> satisfy page-has-heading-one; heading-order sees h1→h2 gapless and PASSES — there is no out-of-sequence level to flag because the missing headings are absent, not mis-leveled. No tool compares the rendered visual weight of 'Method'/'Notes' against 'Ingredients' to notice three identical section labels yielded only one heading.

citation.quote: 1. Each programmatically determinable heading is serving as a visual heading on the page, AND 2. Each visual heading is programmatically defined.

pages.scenario: BOUNDARY PASS: coffee-roastery 'Our Story' page where the giant brand tagline 'Slow coffee, made by hand.' and a centered italic pull-quote 'The best cup I've had in this city.' are large/bold but correctly NOT headings (decorative statement + excerpt), while the three genuine section headings ('Where we started', 'How we roast', 'Visit the bar') are exposed via role=heading aria-level=2 (design-system-without-native-h* persona).
pages.mechanism: The three role=heading paragraphs expose as heading level 2 and each precedes the section it titles; the tagline exposes as paragraph and the pull-quote as blockquote (read in flow, not announced as headings). Live AX returned exactly the three real section headings and neither the tagline nor the pull-quote — every visual heading is programmatically determinable AND no non-heading is falsely a heading (TT 10.B both directions).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Just as tools cannot detect the failures in 01-05, they cannot verify this pass: a scanner cannot confirm 'Slow coffee, made by hand.' correctly is NOT a heading while 'Where we started' correctly IS — both are styled prominently, and role=heading with a valid aria-level passes ARIA validity checks (ACT 4e8ab6) regardless of true heading function. Confirming the verdict requires reading each block's meaning and visual role.

citation.quote: content that is not a visual heading should not have a role of heading (e.g., don't use heading markup for emphasis). Conversely, content styled and functioning like a heading should be programmatically a heading.

aspects.title: Genuine data tables whose header/structure semantics are absent or stripped: all-<td> tables, and real data tables with role=presentation (F91, F92)
aspects.plain: A real data table lacks proper header cells (or hides them), so a screen reader reads bare numbers with no row or column labels for a blind user.
aspects.description: A genuine data table — content where cells are only intelligible via their row/column headers — fails to expose those relationships. Two mechanisms: (1) F91, the table presents headers visually (a bold first row, a labeled first column) but every cell is a plain <td> with no <th>, scope, headers/id, or role=columnheader/rowheader, so a screen reader announces bare values with no context; (2) F92, a structurally correct data table (or list, or heading) carries role=presentation/role=none, deliberately suppressing its semantics from the a11y tree. Both require the human judgments: is this content actually a data table whose cells need headers, and which row/column visually functions as the header? A checker sees either zero header cells (F91 -> rules inapplicable) or a deliberately suppressed tree (F92 -> excluded from scope).
aspects.scLimb: Programmatic determinability of the data-table header-to-data relationship and of table semantics themselves (TT 14.A table identification, 14.B cell-header association); data tables must retain semantics and must not be suppressed.
aspects.whyUncovered: ACT's table rules (a25f45, d0f69e) require a <th> or role=columnheader/rowheader to even be applicable — a table built entirely of <td> returns inapplicable from both, so F91 is silently out of scope. For F92, ACT treats role=presentation / aria-hidden purely as an INAPPLICABILITY trigger (element removed from a11y tree -> structural rule doesn't apply); the corpus therefore uses presentation-role only to exclude elements, never as the failure itself, and never contains a real data table marked role=presentation that should FAIL. Distinguishing 'correctly suppressed layout content' from 'wrongly suppressed data table' is the omitted human judgment.

references.quote: This failure occurs when data tables do not use header elements (th) or other appropriate table mark-up ... to make the headers programmatically determinable from within table content.
This failure occurs when a role of presentation is applied to an element whose purpose is to convey information or relationships in the content.
A data table with role="presentation" will not convey table semantics and fails this test.

aspects.ttWhy: role=presentation fails table identification; all-td tables fail cell-header association.

pages.scenario: SaaS plan-comparison matrix (Starter/Growth/Scale/Enterprise across the top, 8 features down the side) rendered as a real <table> where the first row and first column are visually styled as headers (blue band, bold rail) but every cell, including both header bands, is a plain <td>. F91.
pages.mechanism: F91 — a genuine two-axis data table (cells like '$120' or 'Yes' are meaningless without their plan column AND feature row) exposes table+row+cell to the a11y tree but has zero <th>/scope/headers-id/role=columnheader|rowheader, so the header-to-data relationship is not programmatically determinable; AT navigating a column hears bare values with no plan/feature context (TT 14.B fails).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: ACT rules a25f45 and d0f69e require a header cell (<th> or role=columnheader/rowheader) to be applicable; an all-<td> table returns inapplicable from both, so F91 is silently out of scope. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse raise nothing because a table of only <td> is valid HTML with no empty/missing attribute to lint. Recognising the blue first row as a column-header row and the bold first column as a row-header column — and that the cells are unintelligible without them — is human visual/semantic judgment. Verified via Chromium a11y tree: table:1, row:9, cell:45, zero header roles.

citation.quote: This failure occurs when data tables do not use header elements (th) or other appropriate table mark-up (the scope attribute, headers and id or the ARIA columnheader and rowheader) roles to make the headers programmatically determinable from within table content. Making headers programmatically determinable is especially important when data cells are only intelligible together with header information.

pages.scenario: Finance-intranet 'Q3 departmental expenses' table pasted verbatim from a spreadsheet export: four cost centres down the side, five money columns (July/Aug/Sep/Quarter total/vs. budget) across the top, all cells emitted as <td class='xl-hdr|xl-rowlbl|xl-num'> with dark-blue/light-blue fill styling but no <th> anywhere. F91.
pages.mechanism: F91 — financial figures whose meaning depends entirely on their row/column intersection ('259' = Sales & Marketing / August) lose that relationship: the spreadsheet export wraps the range in <table> and emits only class-styled <td>, so no header cell is programmatically associated and AT announces bare numbers with no month or cost-centre (TT 14.B fails).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The Excel-paste markup is well-formed (valid <table>/<td>, real text, inline classes) so a linter finds nothing; because there is no <th>/role=columnheader, a25f45 and d0f69e are inapplicable and the table is out of scope. Only a human can read the rendered grid, recognise the dark-blue band as the column-header row and the light-blue band as the row-header column, and judge these GBP figures are data that lost their header semantics in copy-paste. Verified via a11y tree: table:1, row:6, cell:36, zero header roles.

citation.quote: items that share a common characteristic are organized into a table where the relationship of cells sharing the same row or column and the relationship of each cell to its row and/or column header are necessary for understanding

pages.scenario: Patient-portal CBC lab-results grid built from <div>s with explicit ARIA roles role=table/row/cell throughout — including the visual header row (Analyte/Result/Reference range/Flag) and the analyte-name column — but with no role=columnheader, no role=rowheader, and no <th> anywhere. F91 (ARIA-grid variant).
pages.mechanism: F91 (ARIA variant) — clinical values ('118', 'Low') are meaningless without their analyte row and column header; the widget is exposed as a table (role=table valid) so the user enters table navigation, but with zero header cells no header is ever announced, so the row/column context is not programmatically determinable (TT 14.B fails; 14.A passes).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: This is the hardest F91 variant: role=cell nested in role=row nested in role=table is a STRUCTURALLY VALID ARIA table and axe does not require a columnheader, so the ARIA-structure rules pass while a25f45/d0f69e stay inapplicable (no header cell exists). No rule fails. Detecting it requires recognising that the first row and first column FUNCTION as headers and should carry columnheader/rowheader, and that real clinical data is unintelligible without them. Verified via a11y tree: table:1, row:6, cell:24, zero header roles.

citation.quote: Inspect the ANDI Output for each data cell and/or the visual highlighting to determine whether the table identifies **all relevant headers** for each data cell.

pages.scenario: A textbook-correct Route 14 bus timetable (five stops x four buses) with <caption>, <th scope='col'> for each bus and <th scope='row'> for each stop — then role='presentation' placed on the <table>, stripping all table semantics from the accessibility tree. F92.
pages.mechanism: F92 — role=presentation removes the table's implicit semantics and its required-owned descendants (thead/tr/th/td and all scope associations) from the a11y API; the data table linearises to a flat run of text with no table mode and no stop/bus header announced for any time, so the correctly-encoded header-to-data relationship becomes invisible (TT 14.A fails: a data table with role=presentation does not convey table semantics).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: ACT treats role=presentation purely as an INAPPLICABILITY trigger — the element leaves the a11y tree so structural rules don't apply, and the corpus never contains a real data table marked role=presentation that should FAIL. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse raise nothing because role=presentation on a <table> is valid for LAYOUT tables. The tool cannot tell whether the suppressed table is harmless layout or a genuine data table wrongly stripped — distinguishing the two requires a human to judge that the times are unintelligible without stop/bus headers. Verified via a11y tree: the table contributes no table/row/header/cell nodes ({}).

citation.quote: A data table with `role="presentation"` will not convey table semantics and **fails** this test.

pages.scenario: A first-aid 'how to use an EpiPen' article with a safety-critical six-step ordered procedure correctly authored as an <ol>, then given role='presentation' to allow custom red number chips; the visible ordinals are a CSS counter() ::before, not real list numbering. F92 (list variant).
pages.mechanism: F92 (list variant) — role=presentation removes the list role and the implicit listitem semantics of the <li> children from the a11y tree, so AT no longer announces 'list, 6 items' or any 'X of 6' position; the only remaining ordinal cue is the CSS ::before generated content, which AT does not announce, making the essential, safety-critical sequence and item count visual-only (TT 10.D fails).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: ACT treats role=presentation only as an inapplicability trigger: the list leaves the a11y tree so list-structure checks don't apply, and no rule fires on 'a real ordered list was suppressed'. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse raise nothing because role=presentation on a list is legitimate for decorative lists and a CSS counter() is valid. Detecting it requires the semantic judgment that THIS list conveys essential sequence/count plus the visual observation that the only ordinal cue is decorative CSS. Verified via a11y tree: the <ol> contributes no list/listitem nodes ({}).

citation.quote: The WAI-ARIA role of presentation on the other hand, is intended to suppress semantic information of content from the accessibility API and prevent user agents from conveying that information to the user. Use of role="presentation" for content which should convey semantic information may prevent the user from understanding that content.

pages.scenario: An order-confirmation email containing TWO tables: (A) a layout table (greeting + order badge) correctly given role='presentation' with no headers, and (B) a genuine order line-items data table correctly built with <caption>, <th scope='col'>, and <th scope='row'>. Both choices are correct. Boundary PASS variant that sharpens the layout-vs-data distinction.
pages.mechanism: Correct retention vs. correct suppression: the layout table's role=presentation correctly removes unneeded table semantics (it reads sensibly in source order), while the data table correctly keeps caption + scope so every cell ('$9.00') announces its column header ('Unit price') and row header ('Reusable filter (size 02)'). No information or relationship is lost (TT 14.A/14.B pass for the data table; 14.C passes for the layout table).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A scanner cannot ORIGINATE this verdict: it sees one valid role=presentation table and one valid table with <th scope> and reports 'no issues' regardless of whether the choices were appropriate — the identical output would appear if the roles were swapped (the failing case-04 pattern). Confirming the suppressed table really is layout and the semantic table really is the data requires the human to recognise which table is which, the exact judgment that makes case-04 fail and this page pass. Verified via a11y tree: layout table suppressed; data table = table:1, row:5, columnheader:4, rowheader:3, cell:11.

citation.quote: The `<table>` element includes `role="presentation"`, OR BOTH: the layout does NOT use `role="table"`/associated ARIA table attributes AND does NOT include table structure/relationship elements or attributes (e.g., `<th>`, `scope="row"`).

aspects.title: Layout tables that falsely assert data-table relationships: th, caption, scope, or summary on a positioning-only table (F46)
aspects.plain: A table used only to position page regions is dressed up with header-cell markup, so a screen reader falsely announces meaningless layout grids as real tabular data.
aspects.description: A table used purely to position page regions (nav | content | sidebar, or a hero/marketing layout) includes data-table semantic markup — a <th>, a <caption>, scope attributes, role=table, or a non-empty summary — which falsely tells AT that the layout grid is meaningful tabular data and that, e.g., 'Page Title' is the header for the nav/content/footer cells. The inverse of the suppression case: here genuine semantic markup is present and syntactically valid, but the relationship it asserts does not exist. Judging this requires recognizing the table is layout (no real row/column data relationship) AND that it nonetheless asserts header semantics. Automated tools see a structurally valid <th>/<caption> and pass; they cannot decide the table is 'really' layout (TT 14.C).
aspects.scLimb: Programmatic relationships must not assert structure that does not exist: a layout table must not designate itself as a table or carry header structure/attributes (TT 14.C).
aspects.whyUncovered: ACT table rules (a25f45, d0f69e) check the INTERNAL correctness of header references and that th cells have assigned cells — they assume the table IS a data table and verify the plumbing. No ACT rule asks 'is this a layout table that should not carry th/caption/summary at all?', so F46 (correct markup, wrong context) is wholly outside the corpus. The layout-vs-data distinction is precisely TT 14.C, a human determination a static checker cannot make.

references.quote: a failure that occurs when a table used only for layout includes either th elements, a summary attribute, or a caption element. This is a failure because it uses structural (or semantic) markup only for presentation.
The example marks the page title as <th>.
The layout table DOES NOT designate the layout table using ARIA role="table" AND DOES NOT include table header structure and relationship elements and/or associated attributes.

aspects.ttWhy: Layout table asserting th/caption/scope/role=table is exactly the 14.C condition.

pages.scenario: County government 'Records & Licensing Portal' positions its entire page chrome (masthead, left services nav, main content with a record-order form, right office-hours sidebar, footer) in a single layout <table>. The top row is a <th colspan=3 scope=colgroup>Northbridge County</th>, falsely asserting that the agency name is the column header governing the nav/content/sidebar cells beneath it.
pages.mechanism: A <th colspan=3 scope=colgroup> on a layout table designates the agency-name cell as the column header for the page-region cells. AT in table-reading mode announces 'Northbridge County Records & Licensing Portal' as the header that classifies the navigation links, the order form, and the office hours — a relationship that does not exist (these are independent page regions, not data observations sharing a header). F46: a <th> in a layout table is structural markup used purely for presentation.
pages.selectorNote: Layout-table masthead falsely a th header; orig table>tr fails due to inserted tbody
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: ACT table rules (a25f45 'th has assigned cells', d0f69e header/headers correctness) assume the table is a data table and only audit internal plumbing; the <th colspan=3> does have assigned cells (the colspan covers row 2), so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse pass and report no violation. Deciding this <table> is LAYOUT — that nav|content|sidebar are page regions with no row/column data relationship — is the TT 14.C human determination no static checker performs. Verified in Chromium: th[colspan=3] parses into a real <table>, scope=colgroup, 3 layout columns; visual render is unmistakable page chrome.

citation.quote: The objective of this technique is to describe a failure that occurs when a table used only for layout includes either th elements, a summary attribute, or a caption element. This is a failure because it uses structural (or semantic) markup only for presentation. The intent of the HTML table elements is to present data.

pages.scenario: An artisan-stationery shop (Marlowe & Finch, en-GB) positions its site header strip — brand logo | centered product search | Account/Cart utility nav — in a one-row, three-column layout <table> that carries a visually-hidden but non-empty <caption>Header layout</caption>. The caption falsely identifies the presentational header strip as a named data table.
pages.mechanism: A <caption> is part of the table and identifies it. AT exposes the header strip as 'table, Header layout, 1 row, 3 columns' and offers table-navigation across the logo/search/cart cells — describing page chrome as a data table named 'Header layout'. F46 explicitly warns that describing a layout table this way 'does not provide value and will only distract users navigating the content via a screen reader.' No row/column data relationship exists.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A non-empty <caption> is exactly what scanners want on a <table> — it gives the table an accessible name and satisfies 'table has caption/name' heuristics, so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse see a well-named table and report nothing. They cannot determine the <table> is layout (logo+search+cart are chrome, not data), which is the precondition for the caption to be a failure — the TT 14.C judgment. Verified in Chromium: caption is a direct child of table.siteheader with text 'Header layout'.

citation.quote: Likewise, there is no need for an additional description of a table which is only used to layout content. Do not include a summary attribute and do not use the summary attribute to describe the table as, for instance, "layout table". When spoken, this information does not provide value and will only distract users navigating the content via a screen reader.

pages.scenario: A scheduling-SaaS landing page (Cadence) lays out its two-column marketing hero — headline + CTA on the left, a decorative aria-hidden calendar illustration on the right — as a <table summary="layout table for hero section">. The non-empty summary provides a textual description of a layout container as if it were a data table.
pages.mechanism: The summary attribute 'provides a textual description of the table that describes its purpose and function' and AT makes it available to users (F46). On this layout table the AT announces the table along with 'layout table for hero section', describing presentational scaffolding as a navigable data table. F46 names describing a table as a 'layout table' via summary as a direct failure. There is no row/column data relationship.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse do not treat a non-empty summary on a <table> as a 1.3.1 violation (summary was historically encouraged for data tables). An HTML5 obsolete-attribute lint, if present, only says 'summary is obsolete' — not 'this layout table fabricates data semantics'; and an EMPTY summary on a layout table is explicitly acceptable, so the defect is specifically the non-empty+layout combination, which requires the TT 14.C layout-vs-data judgment. Verified in Chromium: summary='layout table for hero section' survives parsing on table.hero.

citation.quote: The summary attribute on the table element provides a textual description of the table that describes its purpose and function. Assistive technologies make the summary attribute information available to users.

pages.scenario: A university Marine Biology research-group page lays out its body as a two-column nav-beside-content <table>: each left navigation cell (Research/People/Publications) is a <th scope="row" id="nav-..."> and each right content cell points back with headers="nav-...". The header/headers plumbing is internally flawless but fabricates a row-header relationship between a navigation link and the unrelated content block beside it.
pages.mechanism: In table-reading mode AT prepends each content cell's row header — e.g. landing on the 'Coastal ecosystems under thermal stress' paragraph, the screen reader announces 'Research' as its row header, implying 'Research' classifies/labels that paragraph the way a real row header labels a data cell. But 'Research' is a nav link and the paragraph is page content; there is no row/column data relationship. TT 14.C: a layout table must not include <th> or scope/headers relationship attributes.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: This case is engineered to PASS every internal ACT table rule: a25f45 'th has assigned cells' passes (each <th scope=row> has the data cell in its row) and d0f69e 'headers refers to a cell in the same table' passes (every headers id resolves) — verified in Chromium: 3 row-headers, 3 headers= cells, allHeadersResolve=true. A perfectly-wired FALSE relationship is the hardest variant because the plumbing is valid; no rule asks whether the <table> should carry header structure at all, which requires the TT 14.C judgment that the left column is navigation and the right is independent content.

citation.quote: Although not commonly used in a layout table, the following structural markup would also be failures of Success Criterion 1.3.1 Info and Relationships if used in a layout table: headers attributes [and] scope attributes.

pages.scenario: A DevOps operations dashboard (Helmsman) arranges six independent monitoring widgets in a CSS grid with NO <table> element: the container carries role="table", the top three summary cards carry role="row" + role="columnheader", and the three detail widgets carry role="cell". The ARIA owned-element contract is satisfied, but the widgets are independent panels with no shared row/column axis — the modern ARIA reincarnation of F46.
pages.mechanism: AT exposes the dashboard as a 3-column data table. Navigating to the 'Latency p95' widget in table mode, the screen reader announces 'System Health, Latency p95' — naming the separate System-Health status card as the column header for the latency panel. That relationship is invented; table commands ('read column', 'go to column header') traverse unrelated widgets as a contiguous dataset, and aria-label='Operations metrics' reinforces the false table framing. TT 14.C's first limb is exactly role="table"/ARIA table attributes on layout.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe's ARIA structure rules only check that a declared role has its structurally required parents/children and that role values are valid — all true here (role=table has its required row/columnheader/cell descendants), so 'required ARIA children', 'required parent', and 'valid role' report clean. No rule asks whether these elements genuinely form a table of related data vs. independent panels falsely labeled role=table; answering requires reading the widgets' meaning (separate metrics, no shared axis) and the rendered layout — the TT 14.C human judgment. Verified in Chromium: 0 real <table> elements, role=table + 3 columnheaders + 3 cells; visual render shows six clearly independent cards that do not even align into clean rows.

citation.quote: BOTH: the layout does NOT use `role="table"`/associated ARIA table attributes AND does NOT include table structure/relationship elements or attributes (e.g., `<th>`, `scope="row"`).

pages.scenario: A weekly typography newsletter (The Proof Sheet, Issue 47) is built from deeply nested HTML-email layout tables. Every layout table is correctly role="presentation" EXCEPT the masthead 'header band', which was copied from a data-table block in the ESP snippet library and still carries a <th scope="col">The Proof Sheet</th> and has no presentation role — so that single band re-enters the accessibility tree as a data table whose column header is 'The Proof Sheet'.
pages.mechanism: Because role="presentation" is absent on the header band AND it contains a <th>, AT re-exposes that band as a data table: 'table, 1 column', with 'The Proof Sheet' announced as the column header for the issue-line cell beneath it — a fabricated relationship (it is just a masthead). The surrounding presentational tables read normally, so the experience is one jarring 'table' interruption asserting structure that does not exist. F46 names a <th> in a layout table as a failure; TT 14.C requires layout tables to carry no header structure (or to be role=presentation).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Scanners see a mostly well-formed email: most layout tables are role=presentation and the one <th> that exists has its assigned cell, so internal-correctness rules (a25f45) pass and nothing is flagged. No rule flags 'a <th> on a layout table' because no rule decides the band is layout — it would have to distinguish this masthead band (layout) from a genuine data band (which SHOULD keep its <th>), and notice that exactly one sibling lost its role=presentation. That is the TT 14.C human judgment (TT even instructs testers to IGNORE header alerts on tables that ARE marked presentation — the inverse case). Verified in Chromium: 6 nested tables, 5 role=presentation, 1 leftover th[scope=col]='The Proof Sheet' on a non-presentation band.

citation.quote: If a table has `role="presentation"` and also denotes header relationships (e.g., `<th scope="row">`), ANDI provides an alert; ignore this alert on a layout table (presentation role suppresses semantics).

aspects.title: Valid structural elements asserting relationships that do not exist: heading/blockquote/fieldset used for visual effect (F43)
aspects.plain: Real structural tags are used for looks not meaning (a heading just to enlarge text), so a screen reader announces relationships and an outline that don't really exist.
aspects.description: Genuine structural elements are present and syntactically valid, but they assert a content relationship that is false. An <h3>/<h4> makes an author byline or address big and bold (no new section begins), a <blockquote> wraps text that is not a quotation merely to indent it, or a <fieldset>/<legend> draws a decorative bordered box around prose that is not a group of form controls. Automated tools see a well-formed heading/blockquote/fieldset and pass; only a human reading the content can tell the asserted relationship is untrue. This is the Trusted Tester note 'don't use heading markup for emphasis' and F43's 'relationships that do not exist in the content.' It also fabricates a misleading heading outline (e.g. every ingredient as its own <h5>).
aspects.scLimb: Programmatic relationships must reflect the actual content: structural markup must not indicate relationships (sectioning, quotation, control-grouping) that are not present in the content (TT 10.B note, F43).
aspects.whyUncovered: ACT rules check that structural elements are syntactically correct and carry required properties — never whether the relationship they assert is TRUE of the content. No fixture contains a structurally valid <h4>, <blockquote>, or <fieldset> whose correct verdict is FAIL because the element misrepresents its content. The corpus has no notion of 'valid markup, wrong meaning,' which is precisely the human semantic judgment this aspect needs.

references.quote: a failure that occurs when structural markup is used to achieve a presentational effect, but indicates relationships that do not exist in the content. This is disorienting to users who are depending on those relationships to navigate the content
a heading element is used to display an address in a large, bold font. The address does not identify a new section of the document, however, so it should not be marked as a heading.
content that is not a visual heading should not have a role of heading (e.g., don't use heading markup for emphasis)

aspects.ttWhy: Heading-for-emphasis: programmatic heading isn't a real visual heading (10.B note); blockquote/fieldset misuse uncovered.

pages.scenario: Long-form news article: the byline ("By Marguerite Adler and Tomas Vance") is marked up as <h3> and the dateline as <h4>, between the <h1> title and the real <h2> sections, purely to size them. The byline/date begin no section, fabricating a heading outline (h1 > h3 > h4 > h2) that asserts subsection relationships absent from the content.
pages.mechanism: Screen-reader heading navigation (H key / rotor) announces the byline as a level-3 section and the dateline as a level-4 subsection nested under the title; landing on each, the user finds only author names / a date — no section. Headings assert sectioning relationships (F43) that do not exist; the real first section 'Abstract' is announced after a spurious h3/h4, corrupting the outline.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every heading is valid and non-empty; the only level transition (h1->h3) is at most an axe/Lighthouse 'heading-order' warning, never a hard failure, and h3->h4 is monotonic. No tool can read 'By Marguerite Adler and Tomas Vance' and infer it is a byline that begins no section — that is a semantic reading of the content F43 requires.

citation.quote: However, the h3 and h4 elements between the title and the abstract are used only for visual effect — to control the fonts used to display the authors' names and the date.

pages.scenario: E-commerce product page (Shopify-style theme): the store's OWN shipping/returns/assembly disclaimer — first-party policy prose with no source, no <cite>, no attribution — is wrapped in a <blockquote> only to obtain the theme's indented, left-bordered 'fine print' look. The <blockquote> asserts a quotation relationship that does not exist.
pages.mechanism: <blockquote> carries the implicit role 'blockquote'; AT exposes quotation structure (VoiceOver 'quote'/'end quote', NVDA/JAWS boundary announcements, braille quotation semantic). The AT user is told this binding return policy is something quoted from an external source — a fabricated quotation relationship that can mislead about who is speaking and the standing of the text.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A <blockquote> needs no attributes, can hold any flow content, and is valid and non-empty here. No axe/WAVE/Lighthouse rule inspects whether a blockquote's content is actually a quotation — that needs NL understanding plus knowing this is the store's own voice. Tools see a well-formed quotation container and pass it.

citation.quote:
The following example uses blockquote for text that is
                                not a quotation to give it prominence by indenting it when displayed
                                in graphical browsers.

pages.scenario: Food-blog recipe: under the real <h2> 'Ingredients', each of six ingredient lines ('2 cups all-purpose flour' …) is marked up as its own <h5> to render in a uniform bold serif. Each ingredient is a list item, not a section heading, so six sibling <h5> elements fabricate subsections that reflect no section structure (and the visually apparent list is also not coded as a list).
pages.mechanism: Pulling up the headings list, a screen-reader user hears each ingredient announced as a heading-level-5 section nested under 'Ingredients', asserting that each ingredient introduces a subsection — a relationship that does not exist; the ingredients are peers in one list. Six non-headings between two real sections make the heading rotor useless and misrepresent flat list items as a hierarchy (F43; also TT 10.D list-not-marked-up).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Each <h5> is valid and non-empty; the h2->h5 jump is an axe/Lighthouse heading-order warning at most, and six repeated h5 siblings violate no rule. No automated check recognises '2 cups all-purpose flour' as an ingredient/list item rather than a section title — that needs understanding of the recipe domain.

citation.quote:
The objective of this technique is to describe a failure that occurs when
                        structural markup is used to achieve a presentational effect, but indicates
                        relationships that do not exist in the content. This is disorienting to
                        users who are depending on those relationships to navigate the content

pages.scenario: Nonprofit donation landing page: a 'Matching Gift This Week' promo is built with <fieldset><legend>Matching Gift This Week</legend> … prose … </fieldset> purely for the notched-border look, containing NO form controls. A real, correctly grouped donation-amount <fieldset> (radios + legend) sits below it as a foil. The decorative fieldset asserts a control-grouping relationship that does not exist.
pages.mechanism: <fieldset> has implicit role 'group' with its <legend> as accessible name; AT announces a form-control group named 'Matching Gift This Week' around prose that contains no controls. The markup asserts a grouping relationship between form controls absent from the content; an AT user expecting the implied controls finds none, and the false group pollutes the forms model (F43 fieldset-for-border).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A <fieldset> that HAS a <legend> is the pattern automated tools reward: axe checks that grouped controls sit inside a fieldset and that fieldsets carry a legend, but has no rule that a fieldset must actually contain controls. A fieldset wrapping only prose trips nothing in axe/WAVE/Lighthouse — recognising there is nothing to group requires reading the box.

pages.scenario: SaaS pricing page (CI product): a <dl>/<dt>/<dd> is abused as a two-column spec grid whose rows (Price, Seats, Billing, Included minutes, Support) are independent spec lines, not term->definition pairs — with two rows written <dd>value</dd><dt>label</dt> to force CSS-grid alignment, inverting the programmatic term/description meaning. A second defect: the company's own slogan 'Ship faster. Sleep better.' is wrapped in a <blockquote> (not a quotation).
pages.mechanism: <dl> exposes term/definition structure; AT announces each <dt> as a term defined by its <dd>. The rows are not definitions, so false definition relationships are asserted — and on the two reversed pairs the term/description pairing is literally inverted (AT announces '10 seats included' as the term defined by 'Seats'), scrambling the key/value model for AT users. The <blockquote> (role 'blockquote') additionally asserts the first-party slogan is an external quotation. Both are F43 misuse.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe's dlitem/definition-list rules only verify a <dl> contains <dt>/<dd>/<div> and that dt/dd are inside a dl — all true here. No rule checks whether a term defines its description or whether dt/dd order matches meaning; a reversed pair is structurally legal. A <blockquote> needs no attributes. Detecting spec-rows-not-definitions, the inverted pairs, and the first-party slogan all require reading the content.

citation.quote:
The objective of this technique is to describe a failure that occurs when
                        structural markup is used to achieve a presentational effect, but indicates
                        relationships that do not exist in the content.

pages.scenario: Boundary PASS foil: a law-firm contact page using the SAME three elements F43 warns about, but correctly. The <h2> 'Visit Our Downtown Office' genuinely begins a section whose body is the office address (kept in an <address> element, not a heading), hours, and parking; a <blockquote> wraps a genuine attributed client testimonial with <cite>; a <fieldset>/<legend> actually groups real form controls. Every encoded relationship is true.
pages.mechanism: AT navigating by heading finds 'Visit Our Downtown Office' introducing exactly the office info it promises, with the address announced as ordinary text (not a heading) inside the section. Entering the <blockquote>, AT announces a quotation that IS one (source exposed via <cite>). In the form, the announced group 'How should we reach you?' legitimately labels the name/email/radio controls. Each programmatic relationship reflects the actual content, satisfying SC 1.3.1.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: This is the crux of the aspect: automated tools see valid heading/blockquote/fieldset and return PASS here — the SAME verdict they would wrongly return for the failing cases 01-05, because syntactic validity is identical and tools cannot distinguish this page from them. Only a human reading the content can confirm the relationships are genuine; the discriminating question 'is the asserted relationship true?' is invisible to tools.

citation.quote:
In this example, a heading element is used to display an address in a
                                large, bold font. The address does not identify a new section of the
                                document, however, so it should not be marked as a heading.

aspects.title: Visually apparent lists not programmatically identified as lists (or as the wrong type / lost nesting)
aspects.plain: Content that visually reads as a bulleted, numbered, or definition list isn't coded as the right list type, so a screen reader skips announcing item counts and grouping.
aspects.description:
Content that visually reads as a list — bulleted items, a numbered sequence, or term/description pairs — is not coded as a list of the correct type, or its nesting/hierarchy is flattened. Examples: a bulleted-looking sequence built from
-separated lines or styled
s instead of
    ; a numbered step sequence (where order matters) coded as
      or plain paragraphs instead of
        ; a glossary of terms+definitions coded as paragraphs instead of
        ; a visually nested outline whose programmatic list flattens the sub-list grouping. Trusted Tester 10.D is explicitly driven by VISUALLY apparent lists, not by what markup happens to exist, and requires judging both 'is this visually a list' and 'is its type/nesting correct,' excluding navigation framework unless it appears as a numbered/bulleted list.
aspects.scLimb: Programmatic determinability of list structure and type: visually apparent lists must be programmatically identified as lists of the correct type with consistent nesting/hierarchy (TT 10.D).
aspects.whyUncovered: There is NO ACT 1.3.1 rule for list determinability or list type in the corpus — the only list-adjacent ACT rules concern ARIA owned/context roles (bc4a75, ff89c9: a listbox must own options) and fire only when an explicit listbox/option role is already present. A bulleted-looking set of <div>s, an ordered procedure coded as <ul>, or a flattened nested list has no role for any rule to attach to. Deciding that content visually 'is a list,' which type, and whether nesting matches the visual hierarchy is human visual/semantic judgment.

references.quote: All content with the visual appearance of a list is defined programmatically as a list, by type
Ordered (ol) — numbered sequentially / hierarchically (1, 2, 2.a, 2.a.i) where sequence or reference-by-number matters.
list items are preceded by a bullet and perhaps indented

aspects.ttWhy: Visually apparent lists must be programmatically identified by correct type and nesting.

pages.scenario:
Consumer-product marketing page ('Verdant' countertop composter) shows a six-item bulleted feature list where each '•' is a literal U+2022 glyph and the line breaks are
, all inside one

. Visually a 6-item unordered list; no

    /
  • .
pages.mechanism:
A visually apparent unordered list is encoded as a single paragraph with literal bullet glyphs and
line breaks (F2). A screen reader hears one continuous paragraph — no 'list, 6 items' announcement, no list navigation, and the grouping/count conveyed by the visual bullets is lost.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss:
A

containing '•' glyphs and
is valid HTML and trips no linter; there is no axe/WAVE/Lighthouse rule or ACT rule that says 'this paragraph looks like a list, so it must be a

    .' Recognizing that stacked bulleted lines visually constitute a six-item list whose markup fails to express it requires human visual/semantic judgment.

citation.quote:
1. All content with the visual appearance of a list is defined programmatically as a list, by type:
   a. Unordered list (with/without bullets) → `ul`; b. Ordered list → `ol`; c. Terms+descriptions → `dl`.

pages.scenario: Emergency auto-injector ('AllerStop') instruction card with a banner stating steps must be followed IN ORDER. Six administration steps are visually numbered 1–6 but coded as an UNORDERED list (<ul> + 6 <li>); numerals exist only as typed text. Wrong type — should be <ol>.
pages.mechanism: An order-critical ordered procedure is exposed to AT as an unordered list: a screen reader announces 'list, 6 items' with bullet (unordered) semantics and no ordinal positions ('1 of 6'). The only ordinals are inline text glyphs carrying no positional meaning, so the fixed sequence the safety warning depends on is not programmatically conveyed.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A <ul> with <li> children is structurally valid and passes every list check (the only list-adjacent ACT rules concern listbox/option owned roles, absent here). No tool reads the 'follow in order' warning, judges that sequence matters, and concludes the type should be <ol>. Distinguishing ordered from unordered from content meaning is human semantic judgment.

citation.quote:
**Ordered** (`ol`) — numbered sequentially / hierarchically (1, 2, 2.a, 2.a.i) where sequence or
     reference-by-number matters.

Coffee roaster's field handbook 'Glossary of Cupping Terms': six term/definition pairs presented visually as a bold term line followed by an indented definition line, but coded as alternating

(bold) and

pages.mechanism: A visually apparent description list is encoded as twelve independent paragraphs. A screen reader reads them as unrelated paragraphs with no dl group: nothing signals that each term is paired with its definition, the user cannot navigate term-by-term, and the bold/indent presentation that conveys the pairing is CSS-only and never exposed to AT.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss:
A run of

elements with bold/indent styling is valid HTML and triggers no axe/WAVE/Lighthouse rule; no automated check pairs alternating paragraphs and infers a term/description list owed a

citation.quote: **Description list** (`dl`) — groups terms with their descriptions.

pages.scenario: Course-syllabus 'Outline of Topics' shows a clear two-level hierarchy: three bold top-level topics each with two or three indented sub-topics. Programmatically it is ONE flat <ul> with 11 sibling <li>; the visual nesting is faked with lvl1/lvl2 CSS classes (::before glyph + padding-left). No nested <ul>.
pages.mechanism: The list IS coded as a list but its nesting is flattened: a screen reader announces 'list, 11 items' at one depth and reports no parent/child grouping, so it never conveys that the sub-topics belong to their parent topic. The CSS padding/glyphs that create the visual hierarchy are invisible to AT, violating TT 10.D's requirement that programmatic nesting match the visual hierarchy.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A flat <ul> of <li> is structurally valid; axe/WAVE/Lighthouse have no rule asserting 'these indented items should be a nested sub-list.' Detecting it requires comparing the CSS-rendered indentation hierarchy against the programmatic nesting depth and judging that a grouping was lost — a visual-to-semantic comparison automated tools cannot perform.

citation.quote:
All programmatic list relationships (nesting, hierarchies) are consistent with the list relationships
   presented visually.

pages.scenario: SaaS onboarding card ('Loomly') with a design-system 'Stepper': five steps shown as circular numbered badges 1–5 under 'Finish these steps in order.' Coded as a container <div> with five sibling <div class='step'>; the numbers are drawn by CSS counter() in ::before. No <ol>/<li>, and the ordinals exist only as generated content.
pages.mechanism: A visually apparent ordered list is exposed to AT as generic divs: no 'list, 5 items', no list navigation, and the numbers 1–5 are CSS ::before counter content that is NOT part of the accessible text of those divs — so the user loses both the list structure and the ordinal sequence entirely.
pages.selectorNote: Ordered runbook with list semantics stripped via role=presentation; orig .stepper does not exist
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Divs styled with a CSS counter are valid markup with no role for a rule to attach to; axe/WAVE/Lighthouse have no check that numbered divs should be an <ol>. Worse, the ordinals are pseudo-element content, so even a visible-text scan would not find them in the DOM. Concluding the rendered numbered badges constitute an ordered list missing from the markup requires human visual judgment.

citation.quote: a. Unordered list (with/without bullets) → `ul`; b. Ordered list → `ol`; c. Terms+descriptions → `dl`.

pages.scenario: PASS boundary: a parks 'Trail Conditions' page that does it correctly — three trailheads mentioned as a comma-separated inline run inside a sentence (correctly NOT a list), a genuinely ordered 'Before you hike' procedure coded as <ol>, and a genuinely term/description marker glossary coded as <dl>/<dt>/<dd>.
pages.mechanism: Every visually apparent list is programmatically a list of the correct type: the <ol> exposes ordered/positional list semantics matching the visible numbered steps, the <dl> exposes a description-list group pairing each dt term with its dd, and the comma-separated trailheads are normal sentence prose with no visual list to mismatch — so no list markup is owed (TT 10.D note).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: This is the inverse trap: an over-eager heuristic might flag the comma-separated trailheads as a 'list that should be marked up,' a false positive, because tools cannot tell an in-sentence enumeration from a visually stacked list. A correct PASS requires the human judgment that the run is prose and that the two real lists are already the right type — neither decided by any axe/WAVE/Lighthouse rule.

citation.quote:
Not all lists require markup — a list of items in a sentence separated by commas need not be a
> bulleted/numbered list.

aspects.title: Tabular or multi-column information faked with whitespace, line breaks, or <pre> instead of real structure (F34, F48, F33)
aspects.plain: A table or columns are faked with spaces and line breaks instead of real markup, so it looks aligned but a screen reader reads across into scrambled gibberish.
aspects.description: Tabular or multi-column content is laid out using only spaces, tabs, line breaks, or a monospaced <pre> block, so it looks like a table or two parallel columns on screen but carries no row/column/header structure and linearizes into nonsense for AT ('Monday 2 fried eggs tomato soup garden salad'). The entire relationship lives in the visual alignment of characters. A human must recognize that the ASCII grid encodes a table (with implied row/column headers) or that text is split into parallel columns disrupting reading order; automated tools see a single text node and a syntactically valid <pre> with nothing to flag.
aspects.scLimb: Programmatic determinability of tabular and reading-order relationships conveyed only by character alignment / monospaced layout (F34, F48 tables; F33 columns).
aspects.whyUncovered: These failures involve NO structural element for any rule to attach to — no <table>, <th>, <ul>, or role, just text. The entire ACT 1.3.1 corpus is element/attribute-anchored (ARIA props, header refs, owned roles), so a page whose only 'table' is whitespace-aligned text or a <pre> block is invisible to every rule. Interpreting an ASCII grid as a relationship-bearing table, or detecting that padded spaces split text into columns, is pure human visual/semantic reasoning.

references.quote: using white space characters ... to format tables in text content is a failure to use structure properly. When tables are created in this manner there is no way to indicate that a cell is intended to be a header cell, no way to associate the table header cells with the table data cells
If the pre element is used to markup tabular information, the visually implied logical relationships between the table cells and the headers are lost
Using white space characters to create multiple columns does not provide the information in a natural reading order.

aspects.ttWhy: ANDI detects no table/list in pre/whitespace text, so no TT test isolates it.

pages.scenario:
K-12 school cafeteria 'This Week' page renders the weekly menu as a four-column day x meal grid (Breakfast/Lunch/Snack across Mon-Fri) built entirely from space characters inside a single

— no table, th, role, or list anywhere.
pages.mechanism: F34: white-space characters used to lay out a table; the weekday row-labels and meal column-headers are plain text in the same text run as the food items and never associate with cells. AT reads the paragraph as one node in source order ('Breakfast Lunch Snack Monday Cinnamon oatmeal Turkey & cheese wrap Apple slices...'), collapsing the runs of spaces so the day/meal->food relationship is destroyed and the grid linearizes into a run-on; reflow or a proportional font also collapses the visual grid.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss:
There is no table, th, scope, headers, role, or list element on the page, so every ACT 1.3.1 rule (all element/attribute-anchored) has nothing to attach to; axe/WAVE/Lighthouse see one syntactically valid

of text and report no violation. Deciding the spaces encode a day x meal table with implied headers requires reading the visual alignment and inferring the relationship — human visual-semantic judgment.

citation.quote: The objective of this technique is to describe how using white space characters, such as space, tab, line break, or carriage return, to format tables in text content is a failure to use structure properly. When tables are created in this manner there is no way to indicate that a cell is intended to be a header cell, no way to associate the table header cells with the table data cells, or to navigate directly to a particular cell in a table.

pages.scenario: University LMS course page 'Weekly Schedule' panel where a time x weekday class schedule (Lecture/Lab/Recitation/Office hours) is laid out with literal TAB characters inside a single <pre>, header row and time row-labels implied only by tab alignment; no table/th/role.
pages.mechanism: F48: <pre> used to mark up tabular information. The <pre> preserves only visual formatting; a screen reader exposes it as one text run and collapses each TAB to a single space, flattening the columns ('Monday Tuesday Wednesday Thursday Friday 9:00-9:50 Lecture - Lecture - Lecture...'). The user cannot tell that 'Lab A' is Wednesday at 10:00, cannot navigate by row/column, and the em-dash placeholders read as literal dashes detached from any day/time.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A <pre> containing text is valid HTML with no table semantics to inspect — no element, attribute, or role for any ACT 1.3.1 rule to evaluate — so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse pass it silently; none of them parse tab-aligned text to reconstruct an implied table. Judging that the tab columns encode a schedule with implied row/column headers is human visual-semantic reasoning.

citation.quote: This document describes a failure caused by use of the HTML pre element to markup tabular information. The pre element preserves only visual formatting. If the pre element is used to markup tabular information, the visually implied logical relationships between the table cells and the headers are lost if the user cannot see the screen or if the visual presentation changes significantly.

pages.scenario:
Nonprofit land-trust e-newsletter runs its lead article as a two-column newspaper layout where each line of one

concatenates a LEFT-column fragment, padding spaces, then a RIGHT-column fragment; no CSS multicolumn, no table, no list.
pages.mechanism: F33: white-space characters create multiple columns, breaking reading order. Sighted readers read down the left column then down the right, but the DOM source order is left-chunk then right-chunk per line, so AT reads across each line and splices the columns into shredded sentences ('Each spring the Hollow Creek plant native milkweed, remove Land Trust invites volunteers invasive garlic mustard, and...'). The intended prose is unrecoverable because no column structure exists.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss:
The page contains one valid

and no structural element, attribute, or role for an ACT 1.3.1 rule to attach to; axe/WAVE/Lighthouse see ordinary paragraph text and report nothing. Reconstructing that the padded spaces split the text into two columns whose correct order is column-major (not the line-major DOM order) requires a human to read the visual columns and notice the linearization is scrambled.

citation.quote: The objective of this technique is to describe how using white space characters, such as space, tab, line break, or carriage return, to format columns of data in text content is a failure to use structure properly. Assistive technologies will interpret content in the reading order of the current language. Using white space characters to create multiple columns does not provide the information in a natural reading order.

pages.scenario: Developer-docs 'Troubleshooting a stuck rollout' runbook where the diagnosis instructs operators to 'scan down the STATUS column' and 'cross-reference the same row's READY and RESTARTS' of pasted `kubectl get pods` output — a column-bearing data table — placed verbatim in a space-aligned <pre> with a header row; no table/th/role.
pages.mechanism: F48/F34: load-bearing tabular CLI output in <pre>. AT reads each line as one run, collapsing the alignment spaces, with the header row never associated to data lines, so '0/1' is not mapped to READY nor '8' to RESTARTS; the user hears 'checkout-7d9f8c6b4-pl4mn 0/1 CrashLoopBackOff 8 4m' as a flat string. The instruction 'scan down the STATUS column' is impossible and the cross-row READY comparison (a 2-D operation) is unavailable in a 1-D stream, so the promised diagnosis is unreachable.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Pasted CLI output in <pre> is the most common, entirely valid use of the element; no rule can distinguish a decorative terminal log from a table whose columns must be compared, and there is no table/role/attribute for any ACT 1.3.1 rule to evaluate, so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse report nothing. Determining that THIS <pre> carries load-bearing column relationships requires reading the surrounding instructions plus the aligned data — human semantic judgment.

citation.quote: Instead, the HTML table element is intended to present tabular data. Assistive technologies use the structure of an HTML table to present data to the user in a logical manner. This structure is not available when using the pre element.

pages.scenario: Official municipal (en-CA) 'Unofficial Results' page where a candidate x polling-subdivision results table with right-aligned vote counts uses vertically-stacked, one-letter-per-line angled column headers (the W3C F48 election style) entirely inside one <pre>; no table/th/scope/role.
pages.mechanism: F48/F34: tabular numeric data in <pre>. AT reads top-to-bottom line by line, so the stacked headers come out as isolated letters ('L A M B E R T') rather than 'LAMBERT' — the columns have no human-meaningful labels — and the data rows read as '0103 MILLPOND WARD 290 512 33', three bare numbers with no candidate attached and no per-cell association. Right-aligned-by-spaces numbers lose their column identity once alignment collapses, so 'how many votes did a candidate get in a ward?' is unanswerable.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The page is one valid <pre> of text with no table element, attribute, or role for any ACT 1.3.1 rule to attach to, so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse pass it silently. No tool reconstructs a candidate x subdivision results table — much less recognizes that the vertically-stacked single letters are column headers — from space-aligned characters; that interpretation is pure human visual-semantic reasoning.

citation.quote: Election results displayed using preformatted text

pages.scenario:
Boundary/negative control: a ramen-shop menu uses a

No tabular or multi-column relationship is conveyed by character alignment. The decorative ASCII logo is a

citation.quote: items that share a common characteristic are organized into a table where the relationship of cells sharing the same row or column and the relationship of each cell to its row and/or column header are necessary for understanding

aspects.title: Scripted elements that look like links/buttons but expose a generic role or none (F42)
aspects.plain: A clickable span or div is styled to look like a button but has no real link/button role, so a screen reader won't announce it as clickable.
aspects.description:
An element is styled and behaves like a link or button (cursor:pointer, underlined blue text or a button-shaped box, onclick navigation/activation) but is a bare ,
, or with a JavaScript handler and no , no
aspects.scLimb: Programmatic determinability of an interactive element's role/relationship when its semantics are conveyed only by visual styling and scripted behavior (F42).
aspects.whyUncovered: ACT 1.3.1 role rules (4e8ab6 required-properties, 674b10 valid-role-value) only fire when an explicit role IS present. A <span onclick> with no role attribute is simply outside their applicability, so the F42 failure never appears in the corpus. Judging that a styled <span>/<div> 'is presented as a link/button' from its appearance and behavior is exactly the human visual reasoning the static, attribute-driven corpus omits. (Note: this overlaps SC 4.1.2 but is an explicit F42 1.3.1 failure path.)

references.quote: Failure of Success Criteria 1.3.1, 2.1.1, 2.1.3, or 4.1.2 when emulating links
a screen reader user will hear that the item is a link when the glossary term is encountered

aspects.ttWhy: Wrong/missing control role is a 4.1.2 issue; no 1.3.1 TT test isolates it.

pages.scenario: News/editorial article index (The Ledger Review) whose pagination strip 'Prev 1 2 3 … 9 Next' is built from underlined-blue <span>s with onclick page-changes; '2' is the inert current page. Each control reads unmistakably as a pagination link but is a bare <span> with no <a>, no href, no role, and no tabindex.
pages.mechanism: Each pagination control is a styled <span> with an onclick navigation handler and no <a>/href/role/tabindex; verified in Chrome's accessibility tree as role 'StaticText' (not 'link') and non-focusable, so the link relationship conveyed by blue-underline + pointer cursor + page-changing behaviour is not programmatically determinable (F42 emulated-link path).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: There is no role attribute, so ACT 1.3.1 role rules (4e8ab6 required-properties, 674b10 valid-role-value) are never applicable (they fire only when a role IS present). axe/WAVE/Lighthouse see plain <span>s with a click handler, which matches no 'wrong role' rule. Judging that the strip is PRESENTED AS pagination links and that its exposed generic StaticText role contradicts that is a visual/behavioural call no attribute-anchored rule makes.

citation.quote: This failure occurs when JavaScript event handlers are attached to elements to emulate links. A link created in this manner cannot be tabbed to from the keyboard and does not gain keyboard focus like other controls and/or links. If scripting events are used to emulate links, user agents including assistive technology may not be able to identify the links in the content as links.

pages.scenario: E-commerce product detail page (Fernweh Roastery) whose primary 'Add to cart' CTA is a filled green rounded button-shaped <div> with cursor:pointer, hover/active states, and an onclick that increments the cart and shows a toast. A sibling 'Save to wishlist' is a real <button> styled as a quiet link (foil), so the defect is the specific <div> CTA, not a blanket absence of controls.
pages.mechanism: The primary CTA is <div class="addcart" onclick="addToCart()"> with no <button>/role=button/tabindex; verified as accessibility role 'StaticText' (not 'button') and non-focusable, so the button relationship conveyed by the filled pill + label + activation behaviour is not programmatically determinable and the control is unreachable by keyboard.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The <div> carries no role attribute, so role-validity/required-property rules never apply. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse see a <div> with text and a click handler; no static rule classifies a bare element-plus-listener as 'a button with a missing/wrong role'. Recognising the filled pill + label + hover/press + add-to-cart action as a button, and that its generic role contradicts that, is human visual/behavioural judgment.

citation.quote: Scripted event handling is added to a span element so that it functions as a link when clicked with a mouse. Assistive technology does not recognize this element as a link.

pages.scenario: Real-estate agent dashboard (Harbourline Realty) 'Active Listings' data table with a 'Click a row to open the listing' hint. Each <tr> highlights on hover, shows a pointer cursor, and navigates to the property detail page via location.href, presenting the whole row as one large link. The table markup itself (thead, th scope=col, caption) is correct; only the row-level navigation is role-less.
pages.mechanism: Navigation lives on <tr class="listing" onclick="openListing(...)"> with cursor:pointer and no <a>, no role, no tabindex, and no focusable child; verified that the row exposes only generic 'StaticText' cell content (no link/button role) and is non-focusable, so the link relationship conveyed by the full-row hover highlight/pointer/navigation is not programmatically determinable.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The data table is valid so data-table checks pass; the <tr> has no role so 1.3.1 role rules never apply; every cell has real text so there is no empty/missing-attribute defect. Tools cannot infer that a <tr> with cursor:pointer and an onclick IS PRESENTED AS a link to the listing — concluding 'the whole row is the control' and that its generic row role contradicts that is visual/behavioural reasoning.

citation.quote: For all elements presented as links which use JavaScript event handlers to make the element emulate a link: 1. Check if the programmatically determined role of the element is "link". ... If check #1 is false then this failure condition applies and the content fails Success Criteria 1.3.1 Info and Relationships and 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value.

pages.scenario: Travel flight-search widget (Skylark Air) whose submit control is an rendering a teal disc with a magnifying glass and the baked-in word 'Search'; it has cursor:pointer, a hover scale, and an onclick that runs the search. It is unmistakably the search button, but it is an image with onclick, no role, no tabindex, and an alt that describes the PICTURE rather than the action.
pages.mechanism: Submit control is with no role/tabindex; verified as accessibility role 'image' with the picture-describing name (not 'button') and non-focusable, so the button relationship conveyed by the rendered disc + 'Search' wording + submit behaviour is not programmatically determinable and the form has no keyboard-operable submit.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The has a present non-empty alt (1.1.1 missing-alt passes) and no role (1.3.1 role-validity rules never apply). Tools see a valid image with a click handler; no static rule says 'this image is really the submit button and is exposed as a graphic', nor judges whether the alt names the FUNCTION versus the PICTURE. Both judgments require human visual/behavioural reasoning.

citation.quote: Scripted event handling is added to an img element so that it functions as a link when clicked with a mouse. Assistive technology does not recognize this element as a link.

pages.scenario: SaaS analytics dashboard (Plumeline Analytics) funnel report with a tab strip 'Overview / Acquisition / Retention' drawn as underline tabs; the active tab is darker with a teal underline and switches the panel below. The controls ARE keyboard-focusable (tabindex=0, focus ring, Enter/Space handler) — the harder F42 sub-case — yet each is a role-less <div> and the wrapper is not a tablist.
pages.mechanism: Each tab is <div class="tab" tabindex="0" onclick onkeydown> with no role=tab/button and no enclosing role=tablist, and the selected state is colour/underline only; verified as accessibility role 'generic' while focusable=true, so the control relationship and the selected-state relationship are not programmatically determinable (a focusable thing exposing no role).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: There is no role attribute anywhere, so 1.3.1 role-validity rules never apply and 'tablist must contain tabs' never fires (nothing claims to be a tablist). The <div>s ARE focusable and ARE keyboard-operable, so no keyboard rule trips. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse see focusable <div>s with click/keydown handlers and text — recognising a selected/unselected tab strip whose exposed generic role (and colour-only selection) contradict it is human visual judgment.

citation.quote: This example uses script to make a div element behave like a link. Although the author has provided complete keyboard access and separated the event handlers from the markup to enable repurposing of the content, the div element will not be recognized as a link by assistive technology.

pages.scenario: BOUNDARY/PASS — Nonprofit donation page (Riverbank Trust) whose amount chooser ($25/$50/$100/Other) and 'Continue' action are built from the SAME styled <div> pill building blocks as the failing cases (rounded, filled-when-selected, pointer cursor), but each emulated control correctly EXPOSES the role it presents: role=radiogroup with role=radio children (aria-checked, roving tabindex, arrow-key nav) and role=button with tabindex+keydown.
