pages.mechanism: The amount pills are <div role="radio" aria-checked> inside <div role="radiogroup" aria-labelledby> and 'Continue' is <div role="button" tabindex="0">; verified as accessibility role 'radio' with name '$25' (and the strip as a radio group) and focusable=true, so the control and selection relationships conveyed by the styling ARE programmatically determinable — not an F42 failure, since F42 fails only when the exposed role is generic/absent/wrong.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A scanner can see role=radio/aria-checked/role=button are present and valid and would (correctly) raise nothing here — but it equally raises nothing on the failing cases 01-05 where the same <div>s carry NO role, so the tool cannot distinguish pass from fail. The discriminating judgment — whether the exposed role MATCHES the presented control — requires a human to compare the rendered pill/button to the exposed semantics.

citation.quote: It is possible to use the ARIA role attribute to identify an anonymous element as link control for assistive technologies. However, best practice for ARIA calls for making use of native elements whenever possible, so the use of the role attribute to identify anonymous elements as links is not recommended.

aspects.title: Form field/label and field-group relationships conveyed only by visual layout (programmatic association, grouping, required-cues)
aspects.plain: A form's labels, instructions, required-marks, and field groups are tied to inputs only by visual placement, so a screen reader can't tell which text governs which field.
aspects.description: A form's field-to-label, field-to-instruction, and field-to-group relationships are conveyed only by visual placement and styling, not programmatically. Examples: a label sits visually next to/above an input but is not associated (no <label for>, no aria-labelledby, no wrapping), so AT cannot tell which text describes the field; a set of radio buttons or checkboxes answers a question shown as a visual heading above them with no <fieldset>/<legend> or role=radiogroup, so the group's question is lost; required-field status or a 'pick one' cue is shown only by red text or a visually adjacent note not programmatically tied to the field. Trusted Tester 5.C asks whether the combination of accessible name, description, and OTHER programmatic associations describes each field including instructions and cues, and notes radio/checkbox groups must be associated with their question — a contextual reading-and-layout judgment.
aspects.scLimb: Programmatic determinability of form relationships: which label/instruction/cue governs which field, and which fields form a group sharing a common question (TT 5.C; ARIA17/fieldset grouping; required-cue association).
aspects.whyUncovered: The ACT form rule in scope (e086e5) only checks that a form field has a NON-EMPTY accessible name — a binary presence test a static checker already does. It does not evaluate whether the RIGHT visible label/instruction is the one associated, whether a multi-field group (radios/checkboxes answering one question) is programmatically grouped, or whether a visually-conveyed required/'choose one' cue is tied to the field. Deciding which adjacent text functions as the label, and that several controls share a visually-shown group question, is contextual human judgment outside the corpus.

references.quote: The combination of the accessible name, accessible description, and other programmatic associations (e.g., table column and/or row associations) describes each input field and includes all relevant instructions and cues (textual and graphical).
At minimum, radio buttons and checkboxes should be programmatically associated with their question and response.
Any label associated with the group also serves as a common label or qualifier for individual controls in the group.

aspects.ttWhy: Programmatic label/group/cue association of form fields is exactly the 5.C condition.

pages.scenario: E-commerce/booking 'Reserve a tasting' form whose four text inputs are correctly associated via <label for>/id, but a 2-column CSS grid repaints the input cells swapped within each row so each visible caption sits above a different field than its programmatic label (e.g. 'Preferred date' label over the #guests input). The label-to-field relationship is only correct programmatically, contradicting the visual layout.
pages.mechanism: Every input is correctly labelled: each <label> has a real for= pointing at a real input id with a descriptive name ('Number of guests'->#guests, 'Preferred date'->#visit-date, 'Mobile number'->#mobile, 'Party name'->#party-name), so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse pass. The defect is a visual/programmatic mismatch: the labels and inputs are separate CSS-grid items whose grid-row/grid-column placement paints each label directly above an input it is NOT wired to (the inputs are swapped within each row). A sighted user types into the box captioned 'Preferred date' but its programmatic label is 'Number of guests'; a screen-reader user, following the for/id graph, gets the opposite pairing. The visible label-to-field relationship contradicts the programmatic one.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe e086e5 ('Form field has non-empty accessible name') is a binary presence test and passes because every input has a title-based name. No static rule judges whether the name is the RIGHT descriptive label or that the adjacent unassociated <span> 'Street address' is the text that should govern the field — that requires reading the rendered layout and comparing the meaning of visible text to the computed name, contextual human judgment.

citation.quote: The combination of the accessible name, accessible description, and other programmatic associations (e.g., table column and/or row associations) describes each input field and includes all relevant instructions and cues (textual and graphical).

pages.scenario: Post-purchase coffee survey: the question 'How did you hear about us?' is a bold styled <div class=q> over four radios (Search engine, A friend, Instagram or TikTok, Podcast ad) sharing name='hear' but NOT wrapped in <fieldset>/<legend> or role=radiogroup. A second question on the same form IS correctly wrapped in a fieldset/legend, making Q1's omission a deliberate isolatable contrast.
pages.mechanism: Each radio has a valid accessible name from its own <label for>, so e086e5 passes on all four. But entering the group AT announces 'Search engine, radio button, 1 of 4' and never speaks the question — the styled <div> is unassociated. The option labels ('A friend') are meaningless without the question. TT 5.C requires radios to be programmatically associated with their question; that association is absent for the first group only.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: e086e5 only checks each field has a non-empty accessible name, which every radio satisfies via <label for>. No automated rule requires a set of same-named radios to carry a group label, and none can recognize that the bold <div> above them IS the question they answer. Whether several controls form a group sharing a visually-shown question is a contextual reading-and-grouping judgment.

citation.quote: At minimum, radio buttons and checkboxes should be programmatically associated with their question and response.

pages.scenario: Auto-insurance quote 'Driver details': a one-time styled note says 'Fields shown in red are required'. Required fields (first name, last name, date of birth, license number) have red <label> text via a .required CSS class; optional fields are black. There is no asterisk, no '(required)' token, no required attribute, and no aria-required anywhere — required status is carried only by color plus an unassociated prose sentence.
pages.mechanism:
Every input is correctly labelled (e086e5 passes). The required cue is conveyed only by red label color and a free-floating

note with no aria-describedby tie. AT announces 'Legal first name, edit text' with no indication it is required; users who cannot perceive red cannot distinguish required from optional. TT 5.C requires cues 'including when fields are required' to be in the combination of name+description+associations.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: No automated rule asserts that a field a page visually marks required must expose aria-required/required — a scanner cannot know which fields the author intends as mandatory because that intent lives in a color and a prose note. e086e5 passes (all named). The color overlap is conceptually 1.4.1, which Understanding 1.3.1 explicitly carves out, so even a use-of-color heuristic would not surface the missing programmatic required association. Mapping 'red label' to 'required' and judging the programmatic gap is human reasoning.

citation.quote: ANDI Output includes all relevant instructions and cues for the form element, including when fields are required

pages.scenario:
Municipal building-permit 'Scope' section: two stacked yes/no questions — 'Will the work change the building's footprint?' (name=footprint) and 'Is the property in a flood-hazard zone?' (name=flood). Each question is a styled

; each radio pair is labelled Yes/No via
pages.mechanism: All four radios have valid Yes/No accessible names (e086e5 passes). A screen-reader user navigating by form control lands on 'Yes, radio button, 1 of 2' with no programmatic context about which question it answers; both groups announce the same Yes/No and the questions are unassociated paragraphs. Identical option labels across two ungrouped sets create ambiguous group membership — the disambiguator (the stacked prose question) never reaches the accessibility tree.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss:
e086e5 confirms each radio is named and stops. No rule asserts that two adjacent radio groups with identical option labels must each carry a distinguishing group label, and a scanner cannot read the two

questions and reason that the second 'Yes' belongs to the flood question. Detecting ambiguous group membership requires understanding that the option labels collide and that the only disambiguator is visually-stacked prose — pure contextual/visual judgment.

citation.quote: At minimum, radio buttons and checkboxes should be programmatically associated with their question and response.

pages.scenario: Arabic (lang=ar, dir=rtl) Health-Ministry new-patient form: a split date-of-birth control with three inputs for اليوم/الشهر/السنة (Day/Month/Year) under a single styled <div> heading تاريخ الميلاد (Date of birth). Each input is named via title='يوم'/'شهر'/'سنة', so no input is unnamed, but there is no <fieldset>/<legend> or role=group+aria-labelledby tying the three inputs to the one question they jointly answer; RTL adds a visual-vs-source ordering wrinkle.
pages.mechanism: Each date input has a non-empty accessible name from title (e086e5 passes). AT encounters three independent fields ('Year, edit text', 'Month...', 'Day...') with no announcement that they compose a single Date of birth value; the unifying question is an unassociated <div> never spoken on entry. The sub-names are ambiguous out of context ('Year' of what?). TT 5.C requires the controls be programmatically associated with their shared question.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe e086e5 sees three named inputs and reports nothing. No static rule recognizes that three adjacent inputs jointly answer a single question shown above them, nor that the styled <div> should be the group's programmatic label via fieldset/legend or role=group+aria-labelledby. Deciding that Day/Month/Year compose the one Date-of-birth question — and that the group label never reaches the accessibility tree, across an RTL layout — requires reading the layout and reasoning about group membership.

citation.quote: Social security number fields which are nine digits long and broken up into three segments can be grouped using role="group".

pages.scenario: Nonprofit donation form built as the deliberate PASS counterpart: it contains the same relationship-bearing structures cases 01-05 get wrong (a radio group with a question, a required cue, a second radio group, a multi-part field) but conveys each programmatically — <fieldset>/<legend> for 'Gift frequency', role=radiogroup+aria-labelledby for 'Designate your gift', aria-required + in-label '(required)' token + aria-describedby for the required note, and role=group+aria-labelledby tying the three phone sub-inputs to 'Daytime phone'.
pages.mechanism: Entering the first radio group, AT announces the legend 'Gift frequency (required)' as the group name; the second group announces 'Designate your gift' via role=radiogroup+aria-labelledby; the required email field announces 'required' via aria-required plus the in-label text token, with its description via aria-describedby; the phone group announces 'Daytime phone (optional), group' with each sub-input tied via aria-describedby. TT 5.C is satisfied: name+description+group associations fully describe each field including the required cue and each group's question.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Automated tools also return 'pass' here, but that agreement is not guaranteed by markup alone: a scanner cannot confirm the aria-labelledby target text actually IS the visible question, that the legend matches the group's purpose, or that the required cue is in text rather than color. A human applying TT 5.C must read the rendered layout and confirm the programmatic associations match the visual relationships; this is the true-positive PASS boundary that sharpens where the SC line sits.

citation.quote: However, when an asterisk or other text symbol is associated with the field, using the aria-required property in addition to the visual presentation enables user agents to pass on this important information to the user

aspects.title: Emphasis or special-status meaning conveyed only by visual text variation, with no markup or text equivalent (G117, H49)
aspects.plain: Special status is shown only by bold, strike-through, or font change with no markup or words, so 'on sale' or 'deleted' is invisible to a screen-reader user.
aspects.description: Information is carried solely by a variation in text presentation — bold/italic/underline, a different font face or color, strike-through, larger size — with neither semantic markup (<strong>/<em>/<ins>/<del>) nor an equivalent stated in text. Examples: 'new' or 'on sale' items shown only by bold/red with no '(new)' word; deletions/insertions shown by strike-through/underline with no change list; a glossary term distinguished only by a different font; a warning shown only in red. WCAG explicitly excludes pure color (1.4.1), but bolding/italics/font/strike that convey status, emphasis, or special meaning fall under 1.3.1 (G117/H49): the relationship 'this text has special status' must be exposed via markup OR available in text. Judging which formatting carries meaning (vs decoration) and whether that meaning is otherwise available requires reading the content.
aspects.scLimb: Programmatic determinability OR text-availability of information conveyed by variations in text presentation (emphasis, special status), excluding color which is 1.4.1 (G117, H49).
aspects.whyUncovered: No ACT 1.3.1 rule addresses emphasis or special-status text conveyed by presentation; the corpus is entirely about ARIA properties, roles, owned/context roles, table headers, and accessible-name presence. A page where 'sale' items are bold-only, or insertions are underlined with no markup/text equivalent, has nothing for any rule to evaluate. Deciding that a font/weight/strike variation CARRIES information (not mere decoration) and that the information is not otherwise stated in text is a human content-meaning judgment. (Pure-color cases are deliberately excluded as 1.4.1.)

references.quote: When the visual appearance of text is varied to convey information, state the information explicitly in the text. Variations in the visual appearance can be made by changes in font face, font size, underline, strike through and various other text attributes.
words that have special status are indicated by changing the font family and /or bolding, italicizing, or underlining them
It is not required that color values be programmatically determined. ... Success Criterion 1.4.1 Use of Color addresses the specific case of color, rather than Success Criterion 1.3.1

aspects.ttWhy: Emphasis/status by styling (G117/H49) has no isolating TT test in this SC.

pages.scenario: E-commerce yarn storefront (Shopify Dawn-style grid): three of five products are on sale, signalled ONLY by the product name rendering in bold + one size larger. No '(Sale)' word, no struck original price, no markup, no colour.
pages.mechanism: 'On sale' special status is carried solely by font-weight:700 + larger font-size on the product name; font weight/size are not part of the accessible name or any announced property, so a screen-reader/braille user hears all five names identically and cannot tell which are discounted (F2; G117 not applied).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The DOM is flawless (real list, headings, prices, alt text). font-weight:700 and larger font-size are ubiquitous legitimate styles no checker flags; axe/WAVE/Lighthouse have no rule that reads the copy, notices three of five names are emphasised, and infers the emphasis encodes sale status stated nowhere else. Distinguishing meaningful emphasis from decorative emphasis is human content reading.

citation.quote: When the visual appearance of text is varied to convey information, state the information explicitly in the text. Variations in the visual appearance can be made by changes in font face, font size, underline, strike through and various other text attributes.

pages.scenario: Municipal by-law amendment shown as a tracked-changes redline: insertions underlined and deletions struck through using plain CSS-styled <span> elements (text-decoration), with no <ins>/<del>, no change-history list, no inline '(added)/(removed)' text, no colour.
pages.mechanism: Insertion/deletion status is conveyed only by CSS text-decoration: underline/line-through on <span>, which screen readers do not announce (unlike real <del>/<ins>); repealed clause 6.3 and the struck old times read as live policy text, actively misleading the user, and the change relationship is restated in no change-history text (F2; G117's 'change history' example not applied).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: text-decoration:line-through/underline on a <span> is valid CSS with no lint error; checkers do not require struck text to be <del> or underlined text to be <ins>. No automated rule can read the clauses, recognise the strike means 'repealed' and the underline means 'newly enacted', and confirm it is restated nowhere in text — a legal-content reading.

citation.quote: An online document has gone through multiple drafts. Insertions are underlined and deletions are struck through. At the end of the draft a "change history" lists all changes made to each draft.

pages.scenario: B2B Master Services Agreement where 'defined terms' (Service, Term, Confidential Information) are distinguished from ordinary words ONLY by small-caps styling (font-variant-caps: small-caps), with no <dfn>, no link to the definition, no legend stating 'small-caps = defined term', no colour.
pages.mechanism: font-variant-caps:small-caps changes only glyph rendering; the accessible text is identical, so screen readers announce 'service'/'term'/'confidential information' the same whether the occurrence is the load-bearing defined term or the ordinary word — a distinction that materially changes contract scope — and nothing marks the cross-reference to Section 1 (F2; G117 'different font + separate list' not applied).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: font-variant-caps:small-caps and text-transform are valid common CSS no checker flags; the DOM is a clean definition list. Catching this requires knowing the legal convention that small-caps denotes a defined term, reading the contract to see the defined-vs-ordinary distinction is meaningful, and confirming no legend restates it — three layers of human/domain judgment.

citation.quote: When a sentence in the original document contains a word or phrase that must be used in the summary, the word or phrase is shown in a different font than the rest of the sentence. A separate section also lists all the words and phrases that must be used in the summary.

pages.scenario: University LMS course schedule with a structurally exemplary data table (caption, scoped headers, associated cells), where two CANCELLED sessions are signalled ONLY by italic + strike-through cell styling — no 'Cancelled' word, no status column, no <del>/<s>/ARIA, no colour.
pages.mechanism: The 'cancelled' status is carried solely by font-style:italic + text-decoration:line-through on <td>/<th>, which are not announced; a screen-reader/braille user hears the cancelled lab/lecture as a scheduled class and may attend a session that is not running, while the make-up row reads as ordinary. Table semantics are perfect, so this is purely the text-presentation limb of 1.3.1 (F2; G117 not applied).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The table passes every automated table rule (caption, scoped headers, cell association) — a checker reports it accessible, masking the defect — and italic+line-through on a cell are valid CSS no tool flags. No rule reads the schedule, recognises the strike encodes 'cancelled', and verifies no cell restates it.

citation.quote: Variations in the visual appearance can be made by changes in font face, font size, underline, strike through and various other text attributes. When these types of variations convey information, that information needs to be available elsewhere in the content via text.

pages.scenario: Scholarly journal article-listing page where each paper's CORRESPONDING AUTHOR is designated ONLY by their name being bold (font-weight:700 on a <span>), with no '(corresponding author)' text, no asterisk-and-legend, no email/link tied to the name; the intro additionally uses bold decoratively, making the marker ambiguous.
pages.mechanism: The 'corresponding author' relationship is carried solely by font-weight; screen readers announce every author name identically, so the user cannot tell whom to contact for data/materials even though the intro tells them to 'contact the relevant author'. A second decorative bold use makes the convention undiscoverable from the page (F2; G117 not applied).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: font-weight:700 on a <span> appears on nearly every page as decorative emphasis; flagging all bold would be absurd, so no checker flags it. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse cannot know that in this listing bold encodes 'corresponding author', cannot detect the meaning is stated nowhere, and cannot notice the decoy bold makes the marker ambiguous — layered human/domain judgment.

citation.quote: words that have special status are indicated by changing the font family and /or bolding, italicizing, or underlining them

pages.scenario: BOUNDARY/PASS variant: a product maintenance guide where the one safety-critical step (shut off water before opening housing) is visually emphasised bold+larger — the same risky pattern — BUT uses <strong> markup (H49) AND begins with the literal word 'Important:' in text (G117), so the special status is both programmatically determinable and available in text.
pages.mechanism: The status is conveyed by the word 'Important:' (text equivalent per G117) AND by the <strong> element (programmatically-determinable strong importance per H49), so a screen-reader/braille user gets the warning regardless of styling; the larger font-size is now redundant decoration. Presentation PLUS a text/markup equivalent — 1.3.1 met.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A checker would treat this page and a failing bold-only page nearly identically: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse largely ignore presentation, do not score the presence of the word 'Important:', and never require <strong>, so its absence is never flagged. The pass/fail verdict turns on reading whether the emphasised meaning is ALSO carried by markup or text — exactly the human judgment this aspect isolates.

citation.quote: WCAG 2.2 is new, so is indicated in bold face. To avoid conveying information solely by presentation, the word "(new)" is included after it as well.

aspects.title: CSS visual-vs-DOM reorder: judging whether the source-order read still preserves meaning (F1 FAIL vs Example-2 PASS)
aspects.plain: CSS positions content in a different order than the HTML source, so a screen reader (which follows source order) reads it in a nonsensical sequence.
aspects.description: A page uses CSS (absolute/relative positioning, flexbox order, flex-direction:row-reverse, grid-area/grid-template-areas) so the visual order differs from DOM source order. A tool can mechanically detect 'visual order != DOM order', but that mismatch is ONLY a 1.3.2 failure when reading the content in source order changes the MEANING. The SC pairs the explicit non-failure (Example 2: nav / main / side-story CSS-reordered, meaning unaffected = PASS) directly against the failure (F1 Products/Locations two-column example, where source order reads 'Products Locations Telephones Computers Portable MP3 Players Wisconsin Idaho' and Wisconsin/Idaho bind to the wrong column = FAIL). Note the F1 trap: source order has item5 (Wisconsin) BEFORE item4 (Idaho), so values are swapped even within one logical column — purely semantic, invisible to a DOM-diff tool. The evaluator must linearize the content, read it as prose, and decide whether it still parses as the intended meaning. This is the central, most-tested discrimination of the SC.
aspects.scLimb: Core requirement: 'When the sequence in which content is presented affects its meaning, a correct reading sequence can be programmatically determined' — applied to CSS-positioned content (F1, C27, G57).
aspects.whyUncovered: The SC 1.3.2 inventory reports actRuleCount:0, testCaseCount:0 — there is literally zero ACT coverage of any facet of this SC. Even a hypothetical tool that flagged every visual!=DOM mismatch would fire on the Example-2 PASS case (nav reorder, meaning unaffected) as a false positive, and could not read the linearized text to confirm the F1 FAIL case actually scrambles meaning. Distinguishing FAIL from PASS is a semantic reading task, not a markup or DOM-diff check, so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse cannot reliably do it.

references.quote: The order of content in a sequence is not always meaningful. For example, the relative order of the main section of a web page and a navigation section does not affect their meaning. They could occur in either order in the programmatically determined reading sequence.
Providing a particular linear order is only required where it affects meaning.

it is important
                        not to rely on CSS to visually position content in a specific sequence if this sequence results in a meaning that is different from the programmatically determined reading order.

"Idaho" and "Wisconsin" are listed under Locations (note the different order for
                                Idaho and Wisconsin in the source code order)
Determine whether the reading order of content is still understandable after linearization.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: SaaS two-plan pricing comparison built from position:absolute chips. Plans authored low-to-high (Starter, Growth); the two price chips emitted in REVERSE source order ($79 first, then $19). CSS coordinates land each price in the correct visual column, but linearized the page reads 'Starter ... Growth ... $79 ... $19', binding the expensive price to the cheaper plan and swapping the prices relative to source.
pages.mechanism: position:absolute on every .plan and .price; the .price chips' DOM order is the reverse of the .plan cards' DOM order (F1 archetype), so the programmatically-determined reading sequence binds each price to the wrong plan.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: All elements have visible text; nothing is empty, unlabeled, or low-contrast, so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse find nothing. No checker models which price belongs to which plan, so it cannot detect the reversed price column; even a hypothetical visual!=DOM diff tool could see the mismatch but could not read the linearized stream and judge that the prices bind to the wrong plans.

citation.quote: This describes the failure condition that results when CSS, rather than structural markup, is used to modify the visual layout of the content, and the modified layout changes the meaning of the content.

pages.scenario: Recipe blog 'Brown-Butter Madeleines' with a four-step Method as a real <ol>. flex-direction:row-reverse + flex-wrap:wrap-reverse renders the cards 1,2,3,4 top-to-bottom while the <ol> source order is 4,3,2,1. Because an ordered list is an inherently meaningful sequence, a screen reader announces 'item 1 of 4' on the BAKE step, linearizing the recipe into a dangerous order (bake the batter before mixing it).
pages.mechanism: display:flex with flex-direction:row-reverse and flex-wrap:wrap-reverse on ol.steps inverts the rendered order vs source; the <ol> (a WCAG-defined meaningful sequence) is read 4-3-2-1 by AT, the reverse of the correct cooking order. Hand-typed .n badges mask the reversal visually.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The <ol> is valid, every <li> has text, no empty nodes or contrast issues. Tools do not compute that flex-direction:row-reverse inverted the visual order vs source, and even detecting the geometric mismatch would not tell a tool that THESE steps must be performed in order (a recipe) rather than an unordered set. Judging the reversed sequence is dangerous is human comprehension.

citation.quote: The semantics of some elements define whether or not their content is a meaningful sequence. For instance, in HTML, text is always a meaningful sequence. Tables and ordered lists are meaningful sequences, but unordered lists are not.

pages.scenario: News article 'The tidal marsh is coming back' with TWO deliberate CSS reorders: a position:fixed <nav> that is LAST in source order, and a decorative <blockquote> pull-quote placed FIRST in the DOM but grid-rendered in the side rail. A mechanical visual!=DOM detector fires on both, but neither changes meaning (Example-2 PASS / over-flag trap): the nav, article, and pull-quote are independent blocks and the article is self-contained.
pages.mechanism: position:fixed nav (DOM-last) + CSS-grid-placed blockquote (DOM-first) create visual!=DOM mismatches on independent blocks. Linearized order pull-quote -> article -> nav still conveys correct meaning because no block depends on another's position; this is the SC's own Example 2 non-failure.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: This is the inverse trap: a naive visual-vs-DOM diff tool raises a FALSE POSITIVE because it detects the mismatch but cannot read the linearized prose to confirm meaning survives. Distinguishing this harmless reorder from a genuine F1 failure requires reading the content and judging block independence, a semantic decision automated tools cannot make.

citation.quote: Example 2: CSS is used to position a navigation bar, the main story on a page, and a side story. The visual presentation of the sections does not match the programmatically determined order, but the meaning of the page does not depend on the order of the sections.

pages.scenario: Football full-time scoreboard rendered as 'Hillside Harriers 3 / Riverton Wanderers 1' via CSS grid-template-areas. The four grid items are authored grouped by type, not by team: both team names first, then both scores (DOM 'Harriers, Wanderers, 3, 1'). grid-area re-pairs each score with its team visually, but linearized the scores detach from their teams.
pages.mechanism: display:grid + grid-template-areas + grid-area placement re-pair items visually while the DOM groups team,team,score,score. The accessibility tree follows source order with no programmatic team-to-score association, so AT speaks 'Harriers, Wanderers, 3, 1' and the result is unrecoverable.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Each cell has valid text; no empty nodes, missing names, or contrast failures. Tools do not reconstruct the visual grid pairing from grid-area rules to compare against source order, and detecting the geometric mismatch would not tell a tool that '3' must be read right after 'Hillside Harriers' to convey the score. Binding a number to the adjacent team is content comprehension.

citation.quote: Assistive technologies rely on the source code or other programmatically determined order to render the content in the correct sequence. Thus, it is important not to rely on CSS to visually position content in a specific sequence if this sequence results in a meaning that is different from the programmatically determined reading order.

pages.scenario: Airline booking confirmation itinerary. Each leg visually shows Depart -> Arrive (Outbound 07:15 BUE -> 10:05 SCL; Return 19:40 SCL -> 22:30 BUE) via grid-template-areas. After a two-pass i18n refactor the markup authors ALL departures first, then ALL arrivals, so DOM order is Outbound, Return, 07:15-dep, 19:40-dep, 10:05-arr, 22:30-arr. Linearized, the two departures are read back-to-back then the two arrivals, scrambling which time belongs to which leg.
pages.mechanism: display:grid + grid-template-areas pairs each leg's depart/arrive visually while the DOM is field-grouped (all departures then all arrivals). AT reads the field-grouped source order, detaching each flight's departure from its arrival and binding the return departure (19:40) to the outbound arrival (10:05).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: All times and labels are real text; no empty cells, missing names, or contrast problems. A tool cannot know a flight leg's depart and arrive must be read adjacently, nor reconstruct the grid pairing from grid-area to notice the source groups by field. Judging that the linearized stream scrambles the legs requires reading it as an itinerary.

citation.quote: The order in which items appear on a screen may be different than the order they are found in the source document. Assistive technologies rely on the source code or other programmatically determined order to render the content in the correct sequence.

pages.scenario: Museum exhibition page 'Currents'. On wide screens flexbox order renders the Visit info box (hours/admission/location) in the LEFT rail and the essay on the right, while the DOM is content-first (essay first, Visit aside second). A visual!=DOM detector fires (the DOM-second aside renders left of the DOM-first essay), but it is the G57/Example-2 non-failure: the blocks are independent and each is internally well-ordered. Over-flag trap.
pages.mechanism: display:flex with order:2 on article.essay and order:1 on aside.visit swaps their visual position relative to a content-first DOM. The essay and the Visit box are independent meaningful sequences, and within each block source order is correct (hours in day order; paragraphs intro->detail->closing), so linearizing preserves meaning.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A naive visual-vs-DOM diff tool raises a FALSE POSITIVE: it detects flex order swapped the aside and essay but cannot read the linearized prose to confirm meaning survives. Telling this harmless reorder apart from a genuine F1 failure requires reading the content and judging block independence and internal order, which no automated tool can do.

citation.quote: The links in the navigation bar form a meaningful sequence. The heading, image, and text of the description also form a meaningful sequence. CSS is used to position the elements on the page.

aspects.title: Layout-table linearization that scrambles a meaningful sequence (F49) — reading 2-D content as a linear story
aspects.plain: A layout table looks right as a grid, but read cell-by-cell it interleaves and shreds the text, so a screen-reader user hears a scrambled, meaningless sequence.
aspects.description: An HTML <table> used purely for layout (WCAG explicitly permits layout tables) presents content that reads correctly in two visual dimensions, but when linearized row-by-row, cell-by-cell, the meaningful sequence breaks. F49's two canonical cases: (1) the advertisement where a rowspan stitches 'XYZ mountaineering top!' into one line and separates it from 'XYZ gets you to the', destroying the slogan 'XYZ gets you to the top!'; (2) the museum page where left-column nav links are interleaved with the right-column image/placard/heading/description, so the description is shredded by Link 2, Link 3, Link 4... The evaluator must mentally linearize the cell reading order (first cell of first row to last cell of last row, reading nested cells fully) and judge whether the resulting prose still tells the same story — a semantic reading task over a 2-D structure.
aspects.scLimb: Layout-table-linearization failure mode (F49) + G57 'placement of blocks of content using layout tables may produce a rendering in which related information is positioned together visually, but separated in the content stream.'
aspects.whyUncovered: Zero ACT coverage for 1.3.2; F49 is a failure technique only. Critically, axe/WAVE/Lighthouse do NOT flag layout tables as 1.3.2 failures — a layout table is valid HTML and WCAG permits it — so there is no automated signal. The failure lies entirely in whether the linearized cell order preserves meaning, which requires reading the cells in linearization order and reasoning about the story, something no automated checker does.

references.quote:
This failure occurs when a meaningful sequence of content conveyed through
                        presentation is lost because HTML tables used to control the visual
                        placement of the content do not “linearize" correctly.

Because the navigation bar links are interleaved with the content
                                describing the image, screen readers cannot present the content in a
                                meaningful sequence corresponding to the sequence presented
                                visually.
Since layout tables are read row by row, if the caption of an illustration is placed in the row following the illustration, it may be impossible to associate the caption with the image.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: Mountaineering-retailer promo banner built as a layout table: a wordmark cell and a giant italic 'top!' in a rowspan=2 bottom-aligned cell visually finish the slogan in the row below ('Summit Provisions gets you to the top!'), but the rowspan places 'top!' before the clause in source order. This is F49's canonical advertisement case.
pages.mechanism: A rowspan=2 cell reorders the content stream so the punch word 'top!' is read before the clause it completes; linearized DOM order (verified via Puppeteer) is 'Summit Provisions Mountaineering Outfitters | top! | Summit Provisions gets you to the', splitting the slogan that is a meaningful sequence.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A layout table is valid HTML and WCAG permits it; role=presentation is the correct marking, every cell has text, contrast passes, no attribute is missing. No checker reads the linearized cell stream and judges that '...top! ...gets you to the' has stopped making sense — that is a human semantic reading task over a 2-D structure.

citation.quote: The reading order from this example would be: XYZ mountaineering top! / XYZ gets you to the

pages.scenario: A gallery exhibition page (Thornbury Gallery) where a layout table puts a left-hand nav column, a tall rowspanned artwork image, then a placard + 'About this work' heading + five-paragraph description. Visually the description is one coherent column of prose, but the rowspanned image and per-row nav cells interleave nav links between the description paragraphs when linearized. This is F49's museum case 2.
pages.mechanism: The artwork cell is rowspan=8 while nav links sit one-per-row in the leftmost column, so linearized DOM order (verified) interleaves description paragraphs with 'Membership', 'Plan Your Visit', 'Shop the Catalogue', 'Accessibility' links — the single meaningful sequence describing the painting is shredded by intervening links.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every link has text and an href, the image has a text alternative, the heading is a real h2, role=presentation correctly marks the layout table; nothing is missing or malformed so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse report nothing. Recognizing the description is one block the linearized cell order severs with nav links is a semantic reading judgment outside any checker.

citation.quote: Because the navigation bar links are interleaved with the content describing the image, screen readers cannot present the content in a meaningful sequence corresponding to the sequence presented visually.

pages.scenario: A cafe loyalty coupon (Bean & Leaf) laid out as two side-by-side 'stamps' in a 2x2 layout table with a dashed divider. A divider + stacked typography cue the eye to read DOWN each column (left stamp: 'Buy one'/'get one free'; right stamp: '$10 espresso flight'/'with code SAVE25'), but the table is encoded row-major so linearization scrambles the offer.
pages.mechanism: Visual/intended reading is column-major but the four content cells are in row-major DOM order, so linearized order (verified) is 'Buy one | $10 espresso flight | get one free | with code SAVE25' — the BOGO promise 'Buy one ... get one free' is split with the price line wedged between its two halves.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The 2x2 grid is valid HTML, role=presentation is correct, all four cells have visible text, nothing is empty. Automated tools do not reconstruct the intended visual reading order (here column-major, cued by a divider and stacked layout) nor judge that the row-major linearized stream has ceased to be a coherent offer — a human visual + semantic comparison.

citation.quote: Tables present content in two visual dimensions, horizontal and vertical. However, screen readers present this two-dimensional content in linear order of the content in the source, beginning with the first cell in the first row and ending with the last cell in the last row.

pages.scenario: A bilingual parallel-text page presenting Antonio Machado's 'Caminante, son tus huellas' with the Spanish poem in the left column and a facing English translation in the right column, in a layout table. Each column is a self-contained four-line poem; row-major linearization interleaves the two languages line by line and each cell carries a lang switch. Long-tail i18n variant of F49.
pages.mechanism: The two columns are each a complete poem (a meaningful sequence) meant to be read whole, but row-major DOM order (verified) interleaves them: 'Caminante, son tus huellas | Wanderer, your footprints are | el camino y nada más; | the road and nothing more; ...'. Both poems are shattered as sequences, and per-cell lang=es flips the synthesizer voice on every line.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: This page scores WELL on naive checks: every Spanish cell has correct lang=es, every cell has text, role=presentation is set, and there is no header/data relationship to fault. No tool has a concept that the two columns are each a self-contained poem that row-major linearization splices together — that is a human literary/reading judgment.

citation.quote: if a page contains two independent articles, the relative order of the articles may not affect their meaning, as long as they are not interleaved.

pages.scenario: A food newsletter (The Saturday Kitchen) built as a bulletproof nested-table HTML email. A dish photo sits in the left column with heading/intro/CTA on the right; the photo's caption was placed in a second outer-table row to baseline-align with the body text, so linearization reads photo -> whole recipe blurb -> caption, divorcing the caption from its image.
pages.mechanism: Because layout tables linearize row-by-row and nested tables are read in full first (F49), the verified DOM order is photo aria-label -> 'Red-wine short ribs / intro / Get the full recipe' -> 'Pictured: short ribs after three hours, glaze reduced by half.' The caption arrives after the entire blurb with no figure/figcaption/aria-describedby tie, so the image->caption sequence is broken (G57's caption-in-following-row warning).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The image has an aria-label, every cell has content, the tables are correctly role=presentation, and the nested-table structure is the industry-standard bulletproof email pattern no linter faults. Tools do not reconstruct that the later caption describes an earlier image nor that the linearized order interposes the whole blurb between them — associating caption with image across linearized cells is a human reading judgment.

citation.quote: Since layout tables are read row by row, if the caption of an illustration is placed in the row following the illustration, it may be impossible to associate the caption with the image.

pages.scenario: Control / PASS trap: a 'How returns work' explainer (SwiftShip) built as a 2-column layout table, one row per numbered step ([number badge | step text]) stacked in order 1, 2, 3. It is a genuine layout table marked role=presentation with no th — exactly like the failing cases — but it linearizes correctly, so an annotator must actually linearize rather than reflex-flag every layout table.
pages.mechanism: Row-major linearization (verified) yields '1 | Start your return ... | 2 | Print the label ... | 3 | Drop it off ...' — each number sits immediately before its own step and the steps run 1,2,3, so the linear reading order matches the meaningful sequence conveyed visually (F49 test #2 satisfied; no failure).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Tools also produce no finding here, which is correct this time — and that is exactly why it is hard for a tool-mimicking reviewer: nothing distinguishes this PASS layout table from the FAIL ones in cases 01-05 except the content of the linearized order. A reviewer must read the cells in source order and judge the procedure still makes sense; flagging it merely for being a layout table would be a false positive.

citation.quote: If a layout table is used, however, it is important that the content make sense when linearized.

aspects.title: White space inserted within a word (F32): meaning-breaking spacing vs. carved-out initialisms / inter-word spacing
aspects.plain: Letters of a single word are spaced apart for visual effect, so a screen reader reads it letter-by-letter rather than as the word it spells.
aspects.description:
Authors space out the letters of a single word for visual effect ('W e l c o m e', 'H E L L O', tracked-out hero headings, vertical CJK via
). To AT this reads letter-by-letter or worse, changes meaning (Japanese '東 京' read 'Higashi Kyo' instead of 'Tokyo'; '東
京
都' read 'Higashi Kyo Miyako'). The hard part is F32's own explicit carve-outs: inserting white space into an INITIALISM is NOT a failure, and white space BETWEEN words is NOT a failure. So the evaluator must decide whether a spaced string is a real word being broken (FAIL) or an acronym / legitimate inter-word spacing (PASS) — a linguistic/semantic judgement; for CJK it additionally requires knowing the language to see that the reading (on'yomi/kun'yomi) changed.
aspects.scLimb: White-space-within-a-word failure mode (F32), including its initialism and inter-word carve-outs.
aspects.whyUncovered: Zero ACT coverage for 1.3.2; F32 is a failure technique only. A naive regex for single-letter-then-space patterns would mis-fire on legitimate initialisms ('F B I', 'U S A'), styled monograms, and inter-word spacing — exactly the cases F32 excludes — and could never detect the CJK meaning shift (the failure is a wrong reading, not a space-count). Telling break-the-word from harmless-spacing is the human-judgement core.

references.quote: When blank characters are inserted to control letter spacing within a word, they may change the interpretation of the word or cause it not to be programmatically recognized as a single word.

Inserting white space characters into an initialism is not an example of this
                        failure, since the white space does not change the interpretation of the
                        initialism and may make it easier to understand.

The characters mean "Tokyo," but screen readers say
                                "Higashi Kyo".

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: Boutique yoga studio hero headline reads 'W E L C O M E', built by inserting   between every letter of the single word 'Welcome' (F32 FAIL), on the same page as a primary-nav 'FAQ' link visually tracked the correct way with CSS letter-spacing (initialism carve-out, PASS). Both look identically wide; only one breaks a real word.
pages.mechanism: The <h1> text node is 'W E L C O M E' (U+00A0 between letters), so AT does not recognize the word 'Welcome' and reads it letter-by-letter; the FAQ link's text node is the intact token 'FAQ' (letter-spacing is pure CSS, never entering the text), which F32 explicitly excludes as an initialism.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse have no rule that scans text-node characters for intra-word whitespace, and a naive single-letter-then-space regex would mis-flag the legitimate 'FAQ' initialism too. Deciding that 'Welcome' is a real word being shattered while 'FAQ' is an acronym is a linguistic/semantic judgement no scanner makes.

citation.quote: This example has white spaces within a word to space out the letters in a heading. Screen readers may read each letter individually instead of the word "Welcome."

pages.scenario:
A Japanese logistics dashboard renders data-table row headers (prefecture names) as vertical text by putting a
between every kanji ('東
京
都'), splitting the single word 東京都 (Tokyo-to). The same word appears correctly as one intact token 東京都 in the summary prose below the table.
pages.mechanism:
The
line breaks terminate the text run for AT, so the row header is read as three isolated kanji that take their isolated (wrong) readings — 東='Higashi', 京='Kyo', 都='Miyako' ('Higashi Kyo Miyako') instead of the compound reading 'Tokyo-to'. The intact 東京都 in prose reads correctly, proving the spacing is the defect.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss:
The table passes every structural rule (scoped headers, caption, lang=ja, no empty cells). No automated rule extracts CJK text, segments it into words, and checks whether
-induced splits alter on'yomi/kun'yomi readings. Detecting the 'Higashi Kyo Miyako' mis-reading requires reading Japanese and knowing the compound-vs-isolated reading shift — a language-specific human judgement.

citation.quote: However screen readers are not able to read the words in vertical text correctly because the line breaks occur within the word. In the following example, "東京都"(Tokyo-to) will be read "Higashi Kyo Miyako".

pages.scenario: A county benefits-portal login form uses a wide-tracked uppercase label house style. Two labels are initialisms tracked correctly with CSS ('SSN (last 4)', 'Mailing PIN', PASS); the third label is the single word 'Password' spaced with   inside the <label> ('P A S S W O R D'). Because the <label> supplies the field's accessible name, that field is NAMED letter-by-letter.
pages.mechanism: label[for=pw] is associated to the input via for/id, so its  -broken text 'P A S S W O R D' becomes the input's accessible name; a screen reader announces the field as isolated letters and voice-control users cannot say 'click Password'. The SSN/PIN labels are intact initialism tokens (CSS-tracked only), which F32 excludes, so they read correctly.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: All three inputs have a valid, non-empty, programmatically associated label, so axe label rules, WAVE, and Lighthouse all pass — they verify name presence, not whether the name is a real word vs an initialism vs letters-with-spaces. A letter-space-letter regex would mis-flag 'SSN'/'PIN', which F32 says are not failures. Only a human reading the labels can separate the shattered word from the acronyms.

citation.quote: When blank characters are inserted to control letter spacing within a word, they may change the interpretation of the word or cause it not to be programmatically recognized as a single word.

pages.scenario: A magazine 'partners & sponsors' section fakes two sponsor logos as styled text wordmarks: 'N. A. S. A.' (initialism with periods+spaces, PASS) and 'A M A Z O N' (the single brand word 'Amazon' spaced into letters, FAIL). Both render as big bold letter-separated capitals — visually the same treatment — forcing per-token classification.
pages.mechanism: 'Amazon' is one lexeme; inserting a space between every letter yields the text node 'A M A Z O N', read as six isolated capitals, losing the word. 'N. A. S. A.' is an initialism: there is no single word to break, the letters are meant to be read individually, and F32 says spacing an initialism is not a failure and may aid comprehension.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The wordmarks are live text (not images), markup is valid, no missing attributes. No automated rule distinguishes an initialism from a spaced word; a 'capitals-with-spaces' heuristic would flag both, contradicting F32's initialism carve-out. Only a human who knows 'Amazon' is a word and 'NASA' is an acronym can mark one fail and one pass.

citation.quote: Inserting white space characters into an initialism is not an example of this failure, since the white space does not change the interpretation of the initialism and may make it easier to understand.

pages.scenario: A Korean cultural-heritage exhibition microsite widens the word 대한민국 (Republic of Korea) two ways: the hero uses the CORRECT CSS letter-spacing on an intact text node (PASS), while a later subheading types literal spaces between syllable blocks ('대 한 민 국 의 빛', FAIL). The two render almost identically — the boundary between the correct technique and F32.
pages.mechanism: letter-spacing is a pure CSS rendering property: the hero's accessible text stays 대한민국 and reads 'Daehan-minguk'. The subheading contains U+0020 between syllables, so its text is 대␣한␣민␣국… and a Korean screen reader reads four isolated syllables ('dae han min guk'), losing the word — exactly F32, one step from the correct technique.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Both the hero and the subheading are valid lang=ko text with no missing attributes. No automated rule segments Hangul into words, nor distinguishes 'widened by letter-spacing' (fine) from 'widened by literal spaces in the text' (F32). The two render nearly identically; only reading Korean and inspecting the character stream reveals the difference — a visual+linguistic human judgement.

citation.quote: The objective of this technique is to describe how using white space characters, such as space, tab, line break, or carriage return, to format individual words visually can be a failure to present meaningful sequences properly.

pages.scenario: A coffee roaster's summer-drop page builds a 'SUMMER' wordmark inside a <pre> with a literal TAB character (U+0009) between every letter so the tabs survive whitespace collapsing (F32 FAIL via tabs). The same page has ordinary multi-word prose ('Welcome to our shop', inter-word spacing PASS) and a promo code 'SAVE20' widened with CSS letter-spacing (intact code-identifier token, a subtler carve-out, PASS).
pages.mechanism: <pre> preserves the tabs, so the wordmark's text node is 'S\tU\tM\tM\tE\tR' and AT announces six isolated letters, not 'Summer' — F32 names tab as one of its whitespace mechanisms. The prose has spaces only between words (F32 carve-out), and 'SAVE20' is an unbroken token widened by CSS, not a word broken by spaces.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The <pre> holds live text (not an image), the page is valid, and tabs are legal characters. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse have no rule that detects TAB characters between a word's letters, so the failure is invisible; they equally cannot certify that 'Welcome to our shop' is legitimate inter-word spacing or that 'SAVE20' is a CSS-spaced code rather than a broken word. Word vs inter-word-spacing vs code-identifier is a human semantic judgement.

citation.quote: The use of white space between words for visual formatting is not a failure, since it does not change the interpretation of the words.

aspects.title: Faked columns / faked tables in pre-formatted plain text (F33, F34): visual 2-D structure with zero DOM structure
aspects.plain: Columns or a table are faked with spaces and line breaks inside preformatted text, so a screen reader reads straight across them and interleaves the parts into gibberish.
aspects.description: Content is laid out with literal space/tab/line-break characters inside a <pre>, <textarea>, code block, or monospaced <div>, faking multiple newspaper columns (F33) or a data table (F34, the Breakfast/Lunch/Dinner menu). Visually it looks like two columns or a grid; in the linear character stream a screen reader reads ACROSS the fake columns, interleaving them into gibberish (e.g. 'Web Content Accessibility Guidelines including blindness and low vision'). There is NO table/column markup at all — so the only signal is that the rendered visual implies a 2-D structure the linear character stream destroys. The evaluator must look at the rendering, recognize the implied columnar/tabular structure, then read the character stream and judge that the linear reading scrambles the meaning.
aspects.scLimb: White-space-multi-column-plain-text (F33) and white-space-table-in-plain-text (F34) failure modes (the 1.3.2 facet of these shared 1.3.1/1.3.2 failures).
aspects.whyUncovered: Zero ACT coverage for 1.3.2; F33/F34 are failure techniques only. Automated checkers have nothing structural to assert against — there is no <table>, no CSS columns, just a blob of text in <pre>/<textarea>. axe/WAVE see only text and cannot tell the whitespace encodes a visual grid whose linearization is nonsense. Recognizing the faked 2-D structure from the rendering and judging that the character stream scrambles meaning is inherently visual + semantic.

references.quote:
Using white space characters to create multiple columns does not
                        provide the information in a natural reading order. Thus, the assistive
                        technology user will not be presented with the information in an
                        understandable manner.

When tables are created in
                        this manner there is no way to indicate that a cell is intended to be a
                        header cell, no way to associate the table header cells with the table data
                        cells

This reading order does not make sense since there is no structure in
                                the table for the assistive technology to identify it as a table.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: Desktop-software EULA install screen renders the license body as a single monospaced <pre> inside a focusable scroll region. To fit the page, two unrelated clauses are laid out as newspaper columns with padding spaces: each source line holds a fragment of the LEFT clause, a space gutter, then a fragment of a DIFFERENT RIGHT clause. Sighted users read each column top-to-bottom; AT reads each line across, splicing the grant clause into the middle of the reverse-engineering/transfer restriction clause.
pages.mechanism: F33 — white-space characters create two columns in plain text. The column relationship exists only as space padding inside one <pre> (no <table>, no CSS column-count). A screen reader reads the character stream in line order, so the first spoken line becomes '1. GRANT OF LICENSE. Aperture Software grants and may not be reverse engineered,' — clause 1's opening fused onto the restriction clause's middle. No correct reading sequence can be programmatically determined, so the legalese the user must accept is unintelligible.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The markup is valid and complete: a labelled role=region, a real <pre>, properly-associated checkbox and Continue button. No rule fires for 'this preformatted text visually forms two columns.' axe/WAVE/Lighthouse operate on the DOM/character stream and have no model of the rendered monospace geometry, so they cannot detect that the visual layout implies a two-column reading order the linear DOM order shatters. Recognizing the implied columns from the render and judging that linearization scrambles the legalese is inherently visual + semantic human work.

citation.quote: Using white space characters to create multiple columns does not provide the information in a natural reading order. Thus, the assistive technology user will not be presented with the information in an understandable manner.

pages.scenario: An independent diner's 'This Week's Specials' chalkboard panel presents a genuine data table — rows are weekday ranges (Mon-Tue/Wed-Thu/Fri-Sat), columns are Breakfast/Lunch/Dinner, cells hold a dish plus a price — laid out entirely with space characters in one monospaced <pre>. The header row, the weekday row labels, and the price sub-columns are implied only by alignment. No <table>, <th>, scope, headers, or role exists.
pages.mechanism: F34 — white space formats a table in plain text. Header cells cannot be associated with data cells and the linear read glues unrelated cells together: the first data line is announced 'Mon-Tue Buttermilk stack French dip $12 Meatloaf $15' (three different meals + two prices fused), exactly the F34 'Monday 2 fried eggs tomato soup garden salad' shape. Continuation lines detach sides/prices from their dish, and 'Breakfast Lunch Dinner' is read once with no tie to any cell.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: With no <table> element there is nothing for a table-semantics rule to assert against — no missing <th>, no empty cell, no scope to validate. The <pre> is valid HTML and the section has an accessible name. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse cannot render the monospace layout to discover spaces encode a meal x weekday grid, nor judge that reading the line stream glues unrelated cells together. Distinguishing a faked plain-text table from ordinary preformatted text, and judging the resulting reading order, is human visual + semantic reasoning.

citation.quote: This reading order does not make sense since there is no structure in the table for the assistive technology to identify it as a table.

pages.scenario: A self-service 'Team Email Signature' tool outputs a ready-to-paste signature in a read-only <textarea>. The signature is a directory card whose rows align three columns — Name | Title | Phone — using literal TAB characters (tab-size:12, monospace). Rendered, it is a tidy 3-column staff roster; the columns are carried entirely by tab stops, with no <table>, list, or role.
pages.mechanism: F33/F34 family applied to tabs. Screen readers do not announce tab stops as column boundaries, so AT reads each row as one run — 'Dr. Amara Osei Medical Director x4120 / 555-0142' — with the tab stops collapsed away. Because every row repeats the pattern and names contain spaces, the listener cannot reliably tell where a name ends and a title begins, or which extension pairs with which person. The Name->Title->Phone relationship the layout promises is destroyed on linearization.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A read-only <textarea> with an associated <label> and aria-describedby passes form-label, name, and ARIA checks cleanly. Tab characters are valid content and trip no linter. Automated tools read the textarea value as a string and have no model of the rendered monospace tab-stop geometry, so they cannot see the three columns or judge that collapsing the tabs fuses each row's fields into an ambiguous run-on. Recognizing the faked columns and the scrambled relationship is human visual + semantic work.

citation.quote: The objective of this technique is to describe how using white space characters, such as space, tab, line break, or carriage return, to format columns of data in text content is a failure to use structure properly.

pages.scenario: A 'Your trip is confirmed' airline page shows the itinerary in a read-only <textarea>. The block is a six-column data table — Flight | Date | Route | Depart | Arrive | Gate — aligned with space characters in a monospace font, mimicking the confirmation grids airlines email. The safety-relevant Gate cell sits in the rightmost space-aligned column; alignment alone encodes which value belongs to which field and row. No <table>, role, or list.
pages.mechanism: F34 — white space formats a multi-column table in plain text. AT reads each line straight across as one run: 'MA 933 12 Jul DEN -> ORD 11:55 15:08 B6.' With every row repeating times and a short gate token, the listener must hold six fields in working memory and infer the trailing token is the gate, but the unassociated header row anchors nothing — so the gate detaches from its flight, defeating exactly what the traveler most needs.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A labelled, read-only <textarea> of ordinary text passes every form-label, name and ARIA check. There is no table to validate, no missing header to report. Automated tools treat the value as a string and cannot reconstruct the monospace column geometry, so they cannot see the six columns or judge that reading the line glues the gate to unrelated fields. Detecting the faked columns and broken reading order requires human visual + semantic judgment.

citation.quote: When tables are created in this manner there is no way to indicate that a cell is intended to be a header cell, no way to associate the table header cells with the table data cells, or to navigate directly to a particular cell in a table.

pages.scenario: A user-submitted guitar chord chart for 'Harbor Lights' uses the universal chords-above-lyrics convention: a chord line and a lyric line alternate, and each chord is padded with leading spaces so that, in a monospace font, it sits directly ABOVE the exact syllable where the chord change happens. The musical meaning is the VERTICAL spatial relationship between the two lines. There is no <ruby>, table, or data attribute — only leading-space alignment encodes which chord goes with which word; a <span class=chord> merely colors the chord text.
pages.mechanism: F33 variant — white-space characters create a vertical two-row positional alignment in plain text. A screen reader reads in document order: it speaks the entire chord line as a detached run of chord names ('G C G') and then, separately, the entire lyric line. The vertical alignment that paired each chord with its syllable exists only as runs of spaces, which AT collapses, so the chords are stripped of the words they belong to and the listener cannot reconstruct where any chord change falls.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every line is valid text and the span.chord only changes color/weight (it passes contrast and ARIA checks). There is no table, list, or missing attribute to flag. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse process the character stream and have no notion of the rendered monospace grid, so they cannot perceive that a chord's leading spaces place it above a particular syllable, nor judge that reading the chord line and lyric line separately severs that pairing. Recognizing the vertical alignment as meaningful and seeing that linearization breaks it is inherently visual + semantic.

citation.quote: A sequence is meaningful if the order of content in the sequence cannot be changed without affecting its meaning.

pages.scenario: Boundary PASS / negative control. Release notes for 'fern-cli 2.3.0' show the CHANGELOG in a read-only monospace <textarea>, with a short decorative ASCII rule (role=img with an accessible name) above it. The changelog is deliberately single-column: a release header, then Added/Fixed/Changed sections each followed by indented bullet lines. The indentation expresses simple top-to-bottom nesting; no two facts are placed side-by-side in aligned columns and nothing forms a grid, so the linear character stream IS the intended reading order.
pages.mechanism: No F33/F34 failure. Because no content is aligned into side-by-side columns, every line is a complete independent statement and the screen-reader read order matches the visual order ('Added — fern sync --dry-run previews changes...'). Indentation only signaled nesting, so nothing meaningful is lost on collapse; the decorative divider is exposed as an image named 'Decorative divider' and injects no stray characters. A correct reading sequence is available, satisfying 1.3.2. (Whether the bullets should be a real <ul> is a separate 1.3.1 concern, out of scope here.)
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Symmetry note: just as tools cannot detect the failing column/table cases, they also cannot CONFIRM this pass — they have no model of the rendered monospace layout and so cannot determine that no 2-D grid is being faked. A tool sees a valid labelled <textarea> of text either way. Confirming that the linear order genuinely preserves meaning, and that the indentation is nesting rather than columns, is the same human visual + semantic judgment applied to reach a PASS, making this a clean boundary control rather than a trivially-passing page.

citation.quote: Providing a particular linear order is only required where it affects meaning.

aspects.title: Responsive-breakpoint source-vs-visual desync — order is meaningful at one viewport but reordered at another
aspects.plain: At one screen size CSS reorders items (stacking wizard steps as 2,1,3 on mobile), so the visual order no longer matches the source order a screen reader reads.
aspects.description: A single self-contained page is correct in DOM source order at one width, but a media query reorders flex/grid items at another breakpoint such that the visual order no longer matches the meaningful source order — e.g. a 'Step 1 / Step 2 / Step 3' wizard whose mobile media query uses 'order:' to stack the steps 2,1,3; or an 'Editor's note: read the conclusion first' sidebar that on mobile collapses ABOVE the content it refers to, turning a closing note into a misleading lede. The failure exists only in one rendering state, so the evaluator must render at multiple viewports, recognize that the order is meaningful, and confirm that the visual order diverges from the meaningful source order at the breakpoint where meaning is order-dependent. (Distinct from the F1 single-viewport case: the failure is conditional on viewport and requires comparing rendered states.)
aspects.scLimb: Core requirement applied to CSS flow-order reflow across responsive breakpoints (C27 'each order may be meaningful in itself but may cause confusion'; implied by F1/C27 but named by no failure technique).
aspects.whyUncovered: Zero ACT coverage for 1.3.2, and no failure technique names responsive 'order:' reflow specifically. Automated DOM-vs-visual diff tools typically run at a single viewport and have no notion that a breakpoint reorder changes meaning; they cannot judge whether the reordered sequence still parses, nor will they think to compare across breakpoints.

references.quote:
A sequence is 
         meaningful if the order of content in the sequence cannot be changed without affecting its meaning.

If content is positioned with CSS, the information will display with blue highlighting around the elements and
   those elements will be placed in the page in the **same order in which they appear in the page code**.

The order in which items appear on a screen may be
                        different than the order they are found in the source document.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: E-commerce 3-step checkout wizard (Shipping → Payment → Review) with hard-coded step badges; a max-width:600px flexbox order: reorder stacks Payment above Shipping on mobile, so the badges read out of order ('2' above '1') and the visual order contradicts the meaningful DOM source order.
pages.mechanism: @media (max-width:600px) reassigns flexbox order (.step--payment{order:1}, .step--shipping{order:2}, .step--review{order:3}) so the steps stack visually as Payment, Shipping, Review while the DOM source order stays the correct process order Shipping, Payment, Review. Each step's number is a hard-coded static badge (<span class="step__num" aria-hidden="true">) glued to its content rather than a CSS counter() keyed to visual position, so on mobile the badges travel with their steps and render out of order ('2' Payment above '1' Shipping), visually asserting that payment precedes shipping. A screen reader follows the correct DOM/tab order, so visual order diverges from the meaningful source order at the ≤600px viewport.
pages.selectorNote: Flex container whose step children reorder (Payment before Shipping) under 600px; orig was @media rule
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: DOM order is the CORRECT order, each <li> is valid and labelled, and CSS order is legal. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse evaluate a single viewport, never render <=600px, do not diff rendered geometry across breakpoints, and have no model that 'Payment before Shipping' changes meaning; the only swap signal is a CSS-generated counter, which checkers do not read as content. Requires rendering at mobile width, recognizing the steps are an ordered process, and comparing visual vs source order.

citation.quote: The order of content in the source code can be changed by the author to any number of visual presentations with CSS. Each order may be meaningful in itself but may cause confusion for assistive technology users.

pages.scenario: Investigative long-read whose closing 'Editor's note' deliberately spoils the ending (names the leaker and the outcome) and is acceptable as a last-position afterword. Source order puts the note last and desktop renders it last, but a max-width:680px media query applies order:-1 so on mobile the spoiler note floats above the entire article — turning a closing recap into a misleading lede and making its own phrase 'As detailed above' false.
pages.mechanism: Flexbox order:-1 inside @media (max-width:680px) promotes a meaning-bearing CLOSING aside to the lede at one breakpoint, so the rendered mobile order (note -> body) diverges from the meaningful source order (body -> note); the order of this content affects meaning (spoiler as afterword vs as opener), and the anaphoric 'As detailed above' is broken.
pages.selectorNote: Closing spoiler note that order:-1 floats above the article under 680px; orig was @media rule
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: DOM order is correct (note last), the <aside> is valid with an accessible name, and order:-1 is legal CSS. Single-viewport scanners never render the <=680px state; even rendered, no rule can judge that a closing spoiler floated to the top is now a misleading lede or that 'As detailed above' now points at nothing — that demands reading the prose, understanding the note is a deliberate end-spoiler, and comparing two rendered states.

citation.quote: Content that does not meet this Success Criterion may confuse or disorient users when assistive technology reads the content in the wrong order, or when alternate style sheets or other formatting changes are applied.

pages.scenario: Software license agreement, Section 7 Limitation of Liability, with legally order-dependent sub-clauses 7.1 (cap), 7.2 (exceptions to 7.1), 7.3 ('Notwithstanding the foregoing...'). Source order 7.1,7.2,7.3 and desktop render are correct, but a max-width:640px media query sets flex-direction:column-reverse, so on mobile the clauses render 7.3,7.2,7.1 — an exception appears before the clauses it overrides, and the visible clause numbers run descending and out of order.
pages.mechanism: flex-direction:column-reverse inside @media (max-width:640px) reverses the visual order of cross-referencing, order-dependent legal clauses so the rendered mobile order (7.3,7.2,7.1) diverges from the meaningful source order (7.1,7.2,7.3); backward references ('Notwithstanding the foregoing', 'the cap in Section 7.1') resolve to content that has not yet appeared, breaking the legal meaning.
pages.selectorNote: Flex container reversed via column-reverse under 640px, inverting legal clauses 7.1-7.3; orig was @media rule
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Source order is the correct legal order, clause numbers are real text (no counter trick), and column-reverse is legal CSS. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse test one viewport and never render the reversed <=640px state; even rendered, no rule can read 'Notwithstanding the foregoing' and infer it is a backward reference broken by reversal — that needs legal-semantic comprehension plus cross-state comparison. Desktop and mobile DOM are byte-identical.

citation.quote: The sequence and meaning of the content (in context) is understandable without CSS positioning.

pages.scenario: Canning recipe whose Method is one continuous safety sentence split across two prose blocks (m1 ends '...leaving 1cm headspace, then'; m2 begins 'do NOT seal the jars until the headspace has cooled...'). Desktop uses a 2-column grid ('m1 tip' / 'm2 tip') so m1 and m2 read consecutively in the left column with an unrelated Tip beside them. At max-width:620px grid-template-areas is redefined to 'm1' / 'tip' / 'm2', dropping the unrelated Tip BETWEEN the two halves of the safety sentence so a hurried cook may read the first half ('...then') and seal hot jars.
pages.mechanism: grid-template-areas redefined inside @media (max-width:620px) interleaves an unrelated 'tip' cell between two halves of a single continuous safety instruction; the rendered mobile order (m1, tip, m2) fractures the meaning-bearing sequence while the DOM source order (m1, m2, tip) keeps the sentence intact, so visual order diverges from the meaningful source order. Verified via computed grid: tip beside m1/m2 on desktop, interleaved (same column, after m1, before m2) on mobile.
pages.selectorNote: Grid whose template-areas interleave the tip mid-safety-sentence under 620px; orig was @media rule
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Source/DOM order is correct, all elements valid, the tip has an accessible name, and grid-template-areas is legal CSS. Single-viewport tools never render the <=620px single-column grid; even rendered, no rule can detect that the tip lands between two halves of one continuous sentence — that requires reading the prose, seeing m1 ends mid-sentence ('...then') and m2 completes it, and judging that the interruption changes meaning. The DOM is identical across breakpoints; the defect lives only in rendered grid placement.

citation.quote: Thus, it is important not to rely on CSS to visually position content in a specific sequence if this sequence results in a meaning that is different from the programmatically determined reading order.

pages.scenario: Podcast player transport row whose left-to-right order is fixed in meaning by a caption that is also the group's accessible name ('Use the controls below to move through the episode, left to right: previous chapter, play, next chapter') and by arrow glyphs. Source/DOM order and desktop render are Previous, Play, Next, but a max-width:560px media query reassigns flex order so the row renders Next, Play, Previous — contradicting the caption's stated order and inverting the back-left/forward-right convention; the '<- Previous' button sits on the right and the 'Next ->' button on the left.
