pages.mechanism: Flexbox order reassigned inside @media (max-width:560px) inverts a directionally meaningful control sequence so the rendered mobile order (Next,Play,Previous) contradicts both the captioned/labelled meaning 'left to right: previous, play, next' and the arrow glyphs, while DOM/tab order stays Previous,Play,Next; visual order diverges from the meaningful (captioned) source order at one viewport.
pages.selectorNote: Transport group whose buttons reorder to Next|Play|Previous under 560px; orig was @media rule
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Each control is a real <button> with a correct accessible name, the group is named, DOM order is correct, and flex order is legal CSS. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse evaluate one viewport and never render the <=560px reversal; even rendered, no rule can detect that the visual left-to-right order now contradicts a prose caption defining the intended order, or that an arrow glyph's direction no longer matches its position — that needs reading the caption, knowing the back/forward convention, and comparing rendered states. Desktop and mobile DOM are identical.

citation.quote: A keyboard user may have trouble predicting where focus will go next when the source order does not match the visual order.

pages.scenario: PASS/over-flagging trap: a SaaS analytics dashboard 'Overview' row with a decorative promo banner and three INDEPENDENT KPI cards (Visitors, Revenue, Conversion). It uses the SAME mechanism as the failing cases — a max-width:640px media query applying flex order — to push the decorative banner to the bottom and reshuffle the cards on mobile. Because the items are order-independent (self-contained statistics + decorative banner), the meaning is identical at both viewports and the page must NOT be flagged.
pages.mechanism: Flexbox order reassigned inside @media (max-width:640px) reorders items whose relative order does NOT affect meaning (independent KPI cards + decorative banner), analogous to the Understanding doc's article + callout sidebars; at least one programmatically determinable sequence makes sense at both viewports, no instruction is split, no step/clause/directional sequence is inverted, so 1.3.2 is satisfied.
pages.selectorNote: Container of independent KPI cards reshuffled under 640px (harmless PASS trap); orig was @media rule
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Automated tools would not flag this (correctly) but also cannot certify the pass for the right reason: they cannot tell these particular items are order-independent. The page's value is for the human/LLM evaluator — the identical surface signal (a max-width media query applying order) that caused failures in cases 01-05 is present here, so the evaluator must NOT pattern-match 'breakpoint reorder = fail' and must instead read the content to conclude the reorder does not affect meaning.

citation.quote: The order of content in a sequence is not always meaningful. For example, the relative order of the main section of a web page and a navigation section does not affect their meaning.

aspects.title: Bidirectional / mixed-directionality text where the visual order is fixed by reordering characters, exposing the wrong order to AT (G57 bidi case)
aspects.plain: In mixed left-to-right and right-to-left text, an author physically reorders characters to look right on screen, so a screen reader hears them in the wrong logical order.
aspects.description: A page mixes LTR and RTL scripts (English + Arabic/Hebrew/Persian, or numbers/punctuation embedded in RTL text). G57 names the precise failure: an author 'fixes' the visual rendering by physically moving characters in the content stream (e.g. relocating a trailing period or a price) so the Unicode bidi algorithm happens to position them correctly on screen — but this exposes the WRONG logical character order to AT. The correct fix is markup (dir, <bdi>, <bdo>) that overrides the bidi algorithm so the order is right both visually AND to AT, NOT reordering source characters. Conversely, omitting needed dir/bdi markup can leave the visual correct but the logical order scrambled when spoken. Detecting this requires reading both scripts, knowing their directionality, and judging whether the logical (source) order matches the visual.
aspects.scLimb: Bidirectional / RTL text-order limb (G57: 'using markup to override the bidirectional algorithm' rather than reordering source characters).
aspects.whyUncovered: Zero ACT coverage for 1.3.2; G57 is a general technique with no ACT rule/test. The failure is invisible to automated structural checkers: the markup may be well-formed and the visual rendering correct; only by reading both scripts and comparing logical-vs-visual order can one tell that source characters were reordered (exposing wrong order to AT) or that bidi markup was wrongly omitted. This requires multilingual semantic judgement no checker performs.

references.quote: The visual rendering problem could be corrected by moving the punctuation in the content stream so that the bidirectional algorithm positions it as desired, but this would expose the incorrect content order to assistive technology.
The content is both rendered in the correct order visually and exposed to assistive technology in the correct order by using markup to override the bidirectional algorithm.

It is important that it be possible to programmatically determine at least
         one sequence of the content that makes sense.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: Arabic (RTL) dates-store product price line. The price '$50' plus its sentence period were physically moved to the FRONT of the source byte stream ('.$50 سعر العلبة الواحدة …') so the bidirectional algorithm mirrors them and the screen shows a clean '… $50.' at the visual left end. Verified with a rendering harness: LOGICAL source order is '.$50 سعر…' (price/period first) while VISUAL is '…سعر العلبة الواحدة $50.'
pages.mechanism: G57 source-character reordering: punctuation + an embedded LTR price run relocated in the content stream to satisfy the bidi algorithm, so a screen reader/Braille/copy-paste reads the period and price FIRST, detached from the Arabic clause — the wrong logical order — while the render looks correct. Fix would be <bdi>$50</bdi> with the period in logical final position.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Markup is well-formed, page is lang=ar dir=rtl, no attribute is missing, and the visual render is correct. Detecting it requires reading Arabic, knowing it is RTL, and comparing logical character order to visual order to see the price/period were physically moved. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse perform no multilingual logical-vs-visual order comparison.

citation.quote: The visual rendering problem could be corrected by moving the punctuation in the content stream so that the bidirectional algorithm positions it as desired, but this would expose the incorrect content order to assistive technology.

pages.scenario: Hebrew (RTL) spice-shop out-of-stock notice embedding an English supplier status clause. The sentence-ending period was physically typed BEFORE the English run in source ('… מהמלאי .DUE TO HIGH DEMAND today') so bidi mirrors it to render correctly after 'today.'. Verified with a rendering harness: LOGICAL = '…אזל מהמלאי .DUE TO HIGH DEMAND today' (period before DUE), VISUAL = '…אזל מהמלאי DUE TO HIGH DEMAND today.'
pages.mechanism: G57 source-character reordering of punctuation: the full stop relocated to the front of the embedded LTR clause so the bidi algorithm places it correctly on screen, but a screen reader reads the logical order and announces the sentence period before the English clause, breaking the sentence into the wrong segments. Fix would be <bdi> around the English clause with the period in logical final position.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Page is valid lang=he dir=rtl HTML with every attribute present and a visually correct render; a relocated period is not a missing/empty attribute and trips no linter. Only a human reading both Hebrew and English and comparing the period's logical vs visual position can detect the move. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse do not do this.

citation.quote: the bidirectional algorithm may position punctuation in the wrong location in the visual rendering. The visual rendering problem could be corrected by moving the punctuation in the content stream so that the bidirectional algorithm positions it as desired, but this would expose the incorrect content order to assistive technology.

pages.scenario: English (LTR) museum collections CMS exhibit caption. An Arabic exhibit name ('الأرشيف') and its acquisition year were transposed in source ('… the 2023 الأرشيف collection …') so the bidi algorithm yields a screen layout byte-for-byte identical to the logically-correct '… the الأرشيف 2023 collection …'. Verified with a rendering harness: the two sources render identically; LOGICAL order here is year-before-name.
pages.mechanism: G57 source-token transposition: two adjacent tokens (Arabic name + year) swapped in the content stream so the visual matches the intended order, while a screen reader reads the logical order and announces the acquisition YEAR before the exhibit name — the wrong meaningful sequence. Fix would be <bdi> around the Arabic run with the tokens in logical order.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Page is valid lang=en HTML, every attribute present, render correct; two visually-identical sources differ only in logical token order. No tool can tell the year and Arabic name were swapped because that requires reading Arabic, knowing its directionality, and reconstructing the intended meaning to judge 'year before name' is wrong.

citation.quote: Some techniques permit the content to be rendered visually in a meaningful sequence even if this is different from the order in which the content is encoded in the underlying source file.

pages.scenario: Hebrew (RTL) design-studio invoice. The invoice number must display as 'INV-2024-0731'. The author wrapped it in <bdo dir="rtl"> (which forcibly reverses glyph display but NOT source order) and then typed the characters backwards in source ('1370-4202-VNI'). Verified with a rendering harness: VISUAL = 'INV-2024-0731' (correct), LOGICAL/DOM textContent = '1370-4202-VNI' (reversed, meaningless).
pages.mechanism: G57 inverse case — <bdo> misuse: <bdo dir=rtl> overrides only the display direction, so the DOM text node remains the reversed string. A screen reader announces, and copy-paste/programmatic reads return, '1370-4202-VNI'. The visual is fixed by reversing a deliberately-reversed source rather than using markup that makes the order correct both visually and to AT (<bdi>/dir with digits in logical order).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: <bdo dir=rtl> is perfectly valid, syntactically correct HTML; the page passes every linter and the render is flawless. No tool flags a <bdo> whose contents are a reversed string, because deciding the logical order is wrong requires reading the identifier, recognising it is reversed relative to its intended value, and knowing <bdo> reverses display without reordering source.

citation.quote: The content is both rendered in the correct order visually and exposed to assistive technology in the correct order by using markup to override the bidirectional algorithm.

pages.scenario: Persian (RTL) news article embedding an LTR registration URL. The URL's path segment '2024/' was physically moved before the host in source ('2024/conf.ai-iran.org') so bidi reorders it to render as a clean 'conf.ai-iran.org/2024'. Verified with a rendering harness: LOGICAL = '…نشانی 2024/conf.ai-iran.org مراجعه…' (path before host), VISUAL shows the contiguous correct URL 'conf.ai-iran.org/2024'.
pages.mechanism: G57 source-character reordering of a URL: host and path transposed in the content stream so the bidi algorithm yields a clean visual URL, while a screen reader reads the logical order and announces the URL pieces out of sequence; copy/programmatic reconstruction yields a broken address. Fix would be <bdi> around the URL with segments in logical order.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Page is valid lang=fa dir=rtl HTML, no attribute missing, and the render is a clean URL. Recognising host and path were transposed requires reading Persian, knowing its directionality, parsing the URL's intended structure, and comparing logical vs visual order. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse perform no such analysis.

citation.quote: The visual rendering problem could be corrected by moving the punctuation in the content stream so that the bidirectional algorithm positions it as desired, but this would expose the incorrect content order to assistive technology.

pages.scenario: PASS boundary trap: Arabic (RTL) flight confirmation mixing RTL Arabic with embedded LTR runs (flight code 'EK 0231', price '$50.00', seat '14C', management URL) each correctly isolated with <bdi>. Same class of mixed-direction content as the failing pages, but the logical/source order is the natural meaningful order and the visual is achieved via markup override, not source reordering. Verified with a rendering harness: LOGICAL order matches the meaningful order and VISUAL renders each LTR run correctly.
pages.mechanism: Correct G57-conformant handling: <bdi> isolates each embedded LTR run so the bidi algorithm positions it correctly without relocating any source characters. The content is correct both visually and to AT; a correct reading sequence can be programmatically determined. Present as a negative control so not every RTL+LTR mix is flagged.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Symmetric to the failing cases: automated tools cannot CONFIRM this page is correct either, having no model of intended meaning to compare against. A naive heuristic flagging 'RTL containing LTR runs' or 'uses <bdo>/<bdi>' would false-positive here. Only a human reading both scripts can confirm the logical order matches the meaningful order; this guards against over-flagging.

citation.quote: The content is both rendered in the correct order visually and exposed to assistive technology in the correct order by using markup to override the bidirectional algorithm.

aspects.title: Applicability gate and multiple-valid-orders: deciding whether order is meaningful at all, and that more than one order can be correct
aspects.plain: Deciding when order even matters: two unrelated articles can appear in either order safely, so flagging a page just because blocks could be reordered would be wrong.
aspects.description: 1.3.2 only applies 'when the sequence in which content is presented affects its meaning,' and the Understanding adds three clarifications: providing a particular linear order is only required where it affects meaning; there may be more than one 'correct' order; only one correct order needs to be provided. Two independent non-interleaved articles, a nav-vs-main pairing, and a magazine article with callout sidebars can each appear in EITHER order without failing — the container has no meaningful sequence even though each article does. The evaluator must first decide whether order is meaningful for the content at hand (the applicability gate), and must NOT flag a page merely because its block order could be different, as long as no single block's internal meaning is broken. This is the discrimination that prevents over-flagging the whole SC.
aspects.scLimb: Conditional applicability trigger ('When the sequence... affects its meaning') + multiple-valid-orders limb ('There may be more than one order that is correct... Only one correct order needs to be provided').
aspects.whyUncovered: Zero ACT coverage for 1.3.2. Nothing in ACT tests the applicability gate — deciding whether order is meaningful at all — and no rule/test/technique exercises the multiple-valid-orders case. EN 301 549 frames C.9.1.3.2 as Inspection with a 'Not applicable... does not contain content relevant' clause, wholly absent from ACT. A checker cannot decide whether reordering two articles or a nav/main pair affects meaning; that is a contextual semantic judgement, and getting it wrong means false positives on perfectly conformant pages.

references.quote:
if a page contains two independent articles, the relative order of the
         articles may not affect their meaning, as long as they are not interleaved. In such
         a situation, the articles themselves may have meaningful sequence, but the container
         that contains the articles may not have a meaningful sequence.
There may be more than one order that is "correct" (according to the WCAG 2 definition).

a magazine article contains several callout sidebars.
         The order of the article and the sidebars does not affect their meaning.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: Naturalists' bulletin with two fully independent, non-interleaved articles in a two-column flex layout. The visually dominant photo-led feature ('Return of the curlew') is in the right column but is DOM-second; the short treasurer's notice is DOM-first. Neither article is reordered internally and they are not interleaved, so the container has no meaningful sequence and either order is correct.
pages.mechanism: A screen reader reads the notice in full then the feature in full, each in clean source order and internally coherent, with nothing interleaved. Because the two articles are semantically independent, hearing one before the other does not change either's meaning — the container is order-irrelevant (the Understanding's 'two independent articles' case). The applicability gate is not tripped.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: There is no ACT/axe/WAVE/Lighthouse rule for 1.3.2, so tools emit nothing. The trap is a naive DOM-vs-visual-order heuristic (or over-eager human/LLM) that would FALSE-POSITIVE because the visually dominant block is DOM-second. Deciding the two blocks are independent articles — so EITHER order satisfies the SC — is a contextual semantic judgement no checker can derive from coordinates or DOM order.

citation.quote: if a page contains two independent articles, the relative order of the articles may not affect their meaning, as long as they are not interleaved. In such a situation, the articles themselves may have meaningful sequence, but the container that contains the articles may not have a meaningful sequence.

pages.scenario: Coffee-roastery landing page modelled on the Understanding's Example 2. Visually there is a fixed top nav bar, hero, body, and a pinned bottom-right promo. In the DOM <main> is first and the <nav> landmark is dead last, lifted to the top of the viewport with position:fixed; the promo aside is DOM-after-main and pinned bottom-right. Order of nav vs main carries no meaning.
pages.mechanism: A screen reader reads main first, then promo, then footer, then navigation — each landmark internally coherent. Hearing the nav after the main content does not change either region's meaning, and a landmark/rotor user can jump to Primary navigation at any time regardless of source position. Nav-vs-main order is immaterial, so more than one reading order satisfies the SC and this one is fine.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: No tool runs a 1.3.2 check. The risk is a DOM-vs-visual-order heuristic treating 'visually-first element is source-last' as a focus/reading-order defect. Recognising that nav and main are order-independent regions — so the mismatch is harmless — needs semantic knowledge of what those regions are, which a coordinate or DOM comparison cannot supply.

citation.quote: Example 2: CSS is used to position a navigation bar, the main story on a page, and a side story. The visual presentation of the sections does not match the programmatically determined order, but the meaning of the page does not depend on the order of the sections.

pages.scenario: Co-working start-page dashboard with four independent widgets (weather, stock watchlist, room bookings, transit departures). CSS grid-template-areas places them weather/transit on top and bookings/stocks below; the DOM order is different again (bookings, stocks, weather, transit). Each widget is self-contained and internally ordered, nothing is interleaved, and any permutation reads sensibly.
pages.mechanism: A screen reader reads the widgets in DOM order; each is a complete, internally-ordered unit and none bleeds into another. Because the four widgets are mutually independent, whether weather is heard before or after the bookings changes nothing. This is the 'multiple correct orders' limb: several reading orders all satisfy the SC and the page provides one of them, which is all that is required.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: No tool checks 1.3.2, and a DOM-vs-visual-order heuristic would mis-fire on the grid-area remapping. The correct verdict requires recognising the four cards are independent — so every order is valid — which is a semantic judgement about the content, not a geometric or DOM-order fact a checker can compute.

citation.quote: There may be more than one order that is "correct" (according to the WCAG 2 definition).

pages.scenario: Long-form coastal feature ('The long tide') whose pull-quote callout would be harmless before or after the body, but is instead interleaved INTO the middle of a single running sentence. The sentence is split across p#part-a ('...the river that once fed the marsh') and p#part-b ('was dammed upstream in the 1970s...'), with the entire <aside> pull-quote and attribution sitting between them in the DOM; flex order:99 + float:right place it cleanly in the right margin visually.
pages.mechanism: A screen reader reads the DOM in order: it speaks the opening clause, then jumps into the pull-quote 'We are not losing the marsh... — Dr. Helen Okafor', then returns to 'was dammed upstream in the 1970s...'. The sentence is severed and a quotation+attribution is spoken into the middle of it, so the listener cannot reassemble the author's point. Unlike the harmless article-vs-sidebar case, the blocks ARE interleaved, destroying the body's meaningful sequence.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss:
The
, the two

fragments, and the flex/float CSS are all valid — nothing missing or malformed — and there is no 1.3.2 rule. Detecting the failure requires reading the prose and noticing one sentence has been cut in half by an interleaved aside, a semantic/linguistic judgement no automated checker performs.

citation.quote: it is important not to rely on CSS to visually position content in a specific sequence if this sequence results in a meaning that is different from the programmatically determined reading order.

pages.scenario: Four-step furniture-assembly guide rendered as flex cards (not an <ol>). CSS order: forces the correct visual sequence (attach the wall plate, insert the bracket pins, hang the shelf, tighten and check), but the DOM order is scrambled (shelf, tighten, plate, pins). Headings are unnumbered, so the only cue the order is wrong is the prose 'First/Next/Then/Finally'. Order is genuinely meaningful, so the applicability gate IS tripped — the contrast to the PASS cases.
pages.mechanism: A screen reader and the linearized DOM ignore CSS order: and present the steps as 'Hang the shelf' first, then 'Tighten and check', then 'Attach the wall plate', then 'Insert the bracket pins'. A user following the spoken order would try to hang a shelf onto bracket arms and a wall plate that have not yet been installed. The procedure is meaningful sequence and the programmatically determined order does not match it.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The flex container, the order: declarations, and the <div> cards are all valid; there is no numbered list whose numbers a tool could compare against position, and no 1.3.2 rule. Detecting the failure requires understanding these are sequential assembly steps and that the spoken order ('hang the shelf' before 'attach the wall plate') is physically impossible — a reading-comprehension judgement.

citation.quote: The reading order of the content (in context) is correct and the meaning of the content (in context) is preserved without CSS positioning.

pages.scenario: Saved bank support-chat transcript (a duplicate-charge dispute). Each bubble is a CSS-grid item, and grid-row lays them out in the correct visual conversation order; but the DOM stores messages newest-first (a 'prepend new message' anti-pattern), so the linearized reading order is the exact reverse — the agent's closing 'Glad I could help! The refund will land in 3-5 working days' is read before the customer's opening 'Hi, I was charged twice...'.
pages.mechanism: A screen reader and the linearized DOM ignore grid-row and read source order m6→m1: the resolution is announced before the problem and every answer before its question. A non-sighted user cannot follow the dispute. A conversation is intrinsically meaningful sequence (a reply only makes sense after the message it answers), and the programmatically determined order contradicts it.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The grid, the grid-row rules, the role=log, and the bubble markup are all valid — nothing missing or malformed — and there is no 1.3.2 rule. There are no timestamps or sequence numbers a tool could sort against. Realising the transcript is reversed requires reading the dialogue and recognising that replies precede their prompts, a reading-comprehension judgement automated tools cannot make.

citation.quote: It is important that it be possible to programmatically determine at least one sequence of the content that makes sense. Content that does not meet this Success Criterion may confuse or disorient users when assistive technology reads the content in the wrong order

aspects.title: Inline links distinguished from body text by hue alone (no underline/weight/lightness), incl. hover/focus-only cues that don't rescue
aspects.plain: Links inside paragraphs are shown only by a different color with no underline or bold, so a color-blind user can't tell which words are clickable links.
aspects.description: Links embedded in running text have their underline removed and are set in a color that differs from the surrounding body text by HUE only — there is no bold, italic, size, font-family change, and the link-vs-text lightness contrast is under 3:1. A sighted color-perceiving user can spot the links; a color-blind or grayscale user cannot tell them apart from prose. To flag this an evaluator must (a) recognize which colored spans are actually links (vs decorative emphasis) by reading the markup/meaning, (b) confirm hue is the ONLY differentiator, and (c) judge that any subtle non-color cue present (a faint weight bump, a serif/sans swap) is too weak to count. A critical sub-case: the only non-color cue is injected on :hover or :focus — F73 and G183 are explicit that a cue appearing only on hover/focus is STILL a failure because the resting state is color-only; detecting this requires comparing the resting render to the hover/focus render and applying the rule. This is the canonical 'distinguishing a visual element' failure and is the single most prevalent real-world 1.4.1 defect.
aspects.scLimb: distinguishing a visual element (LIMB 4) + scoping: hover/focus cues do not rescue + 3:1 lightness escape hatch
aspects.whyUncovered:
There are 0 ACT rules and 0 test cases for 1.4.1, so this is entirely unexercised. axe/Lighthouse/WAVE have NO link-vs-surrounding-text contrast rule — their contrast checks measure foreground-vs-background per 1.4.3, not link-color-vs-adjacent-TEXT-color, and they treat an un-underlined colored inside

as fine. Deciding whether a colored span is a real link vs decorative emphasis, whether a subtle non-color cue is 'enough', and whether a hover/focus-only cue rescues the resting state are all perceptual/contextual judgments no automated checker performs.

references.quote: Removing the underline and leaving only the color difference for such links would be a failure because there would be no other visual indication (besides color) that it is a link.
If the non-color cue only happens when the mouse hovers over the link or when the link receives focus, it is still a failure.

Red and pink are the same color (hue) but they have different lightness (which is not color). So red and pink would pass the requirement for "not distinguished by color (hue) alone" since they differ by lightness (which is not color) - as long as the difference in lightness (contrast) is 3:1 or greater.
Hover or focus style changes alone are not sufficient to meet the criterion.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: Dark-mode coffee-industry editorial blog post. Four inline story links are brand blue #6f93cf with text-decoration:none and no weight/size/family/style change on near-white #e8e8ea body text over #0e0f12. Color-perceiving readers see blue; grayscale/color-blind readers cannot find the links.
pages.mechanism: Link #6f93cf vs body #e8e8ea is 2.54:1 lightness contrast (under the 3:1 escape hatch), so hue is the sole differentiator; no underline, weight, italic, size, or hover/focus cue. Link-vs-bg 6.16:1 and body-vs-bg 15.66:1 both pass 1.4.3, which is why contrast scanners stay silent.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse have no link-vs-surrounding-text contrast rule; they measure foreground-vs-background (1.4.3), which the link passes. Judging that 2.54:1 same-direction lightness is below 3:1 and hue is the only cue requires comparing link color to adjacent text color and applying the escape-hatch rule.

citation.quote: Removing the underline and leaving only the color difference for such links would be a failure because there would be no other visual indication (besides color) that it is a link.

pages.scenario: Fintech REST-API developer-docs glossary (<dl> of terms). In-definition cross-reference links (.xref) are a darker shade of the SAME neutral gray hue (#3d3d3d) as the mid-gray body (#6b6b6b), no underline, no weight/family change. Separate blue hover-underlined breadcrumb nav acts as a distractor.
pages.mechanism: Link #3d3d3d vs body #6b6b6b is 2.04:1 lightness and the same hue, so the only difference is a darkness step that does not reach the 3:1 G183/F73 same-hue threshold. Both grays pass 1.4.3 on white (10.86:1 / 5.33:1).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: No fg-vs-bg violation exists (both grays clear 4.5:1 on white) so contrast rules are silent; no scanner compares a link color to adjacent text color, and none knows a 2:1 same-hue darkness step is too weak. Distinguishing real link spans from prose and judging sufficiency of the darkness step is perceptual.

citation.quote: Red and pink are the same color (hue) but they have different lightness (which is not color). So red and pink would pass the requirement for "not distinguished by color (hue) alone" since they differ by lightness (which is not color) - as long as the difference in lightness (contrast) is 3:1 or greater.

pages.scenario: Sourdough-focaccia recipe blog using the literal F73 stylesheet pattern: a:link/a:visited/a:active have text-decoration:none (resting green #1f6f43), and only a:hover (plus a:active) add an underline and red color. No :focus rule, so keyboard users also get color-only at rest.
pages.mechanism: In the resting state the only link-vs-text difference is hue (green vs near-black #2b2b2b) at 2.30:1 lightness, below 3:1. The underline/red cue exists in CSS and fires on mouseover but appears only on :hover/:active, and F73/G183 judge conformance before focus or pointing, so the hover-only cue does not rescue the color-only resting state.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Static scanners parse the resting computed style, see a 1.4.3-passing colored named <a>, and do not simulate :hover/:active or compare resting-vs-hover renders; they have no rule that hover-only cues fail. Catching this needs capturing resting+hover states and applying the F73 still-a-failure rule.

citation.quote: If the visual cue is only provided on hover (as in the example above), it would still fail.

pages.scenario: City government 'Renew your resident parking permit' service page. Inline guidance links inside an ordered step list are gov-blue #2453a6 at rest (no underline, weight 400); the only non-color cue, font-weight:700, is injected via :focus-visible, so it appears only for keyboard users on focus. Mouse/touch/scanning and color-blind users get color-only.
pages.mechanism: Resting link #2453a6 vs body #1b1b1b is 2.35:1 lightness (under 3:1), hue is the sole differentiator; the bold cue requires :focus-visible to appear. F73 states a non-color cue provided only on focus is still a failure. A focus outline satisfies 2.4.7 but not 1.4.1's resting-state visual distinction. Colors pass 1.4.3 (6.96:1 / 16.34:1).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Scanners evaluate the 1.4.3-passing resting style, have no link-vs-text rule, and see a present :focus-visible style plus focus outline that superficially looks accessible. Recognizing the bold cue is keyboard-focus-gated and irrelevant to 1.4.1's resting requirement needs resting-vs-focused comparison and F73 knowledge.

citation.quote: If the non-color cue only happens when the mouse hovers over the link or when the link receives focus, it is still a failure.

pages.scenario: University LMS course page (HIST 214). The theme styles BOTH inline links (<a>) and lecturer emphasis (<strong>) with the identical maroon #9d1b3d + bold + no underline, so 'maroon+bold' is not a link-specific cue; half the maroon-bold phrases are reading-list links and half are non-link emphasis. Only the href reveals which are clickable.
pages.mechanism: The bold weight is real but shared with non-links, so it cannot signal link-ness, leaving color as the only link cue — and color cannot disambiguate links from identically-colored emphasis. Accent-vs-body is 2.01:1 (hue-dominant, under 3:1). Color-blind/grayscale users see uniform bold prose; sighted users must hover or read source. The link is not visually evident as a link.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The <a> and <strong> are valid and 1.4.3-passing (7.90:1 on white); a scanner sees 'links are bold and colored' and would deem it sufficient, unable to know identical styling is reused for non-links or that a shared cue fails to distinguish links. Determining which colored-bold spans are links vs decorative emphasis requires reading meaning and markup.

citation.quote: While some links may be visually evident from page design and context, such as navigational links, links within text are often visually understood only from their own display attributes. Removing the underline and leaving only the color difference for such links would be a failure because there would be no other visual indication (besides color) that it is a link.

pages.scenario: TRUE-NEGATIVE (PASS / escape-hatch boundary). Nonprofit 'Where your gift goes' donation/impact page reproducing the literal G183 example: inline links medium-light blue #3366CC, no underline, on black #000000 body over white. A bonus :hover/:focus underline is added but is not what carries conformance.
pages.mechanism: Link #3366CC vs black body text is 3.91:1 lightness contrast, at/above the 3:1 escape hatch, so links are distinguishable by lightness (not hue alone) even with no color perception or in grayscale. Link-vs-white-bg is 5.37:1, so 1.4.3 also passes. The page does not depend on the hover/focus underline.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: An over-eager 'underline-free colored link = fail' heuristic would false-positive here, while a 1.4.3-only tool stays silent either way because it never measures link-vs-text contrast. Correctly clearing the page requires computing the 3.91:1 link-vs-text lightness ratio and applying the 3:1 escape hatch — guarding against over-reporting.

citation.quote: Because the blue text is light enough, it has a contrast of 3.9:1 with the surrounding text and can be identified as being different from the surrounding text by people with all types of color vision deficiency, including those individuals who cannot see color at all.

pages.scenario: TRUE-NEGATIVE (INAPPLICABLE / non-applicability boundary). Bank Acceptable Use Policy. Three inline clause hyperlinks (.inline-ref) are styled identical to neighboring static text: same color #202124, same weight, no underline, no hover/focus change. A normal blue underlined footer link is a distractor.
pages.mechanism: Link color equals body color (1.00:1), so there is NO color differentiation between the actionable hyperlink and adjacent static text for anyone — full-color, color-blind, or grayscale. 1.4.1 protects information conveyed by color; here color conveys nothing about the link, so a color-blind user is at no disadvantage. Programmatic link-discoverability for AT is governed by 1.3.1/4.1.2, not 1.4.1.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A naive 'colored link without underline = fail' heuristic would mis-flag this; a 1.4.3 tool stays silent. Correctly classifying it as inapplicable requires recognizing link color equals body color (no color differentiation exists) and applying the Understanding note's non-applicability rule — distinguishing color-only differentiation that fails from no color differentiation at all.

citation.quote: For instance, a hyperlink which has been styled to appear no different than neighboring static text would not fail this success criterion, as there would be no color differentiation between the actionable hyperlink text and the adjacent static text.

aspects.title: Required form fields indicated by color alone, with self-referential or absent text instruction
aspects.plain: A form marks required fields only by red color (and any instruction just says 'required fields are red'), so a color-blind user can't tell which are mandatory.
aspects.description: A form marks required fields by coloring their labels (e.g. red) or adding a colored border, with NO asterisk, no '(required)', no icon, and no per-field text cue. The trap that demands human judgment: there may be a general instruction at the top, but it is itself color-keyed ('Required fields are shown in red') — which is useless to someone who cannot perceive red, since it never lets them identify WHICH specific fields are required. An evaluator must (1) see that color is the only visual distinction between required and optional labels, (2) confirm no per-field non-color cue exists, and (3) judge whether any general instruction genuinely RESOLVES which fields are required for a color-blind user, rather than merely mentioning the color rule. 'Required fields are red' passes a literal text-present check yet still fails because the alternative is self-referentially color-dependent.
aspects.scLimb: conveying information (LIMB 1) — 'required fields are red'
aspects.whyUncovered: 0 ACT cases for 1.4.1. Checkers may detect a missing required attribute (a separate 1.3.1/3.3.x concern that does NOT satisfy 1.4.1's VISIBLE-alternative requirement), but no automated rule judges whether the visible required-vs-optional distinction is color-only, nor whether a prose instruction effectively resolves the ambiguity for a color-blind user. The self-referential-instruction failure ('required fields are red' is itself color-keyed) is a pure semantic judgment.

references.quote: To indicate that the phone number field is required, the label "Phone Number" is displayed in a color different from the color used for optional fields, without any other indication that "Phone Number" is a required field. A person with color vision deficiency or low vision may not be able to identify that "Phone Number" is a required field.
The instructions for an online form say, "Required fields are shown in red and marked with (required)." The cue "(required)" is included within the label element.
Examples of information conveyed by color differences: “required fields are red", “error is shown in red", and “Mary's sales are in red, Tom's are in blue".

It would also not fail if the color chosen had sufficient luminosity difference (lightness) from the other text that it would be easily be seen as different if viewed in black and white. A minimum contrast ratio of 3:1 is considered sufficient.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: Volunteer sign-up form (nonprofit/food bank). Required field labels are red (#c62828), optional labels black; that hue difference is the only required-vs-optional distinction. The sole instruction is the self-referential, colour-keyed 'Required fields appear in red' — which never lets a colour-blind user identify WHICH fields are required. No asterisk, no '(required)', no icon, no aria-required.
pages.mechanism: Required fields identified by label colour (hue) only (F81); the 'alternative' instruction is itself colour-keyed and self-referential, so it provides no working visible non-colour means of identifying each required field as 1.4.1 demands.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every label/input is correctly associated and red-on-white passes contrast (5.9:1). No axe/WAVE/Lighthouse rule compares two sets of label colours to infer hue is the sole required differentiator, nor reads the prose 'Required fields appear in red' to judge that, though a text instruction is present, it is circular and never resolves which fields are required for a colour-blind user. It even survives a naive 'is there a required-field instruction?' heuristic — distinguishing a resolving instruction from a self-referential colour-keyed one is pure semantic judgment.

citation.quote: To indicate that the phone number field is required, the label "Phone Number" is displayed in a color different from the color used for optional fields, without any other indication that "Phone Number" is a required field. A person with color vision deficiency or low vision may not be able to identify that "Phone Number" is a required field.

pages.scenario: Job-application form (ATS / job board). Required fields are flagged ONLY by a 3px red left-border on the input/select control itself (.field--required → border-left:3px solid #d32f2f); optional fields keep a plain grey border. No asterisk, no '(required)', no icon, no aria-required, and not even an instruction telling the user the red edge means 'required'. The hue of one edge of the box is the entire signal.
pages.mechanism: Required fields identified by a colour difference only — a coloured border on the control (F81) — with no non-colour cue and no explanatory legend; in greyscale the red and grey edges collapse to near-identical lines, erasing the only differentiator.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Each control has an associated label and accessible name and text contrast passes; the markup is well-formed. No automated rule reads a coloured border on a form control, infers it encodes 'required', and checks for a non-colour equivalent. A 3px coloured border-left is an ordinary decorative style — tools cannot know it carries semantic meaning, let alone that the meaning is colour-only and unstated. Detecting it requires perceiving the rendered controls and reasoning about what the red edge signifies.

citation.quote: For all required fields or error fields in the web page that are identified using color differences: 1. Check that an non-color way to identify the required field or error field is provided.

pages.scenario: Healthcare new-patient intake form. Required fields DO get a marker — a red bullet '•' via .f.req label::before — so a naive 'is a marker present?' check passes. The trap: the identical red bullet glyph (content:'•'; color:#c0392b) is reused decoratively as the list marker on the adjacent 'What to bring' checklist. The required-marker bullet and the decorative bullet are the same glyph in the same red; only colour-keyed context plus the legend 'Fields marked with a red dot are required' tells them apart.
pages.mechanism: The required marker is differentiated from decorative content by colour only (F81), a layered ambiguity where the 'non-colour cue' (a bullet) is itself reused as decoration, so hue is the sole disambiguator; the CSS ::before content is also absent from the accessibility tree.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: It is engineered to defeat the obvious heuristic: a marker glyph IS present next to required fields, satisfying any 'does a non-colour cue exist?' check. CSS ::before content is invisible to axe/WAVE/Lighthouse (not read into the accessibility tree), and even seeing both bullets a tool could not reason that the required marker is indistinguishable from a decorative one except by colour/position, nor that a legend saying 'a red dot' fails to resolve which dots are required. Two visually identical glyphs carrying different meanings separated only by hue is a visual-semantic judgment no scanner performs.

citation.quote: This objective of this technique is to describe the failure that occurs when a required field or an error field is marked with color differences only, without an alternate way to identify the required field or error field.

pages.scenario: Multi-section auto-insurance quote wizard (Step 2 of 4). The 'Driver details' section is correct — required labels are red AND carry '(required)' text per G205. The 'Vehicle details' section fails — required labels (Make, Model, Model year, VIN) are the SAME red but have no '(required)', no asterisk, no aria-required. A single top instruction 'Required fields are marked in red' is colour-keyed and does not resolve the Vehicle fields. Forces per-field, not global, judgment.
pages.mechanism: F81 in one section only: a partially-correct page where the Vehicle section's required cue is colour-only while the Driver section satisfies G205, so a correct verdict requires per-section inspection and the page fails on the Vehicle section.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Both sections are structurally identical, valid, fully-labelled forms; the only differences are section 2's missing '(required)' text and the label colour. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse do not read label prose to notice one group includes '(required)' while the other's red labels do not, and have no rule inferring the page fails because one section's required indicator is colour-only. A tool would pass the whole page or treat both sections identically — it cannot make the per-section, read-the-words distinction the SC requires.

citation.quote: The instructions for an online form say, "Required fields are shown in red and marked with (required)." The cue "(required)" is included within the label element.

pages.scenario: TRUE-NEGATIVE. University course-registration form. Required fields are red AND every required label contains the explicit text cue '(required)' (e.g. 'Student ID (required)'), backed by an at-top legend 'Required fields are shown in red and marked with (required)', plus aria-required='true'. Colour is redundant, not the sole means — implements G205 correctly. Should PASS.
pages.mechanism: G205 satisfied: a visible non-colour textual cue ('(required)') identifies every required field, so use-of-colour is redundant and the required/optional distinction survives greyscale, colour-vision deficiency, and screen-reader announcement; meets 1.4.1.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: This case targets a false positive an over-eager rule would produce: a heuristic that flags 'required labels rendered in red' would wrongly fail it. Automated tools generally do not attempt the use-of-colour judgment at all, so they neither pass nor fail it on 1.4.1 grounds — but a human/LLM evaluator must recognise the '(required)' text is a genuine non-colour alternative and NOT flag it. Its value is confirming the evaluator applies the G205 escape instead of failing any red cue on sight.

citation.quote: A form contains both required and optional fields. Instructions at the top of the form explain that required fields are labeled with red text and also with an icon. Users who cannot perceive the difference between the optional field labels and the red labels for the required fields will still be able to see the icon next to the red labels.

pages.scenario: TRUE-NEGATIVE via the lightness escape hatch. Developer-console 'Create API key' form. Required labels are green (#2e8b2e), optional labels charcoal (#222). No '(required)' text — but the two colours differ in BOTH hue and lightness: their inter-colour contrast is ~3.67:1 (>=3:1), green-on-white is 4.33:1 and charcoal-on-white 15.9:1. The required/optional distinction survives greyscale as a light-vs-dark difference. Should PASS via the escape hatch.
pages.mechanism: The two label colours differ in lightness by a contrast ratio >=3:1, which the 1.4.1 Understanding note counts as an additional visual distinction, so the distinction is not hue-only; passes 1.4.1 even with no text cue (aria-required absence is a separate 1.3.1/3.3.2 matter, not 1.4.1).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: This is the boundary an over-eager rule gets wrong: a heuristic failing any 'colour-coded required field' would wrongly fail it. Automated tools do not compute the luminance difference BETWEEN two label foreground colours and apply the 3:1 escape-hatch from the 1.4.1 Understanding note — they only check foreground-vs-background contrast for 1.4.3. So a tool cannot affirm the pass for the right reason, and a naive judge might fail it. Passing correctly requires computing the inter-label contrast ratio and knowing the escape-hatch rule — a quantitative plus interpretive judgment.

citation.quote: If content is conveyed through the use of colors that differ not only in their hue, but that also have a significant difference in lightness, then this counts as an additional visual distinction, as long as the difference in relative luminance between the colors leads to a contrast ratio of 3:1 or greater. For example, a light green and a dark red differ both by color (hue) and by lightness, so they would pass if the contrast ratio is at least 3:1.

aspects.title: Error / validation feedback conveyed by color alone (red border or red text only) in the post-submit state
aspects.plain: After a failed submit, a wrong field is marked only by a red border or text, with no icon or message, so a color-blind user can't find it.
aspects.description: After a failed submit (or during inline validation), fields that failed are outlined or tinted red, or have their label turned red, with NO error icon, NO inline error message, and NO '(error)' marker — the only signal that THIS field is wrong is its hue. Per F81 and Trusted Tester, an error indicator cannot use color alone. An evaluator must reach/observe the dynamic post-validation state, notice the erroring field is distinguished from valid fields purely by color, and confirm no adjacent non-color error cue exists. This is the 'prompting a response' limb (highlighting a field to prompt correction). Crucially, programmatic exposure via aria-invalid does NOT satisfy 1.4.1, which requires a VISIBLE alternative for sighted color-blind users who are not using AT.
aspects.scLimb: prompting a response (LIMB 3) — 'error is shown in red' / highlighting a field that needs correction; AT-decoupling note
aspects.whyUncovered: 0 ACT cases for 1.4.1. The error state is dynamic (appears after a failed submit), beyond static-page scanners. Even with the state rendered, no automated rule classifies a red border/text as an error indicator (vs decoration) or verifies a non-color error cue exists. aria-invalid presence (4.1.2/3.3.1) is a different, programmatic concern that explicitly does NOT satisfy 1.4.1's visible-alternative requirement — a distinction only a human applying the AT-decoupling note makes.

references.quote: A user submits an online form and leaves a required field blank, resulting in an error. The form field that caused the error is indicated by red text only, without an additional non-color indication that the field caused an error.
An error indicator cannot use color alone as an indicator.
An example of prompting a response would be: using highlighting on form fields to indicate that a required field had been left blank.

Conversely, even if information that is conveyed by color differences is appropriately conveyed to assistive technologies, it does not necessarily pass this criterion, as sighted users who cannot distinguish between certain color may not necessarily be using any assistive technologies. This criterion requires a visible alternative to color.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: Corporate timesheet login rendered in the post-submit error state: the failed password field gets a 2px red border while the still-valid email field keeps a 2px gray border. The red (#d92020) and gray (#8a8f94) borders are tuned to near-equal lightness so the grayscale 3:1 escape hatch does not apply. A generic banner ('We couldn't sign you in.') never names the password field; hue is the only per-field signal.
pages.mechanism: F81 error-field-by-color-only: the only per-field cue that the PASSWORD is wrong is its red border hue, with no text/icon/marker; red↔gray luminance delta is below 3:1 so a color-blind/grayscale user cannot distinguish the invalid field from the valid one.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Both inputs have associated labels, a role=alert banner is present, and all text/borders meet contrast against the page, so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse pass. No rule classifies a 2px red border as an error indicator vs decoration, and none computes whether the red↔gray lightness delta clears 3:1 to decide the escape hatch. A human must reach the error state, view it as a color-blind user (or toggle grayscale), and apply F81.

citation.quote: A user submits an online form and leaves a required field blank, resulting in an error. The form field that caused the error is indicated by red text only, without an additional non-color indication that the field caused an error.

pages.scenario: Healthcare new-patient intake form. An inline submit handler (pre-fired on load) marks each empty required field by turning that field's <label> TEXT red (#c01818) while valid labels stay near-black; no inline message, icon, or '(required)/(error)' word is added. A generic summary ('Some required information is still missing.') never names the failing fields. In the rendered state Date of birth and Member ID have red labels.
pages.mechanism: F81 first example: required/error fields identified by label-text color difference only. Seven visually identical bold labels differ only in hue for the two errored ones; per the Understanding note, relying on perceiving 'red for invalid' needs an additional indicator regardless of contrast.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The error state only exists after submit, so static scans never see it; even after submit, every label is correctly associated via for=, all label text exceeds contrast, and a role=alert summary exists, so tools report clean. No rule decides a red label means 'this field errored' or checks for an accompanying non-color cue. Requires triggering submit and reasoning about meaning.

citation.quote: To indicate that the phone number field is required, the label "Phone Number" is displayed in a color different from the color used for optional fields, without any other indication that "Phone Number" is a required field.

pages.scenario: Job-application page in the post-submit state with an error-summary card at the top listing all eight field names as a two-column checklist. The three failing fields (Phone, Years of experience, Cover note) are re-colored red (#cf1d1d); the five passing ones stay gray. No 'Error:' word, icon, or count pairs a field name with the failure — only hue marks which rows failed. The inputs below carry plain borders, so the summary is the sole place the error surfaces.
pages.mechanism: F81 at the summary level: which fields are in error is conveyed purely by red vs gray list-item color; with hue removed the eight items are an undifferentiated list, so a color-blind user cannot tell which three to fix.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The summary is real, contrast-passing text inside a role=alert region and the inputs are labeled; no empty/unlabeled/low-contrast condition exists, so tools pass. No rule understands 'red list item = errored, gray = ok' or verifies a per-item text/icon backs the color. Distinguishing meaning carried by hue from neutral styling is a human semantic judgment in the post-submit state.

citation.quote: This objective of this technique is to describe the failure that occurs when a required field or an error field is marked with color differences only, without an alternate way to identify the required field or error field.

pages.scenario: Webmail 'Change password' panel with live on-type validation. While typing 'Confirm new password', JS toggles a red 2px outline (box-shadow + border #d31f2f) on the confirm field whenever it does not match 'New password'. The describedby hint below ('Must match the new password above.') is a permanent instruction that never changes on mismatch, so it is not an error message. Pre-rendered in the mismatch state. Only the red outline signals the live error.
pages.mechanism: F81 live error-by-color-outline: on mismatch the sole state change is the outline hue; the unchanging describedby text is an unconditional instruction, not a dynamic non-color error cue, so a color-blind user perceives no live signal that the values disagree.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The error is reachable only by typing, and even then the field has a label, a describedby hint, and a contrast-passing CSS outline, so checkers find nothing. No rule classifies the live red outline as the sole error indicator or reasons that the describedby text is a static instruction rather than a dynamic error message. Requires driving the live validation and judging the meaning of the unchanged text.

citation.quote: if content relies on the user's ability to accurately perceive or differentiate a particular color an additional visual indicator will be required regardless of the contrast ratio between those colors. For example, knowing whether an outline is green for valid or red for invalid.

pages.scenario: State SNAP-renewal wizard (Step 2 of 4) in the post-submit state. The failing 'Number of children' field gets a red 2px border AND aria-invalid='true', but no visible error message, icon, or '(error)' marker; a generic banner does not name it. The AT-decoupling trap: programmatic exposure via aria-invalid does NOT satisfy 1.4.1, which requires a visible alternative for sighted color-blind users not using AT.
pages.mechanism: F81 plus AT-decoupling: the only VISIBLE per-field cue is the red border hue; aria-invalid is a programmatic (4.1.2/3.3.1) channel exposed only to AT, so a non-AT color-blind mouse user gets no visible signal which field failed. Per the Understanding note, conveying info to AT does not satisfy 1.4.1's visible-alternative requirement.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: This markup is the kind axe/WAVE/Lighthouse reward: a labeled input carrying aria-invalid='true' looks like a correctly flagged error, so tools report no issue and the ARIA actively reassures them. None evaluate whether a VISIBLE non-color cue exists for a non-AT color-blind user or encode that programmatic exposure does not satisfy 1.4.1. Recognizing the decoupling requires the AT-decoupling note.

citation.quote: even if information that is conveyed by color differences is appropriately conveyed to assistive technologies, it does not necessarily pass this criterion, as sighted users who cannot distinguish between certain color may not necessarily be using any assistive technologies. This criterion requires a visible alternative to color.

pages.scenario: TRUE-NEGATIVE: festival-ticket payment form in the post-submit state where each invalid field (Name on card empty, Expiry in past) gets a red border PLUS a visible inline text message ('Error: enter the name as printed on the card.' / 'Error: this card has expired...') PLUS a warning-triangle SVG icon. Valid fields (card number, CVC) have plain borders and no message. Error identity is conveyed by text + icon shape + position, so the red border is supplementary decoration.
pages.mechanism: G14/G205 sufficient pattern: error information is also available in text and via a non-color icon shape, so the meaning survives grayscale (the triangle and the word 'Error' remain). Color is not the only visual means, so 1.4.1 is satisfied.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Automated tools also pass this page, but only because they see labeled inputs, describedby links, and contrast-passing text — they cannot affirmatively verify the non-color cue is sufficient for a color-blind user; their pass is coincidentally correct. The genuine judgment (does a non-color visible cue exist?) is human; here it is yes, which a tool can only fail to contradict, not establish.

citation.quote: The objective of this technique is to combine color and text or character cues to convey information.

pages.scenario: TRUE-NEGATIVE (long-tail RTL i18n): Arabic (dir=rtl, lang=ar) mobile-banking transfer form in the post-submit state. The invalid 'amount' field gets a DARK-RED border (#7c0c12) while valid fields keep a LIGHT-GRAY border (#c1c7cd); there is still no text or icon. The two border colors differ in relative luminance by ~6.4:1 (verified), far above 3:1, so in grayscale the invalid border reads as a conspicuously darker, heavier line — a non-hue (lightness) distinction. Passes via the escape hatch.
pages.mechanism: Understanding-note lightness escape hatch: the invalid (#7c0c12, very low L*) and valid (#c1c7cd, high L*) borders have a luminance contrast of ~6.4:1, so the distinction is carried by lightness, not hue alone; the dark border stays distinguishable in grayscale, satisfying 1.4.1. (3.3.1/4.1.2 gaps remain but are out of scope.)
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Tools never reach the post-submit state and do not compute border-to-border luminance deltas to evaluate the escape hatch; they would simply pass a labeled input with a CSS border for the wrong reason. The interesting failure mode is a human over-flagging it as F81 like case-01; the correct verdict requires recognizing the lightness delta clears 3:1 (grayscale test), which is exactly the human reasoning probed.

citation.quote: If content is conveyed through the use of colors that differ not only in their hue, but that also have a significant difference in lightness, then this counts as an additional visual distinction, as long as the difference in relative luminance between the colors leads to a contrast ratio of 3:1 or greater.

aspects.title: Informational image/chart HAS a text alternative, but the alt restates the color RULE instead of resolving the color-encoded fact
aspects.plain: A chart's alt text restates the color rule ('red bars are below quota') but never says which items those are, so a blind user misses the color-coded fact.
aspects.description: An informational bitmap or inline SVG (bar chart, line graph, status dashboard, map) uses color to encode a categorical fact, and it HAS a text alternative — but the alt/caption restates the data values and the color rule ('red bars indicate sales below quota') rather than RESOLVING it (naming WHICH employees fell below quota). Because the alt is present and plausible, an automated checker sees a satisfied alt attribute and passes; only a human who reads the alt against the picture sees that the color-borne distinction is never spelled out in text. This is the canonical F13 failure — 'alt exists but under-describes the color-encoded info'. It requires reading the chart pixels, reading the prose, and comparing meaning.
aspects.scLimb: conveying information (LIMB 1) in non-text content — F13
aspects.whyUncovered: 0 ACT cases for 1.4.1. Even where ACT touches alt text (1.1.1), rules only check alt presence/non-emptiness, never whether the alt CONTENT captures a color-encoded distinction inside the bitmap. Distinguishing 'red = below quota, so Mary and Bob failed' (resolved in alt) from 'red bars indicate below-quota sales' (color rule merely restated, names omitted) requires reading the chart, reading the prose, and comparing their meaning — pure semantic judgment no checker performs.

references.quote: The red bars indicate sales that were below the yearly quota". This text alternative fails to provide the information which is conveyed by the color red in the image.
The alternative should indicate which people did not meet the sales quota rather than relying on color.
Check that the information conveyed by color differences is not included in the text alternative for the image.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: SaaS sales-analytics board-pack panel: a bar-chart (inline-SVG data: URI) of four reps' annual sales vs a $3.0M quota. Fred ($2.6M) and Bob ($2.2M) are drawn red (below quota), Mary/Andrew green. The alt lists all four figures and states 'the bars shown in red indicate sales below the yearly quota' but never names Fred and Bob. Canonical F13 case.
pages.mechanism: F13 — alt restates the colour rule ('red = below quota') and all data values but omits the resolved fact (which reps are below quota); below-quota membership exists only as the red fill of the 2nd and 3rd bars in a raster image, reaching neither AT nor colour-blind sighted users.
pages.primarySelector: figure img[alt^="Bar chart of FY24 annual sales"]
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse only verify alt is present and non-empty (it is, and it reads as a long accurate description). No checker OCRs the chart to find which bars are red, parses the alt to confirm Fred/Bob are never named as below quota, and compares the two meanings — the manual F13 read-pixels/read-prose/compare judgment.

citation.quote: This text alternative fails to provide the information which is conveyed by the color red in the image. The alternative should indicate which people did not meet the sales quota rather than relying on color.

pages.scenario: Nonprofit 'where your gift goes' donation breakdown as an inline SVG pie of five colored <path> wedges with no labels. The wedge→program binding lives only in a color-swatch legend; the caption lists all five programs and dollar amounts and says 'the largest wedge, shown in teal, is our biggest commitment' but never states which program teal is (Direct food aid).
pages.mechanism: F13 — the category↔share binding is conveyed solely by matching wedge fill colour to legend swatch colour; the caption restates the rule ('teal is biggest') without resolving which program the teal wedge represents, so the headline ('most of your gift goes to Direct food aid') is unrecoverable without colour vision.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The SVG is role=img with a non-empty aria-label, the legend swatches are aria-hidden decorative spans, and the caption is valid prose — every alt/name rule passes. No scanner can perceive that the wedge↔program binding is carried only by shared fill colours, nor that the caption never spells that binding out in text.

citation.quote: The objective of this technique is to describe the failure that occurs when an image uses color differences to convey information, but the text alternative for the image does not convey that information.

pages.scenario: County emergency-management heat-advisory choropleth MAP as a flattened (inline-SVG data: URI). Two counties under a Severe Heat Warning (Verde, Calloway) are filled red; three are grey. The alt AND a programmatic aria-describedby long description state the colour rule and the 105F threshold but never name the two warned counties.
pages.mechanism: F13 — both the alt and a high-quality long description state the colour rule ('red = Severe Heat Warning') and threshold, but the warned-county membership (Verde, Calloway) is encoded only as the red fill of two polygons; no text or non-colour cue names which counties are in danger.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The has a long non-empty alt AND a valid aria-describedby target, so every alt/name/description rule passes and the page looks like best practice. No scanner reads the map pixels to find the two red polygons, reads the printed names, and verifies those names are absent from the prose — exactly the manual F13 cross-read. Polished metadata that still omits the fact makes it harder for a human reviewer to catch.

citation.quote: Check that the information conveyed by color differences is not included in the text alternative for the image.

pages.scenario: Startup pitch slide: an inline-SVG line graph of monthly revenue (green) vs cost (red) over Jan-Jun. The two lines cross — cost above revenue (loss) Jan-Mar, revenue above cost (profit) Apr-Jun. The aria-label lists every value for both series and says 'revenue is green, cost is red' but never states which line is on top in any month (the profit/loss crossover the chart exists to show).
pages.mechanism: F13 with a temporal/comparative twist — series identity is carried by line colour and the salient fact (which series is higher each month → profit vs loss) by the relative position of the two colour-coded lines; the alt names the colours and all values but never states the comparison, and the near-identical hues are indistinguishable to a red-green colour-blind viewer.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The SVG is role=img with a long aria-label and nothing malformed; scanners confirm a named graphic and stop. No tool traces the two polylines, detects the crossover, decides 'which series is on top' is the salient colour-encoded fact, and checks that the prose never states it — that needs reading the geometry, the comparison the colours set up, the arithmetic, and the prose together.

citation.quote: This can cause problems for people who are blind, have low vision, or have color vision deficiency, because they will not be able to perceive the information conveyed by the color differences.

pages.scenario: SRE incident runbook embeds a service-health dashboard screenshot (inline-SVG data: URI): a 4x2 grid of service tiles where green = healthy, red = down. auth-gateway and payments-worker are red. The alt names all eight services and states the rule; an aria-describedby long description even says 'two of the eight services are currently down' but never names which two.
pages.mechanism: F13 — the alt and long description list every service, state the colour rule, and even give the COUNT of down services, but the down-services membership (auth-gateway, payments-worker) is encoded only as the red fill of two tiles; the runbook step 'page the owner of each down service' is unactionable for AT and colour-blind users.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The has a rich non-empty alt and an associated aria-describedby description; axe/WAVE/Lighthouse pass every alt/name/description rule and would rate the markup as good practice. No scanner reads the screenshot pixels to find the two red tiles, reads their names, and confirms those names are absent from the prose. Stating the count without the identities is invisible to automation.

citation.quote:
When color is used to convey information, indicate an action, prompt a response, or distinguish a visual
element, another visual, **onscreen** method is used to convey the information which does not use color.

pages.scenario: TRUE NEGATIVE / PASS boundary: the same sales bar chart as case-01 (four reps vs a $3.0M quota, below-quota bars red), but as an inline SVG whose aria-label RESOLVES the fact ('Fred and Bob are the two who fell below the quota; Mary and Andrew met it'). The caption repeats it in bold visible text, a data table repeats it, and the below-quota bars carry non-colour cues (a '▼ below quota' tag and a hatch pattern), making colour redundant.
pages.mechanism: Satisfies G14 — the colour-encoded fact (who is below quota) is conveyed in text (accessible name, caption, table) and via non-colour visible cues (▼ tag, hatch), so no user must perceive red. The inverse of F13; colour is a redundant enhancement, exactly what WCAG permits.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: This PASS is statically near-identical to case-01's FAIL — both are inline graphics with role=img and a long accessible name, and both pass every automated check identically. Automation cannot read either alt against the rendered chart to judge whether the colour-encoded fact is resolved in text; only a human can see case-06 names Fred and Bob (pass) while case-01 only restates 'red = below quota' (fail). That indistinguishability is the point of the aspect.

citation.quote: The objective of this technique is to ensure that when color differences are used to convey information, such as required form fields, the information conveyed by the color differences are also conveyed explicitly in text.

aspects.title: Color-coded charts, maps, diagrams and game pieces distinguished by color with no pattern, icon, or in-graphic label (G111)
aspects.plain: A chart, map, or diagram tells categories apart only by fill color with no patterns, shapes, or labels, so a color-blind user can't distinguish the routes or series.
aspects.description: Non-text graphics rely on solid color to distinguish categories — transit-map routes by color only, a bar/area chart whose series are told apart only by fill color matched to a color-only legend, a flow chart using green-background = pass / red-background = fail with no shape/label difference, an SVG diagram whose elements are identified by color with no number/legend pairing, or game pieces distinguished by color alone. Per G111 the fix is to ADD a pattern (hatching, dots, dashes), a distinct icon/shape, or an in-graphic text/number label so the same information survives without color. An evaluator must read the graphic, identify each color-coded category, and confirm no non-color visual encoding redundantly carries the same distinction. This differs from the F13-alt aspect: here the question is the in-graphic VISUAL encoding (pattern/shape), not whether a sibling alt text resolves it.
aspects.scLimb: distinguishing a visual element (LIMB 4) in non-text content — G111 (the 'and pattern' technique)
aspects.whyUncovered: 0 ACT cases for 1.4.1. No automated checker can render a chart/map/diagram, segment its color regions, and decide whether each color-coded category ALSO carries a pattern, icon, shape, or in-graphic label. Recognizing that a transit-line color or a chart-series fill is the SOLE distinguishing cue — and that the legend itself is color-keyed — is a visual-semantic judgment.

references.quote: The objective of this technique is to ensure that when color differences are used to convey information within non-text content, patterns are included to convey the same information in a manner that does not depend on color.

An on-line map of a transportation system displays each route in a different color. The stops on each route are marked with a distinctive icon such as a diamond, square, or circle to help differentiate each route.
Check that all information that is conveyed using color is also conveyed using patterns that do not rely on color.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: Inline-SVG transit/metro network map (Riverside Metro) with three routes (Crosstown/Harborline/Parkway) drawn as polylines that differ only by stroke color; every station on every line is an identical white dot, and the legend keys each route name to a solid colored swatch with no pattern, shape, icon, or in-line label.
pages.mechanism: Route category is conveyed by line hue alone with no redundant non-color encoding; under CVD/grayscale the three strokes and color-only legend swatches collapse to near-identical greys and the identical dot stations give no fallback, so a sighted user who cannot distinguish color cannot follow a single route or match it to the legend (G111 'color + pattern/icon' not satisfied).
pages.primarySelector: svg polyline[stroke="#0b8457"], svg polyline[stroke="#c0392b"], svg polyline[stroke="#2e86c1"]
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Markup is fully valid: descriptive SVG aria-label, non-empty title, each line color clears 3:1 vs the white background, no missing alt/name attributes. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse find no violation. They cannot rasterize the SVG, segment the overlapping polylines, recognize hue is the sole route differentiator, and confirm the legend is color-keyed with no shape/icon — a visual-semantic judgment.

citation.quote: An on-line map of a transportation system displays each route in a different color. The stops on each route are marked with a distinctive icon such as a diamond, square, or circle to help differentiate each route.

pages.scenario: FinOps dashboard stacked area chart of Q3 cloud spend across four services (Compute/Storage/Networking/Database); the four stacked bands are distinguished only by solid fill color, matched to a swatch-only legend, with no hatch/dot/dash pattern, no direct in-chart band label, and no number keying a band to the legend.
pages.mechanism: Series identity is encoded purely by fill hue; a red-green CVD user cannot separate Storage (red) from Networking (teal) and in grayscale all four bands reduce to similar mid-tone greys, so neither the series nor its mapping to the color-keyed legend survives — no pattern/label redundantly carries the distinction (G111 not met).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: No missing-attribute or contrast violation exists: the SVG has a descriptive aria-label, the title is present, legend text is real, and every fill clears 3:1 against the dark plot. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse pass. They cannot render the stacked chart, identify four categories encoded only by fill hue, see the legend is color-keyed, and judge the distinction vanishes under CVD/grayscale.

citation.quote: A real estate site provides a bar chart of average housing prices in several regions of the United States. The bar for each region is displayed with a different solid color and a different pattern. The legend uses the same colors and patterns to identify each bar.

pages.scenario: CI/CD release-pipeline flow diagram (six sequential stage boxes connected by arrows) where pass/fail status is conveyed solely by box background tint (mint = passed, pink = failed); boxes are otherwise identical in shape/border/size/text and the stage text never states 'passed' or 'failed', with no check/cross icon, status word, border change, or pattern.
pages.mechanism: The boolean pass/fail outcome is carried by background hue alone; identical box shape/border/text means a CVD user, monochrome display, or grayscale screenshot shows six near-identical boxes and cannot tell which stages broke the build — Trusted Tester is explicit that an error indicator cannot use color alone, and G111's flow-chart example pairs color with a distinct line style and wording, both absent here.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Each box is well-formed with real text, no missing labels, and text contrast vs each tint exceeds 4.5:1; the container even has a descriptive aria-label. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse find nothing. No checker can render the pipeline, recognize the two tints encode pass/fail, verify nothing else carries that semantic, and conclude it collapses in grayscale.

citation.quote: An **error indicator cannot use color alone** as an indicator.

pages.scenario: Chemistry worksheet with an inline-SVG ball-and-stick ethanol model where each atom is identified ONLY by sphere color (CPK: dark=carbon, red=oxygen, light=hydrogen) keyed to a color-only legend; there is no element symbol, number, or in-image label, and the graded questions ask the student to count oxygen atoms and name the rightmost atom.
