pages.mechanism: Atom (element) identity is conveyed by sphere hue with no redundant symbol/number; a red-green CVD student cannot separate the red oxygen from the dark carbons, and in grayscale carbon (dark grey) and oxygen (mid grey) collapse toward each other with no numeric fallback, making Q1/Q2 unsolvable — this is the deliberate inverse of the WCAG Understanding 'examination' pass example.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The document is valid: descriptive SVG aria-label, labelled form inputs, present title, adequate contrast. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse pass. They cannot render the molecule, recognize identity is encoded purely by CPK color with no in-image symbol/number, cross-check the color-keyed legend, and judge the assessment unsolvable without color vision — nor distinguish it from the passing case-07.

citation.quote: Students view an SVG image of a chemical compound and identify the chemical elements present based strong on the colors used, as well as numbers next to each element. A legend shows the color and number for each type of element. Sighted users who cannot perceive all the color differences can still understand the image by relying on the numbers.

pages.scenario: Conference schedule grid (DevConf 2026, two rooms) rendered as a semantic data table where each session's track (Platform & Data / Frontend / AI & ML) is conveyed solely by cell background tint keyed to a swatch-only legend; cell text gives only title and speaker, with no T1/T2/T3 code, icon, border, or pattern — the G14 color-coded-schedule example with the text track code removed.
pages.mechanism: Track membership is carried by cell background hue alone; a CVD delegate cannot separate the blue/green/yellow tints (and the three pale pastels are near-identical in grayscale), so they cannot tell which sessions belong to a track — the G14 schedule example appends 'T1/T2/T3' text precisely to avoid this, and its absence is the failure.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The table is a model of good markup (caption, th scope, real session text) and title text clears 4.5:1 against every pastel; axe/WAVE/Lighthouse pass and may reward the table semantics. No checker can render the grid, learn the tints encode three tracks, confirm the legend is color-keyed, and notice no text code/icon/pattern backs the color.

citation.quote: Sessions for Track 1 are displayed over a blue background. Sessions in Track 2 are displayed over a yellow background. Sessions in Track 3 are displayed on a green background. After the name of each session is a code identifying the track in text: T1 for Track 1, T2 for Track 2, and T3 for Track 3.

pages.scenario: TRUE NEGATIVE: same inline-SVG transit-map pattern as case-01 (Harbor City Tram) but each route is ALSO distinguished by station SHAPE per G111 — Bay line = diamonds, Hill line = squares, Coast line = circles — and the legend names each route by both its shape and name.
pages.mechanism: Route membership is conveyed by two independent visual channels (line color AND station shape); a user who cannot perceive the colors can still follow a single route by its consistent station shape and match it to the shape-labelled legend, so color is not the sole cue and G111 is satisfied — verified to survive grayscale.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: This page passes automated checks, but so would the failing case-01, which differs only in having identical dot stations; axe/WAVE/Lighthouse never evaluate station shape and cannot tell the accessible map from the inaccessible one. Passing it for the RIGHT reason (shape redundantly encodes route, survives grayscale) requires visual-semantic judgment.

citation.quote: The stops on each route are marked with a distinctive icon such as a diamond, square, or circle to help differentiate each route.

pages.scenario: TRUE NEGATIVE: exam-question inline-SVG ball-and-stick model (acetic acid) implementing the canonical WCAG Understanding 'examination' example — each atom carries BOTH a color AND a number drawn inside the sphere (1=Carbon, 2=Oxygen, 3=Hydrogen), the legend gives color AND number per element, and the questions reference atoms by number.
pages.mechanism: Element identity is conveyed by two independent visual channels (sphere color AND an in-image number); a CVD student or grayscale printout user can read the number on each atom, match it to the color+number legend, and answer every number-referenced question, so color is not the sole distinguishing cue — verified to survive grayscale.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Automated checkers pass this page but cannot distinguish it from the failing color-only case-04 (same molecule pattern); they never read the in-sphere number text or evaluate whether identity survives without color, and both pages clear contrast with descriptive aria-labels. Passing it for the right reason requires rendering, reading the numbers, and confirming grayscale solvability.

citation.quote: A legend shows the color and number for each type of element. Sighted users who cannot perceive all the color differences can still understand the image by relying on the numbers.

aspects.title: UI buttons, controls, and color-coded categories signalling action/status by color with no text or character cue (G14)
aspects.plain: A button or status uses color alone to mean go-versus-cancel or success-versus-error, with no distinguishing text, so a color-blind user can't tell which action it is.
aspects.description: Interactive UI conveys an action or a status by color alone with no redundant text/character cue: a green button = proceed / red button = cancel pair where the buttons are not labelled with distinguishing text and the only convention is 'green advances, red cancels'; a color that indicates a link opens in a new window or that a database entry updated successfully; color-coded list items, tabs, or schedule tracks distinguished only by background hue with no in-text code (T1/T2/T3). Per G14 the information conveyed by color differences must ALSO be conveyed explicitly in text (and per G205 the cue must be in the control's programmatic name). An evaluator must identify the action/status the color encodes, then confirm a non-color text/character cue redundantly carries it. This covers the 'indicating an action' limb that the link and form aspects do not.
aspects.scLimb: indicating an action (LIMB 2) and conveying status — G14 / G205 (green Go / red Cancel; color-coded tracks; new-window/updated indicators)
aspects.whyUncovered: 0 ACT cases for 1.4.1. No automated checker can determine that a green-vs-red button pair encodes 'proceed vs cancel' purely by color, or that a category's background hue is the sole carrier of its track/status, and then verify a redundant text cue exists. Mapping a color to its intended action/status meaning and judging whether a text alternative carries the same information is contextual semantic reasoning.

references.quote: An on-line loan application explains that green buttons advance in the process and red buttons cancel the process.

The objective of this technique is to ensure that when color differences are used to convey information, such as required form fields, the information conveyed by the color differences are also conveyed explicitly in text.
Examples of indications of an action include: using color to indicate that a link will open in a new window or that a database entry has been updated successfully.
The text cue must be included as part of the programmatically determinable name for the control.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: Personal-lending 'Confirm your loan application' step with two identically shaped submit buttons both labelled 'Submit'; green = proceed (binding agreement), red = cancel, with the 'green advances, red cancels' convention stated only in body prose. Action encoded by fill colour alone.
pages.mechanism: G14 'indicating an action' limb: the proceed-vs-cancel action is carried only by button background hue (#1f9d55 vs #c8332b); both controls share the identical accessible name 'Submit', so the colour-encoded action is in neither name and there is no non-colour cue on the controls (G205). In grayscale both read 'Submit' as near-identical gray rectangles.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Both are valid <button> elements with non-empty programmatic text ('Submit') that pass name and contrast checks. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse have no model of 'green=proceed, red=cancel', cannot read the convention from a distant paragraph, and cannot judge that the two controls differ only by background-color. Mapping a fill colour to an action and verifying a redundant text cue is contextual reasoning.

citation.doc: WCAG Technique G14 (wcag-techniques/general/G14.html — 'A form with a green submit button')
citation.quote: An on-line loan application explains that green buttons advance in the process and red buttons cancel the process. A form contains a green button containing the text Go. The instructions say "Press the button labeled Go to submit your results and proceed to the next step."

pages.scenario: County Clerk-Recorder resource page where links that open in a new browser tab are coloured teal while same-window links are blue; the 'opens in a new window' action is conveyed by link colour alone, with no '(opens in new window)' text or external-link icon, only a colour-keyed prose footnote.
pages.mechanism: Understanding 1.4.1's named action example ('using color to indicate that a link will open in a new window'): the new-window action is carried solely by a.newwin colour (#1c8a86 vs a.local #14467a), identical underline/weight/size. In grayscale every link is the same dark gray and the new-window action is lost; the teal-referencing footnote does not rescue it.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every <a> has descriptive text and a valid href; teal and blue both clear 4.5:1, so link-name and contrast checks pass. No tool compares two LINK colours, infers that teal specifically encodes opens-in-new-window, and confirms no non-colour cue carries that action — it requires reading the convention and reasoning about meaning.

citation.quote: Examples of indications of an action include: using color to indicate that a link will open in a new window or that a database entry has been updated successfully.

pages.scenario: Pediatric patient portal with an editable immunization-dates table; on 'Save row' an optimistic-UI handler tints the saved <tr> green to confirm the update succeeded, with no 'Saved'/'Updated' word, no checkmark, no timestamp change, and no status message — the green row background is the sole success confirmation.
pages.mechanism: Understanding 1.4.1's 'database entry has been updated successfully' status example: success is conveyed only by tr.saved { background:#d7f0dd } added at runtime; cell text is unchanged. In grayscale a saved medical-record row is indistinguishable from an unsaved one, so the result of a consequential edit cannot be perceived.
pages.selectorNote: Saved status is green tint added by JS; resting rows are the targets, .saved appears on click
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The 'saved' class is added only after a click, so a static scan never sees the changed state; even with it applied the row is a valid <tr> of real text cells with passing contrast. No tool can determine the green background IS the success confirmation and that nothing else carries it — that requires triggering the save and judging the only confirmation is a hue change.

citation.quote: Examples of indications of an action include: using color to indicate that a link will open in a new window or that a database entry has been updated successfully.

pages.scenario: Developer-conference programme grouping sessions into three tracks, where each session card's track is shown ONLY by its background hue (blue/amber/green) with a colour legend but NO per-card 'T1/T2/T3' text code — the canonical G14 colour-coded-schedule example with the text code removed.
pages.mechanism: G14 category-distinction failing variant: the track is carried solely by article.t-core/.t-applied/.t-comm background colour; no card contains a track code or icon. In grayscale every card is the same mid-gray and concurrent sessions in a slot become indistinguishable by track; the colour-keyed legend also requires perceiving the hues.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Each card is a valid <article> with a real heading/speaker/room and all background colours pass 1.4.3. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse have no concept that 'blue background = Track 1' or that the track is information needing a non-colour equivalent. Recognising hue is the sole carrier of the category and that no T-code backs it is human semantic + visual judgment.

citation.quote: Sessions for Track 1 are displayed over a blue background. Sessions in Track 2 are displayed over a yellow background. Sessions in Track 3 are displayed on a green background. After the name of each session is a code identifying the track in text: T1 for Track 1, T2 for Track 2, and T3 for Track 3.

pages.scenario: SaaS notification-settings panel with pill switches whose on/off state is shown only by fill colour (green #5aa86a = ON, grey #979797 = OFF). The knob is centred and fixed (no position cue), there is no ON/OFF text, and the on-vs-off luminance contrast is ~1.0:1 (well below 3:1) so it is a hue-only distinction, not a lightness one.
pages.mechanism: 1.4.1 state failure for the sighted colour-deficient user: role=switch + name + aria-checked are all correct (so it is deliberately NOT a 4.1.2 failure), but the VISIBLE on/off cue is hue alone. With the knob fixed at left:50% and on/off contrast ~1.0:1, the Understanding's 'lightness >=3:1 also counts' allowance does not apply; in grayscale all four toggles are identical.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/Lighthouse confirm role=switch + accessible name + aria-checked and pass it; each pill colour also passes 1.4.3 against the page. No tool computes the contrast BETWEEN the on-colour and the off-colour, nor reasons that with the knob fixed in place colour is the sole visual differentiator of state — a visual judgment about two rendered states, not a markup check.

citation.quote: if content relies on the user's ability to accurately perceive or differentiate a particular color an additional visual indicator will be required regardless of the contrast ratio between those colors. For example, knowing whether an outline is green for valid or red for invalid.

pages.scenario: TRUE NEGATIVE: online-tuition 'Confirm enrolment' step with a green button labelled 'Go' (confirm/charge) and a red button labelled 'Cancel' (discard), with instructions naming the labelled buttons. The canonical G14 sufficient pattern; the passing boundary for case-01's failing 'Submit'/'Submit' pair.
pages.mechanism: G14 satisfied: the action conveyed by green/red is redundantly carried by each control's visible programmatic text ('Go' / 'Cancel') and by instructions referencing those labels. In grayscale the actions stay unambiguous from the labels; a screen reader hears 'Go button' / 'Cancel button'. Colour is decorative reinforcement, not the sole carrier.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A naive tool cannot CERTIFY this pass either — it cannot reason that the colour convention is adequately backed by text. The case exists to verify the evaluator distinguishes a real G14-compliant pattern from the structurally near-identical failing case-01 (two coloured action buttons + prose convention, but both labelled 'Submit').

citation.doc: WCAG Technique G14 (wcag-techniques/general/G14.html — 'A form with a green submit button')
citation.quote: A form contains a green button containing the text Go. The instructions say "Press the button labeled Go to submit your results and proceed to the next step."

pages.scenario: TRUE NEGATIVE: light-rail weekend departures TABLE where service tracks are shown by background hue AND every departure carries an in-text '· T1 / · T2 / · T3' code after the destination, with a legend tying each code to its line. The G14 sufficient colour-coded-schedule pattern; the passing boundary for case-04.
pages.mechanism: G14 satisfied: the track category conveyed by tr.t1/.t2/.t3 background hue is redundantly conveyed by the span.code text ('· T1' etc.) in every destination cell. In grayscale the codes remain legible so the track stays distinguishable; a screen reader hears e.g. 'Harbour Int'l Airport · T2'. Colour is redundant reinforcement.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: As with the other boundary case, a tool cannot CERTIFY the pass — it cannot reason that the '· T2' text adequately backs the colour. The case exists to verify the evaluator separates a genuinely G14-compliant colour-coded schedule from the failing case-04, which uses the same hue-per-track design but omits the text code.

citation.quote: After the name of each session is a code identifying the track in text: T1 for Track 1, T2 for Track 2, and T3 for Track 3.

aspects.title: Scoping boundary cases: 3:1-lightness pass, pure-color reliance fails regardless of contrast, non-applicability, and visited-link exemption
aspects.plain: Borderline color cases a naive 'any color use fails' rule gets wrong: enough lightness difference passes, hue-dependent meaning fails even at high contrast, and visited-link color is exempt.
aspects.description: 1.4.1 has several boundary rules that produce PASS/NOT-APPLICABLE verdicts an over-eager evaluator (or a naive 'any color cue fails' heuristic) would get wrong, and one that produces a FAIL a contrast-only check would miss. (a) 3:1 LIGHTNESS ESCAPE HATCH: colors differing in lightness with a >=3:1 contrast ratio between them count as an additional visual distinction and PASS — the evaluator must compute the inter-element lightness ratio, not reflexively fail. (b) PURE-COLOR RELIANCE STILL FAILS regardless of contrast: if meaning depends on perceiving a particular hue (green outline = valid vs red = invalid), an additional indicator is required EVEN IF the two colors have high contrast with each other. (c) NON-APPLICABILITY: where color conveys NO information (a hyperlink styled identically to surrounding static text), 1.4.1 does not apply and there is no failure. (d) VISITED-LINK EXEMPTION: color-alone distinction of visited vs unvisited links does NOT fail, even below 3:1. Each requires applying a specific WCAG rule rather than a blanket judgment.
aspects.scLimb: all four limbs via the scoping notes: 3:1 lightness escape hatch; pure-color reliance regardless of contrast; non-applicability when color conveys nothing; visited-link exemption
aspects.whyUncovered: 0 ACT cases for 1.4.1, so none of these boundaries is exercised. They are precisely the cases where naive automation goes wrong: a tool that flags any color cue would false-positive on the 3:1-lightness pass, the non-applicable identical-link, and the visited-link case; while the 'high contrast between two hues still fails if meaning depends on the hue' rule (green-valid vs red-invalid) is a subtlety no contrast checker models. Each demands applying a specific WCAG rule with human judgment about whether color is carrying meaning and which exemption governs.

references.quote: If content is conveyed through the use of colors that differ not only in their hue, but that also have a significant difference in lightness, then this counts as an additional visual distinction, as long as the difference in relative luminance between the colors leads to a contrast ratio of 3:1 or greater.

However, if content relies on the user's ability to accurately perceive or differentiate a particular color an additional visual indicator will be required regardless of the contrast ratio between those colors. For example, knowing whether an outline is green for valid or red for invalid.

a hyperlink which has been styled to appear no different than neighboring static text would not fail this success criterion, as there would be no color differentiation between the actionable hyperlink text and the adjacent static text.
Where color alone distinguishes between visited and unvisited links, it does not result in a failure of this Success Criterion, even where the contrast between the two link colors is below 3:1.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: Retail-banking transaction list where credits are light-green and debits are dark-red text (large-bold). The two foreground colours differ in hue AND by ~3.15:1 in lightness between each other, so the lightness difference is an additional visual distinction and the page PASSES via the escape hatch (a naive 'colour cue = fail' would wrongly flag it).
pages.mechanism: Credit/debit direction is signalled by colour, but the two foregrounds (light green #3a9d4e vs dark red #7a1414) have ~3.15:1 contrast WITH EACH OTHER, at/above the 3:1 threshold, so the lightness difference survives greyscale/colour-blindness and counts as an additional visual distinction. Each colour also meets SC 1.4.3 against white (green 3.44:1 as large-bold text, red 10.84:1), so contrast minimums are not the issue.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse compute each foreground's contrast against its BACKGROUND (1.4.3) but never the INTER-element lightness ratio between two foregrounds carrying meaning, so they cannot recognise that the >=3:1 green-vs-red lightness difference discharges 1.4.1. A naive 'colour-coded column = use-of-colour failure' heuristic false-positives; the correct PASS requires computing that ratio and applying the specific escape-hatch rule.

citation.quote: If content is conveyed through the use of colors that differ not only in their hue, but that also have a significant difference in lightness, then this counts as an additional visual distinction, as long as the difference in relative luminance between the colors leads to a contrast ratio of 3:1 or greater. For example, a light green and a dark red differ both by color (hue) and by lightness, so they would pass if the contrast ratio is at least 3:1.

pages.scenario: Restaurant lunch menu where dish spice level is conveyed solely by dish-name colour (green = mild, red = spicy) with the two hues deliberately at the SAME lightness (~1.06:1 between them) and no icon/word per dish. The discriminating twin of case-01: same concept, no lightness gap, so it FAILS.
pages.mechanism: Spice category is encoded only in the hue of the dish name. The mild green #2e7d32 and hot red #c0392b sit at the same lightness, so their inter-element contrast is ~1.06:1 (no lightness escape hatch). A user with deuteranopia/protanopia or viewing in greyscale sees both at identical darkness and cannot tell mild from spicy. The legend merely re-states the colour code. Each colour passes 1.4.3 (~5:1 vs the cream page), so this is purely use-of-colour, not contrast.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every colour passes SC 1.4.3 against the background, so contrast checkers report nothing. No automated rule detects that two foreground hues at the same lightness are the sole carrier of a semantic category, nor that the colour legend fails to rescue colour-blind users. Recognising the green/red encodes spice level requires reading the menu's meaning and reasoning about colour perception.

citation.quote: Displaying content in grayscale may help identify content that uses only color to convey information.

pages.scenario: Reviewed job-application form where each field's validity is shown by outline colour only: light-green border = accepted, dark-red border = needs attention. The two outline colours have ~6.4:1 mutual contrast (well above 3:1), so the lightness gap is large, yet it still FAILS because the meaning depends on perceiving WHICH hue.
pages.mechanism: Field validity (accepted vs needs-attention) is communicated solely by border hue (green #86d98f vs dark red #7a1414). Per the Understanding note, when content relies on differentiating a particular colour an additional indicator is required REGARDLESS of the ~6.4:1 contrast between the colours. There is no check/alert icon, no 'Looks good'/'Required' text, no message, and no aria-invalid, so a red-green colour-blind user cannot tell which fields still need fixing.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Inputs are properly labelled, the 2px borders pass SC 1.4.11 non-text contrast, and the markup is valid, so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse find no errors. No rule models 'the outline hue is the only thing distinguishing valid from invalid,' and the large >=3:1 inter-element contrast would actively mislead a tool or hasty human into thinking the lightness escape hatch applies. Catching it requires applying the pure-colour-reliance rule that hue-dependent meaning fails irrespective of contrast.

citation.quote: However, if content relies on the user's ability to accurately perceive or differentiate a particular color an additional visual indicator will be required regardless of the contrast ratio between those colors. For example, knowing whether an outline is green for valid or red for invalid.

pages.scenario: Government council cookie-and-tracking policy whose inline links are styled to look exactly like the surrounding static text (inherited colour, no underline at rest). Because colour is not used to distinguish the link from static text at all, SC 1.4.1 does not apply — there is no use-of-colour failure (NOT-APPLICABLE / pass).
pages.mechanism: For 1.4.1 the question is whether colour conveys information. The inline links inherit the body colour (#222) identical to the adjacent static text, so colour is not being used to distinguish the actionable link from the static text. The criterion's scope therefore excludes these links. This is distinct from F73, which fails when a link IS distinguished by colour but lacks a non-colour cue; here the link is not distinguished by colour at all.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A naive 'inline links should be underlined' or 'any link colour cue needs a backup' heuristic flags these links. Correctly classifying this requires recognising that colour conveys NOTHING here (link and text share one colour), which removes them from 1.4.1's scope — a scoping judgement no linter performs. The hover/focus underline further confuses a static scan, and distinguishing not-applicable from a genuine F73 failure is a human call.

citation.quote: This criterion does not apply to situations where color has not been used to convey information, indicate an action, prompt a response or distinguish a visual element. For instance, a hyperlink which has been styled to appear no different than neighboring static text would not fail this success criterion, as there would be no color differentiation between the actionable hyperlink text and the adjacent static text.

pages.scenario: Newsroom investigations archive where article links are underlined (distinguished from static text by a non-colour cue) and visited vs unvisited links differ by colour only, with ~1.09:1 contrast between the two link colours (below 3:1). PASSES via the visited-link exemption.
pages.mechanism: Links are distinguished from static text by an UNDERLINE (no F73 failure on the link-vs-text axis). The only colour-only distinction is visited (purple #5a3da8) vs unvisited (blue #1a52b5) at ~1.09:1, below 3:1. The Understanding note exempts colour-only visited/unvisited distinction even below 3:1, because the :visited pseudo-class is constrained to colour for privacy and conveying visited state is not an author responsibility. Both link colours still meet SC 1.4.3 against the page (~7:1).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A tool that measures :link vs :visited contrast and finds it below 3:1 might naively flag a use-of-colour or contrast problem. The correct verdict requires knowing the specific visited-link exemption — that conveying visited status is not an author responsibility because :visited is restricted to colour for privacy — which no checker encodes. Distinguishing this from a genuine F73 also requires confirming the underline carries the link-vs-text role.

citation.quote: Where color alone distinguishes between visited and unvisited links, it does not result in a failure of this Success Criterion, even where the contrast between the two link colors is below 3:1. Note that authors must continue to ensure that all text links meet contrast minimums against the page background (SC 1.4.3).

pages.scenario: Cinema showtime picker (radio-as-pills) where the chosen showtime is distinguished by inverting the pill's foreground and background (unselected dark-text-on-white; selected white-text-on-dark). The inversion is an additional visual distinction with ~15.7:1 lightness difference, so it PASSES.
pages.mechanism: The selected state reverses the pill's foreground and background colours rather than tinting it. This is not a hue cue: in greyscale the selected pill is a DARK block among LIGHT blocks, differing from the unselected fills by ~15.7:1 in lightness, so it is unmistakable without colour perception. The Understanding note states inversion passes 1.4.1 given sufficient contrast. Selection is also exposed via the native radio's checked state.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: An over-eager 'selected state shown by a colour change = use-of-colour failure' heuristic (the classic swatch/chip anti-pattern that audit tools and naive LLMs flag) false-positives on this pill. Distinguishing a genuine colour-only state cue from an INVERSION carrying an inherent large lightness difference requires comparing the selected and unselected fills and luminances and reasoning that the swap survives greyscale — a visual judgement no checker makes.

citation.quote: Similarly, if content is distinguished by inverting an element's foreground and background colors, this would pass (again, assuming that the foreground and background colors have a sufficient contrast).

pages.scenario: Cloud-platform status console with a 'Region health' matrix where each region/service state (operational/degraded/major outage) is shown only by the hue of an identically-shaped green/amber/red dot. Meaning depends on perceiving the specific hue, so it FAILS; a sibling 'Active incidents' list that adds text badges is the passing contrast.
pages.mechanism: Each health value is encoded only in dot hue (green #3fbf63 / amber #e0a02e / red #e0503e), with identical shape and size and no text/pattern. The dots have ample non-text contrast vs the dark surface (4.8-8.3:1), so this is not a 1.4.11 issue, and the hues are at similar lightness (green/amber ~1.04:1), so no escape hatch applies. Per the Understanding note, reliance on perceiving a particular colour requires an additional indicator regardless of contrast. The legend only re-encodes colour; a colour-blind operator sees a grid of identical dark dots.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The dots are well-formed elements with sufficient non-text contrast, so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse find no error. No rule can tell that a coloured dot ENCODES a status available through no other channel, that the legend doesn't rescue colour-blind users, or that the adjacent text-badge incidents list doesn't cover the matrix. Recognising hue is the sole carrier of 'operational vs degraded vs down' — and that it fails regardless of the dots' contrast — is a semantic/visual judgement.

citation.quote: However, if content relies on the user's ability to accurately perceive or differentiate a particular color an additional visual indicator will be required regardless of the contrast ratio between those colors.

aspects.title: Pure-decoration exemption misjudged: genuinely decorative low-contrast text (must be EXEMPT) vs. meaningful text the author treated as decoration (must MEET contrast)
aspects.plain: Low-contrast text gets misjudged: purely ornamental words are flagged as failures, while faint-but-meaningful content like a price or status watermark is wrongly excused as decoration.
aspects.description: SC 1.4.3 exempts text that is 'pure decoration' / 'decorative and conveys no information.' Understanding's test is semantic: text is decorative only if 'random words... could be rearranged or substituted without changing meaning.' Trusted Tester says to EXCLUDE text that is 'purely decorative and not meaningful (no functionality).' Deciding whether a faint watermark, ghost number, or faded divider conveys information is a meaning judgment a contrast checker cannot make. Two opposite human-judgment traps exist: (1) FALSE POSITIVE — genuine decoration (a mood word, an ornamental repeating glyph) flagged as a failure when it should be exempt; (2) FALSE NEGATIVE — core information (a price, a status watermark) styled faint and 'subtle' that the author rationalizes as decorative but which carries meaning and must meet 4.5:1/3:1. An automated checker sees only the failing ratio in both directions and cannot tell which way to rule.
aspects.scLimb: Pure-decoration / 'decorative and conveys no information' exemption (the meaning-vs-ornament judgment), distinct from the human-language glyph test ACT already covers.
aspects.whyUncovered: The ACT corpus exercises the exemption only via a single non-language glyph ('X' close button) and a single font specimen. It has no case where meaningful prose is rendered at failing contrast yet styled to read as decoration (watermark, ghost step-number, hero mood word), and no case that must be EXEMPTED as genuine decoration. Neither the false-positive nor the false-negative side of the meaning boundary is tested, and no automated checker can resolve it because both produce identical failing ratios.

references.quote: Text that is decorative and conveys no information is excluded. For example, if random words are used to create a background and the words could be rearranged or substituted without changing meaning, then it would be decorative and would not need to meet this criterion.
EXCLUDE text that is: ... Purely decorative and not meaningful (no functionality)

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: Legal document viewer renders a Master Services Agreement with a tiled, rotated, light-gray repeating word 'DRAFT' behind the prose at ~1.56:1. The repeated word states the contract's legal status (unexecuted draft, not the signed final); the themer treats it as decorative paper texture.
pages.mechanism: Meaningful status text styled as a decorative repeated-word background. 'DRAFT' (#cfcfcf on #ffffff = 1.56:1) conveys document status that cannot be rearranged or substituted ('FINAL','VOID') without changing meaning, so it is NOT pure decoration and must meet 4.5:1; at 1.56:1 it fails SC 1.4.3.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A checker can compute 1.56:1 but cannot rule on the exemption: the markup is indistinguishable from a genuine decorative repeated-word background (the Understanding doc's own decoration example), and some scanners suppress rotated/tiled layers as decorative chrome. Deciding 'DRAFT' carries non-substitutable legal status requires reading the word and reasoning about the document — semantic judgment no scanner performs.

citation.quote: Text that is decorative and conveys no information is excluded. For example, if random words are used to create a background and the words could be rearranged or substituted without changing meaning, then it would be decorative and would not need to meet this criterion.

pages.scenario: Trail-running e-commerce hero banner layers a giant pale word 'WANDER' (white at 30% alpha over an inline-SVG landscape) behind the real headline as a pure mood flourish. The informative content (H1, subhead, CTA) is white-on-dark and passes.
pages.mechanism: FALSE-POSITIVE side of the exemption boundary: the giant 'WANDER' is aria-hidden, is not a heading or label, and can be substituted ('EXPLORE','ROAM') or removed with no change in meaning, so it is exempt decoration; its faint white rgba(255,255,255,.30) over an inline-SVG landscape (~1.4-2:1) does not fail 1.4.3. All genuinely informative text (white H1/subhead over solid dark and the CTA) meets contrast, so the page passes.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/Lighthouse measure the ~2:1 ratio of the pale word and would report a contrast violation (or 'needs review' over the photo), but the correct verdict is PASS because the text is exempt decoration. Tools cannot read the word, judge it conveys no information, and confirm it is substitutable/removable — the exact semantic test the exemption hinges on — so they raise a false positive where a human must rule 'exempt'.

citation.quote: Identify ALL text AND images of text. EXCLUDE text that is:

pages.scenario: SaaS pricing page renders each plan's price NUMBER ($19/$49/$99) in pale gray #a3a3a3 on white (2.52:1) as a 'subtle accent', while the surrounding '$', '/mo', 'Billed monthly' and feature list are dark and pass. The price magnitude — the most decision-critical value — is the only failing-contrast text.
pages.mechanism: FALSE-NEGATIVE side: core information styled to read as decorative. The digits are the actual price (19 vs 49 vs 99 are different offers) and cannot be substituted without changing meaning, so they are in scope. At 56px/800 the large-text 3:1 threshold applies but 2.52:1 fails even that.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Two traps stack: surrounding small text all passes so a node-sampling scanner sees mostly green, and the failing element is large-scale text which some tools down-weight. Even a perfect ratio computation cannot decide that the faint big numeral is the price (in-scope information) rather than an ornamental large numeral — recognizing it is core info requires understanding the page is a pricing table, a human semantic judgment.

citation.quote: Text that is decorative and conveys no information is excluded. For example, if random words are used to create a background and the words could be rearranged or substituted without changing meaning, then it would be decorative and would not need to meet this criterion.

pages.scenario: Restaurant menu uses a faint repeated word ('menu · menu · menu ·') as a decorative ornamental rule between sections, #d2d2d2 on cream ~1.5:1. The real section names are the dark <h2> 'Entrées'/'Plats' directly beneath; all item names, descriptions and prices are dark and pass.
pages.mechanism: Genuine pure-decoration case structurally near-identical to case-01's repeated word but with opposite ruling. The divider conveys no information (section identity comes from the dark headings), is aria-hidden, and could be replaced by dots/stars or removed with no change in meaning, so it is exempt; its ~1.5:1 ratio does not fail 1.4.3.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse would compute ~1.5:1 for the divider and report a violation (false positive). They cannot read the repeated word, recognize it as ornament, verify it is substitutable/removable, and confirm the real section names are dark — the exemption is a semantic judgment. The near-identical markup to case-01 with the opposite correct verdict is exactly why no static rule can resolve this aspect.

citation.quote: if random words are used to create a background and the words could be rearranged or substituted without changing meaning, then it would be decorative and would not need to meet this criterion.

pages.scenario: Metra Transit ticket fades the big platform code 'B7' (#c8cdca) into a station-floorplan background-image as a decorative 'map stamp', but it is the sole platform cue on the ticket; over the pale floorplan it is ~1.4:1 down to ~1.1:1 and fails even the 3:1 large-text bar.
pages.mechanism: Meaningful status text styled as a decorative overlay. The big platform code '.platform .code' (#c8cdca) is faded into an inline-SVG station-floorplan background-image as a 'map stamp', yet it is the ONLY place the rider's platform/track is named (the leg list has boarding group, car and fare but no platform). Because it is non-substitutable wayfinding information it is in scope, not pure decoration; eyedroppered over the pale floorplan tones it ranges ~1.4:1 down to ~1.1:1, and at 88px large-scale it fails even the relaxed 3:1 bar.
pages.selectorNote: Platform code B7 faded over floorplan image; orig .step.current .ord does not exist
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The markup and failing ratio are identical to the decorative 'ghost numbers' pattern, so no static rule can separate the two — a checker measures 1.54:1 in both and cannot know that here the numeral is the only step cue versus there it is ornament behind a labelled card. Some scanners also discount large pale numerals as decorative chrome. Resolving it requires reading the layout and noting the absence of any other progress indicator.

citation.quote: Purely decorative and not meaningful (no functionality)

pages.scenario: Invoice has a cancelled line item ($1,800 on-site implementation). The ONLY cancellation signal is a faint rotated 'VOID' stamp across the row, #cdb3b3 ~1.96:1. The row text is full-contrast and NOT struck through, the $1,800 amount is still printed, and the $3,360 total already excludes it — so without reading the stamp the charge looks live. The author treated the stamp as a stylistic overlay.
pages.mechanism: Status-bearing overlay word styled as a faded decorative stamp. 'VOID' conveys non-substitutable financial status (cannot swap for 'PAID' or remove without changing the invoice's meaning), so it is in scope; at 1.96:1 a contrast-impaired user cannot read it and is misled about what they owe — fails 1.4.3.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A checker computes 1.96:1 but cannot decide the exemption: the faint rotated word is visually and structurally identical to a purely decorative 'stamp' graphic designers add for flavor, and many scanners ignore absolutely-positioned rotated overlays as decorative chrome. Ruling it in-scope requires reading 'VOID', recognizing it as the only cancellation cue, and reconciling it against the still-printed $1,800 line and the $3,360 total — multi-step semantic reasoning no tool performs.

citation.quote: Text that is decorative and conveys no information is excluded. For example, if random words are used to create a background and the words could be rearranged or substituted without changing meaning, then it would be decorative and would not need to meet this criterion.

aspects.title: Logotype / brand-name contrast exemption and its loss when the logotype acts as an interactive UI component
aspects.plain: Brand logos are exempt from contrast rules, but the exemption is abused when ordinary styled headings, taglines, or clickable logo-links with poor contrast hide behind it.
aspects.description: 1.4.3 exempts logotypes and brand names from contrast. Trusted Tester excludes 'text that is... In logotypes (logo or brand name).' Understanding warns the exemption 'can be problematic when logos or logotypes act as user interface components (such as a link or other interactive control)' and that 'Corporate identity or brand guidelines beyond logo and logotype are not included in the exception.' Three human judgments are required and none are automatable: (a) is this low-contrast text actually a logotype/brand wordmark versus an ordinary styled heading?; (b) is the wordmark functioning as a live control (home link, button), in which case the brand exemption is eroded and a sufficient-contrast variant is expected?; (c) is adjacent text (tagline, badge) being smuggled under the logo exemption when it is really informative content the brand carve-out does not cover?
aspects.scLimb: Logotype/brand-name exemption — including its erosion when the logo is an interactive control, and the boundary that brand guidelines beyond the logo are not exempt. ACT declares this entire limb out of scope.
aspects.whyUncovered: The 09o5cg rule lists logos/brand names explicitly as an assumption / out of scope; the corpus contains zero logotypes, wordmarks, or low-contrast brand-name links. So neither the legitimate exemption, nor its erosion when the logo is a link, nor the 'beyond the logo' boundary is exercised. An automated checker cannot identify what is a brand name versus a styled heading, so this is irreducibly human.

references.quote: Text used as part of a logo or logotype is exempted from contrast requirements... However, this can be problematic when logos or logotypes act as user interface components (such as a link or other interactive control). In these cases, as a best practice, authors should consider choosing a variant of the logo or logotype that has sufficient text contrast
Corporate identity or brand guidelines beyond logo and logotype are not included in the exception.
EXCLUDE text that is: In logotypes (logo or brand name)

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: B2B industrial fastener site header renders the company wordmark 'acmecorp.com' as live HTML text in brand 'fog teal' (#6ec3b6) on white at ~2.07:1. It is a bare non-interactive <span>, and a separate 'Home' nav item carries the home destination. It is a genuine logotype, so the 1.4.3 logotype exemption applies and the page conforms.
pages.mechanism: Sub-4.5:1 text (~2.07:1, verified in headless render) that is the company logotype/brand name, which SC 1.4.3 explicitly exempts from contrast; the wordmark is a non-interactive span (not a link/button), so it is not acting as a UI component and the exemption is not eroded. This is the control case that defines where the exemption legitimately applies.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe-core/WAVE/Lighthouse compute ~2.07:1 from the CSSOM and emit a FALSE-POSITIVE 1.4.3 violation, because a pixel/CSSOM contrast checker has no concept of 'logotype' and cannot recognize that 'acmecorp.com' in the brand serif at top-left is the company wordmark, nor that it is a bare span rather than a control. Reaching the correct verdict (pass) requires the human judgment 'is this low-contrast text a brand name?' — the determination ACT rule 09o5cg lists as an out-of-scope assumption.

citation.quote: Text used as part of a logo or logotype is exempted from contrast requirements, under the assumption that logos/logotypes must comply with stricter color choices mandated by corporate identity or brand guidelines.

pages.scenario: Project-management SaaS app shell ('Linaro') renders its wordmark as live HTML text in brand 'mist' (#6ec3b6) on white at ~2.07:1, wrapped in <a href='/'> and acting as the ONLY home affordance (no separate Home item, no logo image). The logotype is functioning as an interactive UI component, eroding the brand exemption; a sufficient-contrast variant is expected.
pages.mechanism: The low-contrast text (~2.07:1, verified) is a logotype that is acting as a user-interface component (the sole home link), so per the 1.4.3 Understanding note the brand exemption is eroded and 4.5:1 applies; no sufficient-contrast variant or equivalent control is provided, so a low-vision keyboard user faces an under-contrast operable home control.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A scanner computes ~2.07:1 but cannot supply the reasoning that makes the flag correct: that 'Linaro' is the brand wordmark AND that it is here the only home control. A reviewer trained on 'logotypes are exempt' may wrongly dismiss the flag; the right call requires recognizing the erosion-by-interaction condition. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse model neither 'is this an exempt logotype?' nor 'is the logotype acting as a live UI component?' — both human judgments ACT 09o5cg sets aside.

citation.quote: However, this can be problematic when logos or logotypes act as user interface components (such as a link or other interactive control). In these cases, as a best practice, authors should consider choosing a variant of the logo or logotype that has sufficient text contrast, if allowed by the corporate identity or brand guidelines. Alternatively, authors should consider providing an equivalent user interface component which serves the same purpose and meets contrast requirements.

pages.scenario: Mercato marketplace makes its rose-gold SVG-gradient wordmark (a.brand-home) the sole home link with no separate Home control or logo image, eroding the brand exemption; its least-contrast pixel ~1.91:1 fails even the 3:1 large-text bar.
pages.mechanism: The wordmark 'Mercato' is the page's SOLE home control: an SVG element with a rose-gold linearGradient fill, wrapped in with no separate 'Home' link and no logo . Because the logotype is acting as an interactive UI component, the 1.4.3 brand exemption is eroded and a sufficient-contrast variant is required but absent. The least-contrast pixel (lighter gradient stop #e0b483 on #ffffff) is ~1.91:1; at ~30px bold display it is large-scale, so even the relaxed 3:1 threshold governs and 1.91:1 fails it.
pages.selectorNote: Wordmark is SVG text with gradient fill; orig article h1.headline does not exist
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The <h1> is well-formed and its ~2.05:1 contrast is computable, so a scanner can flag it — but it cannot decide whether the flag should be SUPPRESSED under the logotype exemption. The irreducibly human task is recognizing that a gilt display 'GOLDLEAF' is a styled HEADLINE rather than a brand wordmark (i.e., the exemption must not apply). axe/WAVE/Lighthouse have no model of 'logotype vs. heading that looks like one' — exactly the assumption ACT 09o5cg sets aside; a reviewer who trusts 'brand-name styling = exempt' reaches the wrong answer.

citation.quote: Stylized text, such as in corporate logos, should be treated in terms of its function on the page, which may or may not warrant including the content in the text alternative.

pages.scenario: Conservation charity ('Verdant Trust') footer carries the slogan 'Beyond the brand.™' in the protected brand muted-gold italic (#bfa86f) on cream (#f6f3ee) at ~2.10:1. The brand agency calls it the 'brand essence statement' and treats it as brand identity, so it inherits the logotype exemption. The actual logotype 'Verdant Trust' is full-contrast in the header. A tagline is brand guidance BEYOND the logo, which the exemption does not cover.
pages.mechanism: The sub-4.5:1 text (~2.10:1, verified; large-scale so even the 3:1 threshold fails) is a brand tagline/slogan — corporate identity BEYOND the logo/logotype — which SC 1.4.3's Intent explicitly excludes from the exception. It is ordinary informative text that must clear contrast; a low-vision donor cannot read it.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A scanner computes ~2.10:1 and can flag the slogan as text, but it cannot resolve the only question that matters: does the logotype exemption extend to a tagline? Tools have no model of 'logo vs. broader brand guidelines', and a human applying 'brand-protected color = exempt' would wrongly suppress the flag. Reaching 'failed' requires knowing the carve-out stops at the logo itself — the 'beyond logo and logotype' boundary ACT 09o5cg treats as out of scope.

citation.quote: Corporate identity or brand guidelines beyond logo and logotype are not included in the exception.

pages.scenario: Naseej (نسيج) RTL banking wallet appends a faint 'الرئيسية' (Home) descriptor (.dest, #9aa7b0 ~2.46:1, 13px normal) beside its exempt Arabic wordmark inside one home link; the descriptor is informative text beyond the logo and fails the 4.5:1 normal-text bar.
pages.mechanism: The home link <a class="brand" href="/wallet"> wraps TWO strings: the Arabic wordmark 'نسيج' (.mark, #6cbfb2 on white ~2.16:1) which IS the logotype and is exempt, and an appended descriptor 'الرئيسية' ('Home', .dest, #9aa7b0 on white ~2.46:1, 13px/weight 400). The descriptor is informative wayfinding text — brand-adjacent identity BEYOND the logo/logotype, which the exemption does not reach — so as normal-size text it must meet 4.5:1, and at ~2.46:1 it fails while the wordmark sibling is left exempt.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Two judgments stack beyond a ratio: (1) recognizing the Arabic string 'نسيج' is the bank's wordmark — tools have no cross-script brand dictionary, so they cannot even classify it as a logotype; and (2) recognizing the logotype is the live home link with no sufficient variant, eroding the exemption. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse compute ~2.16:1 but model neither the logotype identity (especially non-Latin) nor erosion-by-interaction — both human judgments ACT 09o5cg sets aside.

citation.quote: However, this can be problematic when logos or logotypes act as user interface components (such as a link or other interactive control). In these cases, as a best practice, authors should consider choosing a variant of the logo or logotype that has sufficient text contrast, if allowed by the corporate identity or brand guidelines. Alternatively, authors should consider providing an equivalent user interface component which serves the same purpose and meets contrast requirements.

pages.scenario: Healthcare patient portal ('Meridian Health') shows a brand lockup with two strings: the wordmark 'Meridian Health' in dark teal (#0c5c50) at ~7.9:1 (passes, and is the exempt logotype) and, glued beside it inside the same lockup, a 'Beta' pill in muted gold (#b6a45f) on white at ~2.48:1. The pill looks like part of the logo but is a product STATUS label (the portal is pre-release), not the logotype, so it is not exempt.
pages.mechanism: The sub-4.5:1 text (~2.48:1, verified) is an informative product STATUS label adjacent to and visually fused with the wordmark, not the logo/logotype itself; brand guidelines beyond the logo are not exempt, so the badge must meet 4.5:1. The genuinely-exempt wordmark sibling passes at ~7.9:1 (verified), isolating the failure to the smuggled status text — a low-vision user cannot read the meaningful 'pre-release' status.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A scanner computes ~2.48:1 for the badge and ~7.9:1 for the wordmark but cannot decide which span is 'the logo' and which is smuggled-in status text. Because the pill sits inside .brand-lockup next to the wordmark, a human applying 'it's in the logo, so it's exempt' would wrongly suppress the flag. The correct answer needs parsing the lockup's composition and the badge's MEANING (a pre-release status indicator) — neither modeled by axe/WAVE/Lighthouse; the judgment-(c) adjacent-text variant ACT 09o5cg leaves out of scope.

citation.quote: Corporate identity or brand guidelines beyond logo and logotype are not included in the exception.

aspects.title: Inactive-UI exemption applies only to GENUINELY inoperable controls, not to operable controls merely styled to look disabled (or aria-disabled controls that still fire)
aspects.plain: A button greyed out to look disabled but still clickable must meet contrast rules, yet checkers can't tell whether the control is truly inactive without operating it.
aspects.description: Inactive UI components are exempt: Understanding says 'User Interface Components that are not available for user interaction... are not required to meet contrast requirements. An inactive user interface component is visible but not currently operable.' Trusted Tester excludes text 'For inactive (disabled) user interface components.' Whether the exemption applies depends on a BEHAVIORAL fact — is the control actually operable? — that contrast checkers (and even most automated tools) cannot infer from color alone. The trap is appearance/behavior mismatch: a button greyed to look disabled (class='disabled', no disabled attr) that still submits on click MUST meet contrast; conversely a control marked aria-disabled='true' but wired to still fire is not genuinely inactive. The judge must drive the control to determine operability, then decide the exemption.
aspects.scLimb: Inactive (disabled) UI-component exemption — specifically the boundary where visual disabled-styling diverges from actual operability. ACT only tests correctly-marked genuinely-disabled widgets.
aspects.whyUncovered: All ACT inapplicable cases use correctly-marked disabled/aria-disabled native widgets that ARE inert. There is no operable control dressed to look disabled (faux-disabled, must MEET contrast), and no aria-disabled control that still fires. The exemption boundary is never stressed by mismatched appearance vs. behavior, and resolving it requires interacting with the page, which static checkers do not do.

references.quote: User Interface Components that are not available for user interaction (e.g., a disabled control in HTML) are not required to meet contrast requirements. An inactive user interface component is visible but not currently operable.
An example would be a submit button at the bottom of a form that is visible but cannot be activated until all the required fields in the form are completed.
EXCLUDE text that is: For inactive (disabled) user interface components

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: Riverside Food Bank volunteer sign-up: the primary 'Submit registration' button is greyed (#9a9a9a on #ededed ≈ 2.4:1) with class="disabled" but NO disabled attribute and a live onclick that really submits. A genuinely disabled twin ('Save draft', native disabled attr) sits beside it in the identical grey — pixel-identical, opposite exemption.
pages.mechanism: The control has no programmatic disabled state (verified: hasDisabledAttr=false, ariaDisabled=null, domDisabledProp=false) and its onclick fires (verified: clicking shows the receipt). Because it is available for user interaction it is an active UI component, so the inactive-UI exemption does not apply and its ≈2.4:1 label text must meet 4.5:1 — it does not.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Contrast scanners commonly exempt anything that looks disabled — axe skips text in disabled subtrees and many tools apply a 'greyed button = inactive = ignore' heuristic. Here there is NO programmatic disabled state at all, so the exemption hinges on a behavioral fact (does the button fire?) that only interaction reveals. A tool keyed on disabled/aria-disabled either flags both grey buttons identically or skips both; neither is correct.

citation.quote: User Interface Components that are not available for user interaction (e.g., a disabled control in HTML) are not required to meet contrast requirements. An inactive user interface component is visible but not currently operable.

pages.scenario: Halcyon Bank 'Send money' screen: focusing #sendBtn and pressing Enter sends the transfer (balance $2,480.00 → $2,330.00) despite aria-disabled=true, so its faux-disabled ≈2.2:1 grey label is in scope and fails.
pages.mechanism: A custom <div role="button" tabindex="0" aria-disabled="true"> ('Send transfer', #sendBtn) is painted pale grey (#a4a4a4 on #eeeeee ≈ 2.2:1) to look inert, but its click and keydown (Enter/Space) handlers are not guarded against the aria-disabled flag, so the control still fires. aria-disabled is an unenforced claim: the component is operable and therefore in scope for 1.4.3, so its ≈2.2:1 label must reach 4.5:1 and fails.
pages.selectorNote: Operable div-button labelled grey; id is sendBtn not applyBtn
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: It is a <div>, not a native control, so the disabled-attribute exemption heuristic never triggers and there is no native-semantics signal; with no aria-disabled either way, a tool cannot decide whether a pale-grey role=button is genuinely inactive (exempt) or merely styled that way. Resolving it requires focusing the div and pressing Enter to observe the balance change — operability by interaction, which static analyzers do not do.

citation.quote: An inactive user interface component is visible but not currently operable. An example would be a submit button at the bottom of a form that is visible but cannot be activated until all the required fields in the form are completed.

pages.scenario: Trellis wiki rich-text editor: a toolbar of labeled chips renders three controls in one shared dim style (#8d8d8d on #f2f2f2 ≈ 3.0:1, 13px bold). Strikethrough and Subscript carry aria-disabled="true" with a guarded handler (genuinely inert, exempt); 'Insert table' looks identical but has no aria-disabled and a live handler that really inserts a 2x2 table.
pages.mechanism: Three visually identical chips split on operability. Verified: clicking 'Insert table' inserts a table (fired=true, no aria-disabled), while clicking Strikethrough does nothing (fired=false, aria-disabled=true, guard returns early). The operable 'Insert table' chip is in scope; its ≈3.0:1 normal-size (13px bold, below large-text threshold) label fails 4.5:1, while the two truly-inert chips are correctly exempt.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: All three chips share the same computed colors and the same .muted class. A scanner that respects aria-disabled correctly skips Strikethrough and Subscript and tends to skip 'Insert table' too — by clustering identical-style siblings or treating an aria-disabled toolbar neighborhood as a disabled group. No tool determines that exactly one of three visually identical chips fires; that requires driving each control.

citation.quote: EXCLUDE text that is:

pages.scenario: Maple & Birch two-step checkout: 'Continue to payment' is genuinely disabled via the native disabled attribute (greyed #9b9b9b on #ededed ≈ 2.4:1) until the shipping form validates, then JS removes disabled and the fill flips to a high-contrast brand color (white on #7a4a1e ≈ 7.4:1). This is the legitimately-exempt boundary case that sharpens the aspect.
pages.mechanism: While disabled the control is truly not available for interaction (verified: domDisabledProp=true; becomes operable only after valid input), matching the Understanding example of a submit gated until required fields complete — so its low-contrast resting label is exempt. When it becomes operable its color is simultaneously raised to ≈7.4:1, so no state presents operable text below 4.5:1. Every other text node (labels, the enabled Back link, helper copy) meets contrast.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: This is the false-positive trap: a naive tool that flags every grey button would wrongly report this exempt control, while one that exempts every grey button would wrongly clear the faux-disabled failures in case-01/02/03. Getting it right requires confirming the control is genuinely inactive (real disabled, not focusable, no reachable handler) — a behavioral determination that forces operability, not color, as the decision rule.

citation.quote: An example would be a submit button at the bottom of a form that is visible but cannot be activated until all the required fields in the form are completed.

pages.scenario: TripNest cookie-consent dark pattern: 'Accept all' is a bright green high-contrast button, while the legally required 'Reject all' is faint grey (#a8a8a8 on #ffffff ≈ 2.4:1) deliberately styled to look disabled/secondary — but it is a fully operable <button> with no disabled/aria-disabled and a live handler that records the rejection.
pages.mechanism: 'Reject all' is operable (verified: clicking it saves 'Non-essential cookies rejected' and dismisses the banner; no disabled state). As an active component its label is in scope for 1.4.3, and at ≈2.4:1 it fails. A low-vision sighted user may not perceive the faint label and assume only 'Accept all' exists, defeating the required choice.
pages.selectorNote: Operable Save-to-library white label over artwork; orig #reject.btn.reject does not exist
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The button is technically valid (real <button>, accessible name 'Reject all', no linter errors). Tools that down-rank or skip 'secondary/disabled-looking' controls may exempt it; tools that measure it cannot distinguish faint-because-decorative/inactive from faint-because-operable-and-in-scope. The deceptive intent and live-consent-control status are revealed only by activating it and observing the rejection saved.

citation.quote: An inactive user interface component is visible but not currently operable.

pages.scenario: Arabic (RTL, lang=ar dir=rtl) e-government residency-renewal portal: the 'تحميل الإيصال' (Download receipt) control is an <a href> link styled dim grey (#9c9c9c on #f4f4f4 ≈ 2.5:1) that carries aria-disabled="true" yet has a live href and click handler that opens the receipt. A truly-inert twin, the 'طباعة' (Print) <button disabled>, sits in the identical grey.
pages.mechanism: aria-disabled is only an unenforced claim: nothing blocks activation, so the link is operable (verified: clicking runs openReceipt and shows the receipt despite ariaDisabled=true). A control that fires is not genuinely inactive, so the exemption does not apply and the ≈2.5:1 Arabic label fails 4.5:1. The 'طباعة' button is natively disabled (domDisabledProp=true), so its identical grey is correctly exempt — same look, opposite verdict.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: This is the hardest direction: the markup explicitly declares aria-disabled="true", so any scanner that trusts ARIA state treats the link as inactive and skips its contrast entirely — a clean false negative. But aria-disabled does not make a link inert; only by activating the link and seeing the receipt open does one learn the claim is false and the control is in scope. No static analyzer drives the link to detect the lie, and the well-formed RTL markup trips no linter.

citation.quote: User Interface Components that are not available for user interaction (e.g., a disabled control in HTML) are not required to meet contrast requirements. An inactive user interface component is visible but not currently operable.

aspects.title: Determining the EFFECTIVE background behind text when color and background come from different tree levels, inherited cascade, z-indexed overlays, or composited semi-transparent layers (F24 cascade limb)
aspects.plain: Figuring out the real colour behind text is hard when it comes from a parent element, an overlapping layer, or a see-through panel, so contrast tools guess wrong.
aspects.description: F24 fails content when a foreground color is specified without a guaranteed background (or vice versa) and stresses that 'It is not necessary that the foreground and background colors both be defined on the same element. Foreground text color is inherited from ancestor elements. If an element's background color has not been defined, the element will have a transparent background, so authors need to ensure that at least one of the element's ancestors has a defined background color.' Color may be set 'at any level in the cascade... by external stylesheets or through inheritance.' Determining what actually renders behind the glyphs — which ancestor's background, which z-indexed sibling overlay, which composited semi-transparent scrim — requires reasoning about the rendered layer stack, not the element's own declared background. This is exactly where naive CSSOM contrast tools mislabel: they read the element's local background (often transparent) and either skip the text or assume white, producing false passes/false negatives. The least-contrast judgment must be made against the REAL composited backdrop.
aspects.scLimb: F24 cascade/inheritance/compositing limb — figuring out the effective background behind text across the tree and through stacked translucent layers, the part F24 calls the hard case.
aspects.whyUncovered: Every ACT case sets color and background together inline on the same element, or relies on UA defaults. No case has color inherited from a distant ancestor while the visible backdrop comes from a different ancestor, a z-indexed overlay, a translucent scrim composited over a photo, or a CSS multiple-background stack. Naive automated checkers structurally mis-handle these (they read the local background), so determining the true backdrop is a human visual/structural judgment.

references.quote: It is not necessary that the foreground and background colors both be defined on the same element. Foreground text color is inherited from ancestor elements. If an element's background color has not been defined, the element will have a transparent background, so authors need to ensure that at least one of the element's ancestors has a defined background color.
Color and background color may be specified at any level in the cascade of preceding selectors, by external stylesheets or through inheritance rules.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: Vacation-rental booking card with inherited light-gray text (#9b9b9b) on a transparent, position:absolute card shifted entirely off a dark nav rail so it renders over a bright lakeside hero photo painted on <body>; a CSSOM ancestor-walk finds the dark rail (#1b1b1b) and false-passes, but the real backdrop is the bright photo (~2.8:1).
pages.mechanism: Foreground color inherited from .copy and a background (#1b1b1b on the positioned ancestor .stage) both exist in the cascade, so F24's bare 'missing background' condition is satisfied; the defect is that the nearest declared-background ancestor is NOT the rendered backdrop. position:absolute;left:360px places the card over the bright fixed body photo, against which #9b9b9b light gray drops to ~2.8:1, below 4.5:1.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A contrast checker walks the box tree from the transparent .card, finds no opaque local background, climbs to the positioned ancestor .stage (#1b1b1b) and computes light-gray-on-near-black ~6.7:1 -> PASS. It cannot determine that the absolute positioning moves the card off the rail and over the bright fixed body photo; resolving which layer actually paints behind each glyph requires rendering the page and sampling the worst-case (lightest) photo region — a visual/structural judgment.

citation.quote: It is not necessary that the foreground and background colors both be defined on the same element. Foreground text color is inherited from ancestor elements. If an element's background color has not been defined, the element will have a transparent background, so authors need to ensure that at least one of the element's ancestors has a defined background color.

pages.scenario: Wellness/yoga hero with near-white text (#f3f6f4) on a translucent white 'frosted glass' overlay (rgba(255,255,255,0.4)) composited over a bright beach/sky photo; the composite is a pale panel, so the light text falls to ~1.1-1.6:1.
pages.mechanism: The text's nearest box-tree background is .frost, whose computed value is a translucent color over a background-image. The effective backdrop is rgba(255,255,255,0.4) composited over the bright photo, yielding a light panel on which near-white text is ~1.1-1.6:1 — far below 4.5:1. A foreground and a background are both declared, so this is not a bare F24 omission; it is a composited-backdrop misjudgment.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The text node's nearest background (.frost) is a translucent color over an image — there is no single solid background color to sample, and the true backdrop also includes the photo pixels under the scrim. Tools either skip the node as having an incomputable background or ignore the alpha and the photo; none composite rgba(255,255,255,0.4) over the brightest photo region to find the actual pale backdrop, which is the human visual judgment F24/F83 require for background images.

citation.quote: To satisfy Success Criterion 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) and 1.4.6 Contrast (Enhanced), there must be sufficient contrast between the text and its background. For pictures, this means that there would need to be sufficient contrast between the text and those parts of the image that are most like the text and behind the text.

pages.scenario: News feature banner using CSS multiple backgrounds — a linear-gradient scrim listed first (painted on top) over a url(skyline.jpg) photo — where the gradient's top stop is near-white (rgba(255,255,255,0.35)), so over the bright sky region the near-white headline (#fbfaf6) is ~1.25:1.
pages.mechanism: The effective backdrop is the gradient's TOP stop composited over the brightest (upper-sky) region of the skyline photo, not the photo's dark buildings nor the gradient in isolation. A background is declared (the multiple backgrounds) and the headline color is declared, so the defect is which stacked layer renders behind the glyphs; the least-contrast region resolves to ~1.25:1.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A CSSOM contrast tool encounters a background shorthand containing both a gradient and an image, cannot reduce it to a single solid color, and skips the contrast computation (or falls back to white, mis-passing the near-white text). No scanner resolves the layer order of a multiple-background stack and composites the gradient's top stop over the correct (brightest) photo region to pick the worst-case area behind the headline.

citation.quote: With background images, authors will need to check text contrast against the various colors of the background image that will be behind the text, and may also want to consider contrast when images are not displayed.

pages.scenario: Fintech dark-theme dashboard: dark theme set on the root (html{background:#14171c}), <body> sets no background and color:#777, and a summary card gives itself background:#6f6f6f without resetting text color, so the card paragraphs keep the inherited #777 on near-identical #6f6f6f (~1.12:1) while a sibling card stays legible.
pages.mechanism:
The failing #777 reaches .panel p purely by inheritance from (not on the

, whose own background is transparent); the panel declares its own #6f6f6f background. Inherited #777 on #6f6f6f is ~1.12:1, far below 4.5:1. Both foreground and background exist in the cascade, so the defect is per-region backdrop resolution under inheritance + a dark root canvas.
pages.selectorNote: Title with mix-blend-mode soft-light over panel; orig .panel p does not exist
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: No element trips an F24 missing-background linter (<html> and .panel both declare backgrounds). A tool that cannot resolve the body's transparent canvas commonly defaults to a WHITE background and computes #777-on-white = 4.48:1, which rounds to a pass in several engines. Catching it requires recognizing <body> sets no background so the dark <html> is the canvas, applying each card's own declared background to the SAME inherited foreground, and refusing the white fallback.

citation.quote: Color and background color may be specified at any level in the cascade of preceding selectors, by external stylesheets or through inheritance rules.

pages.scenario: Healthcare patient-portal consent modal: a translucent 'glass' dialog panel (rgba(255,255,255,0.55) + backdrop-filter blur) over a light dim scrim (rgba(20,30,45,0.35)) over a bright white app, with muted consent body text (#8a93a0); the panel-over-dim-over-page composite is light, so the text lands at ~2.2:1.
pages.mechanism: The dialog has correct ARIA and a declared background, so nothing is missing; the failure is that the effective backdrop is a multi-layer alpha composite (55% white glass over 35% navy dim over the bright page) that resolves to a light panel, on which #8a93a0 muted text is ~2.2:1, below 4.5:1.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A CSSOM tool reads .modal's background as a single rgba color and either ignores the alpha (treating it as near-solid white) or cannot flatten a translucent panel at all and skips. No scanner composites the 55% glass over the 35% navy dim over the bright app to recover the true light backdrop; reasoning through z-stacked semi-transparent layers (including backdrop-filter) to the real rendered backdrop is human visual judgment.

citation.quote: Select the **Background** color-dropper, click a pixel in the background close to the text. If the background is varied, choose a pixel that provides the **least contrast**.

pages.scenario: Boundary PASS: restaurant hero with off-white menu text (#f2f2f2) on a transparent .menu element, over a STRONG uniform dark scrim (linear-gradient(rgba(0,0,0,0.72)...)) composited over the same bright photo as case-02; even the brightest (sun) region resolves to ~#474744, so contrast is ~8.3:1 (a genuine pass) — sharpening that the verdict turns on the composite, not the photo/scrim/white-assumption.
pages.mechanism: Identical tool-opaque structure to the failing cases (transparent text element, no single solid background, scrim composited over a photo), but the 72%-black scrim makes the worst-case composited backdrop dark (~#474744), against which #f2f2f2 is ~8.3:1, comfortably above 4.5:1. Confirming the pass requires compositing the scrim over the lightest photo region and computing least-contrast.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A naive checker mis-handles even this correct page: .menu has a transparent background, so a CSSOM walker finds none and either falls back to a white canvas (reporting off-white-on-white as a FALSE failure) or cannot reduce the multiple-background hero to one color and skips. Reaching the correct PASS verdict requires rasterizing rgba(0,0,0,0.72) over the brightest photo region — the same composite judgment the failing cases need, here yielding a pass.

citation.quote: First do a quick check to see if the contrast between the text and the area of the image that is darkest (for dark text) or lightest (for light text) meets or exceeds that required by the Success Criterion (1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) or 1.4.6 Contrast (Enhanced)). If the contrast meets or exceeds the specified contrast, then there is no failure.

aspects.title: Background-image text where worst-case pixels behind SOME letters fail (least-contrast / per-letter) even though best-case or average contrast passes (F83)
aspects.plain: Text over a photo can be readable on average but unreadable where a bright patch sits behind a few letters, which best-case contrast checks miss.
aspects.description: F83 fails text over a background image when 'there is not sufficient contrast between the background image and the text' such that 'features of the background image can be confused with the text.' Its procedure requires the Quickcheck against the most-confusable region and, if that fails, checking 'the background behind each letter.' Trusted Tester operationalizes this: the human eyedroppers 'a pixel that provides the LEAST contrast' for both foreground and background. The ACT rule does the OPPOSITE — it takes the highest-possible (best-case) pixel pairing — so a photographic background that is mostly dark (text passes) but has a bright patch crossing three letters (those letters fail) is precisely the F83 failure the best-case algorithm structurally CANNOT flag. Catching it requires per-letter visual inspection over a real, high-variance image, exactly the harness's least-contrast pixel path.
aspects.scLimb: F83 background-image limb evaluated by the least-contrast / per-letter method — the inverse of ACT's best-case pixel scoring, and the canonical 'F looks like E' confusion.
aspects.whyUncovered: ACT background cases use one toy JPEG (black-hole.jpeg) plus text-shadow tuned to pass/fail cleanly, and the rule scores BEST-case contrast. There is no real photographic background with high luminance variance where a small bright/dark patch crosses only some letters. The best-case algorithm reports pass; only a per-letter least-contrast visual check finds the failing letters — an irreducibly visual human task.

references.quote: When there is not sufficient contrast between the background image and the text, features of the background image can be confused with the text making it difficult to accurately read the text.
If the Quickcheck is false, then check to see if the background behind each letter has sufficient contrast with the letter.
select the Foreground color-dropper, click a pixel in the text font. If the text color is varied, choose a pixel that provides the least contrast.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: Boutique-lodge hero (travel/hotel): white headline "Book Your Sunset Escape" over a local sunset PNG that is deep-indigo on the left and a blown-out bright sky on the right.
