The leading words read at ~19:1; only the trailing word "Escape" crosses the bright region and washes out. Best-case/average contrast for the headline is excellent, so a best-case algorithm passes; only the last word fails.
pages.mechanism: Live white text (color:#fff) over a CSS background-image. In-browser pixel sampling: worst-case contrast behind "Book" = 19.35:1 (passes) but behind "Escape" = 1.01:1 (far below 4.5:1). Best-case pixel across the headline ~20:1, so ACT's best-case pixel pairing reports pass while the F83/Trusted-Tester least-contrast pixel behind the trailing word is 1:1.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse cannot read pixels of a CSS background-image; they skip the check or fall back to the solid background-color #101019, against which #fff is ~18:1 and passes. They have no per-region/per-letter worst-case-pixel concept and never sample the bright part of the photo where only the last word fails — catching it requires a human to eyedropper the least-contrast pixel behind the trailing glyphs.

citation.quote: This failure occurs when people with low vision are not able to read text that is displayed over a background image. When there is not sufficient contrast between the background image and the text, features of the background image can be confused with the text making it difficult to accurately read the text.

pages.scenario: Museum wall label (arts/gallery): dark serif caption over a digitised Carrara-marble PNG. The marble is pale cream where dark text reads at ~13:1, but a bold dark-grey vein meanders down the caption column and crosses the strokes of some letters on every line, so a serif glyph merges into the vein (an F reads as an E) — F83's canonical 'lines cross behind the letters' confusion.
pages.mechanism: Live dark text (color:#1b1b1b) over a background-image. In-browser sampling of the whole caption box: worst-case contrast 1.59:1 (a dark glyph stroke sitting on the dark vein) versus best-case ~15:1 (dark text on pale marble). ACT samples the lightest marble pixel and passes; the per-letter least-contrast check finds the ~1.6:1 strokes where the vein crosses.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Scanners cannot sample the marble raster; against the figure's solid fallback #ece7df the dark text is ~12:1 and passes. No automated tool models 'a vein crossing the stroke of this particular glyph' or the perceptual confusion of an F reading as an E — that is an irreducibly visual, per-letter human judgment.

citation.quote: Black text overlays an image with black lines. The lines cross behind the letters making F's look like E's etc.

pages.scenario: Arabic RTL event invitation (events/ticketing, i18n): white headline over a zellige (Moroccan geometric tile) PNG. Because the document is dir=rtl, the line starts on the right, where the raster has a band of pale sand-coloured tiles, so the reading-start word washes out while the rest of the line over deep teal/cobalt tiles reads at ~10:1+.
pages.mechanism: Live white text (color:#fff) over a background-image in an RTL document. In-browser sampling: worst-case contrast behind the reading-start word "يسرّنا" (rightmost) = 1.38:1 (fails); behind "الخط" (later, over teal tiles) = 10.25:1 (passes); best-case pixel ~14:1. The pale tiles sit behind the FIRST glyphs a reader encounters in RTL order.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Scanners cannot read the zellige raster and fall back to the solid #0c4660 where #fff is ~7:1 and passes. They also have no concept of reading order, so even if they sampled the image they would not flag that the failing tiles sit behind the first word a low-vision/AT user encounters — the RTL-reading-order × per-region-luminance interaction is a contextual visual judgment.

citation.quote: Select the Background color-dropper, click a pixel in the background close to the text. If the background is varied, choose a pixel that provides the least contrast.

pages.scenario: Restaurant 'today's specials' board (restaurant menu, pt-PT): dark text over a ceramic-tile PNG whose tiles alternate cream and charcoal-glaze at roughly one letter-advance per tile. Over cream tiles the dark text reads (~5–13:1); over the charcoal tiles it collapses to ~1.2:1, producing a comb of failing glyphs — every other character vanishes.
pages.mechanism: Live dark text (color:#222) over a periodic light/dark tile background-image. In-browser sampling of the heading box: worst-case contrast 1.18:1 (a glyph over a charcoal tile) versus best-case ~13.7:1 (a glyph over a cream tile). ACT samples the cream tile and passes; the per-letter least-contrast check finds the ~1.2:1 characters over dark tiles, so the heading reads as a flickering half-word.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Scanners cannot sample the tile raster; against the board's solid fallback #ece2cf the dark text is ~12:1 and passes. No tool models a periodic background where failing pixels recur under specific letters, nor the resulting 'every other character drops out' legibility loss — it requires a human to scan letter-by-letter which characters sit on a dark tile.

citation.quote: Black text overlays an image with dark gray areas. Wherever the text crosses a dark gray area the contrast is so bad that the text cannot be read.

pages.scenario: Newspaper lead-story hero (news/editorial): large white headline carrying a text-shadow (the common 'make hero text readable over any photo' trick) over a cityscape PNG that is a dark stormy left third ramping to a blown-out bright sky on the right two-thirds. The shadow rescues the dark third but only outlines glyph edges; over the bright sky the stroke interiors still sit on near-white, so the right-hand words fail per-letter.
pages.mechanism: Live white text (color:#fff plus text-shadow) over a background-image. WCAG contrast is computed from fg/bg colours, not the shadow. In-browser sampling: worst-case behind "Bright" = 3.75:1 and behind "Storm Front" = 4.24:1 (both below 4.5:1), while "Skyline" over the dark left = 14.56:1 (passes); best-case ~18:1. The text-shadow darkens only a 1–2px edge halo, not the least-contrast interior pixel.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Three compounding reasons: scanners cannot read the cityscape raster and fall back to the solid #1a2230 (~15:1, pass); their contrast model ignores text-shadow entirely so they neither credit nor discount it; and they have no per-region/per-letter worst-case-pixel concept. Judging that the shadow outlines but does not raise the least-contrast interior pixel over the bright sky is a visual, per-letter determination.

citation.quote: Because authors do not have control over user settings for font smoothing/anti-aliasing, when evaluating this Success Criterion, refer to the foreground and background colors obtained from the user agent, or the underlying markup and stylesheets, rather than the text as presented on screen.

pages.scenario: Tour-operator hero (travel/outdoor booking) — BOUNDARY PASS variant that deliberately mirrors the failing cases: live white headline over a high-variance aurora-over-forest PNG with a bright moon patch that WOULD threaten white text, BUT a solid dark scrim with a hard luminance ceiling is baked into the text band so the worst-case pixel behind every letter stays safe. Sharpens the aspect: a busy image is not automatically an F83 failure.
pages.mechanism: Live white text (color:#fff) over a background-image whose text band has a composited dark scrim (luminance ceiling). In-browser sampling of the whole headline box: worst-case contrast 8.38:1 (at or above 4.5:1 everywhere), best-case ~18:1. Under F83's Quickcheck, white vs the lightest pixel behind the text already meets 4.5:1, so the failure condition does not apply.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: This sharpens the aspect from the tool side too: scanners still cannot read the raster and still fall back to the solid #06140d (~16:1), so they 'pass' it — but for the wrong reason (they never measured the image; they got lucky). A human applying F83 confirms the pass for the right reason (worst-case behind the letters is ~8:1). Distinguishing a correct pass from a coincidental one is itself a judgment automated tools cannot make.

citation.quote: First do a quick check to see if the contrast between the text and the area of the image that is darkest (for dark text) or lightest (for light text) meets or exceeds that required by the Success Criterion (1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) or 1.4.6 Contrast (Enhanced)). If the contrast meets or exceeds the specified contrast, then there is no failure.

aspects.title: Applying the correct AA thresholds (4.5:1 normal / 3:1 large) and the human large-text-size determination, where ACT only scored the stricter AAA limits
aspects.plain: Using the wrong contrast threshold: normal text needs 4.5:1 and large text only 3:1, but deciding whether a given font counts as 'large' takes human judgement.
aspects.description: SC 1.4.3 requires 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large-scale text (>=18pt or >=14pt bold). The ACT 09o5cg rule is calibrated to the AAA 1.4.6 thresholds (7:1 / 4.5:1), so cases it FAILS (e.g. 5.7:1, 6.4:1) actually PASS 1.4.3. Correctly judging 1.4.3 requires (a) applying the right AA threshold, and (b) deciding whether text qualifies as 'large-scale,' which Understanding notes is not a clean pixel cutoff: '18 point and bold can both have different meanings in different fonts but, except for very thin or unusual fonts, they should be sufficient,' anti-aliasing of 'particularly thin or unusual fonts' can render text 'with a much fainter color than the actual text color,' and font size must be 'obtained from the user agent or calculated on font metrics.' The threshold band between 3:1 and 4.5:1 is where the size classification flips the verdict — a human judgment about whether the rendered font is genuinely large-scale (and not a thin/unusual face that should not get the relaxed ratio).
aspects.scLimb: 1.4.3's actual AA thresholds (4.5:1 / 3:1) and the large-scale-text classification (font weight/family/rendered-size judgment near the boundary), neither of which ACT's AAA-calibrated rule exercises.
aspects.whyUncovered: ACT only tests exactly 18pt and 14pt-bold at the AAA boundaries; it never tests the 1.4.3 band where a ratio is between 3:1 and 4.5:1 (passes if large, fails if normal), nor thin/unusual/condensed fonts where the relaxed large-text ratio is arguably unsafe, nor rem/em/zoom/responsive sizing that changes rendered size. Resolving the size classification near the boundary is a human judgment Understanding explicitly says depends on font metrics and weight, not a fixed pixel rule.

references.quote: 18 point text or 14 point bold text is judged to be large enough to require a lower contrast ratio... '18 point' and 'bold' can both have different meanings in different fonts but, except for very thin or unusual fonts, they should be sufficient.

Due to anti-aliasing, particularly thin or unusual fonts may be rendered by user agents with a much fainter color than the actual text color defined in the underlying CSS. This can lead to situations where text has a contrast ratio that nominally passes the Success Criterion, but has a much lower contrast in practice.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: Tidewater Rewards cashback summary card renders a 24px/400 promo strapline (#8a8a8a on white = 3.4522:1) shrunk by transform:scale(0.6) to ~10.8pt rendered; as normal-size text it requires 4.5:1 and fails.
pages.mechanism: A seasonal cashback strapline is set at font-size:24px / weight 400 (= 18.0pt, which axe treats as large-scale and passes at 3:1), but transform: scale(0.6) makes the glyphs RENDER at 24px×0.6 = 14.4px = 10.8pt. The threshold is governed by the rendered size, so this is normal-size text requiring 4.5:1, and #8a8a8a on #ffffff = 3.4522:1 fails. Requires folding the CSS transform into the size determination.
pages.selectorNote: Promo strapline scaled to 14.4px; orig p.context.tone-muted does not exist
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A correct axe run would flag the 16px note, but the corpus's calibrated ACT rule 09o5cg scores the AAA limits (7:1/4.5:1): under it the 24px deck at 3.41:1 is wrongly FAILED (AAA-large needs 4.5) even though it PASSES 1.4.3 at AA. Reaching the right verdict requires applying AA thresholds (4.5/3), not AAA, and making the per-element size determination the AAA-only rule never exercises.

citation.quote: Text that is larger and has wider character strokes is easier to read at lower contrast. The contrast requirement for larger text is therefore lower.

pages.scenario: Coastline Ferries hero headline (#2f4a5e, 20px/400 = 15pt normal) over a pale-to-deep harbour-blue horizontal gradient; the right end resolves to ~2.85:1, below the 4.5:1 normal-text threshold, so it fails.
pages.mechanism: The booking headline (.hero h1, #2f4a5e, 20px/weight 400 = 15.0pt, NOT large-scale, so 4.5:1 applies) sits over a left-to-right gradient (#d8e6f0 → #6f93ad) with no single background colour. Over the deep-blue right end the worst-case backdrop pixels drop the contrast to ~2.85:1, below 4.5:1, so the heading fails. Requires recognising 15pt normal text is not large-scale and resolving the worst-case gradient backdrop.
pages.selectorNote: Booking headline over gradient; orig h2.section-head.is-regular does not exist
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A checker that buckets large-text purely by pixel size (>=18.66px) passes both 18.7px headings at 3:1, missing that the regular-weight one is not bold and must meet 4.5:1. The corpus's AAA-calibrated 09o5cg also wrongly FAILS the bold heading (AAA-large needs 4.5). Correct AA verdict needs font-weight off the computed style plus AA (not AAA) thresholds — a judgment the AAA-only rule never tests.

citation.quote:
18 point text or 14 point bold text is judged to be large
         enough to require a lower contrast ratio.

pages.scenario: Harvest Lights Festival banner shows a white 28px/700 (21pt bold, large-scale) headline over a warm sunset gradient; over the pale straw right end the worst-case contrast is ~2.78:1, below even the relaxed 3:1, so it fails.
pages.mechanism: The festival name (.banner h1) is white 28px/700 = 21.0pt bold, genuinely large-scale, so only 3:1 is required — but large-scale lowers the bar, it does not remove it. Over the pale straw stops at the right of the sunset gradient the worst-case backdrop gives white-on-#c98f55 ≈ 2.78:1 and white-on-#a89a7a ≈ 2.77:1, below 3:1, so it fails even the relaxed threshold. Requires applying 3:1 (not exemption) and resolving the worst-case gradient pixel.
pages.selectorNote: Festival name white on warm gradient; orig h1.title does not exist
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/Lighthouse compute contrast from the declared CSS color (#3d6c6c) and background (#111), get 3.20:1, classify 26.7px as large, compare to 3:1, and report PASS. They have no model of stroke width or anti-aliasing and cannot see the fainter effective color the hairline renders. Understanding 1.4.3 explicitly flags this nominal-pass/practical-fail gap for thin or unusual fonts — a human-only judgment.

citation.quote:
Due to anti-aliasing, particularly thin or unusual fonts may be rendered by user agents with a much fainter
            color than the actual text color defined in the underlying CSS. This can lead to situations where text has
            a contrast ratio that nominally passes the Success Criterion, but has a much lower contrast in practice.

pages.scenario: Riverside Library reading newsletter renders its masthead headline as a flat inline-SVG image of text, #888888 on #ffffff = 3.54:1 at ~15.75pt; as normal-size image-of-text it requires 4.5:1 and fails.
pages.mechanism: The newsletter masthead 'Summer Reading Begins' is an inline-SVG image of text (data: URI), so axe's color-contrast check cannot read the glyph/background colours or measure the glyph size. The glyphs are #888888 on a #ffffff canvas = 3.54:1 and render at ~21px ≈ 15.75pt — below the 18pt large-scale boundary, so it is normal text held to 4.5:1, which 3.54:1 fails. Requires recognising the image of text, eyedroppering the pixels, and measuring glyph height.
pages.selectorNote: Headline is an image of text (SVG data URI); contrast lives in glyph pixels
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The declared 1.5rem strongly reads as 24px/large-scale to anyone skimming the markup; the verdict hinges on noticing the html{font-size:87.5%} rule three rules away and recomputing 21px from font metrics — the exact 'obtain from the user agent / calculate on font metrics' operation the SC calls for. The AAA-calibrated 09o5cg rule only tests fixed-pixel boundary text and never exercises rem/em-cascaded sizing where large-scale status depends on resolving an inherited root.

citation.quote:
When evaluating this Success Criterion, the font size in points should be obtained
            from the user agent or calculated on font metrics in the way that user agents do.

pages.scenario: Glassroom workspace card heading (#8c8c8c, 14pt/weight 400) over a faint white-to-#efefef diagonal gradient; because 14pt is large-scale only when bold, this normal-weight heading needs 4.5:1 and at ~3.36:1 fails.
pages.mechanism: The card heading (.panel h2, #8c8c8c, font-size:14pt/weight 400 = 18.667px) qualifies for the relaxed 3:1 only when BOLD; at weight 400 it is normal text whose large-scale boundary is 18pt, and 14pt < 18pt, so 4.5:1 applies. Over the faint white→#efefef panel gradient the contrast is 3.36:1 (best) down to ~2.92:1 (worst), below 4.5:1, so it fails. The verdict turns on the weight-conditional large-scale rule.
pages.selectorNote: Card heading 14pt normal grey on gradient; orig h2.course-head does not exist
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/Lighthouse classify large-scale by nominal pixel size (24px => large) and compute 3.44:1 vs the 3:1 threshold, returning PASS. They have no notion of font-stretch, glyph width, or x-height and cannot decide a condensed 18pt is effectively smaller than the relaxed ratio assumes. Understanding reserves the relaxed ratio for ordinary faces ('except for very thin or unusual fonts') — a font-metrics judgment requiring a human to view the rendered condensed type.

citation.quote:
"18 point" and "bold" can both have different meanings in
         different fonts but, except for very thin or unusual fonts, they should be sufficient.

pages.scenario: Fern & Field refund-policy page renders body text (#787878, 16px normal) over a white-to-#f4f4f4 paper gradient at 4.4151:1 (top) to ~4.0142:1 (bottom); the threshold is not rounded, so 4.4151:1 < 4.5:1 fails.
pages.mechanism: The refund-policy body (p.policy, #787878, 16px/weight 400 = 12pt normal, so 4.5:1 applies with no large-text relief) sits on a top-to-bottom white→#f4f4f4 'paper' gradient. The contrast is 4.4151:1 over the white top, dropping to ~4.0142:1 over the #f4f4f4 region — both below 4.5:1. The ratio is a normative threshold and must not be rounded up (4.4151:1 is not 4.5:1), so it fails.
pages.selectorNote: Policy body #787878 on paper gradient; orig p.disclosure does not exist
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A precise checker computes 4.40 < 4.5, so this is not a computation blind spot — it is the human disposition near the threshold: auditors routinely round near-threshold values ('4.4 is basically 4.5') and pass low-priority legal fine print, and some tools apply rounding/tolerance slack. Understanding 1.4.3 exists to settle exactly this, stating values 'should not be rounded'. The corpus's AAA-calibrated 09o5cg rule gives no reliable AA-threshold signal at the 4.5 boundary.

citation.quote:
The 3:1 and 4.5:1 contrast ratios referenced in this success criterion are intended to be
            treated as threshold values. When comparing the computed contrast ratio to the Success Criterion
            ratio, the computed values should not be rounded (e.g., 4.499:1 would not meet the 4.5:1 threshold).

aspects.title: Contrast of text only present in non-initial states: placeholder, hover, keyboard focus, active, selected, and error states (and visited-link exclusion)
aspects.plain: Text that only appears on hover, focus, typing, or errors (like placeholder or error messages) must also be readable, but tools only check the initial page.
aspects.description: Understanding explicitly extends 1.4.3 to 'text in the page, including placeholder text and text that is shown when a pointer is hovering over an object or when an object has keyboard focus. If any of these are used in a page, the text needs to provide sufficient contrast.' F24's best-practice note lists 'text, link text, visited link text, link text with hover and keyboard focus.' Trusted Tester warns 'Some text may not initially be visible (appears on mouseover or focus). It must still conform to the contrast requirement wherever it occurs,' while excluding text 'Changed to indicate it is a visited link.' Evaluating these requires DRIVING the page into each state (hover, focus, type into a field, trigger an error) and judging whether the state is genuinely reachable — a behavioral exploration the static, initial-render ACT corpus never performs.
aspects.scLimb: State-dependent presentations of text (placeholder, hover, focus, active, selected, error) that the SC explicitly covers, plus the visited-link exclusion — none scored at static initial render.
aspects.whyUncovered: Every ACT case is scored at static initial render with no interaction; there are no :hover/:focus/:active/::placeholder/aria-selected variants, no error-state styling, and no driven states. The state-coverage breadth Understanding and F24 explicitly demand is entirely absent, and discovering these states requires interacting with the page rather than reading static markup.

references.quote: This success criterion applies to text in the page, including placeholder text and text that is shown when a pointer is hovering over an object or when an object has keyboard focus. If any of these are used in a page, the text needs to provide sufficient contrast.
Best practice is to include all states of the text. For example, text, link text, visited link text, link text with hover and keyboard focus, etc.
Some text may not initially be visible (appears on mouseover or focus). It must still conform to the contrast requirement wherever it occurs.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: Tideline Sea-Swimming Club membership form: the empty postcode field shows a meaningful pale-grey placeholder (#9aa0a6) over a gradient fill at ~2.48→1.53:1, failing 1.4.3; typed dark values pass.
pages.mechanism: A meaningful in-scope placeholder (#tideline-postcode, stating the required postcode format) is painted pale grey #9aa0a6 over a CSS linear-gradient field fill, yielding ~2.48:1 at the light end down to ~1.53:1 at the deep-teal end — below 4.5:1 across the whole range. The 1.4.3 Understanding extends the SC to placeholder text, so this fails; a second faint placeholder (#tideline-promo) is decorative and excluded.
pages.selectorNote: Placeholder over gradient field; resting target is the input (no ::placeholder at load)
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse compute contrast for DOM text nodes; a ::placeholder is generated content with no text node, so axe's color-contrast rule skips it. Every real text node (typed value, headings, prices) passes, so a static scan is all-green. A human must view the empty field, recognise the faint prompt as in-scope text, and measure placeholder-vs-field colour.

citation.quote: This success criterion applies to text in the page, including placeholder text and text that is shown when a pointer is hovering over an object or when an object has keyboard focus. If any of these are used in a page, the text needs to provide sufficient contrast.

pages.scenario: Business-news masthead with a horizontal section nav. Links are dark brand blue (#1a3a6b, ~11.3:1) at rest, but :hover and :focus recolour them to a pale brand blue (#8aa4c8) on the same white bar (~2.55:1) for 15px normal-weight text.
pages.mechanism: The a:hover / a:focus rule sets colour #8aa4c8 on #fff = ~2.55:1, below 4.5:1. Hover and keyboard-focus text are explicitly in scope for 1.4.3, so the link label fails contrast in the states a pointer-user or keyboard-user actually reads it.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Scanners evaluate the static, un-hovered render; no pointer is over any element during a scan and they do not synthesize :hover/:focus, so they read the resting #1a3a6b (~11.3:1, passing). The :hover rule is real CSS that repaints the link, but a scanner never enters that state. Detecting it requires driving the page into hover/focus and re-measuring.

citation.quote: Best practice is to include all states of the text. For example, text, link text, visited link text, link text with hover and keyboard focus, etc.

pages.scenario: Cloud-console billing form with a custom APG listbox country picker driven by aria-activedescendant. Resting options are dark (#1d2733 on white, ~15:1). The keyboard-focused (active descendant) option gets a pale highlight: #9fb0c9 text on a #eef3fb fill (~1.98:1). As the user arrows down, the focused option's label is the hardest to read.
pages.mechanism: The active-option class .opt--active sets colour #9fb0c9 on background #eef3fb = ~1.98:1, below 4.5:1. This is text shown only when an object has keyboard focus — explicitly in scope — so the focused option's label fails contrast for every option as focus roves.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Contrast engines read each option's resting computed style (~15:1, passing) and cannot drive arrow-key navigation to move focus and re-measure the active descendant; in production the listbox is also hidden until opened, so a static initial-render scan never sees the options at all. Confirming the failure requires a human to open the list, arrow through it, and read each highlighted label.

citation.quote: This success criterion applies to text in the page, including placeholder text and text that is shown when a pointer is hovering over an object or when an object has keyboard focus. If any of these are used in a page, the text needs to provide sufficient contrast.

pages.scenario: Bank money-transfer form. On load all text passes. Submitting with an empty amount makes JS inject an inline error 'Enter an amount to transfer.' styled light-red #e98a8a on white (~2.48:1). Long-tail twist: the submit button's label is fine at rest/hover but its :active (pressed) rule recolours the label to #a9c2e8 on the #2f6fd6 button (~2.65:1), unreadable while held down.
pages.mechanism: The injected error text (#e98a8a on #fff = ~2.48:1) and the pressed-state button label (#a9c2e8 on #2f6fd6 = ~2.65:1) both fall below 4.5:1. The error is in-scope state-dependent text present after a failed submit; the button is enabled (not the inactive-control exception), so its :active label is in scope too.
pages.selectorNote: Low-contrast error injected after failed submit; resting host is empty container
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The error element does not exist in the DOM at load — scanners do not submit the form, so they have no node to evaluate. The :active label colour is only computed while the button is pressed, a state scanners never synthesize. Every text node at initial render passes and the markup is well-formed (labels, aria-live, aria-describedby), so naive checks are green. Catching either failure requires driving the page: submit empty and press-and-hold the button.

citation.quote: Some text may not initially be visible (appears on mouseover or focus). It must still conform to the contrast requirement **wherever it occurs**.

pages.scenario: Marketing-analytics app with an APG tablist (Overview, Channels, Audience, Spend). Unselected tabs are dark text (#283543 on #eef2f6, ~11.1:1) and pass. The selected tab gets a 'pill' treatment: white text on a pale-teal gradient (effective #9ad8d4, ~1.60:1). Selection roves, so whichever tab is selected inherits the failing white-on-pale-teal treatment.
pages.mechanism: [role=tab][aria-selected=true] paints white (#fff) text on a ~#9ad8d4 pill = ~1.60:1, below 4.5:1. The selected state is the in-scope presentation here; the SC requires contrast 'wherever it occurs', including state-dependent presentations, and the failure is a property of the selected state for every tab.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A static scan sees exactly one tab selected and the rest passing, and does not activate the other tabs to confirm each fails when selected. Many engines also treat the rounded gradient 'pill' as a component region and down-rank/skip its text rather than measuring white-on-pale-teal as a text-on-background pair. Establishing that the failure follows the selected STATE (true for any tab) requires driving the tablist and re-measuring per selection.

citation.quote: This success criterion applies to text in the page, including placeholder text and text that is shown when a pointer is hovering over an object or when an object has keyboard focus. If any of these are used in a page, the text needs to provide sufficient contrast.

pages.scenario: University coursework-wiki reading list where already-opened links fade (the 'already read' marker). The :visited colour is deliberately faint (#b9b3c9 on white, ~2.03:1, below 4.5:1), but visited-link styling is on the SC's EXCLUDE list. All in-scope states pass: unvisited a:link (~12.1:1), :hover (~14.9:1), :focus-visible (~14.9:1 + outline). Boundary/PASS case that tests whether the judge honours the visited exclusion instead of over-flagging the driven low-contrast state.
pages.mechanism: No in-scope text is below threshold: rest/hover/focus link states all exceed 12:1. The only sub-threshold state is :visited (~2.03:1), and Trusted Tester explicitly excludes text 'Changed to indicate it is a visited link' from the contrast requirement, so the faint visited colour is not a 1.4.3 failure.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: For privacy, browsers never expose the real :visited colour via getComputedStyle and scanners do not synthesize a visited state, so tools never see the faint colour at all — they pass it only by accident of not measuring. The CORRECT human verdict (pass) rests on a judgment tools cannot make: recognising the faint colour is the visited state and that the visited-link exclusion removes it from scope, rather than flagging the measured ~2.03:1 after clicking a link.

citation.quote: EXCLUDE text that is: … Changed to indicate it is a "visited" link

aspects.title: The 'text in a picture that contains significant other visual content' exemption vs. an image of text done purely to get a particular look (which is NOT exempt)
aspects.plain: Text inside a real photo (like a street sign) is exempt, but text drawn as an image just for a fancy look is not.
aspects.description: 1.4.3 exempts text 'that are part of a picture that contains significant other visual content.' Understanding explains the boundary: 'This exception is intended to separate pictures that have text in them from images of text that are done to replace text in order to get a particular look. Incidental text, such as in photographs that happen to include a street sign, are not included.' Trusted Tester excludes text 'Contained within a picture that contains significant other visual content' but requires testing 'an image of text alone (or an image with text and no other significant content)' against 4.5:1/3:1 using the eyedropper. Deciding whether a given image is a 'picture with significant other content' (exempt) versus an 'image of text' styled for look (in scope) is a holistic visual judgment about the image's purpose and composition — not something an automated checker (which cannot read text inside images at all) can do.
aspects.scLimb: The 'picture with significant other visual content' / incidental-text exemption and its boundary against images-of-text-for-look — a limb ACT does not test, requiring image-content judgment.
aspects.whyUncovered: ACT never tests images-of-text at all (it only computes contrast for live text nodes), and certainly not the exemption boundary between an incidental-text photograph (exempt) and an image-of-text crafted for a particular look (in scope at 4.5:1/3:1). Automated checkers cannot read text inside raster images, so both the exemption and the in-scope image-of-text contrast check are human-only.

references.quote: This exception is intended to separate pictures that have text in them from images of text that are done to replace text in order to get a particular look.
Incidental text, such as in photographs that happen to include a street sign, are not included.
If the page contains an image of text alone (or an image with text and no other significant content), test the image of text with CCA

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: Maison Verde bistro renders its dinner menu as a flat image-of-text (img.menu), sepia #9c8e6f on parchment #f3ead7 = 2.70:1 normal-size; in scope and below 4.5:1, so it fails.
pages.mechanism: The bistro's dinner menu is delivered as a single inline-SVG data-URI image, so the dish names and prices are image pixels, not live text. The graphic is a flat parchment fill plus menu lettering with no significant other visual content, so it is an in-scope image of text done for a custom hand-script look (exemption off). The rendered normal-size lettering is sepia #9c8e6f on parchment #f3ead7 = 2.70:1, below 4.5:1, so it fails.
pages.selectorNote: Menu is image of text; orig img#heroHeadingImg.headline does not exist
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse compute contrast only for live text nodes (CSS color vs resolved background); the headline is image pixels with no DOM text node, so the scanner skips it silently and reports no error. No tool OCRs/samples image text or judges that this image is an image-of-text-for-look (in scope) rather than an exempt picture. Both the classification and the eyedropper measurement are human-only.

citation.quote: In this provision there is an exception that reads "that are part of a picture that contains significant other visual content,". This exception is intended to separate pictures that have text in them from images of text that are done to replace text in order to get a particular look.

pages.scenario: Travel article (Meridian Travel, 'Walking Lisbon's Baixa'): the lead photo is a street scene with significant other visual content — sky, sun, tiled buildings, roadway, a tree, pedestrians, a triumphal arch — that incidentally includes a small green 'RUA AUGUSTA' street sign whose lettering measures only ~1.5:1. That incidental text in a picture with significant other visual content is EXEMPT from the contrast requirement; the body prose is live and high-contrast. This is the exempt boundary variant; the trap is a reviewer who reflexively eyedroppers the sign.
pages.mechanism: The low-contrast sign is incidental scenery within a picture that has significant other visual content, so it is exempt and must NOT be measured; nothing rendered as an image of text to convey meaning fails contrast, and the photo's information is carried by a scene-level alt and live high-contrast prose. SC is met.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Checkers cannot read text inside the photograph at all, so they never see the sign — they neither exempt it nor flag it; they have no data. The judgment that makes this a PASS — recognising the image is a photograph with significant other visual content and the sign is incidental, therefore not to be tested — is a holistic visual/purpose judgment no scanner performs.

citation.quote: This requirement applies to situations in which images of text were intended to be understood as text. Incidental text, such as in photographs that happen to include a street sign, are not included.

pages.scenario: E-commerce product page (Olivar del Sol olive oil): two images of identical DOM shape split on the exemption. (A) A product photo of the bottle on a counter (bottle, cork, counter, olive sprig, shadow = significant other visual content) whose printed 'ARBEQUINA / EXTRA VIRGIN' label is ~1.6:1 — incidental, EXEMPT, not tested. (B) A separate flat 'FREE SHIPPING OVER $40 / harvest sale ends sunday' promo banner is an image of text for a custom display look with no other content; lettering 2.95:1 < 4.5:1 — IN SCOPE, FAILS. A correct review classifies each, skips (A), eyedroppers (B).
pages.mechanism: The in-scope promo banner is an image of text (no significant other content) rendered at 2.95:1 < 4.5:1 normal text; a low-vision shopper cannot reliably read the $40 threshold or deadline and cannot restyle an image. The bottle photo's ~1.6:1 label is exempt incidental text in a picture with significant other content. Page fails on (B) alone.
pages.primarySelector: img.promo[alt="Free shipping over $40. Harvest sale ends Sunday."]
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Both are with non-empty alt (no alt error) and contrast checkers measure only live text nodes — neither image has one — so no contrast error fires. No tool reads text inside either image or decides which is an exempt picture vs an in-scope image-of-text-for-look. The page turns on a two-way human classification plus eyedropper, neither automatable.

citation.quote: If the page contains an image of text alone (or an image with text and no other significant content), test the image of text with CCA (ANDI: color contrast cannot detect text inside images).

pages.scenario: Public-health page (Northbridge Public Health, 'How to read a nutrition label'): the explainer is embedded as a single flat infographic. It has boxes and connector lines, but the significant content is the step text itself, rendered as an image of text for a designed look — not a picture with significant other visual content. Body labels are lavender #8d84ac on pale-lilac #ddd8e8 = 2.50:1 (CSS-exact; ~2.62 measured), far below 4.5:1. In scope and failing. The chart-like chrome tempts a reviewer to misread it as an exempt picture.
pages.mechanism: In-scope image-of-text labels at 2.50:1 < 4.5:1; a low-vision user cannot resolve lavender-on-lilac step text and cannot apply a high-contrast stylesheet to an image. The decorative boxes/lines are framing, not significant content that would make the text incidental, so the exemption does not apply. The alt provides an equivalent (1.1.1 passes), isolating the defect to 1.4.3 visual contrast.
pages.primarySelector: figure img[alt^="Infographic: a sample nutrition label"]
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The infographic is one with descriptive alt — no alt error; checkers compute contrast only for live text nodes and cannot OCR/sample the pale labels inside the image, so no contrast error fires. Deciding the diagram's significant content is its text (making it an in-scope image of text, not an exempt picture) and then measuring the worst label is a human-only classification-plus-eyedropper task.

citation.quote: This exception is intended to separate pictures that have text in them from images of text that are done to replace text in order to get a particular look.

pages.scenario: Independent bookstore product page (Harborlight Books, 'The Quiet Tide'): the SAME stylized title appears twice and the exemption flips. (A) A book-cover image with full artwork — moonlit sea, lighthouse beam, gulls, moon, author name, publisher mark — has the low-contrast purple script title integrated into the composition: a picture with significant other visual content, EXEMPT, not tested. (B) A 'Staff Pick' banner lower on the page lifts the same title onto a flat purple panel with no other content; lettering #9488bf on #4a3f6e = 2.93:1 < 4.5:1 — IN SCOPE, FAILS.
pages.mechanism: Identical stylized title is exempt inside rich cover artwork (significant other visual content) but in scope as a flat image-of-text banner; the banner renders at 2.93:1 < 4.5:1 normal text, unreadable for low-vision users and not restylable as an image. The live <h1> and alts carry the book's identity, so the defect is specifically the banner's visual contrast.
pages.primarySelector: section.staff img#staffImg[alt="Staff Pick of the Month: The Quiet Tide"]
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Both images are with non-empty alt (no alt error) and contrast checkers measure only live text nodes — neither image has one — so no contrast error fires. The page hinges on the human judgment that the same stylized title is exempt inside cover artwork but in scope as a flat image-of-text banner (a composition/purpose distinction) followed by an eyedropper measurement, neither of which any scanner can do.

citation.quote: In this provision there is an exception that reads "that are part of a picture that contains significant other visual content,". This exception is intended to separate pictures that have text in them from images of text that are done to replace text in order to get a particular look.

pages.scenario: Nonprofit annual report (Riverkeep Conservancy, '2025 Impact Report'): a founder pull-quote is rendered as a flat image of text (hand-serif look) on a near-white card with no significant other visual content — so it is in scope (not exempt). Lettering #888888 on #f4f2ed = 3.17:1 (CSS-exact; ~3.09 measured): below 4.5:1 for normal text but at/above 3:1 for large-scale text. The image renders large (~40px, > 24px/18pt), so the 3:1 threshold applies and it PASSES. Pass/fail cannot be decided from the number alone — the human must first judge the rendered size.
pages.mechanism: In-scope image of text at 3.17:1; because the rendered text is large-scale (>18pt/24px), the relaxed 3:1 threshold applies and 3.17:1 meets it. Trusted Tester notes there is no tool to compare text size INSIDE an image, so a human must demonstrate large-scale to apply 3:1 — otherwise the default 4.5:1 governs and 3.17:1 would fail. Confirmed by eyedropper plus a size determination.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The quote is an with no live text node, so checkers compute no contrast and cannot read the text or judge its rendered size — they neither flag nor clear it. The decision requires (1) recognising this is an in-scope image of text (not an exempt picture), (2) determining from the rendered pixels that the text is large-scale so 3:1 applies, and (3) eyedroppering 3.17:1. The size determination in particular is the judgment Trusted Tester explicitly leaves to the human.

citation.quote:
if the text in the image is large-scale (≥18pt or 14pt bold), 3:1 applies. TT has not
       identified a tool to compare text size in images, so this determination is not in the process — but
       use 3:1 if it can be satisfactorily demonstrated the text is large-scale.

aspects.title: False logotype / branding exemption — informational text dressed up as a brand mark
aspects.plain: Real logos may be pictures of text, but authors abuse this by saving taglines, slogans, or headings as images so low-vision users can't resize or recolour them.
aspects.description: TT step 1a and the Understanding 'A logo containing text' example exempt logotypes ('text that is part of a logo or brand name') from 1.4.5 because 'the visual presentation of the text is essential to the identity of the logo.' The genuinely hard, human-only judgment is distinguishing a real wordmark/brand identity from ordinary informational text (a tagline, marketing slogan, navigation label, deadline notice, or paragraph of prose) that an author has merely set in a nice typeface, exported as an image, and parked in a header or wrapped in class='logo' to dodge the SC. A one-word company wordmark is exempt; 'Free shipping on orders over $50', 'Apply for your permit before March 31', or a styled <h1> baked into a banner is NOT a logotype even when it sits in a branding zone. A checker cannot OCR the text and reason about whether it functions as a brand identity vs. conveys substantive information; only a human can.
aspects.scLimb: Logotype / branding essential-presentation exception (Intent para 2; TT step 1a)
aspects.whyUncovered: The ACT corpus holds exactly one logo case (W3C logo as role=img CSS background = PASS) and one plain-text-image FAIL (textimage.jpg) at opposite extremes. There is no borderline where an image's text is ambiguous between 'brand identity' and 'ordinary informational text styled nicely' — the exact distinction TT step 1a turns on. The corpus never puts non-logo content into a branding context.

references.quote: Logotypes (text that is part of a logo or brand name) cannot be replaced by text.

The logo contains logotype (text as part, or all, of the logo). The visual presentation of the text is essential to the identity of the logo and is included as a gif image which does not allow the text characteristics to be changed.
This includes instances where a particular presentation of text is essential to the information being conveyed, such as type samples, logotypes, branding, etc.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: Fintech masthead 'brand lockup': a genuine one-word wordmark image ('Northwind', exempt logotype) stacked directly above a second image whose pixels spell the full marketing tagline 'Northwind — the smartest way to manage your money, every day', styled to read as part of the logo. Same branding zone, opposite verdicts; the tagline is ordinary marketing prose that must be live text.
pages.mechanism: The tagline's words are SVG <text> glyphs in an inline-SVG data: URI (verified: string absent from document.body.innerText; rasterises at 200% zoom). A low-vision user cannot resize/recolour the sentence because it is pixels, not text. The wordmark image shares that limitation but is PERMITTED under the logotype exemption; the tagline is NOT, because the same information is expressible as styled live text with the author's technologies, so text must be used (1.4.5).
pages.primarySelector: header.masthead img.tagline-banner[alt="Northwind — the smartest way to manage your money, every day"]
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Both have non-empty, accurate alt, so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse image-alt passes for both and there is no missing-attribute defect. No tool OCRs the pixels, and none can reason that the 'Northwind' image is a brand identity (exempt) while the identically-styled tagline image is a marketing sentence (not exempt). The pass/fail split is a pure logotype-vs-ordinary-text semantic judgment.

citation.quote: The logo contains logotype (text as part, or all, of the logo). The visual presentation of the text is essential to the identity of the logo and is included as a gif image which does not allow the text characteristics to be changed.

pages.scenario: SaaS pricing page where the real brand name 'Quanta' is live text, but the pricing section's heading 'Our 2026 Pricing Plans' is rendered as a flat image and wrapped in <div class="logo" role="img" aria-label="Our 2026 Pricing Plans">, set in the brand display face, argued to be 'branding'. A styled section heading is WCAG's canonical image-of-text example, not a logo.
pages.mechanism: The heading exists only as SVG glyphs inside an wrapped by role="img". The role=img has an accessible name via aria-label so a screen reader hears the words, but 1.4.5 concerns visual customisation: a low-vision user who needs the title at 200% in their own colours gets a blurred raster instead of reflowed, recoloured text. The logotype/branding exemption applies only when presentation is essential to a brand identity; a section heading's information is fully expressible as live CSS text, so text must be used.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The role="img" container has a non-empty accessible name (aria-label), so axe-core's role=img / image-alt name checks pass and there is no empty-name defect. No tool OCRs the SVG to learn the pixels are the section heading, and none can decide that a styled heading is informational text rather than a brand mark. Distinguishing 'branding' from 'a heading dressed as branding' is a human semantic call.

citation.quote: Rather than using bitmap images to present headings in a specific font and size, an author uses CSS to achieve the same result.

pages.scenario: Restaurant site whose primary navigation paints each item's visible label ('Menu', 'Reservations', 'Private Events', 'Find Us') as a CSS background-image of hand-lettered text in the brand signage face; each <a> carries a visually-hidden live-text span for its accessible name. Justified as 'the whole nav is our custom signage font, so it's branding' — but WCAG lists navigation items as text that must be live CSS text.
pages.mechanism: The visible labels are CSS background-images of text, so they cannot be resized by text-zoom, pixelate at page zoom, and are not recoloured by OS forced-colors/High-Contrast mode (where background-image text may vanish). A screen-reader user still hears the link names from the hidden spans, but 1.4.5 protects the visual customisation a low-vision sighted user needs, which is denied. Navigation labels are not a logotype; their information is fully expressible as live CSS text.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every <a> has a discernible accessible name from the visually-hidden span, so axe-core's link-name rule passes with no empty links or missing alts. Automated tools do not inspect background-image URLs to detect images of text, and cannot reason that navigation labels are informational rather than branding. The 'these are nav labels, not a logo' judgment requires a human reading the rendered page plus WCAG context.

citation.quote: A web page contains a menu of navigation links that have both an icon and text to describe their target. CSS is used to display the text's font family, size and foreground and background colors; as well as the spacing between the navigation links.

pages.scenario: Government heavy-vehicle permits portal whose masthead branding strip holds two images of text side by side: a circular departmental crest ('Department of Transport', an exempt logo/seal) and a gold sub-banner image whose pixels read 'Apply for your permit before 31 March 2026'. The deadline notice is styled to sit inside the official lockup, with alt equal to its visible text so a captioned-image heuristic is fooled.
pages.mechanism: The deadline image's alt reproduces its visible text, so the words reach a screen reader (1.1.1 satisfied) — isolating the defect to 1.4.5. The harm is visual: the cut-off date is rasterised glyphs in a fixed-size SVG that pixelates on zoom and is not recoloured by forced-colors mode, so a low-vision citizen cannot read it at large size in a high-contrast palette. The branding/logotype exemption covers marks whose presentation is essential to a brand identity; a deadline notice's information is fully expressible as styled live text, so text must be used. The crest legitimately invokes the exemption.
pages.primarySelector: header.masthead img.deadline[alt="Apply for your permit before 31 March 2026"]
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Both images have correct non-empty alt, so image-alt passes and there is no missing-text-alternative finding; because the deadline's alt even matches its visible text, a 'descriptive alt = compliant' heuristic is actively misled. No automated tool OCRs the two images to discover one is a seal (exempt) and the other a deadline sentence (not exempt). Distinguishing crest from notice is human semantic/contextual judgment.

citation.quote: This includes instances where a particular presentation of text is essential to the information being conveyed, such as type samples, logotypes, branding, etc.

pages.scenario: Fashion product page with two circular badges: a genuine one-word wordmark badge ('AURELIA', exempt logotype) and a promotional badge whose pixels read 'FREE SHIPPING on orders over $50', drawn as an inline <svg role="img"> with a <title> equal to the visible text. The promo states a substantive offer threshold, not a brand name, so the logotype exemption does not reach it.
pages.mechanism: The <svg role="img"> has an accessible name from <title> ('Free shipping on orders over $50'), so a screen reader hears the offer (1.1.1 satisfied). The 1.4.5 harm is visual: the '$50' threshold is rasterised glyphs, so a low-vision shopper who needs the figure at 200% in their own palette gets a blurred badge, and forced-colors mode cannot recolour SVG-fill text inside an image. The exemption covers marks whose presentation is essential to a brand identity; a free-shipping offer's information is fully expressible as styled live text, so text must be used. The wordmark badge legitimately invokes the exemption.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The <svg role="img"> carries a non-empty accessible name via <title>, so axe-core's svg-img-alt / role=img name checks pass; because that name matches the visible words a 'descriptive alt' heuristic is satisfied too. No tool reads the SVG glyphs to learn the badge states an offer threshold, and none can decide that a promotional slogan is not branding. The brand-mark-vs-promotional-information judgment requires a human.

citation.quote: Logotypes (text that is part of a logo or brand name) cannot be replaced by text.

pages.scenario: Charity footer 'Our supporters' logo wall: six identically-styled inline-SVG tiles. Five are genuine partner-company wordmarks (Helix Bank, Verdant Foods, Ardent Mobility, Kestrel Labs, Northstar Media — exempt logotypes); the sixth, given the identical logo treatment, is a legal/financial disclaimer sentence 'Registered charity No. 1180992. Donations are tax deductible where the law allows.' — informational text wearing the logo costume.
pages.mechanism: The disclaimer image's alt reproduces its two lines (1.1.1 satisfied), isolating the defect to 1.4.5. The harm is visual and interactive: the registration number '1180992' is rasterised glyphs at a fixed small size, so a low-vision donor cannot enlarge it without pixelation, cannot recolour it for contrast, and cannot select/copy the number to verify or cite the charity. The logotype/branding exemption covers marks whose presentation is essential to a brand identity; a charity-registration disclaimer's information is fully expressible as styled live text, so text must be used. The five wordmarks legitimately invoke the exemption.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: All six tiles are with correct non-empty alt, so image-alt passes for every one and there is no missing-text-alternative finding. No automated tool OCRs the tiles to separate five brand wordmarks from one disclaimer sentence, and none can reason that a charity-registration statement is informational rather than branding. Spotting the one informational tile hiding in a wall of legitimate logos is a human semantic/visual judgment.

citation.quote: This includes instances where a particular presentation of text is essential to the information being conveyed, such as type samples, logotypes, branding, etc.

aspects.title: Customizability exception — image of text adjustable (or fake-adjustable) via on-page controls (C30)
aspects.plain: A picture of text is allowed if on-page controls truly let users adjust its size, font, and colour, but those controls are sometimes fake, broken, or change nothing.
aspects.description: The SC text itself passes images of text 'where a particular presentation of text is essential or can be visually customized,' and TT Test 7.E condition 2 passes an image of text if it 'can be visually customized: adjust the font, size, color, and background with controls provided by the web page.' Technique C30 (CSS image-replacement with a switch control) and the Understanding 'Dynamically Generated Images' / 'Customizable font settings' examples are the canonical PASS-by-customization route. Evaluating this requires a human to find the controls, operate them, and judge whether activating them actually swaps the image for live text or genuinely re-renders the image to the user's font/size/color — and crucially to catch the FAILURE where controls are present but FAKE (decorative, broken, or only change unrelated styling). A static checker sees pixels and DOM, not whether a button truly re-renders an image of text; this is human-operable judgment.
aspects.scLimb: Customizable-presentation exception (SC clause 'can be visually customized'; TT Test 7.E condition 2; technique C30)
aspects.whyUncovered: Every ACT case is a static flat raster/SVG image with no UI controls at all; the customizability limb of the SC is entirely unexercised in either direction. The corpus has no C30 switch and no dynamically-generated image, so neither a genuine PASS-by-customization nor a fake-controls FAIL is represented.

references.quote: Determine if the image of text can be visually customized: adjust the font, size, color, and background with controls provided by the web page.
Images of text can also be used where it is possible for users to customize the image of text to match their requirements.
Check that when the control is activated the resulting page includes text (programmatically determined text) wherever images of text had been used.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: E-commerce fashion site with a third-party 'accessibility' A-/A/A+ font-scaler toolbar. The campaign headline 'The Spring Linen Edit' is an inline-SVG image of text. The toolbar genuinely resizes the live HTML body copy (via a CSS --fs custom property) but has zero effect on the SVG headline, so the one image of text on the page cannot be customized despite a working customization control.
pages.mechanism: Image of text (inline SVG <text>) sized in absolute SVG user units; the customization control only multiplies a CSS custom property consumed by .scalable HTML text, so activating A+ enlarges paragraphs but never the headline. Customizability exception (TT 7.E condition 2 / C30) not met for the image of text itself. Verified headless: SVG width unchanged after A+ while lede font-size grew (--fs 1->1.3).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The SVG has role=img + a non-empty aria-label, contrast clears 4.5:1, buttons have aria-labels, page is titled — no missing-attribute for a linter. Scanners cannot OCR the SVG to learn it is a styled headline, and cannot operate A+ and diff before/after frames to discover the SVG didn't move while the paragraphs did. Distinguishing 'control customizes the image of text' from 'control customizes only the surrounding live text' requires a human to push the button and watch.

citation.quote: Determine if the image of text can be **visually customized**: adjust the font, size, color, and background with controls provided by the web page.

pages.scenario: Museum exhibition page whose whole campaign poster (title 'Bauhaus in Colour', dates '9 March - 28 July', venue) is a CSS background-image of text. In the poster corner is an 'Adjust poster appearance' toolbar with A-/A+ and three colour swatches, styled and role-marked exactly like a working C30 control. The page contains NO script at all — every control is a decorative span, so the image of text never changes. The deceptive twin: visible controls that a tool 'sees' but that do nothing.
pages.mechanism: role=button spans with tabindex but no event handler anywhere (document has zero <script> elements), driving a fixed background-image data: SVG of text. Activating any control re-renders nothing, so the customizability exception is faked. Verified headless: scriptCount=0, controls are SPAN tag, poster geometry unchanged after click.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Poster has role=img with a complete aria-label, controls are named role=button with tabindex, page is titled, no missing alt/name. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse do not OCR the background-image to learn it is a poster of text, and do not click the controls and diff the rendering to discover they have no effect. A static scanner cannot tell a wired C30 switch from a pixel-perfect decorative imitation; only a human who operates each control and watches the poster (not) change can catch it.

citation.quote: Finally, through the use of server-side or client-side scripting, the author provides a control that allows the user to switch between the available views.

pages.scenario: Higher-ed credential-verification page renders its 'Certificate of Completion' heading into a <canvas> (a genuine image of text). A real C30 customization control (A-/A+ size + a colour <select> incl. a high-contrast black) sits BEFORE the image and truly re-renders the canvas glyphs at the chosen size and colour — it redraws (not CSS-scale), so the text stays sharp at every size with no pixelation and the full wording is always drawn. The canonical PASS-by-customization boundary, confirmable only by operating the control.
pages.mechanism: Canvas image of text re-rasterized on demand: each A+/colour change recomputes canvas dimensions and calls fillText at the new font size/colour (DPR-aware), so output is sharp (no pixelation, satisfying TT note 2a) and complete (same string), with aria-label kept in sync. Control located near the start of the page per C30. Verified headless: canvas.width changed on A+, sizeOut 36px->50px, colour select applied.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A canvas is opaque to scanners: they cannot read the pixels to know they spell 'Certificate of Completion', cannot tell the control re-renders rather than CSS-scales, and cannot verify the enlarged output is sharp and complete. They can neither fail it nor confirm the pass. Establishing this is a legitimate C30 customization (vs the inert twin in case-02) requires a human to operate the control, watch the canvas re-render, and judge the result sharp and equivalent.

citation.quote: Customizing font size for an image of text also implies the ability to adjust the size without pixelation (typically evident when simply using the browser resize functionality to resize images).

pages.scenario: Family-trattoria recipe page presents Nonna's entire ragù recipe (title, 'Serves 6', full ingredient list, numbered method) as a single inline-SVG image of text. A 'Customize reading appearance' panel offers three theme buttons (Cream/Parchment/Mint). Pressing them genuinely changes the PAGE background colour — so the controls feel alive — but the recipe SVG is never re-rendered, recoloured, resized, or swapped. Superficially customizable, substantively not: the customization targets the chrome around the image, not the image of text.
pages.mechanism: Theme buttons' handler sets document.body.style.backgroundColor only; the .recipe-card svg image of text (all quantities and method as <text>) is untouched. Customization must adjust the image of text's font/size/colour/background (TT 7.E condition 2); recolouring the page behind a fixed bitmap does not. Verified headless: body background changed cream->mint while recipe SVG width unchanged.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The SVG has a descriptive aria-label + role=img, the theme buttons are real labelled <button>s with focus styles, the page is titled, and the buttons demonstrably fire JS. Scanners cannot OCR the SVG to learn it contains an entire recipe of text, and cannot reason that the customization the buttons provide (page background) is the wrong target that never reaches the image of text. Telling 'customizes the image of text' from 'customizes only the chrome around it' requires a human to operate the control and notice the content itself never changed.

citation.quote: Images of text can also be used where it is possible for users to customize the image of text to match their requirements.

pages.scenario: Newspaper 'Quote of the Day' pull-quote delivered as a dynamically generated image of text — a 150x52 low-resolution PNG raster of an italic quote. A 'Display size' <select> (Small/Medium/Large/Extra large) re-requests the image at a larger size (the canonical dynamic-image customization). The control works and the card grows, but the quote engine has only the one low-res master raster, so larger sizes are the same pixels upscaled and the text turns blurry/blocky — a borderline FAIL on the no-pixelation sub-requirement.
pages.mechanism: source is a true 150x52 PNG bitmap (naturalWidth 150) with image-rendering: pixelated; the size selector re-assigns the same master src and grows display width (e.g. to 660px, ~4.4x), so the glyphs pixelate rather than re-render sharp. Fails TT 7.E note 2a (size customization must be without pixelation). Verified headless: PNG decodes (150x52), upscales to 660px display, image-rendering computed 'pixelated'; screenshots show crisp Small vs blocky/blurry Extra large.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The has a complete alt reproducing the quote+attribution (1.1.1 passes), the size

citation.quote: Customizing font size for an image of text also implies the ability to adjust the size without pixelation (typically evident when simply using the browser resize functionality to resize images).

pages.scenario: Auto-insurance quote summary renders its legally required 'Important disclosures' block as an SVG image of text. A real C30-style control (A-/A+ size + High contrast colour) genuinely re-renders the disclosure as fresh sharp SVG text at the chosen size/colour. The trap: the re-render template silently OMITS the third line — the 14-day cooling-off / cancellation right present in the default image. The controls work; the customized output is functional yet not equivalent, and the loss lands precisely on the user who must customize to read it.
pages.mechanism: Default SVG markup contains four disclosure lines incl. the cooling-off clause; the JS re-render path rebuilds the SVG from a LINES array that has only three lines (cooling-off dropped). On first interaction the handler replaces #discWrap's SVG with the non-equivalent version. 1.4.5 customizability requires the customized image keep 'the same effect and information' (TT 7.E). Verified headless: default 4 lines with cooling-off present; after A+ -> 3 lines, cooling-off absent.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Both states are clean: SVG has role=img + aria-label, controls are labelled <button>s and a <select>, contrast clears in both colour modes, page well-formed. Scanners cannot OCR either SVG, cannot diff the default glyphs against the re-rendered glyphs, and cannot know one specific regulatory sentence vanished on customization. Catching this requires a human to read the default disclosure, operate the control, and compare the customized output line-by-line for completeness — pure semantic judgment about content equivalence.

citation.quote: Determine if text can be used instead of the image of text to present the **same effect and information**.

aspects.title: 'Significant other visual content' exclusion — graphs, screenshots, diagrams, infographics vs. text-only images
aspects.plain: Charts, screenshots, and diagrams that contain words are exempt, so judging whether an image is mostly-graphic (allowed) or just styled text (not allowed) needs a human.
aspects.description: The images-of-text definition note excludes 'text that is part of a picture that contains significant other visual content,' citing 'graphs, screenshots, and diagrams which visually convey important information through more than just text' (TT adds CAPTCHA). The detection step is explicitly OCR-like: the tester must FIRST decide whether an image that contains text is fundamentally a graph/screenshot/diagram/infographic (out of scope, INAPPLICABLE) or is an image-of-text dressed up (in scope, potentially FAIL). This is the most subjective limb of the SC: a human must weigh whether the non-text graphics are 'significant' enough to exclude the image, or whether it is predominantly text laid out decoratively. No automated checker can make this gestalt judgment.
aspects.scLimb: Definition exclusion: pictures with significant other visual content are not 'images of text'
aspects.whyUncovered: ACT's INAPPLICABLE/PASS pictures contain no text at all (fireworks, Times Square, books — clear non-applicability) and its FAIL images are essentially pure text on a plain field (clear applicability). The genuinely hard middle — an image that is largely text but also carries chart geometry, UI chrome, or diagram structure — is absent. No case forces the 'does the non-text visual content make this NOT an image of text?' judgment.

references.quote: This does not include text that is part of a picture that contains significant other visual content. Examples of such pictures include graphs, screenshots, and diagrams which visually convey important information through more than just text.

EXCLUDE text that is part of a picture that contains significant other visual content such as CAPTCHA, graphs, screenshots, and diagrams, which visually convey important information more than just text.
the tester must first recognize that an image contains text (vs being a photo/diagram), then judge whether that text is essential (logotype) or could have been live text.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: Marketing weekly digest with two flat images side by side: a GENUINE bar chart (bar heights encode the data, words are axis labels — excluded graph) next to a 'Paid campaign breakdown' that wears chart chrome (teal title strip, legend swatch, gridlines, coloured cells) but has ZERO graphical encoding — every spend rectangle is identical width, so all data lives in text laid out in a grid. The right image is a table-as-picture, i.e. an image of text.
pages.mechanism: The right image (#fake-chart) presents tabular data AS an image RATHER THAN as text: dollar values pixelate on zoom, cannot be recoloured/reflowed/selected, and a screen reader gets one alt string instead of a navigable table. None of its visual content (chips, gridlines, legend) conveys meaning beyond the words, so the 1.4.5 'significant other visual content' exclusion does not apply — unlike the left chart whose bar heights genuinely carry the data.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse confirm both have non-empty alt (image-alt passes for both). No scanner OCRs the two pictures, measures that the left bars vary in height (geometry carries meaning, excluded graph) while the right 'bars' are all identical width (geometry carries nothing, table-as-text), and concludes only the right is an image of text. That 'is the non-text visual content significant?' classification is pure human judgment.

citation.quote: The definition of images of text contains the note: This does not include text that is part of a picture that contains significant other visual content. Examples of such pictures include graphs, screenshots, and diagrams which visually convey important information through more than just text.

pages.scenario: A neighbourhood restaurant publishes its daily menu as ONE designed image with a double border, a laurel/dot monogram, an italic display title, an ornamental course rule, and a fork-and-knife glyph. The flourishes make it FEEL like a picture with significant other visual content, but the ornament carries no information — courses, dish names, prices, the soup of the day, and the allergen note are entirely text laid out decoratively. It is an image of text.
pages.mechanism: The menu is presented AS an image RATHER THAN as text: prices pixelate on enlargement, no high-contrast/larger user stylesheet can apply, the two-column price layout cannot reflow on a phone, and text cannot be selected/translated. The laurel/border/monogram are non-text content but not 'significant' (they convey no information), so they do not move the picture into the excluded graphs/screenshots/diagrams category.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: image-alt passes (the alt is a full menu transcript). No automated tool decides whether the laurel/border/monogram is 'significant other visual content' (excluding the image) or mere decoration around an image of text (in scope). Judging that the ornament does no informational work — unlike a real graph/diagram where geometry carries meaning — is exactly the human gestalt the SC requires.

citation.quote: This does not include text that is part of a picture that contains significant other visual content. Examples of such pictures include graphs, screenshots, and diagrams which visually convey important information through more than just text.

pages.scenario: Developer docs 'Exporting a report' page embeds a genuine app screenshot: a window title bar with traffic-light buttons, a menu bar with the File menu open and 'Export…' highlighted, a sidebar report tree, and a modal dialog with a Format dropdown, an 'Include metadata' checkbox, and Cancel/Export buttons. The chrome and layout carry the meaning; the words inside are control labels. Surrounding instructions are live HTML text. This is the sharpening BOUNDARY variant.
pages.mechanism: For 1.4.5 this image is not an image of text: its purpose is to show UI chrome and spatial layout, and the embedded words are control labels, not prose presented as pixels. Converting it to 'live text' would destroy the very information it conveys (the arrangement of the dialog) — precisely the condition the definition note's exclusion exists for. So 1.4.5 is inapplicable to the image (an excluded screenshot); 1.1.1 is separately satisfied by the descriptive alt.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Same blind spot as the failing pages, in reverse: no scanner can tell that THIS image's words are control labels on meaningful UI chrome (excluded, inapplicable) while a near-identical alt-bearing image elsewhere is text-in-disguise (in scope, failed). Reaching the correct INAPPLICABLE is as much a human classification as catching the FAILs.

citation.quote: Detection step is OCR-like: the tester must first recognize that an image *contains text* (vs being a photo/diagram), then judge whether that text is essential (logotype) or could have been live text.

pages.scenario: An HR portal publishes a reimbursement 'Approval flow' as one image, titled 'Approval flow' and captioned 'Approval flowchart' to invite the 1.4.5 diagrams exclusion. But the picture has NO boxes, arrows, connectors, decision diamonds, or branching — it is five numbered sentences stacked on alternating tinted bands. The only structure is top-to-bottom order, which a plain ordered list already provides. It is an image of an ordered list of steps.
pages.mechanism: The steps are presented AS an image RATHER THAN as text: they pixelate on enlargement, cannot be recoloured, and cannot reflow on a narrow screen (the wide image overflows); a screen reader hears one block instead of a navigable ordered list. Because the picture contains no boxes/arrows/branches, none of its visual content is 'significant' — it is an ordered list in disguise, squarely in scope of 1.4.5 (a real flowchart with decision branches would be excluded).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: image-alt passes (the alt is a good transcript). No scanner inspects the picture to confirm there are no boxes or arrows — hence no diagram structure — then concludes the 'flowchart' is really an image of an ordered list. Whether the visual content is 'significant' (a true diagram) or absent (text dressed up as a diagram) is a human visual/semantic judgment.

citation.quote:
EXCLUDE text that is part of a picture that contains significant other visual content such as CAPTCHA,
  graphs, screenshots, and diagrams, which visually convey important information more than just text.

pages.scenario: A municipal permits portal gates an application behind a 'Verify it's you' step that looks like a CAPTCHA (code image, refresh button, input, audio link). Trusted Tester excludes CAPTCHA from images of text — but only because a real CAPTCHA's distortion/noise IS the security function and cannot be reproduced as live text. This image renders the clean word 'SUNFLOWER' in a serif display font on a flat panel: no warping, no per-glyph rotation, no overlapping strokes, no noise, no occluding lines. It is ordinary styled text saved as a picture.
pages.mechanism: A real CAPTCHA's distortion legitimately cannot be replaced by live text (why it is excluded). This clean image's word could be presented as text (or replaced by a genuine accessible challenge) with no loss, so the exclusion fails and 1.4.5 applies: text is presented AS an image RATHER THAN as text, with no way for a low-vision user to enlarge/recolour it without pixelation. Clean styled text is not the 'significant other visual content' (distortion/noise) that defines a CAPTCHA.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The has alt='verification code', so image-alt passes. No scanner measures glyph distortion or noise density to decide 'real CAPTCHA (excluded) vs. clean decorative text masquerading as one (image of text, fail)'. Distinguishing genuine security distortion from cosmetic styling — and thus whether the CAPTCHA exclusion applies — is a human visual judgment.

citation.quote:
EXCLUDE text that is part of a picture that contains significant other visual content such as CAPTCHA,
  graphs, screenshots, and diagrams, which visually convey important information more than just text.

pages.scenario: An insurance broker presents three plan tiers (Essential / Plus / Premier) as a single comparison image with a 'Most popular' ribbon, green check and grey cross glyphs in the coverage rows, and column dividers. The icons/ribbon tempt the 1.4.5 exclusion, but they are redundant: each check/cross marks a yes/no fact already printed as a word, and the ribbon repeats 'Most popular,' also printed. Plan names, prices, deductibles, coverage limits and the yes/no facts are all text in a grid — a comparison table rendered as an image. Tightest borderline in the set.
pages.mechanism: The comparison is presented AS an image RATHER THAN as text: prices/deductibles pixelate on enlargement, cannot be recoloured, and a wide table cannot reflow on mobile (the image overflows); a screen reader gets one alt string instead of a navigable table with row/column headers. Because the check/cross icons and ribbon convey nothing beyond the words, the non-text content is not 'significant' and the exclusion does not apply (a true coverage heatmap encoding values in colour intensity would be excluded).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: image-alt passes (full transcript). No scanner can judge that the check/cross icons and 'Most popular' ribbon are redundant decoration rather than informational graphics — hence that the picture is a table-as-text in scope of 1.4.5. Deciding whether the non-text visual content is 'significant' (unique meaning) versus redundant is exactly the human judgment the SC requires.

citation.quote: This does not include text that is part of a picture that contains significant other visual content. Examples of such pictures include graphs, screenshots, and diagrams which visually convey important information through more than just text.

aspects.title: 'In addition to' MET condition — image of text accompanied by the same content as visible live text
aspects.plain: A picture of text is fine when the exact same words also appear as real visible text nearby, but checkers can't confirm the live text truly matches.
aspects.description: The Understanding note: the SC 'is intended to address situations where images of text are used rather than text. Where images of text are used in addition to text to convey the same information, and where both are presented to the user, this success criterion is met.' The 'event poster + CMS text' example is the canonical PASS: the poster image would fail alone, but because the SAME text is ALSO posted as live, visible text next to it, 1.4.5 is satisfied.
