The hard human judgment is verifying EQUIVALENCE (same information, not a partial summary) AND VISIBILITY (genuinely presented to the user — not an alt attribute, not display:none, not sr-only, not stale content). A checker cannot judge semantic equivalence between an image's pixels and nearby live text, nor that both are 'presented.'
aspects.scLimb: 'In addition to text' met-condition (Understanding para 5 note; distinguishes 1.4.5 from 1.4.9)
aspects.whyUncovered: ACT's decorative-image-plus-text pair (welcome.png with adjacent text) still FAILS, so the corpus never demonstrates the SC being MET because equivalent live text is present in addition to the image. There is no positive 'in addition to' PASS, and no case probing whether the accompanying text is genuinely equivalent and presented vs. only partial/hidden.

references.quote: Where images of text are used in addition to text to convey the same information, and where both are presented to the user, this success criterion is met.

in addition to the image, they can add regular text to the calendar entry, so they post both the poster and the text contained in the image. This text is shown next to the poster image on the site's calendar page.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: Community-arts events calendar: a folk-festival poster (image of text) with the FULL poster contents — date, doors/music times, venue + address, three-act line-up, ticket price, booking URL — reproduced verbatim as visible, restyleable live HTML (a <dl> + <ul>) directly beneath it. The canonical 'in addition to' PASS the ACT corpus lacks.
pages.mechanism: The poster's words exist twice: once as immutable image pixels (inline-SVG data: URI) and once as live HTML. A low-vision user can zoom/recolour the live <dl>/<ul>; a screen-reader user hears the full programme from it. Because the SAME information is presented BOTH as the image AND as adjustable live text, the Understanding-note 'in addition to text … both presented to the user' met-condition is satisfied and 1.4.5 is met even though the image alone would fail.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse have no OCR step, so they never discover the poster pixels contain the same date/venue/line-up/price strings as the live <dl>/<ul>, cannot compare image content to nearby text, and cannot confirm both are rendered. With a non-empty alt, image-alt simply passes and the tools fall silent — they can neither flag a violation nor certify the met-condition. Confirming this PASS is pure human read-the-pixels / read-the-text / compare-meaning judgment.

citation.quote: The success criterion is intended to address situations where images of text are used rather than text. Where images of text are used in addition to text to convey the same information, and where both are presented to the user, this success criterion is met.

pages.scenario: Live-music venue gig listing: a poster image of text states the headline act, tour, date (Fri 7 Nov 2026), doors 7:30, two support acts, 18+ policy, and £24.50 price; the adjacent live text reproduces only the act + tour name in the <h1>, a marketing blurb, and three generic 'tag' chips. Text exists 'in addition to' the image but omits the date, doors, supports, age policy, and price.
pages.mechanism: A blind or low-vision user gets, as live text, only the act/tour name + blurb + tags; the date, doors time, both support acts, the 18+ restriction, and the £24.50 price live ONLY as pixels in the poster (whose alt is just a label). Because the accompanying live text does not convey the SAME information as the image, the 'in addition to' met-condition does not rescue those facts and 1.4.5 fails for them.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: No tool OCRs the poster to learn it contains the date/doors/supports/age/price, none scans the live text to confirm those strings are absent, and none compares image meaning to text meaning. The image has a plausible non-empty alt so image-alt passes, and the live HTML is well-formed, so every rule stays green. Detecting that the accompanying text is a teaser rather than an equivalent is read-both-and-compare human judgment.

citation.quote: Where images of text are used in addition to text to convey the same information, and where both are presented to the user, this success criterion is met.

pages.scenario: Interior-architecture studio testimonial: a designed quote-card image of text, paired in the DOM with a live <blockquote> containing word-for-word identical wording 'in addition to' the image — but the <blockquote> carries the studio's reusable visually-hidden (sr-only 1px clip-path:inset(50%)) helper, so it is removed from the visible page. Equivalence is perfect; visibility is broken.
pages.mechanism: A screen-reader user does hear the full quote from the clipped <blockquote>, but 1.4.5 protects people who can SEE text yet need to restyle it. For a low-vision user who needs the quote at 200% in high contrast, the only thing on screen is the immutable image; the equivalent text is clipped to a 1px offscreen box and cannot be enlarged, recoloured, or reflowed. The note requires BOTH the image and the text be 'presented to the user'; hidden text is exposed to AT but not visibly presented, so the met-condition does not apply.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: visually-hidden/sr-only text is an intentional, ubiquitous pattern; axe/WAVE/Lighthouse treat clipped-but-present text as fine (it is in the a11y tree, has no contrast problem because it isn't painted), and image-alt passes. No tool reasons that, specifically for 1.4.5, the equivalent text must be VISIBLY presented so a low-vision user can restyle it, not merely reachable by a screen reader. Distinguishing 'exposed to AT' from 'presented to the user' for this SC is human judgment about who 1.4.5 protects.

citation.quote: Where images of text are used in addition to text to convey the same information, and where both are presented to the user, this success criterion is met. This allows authors to convey content using any styling they desire, while also presenting the information in text, which can then be manipulated by users to make it more distinguishable.

pages.scenario: Café daily-specials: a photographed chalkboard image of text shows TODAY's specials (Spiced Parsnip Soup £6.50 / Wild Mushroom Risotto £12.50 / Sticky Toffee Pudding £6.00); the live 'Text version' <ul> beneath it was not refreshed this week and still lists LAST week's specials and prices (Carrot & Coriander Soup £6.00 / Beef Lasagne £11.95 / Lemon Cheesecake £5.50). Both are presented, but they convey different menus.
pages.mechanism: A sighted customer reads today's specials off the photo; a blind or low-vision user relying on the restyleable text version hears last week's stale menu and wrong prices — actively misleading. The 'in addition to' met-condition requires the accompanying text to convey the SAME information as the image; stale text conveys DIFFERENT information, so the condition is not satisfied and 1.4.5 is not met.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Nothing is malformed: the board photo has a sensible alt, the <ul> is valid and high-contrast, image-alt passes. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse do not OCR the chalkboard, do not parse the live list, and have no notion of which version is current. Detecting that the two disagree — and that the text is the stale one — requires a human to read both and apply freshness/equivalence judgment.

citation.quote: Determine if text can be used instead of the image of text to present the **same effect and information**.

pages.scenario: District-council garden-waste notice: the entire substantive notice (collection day change, £45 subscription, 20 June deadline, 'will not be emptied' warning, renewal URL/phone) is a single image of text with a faithful, complete alt attribute; there is NO visible live-text version of the notice anywhere on the page. The image of text is used instead of text, with a text alternative bolted on — not in addition to visible text.
pages.mechanism: A screen-reader user hears the full notice from the alt, so 1.1.1 is satisfied. But 1.4.5 protects users who can SEE text yet need to change how it looks; for them the alt is invisible — exposed only to AT, never rendered, so it cannot be enlarged, recoloured, or reflowed on screen. The 'in addition to text' met-condition specifically requires text 'presented to the user' (visible live text alongside the image); an alt attribute is not that, so the condition does not apply and the image of text fails 1.4.5.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The image has a long, accurate alt, so image-alt passes and axe/WAVE/Lighthouse treat it as a model image. None OCRs the graphic to discover its pixels ARE the notice (text that could trivially be HTML), and none has any concept of the 1.4.5 distinction between 'alt present' and 'visible live text present in addition.' Recognising the whole notice is a picture, and reasoning that a text alternative is not text 'presented to the user,' is human visual + semantic judgment.

citation.quote: If authors can use text to achieve the same visual effect, they should present the information as text rather than using an image.

pages.scenario: Residential-building water-shutoff notice: a single bilingual flyer image of text contains both an ENGLISH block and an ESPAÑOL block carrying the same shutoff details; the resident portal renders a live 'Text version' 'in addition to' the image, but a volunteer transcribed only the English half. The Spanish block exists nowhere as live text — only in the image pixels.
pages.mechanism: An English-reading user gets the notice as restyleable live text. A Spanish-reading resident who is blind, or who has low vision and needs to enlarge/recolour, gets their language only as immutable image pixels (the image alt is just a label) — for them the image of text is used instead of text. The 'in addition to' met-condition requires the accompanying text to convey the SAME information as the image; dropping an entire language means it does not, so 1.4.5 is not met for the Spanish content.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The image has a reasonable alt, the live English block is valid, and contrast is fine, so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse stay green. No tool OCRs the flyer to discover it contains a Spanish block, and none reasons that the live 'Text version' reproduces only one of the two languages the image carries. Spotting the dropped language requires a human who can read both languages in the image, read the live text, and notice the Spanish half is image-only — semantic + visual + multilingual judgment.

citation.quote: If the text in the "text alternative" cannot be used in place of the non-text content without losing information or function then it fails because it is not, in fact, an alternative to the non-text content.

aspects.title: Essential-presentation exceptions beyond logos — type samples, font-family specimens, historical documents, symbolic glyphs
aspects.plain: Some pictures of text are allowed because their exact look matters (a font sample, a scanned historical letter), and judging whether the look is essential needs a human.
aspects.description: Intent para 2 and the Understanding enumerate PASS-by-essential-presentation cases distinct from logotypes: a 'Representation of a font family' (substituting another font 'would defeat the purpose of the representation'), 'A representation of a letter' (an original historical document whose original format is essential to information about its time period), 'Symbolic text characters' (B/I/ABC editor buttons whose glyphs 'do not form a sequence that expresses something in human language'), and type samples. Judging these requires understanding WHY the presentation is essential — re-typesetting as live text would destroy the very thing communicated — and rejecting ABUSE where ordinary informational text is wrongly justified as 'a type sample' or 'historical look.' A checker cannot reason about whether a particular visual presentation is essential to meaning.
aspects.scLimb: Essential-presentation exception (non-logo branches): font specimen, historical original format, symbolic non-language glyphs
aspects.whyUncovered: The corpus has the comic-cover type-sample (Ivanhoe) and maps the A/A resize buttons to symbolic characters, but never tests the historical/original-format-essential rationale, the symbolic-vs-human-language editor-glyph distinction in either direction, nor the abuse case where ordinary informational text is wrongly justified under the type-sample/font-representation exception. 'Essential' is asserted by the corpus rather than stress-tested.

references.quote: A web page contains a representation of an original letter. The depiction of the letter in its original format is essential to information being conveyed about the time period in which it was written.
A web page contains information about a particular font family. Substituting the font family with another font would defeat the purpose of the representation.

Some of the buttons use text characters that do not form a sequence that expresses something in human language. For example "B" to increase font weight, "I" to italicize the text and "ABC" to check the spelling.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: A typography magazine feature 'Why Garamond still wins for long reads' bakes its own ordinary body paragraphs (history + argument + recommendation) into a single Garamond image 'so you can see the typeface in real use'. The article ABOUT a font is treated as if it were a font specimen, abusing the 'Representation of a font family' exception. A genuine live-text letterform specimen ('Hh Aa Gg Qq') sits above it for contrast; only the running prose was wrongly imaged.
pages.mechanism: The article's running prose exists only as SVG <text> glyphs inside an inline-SVG data: URI image (verified: 'Claude Garamont cut his romans' absent from live innerText, present in alt). The words are ordinary information, not a demonstration of letterforms, so re-typesetting in the user's own font would lose nothing essential. A user needing a larger/dyslexia-friendly/high-contrast font, wider spacing, or reflow at 200-400% zoom cannot adjust this fixed raster and it pixelates on enlargement. The font-representation exception does not apply because the text is the content, not a specimen.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every img has a non-empty accurate alt (image-alt passes axe/WAVE/Lighthouse), the page has a title, heading hierarchy, landmarks, and good contrast, so no linter rule fires. No tool OCRs the image to learn its pixels are running prose, and none can decide whether that text is an essential font representation (exempt) or ordinary information set in a font (a violation). Recognising 'an article ABOUT a font is not itself a font specimen' is a human semantic judgment about whether re-typesetting destroys essential meaning.

citation.quote: Representation of a font family ... A web page contains information about a particular font family. Substituting the font family with another font would defeat the purpose of the representation. The representation is included as a jpeg image which does not allow the text characteristics to be changed. The image has a text alternative.

pages.scenario: A type foundry's retail specimen page for a new display typeface ('Brume Display') the visitor does not have installed and that is not licensed for web embedding. Specimen images show the actual letterforms ('Velvet Morning', ffi/ffl ligatures, swash Q R K) because the appearance of the glyphs IS what is being sold; re-typesetting in a fallback font would show a different typeface and defeat the representation. The page also provides the same strings as live, selectable, resizable fallback-font text and an editable size-adjustable preview. PASS twin to case-01.
pages.mechanism: The specimen images legitimately use the font-representation exception: substituting the font would defeat the purpose of the representation, so the image of text cannot be replaced by text with the same effect. The page does NOT strand users needing adjustable text — each specimen string also appears as live HTML (verified: 'Velvet Morning' present in BOTH image and live innerText), and an editable preview with a working font-size slider (drives --preview-size) lets low-vision users enlarge/recolour the live copy. This is the conformant 'in addition to' + customizable pattern.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Structurally identical to the abused twins: an automated tool sees img elements with non-empty alt plus live text and cannot tell a genuine font specimen from an abused one. It cannot reason 'this image shows the typeface being sold, and substituting the font would defeat the representation.' Confirming the exception genuinely applies — rather than wrongly flagging or rubber-stamping — is a human judgment; checkers have no concept of 'essential presentation.'

citation.quote: Where images of text are used in addition to text to convey the same information, and where both are presented to the user, this success criterion is met.

pages.scenario: A museum 'Plan your visit' page renders its modern 2024 opening hours and a donation appeal as a faux-antique parchment image — torn-edge border, sepia, cursive quill font — 'to give the page a historic feel'. There is no original artefact: the text was authored today, so its original format is HTML, not a period letter. The 'representation of a letter / original-format-essential' exception is abused to justify avoidable images of text. FAIL twin to case-06.
pages.mechanism: The opening hours, season, and suggested donation exist only as SVG <text> glyphs in an inline-SVG data: URI styled as parchment (verified: 'Harrowby Hall is open Wednesday' absent from live innerText, present in alt). Because the text was authored today and its appearance conveys nothing about a historical time period, the visual presentation is not essential — live HTML would convey the same effect while remaining adjustable. The decorative cursive font additionally harms low-vision/cognitive legibility and the raster pixelates at 200-400% zoom, with no way to resize, recolour, or reflow.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The image has a non-empty accurate alt (image-alt passes), and the page has a title, headings, landmarks, and good surrounding contrast, so no rule fires. No tool OCRs the parchment to learn it contains today's opening hours, and none can know the 'antique' text was authored this year with no original-format rationale. Distinguishing a genuine scanned historical original (exempt) from a modern costume on ordinary informational text (a violation) is a human contextual judgment about whether the original format is essential to information about a time period.

citation.quote: A representation of a letter ... A web page contains a representation of an original letter. The depiction of the letter in its original format is essential to information being conveyed about the time period in which it was written.

pages.scenario: A webmail compose toolbar replaces the symbolic glyphs (B/I/ABC) with images of the FULL WORD LABELS 'Bold', 'Italic', 'Underline', 'Spell check' because single letters were deemed 'too cryptic'. Those are English words — a sequence that expresses something in human language — so the symbolic-text-characters exception does not apply; they are ordinary label text rendered as images and should be live text. Each button also carries a matching aria-label, so AT names are correct.
pages.mechanism: The button labels are human-language words that exist only as SVG <text> glyphs inside images (verified: 'Spell check' absent from live innerText, present via aria-label). The accessible name comes from aria-label so braille/screen-reader output is fine (1.1.1/4.1.2 met), but a sighted low-vision user relying on OS/browser font scaling, a dyslexia-friendly typeface, or forced-colors mode cannot adjust these labels — they are fixed pixels that blur on zoom and won't recolour. Because the words express human language they are not symbolic characters, so live text could and should convey the same effect.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Each button has a correct accessible name (aria-label), the inner image is correctly decorative (alt=""), roles are valid, and contrast is fine, so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse report no violations. No tool OCRs the button faces to discover the labels are full words rather than symbols, and none can apply the 'does this sequence express something in human language?' test that separates an exempt symbolic glyph from a non-exempt word label. That symbolic-vs-language call is the human judgment the exception requires.

citation.quote: Some of the buttons use text characters that do not form a sequence that expresses something in human language. For example "B" to increase font weight, "I" to italicize the text and "ABC" to check the spelling. The symbolic text characters are included as gif images which do not allow the text characteristics to be changed. The buttons have text alternatives.

pages.scenario: A cloud-storage Terms-of-Service page renders its binding clauses (governing law, liability cap, arbitration / class-action waiver) as a single image and labels it 'a type sample of our house legal typeface, Pinevault Text' via both a figcaption and an aria-describedby note. It is not a specimen — it is legally operative contract text the user must read, resize, and reflow. A human reviewer must reject the bogus 'type sample' essential-presentation justification.
pages.mechanism: The operative legal text exists only as SVG <text> glyphs inside an inline-SVG data: URI (verified: 'binding individual arbitration' absent from live innerText, present in alt). A low-vision user needing 200-400% zoom cannot enlarge the arbitration clause without pixelation; a forced-colors user cannot recolour it; reflow to a single column is impossible for a fixed raster. The information is the words of a binding contract, not a demonstration of letterforms, so the visual presentation is not essential and live HTML would convey the same effect. The self-applied 'type sample' label does not change what the content is.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The image has a full accurate alt and the page has a title, headings, landmarks, and good contrast, so nothing fires. Worse, the DOM truthfully states in markup (figcaption + aria-describedby) that this is a 'type sample', and there is no machine-checkable signal the claim is false. No tool OCRs the image or evaluates whether 'type sample' is a legitimate essential-presentation claim for binding legal prose. Rejecting the abuse — recognising operative contract text is not a font specimen — is a pure human contextual judgment.

citation.quote: This includes instances where a particular presentation of text is essential to the information being conveyed, such as type samples, logotypes, branding, etc.

pages.scenario: A museum object page presents a scanned 11th-century Chinese seal-script hanging scroll (山高水長). The artefact IS the brushwork — stroke order, ink density, and the individual calligrapher's hand — so re-typesetting in a modern seal font would show a different object and lose the historical information. The genuine original-format-essential exception. The page also provides the modern Unicode transcription (lang=zh-Hant), romanisation, and English translation beside it as live, selectable, resizable text. PASS twin to case-03.
pages.mechanism: The scroll image's accessible name transcribes the four characters AND describes the calligraphic form (rounded even-weight strokes, the lean of 長, dry-brush flecking on 水 — verified image-side only), so AT users learn both the words and what is visually significant. The irreplaceable information (this hand's brushwork) is what the image preserves, so the image of text is essential and permitted. The page also provides live selectable resizable HTML (zh-Hant transcription + romanisation + translation), so low-vision users can enlarge/recolour adjustable text while researchers get the original form.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Structurally indistinguishable from a page that merely imaged its restaurant menu in Chinese: an img with alt sitting next to live Chinese text. A tool cannot OCR the scroll, cannot tell calligraphy-as-artefact from text-as-image, and has no concept of 'original format essential to information about a time period.' Confirming the exception genuinely applies — and that adjustable equivalent text is provided — is a human art-historical and contextual judgment, not a lint check.

citation.quote: A representation of a letter ... A web page contains a representation of an original letter. The depiction of the letter in its original format is essential to information being conveyed about the time period in which it was written. The letter is included as a gif image which does not allow the text characteristics to be changed. The image has a text alternative.

aspects.title: Core image-of-text-vs-live-text detection across delivery mechanisms and decoy live text
aspects.plain: Words baked into images (CSS backgrounds, SVG, sprites) instead of real text can't be resized or recoloured, and tools often can't even detect that the image contains text.
aspects.description: The SC's foundational requirement — 'If the technologies being used can achieve the visual presentation, text is used to convey information rather than images of text' — depends on a human first recognizing that an image actually contains rendered text (OCR-like detection) and then confirming the same visual effect was achievable in HTML/CSS so the content should have been live text. The hard cases require semantic judgment: text baked into a CSS background-image or pseudo-element (no , no alt, invisible to most checkers), text rendered via SVG inside an image vs. live selectable SVG , web-font glyph text that looks like an image but is real text, and decoys where author-supplied alt or a hidden sr-only string makes a tool believe live text exists when the displayed content is still a bitmap. No automated tool reliably OCRs arbitrary images and judges achievability; this is core human semantic/visual work.
aspects.scLimb: Core SC requirement: live text rather than images of text where the visual presentation is technologically achievable
aspects.whyUncovered: ACT exercises multiple embedding technologies but only at clear extremes (pure-text image FAIL vs. text-free photo PASS, plus one live-SVG-text INAPPLICABLE). It never tests the achievability gating clause (whether the desired visual effect was actually attainable in HTML/CSS), nor the deceptive middle where text is hidden in CSS backgrounds/pseudo-elements or where decoy live text/alt masks a bitmap. The threshold distinguishing achievable-so-must-be-live from genuinely-not-achievable is unexercised.

references.quote: Determine if text can be used instead of the image of text to present the same effect and information.
If authors can use text to achieve the same visual effect, they should present the information as text rather than using an image.
Rather than using bitmap images to present headings in a specific font and size, an author uses CSS to achieve the same result.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: Aurelia Trust bank masthead: the site-name wordmark is an inline-SVG (image of text) delivered via CSS background-image on the <h1>, whose only real DOM text is a visually-hidden sr-only decoy span saying the same words; an identical-looking live-text twin (Aurelia Savings) proves the look was achievable.
pages.mechanism:
Image of text delivered as a CSS background-image (no /alt) on an

; visible serif wordmark is SVG inside the background, absent from DOM/accessibility tree and non-resizable/non-recolorable, while an sr-only span provides programmatic text. Visual presentation is plainly achievable as live text (the twin heading), no logotype/essential exception applies.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss:
No exists so image-alt never fires; the

has a non-empty accessible name from the sr-only span so empty-heading checks pass. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse do not rasterize and OCR background-image SVGs, do not compare the pixels to the sr-only text, and have no rule for 'background image is text whose look is achievable in CSS'. Recognizing it is an image of text and judging achievability/essential is human work.

citation.quote: Rather than using bitmap images to present headings in a specific font and size, an author uses CSS to achieve the same result.

pages.scenario: Lakeshore Public Library reading room: the featured excerpt (opening of The Little Prince) is a genuine raster PNG of a six-line body paragraph embedded in <svg role=img><image href=data:image/png> with a decoy <title>/<desc> naming the book; a sibling block renders Whitman as live, selectable SVG <text> as the PASS/inapplicable foil.
pages.mechanism: A multi-line paragraph of body prose is shipped as a raster PNG inside an SVG <image>, given an accessible name by decoy <title>/<desc>; the prose is fixed pixels (non-resizable, non-recolorable, pixelates on zoom; an 'A+ Larger text' control visibly fails). The same serif body look is achievable with @font-face/live text, proven by the adjacent live SVG <text> block; no essential exception applies to a novel's paragraph.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The PNG is wrapped in an <svg><image> that has an accessible name from <title>/<desc>, so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse report no missing-alt or unnamed-graphic issue. None OCRs the embedded PNG to discover it is a paragraph of body prose, and none can distinguish the visually-similar live-<text> sibling (text) from this raster (image of text) — both are svg role=img with names. Reading the pixels and judging achievability is human OCR-like detection.

citation.quote: If authors can use text to achieve the same visual effect, they should present the information as text rather than using an image.

pages.scenario: Trattoria del Ponte dinner menu: each dish name is painted from a single SVG sprite-sheet set as a CSS background-image and revealed per row with background-position (brush-script 'calligraphy'); the .name span is empty with aria-label="<dish name>" (e.g. 'Tagliatelle al Ragù'), so AT users hear the dish but the visible name is fixed pixels; prices are live text and the live-text 'Dolci' course is the achievable foil.
pages.mechanism: Dish names are images of text delivered as a single CSS sprite-sheet background-image (no /alt), revealed per row via background-position. The .name contains no text node at all (it is empty); the accessible name is supplied by an aria-label of the actual dish name on that span (with role="text"). The brush-script presentation is achievable with a licensed @font-face webfont + live text; the names are words, not a logotype, not a picture with significant other visual content, and not user-customizable.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Names come from background-image so there is no for axe/WAVE to flag; rows have non-empty accessible names (aria-label) so empty-element rules pass; live-text prices make rows look populated; Lighthouse reports nothing. No tool slices and OCRs a sprite-sheet to learn the backgrounds spell dish names, compares them to the off-screen text, or judges a brush-script could have been a licensed webfont — OCR-like detection plus an achievability call.

citation.quote: It is better to use real text for the text portion of these elements, and a combination of semantic markup and style sheets to create the appropriate visual presentation.

pages.scenario: The Meridian Review long-form article: the large italic pull-quote ('We stopped designing streets for cars...') is painted by a CSS ::before pseudo-element whose content box carries a background-image SVG of the quote glyphs; the quote words exist nowhere in the DOM, only a live <figcaption> attribution does. This is the WCAG 'A quote' example built as an image of text.
pages.mechanism:
The pull-quote is an image of text delivered through a ::before generated-content background-image — no , no alt, and the quotation words are entirely absent from the DOM and accessibility tree. Generated-content background images ignore font-size/color/forced-colors and pixelate on zoom. The italic/indented/large-serif effect is the textbook achievable-in-CSS case (live
+ CSS); not essential, not customizable.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: There is no so image-alt never fires; the quote lives in a ::before background-image, which axe/WAVE/Lighthouse do not rasterize or OCR (they cannot read generated-content pixels) and for which they have no 'pseudo-element is an image of text' rule. The figure has a name and the article has ample real text so nothing looks empty. Detecting the styled quotation is an image of text and judging the look was achievable as live HTML+CSS is exactly the human reasoning in WCAG's 'A quote' example.

citation.quote: A web page contains a quote. The quote itself is presented as italicized text, indented from the left margin.

pages.scenario:
Birchwood Outfitters storefront: the 'Summer Clearance Event' category heading is a real raster PNG wrapped in an

, with a perfect descriptive decoy alt ('Summer Clearance Event'); a live-text heading 'New Arrivals for Fall' shows the achievable treatment. A descriptive alt satisfies 1.1.1 but does not satisfy 1.4.5.
pages.mechanism: A styled heading is delivered as a non-resizable raster bitmap image of text; the alt is an exact transcription so 1.1.1 and naive heading checks are satisfied, but the displayed heading pixelates on zoom and ignores user font/color/forced-colors settings. The bold red look is trivially achievable with live HTML+CSS (demonstrated by the adjacent live heading); not a logotype, not essential, not customizable — so it fails 1.4.5 despite correct alt.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: This is the decoy trap: the image has a non-empty, descriptive alt so axe image-alt, WAVE, and Lighthouse all pass — they check 1.1.1-style name presence, not 1.4.5 adjustability. None OCRs the pixels (they trust the alt) and none encodes the rule that a heading rendered as an image of text fails even with perfect alt because the presentation cannot be adjusted and was achievable in CSS. Only a human applying the achievability gate reaches the correct verdict.

citation.quote: Goal: Users can adjust how text is presented.

pages.scenario: Halcyon Type Foundry product page for the typeface 'Meridian Display': the large character-set specimen is a raster PNG showing the actual letterforms of the font being sold (with a descriptive alt), surrounded by live-text price, feature list, buy button, and preview field. The achievability/essential gate makes this a deliberate PASS boundary foil.
pages.mechanism: The specimen is an image of text, but its visual presentation IS the information (the exact glyphs of this specific typeface); rendering it as substitutable live text would defeat the representation, so 1.4.5's essential/not-achievable exception applies. A text alternative satisfies 1.1.1, and all surrounding UI is live text — so the page passes for the right reason.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Tools fail in both directions on 1.4.5: they cannot OCR the specimen to recognize it contains text, and decisively cannot make the human 'is this presentation essential / unachievable as live text?' judgment that separates a legitimate type specimen (PASS) from an avoidable styled heading (FAIL). A naive 'image with text-like alt' flag would wrongly fail this page; ignoring it would pass it coincidentally. Only a human applying the essential clause lands on the correct PASS for the right reason.

citation.quote: A web page contains information about a particular font family. Substituting the font family with another font would defeat the purpose of the representation.

methodology.enNote: Reflow — WCAG 2.1 AA, post-dates Section 508 / WCAG 2.0; no Trusted Tester test.

aspects.title: Non-excepted content forces a horizontal scrollbar at 320 CSS px (fixed-width container, non-wrapping layout, layout-table-as-prose)
aspects.plain: On a narrow phone-width screen, fixed-width or non-wrapping content spills sideways forcing horizontal scrolling, and a human must judge whether that overflow is a real failure.
aspects.description: The defining 1.4.10 failure: when the page is rendered at a width equivalent to 320 CSS px (the 1280px-at-400% equivalent), some section of NON-excepted content forces two-dimensional scrolling. Triggers include a fixed-width container (e.g. width:680px), a body/wrapper min-width, a flex/grid row that refuses to wrap, absolutely-positioned off-canvas content, or a layout table (a <table> used only to position prose side-by-side) that wrongly relies on the data-table exception. The viewport meta is permissive so b4f0c3 passes, yet the rendered page fails Reflow. The judgment that survives automation: a tool can see scrollWidth > clientWidth, but it CANNOT decide whether that overflow is a legitimate exception (real data table, map, video, fixed-dimension media) or a genuine failure, nor whether a wide <table> holds real tabular data versus prose that should reflow. A human must classify the overflowing element and confirm reflow is actually broken for content that should reflow.
aspects.scLimb: The core normative requirement: 'Content can be presented without loss of information or functionality, and without requiring scrolling in two dimensions' at 320 CSS px width for horizontal-language content. The exception for sections that 'require two-dimensional layout for understanding or functionality' governs which overflow is permitted.
aspects.whyUncovered: The lone ACT rule b4f0c3 is a pure DOM-string check of the viewport meta content attribute; it never renders the page, never sets a 320px viewport, and never measures overflow. Its own mapping makes 1.4.4 primary and notes 'most failed examples [actually] satisfy' 1.4.10. The synthetic corpus pages are a title plus a single short Lorem-ipsum paragraph with no content wide enough to overflow. While raw page-overflow is partly machine-detectable, the disposition (legitimate exception vs failure, data table vs layout table) is an irreducible human classification.

references.quote: This criterion requires non-excepted sections of content that are written in horizontal languages reflow when narrowed to a width equivalent to 320 CSS pixels.

When lines of text extend beyond the edge of a viewport, users will be forced to scroll back-and-forth to read line by line. This can cause them to lose their place and can significantly increase both physical and cognitive effort.
The objective of this technique is to be able to present content without introducing a horizontal scroll bar at a width equivalent to 320 CSS pixels

pages.scenario: Independent food-writing essay (Cadence Kitchen Journal) whose article body is hard-pinned to width:680px (not max-width); masthead and footer are fluid. At a 320 CSS-px viewport the whole page gains a horizontal scrollbar and every line of plain prose runs off the right edge.
pages.mechanism: Fixed-width container: .article{width:680px} cannot shrink below 680px, so document scrollWidth (680) exceeds the 320px viewport. Non-excepted running prose (no table/map/media) requires two-dimensional scrolling to read line by line — verified at 320px: scrollWidth=680, prose paragraphs and h2 overflow.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse never render at 320 CSS px nor measure scrollWidth>clientWidth; b4f0c3 (the only ACT rule for 1.4.10) is a pure string check of the viewport meta and passes. Even an overflow detector cannot decide the 680px block is non-excepted prose (fail) rather than a data table or media (legitimate exception) — that classification is human.

citation.quote: This criterion requires non-excepted sections of content that are written in horizontal languages reflow when narrowed to a width equivalent to 320 CSS pixels.

pages.scenario: University LMS course page using a desktop two-column flex shell (fixed 240px sidebar nav + lesson with min-width:520px) and NO flex-wrap. At 320px the columns cannot stack or shrink, so the page scrolls horizontally; both columns are ordinary reflowable content.
pages.mechanism: Flex row that refuses to wrap: .shell is display:flex with no flex-wrap; flex:0 0 240px sidebar + min-width:520px lesson exceed 320px combined. Verified at 320px: scrollWidth=808, nav/lesson/h1/p overflow. No two-dimensional-layout requirement — a nav list and lesson prose should stack into one column.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Static scanners see valid <nav>/<main>/lists and a permissive viewport meta — all green. They do not lay the page out at 320 CSS px to find the non-wrapping flex row, and the deciding question (do these columns require a two-dimensional layout, or should they stack?) is a meaning judgment a tool cannot make.

citation.quote: A common way for many article-driven web pages to meet the Reflow success criterion is to ensure that the presentation of a web page can adjust to a single column of content, fitting into a 320 CSS pixel wide viewport and only requiring a user scroll vertically to read the content of the web page.

pages.scenario: County public-library FAQ (native <details> accordions). Every layout rule is fluid (max-width, percentages) EXCEPT a survivor line in the global reset: body{min-width:600px}. That floor clamps the whole document so it can never reflow below 600px at any zoom.
pages.mechanism: Body/wrapper min-width prevents reflow: body{min-width:600px} sets a hard lower bound, so at a 320px viewport the body stays 600px and scrollWidth>clientWidth. Verified at 320px: scrollWidth=600, h1/h2/p overflow. Content is an accordion of short prose answers — no exception applies.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: No linter/axe rule forbids min-width on body; it is valid and often legitimate CSS. Detecting the failure requires rendering at 320 CSS px to measure overflow (which scanners do not do) and then judging the clamped content is reflowable FAQ prose, not an excepted two-dimensional section.

citation.quote: When content can fit within smaller viewports it not only helps those using mobile devices to read content. It also helps people who need to resize or zoom in a web interface on larger devices, as is the intent of this success criterion.

pages.scenario: Nonprofit annual-report director's letter laid out as two newspaper-style prose columns inside a 700px fixed <table role=presentation> with two 330px <td> cells. The table holds no tabular data; it is a layout table that cannot reflow and wrongly relies on the data-table exception.
pages.mechanism: Layout-table-as-prose: table.letter{table-layout:fixed;width:700px} with two 330px cells of running prose cannot shrink. Verified at 320px: scrollWidth=722, the letter paragraphs overflow. role=presentation confirms there is no tabular semantics, so the data-table exception does NOT apply.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A tool can see a <table> and even role=presentation, but cannot decide whether a wide overflowing table holds genuine tabular data (excepted) or prose that should reflow (not excepted) — the exact classification this aspect targets. Scanners also do not render at 320 CSS px; the markup is well-formed and the viewport meta is permissive, so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse report nothing.

citation.quote: A section of content that requires two-dimensional layout for understanding or functionality, such as a table or map, has an exception to this success criterion. However, sections of content within the two-dimensional layout, such as each cell within a table, would still need to meet this success criterion.

pages.scenario: Volunteer-run trailhead-conditions page with a fluid article and a 'current trail status' <aside> taken out of flow with position:absolute; left:340px; width:280px. At 320px the sidebar's left edge is already off the right of the screen, forcing a page-level horizontal scrollbar to even reach it.
pages.mechanism: Absolutely-positioned off-canvas content: .conditions{position:absolute;left:340px;width:280px} has a right edge at 620 CSS px, beyond a 320px viewport, so the document scrollWidth exceeds clientWidth. Verified at 320px: scrollWidth=620, the aside/h3 overflow. The status box is plain reflowable content that should stack under the article (set static at narrow widths).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A scanner sees a valid named <aside> and a permissive viewport meta — no violation. It does not render at 320 CSS px to find the absolutely-positioned box off-screen forcing horizontal scroll, and even with overflow detection, classifying the off-canvas element as non-excepted content (vs a legitimately fixed-dimension widget) needs a human.

citation.quote: It is strongly suggested that at smaller viewport sizes that such components are modified to have static positioning, or their display can be toggled by the user.

pages.scenario: PASS control / legitimate exception: a sales-ops briefing with a genuine data table (regions x monthly metrics, real th scope row/col relationships) wrapped in a focusable overflow:auto scroll region, while all surrounding prose (max-width:720px) reflows into the 320px column.
pages.mechanism: Correct contained exception: the wide data table (min-width:680px) needs a two-dimensional layout and is isolated inside .table-scroll{overflow:auto} (tabindex=0, role=region, aria-label). Verified at 320px: page scrollWidth==clientWidth==320, zero non-excepted offenders — only the table scrolls inside its own box; all prose reflows.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A naive 'flag any scrollWidth>clientWidth element' detector would FALSELY flag this page's inner table box. Passing it correctly requires the human judgment that the overflowing element is a real data table whose meaning needs two dimensions (excepted) AND that the non-excepted prose around it reflows — the same judgment that distinguishes it from case-04 and case-07.

citation.quote: A data table relies on two-dimensional layout for understanding, but by presenting the table in its own scrollable container it allows other content which does not meet a two-dimensional layout exception to reflow as its containing element adjusts.

pages.scenario: Transit Route-12 timetable: a genuine, excepted data table (stop columns x trip rows), but uncontained (no scroll box) and the content wrapper was sized to the table (.page{width:760px}) so it would 'line up'. The excepted table thus drags the surrounding non-excepted service-notes prose off-canvas — the 'exception does not extend' failure, the inverse of case-06.
pages.mechanism: Exception leaks onto non-excepted content: .page{width:760px} (sized to table.timetable{min-width:760px}) forces every paragraph/heading into a 760px line box, so prose wraps at 760px not at the 320px viewport. Verified at 320px: scrollWidth=780, h2/p overflow off-canvas. The table scrolling is fine (excepted); the prose requiring two-dimensional scrolling is the violation.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: This is the subtlest classification: a tool seeing a wide <table> might wrongly excuse the whole page as 'table exception' (as in case-06), while a flag-all-overflow tool would wrongly flag case-06. Getting case-07 right requires the human, section-by-section distinctions that the table is excepted but the paragraphs are not, and that those paragraphs are themselves forced into two-dimensional scrolling because the table was not isolated.

citation.quote: Fail: Due to the way this example was implemented, the web page has both horizontal and vertical scrollbars. While the table meets the exception for two-dimensional layout for understanding, the paragraphs following the table in the screenshot do not.

aspects.title: F102 — content/functionality present at desktop width disappears at 320px and is not reachable by any equivalent mechanism
aspects.plain: Shrinking the page to phone width hides content (a sidebar, nav links, a search box) with no equivalent way to reach it, so functionality is simply lost.
aspects.description: The dedicated failure technique F102: a section visible at 1280px is hidden at 320px (via display:none in a max-width media query, a collapsed sidebar, a responsive nav that drops links, a search field that vanishes, labels replaced by placeholders) WITHOUT providing the same or equivalent content through a disclosure widget, hamburger menu, dialog, icon, or link to another view. The page reflows (no horizontal scroll) and the viewport meta is fine, so it looks compliant to a tool, but information or functionality has been lost. Judging it requires comparing the desktop and narrow renderings, diffing what content is reachable, and a semantic decision about whether a replacement mechanism genuinely surfaces the same information (does that hamburger button actually expose the dropped nav links, or is it dead? is placeholder text an acceptable label substitute? does the disclosure actually contain the hidden section?).
aspects.scLimb: The 'without loss of information or functionality' half of the SC at 320 CSS px width — distinct from the two-dimensional-scrolling half. Content may legitimately be repositioned or relocated, but it must remain available.
aspects.whyUncovered: F102 has no ACT rule and zero test cases; the corpus only has b4f0c3 (viewport string). Detecting it requires rendering at two widths, diffing reachable content, and a human judgment about whether a replacement mechanism (hamburger, disclosure, link) genuinely surfaces the same information. A tool cannot decide whether a hamburger icon actually leads to the dropped links or whether placeholder text is an acceptable label substitute.

references.quote: a failure that occurs when a change of the viewport width to 320px makes content disappear that was available at wider viewport widths

This content, however, should still be available after reflow to 320px viewport width, either by being repositioned in a single column view, or through some interaction offering the information in some other way, for example, in a disclosure area, a dialog, or via a link to another view.
Labels above text inputs are hidden and replaced by placeholder text after reflow, without a technique showing dedicated labels when focusing the fields.

pages.scenario: Long-form coastal-news investigation: a sticky right-hand 'Continue this investigation' rail holds eight hand-curated related-story links that exist nowhere else. At max-width:600px the page reflows to a clean single column but the rail is display:none, and the eight links are reproduced nowhere — no disclosure, no section index, no inline list. On a phone or at 400% zoom the follow-up investigation is unreachable.
pages.mechanism: Eight unique navigational <a> links (the only place they appear) are removed from the rendering and the accessibility tree by a media-query display:none at 320px, with no repositioned copy, disclosure, dialog, or link to another view — content available at desktop width is unavailable after reflow (F102).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse evaluate one static DOM at one width; the links are well-formed <a href> with text and pass link-name/focus-order checks at every width. No tool renders at 320px, diffs which links remain reachable, and reasons that these specific links exist in no other location. display:none in a media query is a ubiquitous legitimate idiom, so tools never flag it — only a human comparing the wide and narrow renderings can judge the content was dropped with no equivalent.

citation.quote: A block of blog entry links in a side column disappears entirely after reflow (i.e., it is not available further down in the single column view).

pages.scenario: Warehouse-operative job-application form: each input has a real visible <label> (for/id associated) beside it in a two-column grid, plus placeholder text. At max-width:480px the label column is display:none 'to save space', leaving disappear-on-type placeholders. Labels do not reappear on focus and are shown nowhere after reflow.
pages.mechanism: Persistent visible label text present at desktop width is removed at 320px; the only remaining cue is a low-contrast placeholder that is destroyed the instant the user types, and no focus/disclosure/inline mechanism restores the label — the visible labelling information the low-vision/zoom audience relies on is unavailable after reflow (F102 placeholder example).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The for/id associations are present and correct at every width, so name/label rules pass unconditionally and the tools see no problem. They do not render at 320px to observe that the VISIBLE label was removed, that the placeholder is erased on input, or that focusing the field fails to bring the label back. Recognising a persistent label was traded for a disappear-on-type placeholder with no restoration is a human visual-and-behaviour comparison across two widths.

citation.quote: Labels above text inputs are hidden and replaced by placeholder text after reflow, without a technique showing dedicated labels when focusing the fields.

pages.scenario: Municipal transit site: six primary nav links (Plan a trip, Schedules, Fares, Service alerts, Accessibility services, Contact) shown horizontally at desktop. At max-width:768px the nav is display:none and a hamburger 'Menu' button appears — but the button is dead: no click handler, no <details>, no target panel, no links inside it. Activating it does nothing and the destinations exist nowhere else (footer has only legal links).
pages.mechanism: The replacement control is present but decorative: a well-formed <button aria-label aria-expanded> with no wired menu. At 320px the six nav destinations are removed and the hamburger reveals nothing on activation, so the entire primary navigation available at desktop width is unreachable after reflow (F102 hamburger-that-goes-nowhere).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Tools see a valid <button> with an accessible name and aria-expanded (passes button-name/role) and the six <a> links present in the static DOM (display:none narrow). No tool activates the button at 320px to check whether a menu opens and the dropped links became reachable. A working hamburger (PASS, case-04) and a dead one (FAIL) are byte-for-byte identical to a static scanner; telling them apart requires a human to operate the control after reflow.

citation.quote: As zooming continues, most navigation options are eventually behind a "hamburger" menu button. All the information and functionality is still available from this web page.

pages.scenario: PASS control — developer API reference (Pulsegate /docs, Webhooks). Same structural move as case-03 (six nav links collapse to a hamburger at max-width:820px) but done correctly: a native <button aria-expanded aria-controls> wired to a tiny script toggles a panel that reveals all six links at 320px. The 'On this page' sidebar is repositioned above the article rather than deleted. Reflows cleanly, no horizontal scroll, no content lost.
pages.mechanism: All information/functionality at desktop width remains available after reflow: the working disclosure surfaces the same six nav links ('offered in some other way') and the sidebar is repositioned into the single column ('repositioned in a single column view'). The F102 failure condition does not apply.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A static scanner cannot distinguish this PASS from case-03's FAIL: both have a named <button> and the six <a> links in the DOM. Tools never activate the hamburger at 320px, observe the panel open, and confirm the dropped links became reachable, nor that the sidebar truly repositioned. They can neither flag a violation nor certify the met-condition — certifying this PASS requires a human to operate the control after reflow and compare reachable content across widths.

citation.quote: Modern websites and applications commonly employ responsive web design best practices to adjust or relocate sections of content to fit within smaller viewports. Neither adjusting or relocating content is considered a loss of information or functionality, so long as users are still able to access the content.

pages.scenario: Healthcare patient portal care summary: three panels at desktop (Next appointment, Active medications, and an Emergency & advance-directive panel with next-of-kin phone, GP out-of-hours line, and a flagged 'DNACPR in place' note). At max-width:560px the emergency panel is display:none and a 'More details' <details> disclosure appears — and genuinely opens — but it reveals only a generic overnight-update/opening-hours blurb, NOT the dropped emergency data, which appears nowhere else.
pages.mechanism: Disclosure-content mismatch: the replacement mechanism is present and fully operable (native <details>) yet its panel contains different content than the section that was removed. The dropped life-safety information is not repositioned, not inside this or any disclosure, and not linked elsewhere — F102 test step 3 ('same or equivalent content') is explicitly failed despite a working disclosure existing after reflow.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: <details>/<summary> is a valid, operable disclosure that passes every structural/name/role/keyboard check, so a naive 'is there a disclosure after reflow?' heuristic marks the page safe. Tools do not read the dropped panel's text, read the disclosure's text, and reason they are different information. The F102 step-3 semantic comparison — does this disclosure actually contain the dropped content? — is judgment only a human can perform.

citation.quote: For each content element that is not provided at the viewport width of 320px, check that there is a way to reach the same or equivalent content via disclosure widgets, pop-ups, or links to other views

pages.scenario: Fine-dining restaurant menu: each dish carries terse dietary/allergen markers (V, Ve, GF, N, Sf, D) and a right-hand legend column decodes them. At max-width:600px the dish list reflows cleanly to one column but the legend aside is display:none, orphaning the still-present markers. No tooltip, inline expansion, or link to an allergen page reproduces the key, so a guest with a nut/shellfish allergy sees 'N' and 'Sf' with no way to decode them.
pages.mechanism: The decoder/legend for an on-screen code is dropped at 320px while the abbreviation markers it explains remain on every dish. The key (real <dl> text) present at desktop width is removed from the rendering with no equivalent, rendering the existing markers meaningless after reflow (F102 — content needed to use the page is lost).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every element is well-formed real text with adequate contrast — no missing alt, empty label, or contrast failure for a linter to catch — and the legend is simply display:none in a media query. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse do not render at 320px, notice every dish still carries markers while the only key to them is gone, and reason the markers are now undecodable. Recognising that the DECODER for an on-screen code disappeared on reflow with no equivalent is a human semantic-and-reflow comparison.

citation.quote: This content, however, should still be available after reflow to 320px viewport width, either by being repositioned in a single column view, or through some interaction offering the information in some other way, for example, in a disclosure area, a dialog, or via a link to another view.

pages.scenario: Online-banking statements page: each monthly statement row offers View, Download PDF, and Dispute a charge. At max-width:520px each row reflows to a stacked card (clean, no horizontal scroll) but the 'Download PDF' button is display:none 'to reduce clutter' while View and Dispute remain. There is no overflow/kebab menu, no account-level download link, and no separate statements-download view, so a low-vision user at 400% zoom (or any phone user) cannot download a statement PDF.
pages.mechanism: Loss of FUNCTIONALITY (not just content) at narrow width: one action <button> is conditionally removed by CSS while its siblings remain, so the download function available at desktop width is unavailable after reflow to 320px with no equivalent path to perform it (F102 applied to functionality).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The Download PDF button is a valid, named <button> present in the DOM at every width (display:none narrow), passing button-name/role/focus checks at desktop; display:none in a media query is not flagged. No tool renders each row at 320px, enumerates which actions remain operable, diffs that set against the desktop set, and reasons that one specific function vanished with no replacement. That cross-width functional diff plus the 'no other path downloads the PDF' judgment is human work.

citation.quote: This document describes a failure that occurs when a change of the viewport width to 320px makes content disappear that was available at wider viewport widths.

aspects.title: Long unbroken strings (URLs, tokens, hashes, paths, emails, compound words) overflow at 320px without wrapping or a reveal alternative
aspects.plain: A single long unbroken string like a URL, hash, or API key won't wrap, so it forces sideways scrolling even though the rest of the page reflows fine.
aspects.description: Technique C33 addresses long sets of characters with no spaces — a displayed full URL, an API/auth key, a long hash, a deep file path, a blockchain address, a German compound word — that the browser cannot wrap (no break opportunities and no overflow-wrap:break-word / word-break applied, or white-space:nowrap forced). At 320px the one string punches out a horizontal scrollbar even though every paragraph around it reflows perfectly. The viewport meta is fine and the page is 99% fluid, so a viewport-string check sees nothing. The judgment: render at 320px to find the single overflowing element, and decide the correct disposition — whether the string may break mid-word, versus the truncate-with-reveal pattern the Understanding doc describes (truncation is only acceptable if a link or mechanism reveals the full value).
aspects.scLimb: The 'without requiring scrolling in two dimensions' requirement applied to inline text content; the related Understanding nuance that truncating content to save space is only acceptable when the full value remains available via a link or reveal mechanism.
aspects.whyUncovered: No ACT rule renders content or measures string overflow; corpus pages contain only short Lorem-ipsum with normal spaces, never a long unbreakable token. A static checker can heuristically spot a literal very-long string in markup but cannot determine whether it actually overflows at 320px (depends on font, container width, CSS) nor whether the surrounding design already wraps it nor whether a truncation has a valid reveal — this needs visual measurement plus judgment.

references.quote: Long sets of characters without a space, such as URLs shown as content, can break reflow when the page is zoomed.

The objective of this technique is to present URLs without introducing a horizontal scroll bar at a width equivalent to 320 CSS pixels or a vertical scroll bar at a height equivalent to 256 CSS pixels.

A web page presents long strings of text which are truncated to save space. E.g., user generated content that does not fit into the space allocated for the interface's design, or authentication keys which do not wrap

pages.scenario: Help-center password-reset article displays a complete 180-char reset URL (domain + params + opaque JWT-style token) as the visible text of an inline link, in a fully fluid single-column layout. Rendered at 320px the link is 1168px wide and forces a page-level horizontal scrollbar while every paragraph reflows. Head case (head distribution).
pages.mechanism: A long no-space token segment inside a URL has no break opportunity and the link has NO overflow-wrap/word-break, so at a 320 CSS px viewport the single <a> overflows horizontally; probe confirmed document width 1204px and that neutralizing only a.verify-link returns the page to exactly 320px (sole offender). Low-vision/400%-zoom users must scroll in two dimensions to read the link, the barrier C33 addresses.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The only ACT rule for 1.4.10 (b4f0c3) checks the viewport meta allows zoom, which passes here; the link is a valid non-empty link with a correct href/name so link-name rules pass. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse never render at 320px to measure string overflow, and cannot know whether the surrounding fluid CSS already wraps it. Requires visual measurement at 320px plus the judgment that a URL has no two-dimensional exception.

citation.quote: When lines of text extend beyond the edge of a viewport, users will be forced to scroll back-and-forth to read line by line. This can cause them to lose their place and can significantly increase both physical and cognitive effort.

pages.scenario: Payments API docs page (responsive sidebar + content) handles fenced code blocks correctly with overflow-x:auto, but shows the 64-char sandbox bearer token as INLINE <code> with white-space:nowrap so it is 'selectable as one piece'. At 320px the inline token is 503px wide and punches a page-level horizontal scrollbar. Head case.
pages.mechanism: white-space:nowrap on an inline <code> containing a 64-char no-space token actively SUPPRESSES the wrap that would otherwise occur, so the inline text cannot reflow within a 320 CSS px column; probe confirmed document 521px and that neutralizing only code.tok returns the page to exactly 320px. Distinct from case-01: wrapping is suppressed, not merely absent. The visually-similar fenced pre.block right above scrolls in its own container and is NOT the offender.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Viewport-meta rule b4f0c3 passes; the <code> is well-formed with real text so no linter fires. Tools do not render at 320px nor reason that white-space:nowrap on a long no-space inline string overflows a fluid column, and cannot distinguish this failing inline token from the correctly self-scrolling fenced block of the same monospace content immediately above it.

citation.quote: The objective of this technique is to present URLs without introducing a horizontal scroll bar at a width equivalent to 320 CSS pixels or a vertical scroll bar at a height equivalent to 256 CSS pixels. This is done by using CSS techniques that adapt to the available viewport space.

pages.scenario: German legal-protection insurer terms page (lang=de) where fluid serif prose reflows fine, but one genuine 79-letter German compound noun (a Bandwurmwort defined term) is styled word-break:keep-all; overflow-wrap:normal; hyphens:none to never split in PDF export. At 320px the single word is 716px wide and forces a page-level horizontal scrollbar. Long-tail i18n case.
pages.mechanism: A real German compound word with no internal spaces has all break opportunities removed (keep-all + hyphens:none + overflow-wrap:normal), so the one word cannot reflow within 320 CSS px; probe confirmed document 755px and that neutralizing only span.defterm returns the page to exactly 320px. German morphology genuinely produces such single words, which rely on hyphenation or overflow-wrap that the author globally disabled.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: b4f0c3 passes (zoom allowed); the word is valid text so no markup linter objects. Tools do not render at 320px to measure single-token overflow and have no model of German morphology to know word-break:keep-all is fatal on a 79-letter compound while harmless on a 6-letter term elsewhere on the same page. Needs rendering plus linguistic/visual judgment.

citation.quote: By default, a long line of text will wrap to fit within the available viewport. For text written in left-to-right (LTR) and right-to-left (RTL) horizontal languages, it will wrap within the width of the viewport.

pages.scenario: CI 'Build failed' dashboard whose key/value grid, SHA (overflow-wrap:anywhere) and main job-log viewer (pre with overflow-x:auto) all reflow correctly, but a later hand-added 'Failing artifact' callout shows a ~155-char deep filesystem path in a bare <pre> with default white-space:pre and no scroll container. At 320px this one <pre> forces a page-level horizontal scrollbar. Mid case.
pages.mechanism: A <pre> inherits white-space:pre and refuses to wrap the long no-space path, and (unlike the page's other <pre>) has no overflow-x:auto scroll container, so the page itself overflows at 320 CSS px; probe confirmed document 1337px and that wrapping ONLY pre.path returns the page to exactly 320px (sole offender), while the correctly scrollable pre.log contributes nothing. Distinct mechanism: <pre> preformatting + missing scroll container.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: b4f0c3 passes; both <pre> elements are valid markup and no linter distinguishes the scrollable one from the non-scrollable one. Tools do not render at 320px to find that pre.path overflows while the visually similar pre.log is fine, and cannot judge that a slash-delimited path is non-essential preformatting that may wrap versus ASCII art / Python indentation where layout is meaningful and the Reflow exception applies.

citation.quote: The presentation of text where the layout has specific meaning, such as code indentation for Python or "ascii art" as just two examples, would lose meaning if the layout were not presented correctly. This success criterion does not apply where that meaning would be lost. However, this is not the case for most other instances of text where text wrapping can be applied without loss of meaning.

pages.scenario: PASS control: e-commerce order-tracking page shows the SAME kind of long opaque tracking URL as visible link text in the same fluid single-column layout as case-01, but the link has overflow-wrap:break-word / overflow-wrap:anywhere (the C33-prescribed CSS). At 320px the URL wraps cleanly inside the column and the page does not scroll horizontally. Head case (correctly remediated).
pages.mechanism: With overflow-wrap:break-word/anywhere applied, the long no-space token wraps within the 320 CSS px column so the user scrolls only vertically (the reading direction); probe confirmed document width equals the 320px viewport with zero overflow. Nothing is truncated and the full URL remains the link's accessible name. Exists so the evaluator must distinguish a wrapped long string (pass) from a non-wrapping one (cases 01-04).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Symmetry: a tool that cannot detect the failure in cases 01-04 (no 320px rendering/overflow measurement) equally cannot certify this pass. b4f0c3 passes here for the same trivial zoom-allowed reason it passes on the failing pages, so the ACT result is identical across pass and fail and carries no signal about actual reflow behavior. Confirming the URL wraps requires rendering at 320px.

citation.quote: Using the following CSS will cause long URLs to break at appropriate places (hyphens, forward slashes, etc.) and within words without causing reflow.

pages.scenario: Nimbus Cloud console API-keys page truncates the displayed key to a prefix + ellipsis (nk_live_3pQ8vR2tX7…) so cards never overflow, BUT provides a working 'Reveal full key' disclosure (#revealBtn, aria-expanded/aria-controls) that swaps in the full 71-char value (wraps via overflow-wrap:anywhere) plus a Copy button.
pages.mechanism: Truncation-to-save-space would lose the value, but a real reveal mechanism keeps the full content on the page: #revealBtn (aria-expanded toggles, aria-controls=k1) runs reveal() to swap code#k1's text from the masked prefix to its 71-char data-full value, which wraps via overflow-wrap:anywhere; a role=status line announces the change and a Copy button writes the full value. No overflow at 320px and the full value is reachable.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A naive overflow check sees no scrollbar and passes it for the wrong reason; it cannot evaluate the truncation nuance. Judging this correctly needs (1) noticing truncation, (2) finding the reveal, (3) confirming it exposes the full value without reintroducing overflow. No axe/WAVE/Lighthouse rule does steps 1-3, and none can tell this PASS apart from case-07's identical tidy layout where the reveal is absent.

citation.quote: The content is presented as truncated, but a link is provided to a web page where the content is fully visible without truncation, or a mechanism is provided on the web page to reveal the truncated content.

pages.scenario: FAIL (truncation nuance, nothing overflows): crypto-exchange withdrawal receipt shows the destination wallet address and transaction hash middle-truncated to head…tail form (0x4e9a…b71c) with NO reveal, no copy of the full value, and no link to a block explorer. The page reflows perfectly at 320px, yet the complete identifiers a user needs for an irreversible transfer are unavailable. Long-tail counterpart to case-06.
pages.mechanism: Truncation to save space is permitted only when the full content remains reachable; here the middle of the address and hash is permanently dropped with no on-page recovery path, so information available at wider widths is lost after the truncation. Probe confirmed zero horizontal overflow at 320px, so an overflow-only check passes it — but it fails the F102 'content disappears with no equivalent alternative' condition. The DOM contains only the short string (no data-full).
pages.selectorNote: Full SHA-256 digest shown at desktop but display:none at 320px (F102 lost content)
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: This is the inverse blind spot: nothing overflows, so even a hypothetical overflow checker passes. Tools have no concept that a displayed string is a lossy abbreviation of a longer value, and the DOM holds only the short string with nothing to compare against to even detect truncation. Recognizing 0x4e9a…b71c as a lossy abbreviation of an identifier the user needs, with no reveal/link to restore it, is pure human semantic judgment and the precise distinction from case-06.

citation.quote: This content, however, should still be available after reflow to 320px viewport width, either by being repositioned in a single column view, or through some interaction offering the information in some other way, for example, in a disclosure area, a dialog, or via a link to another view.

aspects.title: Two-dimensional-layout exception over-claimed or mis-scoped: non-excepted surroundings of a table/map/grid fail to reflow
aspects.plain: Because one table or map legitimately needs sideways scrolling, the developer lets the whole page scroll sideways, so headings and search boxes that should reflow don't.
aspects.description: 1.4.10 exempts sections that genuinely require two-dimensional layout (data tables, maps, diagrams, grids, code where indentation is meaningful, presentations). The judgment-heavy failure mode is mis-scoping: a developer lets the WHOLE page scroll in two dimensions 'because there's a table', so the heading, intro paragraph, search field, and pagination that surround the table — none of which need 2D layout — also extend off-screen and require horizontal scrolling. The Understanding doc shows exactly this pass/fail pair. Conversely, flagging content that legitimately IS a data table/map/video would be a false positive. Deciding whether a given block legitimately 'requires two-dimensional layout for understanding or functionality', AND scoping the exception to only the excepted section, are irreducibly human contextual calls: is this <table> real tabular data or layout? is this wide block a map (exempt) or a poorly sized banner? must this heading/search/pagination reflow even though the adjacent table need not?
aspects.scLimb: The exception clause itself: 'A section of content that requires two-dimensional layout for understanding or functionality, such as a table or map, has an exception' — plus the normative scoping that the exception 'does not automatically extend to other content that doesn't need two-dimensional scrolling'.
aspects.whyUncovered: The ACT corpus has no rendered pages and no tables/maps/grids, so the exception is never exercised in either direction. The exception turns on the MEANING of the content and on scoping it to only the excepted section — both human judgments. Automated tools cannot distinguish a genuine data table from a layout table, nor decide that a surrounding heading/search/pagination is non-excepted and must reflow.

references.quote: A section of content that requires two-dimensional layout for understanding or functionality, such as a table or map, has an exception to this success criterion. However, sections of content within the two-dimensional layout, such as each cell within a table, would still need to meet this success criterion.
When a section of content is excepted from Reflow, the exception does not automatically extend to other content that doesn't need two-dimensional scrolling for understanding or functionality.
Other content that is related to the table or grid, such as a preceding heading, a search field, or an accompanying pagination to load different sets of data are not excepted from meeting Reflow.

pages.scenario: Municipal treasury property-levy register: a genuine 9-column data table is legitimately excepted, but body{min-width:980px} drags the H1, intro paragraph, search field, and pagination off-screen at 320px. The non-excepted surroundings cannot reflow because the exception was over-scoped to the whole document instead of the one table.
pages.mechanism: body{min-width:980px} sets a 2D-scroll floor on the entire document; at 320 CSS px the heading, intro, search toolbar and pager all extend to right=715-952px and require horizontal scrolling, even though only the table needs 2D layout. The exception is mis-scoped from the table to the page.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse do not lay out the document at 320 CSS px and cannot compute that a non-excepted region overflows; rendered-layout-at-target-viewport is not derivable from static markup. Every checkable attribute is valid (table caption + scope headers, label[for], aria-current pager, accessible nav name), and a scanner seeing 'a table exists' would wrongly treat the page as exempt. Deciding the table may 2D-scroll while heading/search/pager MUST reflow is human scoping judgment.

citation.quote: Other content that is related to the table or grid, such as a preceding heading, a search field, or an accompanying pagination to load different sets of data are not excepted from meeting Reflow. For instance, while a table may require two-dimensional scrolling to maintain its understandability, a heading or paragraph that introduce the table, or a search field and pagination component that allow users to search for or navigate to different "pages" of table content are not extended this exception.

pages.scenario: Business-banking account ledger: a wide, genuine transaction table is correctly excepted AND correctly scoped inside a focusable div{overflow:auto} region, while the account header, balance-summary cards, filter form, 'Load more' button, and disclosure note all reflow into a single 320px column. PASS boundary that mirrors the Understanding pass figure; a naive evaluator might wrongly flag the table's scrollbar.
pages.mechanism: The wide ledger (min-width:880px) is confined to a keyboard-focusable role=region with overflow:auto, so only that container scrolls in 2D. No body min-width; flex-wrap on summary/filters and max-width:320px on the load-more button mean every non-excepted region renders within 302px at a 320px viewport with zero own-scroll.
