Page horizontal overflow = 0.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A scanner can detect that the table container produces a horizontal scrollbar but cannot determine whether it is legitimate (an excepted table confined to its own container, everything else reflows) or a failure (non-excepted content overflowing). Tools have no notion of 'this region is excepted data, the rest must reflow', so they would either skip Reflow or false-positive on the scrollbar. Confirming the PASS requires the same human scoping judgment as confirming a failure.

citation.quote: A data table relies on two-dimensional layout for understanding, but by presenting the table in its own scrollable container it allows other content which does not meet a two-dimensional layout exception to reflow as its containing element adjusts.

pages.scenario: Streaming TV electronic program guide (EPG): the channel x time-slot grid is a legitimate 1.4.10 exception, but one 'featured premiere' cell is built with a fixed 560px internal two-column layout (poster art beside a synopsis and 'how to watch' line, both white-space:nowrap), so that single cell's own content overflows 320px. Cells within an exempt grid must still meet Reflow.
pages.mechanism: After the user scrolls the (excepted) grid to bring the featured cell into a 320px viewport, the cell's .featured-inner is fixed at width:560px and its synopsis/how-to-watch text is white-space:nowrap, so the cell extends to right=730px with a 29px own horizontal scroll. The cell's content fails Reflow even though the grid exception is valid.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A scanner that notices the grid's horizontal scrollbar must NOT flag it (valid exception), and has no model of 'the grid may 2D-scroll, but each cell's internal content must still reflow at 320px'. Detecting that one cell's poster+synopsis layout overruns the cell requires rendering at the target viewport plus the semantic judgment that this is a non-conforming cell inside an otherwise-exempt grid. Nothing is missing in the markup (the cell has role=article and an aria-label).

citation.quote: For example, an "electronic program guide" is a type of grid used to display media programs to stream online. It might be presented alongside other content outside of its grid-based layout. The individual cells of the program guide containing information about how to watch and poster art would be expected to fit within the required width or height.

pages.scenario: Dental-practice 'About' page lays out staff bios and service descriptions in a 1240px-wide 4-column <table> and lets the page scroll horizontally, the author reasoning 'it's a table, tables are exempt'. But it is a LAYOUT table: prose in every cell, no row/column data relationship, no <th>. Prose does not require 2D layout, so the exception does not apply and the content must reflow. Tests data-vs-layout classification.
pages.mechanism: table.team is a fixed table-layout:fixed; width:1240px holding prose paragraphs with td-only cells and no th/scope/caption. At 320px it extends to right=1425px, forcing the user to scroll horizontally to read bios that would wrap perfectly into one column. There is no two-dimensional header-to-data relationship to preserve, so the table is not 'content that requires two-dimensional layout for understanding'.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: An automated checker either ignores Reflow or, on seeing a <table>, may assume the exception applies. The markup is well-formed with no missing attribute. The failure is a CLASSIFICATION judgment: is this real tabular data (excepted) or prose in a layout table (not excepted)? The tells (prose in every cell, no th/scope/caption, no header-to-data relationship) must be read and weighed by a human; axe/WAVE/Lighthouse do not adjudicate data-table-vs-layout-table for the Reflow exception and do not render at 320px.

citation.quote: Data tables and grids have a two-dimensional relationship between column and row headers and their data cells. This success criterion therefore has exceptions for data tables and grids from needing to display without scrolling in the direction of text.

pages.scenario: Public-library 'Summer Reading Challenge' promo banner looks like a graphic and is treated as an exempt fixed-size 'graphic/media', but it is live CSS-styled HTML text set white-space:nowrap at a fixed width:1100px. The text refuses to wrap, forcing a page-level horizontal scrollbar at 320px even though the article prose below reflows fine. Styled text that merely looks banner-like is not a fixed-dimension graphic and must reflow. Wrong exception claim.
pages.mechanism: div.promo holds selectable text in spans but is forced onto one line via white-space:nowrap at width:1100px, so at 320px it extends to right=1152px with a 291px own scroll, producing a page-level horizontal scrollbar. There is no and no role=img: it is text that must wrap, and the author's 'it's a graphic, so it's exempt' claim is invalid.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: There is no , no role=img, no missing alt for a linter to catch. The banner is real text, so a checker cannot OCR/measure an image and cannot decide whether the overflowing region is text that should wrap or a legitimately fixed-size graphic. A scanner has no model of the 1.4.10 exception's content-meaning test; recognizing that this banner is styled text whose exemption claim is invalid (versus case-07's genuine fixed-dimension video, which IS exempt) is the human semantic/visual judgment the SC turns on.

citation.quote: Not all content can fully reflow into smaller viewports without degradation of information or functionality. As already mentioned, this includes tabular data, graphics, maps, presentations,  interfaces that require persistent toolbars for use, and two-dimensional layouts where consistent orientation to related sections of content is important for understandability, functionality, or both.

pages.scenario: EV 'Find a Charging Station' finder shows a genuine interactive SVG map (legitimately excepted) and a control sidebar (filter form, status legend, nearby-results list) together in a single flex-wrap:nowrap row with min-width:1080px. The map keeps its size (acceptable) but the non-excepted sidebar is pushed off the right edge and clipped at 320px instead of stacking below the map and reflowing. Novel map+adjacent-controls scoping case.
pages.mechanism: .finder is a flex-wrap:nowrap row with min-width:1080px; the .controls sidebar (filter selects, legend, results list) has a fixed flex basis of 360px and is pushed to right=1082px at a 320px viewport, clipped off-canvas. These related controls are exactly the 'search field / pagination'-equivalent non-excepted content that must reflow (e.g. stack below the map), but the nowrap row prevents it.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The map's 2D layout is a valid exception, so a tool noticing it must not flag it. There is no missing attribute (filters have labels, the map has role and an accessible name). The failure is the scoping judgment that the map may keep 2D layout but its adjacent filter/legend/results controls must reflow at 320px. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse neither render at the target viewport nor reason about 'excepted map vs non-excepted adjacent controls', so they cannot detect the sidebar is wrongly pinned and clipped.

citation.quote: When a section of content is excepted from Reflow, the exception does not automatically extend to other content that doesn't need two-dimensional scrolling for understanding or functionality.

pages.scenario: Developer-docs tutorial embeds a fixed-720px video player with no max-width:100%, causing a page-level horizontal scrollbar at 320px. A video is a fixed-dimension medium with a 1.4.10 exception, and per the Understanding doc a page-level scrollbar caused solely by such excepted media PASSES as long as all non-excepted content reflows. Here all prose, the on-this-page nav, the callout, headings, and the code block (with overflow-wrap:anywhere; pre-wrap) reflow within 320px. PASS control that mirrors the BBC-Earth-video figure.
pages.mechanism: figure.demo video is width:720px with no max-width:100%, so it overflows to right=738px and produces a 418px page-level horizontal scroll. But every non-excepted region renders within 302px with zero own-scroll: article paragraphs, figcaption, pre (white-space:pre-wrap; overflow-wrap:anywhere wraps even a long Kafka broker string), .callout, headings, and nav.toc. The only 2D scroll is owed entirely to the excepted video, so the page conforms.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A scanner can detect a page-level horizontal scrollbar but cannot determine its cause or whether it is permitted; flagging 'horizontal scrollbar present' would be a false positive here. Tools have no model of 'this scrollbar is owed entirely to an excepted fixed-dimension video, and every other section reflows'. Confirming the PASS, like confirming a FAIL, requires the human judgment that the only 2D scroll comes from excepted media; nothing is missing in the markup.

citation.quote: Pass: A video player without a max-width: 100% CSS property causes it to remain full-sized at smaller (zoomed in) viewports. The rest of the page content reflows within 320 CSS pixel wide container. So, while there is a large horizontal scrollbar at the page level, it is due to the video player which has a reflow exception.

aspects.title: Sticky / fixed-position content (headers, footers, cookie bars, chat widgets, ads) consumes or obscures the 320x256 viewport so reflowed content cannot be read
aspects.plain: On a tiny zoomed viewport, sticky headers, footers, cookie bars, or chat widgets eat most of the screen or cover content, leaving almost nothing readable.
aspects.description: Headers, footers, toolbars, cookie banners, chat widgets, and fixed ads that are reasonable at desktop become viewport-eating obstructions when zoomed to a 320px-wide / 256px-tall viewport. A sticky 130px-tall header over a 256px-tall viewport leaves almost nothing to read; a fixed-bottom cookie bar plus fixed-top nav can sandwich content into a sliver; a fixed-corner ad can cover the focused link, providing no way to dismiss it without keyboard-navigating to its close button. The Understanding doc's Focus-Not-Obscured overlap section and technique C34 both call for un-fixing these at small sizes. The page reflows horizontally (no h-scroll) and the viewport meta is permissive, so tools see nothing — but the rendered experience is broken. Judging it requires rendering at the narrow viewport (especially the 256px height) and a visual proportion assessment of how much readable space the sticky elements leave and whether they obscure content or keyboard focus.
aspects.scLimb: The 'without loss of information or functionality' requirement as it interacts with the SC's overlap with Focus Not Obscured: sticky/fixed regions that, at the reflow viewport, block so much of the screen that content cannot be read or functionality cannot be reached.
aspects.whyUncovered: Corpus pages have no sticky/fixed elements and are never rendered at 256px height. C34 is advisory with no ACT rule. The harm — a sticky element leaving too little room, or covering content/focus — is a visual proportion judgment at a specific small viewport; there is no static signal, and position:sticky/fixed are perfectly valid and ubiquitous, so their mere presence cannot be flagged. Only a human looking at the rendered narrow viewport can judge whether too little remains.

references.quote: when using mobile devices in landscape orientation or when zooming in on the desktop, sticky regions may block a big portion of the screen: the height of the sticky region may leave only a small part of the screen for the display of page content.

Such sticky or fixed content can pose significant issues for those who would benefit from Reflow, as aside from obscuring keyboard focus, such sticky or fixed content can make reading content difficult if not impossible.
It is strongly suggested that at smaller viewport sizes that such components are modified to have static positioning, or their display can be toggled by the user.

pages.scenario: A coastal newspaper long-form article with a position:sticky masthead (wordmark + section nav + dateline, min-height:130px). The article reflows to a single 320px-wide column with zero horizontal overflow, but at the 256px reflow HEIGHT the sticky masthead renders 212px tall, consuming 83% of the viewport and leaving a ~44px sliver to read in.
pages.mechanism: A persistent position:sticky region sized for desktop occupies 83% of the 256px reflow viewport height, so a low-vision user who zooms can read only 2-3 lines at a time and must scroll a near-full screen per couple of lines — the loss-of-function the SC prevents. C34 (un-fix at small height) is not applied.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Zoom is allowed (ACT b4f0c3 passes), content reflows with 0px horizontal overflow at 320px, and position:sticky+min-height:130px is valid ubiquitous CSS no linter flags. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse never render at a 256px-TALL viewport and have no rule computing visible sticky chrome as a fraction of the viewport; judging the remaining sliver is unusable is a human visual-proportion call at the narrow viewport (verified: 212px/256px = 83%).

citation.quote: Such sticky or fixed content can pose significant issues for those who would benefit from Reflow, as aside from obscuring keyboard focus, such sticky or fixed content can make reading content difficult if not impossible.

pages.scenario: A restaurant allergen menu with a position:fixed top nav (min-height:92px) AND a position:fixed bottom cookie-consent bar (min-height:96px). Together they sandwich the menu into a ~13px strip at the 256px reflow viewport (combined 243px = 95%), and the cookie bar's 'Accept all' only sets a data flag — there is no control that removes the bar, so the squeeze is permanent.
pages.mechanism: Two fixed bars on opposite edges consume ~95% of the 256px height, trapping reading content (including allergen lines) in a one-line band; the obscuring consent region has no dismiss path, so the viewport can never be recovered — the SC's 'without loss of information/functionality' limb via the Focus-Not-Obscured overlap.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Both position:fixed bars are standard; the cookie buttons have names, contrast, and focusability so axe/WAVE pass and Lighthouse's viewport audit passes. No tool sums the two fixed-bar heights against 256px or reasons that 'Accept all' never removes the element. Verified: 98px+145px=243px (95%) at 320x256 and the bar persists after activation — recognizing the unreadable sandwich with no dismiss is a human judgment.

citation.quote: It is strongly suggested that at smaller viewport sizes that such components are modified to have static positioning, or their display can be toggled by the user. Doing so will help ensure the zoomed in content can be read by users, as the sticky components will no longer obstruct the view of the web page's content.

pages.scenario: Music-history article ('The Medieval Period of Music') with a position:fixed sponsored ad pinned across the lower band (180px tall, near-full width). The article reflows fine, but the fixed ad obscures the in-article 'listening guide' link when it takes keyboard focus; the only dismiss control (a corner X) is reachable only by advancing focus past the obscured link.
pages.mechanism: Fixed author content obscures the element with keyboard focus at the reflow viewport: aside.ad is position:fixed (left:10px;right:10px;bottom:8px;height:180px) spanning the lower band, so when the in-article 'listening guide' link (a.inline href=#listen) is focused and scrolled toward the bottom edge it lands under the ad. The ad's dismiss control (button.x, aria-label='Close advertisement', onclick removes the ad) is reachable only after tabbing through the whole article; it is the second-to-last focusable element, with the ad's CTA link (a.cta 'Start free trial') following it as the actual last focusable.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The ad is well-formed (X has aria-label, CTA is a real link, contrast OK, zoom allowed). axe/WAVE/Lighthouse do not tab through the page, do not scroll focused elements into view, and have no rule hit-testing whether a fixed element covers the focused element or whether the dismiss control precedes/follows it in focus order. Verified via Puppeteer Tab+elementFromPoint that the focused link is covered — detecting it requires a human keyboard-navigating at the narrow viewport.

citation.quote: They obscure not only the focusable elements of the page, providing no way to dismiss the ad without finding / keyboard navigating to its close button, but significantly reduce the available space for reading.

pages.scenario: A children's-hospice single-page donation flow with a position:fixed support-chat widget expanded by default in the bottom-right (~280px tall). At the 320px reflow viewport the panel parks over the bottom of the form, covering 79% of the 'Give now' submit button; elementFromPoint at the button's center returns the chat's message input. The widget has a title bar but no minimise/collapse/close control, so the page's primary action is unreachable and cannot be uncovered.
pages.mechanism: Fixed author content obscures the primary interactive control at the reflow viewport with no dismiss/collapse affordance — loss of FUNCTIONALITY, not just reading space. A pointer/voice user clicking the button hits the chat input (verified 9258/11750 px2 = 79% coverage, center owned by the chat); a keyboard user reaching the button finds its focus hidden with no way to move the panel.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The chat is a linter model citizen: labelled region, real input with associated label, named Send button, good contrast; the form reflows to one column with zero h-overflow. No tool renders at 320px, computes that the fixed panel covers the submit button, hit-tests the button center, or reasons that no collapse control exists. Verified empirically that the CTA is unreachable — a functional-obstruction judgment for a human.

citation.quote: commonly toolbars, menubars, navigation and other "sidebar" content may be presented with sticky or fixed positions at larger viewport sizes. It is strongly suggested that at smaller viewport sizes that such components are modified to have static positioning, or their display can be toggled by the user.

pages.scenario: PASS control. A higher-ed LMS course page uses the same generously-sized sticky course header (min-height:128px) as the failing cases but implements WCAG technique C34: the header is position:sticky only behind @media (min-height:481px) and resets to position:static under @media (max-height:480px). At the 256px reflow viewport the header un-fixes and scrolls away, so the full lesson is readable (verified: 0px visible fixed chrome).
pages.mechanism: Below 480px viewport height the max-height media query fires and the course header becomes position:static, occupying the top once then scrolling out of view — giving the full 256px to the lesson body with no persistent obstruction and no obscured focus. Information is not lost (scroll to top), satisfying 'without loss of information or functionality.' This is the corrective C34 pattern.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Symmetry point: a tool sees position:sticky inside a media query but cannot evaluate whether the gate actually frees enough space at 256px without rendering and judging proportion. The PASS is therefore also a human visual-proportion judgment that simply resolves the other way (verified: 0px fixed chrome at 320x256). It proves the distinction is 'how much space remains at 256px,' not 'is position:sticky present.'

citation.quote: Disabling, or un-fixing sticky regions, is an effective way to allow for enough available space when users prefer different reading and zoom preferences or when using landscape mode.

pages.scenario: A CMS page editor whose position:sticky formatting toolbar is a single non-wrapping row (white-space:nowrap; overflow-x:auto) of a style select plus ~16 buttons. At 320px the toolbar content is 872px wide vs a 320px client width (552px horizontal overflow), pushing the Publish button (and insert link/image/code/table) off-canvas behind an internal horizontal scrollbar; the same bar is min-height:104px and sticky, eating 41% of the 256px height. The edited content is ordinary prose, not an excepted editing canvas.
pages.mechanism: Dual-axis Reflow failure. Horizontal: to reach Publish (off-canvas at left=793px, viewport 320px) the user must operate a horizontal scrollbar inside the toolbar — a second scroll axis. Vertical: the sticky bar pins 104px (41%) of the 256px height. The editable region is plain prose so the persistent-toolbar exception does not apply; the toolbar is chrome that must itself reflow/wrap.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: overflow-x:auto + white-space:nowrap is a valid pattern; every button has aria-label, contrast, focusability so axe/WAVE pass and Lighthouse passes (zoom allowed) without measuring rendered toolbar width or detecting off-canvas controls. No tool decides whether the editable region qualifies for the persistent-toolbar exception — that requires understanding the content is plain prose. Verified: scrollWidth 872px (552px overflow), Publish off-canvas, sticky bar 104px (41%).

citation.quote: When a section of content is excepted from Reflow, the exception does not automatically extend to other content that doesn't need two-dimensional scrolling for understanding or functionality.

pages.scenario: PASS control. A government transit portal shows a tall position:fixed bottom service-notice banner (~150px) that would otherwise consume 81% of the 256px viewport — identical static markup to a failing cookie bar. It passes because it is genuinely user-dismissible: the 'Dismiss this notice' button removes the banner from the DOM (verified: fixed chrome drops to 0px afterward), and it is the FIRST focusable element (banner precedes main), so a keyboard user reaches Dismiss before the page content.
pages.mechanism: The obscuring fixed content is dismissible by a control reachable without advancing focus past the obscured content: the first Tab lands on Dismiss, activation removes the banner, and the full schedule reflows into one readable column with no persistent obstruction. The banner's info is also conveyed inline so dismissing it costs nothing — the Focus-Not-Obscured overlap satisfied via an explicit dismiss path.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A tool cannot tell a dismissible banner from a permanent one from static markup — both are position:fixed with a button. Whether activating Dismiss truly frees the viewport (vs only setting a flag, like case-02) and whether the control precedes the obscured content in focus order are behavioural facts requiring interaction. Verified via Puppeteer: Dismiss is first in focus order and .remove() drops fixed chrome to 0px — neither confirmable nor distinguishable from case-02 without rendering, tabbing, and activating.

citation.quote: in the case author created content does obscure content, there is a way for a user to dismiss the obscuring content without requiring the advancement of keyboard focus.

aspects.title: Horizontally-scrolling carousel where an individual panel does not fit within 320 CSS px (G225)
aspects.plain: A sideways-scrolling carousel is allowed, but one over-stuffed panel doesn't fit the narrow width, forcing extra horizontal scrolling inside that single panel.
aspects.description: Horizontally-scrolling carousels are explicitly allowed: the strip scrolls horizontally to move between panels, but EACH individual panel must fit within 320 CSS px so the user need only scroll vertically to read one panel's content. The Understanding doc gives a pass (each home-listing panel fits 320px) and a fail (the second panel's content does not fit 320px). The failure is subtle: the carousel mechanism is fine and most panels fit, but one over-stuffed panel (longer text, an extra-wide image, a wider card) forces horizontal scrolling WITHIN that panel. Catching it requires rendering at 320px, advancing through each panel, and judging per-panel whether its content overflows — AND judging that the horizontal strip-scroll itself is the intended carousel navigation and NOT the violation. A tool cannot tell which overflow is 'the carousel working' versus 'a panel too wide'.
aspects.scLimb: The single-direction-scrolling requirement applied to carousel/panel widgets: the strip may scroll horizontally to change panels, but each panel's content must be readable with vertical-only scrolling within 320 CSS px.
aspects.whyUncovered: No carousels exist in the corpus and nothing is rendered. G225 has no ACT rule. The distinction between acceptable strip-level horizontal scrolling (navigation between panels) and unacceptable within-panel horizontal scrolling requires interpreting the widget's purpose and inspecting each panel individually at 320px — beyond static markup analysis.

references.quote: Section panels that scroll horizontally are designed to fit within a width of 320 CSS pixels on a vertically scrolling page
As long as each individual panel within the carousel can fit within a 320 CSS pixel viewport, then a user need only scroll in a single direction to read an individual panel's content.
Fail: In this modified version of the previous carousel, the second panel's content does not fit within the 320 CSS pixel viewport.

pages.scenario: E-commerce outdoor-gear product carousel (flex overflow-x:auto strip). Four product cards are width:300px and read top-to-bottom; one featured 'Trail Pack Bundle' promo card is hard-coded width:420px with a 396px inner image and a no-wrap price/save row, so that single panel cannot fit a 320px viewport and forces within-panel horizontal scrolling.
pages.mechanism: Strip-level horizontal scroll is allowed carousel navigation; the violation is per-panel: at 320 CSS px the promo card (width:420px, with img.feature 396px and white-space:nowrap pricerow) exceeds the viewport, so a low-vision user at 400% zoom must scroll horizontally within that one panel to read it — the two-direction reading the SC forbids. Rendered at 320px: the .card.promo panel is 420px wide (widerThanViewport=true) while all four sibling .card panels are 300px and fit.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Markup is clean (alt on every image, nested headings, valid list roles, passing contrast) so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse find nothing. Reflow is a rendered-layout property at a specific viewport that static analyzers never compute at 320px. Even an overflow detector sees overflow on the STRIP (allowed carousel behavior) and cannot distinguish 'the carousel working' from 'one panel too wide' — that needs judging the widget's purpose and inspecting each panel individually at 320px (human semantic + visual judgment).

citation.quote: As long as each individual panel within the carousel can fit within a 320 CSS pixel viewport, then a user need only scroll in a single direction to read an individual panel's content.

pages.scenario: SaaS email pricing carousel ('Northwind Mail', flex overflow-x:auto strip of plan panels). Every plan panel clamps to max-width:296px and fits 320px EXCEPT the 'Business' panel, whose embedded two-column 'Business vs Pro' comparison (two fixed 220px text columns, ~460px) cannot fit a 320px viewport and forces within-panel horizontal scrolling.
pages.mechanism: Strip-level horizontal scroll between plan panels is allowed carousel navigation; the failure is one over-stuffed panel. The 'Business' plan panel embeds a side-by-side two-column TEXT comparison (section.plan .compare, a flex row of two fixed columns .col{width:220px;flex:0 0 220px}, together ~460px with no per-column scroll and no fluid sizing), so at a 320px viewport that one panel's comparison overflows and forces within-panel horizontal scrolling. The comparison is plain text (feature names + check/dash + values) that would read fine stacked, so no two-dimensional-layout exception applies. The other panels are width:90vw;max-width:296px and fit.
pages.selectorNote: The rogue two-column Business-vs-Pro comparison (~460px) overflows the panel at 320px
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The screenshot image has descriptive alt and a fixed width is legal HTML, so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse report nothing. Reflow at 320px is a rendered measurement no static tool performs. An overflow detector flags the strip's horizontal scroll (allowed) and cannot isolate the one PANEL whose content overflows. Deciding this image needs max-width:100% so its panel fits 320px — while the strip is supposed to scroll — requires understanding the carousel's purpose and per-panel inspection at 320px.

citation.quote: By providing the video player a max-width: 100% CSS property, the video fits within the container element. A horizontal scrollbar no longer appears on the page...

pages.scenario: Healthcare patient-portal 'Upcoming Visits' carousel (horizontal row of appointment cards). Every card is width:300px and reads top-to-bottom; the 'Medication Review' card embeds the medication schedule in a <pre> block (white-space:pre, does not wrap) whose longest line (~430px) overflows the panel and the 320px viewport, forcing within-panel horizontal scrolling. The schedule's meaning survives wrapping into label/value pairs, so the Reflow 2D-layout exception does NOT apply.
pages.mechanism: Strip scroll is allowed navigation between visits; the failure is one panel's non-wrapping preformatted block. At 320 CSS px the pre.schedule lines extend past the panel, so a low-vision user must scroll horizontally within that panel to read dose times/notes. Critically, this is a simple drug/dose/time list whose meaning is preserved when reflowed (unlike Python indentation or ASCII art) — so it is NOT an excepted 2D-layout section but a genuine within-panel reflow failure. Rendered at 320px: only the 2nd section.visit reports inner overflow via pre.schedule.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The <pre> is valid, the text is readable, headings nest — axe/WAVE/Lighthouse report nothing. Reflow at 320px is a rendered measurement static tools do not perform. Even an overflow detector, on hitting the <pre>, cannot decide the load-bearing question: does this preformatted layout carry essential meaning (Reflow exception, pass) or is it over-wide content that should wrap (fail)? That meaning judgment is exactly what WCAG assigns to a human.

citation.quote: The presentation of text where the layout has specific meaning, such as code indentation for Python or "ascii art" as just two examples, would lose meaning if the layout were not presented correctly. This success criterion does not apply where that meaning would be lost. However, this is not the case for most other instances of text where text wrapping can be applied without loss of meaning.

pages.scenario: Real-estate page with TWO sibling carousels from the same component. 'Just Listed' clamps panels to width:min(86vw,300px) (every panel fits 320px — PASSES); 'Luxury Collection' overrides panels to a fixed width:380px (every panel overflows 320px — FAILS). Both strips legitimately scroll horizontally. Same-page pass/fail contrast on the identical widget; the page fails because the luxury rail's panels don't fit.
pages.mechanism: Strip-level horizontal scroll on both rails is allowed navigation. In '.good' each panel clamps to <=300px and fits 320px (pass). In '.lux' each panel is fixed 380px, so at 320px every panel exceeds the viewport and the user must scroll horizontally within each panel to read price/address/stats. The sole difference is one CSS width value (min(86vw,300px) vs 380px) and its effect at 320px. Rendered at 320px: all three .good panels are 275px and fit; all three .lux panels are 380px (widerThanViewport=true).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Both rails are valid, well-formed markup that look identical to a static parser (alt + headings present), so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse report nothing. Reflow at 320px is a rendered measurement no static tool computes, and the only difference is a CSS width whose consequence appears solely AT 320px. An overflow detector sees horizontal scroll on BOTH strips (allowed) and cannot tell one carousel's panels fit while the other's don't — that requires rendering at 320px and judging each carousel's panels individually.

citation.quote: Although the entire section requires horizontal scrolling to navigate between panels, each panel is designed to fit within a fixed width of 320 CSS pixels. This ensures that when a 320 CSS pixel wide viewport is used, and the card is in the viewport, each card will remain fully visible without the need for additional horizontal scrolling to read its content.

pages.scenario: PASS CONTROL: a correctly-built civic-news 'Top Stories' carousel. The strip scrolls horizontally (allowed); each of five story panels is clamped to width:min(90vw,300px), uses overflow-wrap:anywhere so long words break, and has only a width:100% image. At 320px every panel fits and reads top-to-bottom; the user scrolls horizontally ONLY to change stories. Exists to test that the evaluator does NOT wrongly fail the page just because a horizontal scrollbar is present.
pages.mechanism: A low-vision user at ~400% zoom (~320px viewport) sees one story panel at a time, reads it top-to-bottom with vertical-only scrolling, and swipes the strip horizontally to advance — the carousel's intended navigation, not two-direction reading of a section. Each panel fits 320px and wraps its text, so no within-panel horizontal scrolling is ever needed; the SC is satisfied. Rendered at 320px: every article.story panel is 288px and fits; no panel fails; only the strip overflows (allowed).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A naive 'horizontal scrollbar present -> Reflow fail' heuristic would FALSE-POSITIVE on this perfectly conforming carousel. Confirming the actual pass condition — that each panel fits 320px AND that the horizontal scroll is allowed strip-level navigation — is a rendered measurement at 320px combined with judgment about the widget's purpose, neither of which axe/WAVE/Lighthouse perform. The control proves the evaluator must reason about carousel intent rather than flag any horizontal scroll.

citation.quote: Within vertically scrolling web pages, implementations of carousels can allow for horizontal scrolling of their content. As the carousel scrolls, a new carousel panel or panels are displayed within the visible viewport. As long as each individual panel within the carousel can fit within a 320 CSS pixel viewport, then a user need only scroll in a single direction to read an individual panel's content.

pages.scenario: Recipe carousel ('Brambleway Kitchen', flex overflow-x:auto strip of recipe cards). Image and title block are pinned to 280px so normal cards fit, but the six-tile 'Slow-Braised Lamb Ragù' card's no-wrap .stats bar (~470px) overflows 320px and forces within-panel horizontal scrolling while the strip scroll stays allowed.
pages.mechanism: Strip-level horizontal scroll between recipe cards is allowed carousel navigation; the failure is per-panel and content-dependent. Each article.recipe is width:max-content with its image and .head pinned to 280px, so a normal four-tile card fits 320px; but .stats is a flex row set flex-wrap:nowrap with tiles flex:0 0 auto (never wrap, never shrink). The 'Slow-Braised Lamb Ragù' card carries SIX stat tiles (Prep/Cook/Total/Serves/Cal/Level), so its no-wrap stats bar is ~470px and drives that one content-sized card past 280px and the 320px viewport, forcing within-panel horizontal scrolling. The stats are a plain linear set of facts (not an excepted 2-D grid), so the content must reflow.
pages.selectorNote: Lamb-ragu card's six-tile no-wrap stats bar drives the card past 320px
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Markup is valid (image alt, figure/figcaption correct, contrast fine) so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse report nothing; white-space:nowrap is legal CSS. Whether it overflows 320px depends on the LENGTH of this particular caption AT 320px — a content-dependent rendered measurement no static tool performs. An overflow detector sees the allowed strip scroll and cannot isolate which single panel's caption overflows due to nowrap. Catching it requires rendering at 320px, advancing the strip to that thumbnail, and judging the overflow is within-panel (violation) rather than strip-level (allowed).

citation.quote: When lines of text extend beyond the edge of a viewport, users will be forced to scroll back-and-forth to read line by line. This can cause them to lose their place and can significantly increase both physical and cognitive effort.

aspects.title: Preformatted text / nested-list / code indentation: distinguishing meaningful (excepted) layout from gratuitous non-wrapping that should reflow
aspects.plain: Code and nested lists may keep meaningful indentation that needs sideways scrolling, but ordinary prose forced not to wrap overflows when it should simply reflow.
aspects.description: Lists and code blocks often rely on indentation to convey hierarchy or meaning (nested <ul> levels, Python block structure, ascii art). Where indentation is genuinely meaningful, the section may legitimately need two-dimensional scrolling and is excepted (G224 / the Understanding 'Preformatted text conveys meaning' example). The judgment-heavy failure: a developer wraps ordinary prose in <pre> or applies white-space:nowrap to text whose layout carries NO meaning, so it refuses to wrap and overflows 320px when it should simply reflow — OR conversely, genuinely meaningful indented code that is force-flattened, losing meaning. Deciding whether the layout's meaning would be lost by wrapping (exempt) versus whether the non-wrapping is gratuitous (must reflow) is a semantic content call no tool can make. G224 also notes the conforming middle path: keep meaningful indentation but reduce it at zoomed levels and allow each nested level to be horizontally scrolled into view while its items read vertically.
aspects.scLimb: The exception for content where 'consistent orientation... is important for understandability, functionality, or both' applied to preformatted/indented text, and the corresponding requirement that text whose layout carries no meaning must reflow (wrap) at 320px.
aspects.whyUncovered: The corpus has only plain Lorem-ipsum prose, no <pre>, code, or nested lists, and nothing is rendered. G224 has no ACT rule. Whether indentation/non-wrapping is meaningful (exempt) or gratuitous (must wrap) depends on reading and understanding the content's semantics — a tool sees white-space:pre and cannot decide if flattening would destroy meaning.

references.quote: The presentation of text where the layout has specific meaning, such as code indentation for Python or "ascii art" as just two examples, would lose meaning if the layout were not presented correctly. This success criterion does not apply where that meaning would be lost. However, this is not the case for most other instances of text where text wrapping can be applied without loss of meaning.

There can be instances where indentation of text is considered important to the presentation and understandability of the text content. If the indentations were to be removed, then meaning or functionality could suffer.

the indentation of code blocks like these could be adjusted at different viewport sizes... each nested list can be horizontally scrolled into view. Only vertical scrolling is necessary to read the content of list items within each specific nested list level.

pages.scenario: Public-library blog announcement: ordinary multi-paragraph prose was mis-rendered by a Markdown converter into non-wrapping <pre><code> code blocks (source paragraphs were indented). At 320px each prose paragraph is one unbreakable line that scrolls horizontally; its layout carries no meaning, so it must reflow.
pages.mechanism: Three <pre><code> blocks contain plain English announcement prose with white-space:pre + overflow-x:auto. At a 320 CSS px viewport each paragraph self-overflows ~2200-2336px and exposes a horizontal scrollbar, forcing a low-vision reader to scroll left-and-right to read every sentence. No code, indentation hierarchy, or ascii layout exists, so the 'preformatted text conveys meaning' exception does not apply and the content must reflow.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The markup is semantically correct (<pre><code> is the proper element for preformatted text), so no linter flags it; axe/WAVE/Lighthouse have no rule that renders at 320px and computes horizontal overflow, and even a hypothetical overflow detector cannot read the bytes inside <pre> and decide this is prose with no meaningful layout (must wrap) versus Python/ascii-art (exempt). That read-the-content exception test is human judgment.

citation.quote: The presentation of text where the layout has specific meaning, such as code indentation for Python or "ascii art" as just two examples, would lose meaning if the layout were not presented correctly. This success criterion does not apply where that meaning would be lost. However, this is not the case for most other instances of text where text wrapping can be applied without loss of meaning.

pages.scenario: Data-engineering developer docs embed a real Python backfill function whose block-structure indentation is load-bearing syntax. The deepest nested line exceeds 320px so the <pre> scrolls horizontally, but flattening/wrapping would destroy the if/for/else block mapping — a legitimately excepted overflow. The author also applies the G224 conforming-extra (reduced tab-size at narrow widths).
pages.mechanism: figure.code pre with white-space:pre self-overflows ~323px at 320 CSS px. The indentation is Python control-flow syntax: a magnifier/low-vision user relies on indent level to see which block each statement belongs to, and the code would not run if whitespace were altered. SC 1.4.10 does not apply where wrapping loses meaning, so the horizontal scroll of this single section is permitted; a tab-size media query further reduces it.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A scanner sees a <pre> with white-space:pre overflowing 320px — byte-for-byte the same signal as case-01's failing prose block. It cannot read the content and conclude this is Python (indentation load-bearing, overflow exempt) while the other is prose (must wrap). The exempt/not-exempt determination requires understanding the content's semantics.

citation.quote: A website providing code snippets needs to maintain line indentations, as the indentations are meaningful not only to the structure of the code, but in some languages - such as with Python, are requirements when defining blocks of code.

pages.scenario: Open-source message-bus architecture doc embeds a hand-drawn ASCII network/topology diagram (boxes of +-|, arrows -->/v) whose positions encode which service connects to which and a parallel fan-out. It is wider than 320px and uses white-space:pre, so it scrolls horizontally — but its layout IS the content (ascii art), a legitimately excepted overflow. A role=img + aria-label transcript serves AT users.
pages.mechanism: figure.diagram pre.ascii self-overflows ~255px at 320 CSS px and exposes a horizontal scrollbar. This is two-dimensional content requiring consistent orientation for understanding — equivalent to a drawn graphic/map; the Understanding doc explicitly cites 'ascii art'. Wrapping would shatter the box/arrow alignment and convey nothing, so the scroll of this one figure is exempt while all surrounding prose, headings, and links reflow; the aria-label gives screen-reader users an equivalent.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A scanner sees a <pre> overflowing 320px — structurally identical to case-01's failing prose block. No tool can examine the characters and recognize an arrangement of + - | > as a meaningful diagram (exempt) versus prose that should wrap. The role=img/aria-label satisfies a name linter, but whether the overflow is exempt is a read-the-content meaning call.

citation.quote: Graphics and video are by their nature two-dimensional. Slicing up a graphic (photograph, drawing, graph, etc.) and stacking the blocks would make the graphic difficult to understand, if not rendering it unintelligible.

pages.scenario: Lexbridge Regulatory Research product: a '42 CFR' regulatory issue-tree sidebar (Title > Chapter > Part > Section > Subsection) in a horizontally-scrollable .issuetree container that mimics the G224 conforming nested-list pattern, but forces every long regulatory item label onto a single non-wrapping line (white-space:nowrap), so item text cannot reflow at 320px.
pages.mechanism: EXPECTED OUTCOME SHOULD BE failed, not passed. A nested semantic <ul>/<li> regulatory issue tree lives in .issuetree (overflow-x:auto, an indent-reducing @media(max-width:480px) — the G224 scaffolding), but .issuetree li > .node is white-space:nowrap, so each long regulatory label is locked to one physical line. At 320px the meaningful level-indentation may be preserved, yet even after a level is scrolled into view every item's prose runs off the right edge — violating G224 list-procedure check 4 ('only vertical scrolling necessary to read the content of the nested list's items'). The per-item prose carries no meaning that wrapping would lose, so it must reflow and does not.
pages.selectorNote: Horizontally scrollable outline whose nowrap item prose forces left-right reading at 320px
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A tool can detect overflow-x:auto and a deep list but cannot judge that (a) the indentation is meaningful hierarchy so flattening would lose information, and (b) the per-level-scroll + wrapping-item-text arrangement is the conforming G224 pattern rather than a wide list whose line text runs off-screen (a failure). Distinguishing the conforming pattern from a failure requires understanding what the layout means.

citation.quote: At this breakpoint, each nested list level can be horizontally scrolled into view, and once a nested list is visible within the viewport, only vertical scrolling will be necessary to read the content of the nested list's items.

pages.scenario: SaaS onboarding 'Quick start' shows a long curl|sh install command and a one-line SQL INSERT in <pre> with white-space:pre and only a Copy button (no wrap toggle). Shell and SQL are wrappable — a soft-wrap loses no meaning — yet the lines are forced non-wrapping, so at 320px the user must scroll each command horizontally. Wrappable code with no wrap mechanism must reflow per G224.
pages.mechanism: The two .codecard pre blocks self-overflow ~1229-1343px at 320 CSS px and expose horizontal scrollbars. For shell/SQL nothing is lost by wrapping, so the 'preformatted conveys meaning' exception does not apply; because no wrapping mechanism (pre-wrap or a wrap toggle) is offered, a low-vision user is forced into horizontal scrolling to read each command — the barrier 1.4.10 prohibits.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The signal is identical to case-02's PASS: a <pre> with white-space:pre overflowing 320px. A tool cannot read the bytes and decide this is shell/SQL (wrapping loses nothing, must wrap) while that is Python (wrapping loses meaning, exempt); worse, the common heuristic 'it is in <pre> so the code is exempt' is itself wrong per G224. Only a human who reads the code and knows the language's wrapping semantics can call it.

citation.quote: Or, for code where non-wrapping lines are not essential, the code wraps or a mechanism is provided to allow line wrapping.

pages.scenario: Webhooks API reference shows a long docker run command and a long single-line JSON payload (both wrappable). Default is preformatted, but each code card provides a real keyboard-operable 'Wrap lines' toggle (button[aria-pressed]) that switches the <pre> to white-space:pre-wrap. When wrapped, every command and payload fits 320px in a single column — the conforming counterpart to case-05 via the G224/G206 wrappable-code mechanism.
pages.mechanism: By default the .codecard pre blocks overflow 320px (~1295-1668px self-overflow, same as case-05). Activating the keyboard-reachable Wrap lines button (correct aria-pressed state, focus-visible outline) adds white-space:pre-wrap; overflow-wrap:anywhere, verified to drop self-overflow to 0 with aria-pressed=true, so the whole command/JSON fits a single 320px column with vertical scrolling only. Wrappable content plus a working wrap mechanism conforms even though the default scrolls horizontally.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A tool sees a <pre> overflowing 320px by default (identical to case-05's failing default) plus a generic <button>. It cannot determine that the button toggles wrapping, that wrapping is an adequate remedy for THIS content (because it is wrappable code, not Python), or that the toggle is the G224/G206 mechanism. That chain — content is wrappable, control wraps it, wrapping suffices — is human reasoning over both meaning and behavior.

citation.quote: Providing options within the content to switch to a layout that does not require the user to scroll horizontally to read a line of text

methodology.enNote: Non-text Contrast — WCAG 2.1 AA; no Trusted Tester test.

aspects.title: Border/boundary contrast bites ONLY when it is the sole cue that a control exists
aspects.plain: A faint border only needs strong contrast when it is the single hint a control exists, so the same grey border can fail on a borderless input yet pass elsewhere.
aspects.description: The SC's UI-component requirement only applies to the visual information NECESSARY to identify that a control is present. The Understanding text is explicit: a border indicating the hit area is required to contrast 3:1 only 'when there is no other visual way to identify the presence of the control'; if the control has visible text or a sufficiently contrasting icon, a low-contrast surrounding border is NOT subject to the requirement. So the identical low-contrast 2px grey border can be a PASS on a labelled, clearly-styled button and a FAIL on a borderless 'ghost' input whose ONLY cue is that same border. The verdict flips on a semantic reading of the whole component (is there any OTHER visual way a sighted low-vision user would know the control is there?), not on the border's contrast number alone. A purely automated checker either measures every border in isolation (false-positives on the labelled button) or does not measure non-text borders at all (misses the ghost input) -- neither evaluates 'is the boundary the only way to identify the control'.
aspects.scLimb: UI-component boundary contrast (Understanding 'Boundaries'): boundary contrast required only when no other visual cue identifies the control
aspects.whyUncovered: Zero ACT test cases exist (testCaseCount:0). The discrimination resists encoding because the outcome turns on whether label text / contrasting icon / positional context already identify the control -- a human reading of the whole component, not a property of the border. Automated tools either over-flag every faint border or never measure non-text borders; neither performs the 'is the boundary the only cue' judgement.

references.quote: Having a visual boundary indicating the hit area is only required when there is no other visual way to identify the presence of the control – and in those cases, the boundary must have sufficient non-text contrast in order to pass this success criterion.

If a control has visible content (such as text or a sufficiently contrasting icon), which helps users identify the presence of the control, then a border or other indication of the overall boundary of the hit area is not required, as is therefore not subject to non-text contrast requirements.

The text input lacks any form of label to hint at its presence. The border color (#AAA) has contrast lower than 3:1 against its adjacent white background. As the border here is required to identify the presence of the input, it must have sufficient contrast to pass this criterion.

pages.scenario: Civic permit-search page with two side-by-side search inputs sharing the identical 2px #AAAAAA border (2.32:1): the left has a visible 'Search by address' label + placeholder (PASS, border exempt); the right 'case number' box is bare with no label/placeholder/icon (FAIL, border is the only cue and required).
pages.mechanism: The case-number input's only visual cue that a control exists is a 2.32:1 grey border, below the 3:1 threshold; because no other visual way identifies the control, the boundary is required and fails. The identical border on the labelled address input is exempt because its visible label identifies the control.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse do not measure non-text/input border contrast at all (miss the ghost box), and a 'measure every border' checker would false-positive on the labelled box too; neither performs the 'is this border the only cue?' judgement. Both inputs have valid accessible names (label vs aria-label), so name/label linters are green.

citation.quote: Having a visual boundary indicating the hit area is only required when there is no other visual way to identify the presence of the control – and in those cases, the boundary must have sufficient non-text contrast in order to pass this success criterion.

pages.scenario: Credit-union login card: username field has a visible label + 6.47:1 person icon + placeholder (PASS), stacked above a password field that is a bare white box on white with a visually-hidden (.sr-only) label, no icon, no placeholder. Both inputs share a 1px #ABABAB border (2.30:1).
pages.mechanism: The password input is a white box on a white card whose only visual cue is a 2.30:1 border; with the label hidden and no icon/placeholder, that boundary is required to reach 3:1 and fails. The username's identical border is exempt because its visible label + contrasting icon + placeholder identify the control.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The label is present but .sr-only, so name/label checks pass; axe/Lighthouse never measure input border contrast. A tool cannot infer that the username border is exempt (visible label/icon) while the identical password border is required (sole cue) — that flip is a human reading of which fields carry an alternative visual identifier.

citation.quote: If a control has visible content (such as text or a sufficiently contrasting icon), which helps users identify the presence of the control, then a border or other indication of the overall boundary of the hit area is not required, as is therefore not subject to non-text contrast requirements.

pages.scenario: Document-editor toolbar on a #5b6675 slate bar: three icon-only buttons (Bold/Italic/Bulleted list) drawn with #788294 glyphs at 1.50:1 (FAIL, the faint icon is the only cue of presence), beside a 'Comment' button that uses the same 1.50:1 glyph but adds a white 5.83:1 text label (PASS).
pages.mechanism: The Bold/Italic/List buttons have no text and no border; the only graphical object identifying that a control is present is a 1.50:1 icon, far below 3:1, so it is required and fails. The Comment button's identical faint icon is supplemental because its white text label (5.83:1) identifies the control.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every button has a valid accessible name (aria-label or visible text), so name/role checks pass. Scanners do not compute SVG-glyph-vs-toolbar contrast, and cannot distinguish an icon that is required for identification (icon-only buttons) from one that is supplemental to a visible text label (Comment) — the exact semantic judgement the SC demands.

citation.quote: A button which has a distinguishing indicator such as position, text style, or context does not need a contrasting visual indicator to show that it is a button, although some users are likely to identify a button with an outline that meets contrast requirements more easily.

pages.scenario: Sales-pipeline data grid whose 'Forecast' column cells are inline-editable (contenteditable/role=textbox); the only cue that they are editable controls rather than static text is a faint 1px #B4B4B4 inset border (2.07:1) — FAIL. The bottom row instead uses an explicit 'Edit 410' button with a visible text label (and the same 2.07:1 pencil) — PASS.
pages.mechanism: At 2.07:1 the inset cell borders wash out, so the editable forecast figures are visually indistinguishable from adjacent static owner text; the boundary that is the sole signal of editability is required to reach 3:1 and fails. The 'Edit' button is identified by its visible text regardless of its identical faint border.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The editable cells have correct role=textbox + aria-label, so role/name checks pass; no scanner measures a cell's inset border contrast. Distinguishing an editable cell from adjacent static text by its faint boundary, and recognising the labelled 'Edit' button's border is exempt, is a meaning-level judgement static analysis cannot make.

citation.quote: Unless the control is inactive, any visual information provided that is necessary for a user to identify that a control is present and how to operate it must have a minimum 3:1 contrast ratio with the adjacent colors.

pages.scenario: RTL Arabic nonprofit donation card: a 'monthly amount' field has a visible label + a 9.11:1 green 'ر.س' currency mark + placeholder (PASS), above an 'other amount' field that is a bare white box on white with a .sr-only label, no currency mark, no placeholder (FAIL). Both money inputs share a 2px #A8A8A8 border (2.38:1).
pages.mechanism: Contrast is layout-direction-agnostic; the 'other amount' box is a blank region of the white card whose only visual cue is a 2.38:1 border, which is therefore required to reach 3:1 and fails. The monthly field's identical border is exempt because its visible label and high-contrast currency mark identify it.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The bare field has a programmatic name via its .sr-only label, so name/label checks pass; axe/Lighthouse do not measure input border contrast. The RTL mirroring and Arabic-Indic numerals add surface complexity but do not change the human judgement of whether any other visual cue identifies the control, which no scanner performs.

citation.quote: If a control has visible content (such as text or a sufficiently contrasting icon), which helps users identify the presence of the control, then a border or other indication of the overall boundary of the hit area is not required, as is therefore not subject to non-text contrast requirements. Having a visual boundary indicating the hit area is only required when there is no other visual way to identify the presence of the control – and in those cases, the boundary must have sufficient non-text contrast in order to pass this success criterion.

pages.scenario: Flight-search filter bar with three fields sharing the identical 2px #ADADAD border (2.24:1): Origin has a visible 'Origin city' label + placeholder (PASS, exempt); Destination is an active bare input with only an aria-label (FAIL, border is the sole cue); Airline is a disabled/inactive input (NOT APPLICABLE, inactive components are exempt). The page fails overall on Destination.
pages.mechanism: The active Destination input's only visual cue is a 2.24:1 border, below 3:1, so it is required and fails. The same number lands on three different SC outcomes: Origin's border is exempt (visible label identifies it) and Airline's is exempt (inactive control), demonstrating the verdict turns on label-presence and active/inactive state, not the contrast number.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: All three inputs have accessible names, so name/label checks pass; no scanner measures input border contrast. A naive 'measure every border' checker would false-positive on Origin (label-exempt) and Airline (disabled-exempt) while a 'skip non-text borders' tool false-negatives on Destination; getting all three right needs the label-identifies judgement plus the disabled-exemption judgement layered on one 2.24:1 value.

citation.doc: WCAG 2.2 Understanding 1.4.11 — Inactive User Interface Components
citation.quote: User Interface Components that are not available for user interaction (e.g., a disabled control in HTML) are not required to meet contrast requirements. An inactive user interface component is visible but not currently operable.

aspects.title: State-indicator (checked/selected/expanded) contrast against the CORRECT adjacent surface within the component
aspects.plain: The mark showing a control's state (a checkbox's tick, a toggle's thumb) must contrast 3:1 against the correct neighbouring surface, which is easy to pick wrong.
aspects.description: Beyond identifying that a control exists, the SC requires the non-text information that conveys STATE -- the check in a checkbox, the dot in a radio, the thumb of a toggle/slider, the chevron showing an accordion is open -- to have 3:1 against ITS adjacent color, which may be another part of the component rather than the page. Two semantic judgements are needed that automation cannot make: (a) identifying which mark conveys state versus which is decorative, and (b) choosing the correct comparison surface (the check is measured against the box fill, not the page; the toggle thumb against the track, not the page). A flat-fill design where the indicator does NOT contrast with the component but the whole filled component contrasts with the page is explicitly allowed -- so the same physical pair of colors passes or fails depending on which surface is the relevant 'adjacent' one. Picking the wrong surface gives the wrong verdict.
aspects.scLimb: UI-component STATE-indicator contrast: 'any visual information necessary to indicate state ... must ... have a minimum 3:1 contrast ratio' measured against the adjacent color (which may be another part of the component)
aspects.whyUncovered: No ACT cases exist for checked/selected/expanded indicators. The hard part is not arithmetic but segmenting a custom control into 'state mark' + its correct adjacent surface, and recognizing the flat-fill exception (compare filled component to page) versus the mark-on-fill pattern (compare mark to fill). Automated tools cannot reliably segment a styled/SVG control into these regions, so they can neither locate the right two colors nor decide which design pattern applies.

references.quote: any visual information necessary to indicate state, such as whether a component is selected or focused must also ensure that the information used to identify the control in that state has a minimum 3:1 contrast ratio.
non-text indicators such as the check in a checkbox, or an arrow graphic indicating a menu is selected or open must have sufficient contrast to the adjacent colors.
It is possible to use a flat design where the status indicator fills the component and does not contrast with the component, but does contrast with the colors adjacent to the component.

pages.scenario: Healthcare patient-portal consent form with custom checkboxes. Two boxes are CHECKED: the box fills brand-purple #6221EA and contrasts ~7:1 with the white card (distractor PASS), but the check mark is a brand tint #9D85DB drawn on that fill at 2.33:1 — the checked-state mark fails its correct adjacent surface (the box fill).
pages.mechanism: The checked-state indicator (SVG check stroke #9D85DB) sits on the purple fill #6221EA at 2.33:1, below the 3:1 required for non-text information that indicates state. The correct adjacent color for an internal state mark is the box fill, not the page; box-vs-page (7.18:1) is a distractor.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse have no rule that segments a custom control into 'state mark' + 'the surface that mark sits on' and tests that pair; they measure text contrast (none in the SVG) and at most sample component-vs-page, which here is the 7:1 passing distractor. Deciding the check is the state mark and its adjacent color is the fill is a two-step human visual/semantic judgment. The native input, label association, and programmatic checked state are all valid, so no linter fires.

citation.quote: For visual information required to identify a state, such as the check in a checkbox or the thumb of a slider, that part might be within the component so the adjacent color might be another part of the component.

pages.scenario: SaaS analytics notification settings with custom toggle switches. Three are ON: the track turns green #4E9E52 (~3.31:1 vs the white page, distractor PASS), but on/off is conveyed by thumb POSITION, and the pale frosted thumb #74B97A rides directly on the green track #4E9E52 at ~1.32:1 — the state-conveying part fails the surface it travels along.
pages.mechanism: The ON-state indicator is the thumb's position, read from the thumb against the track it rides. On the ON switches the thumb is recoloured a pale 'frosted' green #74B97A sitting inside the green ON-track #4E9E52 at ~1.32:1, far below 3:1, and its drop-shadow is removed, so the only ON/OFF cue cannot be located. The green-track-vs-white-page (~3.31:1) is the wrong, exonerating comparison.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: No automated checker isolates 'the thumb' as the state-conveying graphical object and tests it against 'the track it rides'; there is no text pair to flag, and a component-vs-page heuristic lands on the green-vs-white passing distractor. Recognizing that thumb position (not track color) is the ON cue, and that the relevant adjacent surface is the inner rail, requires human visual reasoning. The native checkbox, label, and checked state are valid.

citation.quote: the component must not lose contrast with the adjacent colors, and non-text indicators such as the check in a checkbox, or an arrow graphic indicating a menu is selected or open must have sufficient contrast to the adjacent colors.

pages.scenario: State DMV FAQ accordion. Header bands #5C6B7E contrast ~5.4:1 with the white page, and aria-expanded is correct. The only visual open/closed cue is a rotating chevron drawn 'soft slate' #8A96A6 on the band at 1.81:1 — the expanded-state graphic fails its adjacent surface, so a sighted low-vision user cannot tell open panels from closed.
pages.mechanism: The expanded-state indicator (SVG chevron #8A96A6) is 1.81:1 against the header band #5C6B7E it overlays, below 3:1. Correct programmatic aria-expanded does not satisfy 1.4.11, which is a visual contrast requirement; the chevron's adjacent color is the band, not the page (5.44:1 distractor).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: aria-expanded is present and correct, so state-exposure checks pass; axe/WAVE/Lighthouse do not measure an SVG chevron's contrast against the specific band it overlays, nor know it is the sole open/closed cue, and a component-vs-page sample tests the passing band. Identifying the chevron as the state graphic and the band as its adjacent surface is human visual judgment over exemplary APG markup.

citation.quote: any visual information necessary to indicate state, such as whether a component is selected or focused must also ensure that the information used to identify the control in that state has a minimum 3:1 contrast ratio.

pages.scenario: Auto-insurance quote wizard with two custom radio groups, the adjacent-surface boundary page. Group A (liability) uses a flat-fill selected state: the whole control fills solid #1565C0 at 5.75:1 vs the page (PASS, fill is the indicator). Group B (deductible) uses mark-on-fill: a faint inner dot #7BB0E6 on a #4A90D9 fill at 1.46:1 (FAIL). Same blue palette, opposite verdicts depending on the correct adjacent surface.
pages.mechanism: Group B's selection mark (inner dot #7BB0E6) is 1.46:1 against its fill #4A90D9, below 3:1; the dot's adjacent surface is the fill, not the page (3.34:1 distractor). Group A is the explicitly-allowed flat-fill pattern (fill vs page 5.75:1) and passes — included to force the correct adjacent-surface choice. A reviewer measuring both controls against the page would wrongly pass B.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Both groups use real native radios with correct labels/checked state, so nothing trips a linter; axe/Lighthouse compute no contrast for these CSS shapes/pseudo-elements, and a component-vs-page heuristic passes BOTH (A legitimately, B via the 3.34:1 fill-vs-page distractor). Distinguishing 'flat fill = indicator, compare to page' from 'inner dot = indicator, compare to fill,' and seeing the same blue yields opposite verdicts, is human-only segmentation and pattern classification.

citation.quote: It is possible to use a flat design where the status indicator fills the component and does not contrast with the component, but does contrast with the colors adjacent to the component.

pages.scenario: ATS candidate shortlist as an aria-multiselectable listbox. Two rows are selected; aria-selected is correct and announced. The sole visual selected cue is a 4px left accent bar #9FB4CF on the pinned row surface #EEF2F7 at 1.89:1 — too faint for a low-vision recruiter to see which candidates are on the interview panel.
pages.mechanism: The selected-state indicator (border-left accent bar #9FB4CF) is 1.89:1 against the row background #EEF2F7 it abuts, below 3:1. There is no other visual selected cue (no checkmark, no extra background change). Correct aria-selected exposure does not satisfy the visual contrast requirement; the bar's adjacent color is the row surface.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: aria-selected is present and correct so state-exposure checks pass; all row text contrasts amply, and axe/WAVE/Lighthouse have no rule treating a border-left-color as a selection indicator tested against the row fill — there is no foreground/background text pair to flag. Recognizing the thin left bar is the only selected cue and that its adjacent color is the row background is human visual judgment over clean APG listbox markup.

citation.quote: any visual information necessary to indicate state, such as whether a component is selected or focused must also ensure that the information used to identify the control in that state has a minimum 3:1 contrast ratio.

pages.scenario: Restaurant review star ratings, the 1.4.1-vs-1.4.11 boundary. Each rating is also text ('4 of 5'), so Use of Color is satisfied (not hue-only). Default reviews still FAIL 1.4.11: a 'filled' star is distinguished from empty only by an inner glow #C99A3E on the gold body #A67C2E at 1.47:1. The editor's-pick widget uses a solid dark fill #1A1A1A (~17:1) for filled vs an outline (PASS variant).
pages.mechanism: The filled-state mark (inner glow #C99A3E) is 1.47:1 against its adjacent surface, the star body #A67C2E, below 3:1; filled and empty stars share the same gold body, so the state hinges entirely on that low-contrast glow. The value-as-text removes the 1.4.1 concern, isolating the 1.4.11 mark-vs-body failure. The solid-fill variant (17:1) marks the conforming boundary.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Both widgets have correct role=img + aria-label and an adjacent text value, so name/role and 1.4.1 checks pass; axe/WAVE/Lighthouse compute no contrast for SVG fills and have no rule segmenting a star into 'body' + 'filled-state glow' to test the glow against the body, and a star-vs-page sample lands on the 3.7:1 gold-vs-cream passing distractor. Recognizing the inner glow is the filled-vs-empty mark and its adjacent surface is the star body is human visual judgment.

citation.quote: The second example fails the Non-text contrast criterion due to the yellow (#FFF000) to white contrast ratio of 1.2:1.

aspects.title: Selecting WHICH parts of a complex graphic are 'required for understanding' and whether equivalent text exempts them
aspects.plain: Parts of a chart or diagram needed to understand it must contrast 3:1, but deciding which parts matter, and whether nearby text labels excuse them, needs a human.
aspects.description: G207/G209 require 3:1 contrast only for graphical objects 'required for understanding.' The whole judgement is meaning-level: in a multi-part graphic (chart line, pie slice, infographic circle + its icon, map region, the magnet's U-shape and tips) the evaluator must decide WHICH parts a viewer must perceive to grasp the meaning, then test only those -- and crucially the graphic is EXEMPT if equivalent text (visible labels AND values, or a data table via a Long Description) conveys the same information. So a pie chart with adjoining 1.5:1 slices is a FAIL when the slices are the only data, NOT APPLICABLE when the same chart carries visible numeric labels and values, and a PASS only after a 3:1 border is added between slices (G209). The 'is it required / is the same info available another way' decision is exactly the determination only a human reading the graphic can make.
aspects.scLimb: Graphical-object contrast for multi-part graphics 'required for understanding' (G207/G209): chart lines, pie slices, infographic circles/icons, map regions; with the equivalent-text NA exemption
aspects.whyUncovered: No chart/diagram/infographic ACT cases exist. Automated tools cannot parse a raster or SVG chart into 'graphical objects', cannot judge which are required for understanding, and cannot determine whether adjacent visible labels+values render the graphic non-essential. The same pixel pattern flips between Fail, NA, and Pass depending on accompanying text -- a semantic determination.

references.quote: Not every graphical object needs to contrast with its surroundings - only those that are required for a user to understand what the graphic is conveying.
Not applicable: The pie chart has visible labels and values that convey equivalent information to the graphical objects (the pie slices).
If adjoining colors have less than 3:1 color contrast ratio difference add a border with at least a 3:1 color contrast with each color.

pages.scenario: SaaS analytics dashboard renders a 'Browser market share Q2 2026' pie chart as inline SVG with four adjoining pastel wedges (~1.1-1.3:1 between neighbours) and NO labels, values, legend, or data table. The slice boundaries are the only data and are the graphical objects required for understanding.
pages.mechanism: Adjoining pie wedges (#6FA8DC / #93C47D / #E0A0A0 / #E8C8E0) differ by only ~1.1-1.3:1 with no 3:1 separating border; per G209 the slice boundaries are graphical objects required for understanding and must reach 3:1 (or carry a 3:1 border). With no labels+values to exempt them, the chart fails.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The SVG is well-formed with role=img and a non-empty aria-label, so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse register a labelled graphic and stop. None parse an SVG into its constituent wedges, compute wedge-to-wedge boundary contrast, or reason that -- absent any labels/values/legend/table -- the wedge edges are the sole carrier of the data and therefore required for understanding. The identical pixels become Not Applicable the moment visible labels+values are added (case-02), a semantic reading-the-chart judgment.

citation.quote: The pie chart has labels for each slice (so passes 1.4.1 Use of Color), but in order to understand the proportions of the slices you must discern the edges of the slices (the graphical objects conveying essential information), and the contrast between the slices is not  3:1 or greater.

pages.scenario: A district council publishes 'Household recycling rate 2021-2025' as an inline-SVG bar chart. The bars are pale mint (~1.34:1 vs the white plot) but every bar is captioned in conforming text with its exact numeric value (42/45/48/51/55). The labels and values convey the same information, exempting the low bar contrast.
pages.mechanism: The graphical objects (the <rect> bars at ~1.34:1 vs the white plot) carry a visible label AND value adjacent to each bar; per the Understanding 'Required for Understanding' list a graphic with text conveying the same information (labels and values on a chart) is not required for understanding, so the low bar contrast does not fall under 1.4.11.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A scanner that did parse the SVG would likely flag the pale bars (~1.34:1) as a non-text-contrast failure -- a false positive. No tool can read the <text> value nodes, associate each value with its bar, and conclude the graphic carries equivalent text and is therefore exempt. The judgment 'is there a visible label AND value for each graphical object?' which flips the verdict from Fail to Not Applicable is the human reading-the-chart determination automation cannot make.

citation.quote: However, that is not a requirement when:

pages.scenario: A healthcare on-call dashboard shows 'Mean ambulance response time by region' as an inline-SVG line chart with four pale series strokes (~1.5-2.1:1 vs the white plot). A colour-swatch legend maps each colour to a region NAME but gives no values; you must still trace the low-contrast lines. No data table or per-point values exist.
pages.mechanism: The four <polyline> series (#9FC5E8 ~1.8:1, #B6D7A8 ~1.6:1, #F9CB9C ~1.5:1, #D5A6BD ~2.1:1) are graphical objects required for understanding and each is below 3:1 against the white plot. The legend only names the colours (no values), so it is not the equivalent text that would exempt the lines (G207).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The SVG is labelled and the legend is genuine text, so tools see a labelled chart with a key and report nothing. None compute each polyline stroke against the white plot, decide the lines are required for understanding because no per-point values/table exist, or reason that a legend which only NAMES the colours is not equivalent text. Distinguishing a legend that exempts the graphic (labels AND values) from one that merely names colours -- and the colour-name key masks the failure from a naive 'does it have a key?' heuristic -- is a meaning-level judgment.

citation.quote: The lines should have 3:1 contrast against their background, but

pages.scenario: A neighbourhood bakery shows a 'Same-day delivery zones' choropleth map as inline SVG split into four adjoining pastel regions (~1.05-1.1:1 between neighbours) with NO boundary lines (stroke=none). Zone names and a cut-off-time key are present, but a user must perceive the region boundaries to answer 'which zone am I in?'.
pages.mechanism: Adjoining region <path> fills (#FBE3C2 / #FAD7B0 / #F8CDA0 / #F6DFC0) differ by ~1.05-1.1:1 with stroke=none; per G209's map example, adjoining region colours below 3:1 must carry a boundary line of at least 3:1. The region boundaries are required for understanding and the labels/key do not establish where one zone ends and the next begins.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The map SVG is labelled and the regions carry text names, so tools pass it. None compute adjoining-region fill contrast, and none can reason that the region boundaries (not the names, not the key) are what a user must perceive to find their zone. The key lists cut-off times by zone name, which a naive 'the data is in text' heuristic might count as an exemption, but it is not equivalent because you still must read the sub-3:1 border-less boundaries. Recognising this as a G209 map-boundary failure the labels do not exempt is a meaning-level judgment.

citation.quote: The color contrast of areas within the map range between 1.3 and 1.8. A boundary line is added with a color contrast ratio of at least 3:1 with the area colors.

pages.scenario: An open-data site shows 'Electricity generation mix 2015-2024' as an inline-SVG stacked-area chart on a dark panel; the five bands sit ~1.05-1.3:1 apart with no inline values. A working <details> 'View data table (Long Description)' discloses a conforming <table> with every value for every year and source, exempting the low-contrast bands.
