pages.mechanism: The band-to-band boundaries between the stacked <polygon> elements (~1.1:1) are the graphical objects, but per the Understanding 'Required for Understanding' list, when the information is available in a table revealed by a Long Description button the graphic is not relied upon for understanding -- so the low band contrast does not fall under 1.4.11. This is a distinct exemption mechanism (long-description data table) from case-02's inline labels+values.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A scanner that did parse the SVG could flag the ~1.1:1 band boundaries as a failure -- a false positive. The correct outcome is Not Applicable, but no tool can find the <details> sibling, verify the disclosed table actually contains the chart's data for every series and year, and conclude the bands are exempt. 'Does a long description / data table convey the equivalent information so the graphic is not relied upon?' is the human judgment separating Fail from Not Applicable -- and a different exemption from case-02 that a single hard-coded rule could not capture.

citation.quote: The information is available in another form, such as in a table that follows the graph, which becomes visible when a "Long Description" button is pressed.

pages.scenario: A college advancement report shows 'Where our alumni connect' as a bubble infographic in inline SVG: five circles whose AREA encodes community size, each with a faint inner icon marking the platform. Circle-vs-page (~1.26:1) and icon-vs-circle (~1.30:1) are both below 3:1, with no member counts/legend/table; the text names give identity but not size.
pages.mechanism: Two graphical-object families per item are required for understanding -- the bubble <circle fill=#DCE6F1> measured against the white page (~1.26:1) and the inner icon (#B8CCE4) measured against the circle (~1.30:1) -- and both are below 3:1 (G207). The platform text names convey identity but not the size the circles encode, so no equivalent text exempts the circles.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The infographic SVG is labelled and each circle has a text platform name, so tools pass it. None recognise this as a bubble chart where circle AREA is the data, compute circle-vs-page AND icon-vs-circle contrast as two separate required graphical objects, or reason that the names convey identity but not size so the faint circles remain required. Treating one infographic as a SET of graphical objects each measured against its own adjacent surface, and judging which are required, is a human determination; the identical layout with dark borders/icons/counts would pass and nothing in the markup tells a scanner which it is.

citation.quote: Discerning the circles is required to understand the size of network and discerning the icons in each circle is required to identify which network it shows.

aspects.title: F78: an author focus indicator that technically exists but is rendered non-visible by surrounding styling
aspects.plain: A focus outline technically exists but is hidden by look-alike borders, so a keyboard user genuinely can't tell which control is currently focused.
aspects.description: F78 names failure modes beyond the trivial outline:none: (a) a non-focus outline/border that looks identical to the browser focus ring, so the user cannot tell which element is focused; and (b) a thick element border the same color as the focus indicator drawn just outside it, so the focus ring is swallowed by the border. In both cases an outline IS present on focus -- a CSS scraper or rule that merely detects a focus style reports a pass -- but a sighted keyboard user cannot perceive WHICH control has focus or that focus moved at all. Deciding this requires comparing the focused appearance against the persistent decorative styling and judging whether the change is humanly discernible.
aspects.scLimb: Focus-indicator non-text contrast (Understanding 'Relationship with Focus Visible' + failure technique F78): focus indicator present but visually indistinguishable / occluded
aspects.whyUncovered: The 1.4.11 ACT corpus has zero cases (testCaseCount:0); F78 exists only as a technique document with no synthetic page. Its own test procedure ('Set the focus to all focusable elements ... Check that the focus indicator is visible') is a manual keyboard-and-eyeball check no ACT rule encodes. Automated tools detect outline:none but cannot judge 'looks the same as the focus indicator' or 'occluded by a same-color border' -- both require visually comparing the focused state against the resting state and a same-element border.

references.quote: Other styling may make it difficult to see the focus indicator even though it is present, such as outlines that look the same as the focus outline, or thick borders that are the same color as the focus indicator so it cannot be seen against them.
the focus indicator is drawn just outside the border, but as both are black and the border is thicker than the focus indicator, it no longer meets the definition of "visible".

the visual focus indicator for a component must have sufficient contrast against the adjacent background when the component is focused, except where the appearance of the component is determined by the user agent and not modified by the author.

pages.scenario: Glyphwright SDK API-reference 'On this page' link rail: every TOC link permanently carries a 1px dotted #1b1b1b outline, and :focus re-declares the identical 1px dotted #1b1b1b outline at the same offset. Page loads (autofocus) with the Pagination link focused; it is visually indistinguishable from its eight siblings.
pages.mechanism: F78(a): the author's always-on decorative outline is byte-identical to the focus indicator (same 1px/dotted/#1b1b1b/offset), so the focused link's appearance equals the resting appearance of every other link — focus state carries zero discriminating signal even though a focus outline genuinely renders. Verified in Chrome: the focused Pagination link looks exactly like the other links.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse have no focus-visibility rule and cannot reason about indistinguishability. A 'does a contrasting :focus outline exist?' heuristic returns true (1px #1b1b1b on white ~17:1), and contrast on either state passes. The defect only appears by rendering the resting and focused states of the same element and judging a human cannot tell them apart — a two-state visual diff no static checker performs.

citation.quote: The following CSS example will create an outline around links that looks the same as the focus indicator. This makes it impossible for users to determine which one in fact has the focus, even though the user agent does draw the focus indicator.

pages.scenario: City of Marrowfield parking-citation review step: action buttons have a permanent 4px solid #000 border, and the author focus indicator is a 2px solid #000 outline (outline-offset 1px) drawn just outside that border. Page loads (autofocus) with the 'Continue to payment' button focused.
pages.mechanism: F78(b): the focus outline is the same color (black) as a thicker (4px) element border drawn immediately inside it, so the focus ring is swallowed — it reads as one continuous black edge with only a hairline gap. Verified in Chrome close-up: the focused button differs from the unfocused one by an imperceptible thin black line, not a discernible focus change. (An explicit black author outline is used rather than the UA default, which modern Chrome paints in the accent color and would not be occluded.)
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: outline:none is not used and a real author :focus outline is declared, so outline-removal and focus-style-exists linters pass; the focus outline measured in isolation against white is ~21:1 so a contrast checker passes. No tool encodes 'focus ring occluded by a same-color thicker border.' Detecting it needs the focused state rendered, the black-on-black adjacency observed, and the human judgment that focus is not perceivable.

citation.quote: In this case the focus indicator is drawn just outside the border, but as both are black and the border is thicker than the focus indicator, it no longer meets the definition of "visible".

pages.scenario: Cohortly analytics-app top nav: every primary-nav button permanently carries a 2px solid #2f6df6 'chip' outline, and :focus re-uses the identical 2px solid #2f6df6 outline. Page loads (autofocus) with the Funnels item focused; all five nav items look identical.
pages.mechanism: F78(a) applied to a sibling toolbar: the uniform decorative outline on every nav button equals the focus indicator, so the focused item is indistinguishable from its four peers. Verified in Chrome: five identical blue-outlined buttons, no perceptible focus on Funnels. Each outline individually has fine contrast (blue #2f6df6 on white ~4:1) — this is a relational distinguishability failure, not a contrast shortfall.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A real 2px solid blue :focus outline of good contrast is declared, so any focus-style heuristic passes. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse have no rule comparing the focused element to its unfocused siblings; uniform decorative nav outlines are legitimate. Only a human rendering the focused state and scanning the row can see the focused item matches the others.

citation.quote: Also, any visual information necessary to indicate state, such as whether a component is selected or focused must also ensure that the information used to identify the control in that state has a minimum 3:1 contrast ratio.

pages.scenario: Northvale Health MyChart segmented 'appointment type' radio group: the selected state uses a 3px solid #0f8a8a border and :focus re-uses the identical 3px solid #0f8a8a border (with outline:none). Page loads with the Video visit segment selected and the In-person visit segment focused — both show identical teal borders.
pages.mechanism: F78 state-collision: the focus indicator is visually identical to a DIFFERENT state indicator (selection), so a focused-but-unselected segment is indistinguishable from the selected one, and focus cannot be told apart from selection. Verified in Chrome: two teal-bordered segments, ambiguous which is chosen vs focused. Teal #0f8a8a on white (~3.3:1) is fine standalone — this is a state-distinguishability failure.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Markup is exemplary (role=radiogroup/radio, aria-checked correct) and a real focus style exists with fine contrast, so structural and contrast checks pass. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse cannot reason that the focus treatment is byte-identical to the selection treatment and therefore collapses two distinct states into one appearance — a live-state collision comparison no static rule performs.

citation.quote: The following CSS example will create an outline around links that looks the same as the focus indicator. This makes it impossible for users to determine which one in fact has the focus, even though the user agent does draw the focus indicator.

pages.scenario: Meridian Bank money-transfer form: every field has a permanent 3px solid #10243f (navy) border, and :focus adds only a 1px solid #10243f outline at offset 0 (caret also navy). Page loads (autofocus) with the Amount field focused.
pages.mechanism: F78(b) on a text input: a 1px navy focus outline flush against a 3px navy border of the same color fuses into a single slightly-thicker navy edge — no perceivable 'focus moved here' change, and the navy caret does not rescue it. Verified in Chrome: the focused Amount field is indistinguishable from the other navy-bordered fields. Navy on white (~13:1) is fine standalone — the focus indicator is occluded, not low-contrast.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: outline:none is not used and an author :focus outline is declared, so outline-removal and focus-exists checks pass; each color is individually high-contrast so any contrast calculator passes. No tool encodes 'thin focus outline occluded by a thicker same-color adjacent border.' Detecting it needs the focused field rendered and the human judgment that the navy-on-navy change is not perceivable.

citation.quote: A focus indicator is required. If the focus indicator is styled by the author, it must meet the 3:1 contrast ratio with adjacent colors.

pages.scenario: Hearthline real-estate listing card grid (PASS boundary): every card has a subtle resting box-shadow, but :focus-visible swaps to a thick high-contrast offset ring — outline:3px solid #1b3a2b, outline-offset:4px, plus a wide 6px colored halo. Page loads (autofocus) with the 8 Meadowgate Ct card focused.
pages.mechanism: Correct F78 avoidance: the focus indicator differs from the resting decoration on multiple axes at once (solid vs soft, dark-green vs translucent grey, 4px offset vs flush, plus wide halo), so the focused card is unmistakably distinct and the ~9:1 ring exceeds the 3:1 focus-state threshold. Verified in Chrome: the focused card is clearly identifiable among its neighbours. Included so the judge must reason about discernibility, not mere presence of a focus style.
pages.selectorNote: The listing card that loads focused; its focus ring is distinct from resting shadow
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Symmetric to the failures: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse cannot PROVE this passes any more than they can prove the others fail — no tool confirms a focus indicator is perceptibly DISTINCT from a resting box-shadow. A tool sees a :focus-visible rule and can only guess; a human renders the resting and focused cards and confirms the difference is unmistakable, establishing the pass for a reason no static analyzer can reach.

citation.quote: Using a change of contrast for focus and other states is a technique to differentiate the states. This is the basis for G195: Using an author-supplied, highly visible focus indicator, and more techniques are being added.

aspects.title: Choosing the correct comparison surface: subsumed borders/shadows and controls between two backgrounds
aspects.plain: Deciding which neighbouring colour to compare against is tricky: decorative borders and shadows should be ignored, and measuring the wrong pair gives the wrong pass/fail result.
aspects.description: The 'Adjacent colors' guidance requires the evaluator to pick the meaningful comparison and ignore decorative elements. A border between two contrasting backgrounds, or a 3D drop-shadow, is 'subsumed into the color closest in brightness' and is NOT measured; instead you measure inside vs outside background. A background-color-only input (no border) is measured against the page (#043464 example). Getting the verdict right means deciding which color is the meaningful adjacent one and which decorative element to ignore -- e.g. an input on a dark panel whose silver border is irrelevant because the white interior already contrasts with the dark panel. A naive tool that measures the silver border against the dark panel (and flags it) gets the WRONG answer; the correct test ignores the border entirely and compares interior-to-panel.
aspects.scLimb: UI-component 'Adjacent colors' measurement incl. the subsumption rule (Understanding 'Adjacent colors'): pick the right adjacency; ignore subsumed borders/shadows; background-color-only inputs vs page
aspects.whyUncovered: No ACT cases exercise input-border-vs-internal-vs-external-background or background-color-only inputs. The subsumption rule ('considered to be subsumed into the color closest in brightness') is an interpretive step -- deciding a border doesn't interfere with identifying the component -- that contrast checkers don't perform; they measure each declared border/background pair literally and over- or under-report.

references.quote: if an input has a white internal background, dark border, and white external background the 'adjacent color' to the component would be the white external background.
a 3D drop-shadow on an input, or a dark border line between contrasting backgrounds is considered to be subsumed into the color closest in brightness (perceived luminance).
Text inputs that have no border and are differentiated only by a background color must have a 3:1 contrast ratio to the adjacent background (#043464).

pages.scenario: Online-banking wire form. Text inputs with a white interior and a thin graphite border (#3E5168) sit on a dark-blue panel (#003366). A per-edge tool measures border-vs-panel = 1.55:1 and reports a 1.4.11 failure; the correct verdict is PASS because the graphite border is subsumed into the dark panel and the meaningful adjacency is the white interior vs the dark-blue panel (12.6:1).
pages.mechanism: Subsumption rule: a dark border line between contrasting backgrounds is 'subsumed into the color closest in brightness', so it is not measured; the identifying cue is the white interior vs the #003366 panel at 12.6:1. The border (1.55:1 vs panel) does not interfere with identifying the control and is ignored.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A contrast checker measures every declared border against its declared neighbor and reports border #3E5168 vs panel #003366 = 1.55:1 as a FAILURE — the wrong answer. It cannot perform the interpretive step of recognizing the border is subsumed and that the white interior (not the border) is the identifying cue; deciding which adjacency is meaningful is human judgment.

citation.doc: WCAG 2.2 Understanding SC 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast — 'Adjacent colors' (wcag-understanding/non-text-contrast.html)
citation.quote: If components use several colors, any color which does not interfere with identifying the component can be ignored for the purpose of measuring contrast ratio. For example, a 3D drop-shadow on an input, or a dark border line between contrasting backgrounds is considered to be subsumed into the color closest in brightness (perceived luminance).

pages.scenario: Government SNAP-renewal wizard with borderless inputs differentiated only by background fill. The 'Street address' input uses navy #043464 on the white page (12.5:1, the canonical PASS); the 'City or town' and date-of-birth inputs use a very pale blue #EAF2FB on the same white page (1.13:1) — the fill is the only cue an input exists, so those FAIL.
pages.mechanism: For a borderless input the differentiating background color is the sole control-identification cue and must reach 3:1 against the adjacent page. The pale-blue fill (#EAF2FB) vs the white page is 1.13:1, so the input's presence and extent are imperceptible to a low-vision user.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse compute text/foreground contrast; the labels and entered text are dark-on-pale-blue and pass 1.4.3, so they report no issue. No automated rule treats a borderless field's tint as the required identifying cue that must reach 3:1 against the page. Distinguishing 'the fill is the required cue' from 'the fill is decorative' is human interpretation.

citation.doc: WCAG 2.2 Understanding SC 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast — 'Text input using background color' passing example (wcag-understanding/non-text-contrast.html)
citation.quote: Text inputs that have no border and are differentiated only by a background color must have a 3:1 contrast ratio to the adjacent background (#043464).

pages.scenario: Skeuomorphic transport buttons in a DAW. Each button has a mid-grey filled face (#6E6E6E) on a light-grey page (#ECECEC) = 4.32:1, plus a 3D bevel built from a faint inset highlight (#F4F4F4, ~1.07:1) and inset shadow (#C4C4C4, ~1.48:1) and a drop-shadow. A per-edge tool flags the faint bevel rings; the correct verdict is PASS because the bevel is a subsumed 3D shadow and the filled face identifies the control.
pages.mechanism: Subsumption rule for 3D drop-shadows: the embossed highlight/shadow edges are subsumed into the color closest in brightness and do not interfere with identifying the component; the identifying cue is the filled button face vs the page at 4.32:1.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A naive checker that enumerates each box-shadow ring (or a thin painted edge) measures the bevel highlight (~1.07:1) and shadow (~1.48:1) against the page and reports a failure on those edges. It cannot apply the rule that a 3D drop-shadow is subsumed and that the face (not the bevel) is the cue — that requires human reasoning about what identifies the control.

citation.doc: WCAG 2.2 Understanding SC 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast — 'Adjacent colors' subsumption rule (wcag-understanding/non-text-contrast.html)
citation.quote: If components use several colors, any color which does not interfere with identifying the component can be ignored for the purpose of measuring contrast ratio. For example, a 3D drop-shadow on an input, or a dark border line between contrasting backgrounds is considered to be subsumed into the color closest in brightness (perceived luminance).

pages.scenario: Insurance quote wizard. Two inputs on the same lavender panel (#DDE3F0). Input A (white interior, #6E8FB5 border): border-vs-interior 3.36:1 but interior-vs-panel only 1.29:1 and border-vs-panel only 2.61:1 -> FAIL. Input B (violet #6E5A86 interior, #7A4A8A border): border-vs-interior only 1.09:1 but fill-vs-panel 4.70:1 -> PASS. A literal per-edge tool gets both backwards.
pages.mechanism: The verdict requires choosing the meaningful adjacency that identifies each control on the shared panel. For input A that is interior-vs-panel (1.29:1, fail) with the border as a failed fallback (2.61:1); the white field is nearly invisible against the lavender panel, so the control is not identifiable.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A per-edge checker is fooled in opposite directions: for input A it picks border-vs-interior (3.36:1) and reports PASS (wrong); for input B it picks border-vs-interior (1.09:1) and reports FAIL (wrong). It never decides WHICH adjacency identifies each control (interior/fill-vs-panel); only a human reasoning about the meaningful comparison surface gets both right.

citation.doc: WCAG 2.2 Understanding SC 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast — 'Adjacent colors' (wcag-understanding/non-text-contrast.html)
citation.quote: For user interface components 'adjacent colors' means the colors adjacent to the component. For example, if an input has a white internal background, dark border, and white external background the 'adjacent color' to the component would be the white external background.

pages.scenario: Forum tag-filter 'pill' buttons whose interior fill equals the page (#F4F6F8), so the outline is the only cue a control exists. Two pills use #7E8B96 outline = 3.22:1 (PASS); three pills use a near-identical #8E9BA6 outline = 2.62:1 (FAIL). The two greys look almost the same to a casual eye.
pages.mechanism: Because the pill interior matches the page, there is no other visual way to identify the control, so the boundary outline is required and must reach 3:1. The .pill.bad outline is 2.62:1 against the page, below threshold, so three of five filters are not reliably perceivable as controls.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Two human judgments defeat automation: (1) deciding the outline is REQUIRED because the interior gives no other cue (a tool treats every button border as a decorative, non-required boundary and does not flag it); and (2) even if measured, distinguishing the 2.62:1 fail from the visually near-identical 3.22:1 pass is the sub-perceptual boundary the SC is calibrated to.

citation.quote: Having a visual boundary indicating the hit area is only required when there is no other visual way to identify the presence of the control – and in those cases, the boundary must have sufficient non-text contrast in order to pass this success criterion.

pages.scenario: Dark-mode fintech 'API keys' panel — the inverse of the canonical subsumed-border pass. Inputs have a near-black interior (#1B2230) and a faint border (#3A4658) on a near-black panel (#11151C). A per-edge tool flags the border (1.91:1 vs panel) and points at the wrong element; once the subsumed border is correctly ignored, the meaningful interior-vs-panel adjacency is 1.15:1, so the inputs are not identifiable -> FAIL.
pages.mechanism: The faint border is closest in brightness to the near-black surroundings and is subsumed into them (same reasoning that makes a subsumed border a PASS in the light-mode figure). With the border removed from consideration, the remaining cue is the interior fill vs the panel at 1.15:1 — no perceptible visual information identifies the control.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A per-edge checker flags the declared border (#3A4658 vs panel 1.91:1) and points the developer at the wrong element, encouraging a border tweak that leaves the control just as invisible. Reaching the correct verdict requires two interpretive steps — recognizing the border is subsumed and dropping it, then measuring interior-vs-panel as the governing adjacency — which tools do not perform.

citation.doc: WCAG 2.2 Understanding SC 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast — 'Adjacent colors' dark-background example (wcag-understanding/non-text-contrast.html)
citation.quote: The input also has a dark grey border which is considered to be subsumed into the dark background. The border does not interfere with identifying the component, so the contrast ratio is taken between the white background and dark blue background.

aspects.title: Focus-indicator geometry: which adjacency the indicator must contrast with (inner / on-the-border / partly-outside)
aspects.plain: Where a focus indicator sits (inside, outside, or on the control's edge) decides which surface it must contrast against, so geometry, not one number, determines pass or fail.
aspects.description: Where a focus indicator sits determines which adjacency it must contrast with, and the SC carves out specific patterns that automation cannot disambiguate. An indicator entirely OUTSIDE need only contrast with the page the component sits on. An indicator entirely INSIDE must contrast with the adjacent color(s) within the component. An indicator that IS the component's border must contrast with BOTH adjacencies. A partly-inside/partly-outside indicator passes if EITHER part contrasts. So an inner green border that contrasts with the black outer border but NOT with the blue component background FAILS, while an inner WHITE border that contrasts with both PASSES -- the geometry, not just a single contrast number, decides it. Determining where the indicator sits relative to the visible boundary, and therefore which surface(s) it must beat, is a visual/structural judgement.
aspects.scLimb: Focus-indicator non-text contrast geometry (Understanding 'Relationship with Focus Visible'): outer-vs-page, inner-vs-component, border-needs-both, partly-inside/partly-outside either-part-suffices
aspects.whyUncovered: No ACT cases build from these figures. The verdict depends on segmenting the indicator's position relative to the component's visible boundary (inside / on the border / straddling) and then choosing the correct one-or-two adjacencies -- a structural/visual determination automated contrast checkers cannot perform; they have no notion of 'inner vs outer indicator' or 'either part may contrast'.

references.quote: only inside the component and need to contrast with the adjacent color(s) within the component.
the border of the component (inside the component and adjacent to the outside) and need to contrast with both adjacent colors.
An inner border of dark green (#008000) does contrast with the black border, but does not contrast with the blue component background.

pages.scenario: Meridian online-banking transfer-confirm screen. Two brand-blue (#4189B9) primary buttons with a 2px black border, side by side. On focus each draws a 3px INSET ring inside the visible boundary: #btn-confirm uses dark-green #008000 (FAIL), #btn-schedule uses white (PASS). The only difference is the ring colour; the verdict flips on which INNER adjacency the indicator must beat.
pages.mechanism: An inner focus indicator (box-shadow inset) must contrast with the adjacent colour WITHIN the component. The green inset ring contrasts the black border (4.09:1) but, being entirely inside the blue button, must beat the blue interior (#4189B9) — green-on-blue is 1.35:1, far below 3:1, so the focused state is imperceptible to a moderately-low-vision user. The white-ring sibling beats the blue interior at 3.82:1 and passes.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse have no model of inner-vs-outer indicator geometry; they cannot determine that an inset ring sits inside the fill and so must contrast with the interior rather than the abutting black border. A pixel checker sampling the green against the nearest dark pixels (the black border) would compute 4.09:1 and wrongly pass it. Both buttons have real <button> semantics, accessible names and a visible focus change, satisfying every automatable focus-visible heuristic.

citation.quote: Fail: An inner border of dark green (#008000) does contrast with the black border, but does not contrast with the blue component background.

pages.scenario: Cascade County 'Renew vehicle registration' wizard (step 3 of 4). Two flat text-only ghost buttons on a white page; with no fill or resting border, the outer focus outline is their only focus signal. #btn-continue uses a yellow #FFFF00 outer outline (FAIL); #btn-back uses green #008000 (PASS). Identical geometry — outer outline on a white page — so the verdict turns on whether the outer indicator beats the page.
pages.mechanism: An outer focus indicator must contrast with the background the component sits on (the page). Yellow #FFFF00 on white #fff is 1.07:1, so the focused state of the most important control on the step is invisible to a low-vision user. The green sibling outline is 5.14:1 on the same white page and passes.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A focus indicator is present and changes on focus, so focus-visible heuristics pass. No automated tool computes the contrast of an author-supplied focus OUTLINE against the page surface, and none selects 'the page' as the adjacency for an outer indicator to evaluate 1.07:1. The bright yellow also looks vivid on dark previews, masking the failure to casual visual checks.

citation.quote: Fail: The external yellow indicator (#FFFF00) does not contrast with the white background (#FFF) which the component is on.

pages.scenario: Cedar Park Health appointment-confirm screen. The 'Confirm appointment' CTA is a solid brand-blue (#4189B9) primary button with a 2px blue border at its visible edge. On focus it recolours that border in place from blue to green #4B933A — a change within the visible boundary; green vs the blue interior is 1.005:1.
pages.mechanism: The 'Confirm appointment' button is a SOLID brand-blue primary button: interior fill #4189B9 with a 2px #4189B9 border tracing its visible edge. On focus it adds no outer outline — it recolours its own border in place from blue to green #4B933A, staying at the visible boundary. Because the recoloured border sits within the visible boundary it must contrast with the component it borders (the blue interior); green-on-blue is 1.005:1, so the focus indicator is imperceptible.
pages.selectorNote: Confirm button whose focus recolours its own border green vs blue interior; id was wrong
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A visible change does occur on focus (border colour changes), so 'is there a focus change?' heuristics pass. No tool recognises the in-place recoloured border AS the focus indicator, locates it within the visible boundary, and requires it to beat the interior. A blunt border-vs-page check would read the green border against the white card (high contrast) and wrongly pass it — the wrong adjacency.

citation.quote: Fail: The border of the control changes from blue (#4189B9) to green (#4B933A). This is within the component and does not contrast with the inside background of the component.

pages.scenario: Northwind Air seat-map on a light cabin-grey page (#f4f4f4); available seats are blue (#4189B9) buttons. The focus indicator is a 4px yellow (#FFFF00) ring that STRADDLES each seat's boundary — a 2px inset half (inside the seat) plus a 2px outset half (outside on the cabin page), via two stacked box-shadows. Boundary PASS case that exercises 'either part suffices'.
pages.mechanism: A partly-inside/partly-outside focus indicator passes if EITHER part contrasts with its respective adjacency. The outer half fails the page (yellow vs #f4f4f4 = 1.02:1) but the inner half beats the seat fill (yellow vs #4189B9 = 3.55:1), so the focus state is perceivable and the indicator passes. Confirming this requires segmenting the ring into halves and applying the either-part rule, not reading one number.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Establishing this pass requires segmenting the ring into inner and outer halves, choosing the correct adjacency for each (seat fill vs cabin page), and applying 'either part may contrast'. No automated tool models a straddling indicator. A pixel checker sampling the yellow against the dominant nearby surface could just as easily report a FALSE FAIL (vs the grey page, 1.02:1) as a coincidental pass — only human geometric reasoning concludes it passes via its inner half.

citation.quote: Pass: The focus indicator is partially inside, partially outside the button. The internal part of the yellow indicator (#FFFF00) contrasts with the blue button background (#4189B9).

pages.scenario: Pulse Analytics cohort-report panel with an icon-only role=toolbar on a white surface. Every button uses the same outer grey focus ring, but one button's design token differs: most buttons use #949494 (3.03:1, PASS — the spec's canonical 3:1 focus indicator), while #tool-export uses #aaaaaa (2.32:1, FAIL). The two greys are visually almost identical, separated only by the exact unrounded 3:1 threshold.
pages.mechanism: An outer focus ring is measured against the page/surface the component sits on, and the 3:1 threshold is exact (not rounded). #aaaaaa on white is 2.32:1, below 3:1, so the focus on the export action is too faint for a low-vision user to confirm which icon they are activating. The #949494 siblings sit at 3.033:1 and pass.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A focus ring is present and changes on focus for every button, so focus-visible heuristics pass uniformly and cannot distinguish the export button. No tool measures an author focus RING against the toolbar/page surface, and none polices the exact unrounded 3:1 boundary separating #949494 (pass) from #aaaaaa (fail). The two greys are indistinguishable to a casual eye, so manual spot-checks miss it too.

citation.quote: When comparing the computed contrast ratio to the success criterion ratio, the computed values should not be rounded (e.g. 2.999:1 would not meet the 3:1 threshold).

pages.scenario: RTL Arabic settings screen (dir=rtl lang=ar) for a city-transit app. The ON 'delay alerts' switch is a custom role=switch with a brand-blue (#4189B9) track on a white card. On focus it draws a 3px INSET border inside the track coloured dark-green #008000; being inside the component, the relevant adjacency is the blue track, where green is 1.35:1.
pages.mechanism: An inner focus indicator on a switch must contrast with the adjacent colour within the component — the track fill. Green inset border vs blue track #4189B9 is 1.35:1, so the focused state is invisible against the surface it sits inside, risking accidental toggling of a setting. Green would clear the white card (5.14:1) but that is the wrong adjacency for an inner indicator. Screen-reader role/aria-checked semantics are correct; the failure is purely the visual focus-indicator contrast.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The switch has correct role=switch/aria-checked and a visible focus change, so role/name/value and focus-visible heuristics pass. Tools cannot tell the inset border sits inside the track and must beat the blue track fill rather than the white card; a checker sampling green against the nearest white card pixels would read 5.14:1 and wrongly pass it. The RTL/Arabic context moves the case away from the spec's English figures, defeating pattern-matching.

citation.quote: Other cases include focus indicators which are: only inside the component and need to contrast with the adjacent color(s) within the component.

aspects.title: Negative/NA boundaries: inactive controls, hover-only treatments, essential graphics & author-choice logos, and symbolic text characters
aspects.plain: Several borderline cases (disabled controls, hover-only highlights, brand logos, symbolic glyphs like 'X' for close) need a human to decide whether the 3:1 contrast rule even applies.
aspects.description: The SC defines several carve-outs whose correct answer is 'Not Applicable / Pass' and which a naive contrast scan will wrongly FAIL, plus one inclusion (symbolic text) it will wrongly ignore. (1) Inactive/disabled controls are exempt -- a faint disabled button is NOT a failure. (2) Author-supplied HOVER treatments are supplemental and need not contrast 3:1 because the pointer position is the indicator. (3) The Essential exception exempts logos/flags/sensory photos/heatmaps/medical schematics -- BUT a logo presented low-contrast by AUTHOR CHOICE (not brand-mandated, e.g. dark-grey logos on a black page revealed only on hover) is NOT exempt and DOES fail. (4) Conversely, symbolic text characters used for appearance not language (an 'X' for close, '>' as an arrow) ARE non-text content and DO need 3:1. Every one of these requires deciding category/intent (is it disabled? is this hover or a persistent state? is the low contrast brand-mandated or an author choice? is this glyph linguistic or symbolic?), which is a semantic judgement, not a measurement.
aspects.scLimb: Scope carve-outs & inclusions: Inactive components exemption; Hover-state carve-out; Essential exception incl. author-choice-logo non-exemption; Symbolic text characters as non-text content
aspects.whyUncovered: No ACT cases verify these negative/NA boundaries or the symbolic-text inclusion. Automated checkers measure contrast on every element and will FAIL disabled controls, supplemental hover treatments, and brand logos that are genuinely exempt, while having no way to recognize the author-choice-logo reversal or to treat an 'X'/'>' glyph as a graphical object. Each verdict hinges on category/intent recognition (disabled? hover vs state? brand-mandated vs author choice? symbol vs language) -- pure semantic judgement.

references.quote: this requirement does not apply to inactive user interface components.

additional author-supplied visual treatments for hover are not "required to identify" the hover state. Those treatments can be considered supplemental and do not themselves need to contrast 3:1 against the background.

If logos are presented with an insufficient contrast, but their presentation was an author choice rather than being mandated by corporate identity or brand guidelines, then that particular low contrast presentation is not "essential", and the logo is not exempt from the contrast requirements.
When text characters are used as symbols – used for their visual appearance, rather than “expressing something in human language” – they fall under the definition of non-text content.

pages.scenario: Auto-insurance checkout: an operable 'Pay now' submit button and a natively-disabled 'Enroll in AutoPay' button share pixel-identical 'ghost' styling — a 2px #c9c9c9 border (~1.66:1 on white). The active button FAILS (its identifying border is the only thing marking the control and must reach 3:1); the disabled twin is exempt (inactive UI).
pages.mechanism: An active UI component's identifying boundary (2px #c9c9c9 border ≈1.66:1 vs white) is below the 3:1 non-text-contrast threshold; the inactive-UI exemption applies only to the disabled twin, not to the operable #pay-now submit, so the surface fails.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Both buttons resolve to the identical #c9c9c9 border on white, so a pixel scanner can only flag both or skip both; axe-style tools skip the disabled subtree but have no rule that the OTHER faint button is active and therefore failing. Separating the exempt from the failing one requires recognizing operability (does it submit? is it in the tab order?) — a behavioral judgement, not a measurement.

citation.quote: User Interface Components that are not available for user interaction (e.g., a disabled control in HTML) are not required to meet contrast requirements. An inactive user interface component is visible but not currently operable. An example would be a submit button at the bottom of a form that is visible but cannot be activated until all the required fields in the form are completed.

pages.scenario: Developer-docs cookie/telemetry preferences. Custom checkboxes are identified at rest by a 2px solid black border (#111 on white = 18.8:1). On hover the row gains a faint grey wash (#ededed, ~1.17:1 vs white). A scanner sampling :hover would flag the faint wash, but the wash is a SUPPLEMENTAL hover treatment (pointer position is the indicator) and the control passes.
pages.mechanism: The resting identifying indicator (2px #111 border) is 18.8:1 and stays ~16:1 even against the #ededed hover wash, so the control never loses contrast; the ~1.17:1 hover wash is an author-supplied supplemental treatment that the SC explicitly exempts from the 3:1 requirement.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A checker instructed to evaluate the :hover pseudo-state simply measures the new #ededed background's ~1.17:1 ratio and emits a 1.4.11 violation — a false positive. It cannot distinguish a REQUIRED state indicator from a SUPPLEMENTAL hover decoration, which requires knowing the pointer position already conveys hover and the resting black border already identifies the control.

citation.quote: The pointer itself, via its location, is the indicator of whether the user is hovering on a component. Therefore, additional author-supplied visual treatments for hover are not "required to identify" the hover state. Those treatments can be considered supplemental and do not themselves need to contrast 3:1 against the background.

pages.scenario: SaaS 'Trusted by' logo wall on a black page. Nine company wordmarks are set in #1c1c1c (~1.23:1) and turn white only on hover — an author-choice low-contrast presentation that is NOT essential and FAILS. A tenth wordmark (BNØRD) is set in its brand-mandated navy #11203a (~1.29:1) and is genuinely Essential/exempt (NA).
pages.mechanism: The nine #1c1c1c wordmarks are logos presented low-contrast by AUTHOR CHOICE (a hover-reveal styling effect), so the logo/Essential exemption is forfeited and they fail 3:1; only the brand-MANDATED navy wordmark retains the Essential exemption.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A scanner sees ten low-contrast wordmark elements on black and cannot tell which color is brand-mandated (Essential, exempt) from which is an author styling choice (in scope, failing), nor whether a hover-reveal masks a non-essential too-faint default. The correct nine-fail/one-NA split depends entirely on knowing brand intent — knowledge a tool has no access to.

citation.quote: If logos are presented with an insufficient contrast, but their presentation was an author choice rather than being mandated by corporate identity or brand guidelines, then that particular low contrast presentation is not "essential", and the logo is not exempt from the contrast requirements.

pages.scenario: Festival ticketing photo-gallery dialog whose only controls are text-character glyphs used as symbols: '✕' (close) and '‹'/'›' (prev/next) at #5e6b82 on the #4a5366 bar (~1.43:1). A reference row shows the identical glyphs in #e9edf3 (~6.6:1) which PASS. The symbolic glyphs are non-text content requiring 3:1.
pages.mechanism: Text characters used as symbols (✕ as close, ‹/› as arrows) fall under the definition of non-text content and must reach 3:1; at ~1.43:1 these graphical-object glyphs fail, and a valid aria-label does not substitute for visible non-text contrast.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A <button> whose content is the single character '✕' looks like TEXT, so a tool either evaluates it under the 1.4.3 text rule, ignores it as a trivial one-glyph node, or marks the control passing because it has an accessible name. None recognizes that the glyph is a graphical object whose appearance — not its character value — carries meaning; classifying 'X' as symbol vs letter is a meaning judgement a parser cannot make.

citation.quote: When text characters are used as symbols – used for their visual appearance, rather than "expressing something in human language" – they fall under the definition of non-text content.

pages.scenario: Ophthalmology patient-portal imaging card with three low-contrast graphics: an essential fundus schematic (anatomical colors, NA), an essential retinal-thickness heat-map gradient (measurement scale, NA), and an overlaid clickable annotation ring (.pin, role button) whose #b8c0c8 outline is ~1.6:1 against the schematic — a real UI control that FAILS.
pages.mechanism: The schematic and heat-map qualify for the Essential exception (recoloring would undermine clinical meaning), so they are NA; but the overlaid annotation marker is a user-interface component whose only identifying visual (a ~1.6:1 hollow ring) is below the 3:1 requirement and fails.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A scanner cannot recognize the Essential exception — it cannot know a red→blue gradient is a clinical measurement scale (NA) rather than a recolorable decoration, nor that beige regions are anatomically mandated; and it cannot tell the overlaid hollow ring is an operable control (whose 1.6:1 outline truly fails) versus a decorative dot. Both judgements ('essential' and 'is this a control') are semantic/domain calls.

citation.quote: Diagrams of medical information that use the colors found in biology ... color gradients that represent a measurement, such as heat maps

pages.scenario: RTL (Arabic) transit-authority route-map editor. One role=toolbar holds four visually-similar controls needing different verdicts: a disabled Delete tool (~1.7:1 icon, NA/inactive), an active Draw tool (same ~1.7:1 icon, FAILS), an active Zoom tool (#3a3a3a icon ~7.6:1 plus a supplemental hover glow, NA), and a symbolic ✕ close glyph (~2.0:1, FAILS as non-text content). RTL places the close glyph on the visual left.
pages.mechanism: One role=toolbar holds four visually-similar controls needing different verdicts: a disabled Delete tool (~1.7:1 #b9b9b9 icon, NA/inactive); an active Draw tool (.tool--active-fail, same ~1.7:1 #b9b9b9 icon, FAILS as it must reach 3:1); an active Zoom tool (#3a3a3a icon ~7.6:1 plus a supplemental hover glow, NA); and a symbolic ✕ close glyph #9c9c9c at ~2.0:1 (FAILS as non-text content). Multiple active controls below 3:1 make the surface fail.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The two ~1.6:1 icons (Delete and Draw) are pixel-identical to a scanner, which would flag or skip both together though only the operable Draw fails; the scanner cannot tell the Zoom hover glow is supplemental rather than a required state, and reads the ✕ as plain text rather than a graphical symbol. Four differing verdicts require reasoning about active-vs-inactive, hover-vs-state, and symbol-vs-language — none measurable; the RTL layout additionally defeats 'close is top-right' heuristics.

citation.quote: Inactive components, such as disabled controls in HTML, are not available for user interaction.

methodology.enNote: Content on Hover or Focus — WCAG 2.1 AA; no Trusted Tester test.

aspects.title: F95 — author hover content is not itself hoverable (pop-up vanishes on the cursor path from trigger to content)
aspects.plain: A tooltip or pop-up that appears on hover vanishes the moment you move the mouse toward it, so you can never reach it to read it.
aspects.description: The single normative failure technique for 1.4.13 (F95) describes author-built additional content that appears on pointer hover but DISAPPEARS the moment the user moves the pointer off the trigger toward the content to read it — because visibility is bound only to mouseover/mouseout on the trigger, there is a physical gap between trigger and pop-up, or there is no shared hover region. Judging this is a SPATIAL + BEHAVIORAL call: a reviewer mentally traces the cursor path and asks whether the pop-up is reachable without the mouseout firing. A static checker sees a span[role=tooltip] that toggles display:none on mouseout and cannot tell whether the content overlaps/adjoins the trigger or is separated by a dead-zone; the Understanding states the passing arrangement 'generally implies that the additional content overlaps or is positioned adjacent to the target.' This is the geometric/event-handler reasoning a human does by simulating pointer travel under magnification.
aspects.scLimb: Hoverable
aspects.whyUncovered: testCaseCountsByExpected = {} — 0 ACT rules and 0 test cases for 1.4.13, so the only normative failure technique (F95) has no failing fixture and no passing counter-fixture. Nothing in the corpus exercises pointer travel from trigger to pop-up.

references.quote: A pop-up opens on pointer hover. Due to the chosen screen magnification, the content is only partially visible. However, as soon as the pointer is moved away from the trigger towards the pop-up content so it can be read, the pop-up automatically closes.
The pointer can be moved over the new content without the additional content disappearing.

A technique to view the content fully in both situations is to move the mouse pointer directly from the trigger onto the new content.  This capability also offers significant advantages for users who utilize screen reader feedback on mouse interactions.  This condition generally implies that the additional content overlaps or is positioned adjacent to the target.

pages.scenario: SaaS billing page: a "?" help button beside "Seat overage" shows a custom tooltip positioned 30px BELOW the trigger, separated by a transparent .gap spacer (pointer-events:none). Show/hide is bound only to the trigger button's mouseover/mouseout; the tooltip has no hover handler and is not a descendant of the trigger. Moving the pointer down to read the tooltip crosses the gap, fires mouseout, and the tooltip vanishes before the pointer reaches it.
pages.mechanism: Hoverable (F95) pure dead-zone: trigger-to-popup geometry is a transparent gap (top:50px on a 20px trigger with a 30px spacer), not adjacency/overlap, and the popup carries no mouseenter, so the trigger's mouseout fires on the travel path and hides the tooltip; no continuous pointer path keeps the content visible.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: No engine implements 1.4.13. The markup is impeccable (real <button>, role=tooltip, aria-describedby, appears on focus, ~16:1 contrast), so a "tooltip toggles on hover" heuristic passes. Catching it requires mentally tracing the pointer from the 20px trigger down across a 30px transparent gap and reasoning that mouseout fires before the pointer arrives — a spatial + event-handler simulation no static checker performs. Verified in Puppeteer: tip visible on trigger, hidden after pointer enters the gap.

citation.quote: A pop-up opens on pointer hover. Due to the chosen screen magnification, the content is only partially visible. However, as soon as the pointer is moved away from the trigger towards the pop-up content so it can be read, the pop-up automatically closes.

pages.scenario: Community forum thread: a GitHub/Twitter-style profile "hover card" appears when hovering a username. It is rendered into a detached portal layer (#hovercard-layer, sibling of the content) positioned 12px below the username. Show is delayed 180ms (hover-intent); hide is immediate on the username's mouseleave; the card has no mouseenter of its own. Moving the pointer down to the card crosses the 12px transparent gap, fires mouseleave, and the card vanishes instantly.
pages.mechanism: Hoverable (F95) with timing asymmetry: delayed-show / immediate-hide, popup is a portal sibling (no DOM proximity to the trigger), a 12px transparent gap sits on the travel path, and there is no popup mouseenter to cancel the hide — so a continuous pointer path cannot keep the card open.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: No 1.4.13 rule exists, and the portal actively misleads a DOM-proximity heuristic (the card is nowhere near the trigger in the DOM, yet that does not help). The card is statically exemplary: role=dialog, aria-label, real controls, good contrast, opens on focus. The failure requires reasoning jointly about the 180ms-show/instant-hide asymmetry, the 12px gap, and the missing card mouseenter — a behavioral+geometric pointer-travel simulation. Verified in Puppeteer: card shows after delay, hidden after pointer enters the gap.

citation.quote: When the added content is large, magnified views may mean that the user needs to scroll or pan to completely view it, which is impossible unless the user is able to move their pointer off the trigger without the additional content disappearing.

pages.scenario: Fintech dashboard: an SVG line chart of daily NAV where each <circle> data point shows a detail pop-up on mouseenter, offset above-and-right of the point. Points are closely spaced (~26px) and share one reusable pop-up. To read the offset pop-up for a point under magnification, the pointer must travel toward it — crossing the next data point, whose mouseenter replaces the wanted pop-up with the neighbour's (the exact F95 chart example).
pages.mechanism: Hoverable (F95) chart variant: the pop-up is offset (+14,-46) from its point with pointer-events:none and there is no shared hover region; because adjacent points are ~26px apart, the cursor path to one pop-up crosses a neighbour whose mouseenter re-renders the shared pop-up, destroying the one the user wanted.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: No 1.4.13 rule, and the page passes the checks a scanner can do (svg role=img + aria-label, a real <table> data fallback for 1.1.1, focusable points with handlers for 2.1.1). The failure is purely a function of pixel geometry — point spacing vs. pop-up offset vs. which point the travel vector intersects. Verified in Puppeteer: pop-up read "Jun 11 $1.041 +1.0%" then changed to "Jun 12 $1.037 -0.4%" when crossing the neighbour.

citation.quote: Hovering over a chart with data points, pop-ups open to show details of the respective data point, somewhat offset from the data point itself. When moving the pointer towards the pop-up so it can be fully read with magnification, the pointer travels over other data points that cause the appearance of other pop-ups that replace the particular pop-up the user wanted to see.

pages.scenario: E-commerce category sidebar: hovering a top-level category ("Camp & Hike") reveals a CSS-only flyout submenu offset to the right (left:230px against a 210px row, leaving a ~20px transparent corridor). The flyout is a DOM child of the category but not geometrically contiguous; reaching lower submenu items requires a diagonal down-and-right path that exits both hot-zones, ending the :hover state and collapsing the flyout before the cursor arrives.
pages.mechanism: Hoverable (F95) diagonal dead-zone: popup is a DOM descendant (li.cat:hover > .flyout) but positioned with a horizontal gap and a taller box, so the natural diagonal travel vector passes through empty space belonging to neither li.cat nor .flyout; :hover on li.cat goes false and the CSS reveal rule stops matching mid-travel. No JS hover-intent bridge spans the corner.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: No 1.4.13 rule, and the most plausible static heuristic is fooled: the flyout IS a DOM child of the trigger, so "popup nested in trigger? probably hoverable" passes — yet DOM nesting does not imply geometric contiguity here. Markup is a clean nested ul/role=group with good contrast and :focus-within keyboard reveal. Judging it requires tracing a realistic diagonal pointer path against the two bounding boxes and the 20px gap. Verified in Puppeteer: flyout visible on hover, hidden when the pointer sits in the diagonal corridor.

citation.quote: A technique to view the content fully in both situations is to move the mouse pointer directly from the trigger onto the new content.  This capability also offers significant advantages for users who utilize screen reader feedback on mouse interactions.  This condition generally implies that the additional content overlaps or is positioned adjacent to the target.

pages.scenario: Pharmacy prescription page: a glossary term <dfn> ("contraindication") shows a definition pop-up that DIRECTLY overlaps/adjoins the term (top:-2px, no gap) — visually the passing arrangement the Understanding describes. But the pop-up carries pointer-events:none and reveal is keyed only to the term's :hover, so moving the pointer onto the pop-up means the cursor is no longer counted as over the term, :hover collapses, and the content vanishes. Adjacency is present but the content is not actually hoverable.
pages.mechanism: Hoverable (F95) "adjacency present but un-hoverable": geometry satisfies overlap/adjacency, yet pointer-events:none makes the popup transparent to the cursor; the pointer entering the popup region is not counted as hovering the trigger, so dfn.term:hover .def stops matching and the popup hides. There is no continuous pointer path despite perfect visual adjacency.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: No 1.4.13 rule, and this case specifically defeats the smarter heuristics: a geometry/overlap check passes (the overlap is real) and a markup review passes (<dfn>, role=tooltip, aria-describedby, tabindex, focus parity, ~15:1 contrast). The single breaking line, pointer-events:none, is a common harmless tooltip style; no linter knows it makes a hover-revealed popup un-hoverable. Catching it requires reasoning about CSS hit-testing — that the cursor over the popup is not hovering the trigger. Verified in Puppeteer: definition visible on the term, computed pointer-events:none confirmed.

citation.quote: The intent of this condition is to ensure that additional content which may appear on hover of a target may also be hovered itself.  Content which appears on hover can be difficult or impossible to perceive if a user is required to keep their mouse pointer over the trigger.

pages.scenario: Government parking-permit form: a "?" help tooltip beside the "Parking zone" select, built correctly as the PASS anchor on the same component family. Trigger and tooltip share one wrapper (.help) whose box encloses both; reveal is keyed to the wrapper's mouseenter/mouseleave and focus-within. The tooltip is adjacent/overlapping (4px overlap, no gap), has pointer-events:auto and its own mouseenter, a 120ms hide delay tolerates the sub-element transition, and Esc dismisses it. A continuous pointer path from button to tooltip keeps the content visible.
pages.mechanism: Hoverable satisfied (aligns with SCR39): shared hover region (wrapper encloses both elements), popup is itself hoverable (pointer-events:auto + tip.mouseenter cancels close), no transparent dead-zone (4px overlap), and a 120ms close delay bridges the button-to-tip boundary; moving the pointer onto the tooltip keeps it visible and Esc closes it.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: No engine evaluates 1.4.13, so a tool can neither flag nor confirm this PASS — it is silent. Confirming the page actually passes requires a human to trace the pointer from the button onto the tooltip and verify the shared hover region, the popup's mouseenter, and the hide delay keep it visible (and that Esc dismisses it) — the same pointer-travel simulation the FAIL cases need, here resolving to PASS, which is why a correct PASS and a subtle FAIL look near-identical to a scanner. Verified in Puppeteer: visible on trigger, pointer-events:auto, still visible when pointer moves onto the popup, hidden after Esc.

citation.quote: The pointer can be moved over the additional content without the additional content disappearing.

aspects.title: Applicability gate — author-controlled tooltip vs. user-agent title= tooltip (and modal-dialog carve-out)
aspects.plain: Telling apart a browser's built-in title= tooltip (which this rule ignores) from a custom one the developer built to look identical, since only the custom one has to follow the rules.
aspects.description: The SC explicitly does NOT apply when the additional content's appearance is 'completely controlled by the user agent' — canonically the browser rendering of the title attribute — and modal dialogs are also out of scope. F95 bakes the UA carve-out into its test (condition #2: 'controlled by the user agent, not the author'). The judgment-heavy case is attributing WHO controls the appearance: distinguishing (a) a plain title= tooltip (out of scope, passes by exclusion) from (b) an AUTHOR-built div styled/scripted to LOOK native (in scope, must meet all three conditions) and (c) the inverse where the author suppresses the native tooltip (title='') and reimplements it in JS. A static tool sees both a title= and a div and cannot reason that the visible bubble is the author's div, not the UA's tooltip — yet getting this attribution wrong flips PASS↔FAIL for the entire criterion. The modal-dialog exclusion likewise needs an N/A judgment (a dialog takes focus, so it is not hover/focus-transient content).
aspects.scLimb: Applicability / Trigger gate (UA-exclusion + modal exclusion)
aspects.whyUncovered: The exclusion carve-outs are listed as corpus gaps (no case distinguishes a native title tooltip from an author-built tooltip; no N/A case for modals). With 0 fixtures there is no example anchoring the in-scope/out-of-scope boundary, so the whole gating predicate is unmodeled.

references.quote: This criterion does not attempt to solve such issues when the appearance of the additional content is completely controlled by the user agent. A prominent example is the common behavior of browsers to display the title attribute in HTML as a small tooltip.
Modal dialogs are out of scope for this criterion because they must take keyboard focus  and thus should not appear on hover or focus.
The appearance of the additional content is controlled by the user agent, not the author.

pages.scenario: Ledgerline invoicing toolbar: every button (Save/Export/Send/Duplicate) carries only a native title= attribute (e.g. title='Save your work'). There is zero JavaScript and no author popup DOM, so the hover bubble is rendered entirely by the user agent. This is the out-of-scope boundary anchor: visually similar to the author-built failing cases, but UA-controlled and therefore inapplicable / PASS by exclusion.
pages.mechanism: The hover bubble is the browser's native rendering of the title attribute. SC 1.4.13 explicitly excludes content whose appearance is completely controlled by the user agent (canonically the title tooltip), and F95 condition #2 ('controlled by the user agent, not the author') is satisfied — so the failure does not apply. Verified with Puppeteer: 0 script tags, 0 inline on* handlers, Save title='Save your work', no author bubble element in the DOM.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A scanner sees title= attributes and a tooltip appearing on hover and could flag it for 1.4.13 (native title tooltips are famously not hoverable/dismissible/persistent). The judgment a tool cannot make is the attribution that this bubble is UA-rendered (no author script/DOM), which triggers the explicit UA-exclusion and makes the criterion inapplicable — distinguishing this PASS from an author bubble dressed to look native.

citation.quote: This criterion does not attempt to solve such issues when the appearance of the additional content is completely controlled by the user agent. A prominent example is the common behavior of browsers to display the title attribute in HTML as a small tooltip.

pages.scenario: Northwind Pharmacy refill queue: each status help icon shipped with a native title=, but a Bootstrap/jQuery-UI-style tooltip plugin strips the native title on load (removeAttribute('title')) and renders its own gray span.nwtip styled to mimic the native UA tooltip. The author bubble is pointer-events:none, toggled only on mouseenter/mouseleave of the 18px icon, with no Escape handler. Visually near-identical to the case-01 native tooltip, but author-owned, so 1.4.13 applies and it fails.
pages.mechanism: Because the JS blanks the native title and shows an author span, the visible bubble is author-controlled (UA-exclusion does NOT apply -> in scope). The bubble is pointer-events:none and only listens on the trigger, so moving the pointer toward it fires mouseleave and it vanishes (not hoverable, F95); there is no keydown/Escape handler (not dismissible). Verified with Puppeteer: after init .info title===null, .nwtip computes pointer-events:none and becomes visibility:visible on hover (screenshot showed the gray author bubble).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: At rest the icons are plain spans (title stripped at runtime; even a bare title= trips no rule). A scanner cannot determine that the gray bubble on hover is an author span rather than the browser's native title tooltip — yet that attribution flips the verdict from out-of-scope (UA title) to in-scope. The conditions it then fails (hoverable, dismissible) are interaction-time properties requiring actual hover-toward and Escape, which static checkers never exercise.

citation.quote: The objective of this failure is to describe a situation where users find it difficult or impossible to move the pointer over additional content that appears on hover.

pages.scenario: Aurora Transit trip planner: each leg has a round service-note icon where the author sets title='' to suppress the native tooltip, then paints an identical gray bubble with a pure-CSS ::after { content: attr(data-hint) } (no JavaScript). The bubble appears only while the 22px icon itself is :hovered; a ::after pseudo-element cannot receive the pointer and there is no Escape affordance. Indistinguishable from a native tooltip, but author CSS owns it, so 1.4.13 applies and it fails.
pages.mechanism: title='' yields no UA tooltip; the visible gray bubble is an author CSS ::after, putting the content in scope. A ::after pseudo-element is generated content with no DOM/accessibility-tree node and cannot take the pointer, so moving off the 22px icon ends :hover and the bubble vanishes (not hoverable, F95); there is no dismiss path (not dismissible). Verified with Puppeteer: .feat has title='', getComputedStyle(.feat,'::after').content equals the data-hint text, and on a real mouse hover ::after opacity goes to 1 (screenshot confirmed the bubble).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The element carries title='' so a scanner reads 'has a native tooltip', but an empty title produces no UA tooltip, so a tool may instead conclude nothing is on hover. Neither view captures that the visible bubble is an author CSS ::after (in scope). Recognizing the bubble is author-painted, that a pseudo-element cannot be hovered into, and that there is no dismiss path are all human visual/semantic judgments.

citation.quote:
1. The pointer can be moved over the new content without the additional content disappearing.
          2. The appearance of the additional content is controlled by the user agent, not the author.

pages.scenario: The Tidewater Review economics article: FOMC and bps are plain abbr title= (native, UA-controlled, out of scope / PASS), while GDP looks identical (same dotted underline) but is an abbr.gloss wrapping a span.bub author tooltip that JS reveals on hover/focus. The author bubble is pointer-events:none with no Escape handler. Two visually identical abbreviations, different owners — only the GDP one is governed by 1.4.13, and it fails; the reviewer must attribute each bubble element-by-element.
pages.mechanism: FOMC/bps hover bubbles are the browser's title rendering (UA-controlled -> 1.4.13 does not apply -> PASS by exclusion). GDP's .gloss reveals an author span via JS on mouseenter/focus; it is pointer-events:none and toggles only on the trigger with no Escape, so it is not hoverable (F95) and not dismissible. Author-controlled -> in scope -> FAILS. Verified with Puppeteer: FOMC abbr has title='Federal Open Market Committee'; .gloss has NO title and contains an author .bub that becomes visibility:visible on hover (screenshot showed the author footnote bubble).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A scanner sees two abbr elements that look the same and no rule fires for either. It cannot reason that FOMC's bubble is the browser's title rendering (out of scope, PASS) while GDP's is an author span driven by JS (in scope, failing hoverable/dismissible). The per-element attribution of who renders each bubble, plus the interaction-time hoverable/dismissible test on the author one, are human judgments static tools cannot make.

citation.quote: Examples of such interactions can include custom tooltips, sub-menus and other non-modal popups which display on hover and focus.

pages.scenario: Helios Energy kWh bar chart: each SVG rect bar has an SVG <title> child (UA-rendered native tooltip, e.g. 'February: 612 kWh', out of scope) AND an author .vtip floating overlay shown on hover with DIFFERENT, richer text ('Feb · 612 kWh · $84.10 · 18% below your 12-mo avg'). The overlay is pointer-events:none, repositions under the cursor via mousemove, and has no Escape handler. Two on-hover sources, two owners, two divergent texts — the reviewer must separate which content the SC governs (only the author overlay) and judge its behavior.
pages.mechanism: The SVG <title> tooltip is user-agent-controlled (out of scope). The author .vtip overlay is shown on mousemove, is pointer-events:none and follows the cursor, so moving toward it under magnification chases it or leaves the bar and it disappears (not hoverable, F95); no Escape/dismiss path (not dismissible). Author-controlled -> in scope -> FAILS. Verified with Puppeteer: each rect.bar's SVG <title> ('February: 612 kWh') differs from its data-rich ('Feb · 612 kWh · $84.10 · 18% below your 12-mo avg'); on real hover .vtip shows the rich text at opacity 1 and computes pointer-events:none (screenshot confirmed).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Each bar has two hover-content sources with two owners. A scanner sees a valid SVG <title> (and may credit it as an accessible name) plus a JS-built div, and cannot reason that only the author overlay is governed by 1.4.13, that the SVG <title> is out of scope (UA-controlled), or that the two carry different text. Nor can it test that the overlay (pointer-events:none, cursor-following, no Esc) fails hoverable + dismissible.

citation.quote: Hovering over a chart with data points, pop-ups open to show details of the respective data point, somewhat offset from the data point itself. When moving the pointer towards the pop-up so it can be fully read with magnification, the pointer travels over other data points that cause the appearance of other pop-ups that replace the particular pop-up the user wanted to see.

pages.scenario: Meridian Bank wire-transfer form: focusing the high-risk Amount field opens a modal security step-up dialog (role='dialog' aria-modal='true') that dims the page, moves keyboard focus to its confirm button, traps Tab, and is dismissed via Escape/Cancel. Superficially this is content appearing on focus (the 1.4.13 trigger pattern), but modal dialogs are explicitly out of scope — the correct disposition is NOT-APPLICABLE to 1.4.13 (evaluate under 3.2.1 On Focus). This is the N/A modal carve-out anchor.
pages.mechanism: The focus-triggered content is a modal: it takes keyboard focus (focus moved into the dialog), traps it, dims the page, and must be acknowledged. The 1.4.13 modal exclusion states modals must take keyboard focus and thus should not appear on hover/focus in the transient sense the SC governs, routing such content to 3.2.1 On Focus. So 1.4.13 does not apply. Verified with Puppeteer: dialog has aria-modal='true'; focusing #amount sets backdrop data-open='true' and moves document.activeElement to dlg-confirm (focus enters the dialog) — confirming modal behavior (screenshot showed the dimmed page + modal).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The DOM shows additional content appearing on focus — the literal 1.4.13 trigger — so a naive rule could apply 1.4.13 and start testing hoverable/dismissible/persistent. Deciding that this focus-triggered content is a modal (takes/traps focus, dims the page, must be acknowledged) rather than a non-modal tooltip is a judgment about behavior and intent; both look like 'content appears on focus' in markup, and only a human can make the N/A call and re-route it to 3.2.1.

citation.quote: Modal dialogs are out of scope for this criterion because they must take keyboard focus  and thus should not appear on hover or focus.  Refer to Success Criterion 3.2.1 On Focus.

aspects.title: Dismissible Method 2 — no/broken keyboard dismiss (cannot clear content without moving hover or focus)
aspects.plain: A hovered or focused pop-up covers other content but offers no key (like Escape) to clear it, forcing low-vision users to move the mouse and lose what they were reading.
aspects.description: SCR39 requires hover content 'can be closed without moving the pointer away from the trigger' and focus content 'closed without moving the focus away from the trigger' — by Esc, another documented shortcut, or activating the trigger. The judgment-heavy failures: (a) NO dismiss mechanism at all, so the user must physically move the pointer/focus to clear it, defeating the low-vision pan workaround; (b) an Esc handler scoped wrong (e.g., bound to the trigger which has lost focus, so Esc is inert while the bubble shows); (c) a 'close' that only works by moving focus INTO the pop-up, which can re-obscure. A static tool can detect that a keydown listener exists but cannot judge whether pressing Esc actually clears THIS content while hover/focus is retained on the trigger — that requires interpreting handler scope against the user's physical situation. The Understanding's whole motivation is the magnified user who cannot afford to move the pointer to dismiss obscuring text.
aspects.scLimb: Dismissible (Method 2: dismiss mechanism)
aspects.whyUncovered: The Dismissible-mechanism limb is listed as absent — no case tests presence/absence of an Esc/keyboard dismissal without moving hover/focus. With no fixtures there is no failing 'no-Esc' or 'wrongly-scoped-Esc' example.

references.quote: The content can be closed without moving the pointer way from the trigger. Either by pressing <kbd>Esc</kbd>, by pressing another documented keyboard shortcut, or by activating the trigger.
Provide a mechanism to easily dismiss the additional content, such as by pressing Escape.

low vision users who can only navigate via the keyboard do not want the small area of their magnified viewport cluttered with hover text. They need a keyboard method of dismissing something that is obscuring the current focal area.

pages.scenario: Online-banking transfer-limit screen: a round 'i' info button shows a tooltip on hover AND keyboard focus that overlaps the help paragraph and the Continue button. The tooltip is keyboard-reachable (meets 2.1.1) but there is NO Escape handler, no documented shortcut, and activating the trigger does not toggle it off — the only way to clear the obscuring content is to move focus/pointer off the trigger.
pages.mechanism: Additional content appears on focus and obscures other content (Method 1 not satisfied), and Dismissible Method 2 is entirely absent: no keydown/Escape listener exists and the click handler only re-asserts focus, so a magnifier/keyboard user cannot clear the tooltip without moving focus away from the trigger.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse have no rule that focuses the trigger, presses Escape, and checks whether obscuring content clears. The button has a valid accessible name, role=tooltip is wired via aria-describedby, and the CSS is well-formed — every static check is green. Detecting the failure requires a human to focus the trigger, observe the tooltip covers real content, press Escape, and judge that nothing happens while focus is retained.

citation.quote: Alternatively, low vision users who can only navigate via the keyboard do not want the small area of their magnified viewport cluttered with hover text. They need a keyboard method of dismissing something that is obscuring the current focal area.

pages.scenario: Patient-portal medication list: an 'interactions' pill on Warfarin opens a drug-interaction warning box that covers the dosage text. An Escape handler exists but is bound to the trigger button; the trigger's own click handler calls this.blur(), moving focus to document.body, so the keydown never reaches the handler and Escape is inert while the box obscures the dose.
pages.mechanism: Esc handler scoped wrong: the keydown/Escape listener is on the trigger element, but after activation focus is blurred to <body>, so keydown is dispatched to the body where no listener exists. The obscuring popover cannot be dismissed without moving focus — a runtime scope mismatch between where the listener lives and where focus actually is.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A static scan sees a keydown listener that checks for 'Escape' (superficially 'has a dismiss mechanism') plus a valid button and role=tooltip. No tool models the runtime focus path — that this.blur() in the click handler moves focus to <body> while the listener is on the button, so the two never meet. Confirming the failure requires activating the trigger, pressing Escape, observing nothing happens, and reasoning that handler scope no longer matches live focus location.

citation.quote: The content can be closed without moving the focus way from the trigger. Either by pressing Esc, by  pressing another other documented keyboard shortcut, or by activating the trigger.

pages.scenario: SaaS analytics dashboard: a '?' badge on a conversion KPI opens a definition popover that covers the device-breakdown list. The popover is hoverable and persistent, but its only dismiss affordance is a close '×' button positioned INSIDE the popover, reachable only by Tab-ing focus off the trigger and into the additional content. No Escape handler and no toggle-on-trigger.
pages.mechanism: The sole dismissal requires moving focus INTO the additional content (Tab to the in-popover × button), violating SCR39's 'closed without moving the focus away from the trigger.' For a magnifier user the viewport follows focus into the popover, which can re-obscure the data they wanted to read.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The popover has an explicitly labelled close button (aria-label='Close definition'), valid role=tooltip, and a named trigger, so all static checks pass; a naive 'is there a close button?' heuristic would wrongly mark it dismissible. No tool can judge that reaching that button requires moving focus into the content — the exact condition SCR39 forbids. A human must focus the trigger, try Escape (nothing), and reason that Tab-ing to the × breaks the no-move rule.

citation.quote: The content can be closed without moving the focus way from the trigger. Either by pressing Esc, by  pressing another other documented keyboard shortcut, or by activating the trigger.

pages.scenario: RTL (Arabic) API-reference docs: a dotted-underline glossary term 'cursor' shows a hover-only tooltip on a non-focusable span that covers the curl example block. A document-level Escape handler exists but its dismiss branch is gated on document.activeElement being a text input (copied from the filter box's clear-on-Esc behavior); while hovering the term nothing is focused, so the guard is false and Escape is inert.
