pages.mechanism: Esc is captured only when an input is focused; the tooltip is hover-only on a tabindex=-1 span, so when it is visible activeElement is <body>, the guard fails, and the dismiss code is dead. The obscuring tip can only be cleared by physically moving the pointer off the term, defeating the magnifier pan workaround.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A scanner sees document.addEventListener('keydown', ...) that checks for 'Escape' and even hides .tip elements — a present, document-scoped dismiss mechanism on paper. It cannot evaluate the activeElement guard at runtime and reason that for a hover-only tooltip on a non-focusable span the guard is always false when the tooltip is visible, making the dismiss unreachable. Catching it requires hovering, pressing Escape, seeing nothing, then reading the handler's control flow.

citation.quote: almost the entire portion of the page visible in this restricted viewport may trigger the additional content, making it difficult for a user to pan without re-triggering the content. A keyboard means of dismissing the additional content provides a workaround.

pages.scenario: City government primary nav: a 'Residents & Services' submenu opens on hover and on activation/focus of its toggle and covers the page banner and intro text. It carries aria-haspopup/aria-expanded/aria-controls, but the only way it closes is a document-level click outside the menu (pointer only) — no Escape handler and activating the toggle only re-opens it, so keyboard/magnifier users cannot dismiss the obscuring panel without moving focus away.
pages.mechanism: Obscuring content on focus/hover whose only dismiss path is a pointer click on empty page area; Escape is completely unhandled and the trigger's click only opens, so there is no keyboard mechanism that keeps focus on the trigger while clearing the panel.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The component carries all the ARIA a scanner checks for — aria-haspopup, aria-controls, and an aria-expanded that actually toggles — so audits report a well-formed 'accessible' menu. No tool opens the panel by keyboard, presses Escape, and verifies the obscuring content clears with focus retained, nor can it tell the only dismiss handler is a click-outside (pointer) with no keyboard equivalent. A human must open by keyboard, try Escape and re-activation (both fail), and reason that only the mouse works.

citation.quote: Mouse users frequently move the pointer to pan the magnified viewport and display another portion of the screen. However, almost the entire portion of the page visible in this restricted viewport may trigger the additional content, making it difficult for a user to pan without re-triggering the content. A keyboard means of dismissing the additional content provides a workaround.

pages.scenario: Museum object-label page: a dotted-underline glossary term 'maki-e' (button#term) opens a definition popup (#defn) on hover AND keyboard focus, deliberately overlapping the paragraph below; a document-level Escape clears it while focus stays on the trigger, and activating the trigger also toggles it closed.
pages.mechanism: Correct Dismissible Method 2: a document-scoped keydown (keyCode 27 / Escape) listener on document hides the popup #defn while focus REMAINS on the trigger button#term (focus is never moved); activating button#term toggles the popup closed in place as a second SCR39-allowed dismissal. Hover-and-focus parity opens it; a `dismissed` flag stops trailing focus/hover from re-opening it after an in-place dismiss.
pages.selectorNote: maki-e glossary trigger; popup hidden until hover/focus, id was c1
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: This passing case is statically indistinguishable from the failing ones — same role=tooltip, named trigger, and a keydown Escape listener present in all of them. A tool cannot tell that here the handler is document-scoped, fires while the trigger keeps focus, and does not move focus — the very properties that flip case-02/case-04's identical-looking handlers from fail to pass. Confirming the pass requires a human to focus the trigger, press Escape, and observe the obscuring content clears with focus retained.

citation.quote: document.addEventListener("keydown", (e) => { if ((e.keyCode || e.which) === 27) document.getElementById("popup").style.display = "none"; });

aspects.title: Dismissible Method 1 — pop-up obscures meaningful content (beyond the white-space / decorative exception)
aspects.plain: A pop-up with no dismiss key sits on top of real content or controls rather than empty space, hiding information the user still needs.
aspects.description: When no dismiss mechanism is provided, the SC can still be met if the content is positioned 'so that it does not obscure any other content including the trigger, with the exception of white space and purely decorative content.' This is a VISUAL + SEMANTIC judgment: does the pop-up cover meaningful content/controls, or only white space or a 'background graphic which provides no information'? A checker can compute that two boxes overlap, but cannot judge whether the covered region is purely decorative versus information-bearing. It also cannot apply the Understanding's nuance that for a LARGE trigger, positioning content away to avoid overlap may itself harm discoverability, so only Method 2 is appropriate — meaning 'obscures the trigger/content' is not always disqualifying. Distinguishing acceptable overlap of decorative whitespace from unacceptable obscuring of content is squarely human and visual.
aspects.scLimb: Dismissible (Method 1: non-obscuring positioning)
aspects.whyUncovered: The positioning/obscuring limb is listed as absent — no case tests obscuring vs. non-obscuring placement, and there is no low-vision/magnification fixture exercising content that obscures the trigger or adjacent meaningful content.

references.quote: Position the additional content so that it does not obscure any other content including the trigger, with the exception of white space and purely decorative content, such as a background graphic which provides no information.

For most triggers of relatively small size, it is desirable for both methods to be implemented.  If the trigger is large, noticing the additional content may be of concern if it appears away from the trigger.  In those cases, only the second method may be appropriate.

It does however obscure content below the button (the next red button, called ~comment-zoom-content). To meet the Dismissible requirement, a user can press the Escape key to clear the tooltip without moving the mouse

pages.scenario: Long-form policy article: an inline glossary-term tooltip (Emissions Trading System) opens downward on hover/focus with no Esc dismiss, landing on the first ~3 lines of the next body paragraph. Method 2 absent, so Method 1 is the only path — and it obscures meaningful body text.
pages.mechanism: Additional content shown on focus/hover is absolutely positioned downward (top:1.7em) and overlaps the following information-bearing paragraph; with no dismiss mechanism the low-vision/magnifier user cannot clear it in place to read the obscured prose. Method 1's non-obscuring condition is violated and Method 2 (dismiss) does not exist.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Markup is flawless (real <button>, role=tooltip, aria-describedby, focus styles, passing contrast). Scanners never enter the hover/focus state, never compute the tooltip box vs. the next paragraph box, and cannot judge that the covered region is meaningful body text rather than exempt white space — the meaningful-vs-decorative call is human and visual.

citation.quote: Position the additional content so that it does not obscure any other content including the trigger, with the exception of white space and purely decorative content, such as a background graphic which provides no information.

pages.scenario: Healthcare new-patient intake form: a 'What's this?' help popover on the Insurance Member ID field opens down-right with no Esc dismiss and overlaps the next field's required asterisk + label (Patient date of birth) and the input being filled.
pages.mechanism: On hover/focus the popover (role=tooltip) covers an adjacent required-field marker, its label, and the active input; with no dismiss key a magnifier user cannot clear it in place to see the required indicator/format hint. Method 1 violated (covers meaningful, action-critical content), Method 2 absent.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every linter-checkable property is correct: real label[for], aria-required, aria-describedby for both helper text and popover, role=tooltip, passing contrast. Tools do not render the open popover, do not measure its rectangle against the adjacent field's asterisk/label, and cannot decide the covered pixels carry required-field information rather than white space.

citation.quote: low vision users who can only navigate via the keyboard do not want the small area of their magnified viewport cluttered with hover text. They need a keyboard method of dismissing something that is obscuring the current focal area.

pages.scenario: SaaS analytics dashboard: a KPI-card metric-definition popover opens downward into the large empty dashboard canvas below the cards, with no Esc dismiss. Overlap exists but covers only empty space — PASS by the white-space exception (inverse/false-positive anchor).
pages.mechanism: The popover (role=tooltip) lands in empty canvas below the cards — verified to overlap no text, control, or informational graphic. Because Method 1's non-obscuring condition is met (overlap is exempt white space), the absence of a dismiss mechanism is acceptable and the page passes.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A naive 'any overlapping boxes fail' detector would wrongly flag this because the popover's rectangle intersects the page region; only a human can see the intersected area is empty canvas, invoke the white-space exception, and rule PASS. This is the precise false positive an automated overlap heuristic produces — the inverse error to the FAIL cases.

citation.quote: Position the additional content so that it does not obscure any other content including the trigger, with the exception of white space and purely decorative content, such as a background graphic which provides no information.

pages.scenario: Restaurant menu: a dish allergen tooltip opens into an empty menu band occupied only by a large decorative olive-branch SVG flourish (aria-hidden, no information), with no Esc dismiss. Overlap is with purely decorative content — PASS by the decorative carve-out.
pages.mechanism: The tooltip (role=tooltip) overlaps only svg.flourish (aria-hidden, conveys nothing) and is verified clear of every dish name/description/price/heading. Because the only covered thing is 'a background graphic which provides no information,' Method 1's exception applies and the missing dismiss mechanism is acceptable.
pages.selectorNote: Conditions help trigger; tooltip opens down over the difficulty key
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: An overlap detector would wrongly flag this because the tooltip box intersects the visually-large flourish — exactly the kind of element a machine cannot tell apart from informational content. Recognizing the covered SVG as decorative-and-exempt requires a human to look at it and judge it; treating the eye-catching flourish as content would over-report.

citation.quote: Position the additional content so that it does not obscure any other content including the trigger, with the exception of white space and purely decorative content, such as a background graphic which provides no information.

aspects.title: Persistent — auto-dismiss on timeout / closing for a disallowed reason vs. legitimate info-invalidation
aspects.plain: A hover or focus pop-up closes itself on a timer or a stray mouse move while the user is still reading it, instead of staying until they leave or dismiss it.
aspects.description: SCR39 requires the content 'stays visible and does not automatically close after a time,' and the Understanding says it should remain until exactly one of: the user removes hover/focus, the user dismisses it, OR the conveyed information becomes invalid (e.g., a 'busy' message). The judgment-heavy failures: (a) a tooltip on a setTimeout that auto-hides after N seconds while the user is still hovering/focused (a magnifier user needs that time to change magnification and pan); (b) content that closes for the WRONG reason (scroll, slight pointer jitter within the trigger); versus the legitimate exception — (c) content that disappears because its info BECAME INVALID (a 'saving…' that becomes 'saved'), which must NOT be flagged. Telling a disallowed timeout from a legitimate information-invalidation requires understanding the MEANING of the content over time — a human reasoning, not a timer-presence check. A static checker that merely sees setTimeout cannot tell which case it is.
aspects.scLimb: Persistent
aspects.whyUncovered: The Persistent limb is listed as absent — none of the three persistence-end conditions, nor the auto-dismiss-on-timeout failure ('does not automatically close after a time'), is tested; there is no outcome variety to anchor the valid-info-invalidation exception.

pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse see well-formed role=tooltip, a real button with an accessible name, aria-describedby, hover+focus triggers, a hoverable popup and an Esc handler — all static checks pass. The defect is purely temporal (a 4s timer hides still-valid content), and a scanner cannot tell a disallowed auto-dismiss from a legitimate info-invalidation; that needs a human watching the timeline and judging whether the info is still valid.

aspects.title: Perceive-on-focus — hover-triggered content with NO keyboard-focus path to reveal it
aspects.plain: Useful content shows only when you hover with a mouse and never appears on keyboard focus, so keyboard-only users can never see information that mouse users get.
aspects.description: The Additional Notes require that 'content which can be triggered via pointer hover should also be able to be triggered by keyboard focus' (cross-referencing 2.1.1), because the SC's core intent is that users can PERCEIVE the additional content; if the only reveal is mouse hover, keyboard and many AT users can never perceive it. The judgment is semantic and two-part: the reviewer must (a) recognize that the hover content carries information not otherwise available (not redundant decoration) AND (b) determine the trigger is non-focusable or has no focus handler. A static tool can note that a tooltip is bound to mouseover-but-not-focus, but cannot judge whether the trigger SHOULD be focusable (is it interactive? is the content meaningful?) — recognizing 'this hidden content matters and is unreachable by keyboard' is a contextual call. This is the focus-modality half of SCR39, which carries a DIFFERENT checklist than hover (persistent + dismissible only; no hoverable requirement).
aspects.scLimb: Trigger / focus-modality (perceive on focus; cross-ref 2.1.1)
aspects.whyUncovered: The keyboard-focus-triggered variant is listed as wholly absent, and there is no input-modality split in the corpus (hover vs. focus require different SCR39 checklists). With 0 fixtures, the focus path of the trigger is entirely unmodeled.

aspects.title: Pointer-only (mouse/touch/gesture) handlers on non-native elements with no keyboard equivalent (F54)
aspects.plain: A control built from a plain div, span, or image fires only on mouse or touch events with no keyboard handler, so keyboard-only users can never reach or trigger it.
aspects.description: A function is wired up exclusively through pointing-device events (onclick/onmousedown/onmouseup/onmouseover, or touch/pointer/gesture listeners) on an element that has no native keyboard behaviour and no tabindex, role, or key handler — typically a div, span, img, li, or svg. The page looks fully operable, but a keyboard-only user can never reach or invoke the function. The human-judgment core is recognizing that a given visual control (a 'Next' arrow image, a star-rating widget, a custom 'Add to cart' tile, a swipeable carousel) actually IS interactive functionality whose only trigger is a pointer event — i.e. mapping pixels-that-do-something to the absence of any keyboard path — then confirming there is no keyboard route anywhere on the page. This is the canonical F54 failure and the core of Trusted Tester's 'use the mouse to determine available functions, then operate them with the keyboard' procedure.
aspects.scLimb: 2.1.1 'all functionality is operable through a keyboard interface' — reachability AND activation of explicit/custom interactive controls (not scroll regions). Does not exercise the keystroke-timing limb. Also maps to 2.1.3.
aspects.whyUncovered: Neither ACT rule (0ssw9k scroll reachability, akn7bn iframe tab order) inspects element event handlers at all. The corpus contains zero pages where 'this thing does something on click but nothing on keyboard'. The judgment requires using the mouse to discover that a visually-styled element is functional and is semantic, not detectable by a static checker that has no concept of which non-native elements are 'meant' to be operable.

references.quote: When pointing device-specific event handlers are the only mechanism available to invoke a function of the content, users with no vision ... as well as users who must use alternate keyboards or input devices that act as keyboard emulators will be unable to access the function of the content.

Use the mouse/pointer to determine **available functions** provided by interactive elements (drop-down menus, form fields, revealing/hiding content, tooltips, AND all interactive interface components).

aspects.ttWhy: F54 pointer-only control must be reachable and executable by keyboard.

pages.mechanism: The rating-setting function is invokable solely through a pointer click on a generic <span>. The spans are not in the tab order and not exposed as controls (no role/tabindex/keydown), so a keyboard-only or switch user can never reach or operate them; there is no alternative keyboard path to set the rating anywhere on the page. Canonical F54: pointing-device-only handler is the sole mechanism to invoke a non-path-dependent function.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Each span contains a non-empty '★' glyph (no empty-name/missing-alt violation) and nothing in the static DOM declares the spans interactive (no role, no href, no form control; handler is a plain onclick on a generic element), so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse have no rule that treats them as controls to test for keyboard operability. Recognising the five stars ARE a functional rating control and confirming no keyboard route exists is a visual/semantic human judgment. Verified in Puppeteer: stars never receive focus across a full Tab sweep; a mouse click sets rating=4.

The product-open function therefore has no keyboard route via the card. F54 escalated past the linter by adding a valid role+name so static checks pass.

pages.scenario: Credit-union money-transfer confirmation screen whose final 'Confirm & send £420.00' action is a <div role="button" tabindex="0"> with a clear accessible name — focusable and ARIA-correct — but activation is wired ONLY to dblclick/pointerup (a 'double-click to confirm' guard) with no keydown/keyup handler, so Enter and Space do nothing. A real keyboard-operable <button>Cancel</button> sits beside it.
pages.mechanism: The tile is exposed as a focusable button with a valid name, so every static signal looks correct; but the activation logic listens only for dblclick and pointerup (gated to pointerType mouse/touch/pen), so neither Enter nor Space — the platform keys a button role implies — invokes the confirm. The transfer cannot be sent from the keyboard at all (only Cancel is keyboard-reachable, which is not an equivalent). Per the Understanding note a custom button may respond to only one key, but it must respond to some key; here it responds to none. F54 with the element fully ARIA-correct and focusable, so the failure is purely missing keyboard activation.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every static check passes: valid role="button", non-empty accessible name, and tabindex="0" (focusable, so not flagged as an unreachable interactive element). axe/WAVE/Lighthouse have no rule that verifies a role=button element actually responds to Enter/Space — that is runtime behaviour — and the activation is bound to dblclick/pointerup, events no static rule maps to a keyboard requirement. The only way to catch it is to focus the tile and press Enter and Space and observe nothing happens. Verified in Puppeteer: tile receives focus (activeElement=confirmTile), Enter+Space produce no result, a dblclick sends the transfer.

citation.quote: For instance, buttons that have focus can generally be activated using both the Enter key and the Space bar. If a custom button control in a web application instead only reacts to Enter (or even a completely custom key or key combination), this still satisfies the requirements of this success criterion.

pages.scenario: Furniture product page where the colour chooser appears twice: a labelled native <select id="colour"> (fully keyboard operable) and a row of pointer-only colour chips <li onclick="pickColour(...)"> with no tabindex/role/keydown. Both call the same pickColour() routine; the chips are a mouse shortcut layered on the real menu and are aria-hidden so AT users are routed to the <select>. Boundary PASS variant that sharpens the aspect.
pages.mechanism: Taken alone each <li onclick> is the F54 shape (pointer-only, no tabindex/role/keydown), but 2.1.1 asks whether the FUNCTION is keyboard operable, not whether every visible control is focusable. The colour-selection function is fully available from the keyboard via the labelled <select> (in tab order, arrow/typeahead operable, calls the same pickColour()), and the chips are aria-hidden so screen-reader users use the menu. Because an equivalent keyboard method for the same action exists, this passes 2.1.1 — demonstrating that a pointer-only handler is not automatically a failure.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: This is the inverse trap for automation: a naive heuristic flagging '<li> onclick with no keyboard handler' would FALSE-POSITIVE here, while scanners that ignore the chips report nothing. Neither can perform the deciding judgment — recognising the chips are an F54-shaped control AND that the adjacent <select> provides the equivalent keyboard route for the same function, so no failure exists. That two-controls-to-one-function equivalence reasoning is the human Trusted-Tester step. Verified in Puppeteer: changing the <select> via keyboard recolors the preview (rgb(44,47,54) ink after the transition settles) and announces 'Colour: …'; clicking a swatch does the same and syncs the <select>.

citation.quote: This success criterion does not require that every visible control that can be activated using a mouse or touchscreen must also be focusable and actionable using the keyboard. The normative requirement is only that there must be a way for keyboard interface users to perform the same, or comparable, actions and to operate the content.

aspects.title: Emulated links/controls that are reachable but not truly activatable by keyboard — wrong element, Enter-only, or no-op handler (F42)
aspects.plain: A fake button or link you can Tab to but that ignores Enter or Space (or only one of them), so it looks operable yet does nothing for keyboard users.
aspects.description: The subtle slice between a bare pointer-only fake control and a properly built one. Markup that reads as compliant (tabindex present, an onkeypress/onkeydown attribute present, role=button/link) but where keyboard ACTIVATION silently fails: (a) a <div tabindex=0 onclick> with no key handler at all — focusable, so it appears 'in the tab order', but Enter/Space do nothing because a div has no implicit activation; (b) an onkeypress that listens ONLY for Enter (keyCode 13) while onclick does the work, so Space (and any keydown-only AT) gets nothing; (c) a handler that calls preventDefault/returns early on keyboard, swallowing activation; (d) an <a> WITHOUT href (just onclick) that drops out of the tab order entirely despite looking like a real link in source. F42 only fails 2.1.1 when keyboard activation actually fails — so the human must FOCUS the element and actually PRESS the key, in both Enter and Space, rather than trust the presence of attributes.
aspects.scLimb: 2.1.1 'operable through a keyboard interface' — specifically the activation half (reach-AND-execute). The note in Understanding that a custom button reacting only to Enter still passes makes this a genuine judgment call, not a mechanical rule. Also maps to 2.1.3.
aspects.whyUncovered: The ACT corpus has no scripted-control cases at all; its only 'pass via focusable descendant' uses a genuine native <a href>. There is no case where a fake control is keyboard-reachable-but-not-activatable, no Enter-only/Space-missing handler, and no href-less anchor — so the activation-verification dimension is entirely untested. A static checker sees tabindex+role+a key listener and reads it as compliant; only behavioural key-press verification reveals the gap.

references.quote: This failure occurs when JavaScript event handlers are attached to elements to emulate links. A link created in this manner cannot be tabbed to from the keyboard and does not gain keyboard focus like other controls and/or links.
Fake link
Use the keyboard to operate identified functionality and/or access the essential information: tab to the element and execute (e.g., press Enter with focus on the element).

aspects.ttWhy: F42 focusable fake control fails keyboard activation; tab then press Enter.

pages.scenario: UK council-tax services portal. The primary 'Make a payment' service tile is a <div role=button tabindex=0 onclick> with NO key handler at all, sitting between two genuine <a href> tiles. It receives focus and announces as a button (reads as 'in the tab order') but a div has no implicit activation, so Enter/Space do nothing and there is no alternative keyboard path to card payment.
pages.mechanism: Focusable (tabindex=0) + role=button gives a tab stop announced as a button, but only onclick is wired and no keydown/keypress/keyup handler exists; a div has no implicit activation, so keyboard Enter/Space never executes startPayment(). Reachable but not operable. Verified in headless Chromium: focusable=true, Enter-activates=false, Space-activates=false, mouse-click=true.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse see a focusable element that HAS a role (button) and IS reachable (tabindex=0); the presence of role=button suppresses the naive 'div with onclick but no role' lint. No static rule asserts 'a key handler must exist to execute the action' — confirming the dead activation requires actually focusing the tile and pressing Enter and Space and observing nothing happens.

citation.quote: Set keyboard focus to the control … Check that pressing Enter or Space invokes the scripting action.

pages.scenario: Recipe blog card with a matched pair of visually/structurally identical <span role=link tabindex=0> controls: 'Save to recipe box' has onclick AND onkeypress(Enter) so it is operable (passes per the Understanding note), while 'Print this recipe' is byte-for-byte the same except the onkeypress was deleted in a cleanup commit, so its keyboard activation is silently dead. The page's verdict hinges on actually pressing keys on each control, not on attribute inspection.
pages.mechanism: Two sibling pseudo-links share class/role/tabindex/onclick. Save's onkeypress fires saveRecipe() on Enter (conformant Enter-only). Print has no key handler, so Enter and Space never reach printRecipe(); mouse still works. The page fails because the in-scope Print function is keyboard-reachable but not operable. Verified: Save Enter-activates=true; Print Enter-activates=false and Space-activates=false; both mouse-activate.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Both controls present a valid role=link, tabindex=0 and onclick; one also has onkeypress. A scanner checking focusable/role/name passes both identically and cannot use 'one looks suspicious' reasoning because they are matched siblings with the same class and shape. Separating the operable from the dead one requires focusing each and pressing Enter and Space and watching the live-region output — a runtime behaviour.

citation.doc: WCAG Failure Technique F42 — Expected Results (wcag-techniques/failures/F42.html)
citation.quote: If check #2 is false then this failure condition applies and the content fails Success Criteria 2.1.1 Keyboard and 2.1.3 Keyboard (No Exception).

pages.scenario: Webmail reading-pane message-action toolbar (Reply, Reply all, Forward, Archive, Delete) built from <a class=action onclick> anchors that have NO href and no tabindex. They look like ordinary clickable link/buttons in source and are fully mouse-operable, but an href-less, tabindex-less anchor is not focusable and never enters the Tab sequence, so the entire toolbar drops out of the tab order with no alternative keyboard path.
pages.mechanism: An <a> with neither href nor tabindex is not a focusable element, so it is excluded from sequential focus navigation; Tab skips all five toolbar actions and AT does not expose them as real links. Core message actions are therefore keyboard-unreachable. Verified: calling .focus() on a toolbar anchor does not make it activeElement; 30 Tab presses from body never land on .msg-toolbar a.action.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The markup is well-formed: legal <a> elements inside role=toolbar, each with visible text (accessible-name checks pass). Scanners typically flag a problematic href (#, javascript:) or a div/span-with-onclick-and-no-role, neither of which applies. No static rule asserts 'this href-less anchor SHOULD be focusable'; discovering that Tab never reaches the toolbar requires running the focus sequence — a behavioural test.

citation.quote: This failure occurs when JavaScript event handlers are attached to elements to emulate links. A link created in this manner cannot be tabbed to from the keyboard and does not gain keyboard focus like other controls and/or links.

pages.scenario: Museum virtual-exhibitions gallery where each clickable cover enters a virtual room. Each has onclick AND an onkeypress, so it appears keyboard-wired, but the handleKey handler calls event.preventDefault() and returns false BEFORE any activation branch — so for every key, including Enter and Space, it stops default behaviour and exits without calling enterRoom(). The key handler is present but swallows activation; no fallback control exists.
pages.mechanism: The element is focusable with a button role and accessible name (alt) and has an onkeypress, so all static keyboard signals are satisfied. But the handler body does event.preventDefault(); return false; making the if(Enter/Space) enterRoom() branch unreachable, so the dialog never opens from the keyboard. Mouse onclick is untouched. Verified: Enter-activates=false, Space-activates=false, mouse-click=true.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every static signal — tabindex=0, role=button, alt name, onclick, AND onkeypress — says 'focusable, named, keyboard handler present', satisfying 'interactive element must have a keyboard handler' heuristics. The defect is entirely in the runtime control flow of the handler (preventDefault + early return before activation). No static analyzer evaluates handler bodies to prove the activation branch is unreachable; only pressing Enter/Space and watching the room never open reveals it.

citation.doc: WCAG Failure Technique F42 — Tests / Procedure (wcag-techniques/failures/F42.html)
citation.quote: Check if the emulated link can be activated using the keyboard.

pages.scenario: Cloud-console deployments table where each row has a 'more actions' kebab built as <div role=button tabindex=0 aria-haspopup aria-expanded onclick onkeydown>. It looks like a textbook keyboard-ready menu button, but the onkeydown handler gates on event.charCode against 13/32 — and charCode is ALWAYS 0 on a keydown event — so the Enter/Space branch never matches and the menu (containing Redeploy/Roll back/View logs) cannot be opened by keyboard in any browser.
pages.mechanism: kebabKey reads event.charCode on a keydown event; charCode is only ever populated for keypress (and only printing characters), so it is 0 for Enter and Space, 0===13||0===32 is false, toggleMenu() is never called and aria-expanded stays false. The menu items have no other keyboard path. Verified in headless Chromium: Enter-activates=false, Space-activates=false, mouse-click=true (fails universally, not a single-browser quirk; confirmed via Gemini that charCode is 0 on keydown in all current browsers and that window.event would NOT have failed because all browsers now populate it).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The control is over-decorated with valid ARIA (role=button, tabindex, aria-haspopup, aria-expanded, aria-label, onclick AND onkeydown), so every static 'is this a keyboard-ready button?' signal passes — a keydown handler literally exists. The bug is a semantic error inside the handler (reading charCode, which is 0 on keydown). No scanner evaluates whether the key-matching condition can ever be true at runtime; only pressing Enter/Space and seeing the menu never open (and aria-expanded never flip) exposes it.

citation.doc: WCAG Technique SCR29 — Tests / Expected Results (wcag-techniques/client-side-script/SCR29.html)
citation.quote: Set keyboard focus to the control … Check that pressing Enter or Space invokes the scripting action. … All of the checks are true.

pages.scenario: Online-banking transfer form whose primary control is a custom <span role=button tabindex=0 onclick onkeydown(Enter only)> 'Review transfer'. It is focusable and activates on Enter but deliberately does NOT respond to Space. This is the PASS boundary: a naive reviewer who presses Space, sees nothing, and fails it would be wrong — the WCAG Understanding note states a custom control reacting only to Enter still satisfies 2.1.1. The action is both reachable and executable by keyboard and the rest of the form is operable, so the page passes.
pages.mechanism: onkeydown matches event.key==='Enter', calls preventDefault() and runs reviewTransfer(), revealing the summary region; the function is reached AND executed via keyboard. Space intentionally does nothing, which is acceptable for a custom control per the Understanding note. All other controls (selects, amount input, Cancel link) are native and fully operable. Verified: focusable=true, Enter-activates=true, Space-activates=false.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Automated tools cannot make the JUDGMENT that this PASSES; a heuristic firing on 'custom role=button does not handle Space' would produce a FALSE POSITIVE here. A correct verdict requires both verifying at runtime that Enter genuinely activates the control AND knowing that Enter-only is conformant for a custom control under the normative Understanding note — neither the runtime activation check nor the note interpretation is something axe/WAVE/Lighthouse perform. This case tests that the evaluator does not over-fire on a conformant Enter-only control.

citation.quote: If a custom button control in a web application instead only reacts to Enter (or even a completely custom key or key combination), this still satisfies the requirements of this success criterion.

aspects.title: Drag-and-drop / endpoint-style functions without the path exception, lacking a keyboard equivalent (G90 / G202 / Understanding)
aspects.plain: A drag-and-drop action like reordering a list or dropping a file has no keyboard alternative, locking out keyboard users from a task mouse users can do.
aspects.description: The SC exempts only functions whose input depends on the PATH of movement, not just the endpoints (free-hand drawing, watercolour). Reordering a list by drag, dragging a file into a dropzone, sorting kanban cards, dragging a map pin, or resizing a panel are endpoint-dependent and therefore do NOT qualify for the exception — they REQUIRE a keyboard equivalent (cut/paste, move up/down buttons, an 'enter position' field, type-to-set coordinates). Two human judgments no checker can make: (1) decide whether a given drag operation is genuinely path-dependent (exempt) or merely endpoint-dependent (must be keyboard-operable) — a semantic call about the underlying function; and (2) determine whether SOME keyboard alternative for the same function exists ANYWHERE on the page, since G202/Understanding allow a separate keyboard mode rather than per-control parity. A drag-to-reorder list with no up/down buttons fails; the same list WITH up/down buttons passes — identical drag markup, opposite verdicts.
aspects.scLimb: 2.1.1 'all functionality is operable through a keyboard interface' at the FUNCTION level, plus the path-vs-endpoint EXCEPTION clause — the only part of the SC's normative text that carves out functionality. G202's 'multiple methods to perform the same function' is the parity-not-per-control allowance.
aspects.whyUncovered: There is no drag-and-drop, sorting, resizing, or dropzone case anywhere in the 2.1.1 corpus. The exception clause (path of movement vs endpoints) is never exercised, and the 'keyboard alternative exists elsewhere on the page' allowance is never modeled. Both ACT rules check single-control reachability, not function-level keyboard parity, and a checker cannot reason about whether a drag is path- or endpoint-dependent.

references.quote: Drawing straight lines, regular geometric shapes, re-sizing windows and dragging objects to a location (when the path to that location is not relevant) do not require path dependent input.
This does not necessarily mean that each of the individual controls can be used from the keyboard as long as there are multiple methods to perform the same function available on the page.
make sure that all event handlers triggered by non-keyboard UI events are also associated with a keyboard-based event, or provide redundant keyboard-based mechanisms to accomplish the functionality

aspects.ttWhy: Endpoint-dependent drag function must be operable by keyboard somewhere on page.

pages.scenario: Fresh&Co grocery shopping-list reorderable ONLY by native HTML5 drag-and-drop (draggable=true + dragstart/dragover/drop + insertBefore). Every other control (Add form, picked checkboxes) is keyboard-operable, but the reorder function has no keyboard route: no Move-up/Move-down buttons, no position field, and the li items are not focusable and have no key handlers.
pages.mechanism: Reordering a list is endpoint-dependent (only the destination index matters, not the pointer path), so the SC 2.1.1 path-of-movement exception does NOT apply and the function requires a keyboard equivalent. None exists anywhere on the page, so the reorder function is operable by pointer only — a pointing-device-specific mechanism is the sole way to invoke a non-path-dependent function (F54).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Verified in headless Chrome: list items not focusable (tabIndex<0), zero move buttons, 5 draggable items. No missing/empty attribute, every named control has a role+name, no broken ARIA — axe/WAVE/Lighthouse pass. No scanner models a draggable li as a reorder FUNCTION that needs a keyboard equivalent, nor decides this drag is endpoint- (not path-) dependent and thus in scope. Requires the human judgments: recognize reorder as a function, judge it endpoint-dependent, and confirm no keyboard alternative for that function exists anywhere.

citation.quote: Drawing straight lines, regular geometric shapes, re-sizing windows and dragging objects to a location (when the path to that location is not relevant) do not require path dependent input.

pages.scenario: PollForge survey-question reorder screen. The list uses native HTML5 drag-and-drop markup essentially IDENTICAL to case-01, BUT each card also has real Move-up/Move-down <button> controls that reorder the list via keyboard, disable at the list ends, keep focus on the moved control, and announce the new position via a role=status live region. This is the deliberate matched-PASS partner of case-01.
pages.mechanism: Per G202 / the Understanding note, SC 2.1.1 requires the FUNCTION to have a keyboard route, not every individual control. The same reorder function is fully keyboard-operable through the up/down buttons even though the drag handle itself is pointer-only, so the page passes — function-level parity (multiple methods to perform the same function).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Verified: focusing the first card's Down button and pressing Enter actually reordered the list (first item changed; live region announced 'moved to position 2 of 4'); 4 down buttons present. A naive 'drag-only reorder is a 2.1.1 fail' heuristic would FALSE-POSITIVE this page because the draggable markup matches case-01. No static scanner can recognize the up/down buttons as the keyboard equivalent of the drag function — that semantic association (two controls, one function) plus the G202 allowance is not expressible as a DOM lint. Correctly passing requires the same function-level reasoning that correctly fails case-01.

citation.quote: Example 2: A reorder feature A web application that allows users to create surveys by dragging questions into position includes a list of the questions followed by a text field that allows users to re-order questions as needed by entering the desired question number.

pages.scenario: Northwind Talent job-application page. Attaching a resume is required. A native <input type=file id=resume> exists with an associated <label>, but it is display:none and is NEVER surfaced to keyboard users: no clickable/visible <label>, no button calling resume.click(), and the dashed 'Drag your resume file here' area is a plain <div> with only dragover/drop handlers (no role, no tabindex, no key handler). The only surfaced upload affordance is dragging a file in.
pages.mechanism: Attaching a file is endpoint-dependent (the drop target is what matters, not the pointer path), so the exception does not apply and the upload function must be keyboard-operable. The dropzone div is not focusable/has no key handler, and the display:none input is never reachable (removed from tab order, never .click()-ed), so a keyboard user cannot attach the required resume — pointer-only mechanism (F54). A hidden input with a clickable <label for> or a button calling .click() would pass; the difference is purely keyboard reachability.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Verified: input display=none, dropzone tabIndex<0 and role=null. The file input has a programmatically associated <label>, so axe/WAVE report a correctly labeled form control and raise no error. They do not detect that the input is display:none with no surfaced trigger, that the visible dropzone is the only upload affordance, or that 'attach a file' is therefore keyboard-unreachable. Distinguishing the failing hidden-and-untriggered input from a passing hidden-input-with-clickable-label requires tracing the interaction and judging the function has no keyboard route.

citation.quote: When pointing device-specific event handlers are the only mechanism available to invoke a function of the content, users with no vision (who cannot use devices such as mice that require eye-hand coordination) as well as users who must use alternate keyboards or input devices that act as keyboard emulators will be unable to access the function of the content.

pages.scenario: Stripe-style API-reference reader with a draggable splitter between a nav pane and content pane. The splitter is marked up as a textbook ARIA window-splitter — role=separator, aria-orientation=vertical, aria-valuemin/max/now, an aria-label, and tabindex=0 (focusable) — but has NO keydown handler, so arrow keys do nothing and aria-valuenow never changes. Resize works by mouse drag only.
pages.mechanism: Resizing a region is endpoint-dependent (only the final width matters; the Understanding text lists 're-sizing windows' as explicitly NOT path-dependent), so the exception does not apply and resize must be keyboard-operable. The separator advertises itself as adjustable and is focusable, but ArrowLeft/Right/Home/End do nothing (no keydown listener), so the resize function is pointer-only — and the valid ARIA actively masks the failure by making a non-operable control claim to be operable.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Verified: splitter focusable with role=separator, but after two ArrowLeft presses aria-valuenow stayed at 280. axe/WAVE validate the ARIA (role=separator with aria-valuenow in min/max is syntactically correct and focusable), so every static check passes and the ARIA presence makes the widget LOOK fully accessible. No scanner presses ArrowLeft on the focused separator and observes the value does not move; verifying the keyboard contract is a runtime interaction, plus the human judgment that resizing is endpoint- (not path-) dependent.

citation.quote: Drawing straight lines, regular geometric shapes, re-sizing windows and dragging objects to a location (when the path to that location is not relevant) do not require path dependent input.

pages.scenario: Meridian Bank auto-loan e-signing page. The borrower draws their handwritten signature in a <canvas> with finger/stylus/mouse; strokes are captured free-hand via pointermove and the recorded value is the literal shape of the curves. Every other function (Clear signature button, Type-your-legal-name field, Agree & sign submit) is keyboard-operable. The canvas carries a descriptive accessible name. This is the exception-handling boundary that must NOT be flagged.
pages.mechanism: A handwritten signature is, by definition, input whose value depends on the PATH of the user's movement (the shape of strokes), not on endpoints — the same class as free-hand drawing/watercolour painting that the SC's normative text and Understanding Example 4 explicitly carve out, with no known keyboard equivalent. The drawing surface legitimately invokes the path-of-movement exception, and all other functions are keyboard-operable, so the page satisfies SC 2.1.1.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Verified: canvas not focusable (pointer-only, exempt) but has an accessible name; Clear is a real <button> and the name field is focusable. This is the inverse failure mode: a naive 'pointer-only canvas with no keyboard interaction' rule would FALSE-POSITIVE it. No tool can decide that THIS drag is genuinely path-dependent (a handwritten signature) and therefore exempt, versus an endpoint-dependent drag (reorder/resize/drop) that is NOT — that distinction is the exact human semantic judgment the exception clause demands.

citation.quote: The phrase "except where the underlying function requires input that depends on the path of the user's movement and not just the endpoints" is included to separate those things that cannot reasonably be controlled from a keyboard.

pages.scenario: Canvasly brand-kit colour editor with a classic HSV picker: a 2D saturation/brightness square (drag the handle anywhere inside) plus a hue slider below. The hue slider is a native <input type=range> — fully focusable and arrow-key operable. The 2D square is a plain <div role=application> with pointer drag handlers only: no role=slider(s), no tabindex, no key handler, so saturation and brightness cannot be set by keyboard at all.
pages.mechanism: Two judgments make this a failure: (1) the S/V square is endpoint-dependent — only the final (x=saturation, y=brightness) position the handle lands on matters, the wandering drag path is irrelevant — so it is NOT the free-hand exception (contrast case-05) and DOES require a keyboard equivalent; (2) the keyboard-operable hue slider sets a DIFFERENT dimension, so its operability does not provide a keyboard route to saturation/brightness, and the G202 'keyboard alternative exists elsewhere' allowance does not apply because no control anywhere lets a keyboard user change S or V.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Verified: hue is a native range and ArrowRight changed the hex (#6A2BC2 -> #6F2BC2), but the S/V square #sv is not focusable (tabIndex<0). axe/WAVE see a real focusable labeled range for hue and conclude the picker has keyboard support; the S/V square is just a div, not recognized as a control needing keyboard operation. Catching the failure needs both human judgments — that the square is endpoint- (not path-) dependent and thus in scope, and that the hue slider is a different FUNCTION so its keyboard operability does not count as parity. Neither is expressible as a DOM lint.

citation.quote: This does not necessarily mean that each of the individual controls can be used from the keyboard as long as there are multiple methods to perform the same function available on the page.

aspects.title: Hover/pointer-only revealed content carrying essential information or controls, with no keyboard path (Trusted Tester essential-information branch)
aspects.plain: Menus, tooltips, or row buttons appear only on mouse hover and never on keyboard focus, hiding essential information or the only way to act from keyboard users.
aspects.description: Content or controls that appear only on mouseover/hover (CSS :hover dropdowns/megamenus, JS mouseover tooltips, hover-revealed action buttons on table rows or cards) with no focus/keyboard trigger and no equivalent elsewhere. Trusted Tester explicitly splits the SC into operable-functionality AND access-to-essential-information, and gives the precise tooltip nuance: place keyboard focus and if the information does not appear within two seconds, keyboard focus will not reveal it — then ask whether that information is available elsewhere on the page. Two human judgments: (1) is the hover-revealed content merely decorative/redundant (no failure) or does it carry ESSENTIAL information or the only access to a function (failure if keyboard can't get it AND it's not elsewhere)?; (2) does focus actually reveal the same content that hover does? Both demand reasoning about meaning and interacting in two modalities. Distinct from 1.4.13's persistence/dismissal requirements — this is purely about keyboard reachability of the function/info.
aspects.scLimb: 2.1.1 'all functionality is operable through a keyboard interface' AND the essential-information access branch, with the 'available elsewhere on the page' allowance. The essential-vs-decorative call and the two-second title-reveal check are the human-judgment core.
aspects.whyUncovered: The ACT corpus has no hover-revealed menus, tooltips, or row-action affordances, and never models the 'essential information available elsewhere' allowance. 0ssw9k/akn7bn never inspect :hover or mouseover content. The essential-vs-decorative distinction and the two-second title-reveal check are wholly absent, and neither is decidable by a static checker (it cannot judge whether hidden text is 'essential' or redundant).

references.quote: Use the mouse to identify instances where interactive elements provide **information essential** to understanding or operating page content.
For interactive elements with `title` attributes, place keyboard focus; if the tooltip does not appear within **two seconds**, keyboard focus will not reveal the title information.
If an element does not provide access to essential information via keyboard, determine whether the information is **available elsewhere** on the page (e.g., as text).

aspects.ttWhy: Hover-revealed function/essential info must be keyboard-accessible or available elsewhere.

pages.scenario: County government site whose primary mega-menu submenus (Pay water bill, Apply for marriage license, Pay traffic ticket, Register to vote) open only on li:hover via CSS, with no :focus-within or JS focus handler; keyboard users can activate the top-level links but the specific essential service deep-links are never tab stops and exist nowhere else on the page.
pages.mechanism: ul.submenu is display:none except under `nav.primary > ul > li:hover ul.submenu`; display:none removes the second-level <a href> service links from the tab order, and there is no :focus-within rule or keydown handler, so keyboard focus never reveals or reaches them — the page's primary government functions are pointer-only.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The DOM is impeccable: semantic <nav aria-label>, well-formed nested <ul>/<li>, every submenu entry a real <a href> with descriptive text, no empty/missing attributes. Static scanners do not compute that a :hover-descendant display:none removes those anchors from the tab order, do not exercise Tab to see the submenu never opens on focus, and cannot judge that the lost links are ESSENTIAL services absent elsewhere on the page.

citation.quote: PASS if BOTH true: 1. All functionality can be accessed and executed using the keyboard, AND 2. All essential information can be accessed via keyboard OR is available elsewhere on the page.

pages.scenario: SaaS admin (Mailroom) subscriber data-table where each row's only Edit/Delete controls are wrapped in span.row-actions that is visibility:hidden and revealed only under tr:hover; keyboard users can reach search and Add subscriber but can never edit or delete any existing row, and the hinted bulk-action column is 'coming soon' (absent).
pages.mechanism: The Edit/Delete <button>s sit inside a visibility:hidden container revealed only by `tbody tr:hover`; visibility:hidden removes elements from the tab order, and there is no tr:focus-within rule, so Tab never lands on the buttons — the sole edit/delete path is pointer-only with no keyboard equivalent on the page.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every Edit/Delete is a real <button> with a clear accessible name inside a semantic <table> with <th scope>; nothing is missing, empty, or malformed, so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse report no error. The defect is a runtime visual-state fact (visibility:hidden makes the buttons un-focusable until a hover a keyboard user cannot perform) and requires judging that edit/delete are ESSENTIAL operations with no keyboard-reachable equivalent.

citation.quote: If an element has no keyboard access, determine whether another keyboard-accessible method on the page provides the same functionality (e.g., one of two print methods is keyboard accessible).

pages.scenario: Cloud-GPU pricing page where the Starter plan's 'Spot capacity' info dot reveals, on mouseover only, a JS tooltip stating spot instances can be reclaimed with 30 seconds' notice and in-progress renders are lost and not refunded — a make-or-break caveat disclosed nowhere else. A decoy tabindex=0/role=button/aria-label makes the first dot focusable, but the reveal is bound only to mouseover so focus shows nothing within two seconds, and there is no aria-describedby.
pages.mechanism: The tooltip reveal is registered only on the 'mouseover' event with no 'focus'/'keydown' listener and no aria-describedby; focusing the (decoy-focusable) dot produces no tooltip within two seconds, so the essential plan caveat is unreachable by keyboard and unavailable elsewhere on the page.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The trigger has role=button, tabindex=0 and an aria-label, and the tooltip payloads are non-empty real elements, so scanners see a named, focusable control and well-formed content and pass it. They cannot read the tooltip text to judge it ESSENTIAL, cannot detect that the reveal is mouseover-only so keyboard focus yields nothing within two seconds, and cannot verify the caveat appears nowhere else.

citation.quote: For interactive elements with `title` attributes, place keyboard focus; if the tooltip does not appear within two seconds, keyboard focus will not reveal the title information.

pages.scenario: Government sales-tax return (Form ST-100) where two fields carry return-critical filing instructions only inside a title attribute on a decorative '?' span — do NOT enter collected tax on the exempt-sales line (most common cause of a rejected return), and use the delivery county code not the business county — with no tabindex on the marker, no aria-describedby on the input, and the instruction nowhere else on the page.
pages.mechanism: Essential instruction stored only in a `title` attribute on a non-focusable <span> (no tabindex); a title surfaces visually as a tooltip on mouse hover but is not reliably rendered on keyboard focus (two-second rule), and with no aria-describedby the field never programmatically exposes the warning — so the essential, return-rejecting instruction is pointer-only.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every input has an associated <label>, the title attributes are present and non-empty, and there are no empty/missing attributes or contrast issues, so scanners pass it (a non-empty title is treated as positive). A tool cannot judge the title text is ESSENTIAL rather than a nicety, cannot reason that a title on a non-focusable span will not surface on keyboard focus within two seconds, and cannot confirm the instruction is absent elsewhere.

citation.quote: Not all browsers visually display the `title` as a tooltip on keyboard focus.

pages.scenario: Recipe page where ingredient amounts reveal a metric conversion (e.g. 2 cups -> 240 g) only on mouseover via JS on non-focusable spans, BUT every conversion is also printed verbatim as visible text in a keyboard-accessible 'Metric conversions' <table> lower on the page — a pass via the 'available elsewhere on the page' allowance that forces the redundancy judgment.
pages.mechanism: The hover reveal is pointer-only (mouseover on non-focusable .amt spans), but the identical conversion data appears as plain visible text in a semantic <table> with <th scope> headers that is fully reachable by keyboard and screen reader; per Trusted Tester, essential info not provided via keyboard still passes if available elsewhere on the page as text — and the tooltips carry no action, only redundant data.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A tool would also not flag this — but for the wrong reason and with no understanding: it never reads the tooltip text, never reads the table, and has no mechanism to reason that one is a redundant copy of the other. The genuine PASS turns on the human judgment that the hover content is merely redundant AND that an equivalent keyboard-accessible text source exists on the same page.

citation.quote: If an element does not provide access to essential information via keyboard, determine whether the information is available elsewhere on the page (e.g., as text).

pages.scenario: Kanban sprint board where each card's overflow '...' button is the only way to move/assign/archive a card; it is visually hidden by opacity:0 (resembling case-02) but, unlike visibility:hidden, stays focusable and in the tab order, and the CSS reveals it on BOTH hover AND focus (:focus / :focus-within), with Enter opening the menu and Esc closing it and restoring focus — modality-equivalent, so it passes.
pages.mechanism: The control is hidden with opacity:0 (which keeps it focusable and in the tab order, unlike visibility:hidden/display:none) and revealed by `.card .more:focus` and `.card:focus-within .more` exactly as by `.card:hover .more`; a keyboard user Tabs to it, it appears on focus, Enter opens the same role=menu the mouse user gets, and Esc returns focus — keyboard focus reveals the same content as hover.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A scanner sees a focusable, named <button> with aria-haspopup and a role=menu here — and the SAME shapes in case-02's failing version. It cannot distinguish visibility:hidden (removes from tab order -> fails) from opacity:0 + :focus reveal (stays focusable -> passes), nor confirm the keyboard reveal produces the same control as hover; the pass/fail turns on a CSS-mechanics and two-modality interaction judgment a human must make.

citation.quote: The normative requirement is only that there must be a way for keyboard interface users to perform the same, or comparable, actions and to operate the content.

aspects.title: Scripts that remove or steal focus the moment it is received (F55) — focus cannot rest on a control
aspects.plain: A script yanks focus away the instant a control receives it, so even though you can Tab to the control, focus never stays long enough for you to use it.
aspects.description: Content that would normally receive focus has that focus stripped by script (onfocus="this.blur()", a handler that immediately moves focus elsewhere, or a focusin listener that bounces focus back to the top on every Tab). The element appears in the tab order and is technically reachable, but focus cannot remain on it long enough to operate it, so keyboard operation is impossible. This is dynamic behaviour: the static DOM shows a normal, well-formed, focusable control — only by actually tabbing through and watching where focus lands does a human discover focus being yanked away. The judgment is temporal/behavioural: 'I pressed Tab, the indicator flashed on the field, then jumped away.' Real-world variants include an overlay that re-focuses its first element on every focusin, or a sticky-header script that re-focuses the logo whenever a lower control gains focus.
aspects.scLimb: 2.1.1 'operable through a keyboard interface' — the persistence dimension: reachable is necessary but not sufficient; focus must be able to REST so the control can be operated. Orthogonal to scroll-region/iframe reachability.
aspects.whyUncovered: 0ssw9k only checks whether a tab stop EXISTS on/within a scroll region; it never checks whether focus can persist there. akn7bn checks iframe tab inclusion. Nothing in the corpus runs a focus-event handler or models focus being removed after receipt, so the 'reachable but focus won't stay' failure has zero coverage. Detecting it requires running the page and observing focus movement — a behavioural trace, not static markup analysis.

references.quote: Content that normally receives focus when the content is accessed by keyboard may have this focus removed by scripting. ... this practice removes focus from the content entirely, which means that the content can only be operated by a pointing device such as a mouse.
Check that when focus is placed on each element, focus remains there until user moves it.
<input type="submit" onFocus="this.blur();">

aspects.ttWhy: F55 strips focus on receipt; focus must rest so control is operable.

pages.scenario: Credit-union online-banking sign-in form. The username/password fields are operable, but the primary submit control carries onfocus="this.blur()" (the canonical F55 one-liner). A keyboard user can Tab to the Sign in button but focus is stripped the instant it lands, throwing focus to <body>, so the button can never be activated by keyboard.
pages.mechanism: Inline onfocus HTML event-handler attribute on a native <input type=submit> synchronously calls this.blur() when the element receives focus, so focus is removed on receipt and relocated to document.body; the named, focusable control cannot retain focus to be operated.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: In a static DOM snapshot the submit button is a valid, named, focusable native control with no missing/empty attributes. The defect is purely behavioural: it only manifests when the focus event fires at runtime and the handler blurs the element. No static rule dispatches focus to each control and re-reads document.activeElement after the event loop turns; an onfocus attribute is not itself an error, so its presence cannot be flagged. Verified with Puppeteer: focusing input.signin leaves activeElement=body.

citation.quote: Content that normally receives focus when the content is accessed by keyboard may have this focus removed by scripting. ... this practice removes focus from the content entirely, which means that the content can only be operated by a pointing device such as a mouse.

pages.scenario: German municipal services portal (de-DE). The site-search field has a mis-wired 'select on focus' helper whose early-return branch calls document.body.focus(). Because the box ships with a remembered query, the buggy branch fires on the first focus: every Tab into the search field bounces focus to <body> (made focusable via script-set tabindex=-1), so a keyboard user can never land in the box to type.
pages.mechanism: An onfocus handler relocates focus to a different, non-operable element (document.body, programmatically focusable via tabindex=-1) on receipt, conditional on the field holding its remembered value; the labelled type=search input cannot retain focus so free-text search is not keyboard-executable.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Scanners see a correctly labelled type=search input and a valid submit button — zero markup errors. The focus theft only occurs at runtime when the focus event fires AND the field still holds its remembered value (stateful, conditional). A linter cannot know the helper calls document.body.focus() nor that body was made focusable via a script-set tabindex; there is no static signature for 'focus moves to body on receipt'. Verified with Puppeteer: focusing #q ends with activeElement=body.

citation.quote: Use the keyboard to operate identified functionality and/or access the essential information: tab to the element and execute (e.g., press Enter with focus on the element).

pages.scenario: Newspaper article page with a sticky masthead. A page-wide document focusin listener re-focuses the masthead logo on every focus change ('keep the brand the anchor'), and its exclusion guard compares the wrong property so it never excludes anything. Every Tab to a section-nav link, an article-tool button, the newsletter field, or an in-article link snaps focus back to the logo, freezing the whole page at the masthead for keyboard users.
pages.mechanism: A document-level focusin listener relocates focus to a fixed element (#brandLogo) whenever ANY downstream control receives focus (the guard if(e.tabIndex===logo) is always falsy because FocusEvent has no tabIndex), so every interactive control on the page loses focus on receipt and cannot be operated by keyboard.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The DOM is exemplary — semantic header/nav, real <a>/<button>, a labelled email input — so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse find no errors. The failure lives in a runtime focusin handler attached to document; static scanners do not execute Tab sequences and do not model that a global listener re-focuses the logo after every focus change. There is no markup signature for page-wide focus theft. Verified with Puppeteer: focusing the first nav link ends with activeElement.id=brandLogo.

citation.quote: Use the keyboard to verify that you can get to all interactive elements using the keyboard. Check that when focus is placed on each element, focus remains there until user moves it.

pages.scenario: E-commerce storefront newsletter overlay (role=dialog, aria-modal). A marketing-popup plugin's focus management is a modal-scoped focusin listener that re-focuses the email input on every focus-in, with no exclusion for Close (x), the decline link, or Submit. A keyboard user can never Tab off the email field: every attempt to reach Close/Submit rebounds to the email box, so the overlay can neither be dismissed nor submitted by keyboard.
pages.mechanism: A modal-scoped focusin listener defers (setTimeout 0) and re-focuses a single element (the first input) on every focus-in, so the dismiss/submit controls receive focus momentarily then have it stripped and re-granted to the email field. This is a 2.1.1 'focus cannot rest' failure (focus actively relocated to one element), distinct from a 2.1.2 Tab-cycle trap.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The static markup is a well-formed dialog (role=dialog, aria-modal, aria-labelledby, named Close button, labelled email input) so scanners report nothing. The defect is the runtime focusin re-grab, manifesting only when focus moves between in-modal controls; the setTimeout(0) deferral wins the race against the browser's focus assignment and is invisible to any inline-onfocus heuristic, and tools cannot distinguish it from a legitimate 'focus first field on open' pattern without observing it re-fire on every focus change. Verified with Puppeteer: focusing #nlClose ends with activeElement.id=nlEmail.

citation.quote: All functionality can be accessed and executed using the keyboard, AND ... All essential information can be accessed via keyboard

pages.scenario: SaaS analytics dashboard with a custom APG 'Date range' listbox (role=button trigger + role=listbox/option, correct aria-expanded/aria-selected, full Arrow/Enter/Escape). It opens by keyboard, but each option has a deferred self-blur added to fix a flicker: on the option's focus event a setTimeout(0) later calls opt.blur() then trigger.focus(). The ring flashes on an option then snaps back to the trigger, so no option can be selected by keyboard.
pages.mechanism: A per-option focus handler asynchronously (setTimeout 0) blurs the option and re-focuses the trigger on every option focus, so options are reachable via Arrow keys but focus is removed on receipt and relocated to the trigger — no option can retain focus to be activated/selected by keyboard.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: This is the ARIA-complete, passes-structural-checks, fails-at-runtime trap: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse confirm valid role/aria-haspopup/aria-expanded/aria-selected and intact names. The focus theft is deferred inside a runtime focus handler, so there is no inline onfocus=this.blur() to grep and even a synchronous post-focus() snapshot still shows the option focused — you must wait an event-loop turn and re-read activeElement. No static tool arrows through options and re-checks focus after a macrotask. Verified with Puppeteer (menu open): focusing an option ends with activeElement.id=drTrigger.

citation.quote: Check that when focus is placed on each element, focus remains there until user moves it. ... If #2 is false then this failure condition applies and content fails the Success Criterion.

pages.scenario: Rich-text document-editor toolbar over a contenteditable. Each formatting button declines focus ONLY on pointer interaction via mousedown -> e.preventDefault() (the standard pattern that keeps the caret in the editor when you click Bold). There is no onfocus=this.blur() and no focusin re-grab: a keyboard user can Tab to every button, focus RESTS on it, and Space/Enter toggles aria-pressed. Boundary variant proving mouse-only focus suppression is not F55.
pages.mechanism: mousedown -> preventDefault() cancels the default MOUSE focus assignment only (it fires on physical pointer press, never on Tab), so keyboard focus is never removed: focus lands on the toolbar button and remains, and the click handler toggles aria-pressed. F55's passing condition ('focus remains there until user moves it') holds for the keyboard path.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: This tests the inverse error: a tool or reviewer that flagged anything resembling focus suppression near preventDefault would FALSELY fail this page. Tools cannot tell from static markup whether the suppression affects keyboard focus or only pointer focus — distinguishing a mousedown-scoped preventDefault() (legitimate) from a focus/focusin self-blur (F55) requires running the page and tracing focus. Verified with Puppeteer: focusing the Bold button leaves activeElement on that button after the event-loop turn (focus rests).

citation.quote: This success criterion does not require that every visible control that can be activated using a mouse or touchscreen must also be focusable and actionable using the keyboard. The normative requirement is only that there must be a way for keyboard interface users to perform the same, or comparable, actions and to operate the content.

aspects.title: Keystroke-timing dependence: functions that require specific timing of individual keystrokes (Test 4.B / second SC limb)
aspects.plain: A control only works if you hold a key down, press keys within a tight window, or type at a set speed, which many keyboard users cannot reliably do.
aspects.description: The second normative limb of 2.1.1: 'without requiring specific timings for individual keystrokes.' A function may be fully keyboard-reachable and activatable yet still FAIL because it demands a timing of keystrokes that keyboard-interface users (especially speech-input, sip-and-puff, switch, and on-screen-keyboard users) cannot reliably produce: keys that must be held down for an extended period before registering, multiple keystrokes that must be entered within a short window, double-press/rapid-repeat shortcuts with a tight interval, or input where the speed/rhythm of typing is itself part of the function (e.g. keystroke-dynamics 'authentication'). Understanding gives the exact examples. The judgment is behavioural and temporal — a human must notice that activation depends on HOW FAST or HOW LONG keys are pressed, not merely on WHICH keys. Per Test 4.B, a pass is still possible if another keyboard-accessible method on the page does not require specific timing.
aspects.scLimb: 2.1.1 second limb — 'without requiring specific timings for individual keystrokes.' This limb is entirely separate from the operability limb both ACT rules target; Trusted Tester isolates it as Test 4.B.
aspects.whyUncovered: Both ACT rules (scroll reachability, iframe tab order) test only the operability limb and never the timing limb. There is no corpus case where a control activates only with a held key, a rapid key sequence, or speed-of-typing input. A static checker cannot infer timing requirements from markup; this requires observing time-dependent input behaviour, and judging whether an untimed keyboard alternative exists elsewhere.

references.quote: Examples of "specific timings for individual keystrokes" include situations where a user would be required to repeat or execute multiple keystrokes within a short period of time or where a key must be held down for an extended period before the keystroke is registered.

Determine whether there are instances where the **timing of keystrokes** is required to activate the element (e.g., the speed at which password keystrokes are typed is part of password authentication).
If timing-dependent functionality exists, determine if another keyboard-accessible method on the page does **not** require specific timing.

aspects.ttWhy: Activation depends on keystroke timing; isolated by no-keystroke-timing test.

pages.scenario: SaaS account 'Danger zone': the 'Delete account' button is a real, focusable, named <button> wired for keyboard, but its keydown/keyup handler only fires the destructive action once Enter/Space has been HELD continuously for 2000 ms. A normal tap of Enter (keydown immediately followed by keyup) never reaches the threshold and does nothing; no other keyboard control deletes the account.
pages.mechanism: Keystroke-HOLD-duration gate (2.1.1 second limb): activation requires a single key to be held for an extended period (2 s). Discrete-activation users (switch, sip-and-puff, speech input, on-screen keyboard, scanning) cannot emit a 2-second-long held keystroke, and no untimed keyboard path to the function exists, so Test 4.B has no passing path.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse confirm the control is a real button, focusable, with an accessible name and keyboard handlers — all present and correct. None of them holds a key for a measured duration to observe that a discrete keypress fails to activate it; the timing dependency lives only in the runtime keydown/keyup duration check (REQUIRED_MS=2000) and is invisible to static markup analysis.

citation.quote: Examples of "specific timings for individual keystrokes" include situations where a user would be required to repeat or execute multiple keystrokes within a short period of time or where a key must be held down for an extended period before the keystroke is registered.

pages.scenario: Public-transit trip planner with a route map. The 'center on your live location / turn on real-time vehicle tracking' function is bound to a documented G keyboard shortcut, but the handler fires geolocation only when two G keydown events arrive within 250 ms of each other. A single press of G arms a window but does nothing; two presses >250 ms apart never fire; there is no single-press button or menu item for the same function.
pages.mechanism: Rapid double-press gate (2.1.1 second limb): the only trigger for an essential function (geolocation/live tracking) is two keystrokes within a 250 ms inter-keypress window. Speech-input (one key at a time), switch/scanning (slow cadence), tremor, and on-screen-keyboard users cannot produce a sub-250 ms double-press, and no single-press/untimed alternative exists.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A static scan sees a focusable, named role=application region with a documented (and visibly self-described) keyboard shortcut and reports no problem. No checker presses a key twice at two different speeds to discover that only the fast double-press works; the 250 ms inter-keypress window exists solely in the runtime keydown timing comparison (DOUBLE_MS=250).

citation.quote: A keyboard method is provided for functionality to be activated without requiring users to perform specific timings for activation.

pages.scenario: Online-banking sign-in form (member number + 6-digit PIN). A hidden 'keystroke-dynamics' layer measures the interval between consecutive PIN keystrokes and rejects the login as an identity-verification failure if any gap exceeds 400 ms — even when the PIN entered is exactly correct. Visible help frames it as security ('we verify how you type'). No slow-typing-tolerant or alternative sign-in path is offered.
pages.mechanism: Typing speed/rhythm as authentication (2.1.1 second limb; the exact Trusted Tester Test 4.B example). Successful sign-in requires each PIN keystroke gap to be fast (<=400 ms). Slow typists, on-screen-keyboard, switch/scanning, sip-and-puff, speech-input, and paste users supply the correct credential but fail the rhythm check; the timed login is the only mechanism, so no untimed keyboard path exists.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The DOM is a textbook-accessible login form (associated labels, aria-describedby help, native submit, full keyboard reachability) and passes axe/WAVE/Lighthouse. None of them types a correct PIN slowly to observe rejection; the requirement lives entirely in the runtime inter-keystroke-interval comparison (MAX_GAP_MS=400) and the submit-time slowGapSeen check.

citation.quote: Determine whether there are instances where the **timing of keystrokes** is required to activate the element (e.g., the speed at which password keystrokes are typed is part of password authentication).

pages.scenario: Payment confirmation screen ($248 rent). The primary control is a 'Hold to slide & pay' slider that confirms only after the Space bar is held for 1500 ms (a keystroke-timing barrier on its own), BUT directly beneath it the page provides a plain 'Confirm payment' button that completes the identical payment with a single, untimed Enter/Space press. Both paths invoke the same pay() function.
pages.mechanism: Test 4.B allowance: a timed path (Space-hold slider, HOLD_MS=1500) coexists with an untimed keyboard method for the same function (single discrete activation of button#confirmBtn). Because a keyboard method free of specific keystroke timing is provided, the second limb of 2.1.1 is satisfied despite the slider's hold requirement.
