citation.quote: Applies when content creates a situation where the user can enter the content using the keyboard, but cannot exit the content using the keyboard.

aspects.title: Documented custom-exit advice that is unreachable or inaccurate beyond the corpus's Ctrl+M-before-trap pattern
aspects.plain: When escaping a focus loop needs a special key combo, the instructions must actually reach the trapped keyboard user and correctly name the key, not be hidden or wrong.
aspects.description: TT Evaluate-Results 1.b requires custom escape keystrokes to be DOCUMENTED AND AVAILABLE, and How-to-Test 3.a/3.b require checking that contextual help discloses the alternate command and that the command actually works. The corpus covers advice-before-trap, advice-within-trap, and a help-link inside the subset (Passed 4/5/6), plus three failure modes (never advised, generic/non-instructive, named-but-broken). But it tests these only on the Ctrl+M-on-flat-buttons template and only with advice that is either plainly present or plainly absent. The uncovered judgment surface is advice REACHABILITY and ACCURACY in harder forms: advice that exists but is itself only reachable by mouse or after the trap; advice located only in collapsed/off-screen help the keyboard user inside the trap cannot get to; advice that names a key combo with a subtle defect (right key, wrong modifier); or advice that is technically present but describes a DIFFERENT trap. Judging whether documented advice is genuinely AVAILABLE to a trapped keyboard user, and whether it accurately matches the working escape, requires reading intent and driving the keyboard.
aspects.scLimb: Conditional-pass clause: the user IS ADVISED of the method for moving focus away — applied to the REACHABILITY and ACCURACY of the advice (G21: 'document the feature in an accessible manner within the subset'), beyond the corpus's plainly-present/plainly-absent Ctrl+M cases.
aspects.whyUncovered: ACT tests advice only as plainly-present (before/within trap, help link) or plainly-absent/generic/named-but-broken, all on the Ctrl+M-flat-button template. It never tests advice that is present but unreachable by a trapped keyboard user, hidden in collapsed/off-screen help, located only AFTER the trap, or accurate-looking but subtly mismatched — the reachability/accuracy judgment G21 demands ('accessible manner within the subset'). A checker cannot judge whether advice is genuinely reachable from inside the trap or whether it matches the real escape.

references.quote: Inspect any contextual/application help and documentation for notification of **available alternate keyboard commands** (non-standard controls, access keys, hotkeys) to escape/avoid the trap.
Custom keystrokes that are **documented and available** to users in the application.
Providing a keyboard function to move the focus out of the subset of the content. Be sure to document the feature in an accessible manner within the subset.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: County property-tax estimator: a Millage Worksheet loops focus internally; the working custom exit (Ctrl+M) is documented ONLY inside a collapsed <details> placed in DOM/visual order AFTER the trap, so a trapped keyboard user can never reach or open it.
pages.mechanism: Focus is trapped (blur re-focuses the first field); Ctrl+M genuinely exits, but its sole instruction lives in a post-trap collapsed disclosure unreachable from inside the loop — advice present but not reachable within the subset (G21 'accessible manner within the subset' violated by placement).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Scanners see a valid <details>/<summary>, plain-text instruction, labeled fields, and a working handler. They do not Tab to discover the focus loop and cannot reason about WHEN the advice becomes reachable relative to the trap — i.e. that a collapsed disclosure downstream of the loop is undiscoverable from inside it. Requires driving the keyboard and judging advice reachability.

citation.quote: Providing a keyboard function to move the focus out of the subset of the content. Be sure to document the feature in an accessible manner within the subset.

pages.scenario: Webmail compose: a contenteditable rich-text editor captures Tab (WYSIWYG indent) and exits on Alt+0, but the only documentation of that keystroke is a title= tooltip on a non-focusable '?' badge — revealed on pointer hover only, never reachable or announced for the trapped keyboard user.
pages.mechanism: Editor traps focus (Tab captured); Alt+0 works; the exit advice is delivered solely via title on a non-interactive <span> with no tabindex/role — hover-only and not reliably exposed by AT, so the trapped keyboard user is never told how to escape.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The badge HAS a title (associated text present) and the editor has role=textbox + aria-label, so linters pass. A tool cannot determine that the escape instruction is hover-only, on a non-focusable element, never reachable by keyboard, and not announced as the editor's operating instruction. Requires knowing how title is exposed and trying to reach the advice from inside the trap.

citation.quote:
When the editing area receives focus, an instruction appears, letting users know that
               they can use <kbd>Alt+F10</kbd> / <kbd>Option+F10</kbd> to move focus back out of the
               area and to the editor toolbar.

pages.scenario: Rail-booking seat grid (arrow-key roving tabindex) traps focus; the visible, reachable legend says 'press Ctrl+M' to leave, but the keydown handler actually releases on Alt+M (right key letter, wrong modifier), so following the documented combo keeps the user trapped.
pages.mechanism: Grid captures Tab and roves with arrows; the release branch fires on e.altKey+'m'. The on-screen advice names Ctrl+M, which is dead — the documented keystroke does not match the working escape (Alt+M), so the user is advised of a non-working exit.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: All controls are real buttons with names, the instruction is present/reachable, and the grid has roles — nothing empty or malformed. The defect is a semantic mismatch between prose ('Ctrl+M') and the handler's modifier check (altKey). Scanners do not read instructions, parse keydown modifier logic, or cross-reference the two. Only a human reading the advice then driving the keyboard finds Ctrl+M dead and Alt+M live.

citation.quote: Determine whether the alternate command(s) work.

pages.scenario: Patient-portal Care Plan Builder with two side-by-side focus-trapping panels: Morning (escapes Ctrl+J) and Evening (escapes Ctrl+K). Both panels display identical 'press Ctrl+K' help; correct for Evening but inaccurate for Morning, whose real escape is Ctrl+J.
pages.mechanism: Each region loops focus and has its own working exit; region A's help text documents region B's keystroke. The advice in A is present, reachable, and even names a real shortcut working elsewhere — but it does not move focus out of A (Ctrl+K is dead in A; only the undocumented Ctrl+J exits A). Per-region advice/escape mismatch.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Both panels are well-formed, the help is real visible text, and BOTH documented shortcuts genuinely work somewhere on the page — so there is no missing instruction and no dead key for a scanner to find. The defect is purely relational (A documents B's key). No static tool models which trap a sentence belongs to; detecting it requires reading each panel's prose, discovering each region's real escape by keyboard, and cross-matching.

citation.quote:
Keyboard focus can be moved away from each section of the page containing elements (not trapped in a "loop"
   preventing access to other elements) using either standard navigation keys OR documented custom keystrokes.

pages.scenario: LMS submission grader: an annotation panel loops focus among rubric buttons and a comment box; a help disclosure button INSIDE the trapped subset (in the tab loop, with aria-expanded/aria-controls) reveals 'press Ctrl+Q', and Ctrl+Q genuinely exits — advice both reachable in-subset by keyboard and matching the working exit.
pages.mechanism: The disclosure is part of the focus loop, so a keyboard user reaches it before being stranded; activating it exposes the in-flow instruction read in context; the documented keystroke (Ctrl+Q) is exactly the one the handler releases on. All three G21 conditions hold: exit exists, documented in an accessible manner within the subset, and accurate.
pages.selectorNote: Focus-looping interpretation booth present at load; not a dialog, so target the trapping section
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A clean conditional pass that a static tool also cannot CONFIRM: it cannot tell focus loops here, cannot confirm the disclosure is reachable before the loop strands the user, and cannot check that 'Ctrl+Q' in the revealed text equals the handler's key. Confirming the PASS needs the same human keyboard-driving judgment the FAIL cases need, which sharpens the reachability/accuracy aspect.

citation.quote: The help information available from the content that is not accessibility supported documents how to move focus back to the accessibility-supported content via the keyboard, and the help information can be accessed via the keyboard.

pages.scenario: Lease e-signature step: the signature region loops focus and exits on Ctrl+M, but the escape advice is locked in a popover opened ONLY by a mouse-only div[onclick] info badge (no tabindex/role/keydown). Even if opened, the tip says 'press Esc' — which is dead — so the advice is both keyboard-unreachable and inaccurate.
pages.mechanism: Focus loops on the legal-name field/Clear button; Ctrl+M is the real exit. The only advice sits in a popover whose sole trigger is a non-focusable <div onclick> absent from the tab order and the a11y tree as a control; and the tip names Esc, which the handler does not honor. Reachability AND accuracy both fail.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Markup looks fine: aria-labeled field, real Clear/Finish buttons, an escape string present in the DOM. axe may not flag the <div onclick> (no name to be 'wrong') and cannot know that popover is the sole home of the exit instruction, nor that 'Esc' in the tip mismatches the Ctrl+M handler. Catching either defect requires driving the keyboard to find the popover unopenable then the documented key dead.

citation.quote: The objective of this technique is to ensure that keyboard users do not become trapped in a subset of the content that can only be exited using a mouse or pointing device.

aspects.title: Title is a non-empty but non-identifying artifact: authoring-tool default, unfilled placeholder, or filename/code string
aspects.plain: The page title is a leftover like 'Untitled Document', a 'TODO' placeholder, or a filename such as 'report.html', which is technically present but tells the user nothing about the page.
aspects.description: F25 names a family of title strings that are non-empty, valid, and pass the presence rule (2779a5), yet fail 2.4.2 because the string itself identifies nothing about the page's content. Three sub-classes, all requiring semantic recognition that the string is residue rather than content: (a) authoring-tool defaults ('Untitled Document', 'Enter the title of your HTML document here', 'No Title', 'New Page 1'); (b) filler/placeholder/unfilled-template text ('Lorem ipsum', 'TODO: title', 'PAGE TITLE HERE', 'xxxxx', 'test'); (c) filenames or machine identifiers that are not descriptive in their own right ('report.html', 'spk12.html', SKUs, build hashes, Drupal-style 'node/3387', raw slugs like 'page_2_final_v3'). The c4a8a4 descriptiveness corpus contains NONE of these named strings — its only non-descriptive case is a wrong-real-subject title (apple vs clementine) and a site-name-only search page. A checker cannot flag any of these because each is non-empty, valid UTF-8, often dictionary words, and structurally indistinguishable from a legitimate terse title; only semantic recognition that 'Untitled Document' announces no-title, or that '.html' / a hash signals machine residue, catches it.
aspects.scLimb: Limb (b), 'titles that describe topic or purpose' — specifically the F25 case where the title exists and is non-empty but identifies nothing about the page. Limb (a) presence is satisfied and carved out to 2779a5.
aspects.whyUncovered: c4a8a4's failing titles are all natural-language phrases ('Apple harvesting season', 'University of Arkham'); the corpus never presents an authoring default, a placeholder/unfilled-template token, or a filename/code-string title. 2779a5 explicitly passes any non-whitespace title, so 'Untitled Document', 'TODO: title' and 'report.html' sail through both ACT rules. Fully-automated tools cannot distinguish these from a real title: they are non-empty and valid; distinguishing 'report.html' from a genuine 'Report 2024', or 'New Page 1' from a legitimate title, requires understanding that the string is a vestigial tool artifact or unfilled template, not page-identifying content.

references.quote: Authoring tool default titles, such as ... "Enter the title of your HTML document here," "Untitled Document" "No Title" "Untitled Page" "New Page 1"
Filenames that are not descriptive in their own right, such as report.html or spk12.html
Empty text ... Filler or placeholder text
Titles identify the current location without requiring users to read or interpret page content.

aspects.ttWhy: Title is present and non-empty but identifies nothing about the page's content.

pages.scenario: A finished quarterly-revenue investor-relations article (masthead, prose, management quotes, a revenue-by-segment data table) whose <title> is the literal Adobe Dreamweaver new-document default 'Untitled Document'.
pages.mechanism: F25 sub-class (a): authoring-tool default title. The <title> text node is 'Untitled Document', which announces the absence of a title and identifies nothing about the Q3-revenue subject; AT/tab/bookmark/search-result readers cannot distinguish it from any other 'Untitled Document'.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe document-title / WAVE / Lighthouse / ACT 2779a5 only verify a non-empty <title> exists. 'Untitled Document' is non-empty, valid UTF-8 and a grammatical noun phrase, so it passes every presence/format heuristic. Recognizing it as an authoring-tool default that means no-title requires semantic knowledge a checker lacks.

citation.quote: Authoring tool default titles, such as "Enter the title of your HTML document here," "Untitled Document" "No Title" "Untitled Page" "New Page 1"

pages.scenario: A shipped Vite + React single-page app rendering a real 'New Engineer Onboarding Checklist' HR console view, whose document <title> is left at the build scaffold default 'Vite + React' and is never updated on route change.
pages.mechanism: F25 sub-class (c) + SPA dynamic-state: the <title> is the build tool's name, not the page's. The inline script never sets document.title and the SPA never updates it per view, so every route reports 'Vite + React' to AT and the tab, identifying tooling not content and failing to distinguish views served from one URL.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: 'Vite + React' is a non-empty valid title so document-title / 2779a5 pass on the served HTML; scanners also evaluate the initial DOM and do not model that the SPA never updates document.title per view. Knowing it is a generator default describing the framework, not the onboarding page, is semantic judgment.

citation.quote: In cases such as Single Page Applications (SPAs), where various distinct pages/views are all nominally served from the same URI and the content of the page is changed dynamically, the title of the page should also be changed dynamically to reflect the content or topic of the current view.

pages.scenario: A complete Returns & Refunds policy page (breadcrumb, h1, effective date, return steps, refund timing, FAQ definition list) whose <title> is the unfilled CMS placeholder 'TODO: add page title'.
pages.mechanism: F25 sub-class (b): filler/placeholder/unfilled-template text. The theme echoed the CMS page-title field, still holding its authoring-hint placeholder, into <title>. AT and tab/bookmark/search-result users receive an editorial instruction to the author ('TODO: add page title') that identifies nothing about returns/refunds and even signals the page is unfinished.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The string is non-empty, valid, sentence-case, and even contains the dictionary token 'title', so document-title / 2779a5 pass. No linter knows 'TODO: add page title' is an unfilled template token rather than a real title; distinguishing residue from content is semantic recognition.

citation.quote: Examples of text that are not titles include: ... Empty text ... Filler or placeholder text

pages.scenario: A finished field-research brief (descriptive h1 on riparian-buffer stream-temperature study, metadata list, executive summary, key findings, recommendation, methods) whose <title> is the source filename 'report.html' — F25's own literal example.
pages.mechanism: F25 sub-class (c): a filename not descriptive in its own right. A docs generator used the filename as <title> when no front-matter title was supplied, emitting 'report.html' with the extension. The string identifies a file ('report' of what?), not a subject, and the '.html' is machine residue; it does not distinguish this brief from any other report.html.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: 'report.html' is non-empty and valid so document-title / 2779a5 pass; a scanner cannot tell a non-descriptive filename ('report.html') from a genuine terse title ('Report 2024') since both are short strings. Recognizing '.html' as a filename extension signalling residue, and 'report' as non-identifying alone, is semantic judgment.

citation.quote: Filenames that are not descriptive in their own right, such as report.html or spk12.html

pages.scenario: A complete conference keynote-speaker profile (name, role, featured-talk card, bio, speaking topics for Dr. Lena Okafor at DataShift 2025) whose <title> is the internal record slug 'spk12.html' — F25's other literal filename example.
pages.mechanism: F25 sub-class (c): machine slug filename. A speakers CMS fell back to the output filename when the title field was blank, emitting 'spk12.html'. AT and tab/search-result users get a build artifact identifying speaker record twelve, not the page's human subject; comparing 'spk12.html' vs 'spk13.html' tabs cannot reveal who is who.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: 'spk12.html' is non-empty and valid so document-title / 2779a5 pass; the string even 'looks technical/intentional', which can reassure naive heuristics. Knowing it is a machine slug that says nothing about the bio's subject requires semantic recognition.

citation.quote: Filenames that are not descriptive in their own right, such as report.html or spk12.html

pages.scenario: A help-centre article (sidebar nav + complete 'Set up two-factor authentication' guide with numbered steps and recovery-codes tip) whose <title> is the raw Drupal internal node path 'node/3387'.
pages.mechanism: F25 sub-class (c): a machine identifier / internal path used as the title. A misconfigured Drupal title token (or empty Title field) rendered the node's system path into <title>. AT and tab/history readers get a database row reference ('node/3387') that says nothing about two-factor authentication and cannot distinguish this from 'node/3388'.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: 'node/3387' is non-empty and valid so document-title / 2779a5 pass; a scanner has no model of Drupal node paths and cannot tell an internal identifier from a deliberate terse title. Recognizing it as a CMS row reference, not content, is human semantic judgment.

citation.quote: This describes a failure condition when the web page has a title, but the title does not identify the contents or purpose of the web page.

pages.scenario: PASSED BOUNDARY: a real Contact page (Riverside branch of Cedar Hollow Veterinary Clinic, with address, hours table, map, labelled form) whose <title> wears the same code-ish texture as the failing cases — embedding a location slug 'loc-04' and release stamp '(rev 2025-06)' — yet still leads with genuinely identifying natural language.
pages.mechanism: Control/discriminator: the title 'Contact Cedar Hollow Veterinary Clinic — Riverside Branch · loc-04 (rev 2025-06)' DOES identify topic (contacting the clinic) and distinguishes the branch (Riverside) from other locations. The artifact-shaped suffix is harmless decoration, proving the failure is NON-IDENTIFICATION, not the mere presence of filename/code/version texture.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Symmetry point: a checker passes this for the wrong reason (presence only) and would ALSO pass the failing cases 04-06. Only a human evaluating meaning can both pass this page (identifying content present) and fail the others (identifying content absent); the checker's pass signal is therefore not evidence of conformance.

citation.quote: The title of each web page should: Identify the subject of the web page; Make sense when read out of context, for example by a screen reader or in a site map or list of search results; Be short

aspects.title: Title describes a secondary/peripheral block instead of the page's primary topic (rich mixed-content pages)
aspects.plain: On a busy page the title names a sidebar, ad, or banner instead of what the page is actually about, so users picking from open tabs or search results are misled.
aspects.description:
F25 fails titles that do not identify the contents or purpose of the OVERALL page. On a realistic page with mixed content (a main article plus a sidebar, ad rail, promo banner, related-links, footer tagline), a title can be non-empty and genuinely describe SOMETHING present on the page while completely missing the page's primary subject — e.g. a detailed page about a city budget vote titled after the top promo banner ('Summer Sale - 20% Off'), or a recipe page titled after its sidebar newsletter widget. The c4a8a4 corpus only ever has a single short

as the entire body, so the page's topic is unambiguous by construction and 'which of several content blocks is this page about' is never exercised. Identifying a busy page's PRIMARY topic versus peripheral blocks, and checking the title against the dominant content region, is a quintessential human reading-comprehension/visual-prominence judgment that no presence-or-emptiness checker performs.
aspects.scLimb: Limb (b), 'describe topic or purpose' — the title must identify the OVERALL/primary content of the page, not merely some element that appears on it.
aspects.whyUncovered:
Every c4a8a4 case has one sentence of body content, so there is exactly one possible topic and no competition between primary and peripheral content; the corpus's own syntheticNarrowness admits 'a single short

as the entire page content'. Real pages have headers, sidebars, ads, and related-content rails. Automated tools cannot identify a page's primary topic versus peripheral blocks, have no model of visual or semantic prominence, and do no title-versus-dominant-content comparison; a human must read the page, determine what it is principally about, and judge whether the title names THAT.

references.quote: This describes a failure condition when the web page has a title, but the title does not identify the contents or purpose of the web page.
Identify the subject of the web page
Determine whether the Page Title is a meaningful representation or indication of page content.

aspects.ttWhy: Title exists but names a peripheral block, not the page's overall purpose.

pages.scenario: Long-form local-news article (~600 words) on the Cedar Falls City Council adopting a $214M municipal budget after a contested vote on police and parks funding. The page is a rich news layout (promo banner, masthead, section nav, article, sidebar with most-read/ad/newsletter, footer), but the <title> 'Summer Sale — 20% Off Annual Subscriptions | Cedar Falls Tribune' is lifted from the top rotating subscription promo banner — a peripheral marketing block, not the budget story that is the page's primary topic.
pages.mechanism: F25 limb (b): the <title> is non-empty and accurately describes a real, present PERIPHERAL block (.promo-banner), but does not identify the OVERALL/primary content (the article#hl headline about the $214M budget vote). A screen reader announces the page as a sale promo; in tabs/history/bookmarks/search the budget story is filed under marketing copy, and two different stories could share the identical promo title, so it also fails to distinguish the page.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe-core document-title, WAVE, and Lighthouse only verify a non-empty <title> exists; the title's words ('Summer Sale', 'Subscriptions') literally appear in the .promo-banner DOM, so even a keyword-presence heuristic finds a match. No tool models which region is the page's primary topic versus a promo rail, and none compares the title against the dominant content region. Deciding the budget article — not the sale banner — is the page's subject requires human reading comprehension and a sense of visual/semantic prominence.

citation.quote: This describes a failure condition when the web page has a title, but the title does not identify the contents or purpose of the web page.

pages.scenario: A food-blog recipe page whose dominant main column is a complete recipe for 'Brown Butter Miso Chocolate Chip Cookies' (full ingredient list + five-step numbered method). The <title> 'Sign up for our newsletter — sweetcrumb.kitchen' is the heading of the sidebar newsletter-signup card — a peripheral conversion widget — rather than the recipe that is the page's subject.
pages.mechanism: F25 limb (b): the <title> names the sidebar newsletter widget heading (aside .card.nl > h2) instead of the primary recipe (main.recipe > h1#rtitle). The title is non-empty and its words are present in the DOM, but it identifies a peripheral widget, not the overall content. Because every recipe page carries the same widget, the title also fails to distinguish the page — a screen reader announces 'Sign up for our newsletter' for what is actually the cookie recipe.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The <title> is present and non-empty so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse pass; the phrase 'Sign up for our newsletter' appears verbatim in the sidebar DOM, so token-overlap between title and page text scores a match. No tool can tell that the recipe — not the newsletter card — is the page's primary topic, which requires recognizing the recipe as the visually/semantically dominant region and reading its meaning.

citation.quote: Determine whether the Page Title is a **meaningful representation or indication** of page content.

pages.scenario: An ATS job-posting page whose entire main column is a specific posting: 'Senior Backend Engineer (Payments)' at Northwind Robotics (role summary, responsibilities, requirements, compensation, Apply button). The <title> 'Building robots that give people their time back. — Northwind Robotics' is the company's generic mission-statement tagline that appears only in the footer — a peripheral brand block — and is emitted as the title of every posting in the set.
pages.mechanism: F25 'same title for each page' + limb (b): the <title> is the global footer tagline (footer > p.tagline), not the posting headline (h1#jtitle). It is non-empty but describes the company brand, not THIS job, and is duplicated across every posting — so a screen-reader user hears every Northwind job tab announced identically and cannot distinguish the Senior Backend Engineer role from any other open posting.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The <title> is non-empty so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse pass; the tagline's words appear verbatim in the footer so token-overlap heuristics match. Detecting that every posting carries the SAME tagline-title requires crawling and comparing multiple pages, which single-URL scanners never do; and judging that the title fails to name the specific job requires reading the posting and understanding it is the page's primary subject.

citation.quote:
A site generated using templates includes the same title for each
                                page on the site. So the title cannot be used to distinguish among
                                the pages.

pages.scenario: A bilingual (EN/FR) help-center article whose dominant main column is the support article 'Resetting your password'. The <title> 'Maintenance planifiée samedi 02 h–05 h HE — Aide Cendre' is the text of the transient top service-status announcement bar (written in French because the product is bilingual). The title names a peripheral status banner about Saturday maintenance, not the password-reset article — and is in a different language than the document's lang="en".
pages.mechanism: F25 limb (b), long-tail/i18n variant: the <title> is taken from the transient announcement region (.announce, role='Avis de service', span[lang='fr']) rather than the article topic (article.kb > h1#atitle). The title is non-empty but names a peripheral banner that will be stale after maintenance ends; additionally, under <html lang='en'> a screen reader announces the French title with English pronunciation, so a user cannot locate the password-reset article among open tabs.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The <title> is non-empty (axe/WAVE/Lighthouse pass), the announcement words appear in the DOM (keyword match passes), and <html lang='en'> is present so a naive language-attribute check is also satisfied. No tool can determine the page is principally about resetting a password rather than Saturday maintenance — that requires reading the article, recognizing the announcement as a transient peripheral banner, and judging which region is the page's primary topic.

citation.quote:
The intent of this success criterion is to help users find content and orient themselves
         within it by ensuring that each web page has a descriptive title. Titles identify
         the current location without requiring users to read or interpret page content.

pages.scenario: An e-commerce product-detail page whose primary content is the 'Aria 14 Ultralight Laptop Stand' (gallery, price, description, full technical-spec table, Add-to-cart). The <title> 'Veza Mechanical Keyboard (Walnut) | Lumen Goods' is one of the items in the 'You may also like' related-products rail near the bottom — a peripheral cross-sell suggestion, not the product the page is about. The title names the wrong product.
pages.mechanism: F25 limb (b): the <title> is bound to a related-rail item (section.related .rail .card .name) instead of the canonical product (section.pdp .buybox > h1#ptitle). The title is non-empty but actively misleads — the laptop-stand tab is announced as a keyboard, so in tab comparison, history, or a bookmark the page is filed under the wrong product entirely, defeating SC 2.4.2's orientation/identification purpose.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The <title> is non-empty so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse pass; the keyboard's name appears verbatim in the related-rail DOM so token overlap is high and a naive descriptiveness heuristic is satisfied. No tool models which product region is the page's canonical subject versus a 'you may also like' suggestion rail, and none compares the title against the primary product. Determining the laptop stand — not the suggested keyboard — is the page's topic requires human reading and a sense of layout prominence.

citation.quote: Check that the title is relevant to the content of the web page.

pages.scenario: BOUNDARY PASS / contrast case: a museum exhibition feature page deliberately as busy and mixed-content as the failing cases — membership-promo strip, sponsor logo rail, 'Gift shop pick of the week' sidebar promo, newsletter widget, 'Now on view' related-exhibitions rail, footer tagline — whose dominant main column is the exhibition 'Hokusai: Beyond the Great Wave'. Here the <title> 'Hokusai: Beyond the Great Wave — Pelham Museum of Art' CORRECTLY names the primary exhibition, not any peripheral block.
pages.mechanism: Limb (b) satisfied: the <title> matches the dominant primary region (article.exhibit > h1#ex), not the gift-shop promo, sponsor rail, newsletter, related shows, or footer tagline. A screen reader announces 'Hokusai: Beyond the Great Wave, Pelham Museum of Art', so the user immediately recognizes and can distinguish the page despite surrounding promotional clutter — the affirmative of the aspect, proving the failure is about WHICH region the title names, not about page busyness.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Automated tools pass this only for the trivial reason a non-empty <title> exists — the same reason they passed the failing cases 01–05, so their 'pass' carries no signal. Worse, a naive descriptiveness heuristic of the form 'flag busy pages whose title matches only a small fraction of visible text' could FALSE-POSITIVE here, because most of this page's words belong to peripheral blocks and the title's token overlap with the full page text is modest — yet the title is correct. Reaching the right verdict (PASS) requires the same human judgment as the failures applied affirmatively: identify the primary topic, then confirm the title names THAT region.

citation.quote: Identify the subject of the web page

aspects.title: Stale / copy-paste title: right subject family, wrong specific instance (date, name, version, account)
aspects.plain: The title is on-topic but names the wrong specific item, like last month's date or the previous product, usually left over from copying a template or a sibling page.
aspects.description: F25 and Trusted Tester 12.B require the title to accurately identify THIS page. A pervasive real-world failure is a title carried over from a template clone or a prior edit: it is on-topic for the section and looks entirely plausible, but names the wrong specific item — last month's statement title on this month's statement, last year's gala date on this year's event, the donor product's name on a duplicated product page. c4a8a4's 'Apple harvesting season' on a clementine page is the only wrong-subject case, and it is a gross, obvious cross-domain swap (different fruit). The corpus has no subtle in-family mismatch where title and body share the domain and vocabulary but disagree on the specific instance — precisely the case that needs careful human cross-checking of identifiers (date/name/version/number) against the body, and that no presence/emptiness checker, and even a keyword-matcher, can detect (both 'Q3 Report' and a Q4 body contain 'Report').
aspects.scLimb: Limb (b), 'describe topic or purpose' — the title must ACCURATELY identify the specific content of THIS page, not merely be domain-plausible.
aspects.whyUncovered: c4a8a4's single wrong-subject case is a blatant cross-domain topic swap; there is no near-miss where title and content share the domain but differ in the specific instance, date, name, or version. The corpus never models a body that the title must be cross-checked against beyond one obvious sentence. Automated tools do no title-versus-content comparison for descriptiveness at all; even a keyword-overlap tool would pass a stale title that shares vocabulary with the body. Catching it requires reading the body and noticing that the specific identifiers in the title disagree with the page's actual subject.

the title does not identify the contents or purpose of the web page
"Bank XYZ, December 2005 statement for Account 1234-5678"

aspects.ttWhy: Title present but names wrong instance, so it misidentifies this page's content.

pages.scenario: Online-banking statement view. The body is unambiguously the December 2005 statement for Account 1234-5678 (H1, statement-period metadata 1-31 Dec 2005, every transaction date 02-30 Dec 2005, closing-balance row, breadcrumb current page, PDF download filename ...-2005-12-..., footer). The <title> reads 'Meridian Bank — November 2005 statement for Account 1234-5678' — the statement template carried over the prior month's title. Mirrors the WCAG Understanding bank example run in reverse: same bank/document-type/account, plausible month, one stale identifier (the month).
pages.mechanism: F25 descriptiveness limb (Trusted Tester 12.B): a present, on-topic <title> names a DIFFERENT (sibling) statement than the page's content. The month is the identifier that distinguishes monthly statements in a set; the title's month (November) contradicts the body's true period (December), so within the set it neither identifies this page nor distinguishes it.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse verify only that a <title> exists and is non-empty (ACT 2779a5). The title is valid, non-empty, unique, human-sounding, and shares vocabulary with the body ('statement','Account 1234-5678', a month name), so a keyword-overlap heuristic also passes it. Catching it requires extracting the body's true period (December — from H1, period metadata, transaction dates, download filename) and noticing the title's month is the prior instance. No linter knows November != December in a way that matters.

citation.quote: The web application dynamically generates titles for each web page, e.g., "Bank XYZ, accounts for Alex Smith" "Bank XYZ, December 2005 statement for Account 1234-5678".

pages.scenario: A nonprofit cloned last year's annual-gala page to build this year's. The body is updated throughout to the 2026 event — an inline-SVG hero date banner reading 'SATURDAY 14 MARCH 2026' (with correct aria-label), the 'This year at a glance' date, the 2026 honoree, 2026 ticket prices, 'Program for the evening of 14 March 2026', and footer. The <title> still says 'Annual Hope Gala 2025 | Riverside Children's Fund' — the year token from the cloned page. The gala recurs annually so 2025 is a real sibling page.
pages.mechanism: F25 descriptiveness limb: the <title> names last year's edition (2025) while the body — including the SVG banner's aria-label, which AT reads — establishes 14 March 2026. AT receives two contradictory year signals and the orientation-authoritative one (the title) is wrong; within an annually recurring set it fails to distinguish this edition.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse confirm a present, non-empty, unique, organization-qualified, on-topic title (ACT 2779a5) and stop. A keyword-overlap tool passes it because title and body share 'Annual Hope Gala','Riverside Children's Fund', and a four-digit year. No automated check reconciles the title's year against the body's date (partly conveyed as text inside an SVG), so none can tell 2025 should read 2026; only a human reading the body's true date catches that the title names the prior edition.

citation.quote: A website that permits editions from different dates to be viewed titles its web page, "National News, Front Page, Oct 17, 2005".

pages.scenario: An e-commerce product detail page duplicated from a sibling SKU. A merchandiser cloned the 500 mL Tundra bottle listing to create the 750 mL one and updated the body end-to-end — breadcrumb, H1, price-line SKU (TND-750-SLT), Add-to-cart button, description, every spec row (capacity 750 mL, height 27 cm, weight 415 g), the product-image SVG label (aria-label '750 millilitres'), and footer all read 750 mL. The <title> still reads 'Tundra Stainless Steel Bottle 500ml — Slate | NorthPeak Gear'. 500 mL is a real sibling SKU, so the title looks legitimate.
pages.mechanism: F25 descriptiveness limb: capacity is the only attribute distinguishing this PDP from its 500 mL sibling, so the title must distinguish pages in a set. The title's '500ml' identifies a different variant than the body's 750 mL (H1, spec table, SKU, SVG image accessible name), misdirecting a shopper comparing sizes by the announced title.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse verify only a present, non-empty title (ACT 2779a5). The title is valid, unique, brand-qualified, on-topic. A keyword-overlap heuristic passes it because title and body share 'Tundra','Stainless Steel Bottle','Slate','NorthPeak' and a millilitre figure. The deciding fact — capacity should be 750, established by H1/spec-table/SKU/SVG accessible name — needs reading and reconciling the body's identifiers; no checker compares '500ml' to '750 mL' as both are valid capacity strings.

citation.quote: Titles identify the current location without requiring users to read or interpret page content.

pages.scenario: A developer-docs release-notes page built by a static-site generator from markdown front matter. The body is unambiguously the v4.2.0 notes: the version <select> shows 'v4.2.0 (current)' selected, the H1 reads 'Release notes — Quartzdb v4.2.0', the release date and package line read quartzdb@4.2.0, the install snippet pins quartzdb@4.2.0, and every changelog heading/item is scoped to 4.2.0. The <title> reads 'Release notes — v4.1.0 · Quartzdb Documentation' — the version was bumped everywhere except the page's front-matter title: field. The body deliberately also MENTIONS 4.1.0 in context ('Upgrading from 4.1.0 to 4.2.0', 'regression present since 4.1.0').
pages.mechanism: F25 descriptiveness limb, sharpened: the title's version (4.1.0) is not absent from the body — it appears as a REFERENCED prior version, not the page's SUBJECT version (4.2.0, set by the H1, selected version control, release date, install pin). The title names a different release than the page documents; among versioned release-notes pages it fails to distinguish this page.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse confirm a present, non-empty, product-qualified, on-topic title (ACT 2779a5). A keyword-overlap heuristic is actively fooled: '4.1.0' appears in BOTH the title and the body (upgrade/regression sentences), so naive title-vs-content overlap scores it consistent. Determining the page's true subject version requires distinguishing the subject (H1 + selected version control + install pin) from referenced versions — a semantic distinction no linter or overlap metric makes.

citation.quote: This describes a failure condition when the web page has a title, but the title does not identify the contents or purpose of the web page.

pages.scenario: A pharmacy patient-portal 'refill ready' confirmation. After a dose increase the patient has two Lisinopril prescriptions: the discontinued 10 mg (Rx 4471829) and the active 20 mg (Rx 4471830). This page is the 20 mg refill: the H1, patient/Rx subheading (Rx 4471830), a bilingual EN/Simplified-Chinese image-of-text dispensed label (inline SVG, aria-label 'Lisinopril 20 mg ... Rx 4471830'), the strength field (20 mg), directions, pickup line ('your 20 mg refill'), an explicit note that the 10 mg was discontinued, and footer all say 20 mg / Rx 4471830. The <title> reads 'Refill ready: Lisinopril 10 mg — Rx 4471829 | BayCare Pharmacy', built from a stale cached prescription summary naming the discontinued strength.
pages.mechanism: F25 descriptiveness limb (safety-critical): the <title> names the discontinued 10 mg / Rx 4471829 while the body — including the image-of-text label's aria-label that AT reads — establishes the refill is 20 mg / Rx 4471830. Strength is what distinguishes this confirmation from the sibling Rx; a patient trusting the announced title is told the wrong (old) dose, risking the wrong medication strength.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse verify only a present, non-empty, pharmacy-qualified, on-topic title (ACT 2779a5). A keyword-overlap tool passes it because title and body share 'Refill ready','Lisinopril','BayCare Pharmacy','Rx','mg' — and the body even mentions 10 mg / Rx 4471829 in the discontinuation note, so naive overlap finds the title's tokens present and scores it consistent. The deciding facts (subject = 20 mg / Rx 4471830; 10 mg = referenced discontinued prior) live in the H1, the SVG label's accessible name, the strength field, and the note's semantics, none of which a checker parses or reconciles against the title.

citation.quote: People with cognitive disabilities, limited short-term memory and reading disabilities also benefit from the ability to identify content by its title.

pages.scenario: PASS boundary variant. A municipal transit timetable, which ships as a set of near-identical sibling pages (Weekday / Saturday / Sunday & Holiday) — exactly the situation that breeds stale copy-paste titles. Here the author got the specific instance RIGHT: the <title> reads 'Route 12 Riverside — Saturday Schedule | Metro Transit', and the body — breadcrumb current page, H1, day-selector (Saturday marked aria-current=page), service note ('Saturday service runs every 30 minutes...'), table caption ('Saturday departures — Route 12 Riverside'), 'All times are Saturdays only', and footer — is unambiguously the Saturday schedule for the same route. Title and body share the route family and timetable vocabulary AND agree on the one critical identifier (the service day).
pages.mechanism: No F25 failure: the title is present AND identifies the contents AND distinguishes the page within its set of sibling timetables — the service day in the title matches the service day throughout the body. This is the in-family MATCH the five failing cases are contrasted against, proving the judgment under test is 'does the title's specific instance match the body's?', not 'does a title exist?'.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Irrelevant to the verdict but instructive: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse would report PASS here for the same shallow reason they wrongly PASS the failing cases — a present, non-empty title (ACT 2779a5). They cannot see whether the title's service day agrees with the body's. The correct PASS here comes only from a human (or model) cross-check succeeding; the identical cross-check fails in case-01 through case-05. This case confirms a detector keys on the title-vs-body identifier MATCH rather than on surface presence or on mere structural similarity to the failing cases.

citation.quote: The Page Title accurately identifies the contents or purpose of the web page, AND if the web page is part of a set of web pages, the Page Title accurately distinguishes the web page from other pages in the web site.

aspects.title: Title is correct but too generic to distinguish this page from its siblings (site-name-only / template-shared on an inner page)
aspects.plain: An inner page's title is only the site name or a shared label every page uses, so users cannot tell this page apart from its siblings in tabs or history.
aspects.description: F25's second example is a distinct failure: 'A site generated using templates includes the same title for each page on the site. So the title cannot be used to distinguish among the pages.' G88 and Trusted Tester 12.B both make distinguish-within-the-set a pass requirement. Here the title may be perfectly accurate about the SITE ('Acme Corporation', 'Online Store', 'Help Center') yet fail 2.4.2 because it carries no page-level information and so cannot distinguish THIS page (Contact) from siblings (Products, About). The single-page-detectable form of this failure — an inner page of an obvious set whose title is only the site name or only the shared template/section label — IS testable on a self-contained HTML page: the body unambiguously reveals the page's specific role, while the title carries only site-level information. Deciding whether 'Acme Corporation' adequately distinguishes the Contact page requires knowing the page's specific role — a human judgment about whether the title carries page-level, not just site-level, information.
aspects.scLimb: Limb (b), 'describe topic or purpose' — within the SC's distinguish-among-a-set requirement: the title must identify THIS page, not merely the site/template it shares with its siblings.
aspects.whyUncovered: ACT test cases are single self-contained files with no sibling pages, so 'same title across the set' cannot be encoded; the corpus's only inner-page case is one search page, and c4a8a4's 'University of Arkham' touches site-name-only but as an isolated single page, never as the distinguish-among-siblings problem F25 describes. Fully-automated single-page tools have no cross-page corpus to compare titles against, and even on one page cannot decide whether a site-name-only or template-shared title adequately distinguishes this page's specific role — that requires reading the body to learn the page's role and judging whether the title carries any page-level signal.

references.quote: A site generated using templates includes the same title for each page on the site. So the title cannot be used to distinguish among the pages.
Be unique within the site or other resource to which the web page belongs
If the web page is part of a set of web pages, determine whether the Page Title is sufficient to distinguish the web page from other pages.

aspects.ttWhy: Site-name/template title is present but fails to distinguish this page from siblings.

pages.scenario: A specific e-commerce product detail page (Stainless Steel Insulated Water Bottle, 750 ml) in an obvious multi-page storefront whose <title> is only the Shopify Dawn theme default 'Online Store' — the same string the cart and every collection/product sibling carries. Breadcrumb, category nav, h1, and SKU establish the page's specific role; the title carries zero page-level information.
pages.mechanism: F25 example 2 (template-shared, site-name-only title). The <title> 'Online Store' is accurate about the SITE but identical across every product, collection, and cart page, so it cannot distinguish THIS product from its siblings. AT exposes <title> for tab/window/history/search orientation, and that cue is non-distinguishing; the page-level identity exists only in the h1/breadcrumb/SKU which AT does not use for cross-page orientation.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe-core document-title, WAVE, and Lighthouse only verify a non-empty <title> exists, which 'Online Store' satisfies. They have no sibling-page corpus to compare against and cannot read the body to learn the page is a specific product, so they cannot judge that the title carries only site-level, not page-level, information.

citation.quote: A site generated using templates includes the same title for each page on the site. So the title cannot be used to distinguish among the pages.

pages.scenario: Step 3 (Payment) of a 4-step checkout flow on the Loomwell Home store. The progress bar (Cart -> Shipping -> Payment -> Review), the h1 'Step 3 of 4 — Payment', and the payment fieldset make the step unmistakable, but the <title> is the section-shared label 'Checkout' carried by all four steps from one Express layout template.
pages.mechanism: F25 — one title reused across every page (step) in the set. The <title> 'Checkout' distinguishes the flow but not the step; a screen-reader user with multiple steps open in tabs, or recovering a session from history, hears 'Checkout' on every step with no step-level signal. The step identity lives only in the visual progress bar and the h1.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Each step's snapshot has a valid, non-empty <title>, so per-page scans pass 2.4.2 on every step. Detecting the failure requires comparing the title across the four steps and recognizing it carries no step-level information — a cross-page comparison plus semantic judgment single-page automated scans never perform.

citation.quote: A site generated using templates includes the same title for each page on the site. So the title cannot be used to distinguish among the pages.

pages.scenario: The 'Authentication API Reference' page of the Quilltail Pay developer docs. The sidebar tree-nav lists sibling pages (Quickstart, Authentication, Charges, Refunds, Webhooks, Errors, Rate limits) and the h1/token-endpoint/parameter-table make the page specifically the Authentication reference, but the <title> is the docs-generator default 'Documentation' (front-matter title line was deleted), identical across every doc page.
pages.mechanism: F25 — authoring-tool/template default that names the whole collection. The <title> 'Documentation' names the docs site, not this page, so it cannot distinguish the Authentication reference from Webhooks or Errors. A developer with several reference pages open in tabs hears 'Documentation' on all of them; bookmarks and search results collapse to one string.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: 'Documentation' is a non-empty <title>, so the presence check passes on every doc page. No single-page tool can compare it across the doc set, and none reads the body to learn this is specifically the Authentication reference — judging it is the shared template default is human-only.

citation.quote: Make sense when read out of context, for example by a screen reader or in a site map or list of search results

pages.scenario: A Japanese (lang=ja) municipal transit route-detail/timetable page for one specific bus route — Route 32 'Minato Loop' (32系統 みなと循環線) — on the Sakurai City Transit Bureau site. A route chip-nav lists sibling routes (11, 21, 32, 45, 58) and the h1/direction-tablist/timetable table make the page specifically Route 32, but the <title> is only the agency name '桜井市交通局', identical across every route page and the home page. The body is fully localized; the defect is set-distinguishing, not translation.
pages.mechanism: F25 — one site/agency name reused as the title of every route page. The <title> names the agency, not the route, so a commuter using a Japanese screen reader who opens Route 32 and Route 45 in tabs hears '桜井市交通局' for both with no way to tell them apart. The route identity exists only in the h1, the active route chip, and the table caption.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The <title> is present and non-empty, so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse pass the presence check. They cannot parse the Japanese body to learn this is the Route 32 timetable, and they have no sibling corpus to notice every route page carries the same agency name, so the distinguish-within-set failure is invisible.

citation.quote: If the web page is part of a set of web pages, the Page Title accurately distinguishes the web page from other pages in the web site.

pages.scenario: A specific government service page on the Marisol DMV site: 'Renew your driver license online'. A mega-menu lists sibling services (Vehicles, Driver licenses, ID cards, Tests & scheduling, plus renew/replace/permit sub-services) and the h1/eligibility-callout/steps make the page specifically the license-renewal service, but the <title> is only the agency name 'Department of Motor Vehicles' (CMS migration mapped the site-name field), identical across every service page.
pages.mechanism: F25 — agency/department name reused as the title of every service page. The <title> names the department, not the service, so a resident who opens 'Renew online' and 'Register a vehicle' in two tabs hears 'Department of Motor Vehicles' for both. The service identity is only in the h1, breadcrumb, and active mega-menu link — none of which AT uses for cross-page tab/history/bookmark orientation.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: 'Department of Motor Vehicles' is a present, non-empty <title>, so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse pass. They cannot read the body to learn the page is the license-renewal service, and they have no view of sibling service pages to notice the department name is repeated as every title — the distinguish-within-set judgment is human-only.

This describes a failure condition when the web page has a title, but the
                        title does not identify the contents or purpose of the web page.

pages.scenario: PASS boundary/control. Same structural family as the failures — an inner page of an obvious multi-page set (MyHealth Patient Portal) with sibling section nav (Dashboard, Appointments, Lab results, Messages, Medications, Billing), a footer, a specific h1, and a CBC results table. The difference: the <title> is 'Lab Results — MyHealth Patient Portal', leading with page-level info before the site-level part, so it distinguishes this page from its siblings.
pages.mechanism: Correct G88-style ordering: the <title> carries page-level information (the 'Lab Results' section) ahead of the site name, so it identifies the current location and distinguishes the page within the set — a screen-reader user with Lab Results, Appointments, and Billing in tabs hears three distinct, page-identifying titles. This is the deliberate control showing what a correctly distinguishing inner-page title looks like.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: An automated tool sees only a present, non-empty <title> here — exactly what it sees on the five failing cases. It cannot confirm that the leading 'Lab Results' segment actually matches this page's role and distinguishes it from siblings; that confirmation is the same human judgment the failures require, which is why even the PASS verdict is not machine-decidable.

citation.quote: A web page is published by a group within a larger organization. The title of the web page first identifies the topic of the page, then shows the group name followed by the name of the parent organization.

aspects.title: Title is locally descriptive in-page but loses meaning out of context / fails to convey collection position (G88 out-of-context, G127)
aspects.plain: A title like 'Step 2' or 'Chapter 3' is clear while on the page but meaningless when seen alone in a tab list or search results, with no surrounding context.
aspects.description: G88 makes 'Make sense when read out of context, for example by a screen reader or in a site map or list of search results' a core requirement, and G127 covers titles that identify a page's RELATIONSHIP to a larger collection (its position in a hierarchy, its parent section). A title can be perfectly clear while reading the page ('Chapter 3', 'Settings', 'Step 2', 'GET /users') yet be uninformative when isolated in a list of open tabs, a search-results list, or a screen-reader page list, because it strips all collection/parent context. The Understanding examples model exactly the good pattern ('Alert Dialog Example | APG | WAI | W3C'; 'Bank XYZ, December 2005 statement for Account 1234-5678'). The ACT corpus has no hierarchical or collection-structured cases — every page is a standalone leaf with no parent context — so the 'descriptive in-page but meaningless out of context' failure is never exercised. Judging whether a title 'makes sense out of context' or conveys collection position requires imagining it isolated and understanding the page's role in a larger information architecture — a human contextual judgment.
aspects.scLimb: Limb (b), 'describe topic or purpose' — the title must identify the page in a way that orients the user, including when read out of context, per G88/G127; a context-dependent fragment does not.
aspects.whyUncovered: The ACT corpus has no multi-level or collection-structured examples; the richest is a flat search-results page, and every case is a standalone leaf with no parent/hierarchy modeled. It never tests a title that is locally descriptive but loses meaning out of context. Automated tools cannot judge whether a title 'makes sense out of context' or conveys collection position — that requires understanding the page's role in a larger information architecture and imagining the title isolated in a list of tabs or search hits; 'Chapter 3' is fine in-page but uninformative as a standalone title, and only a human weighs that.

aspects.ttWhy: Title is present but too context-dependent to identify the page out of context.

pages.scenario: Online textbook reader: the page is Chapter 3 ('Newton's Laws of Motion') of 'University Physics, 8th ed.', Part I: Mechanics, chapter 3 of 41 — all named in the body — but the document <title> is the bare positional fragment 'Chapter 3'.
pages.mechanism: The <title> 'Chapter 3' is descriptive only while the body (book, part, chapter title, edition) is on screen. In a tab list, browser history, bookmark, screen-reader page-title query, or search result it identifies neither the topic nor the book, and conveys no collection position — it collides with the 'Chapter 3' of every other book in the LMS. Fails limb (b) for descriptiveness out of context and G127 collection-position.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A non-empty <title> is present so axe document-title / WAVE / Lighthouse pass; 'Chapter 3' is on no placeholder blocklist. Recognizing that the title is meaningless once isolated from the body — and cannot convey position in the named collection — requires imagining it beside other books' identical 'Chapter 3' pages, i.e. human reasoning about information architecture, not a DOM check.

citation.doc: WCAG Technique G127 (general/G127.html), Examples — Chapters in an online textbook
citation.quote: An online textbook is divided into chapters. The title of each web page includes the number and title of the chapter as well as the title of the textbook.

pages.scenario: Multi-pane SaaS settings area (Cadence CRM): the current pane is Notifications (active sidebar item, breadcrumb 'Settings > Workspace > Notifications', H1 'Notification settings'), but the <title> is the single bare word 'Settings' — the same word every sibling pane (Profile, Security, Billing, Integrations, API keys) would emit.
pages.mechanism: This is a 'set of web pages'. The shared <title> 'Settings' cannot distinguish the Notifications pane from Billing or API-keys; a user with several panes in tabs hears 'Settings' on every one and gets no orientation cue on navigation. Fails limb (b) out of context AND the within-a-set distinguishing requirement.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A single-page scan finds a present, non-empty title that even reads like a plausible one, so 2.4.2 passes. A scanner audits one DOM state and has no concept that five sibling routes ship the identical word, nor that this route is really the Notifications pane. Detecting a non-distinguishing title across a set requires crawling siblings and comparing — a manual step.

citation.quote: If the web page is part of a set of web pages, the Page Title accurately distinguishes the web page from other pages in the web site.

pages.scenario: Auto-generated REST API reference (Helios Identity API v3): the masthead, sidebar group 'Users', and breadcrumb all establish product/version/section, but the OpenAPI generator set the <title> to the bare operation 'GET /users' with no product, version, or section.
pages.mechanism: 'GET /users' is one of the most common endpoint strings on the web. In a tab strip, bookmark, or search result it cannot be told apart from the same product's Billing API, a competitor's docs, or an old version — the product/version/section that make it meaningful are stripped. The title identifies the operation but not the page out of context, and does not distinguish it from countless near-identical pages. Fails limb (b).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The <title> is present and non-empty so 2.4.2 passes mechanically; 'GET /users' is not a placeholder. Recognizing that it is so generic it collides with countless pages across the wider web — and so cannot identify THIS page out of context — needs world knowledge of how common the string is and how API docs are navigated. Pure human judgment.
