pages.scenario: Court electronic-filing document viewer (CM/ECF-style): the body shows the full case caption (Marisol Vega v. Brightline Logistics, Inc., 3:24-cv-04417-WHA, doc #42-2, 'Exhibit B — Commercial Lease Agreement dated March 14, 2022'), but the viewer derived the <title> from only the short-label field, yielding the bare 'Exhibit B'.
pages.mechanism: An attorney keeps many exhibit tabs open across active cases; the tab strip, history, bookmarks, and screen-reader page-title query all read 'Exhibit B' — identical across every case's Exhibit B, with no case name, document number, or statement of what the exhibit is. Meaningful only beside the on-page caption; isolated it conveys nothing and cannot distinguish among open documents. Fails limb (b) out of context and the distinguish-within-a-set requirement.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A non-empty <title> is present so document-title checks pass; 'Exhibit B' is not a known placeholder, so heuristic blocklists don't fire. Knowing 'Exhibit B' is a positional fragment meaningless once it leaves the on-page caption — and that every case has one, so pages aren't distinguishable — is contextual legal-document reasoning no tool can perform.

citation.quote: The title can be used to identify the web page without requiring users to read or interpret page content.

pages.scenario: Museum digital-collection object viewer (Spanish locale, lang=es): the body fully identifies the object (collection, portfolio 'Flora Mexicana, Tomo II', plate caption 'Lamina 12: Dalia silvestre', accession no.), but the i18n template built the <title> from only the localised plate label + number, yielding the bare fragment 'Lamina 12' (Plate 12).
pages.mechanism: 'Lamina 12' (Plate 12) strips the portfolio, subject, and collection the body carries, and is identical to plate 12 of every other digitised work. In a tab list, a Europeana/Google result, or a screen-reader page-title query it gives nothing to choose by. Meaningful only beside the on-page metadata; isolated it conveys no topic and no collection position. Fails limb (b). The defect being in well-formed Spanish compounds the difficulty.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A <title> is present and non-empty (2.4.2 passes); 'Lamina 12' is well-formed Spanish on no placeholder list. Judging descriptiveness is already a human task, and doing it across a different natural language compounds it — a tool has no notion that this localised 'Plate 12' loses all collection context or collides with every other work's plate 12.

citation.quote: The objective of this technique is to enable users to identify the relationship between the current web page and other web pages in the same collection (e.g., on the same website).

pages.scenario: BOUNDARY PASS variant. Docs leaf with the same shape as the failing cases — the in-page H1 is the bare action 'Installing' and the sidebar shows hierarchy position — but the <title> correctly carries collection context most-specific-first: 'Installing the CLI - Aurora CLI Tools - Aurora Docs', per G127/G88 and the APG example pattern.
pages.mechanism: Read out of context the title still identifies topic ('Installing the CLI'), section ('Aurora CLI Tools'), and product ('Aurora Docs'), distinguishing the page from siblings ('Authentication...') and from any other Aurora product's install page. A screen-reader user with several docs tabs knows exactly which page without the body. Passes limb (b) and the distinguish-within-a-set requirement; the bare H1 'Installing' is the trap the failing cases fall into.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A tool sees only a present, non-empty <title> in every case, failing and passing alike; it cannot tell that THIS title survives isolation while a bare 'Installing' would not, nor that it conveys collection position. Confirming the pass requires the same out-of-context reasoning the failures require — a static checker has no basis to distinguish case-06 from case-01.

citation.doc: WCAG Technique G88 (general/G88.html), Examples — A web page with a descriptive title in three parts
citation.quote: The title is separated into three parts by dashes. The first part of the title identifies the organization. The second part identifies the sub-site to which the web page belongs. The third part identifies the web page itself.

aspects.title: CSS-reordered visual layout makes DOM/tab order contradict the meaningful order (no tabindex, no script)
aspects.plain: CSS like flexbox order or absolute positioning rearranges the page so it reads one way visually but Tab moves focus in the unrelated DOM order, confusing keyboard users.
aspects.description: A page uses NO positive tabindex and NO focus-managing script, so every static 'tabindex misuse' heuristic finds nothing. But CSS (flexbox `order`, grid placement, float, absolute positioning) reorders the visual presentation so that the natural DOM tab order no longer follows the meaning conveyed by the rendered layout. G59's core point applies: 'When the source order does not match the visual order, the tab order through the content must reflect the logical relationships in the content that are displayed visually.' Judging a violation requires looking at the RENDERED page, inferring the intended reading/operation sequence from the visual hierarchy, and comparing it to the keyboard sequence. The Understanding makes this an explicit judgment: independent columns out of order do NOT fail, but interdependent content out of order DOES. This is the most semantically demanding limb and the highest-value uncovered space.
aspects.scLimb: Focus-order-vs-reading-order independence limb / core meaning limb: 'Focus order does not necessarily need to follow the visual layout... as long as the order in which elements receive focus is logical, and the hierarchy and relationship of content implied by the visual presentation is preserved.'
aspects.whyUncovered: 0 ACT rules/cases for 2.4.3. F44 (the only automatable-adjacent failure) is scoped to the tabindex attribute; a page with zero tabindex and zero script presents nothing for a static rule to inspect. No automated tool can decide whether visually-reordered DOM content is 'independent' (passes) or 'interdependent' (fails) — that is the exact distinction the Understanding flags as requiring human consideration of the rendered presentation.

references.quote: When the source order does not match the visual order, the tab order through the content must reflect the logical relationships in the content that are displayed visually.

if the two columns are independent of each other, and meaning/operation are not affected, it is not a failure if elements in the right-hand column receive focus first, followed by the elements in the left-hand column.

Focus order does not necessarily need to follow the visual layout of the web page, as long as the order in which elements receive focus is logical, and the hierarchy and relationship of content implied by the visual presentation is preserved.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: Single-page e-commerce checkout (Maple & Thread). A flex column whose 'Place order & pay' submit block is authored first in the DOM but pushed to the visual bottom with order:99. No tabindex, no JS. Verified tab order: T1 = the submit button (at y=1213, the visual bottom), then Quantity, Shipping, Payment — so Tab reaches the irreversible commit before any field.
pages.mechanism: CSS flexbox `order:99` on a DOM-first submit block makes the commit control the FIRST keyboard tab stop while it renders visually last; the operational sequence (fill fields, then submit) is inverted for keyboard users, so focus order does not preserve operability.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: No positive tabindex and no script, so F44 and tab-order linters have nothing to inspect; every input is labelled and contrast is fine, so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse pass. Both the DOM order and the CSS `order` value are individually valid. Catching it requires rendering the page, inferring from the visual layout that submit is meant to be the final step, and comparing that to where Tab actually goes first — a visual/semantic judgment no DOM scan performs.

citation.quote: Focus order needs to allow the user to navigate focusable elements in a logical order, and that order needs to preserve any meaning or operation that the page is conveying. Focus order does not necessarily need to follow the visual layout of the web page, as long as the order in which elements receive focus is logical, and the hierarchy and relationship of content implied by the visual presentation is preserved.

pages.scenario: Joint mortgage pre-approval form (Northgate Mutual) rendered as two titled columns — Primary applicant left, Co-applicant right — built with CSS Grid. The DOM interleaves the columns field-by-field and grid-column placement sorts each into its visual column. No tabindex, no JS. Verified tab order ping-pongs Primary-name, Co-applicant-name, Primary-DOB, Co-applicant-DOB, ... across two interdependent applicants.
pages.mechanism: CSS Grid (grid-template-columns + per-field grid-column/grid-row) presents two top-to-bottom columns, but interleaved DOM order makes Tab alternate between two INTERDEPENDENT applicants on every field instead of completing one column then the next — the Understanding's explicit failing 'tab order skips between fields in different sections' case.
pages.selectorNote: Co-applicant name input; tab reaches it 2nd though it is the right column, ping-ponging columns; orig div.compare input.c2 matched nothing (class is on .field parent)
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: No positive tabindex/JS, so F44/linters find nothing; all inputs are labelled and structurally valid, so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse pass. CSS Grid placement plus interleaved DOM are both legal. Detecting the failure requires rendering the two columns, recognizing they are two interdependent parties to the same application, and judging that the intended fill order is column-by-column — the exact interdependent-vs-independent distinction the Understanding reserves for a human.

citation.quote: However, the tab order for the form skips between fields in different sections of the form, so that focus moves from the name field to a checkbox, then to the street address, then to another checkbox.

pages.scenario: LMS course home (BIO 210): a wide main course-content column (module links + Start quiz) on the left and a narrow, UNRELATED site-wide 'Annual Fund' donation widget on the right. The donation aside is DOM-first but flex order paints it right. No tabindex, no JS. Verified tab order: donation amount, Donate now, THEN the course links/quiz — right column focuses first, but the columns are independent.
pages.mechanism: Flexbox `order` swaps a DOM-first independent sidebar to the visual right so it tabs first, but the donation widget and the coursework are independent regions — completing or skipping either does not affect the meaning or operability of the other — which the Understanding explicitly says is NOT a failure.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A naive 'visual order != DOM order' rule would WRONGLY fail this; no such rule ships precisely because the pass/fail turns on whether the two regions are independent — a semantic judgment about content relationships (a tool cannot know 'BIO 210 modules' and 'Annual Fund donation' are unrelated). axe/WAVE/Lighthouse see valid labelled controls and correctly report nothing. Included to measure against over-flagging.

citation.quote: However, if the two columns are independent of each other, and meaning/operation are not affected, it is not a failure if elements in the right-hand column receive focus first, followed by the elements in the left-hand column.

pages.scenario: Municipal parking-permit page (City of Aldergrove): a left-hand 'Parking services' nav and a wide application form on the right. The nav is authored AFTER <main> in the DOM and CSS Grid (grid-template-areas) paints it left. No tabindex, no JS. Verified tab order reaches the main form (plate, zone, email, submit) FIRST, then the side-nav links — the Understanding's own passing source-order technique.
pages.mechanism: CSS Grid grid-template-areas places a DOM-second <nav> into the visual left column while <main> (DOM-first) renders right, so the primary task receives focus before the secondary navigation. This is the Understanding's explicitly passing 'left nav in HTML after main content, styled left' construction — focus order preserves the visual hierarchy (primary task first).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A naive visual-vs-DOM diff would flag the Understanding's own PASSING example. No automated tool ships such a rule because judging that the reorder preserves meaning is a human task; axe/WAVE/Lighthouse see a valid grid, real <nav>/<main> landmarks, and labelled inputs and correctly pass. Included so a judge recognizes an intentional, passing source-order technique rather than failing any reorder.

citation.quote: An HTML web page is created with the left hand navigation occurring in the HTML after the main body content, and styled with CSS to appear on the left hand side of the page. This is done to allow focus to move to the main body content first without requiring tabindex attributes or JavaScript.

pages.scenario: SafeHarbor auto-insurance 'Quick Quote' wizard on one screen: numbered steps (1) About you, (2) Your vehicle, (3) Coverage & quote shown top-to-bottom with circular number badges. Panels are placed by CSS Grid grid-row but emitted in DOM order 3,1,2. No tabindex, no JS. Verified tab order: T1 = Step 3 coverage radio, T2 = 'Get my quote', then jumps up to Step 1 name/age/zip, then Step 2.
pages.mechanism: CSS Grid `grid-row` paints step panels 1->2->3 visually, but DOM order 3,1,2 makes Tab enter the LAST interdependent step (coverage selection + submit) before the prerequisite earlier steps, inverting the explicitly-numbered operational sequence and allowing submit before the required fields.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: No positive tabindex/JS, so F44/linters find nothing; the radio group, fieldset, headings, and labels are all valid, so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse pass. grid-row placement and the chosen DOM order are legal. Detecting it requires rendering the page, reading the visual numbering (1,2,3) to infer the intended sequence, and comparing it to the Tab order to see a later interdependent step focuses first — human visual/semantic reasoning no DOM scan does.

citation.quote: Determine if the focus order impacts the page meaning (e.g., form fields for a mailing address are presented in the expected sequence). Most noticeable when focus order does not follow the logical order of operation (normally top to bottom, left to right).

pages.scenario: Bakery (Birchwood Bakehouse) footer with a flex row of five social-media links. DOM order is Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, Pinterest, YouTube; CSS `order` paints them Instagram, Facebook, YouTube, TikTok, Pinterest. No tabindex, no JS. Verified tab order (DOM) differs from visual left-to-right order, but the links are an orderless set.
pages.mechanism: Flexbox `order` rearranges an unordered set of social links so tab order != visual order, but the links carry no sequence, dependency, or relationship, so the focus-order mismatch does not affect meaning or operability — the Trusted Tester's explicit 'row of social-media icons' Does-Not-Apply carve-out.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A naive visual-vs-DOM diff would flag this real mismatch; no tool ships such a rule because the disposition hinges on whether the focusable elements form a MEANINGFUL sequence — a human judgment. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse see five valid named links and correctly report nothing. Included so a judge recognizes an orderless link set and declines to flag it.

citation.quote: When focus order does not affect meaning or operability, this test Does Not Apply (e.g., a row of icons linking to social media may not need to be navigated in a particular order).

pages.scenario: Riverbank Playhouse seat-selection chart ('An Evening of Chamber Music'): an 8-column x 5-row (rows A-E) grid of seat <button>s numbered 1-40, placed by CSS grid-column/grid-row so they ascend left-to-right then top-to-bottom. The buttons are emitted column-major in the DOM (col1: 1,9,17,25,33; col2: 2,10,18,26,34; ...). No tabindex, no JS. Tab walks down each seat column (1,9,17,25,33, then 2,10,18,26,34, ...) rather than the visible 1..40 reading order.
pages.mechanism: CSS Grid 2-D placement (grid-column + grid-row) renders a seat chart numbered 1-40 left-to-right then top-to-bottom, but the seat <button>s are emitted COLUMN-MAJOR in the DOM (all of column 1's seats, then column 2's, ...), so with no tabindex/JS Tab traverses DOWN each column (1,9,17,25,33,2,10,18,...) instead of the visible seat-number sequence, destroying the meaning/operability of seat selection.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: No positive tabindex/JS, so F44/linters find nothing; every day is a real <button> with an aria-label date name and the group is named, so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse pass. Grid 2-D placement and the column-major DOM order are both valid. Detecting it requires rendering the calendar, recognizing the cells form an ordered date sequence read row-wise, and comparing that to the Tab path to see it walks columns — reconstructing a 2-D grid's intended visual reading order is a human visual/semantic task.

citation.quote: When the source order does not match the visual order, the tab order through the content must reflect the logical relationships in the content that are displayed visually.

aspects.title: Focus order interleaves between two semantically distinct sections/groups (the canonical Understanding form failure)
aspects.plain: Tabbing through a form jumps back and forth between two unrelated sections instead of finishing one before starting the next, breaking the user's sense of what belongs together.
aspects.description: The Understanding's own failing example: a form has a mailing/marketing-data section (name, address, city, state, postal) and a separate newsletter-checkbox section, but the tab order jumps between sections — name, then a checkbox, then street address, then another checkbox. Every field has a correct visible label, correct programmatic name/role, and is fully keyboard-operable; the interleaving can be produced purely by DOM order with no tabindex for a tool to flag. The failure is visible ONLY to an evaluator who understands which fields 'belong together' semantically (mailing-address fields form one group; newsletter choices form another) and that crossing between groups mid-sequence destroys the user's mental model. G59's applicant/spouse example is the passing mirror.
aspects.scLimb: Core meaning limb: 'focusable components receive focus in an order that preserves meaning'. Concretely the Understanding's failing example of tab order skipping between distinct form sections.
aspects.whyUncovered: 0 ACT cases. The fields are individually valid (labels present, operable), so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse report nothing — they have no model of which fields belong together semantically. Deciding that 'street address' belongs with 'city/state/postal' and NOT between two newsletter checkboxes is pure content-meaning grouping, exactly what the SC leaves to human judgment.

references.quote: the tab order for the form skips between fields in different sections of the form, so that focus moves from the name field to a checkbox, then to the street address, then to another checkbox.
All the interactive elements in the applicant section receive focus before any of the elements in the spouse section. The elements in each section receive focus in the reading order of that section.
Determine if the focus order impacts the page meaning (e.g., form fields for a mailing address are presented in the expected sequence).

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: E-commerce checkout (Northwind Outfitters) with two side-by-side boxed sections — Billing address and Shipping address — each visually holding Full name/Street/Apt/City/Postal in order. The whole form is one CSS grid; the DOM emits the two addresses interleaved line-by-line (billing-name, shipping-name, billing-street, shipping-street, ...), so with no tabindex the keyboard focus zig-zags between the billing and shipping cards on every Tab.
pages.mechanism: Focus order interleaves two semantically distinct address groups: pure DOM source order alternates billing-field then shipping-field for each line, so a keyboard user is pulled from the billing recipient to the shipping recipient before finishing the billing block. The fields are placed into their correct visual cards by CSS grid-template-areas, so visual grouping is intact while the focus sequence crosses the billing/shipping boundary on every Tab, destroying the user's 'I am entering my billing address' mental model.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: No tabindex exists to flag (tab order is the DOM default); every input has a correct label-for/programmatic name, every control is operable, contrast is fine — so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse pass the form. They have no model of which fields belong to the same address, so they cannot tell that 'shipping street' must not come between 'billing name' and 'billing street.' Recognising that street/apt/city/postal belong with the address they started, and that crossing into the other address mid-sequence breaks meaning, is content-grouping judgment the SC leaves to a human.

citation.quote: However, the tab order for the form skips between fields in different sections of the form, so that focus moves from the name field to a checkbox, then to the street address, then to another checkbox.

pages.scenario: Nonprofit contact form (Riverbend Animal Rescue) with a contact-message column (Name, Email, Message) on the left and a 'How did you hear about us?' checkbox group (Instagram, From a friend, Web search, Event or flyer) on the right. The checkbox divs are spliced between the contact fields in DOM source order, so with no tabindex the tab sequence is Name -> Instagram -> Email -> From a friend -> Message -> Web search -> Event -> Send — the Understanding document's own failing example recast as a contact form.
pages.mechanism: A second semantic group (marketing checkboxes) is interleaved INTO the middle of the first group (contact message). Pure DOM order places a checkbox after Name (before Email) and another after Email (before Message), so keyboard focus alternates between the contact group (left column) and the checkbox group (right column). The user composing a message is repeatedly interrupted to answer an unrelated marketing question one checkbox at a time, so neither group can be completed as a coherent unit.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: No tabindex; every text field and checkbox has a correct label-for and is operable; the group heading is a real visible element; contrast passes — so the page is clean to axe/WAVE/Lighthouse. They cannot tell that Email and Message belong with Name while the checkboxes are a separate question — that is content meaning. Detecting that the checkbox group has been interleaved into the contact group, rather than placed after it, requires a human reading the two questions and knowing they should be answered as two coherent blocks.

citation.quote: Another section of the form includes several checkboxes so that users can indicate newsletters they want to receive. However, the tab order for the form skips between fields in different sections of the form, so that focus moves from the name field to a checkbox, then to the street address, then to another checkbox.

pages.scenario: Round-trip flight search (SkyHop) with two vertically stacked, headed panels — Outbound flight (From, To, Depart date, Passengers) above Return flight (From, To, Return date, Cabin). The DOM emits the eight fields in alternating legs (outbound-From, return-From, outbound-To, return-To, ...) and CSS grid routes each field back into its panel, so with no tabindex keyboard focus bounces between the outbound and return legs on every Tab while a sighted user sees two clean stacked cards.
pages.mechanism: Two semantic groups (the outbound and return trip legs) are interleaved by raw source order, so focus alternates between the two stacked panels instead of completing one leg before the other. For a round trip the legs are conceptually sequential (go, then return); interleaving them mid-entry forces the user to specify the return origin before finishing the outbound leg and makes it easy to type a return city into an outbound field, corrupting the model of which leg is being edited.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: No tabindex; every input/select has a correct label-for and is operable; both panels have visible headings; contrast passes — so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse see a valid form. They have no model that 'Depart date and Passengers belong with the outbound From/To' and that the return fields are a separate leg, so they cannot detect that the return fields are woven into the outbound leg. Recognising the two trip legs as distinct groups requires understanding the travel content.

citation.quote: Determine if the focus order impacts the page meaning (e.g., form fields for a mailing address are presented in the expected sequence).

pages.scenario: Joint loan application (Meridian Credit Union) with two side-by-side boxed sections — Applicant and Co-applicant — each with Full name, Date of birth, Annual income, Employer. Visually near-identical to the failing dual-section cases, but each section is a real fieldset containing its own fields in order, so the natural DOM order keeps each group whole: all four applicant fields are tabbed before any co-applicant field (the G59 passing pattern). PASS counter-example included so a judge cannot pass the failing cases by merely detecting 'two groups exist.'
pages.mechanism: Focus order follows the sequences and relationships in the content (G59): each applicant fieldset contains its own four fields in order, so the keyboard sequence completes the entire Applicant group (left column) before entering the entire Co-applicant group (right column). Focus does not follow visual left-then-right field-by-field; it follows the meaningful order (one applicant, then the other), which the Understanding explicitly permits — so meaning is preserved and the SC is satisfied.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Automated tools also report no violation here, but for the wrong reason: they cannot distinguish this passing page from the failing interleaved pages, because both have valid labels, valid names, no tabindex, and two grouped sections — the same clean markup signature. Only a human (or a model reasoning about content) can confirm that here the focus order keeps each applicant whole, whereas in the failing cases it crosses the group boundary mid-sequence. The discriminator is the focus-order-vs-meaning judgment, not 'two groups exist' detection.

citation.quote: One section contains information about an applicant; the other section contains information about the applicant's spouse. All the interactive elements in the applicant section receive focus before any of the elements in the spouse section.

pages.scenario: RTL Arabic (lang=ar, dir=rtl) two-attendee conference registration (مؤتمر الابتكار التقني) with two grouped, headed cards — الحاضر الأول (Attendee 1, on the right per RTL) and الحاضر الثاني (Attendee 2, on the left) — each with full name, email, job title, dietary preference. The DOM interleaves the two attendees field-by-field, so with no tabindex keyboard focus alternates between the right (Attendee 1) and left (Attendee 2) cards on every Tab.
pages.mechanism: Two semantic groups (two attendees) are interleaved by raw DOM order in an RTL context where the expected logical order is right-to-left. Pure source order alternates attendee1-name, attendee2-name, attendee1-email, attendee2-email, ..., so focus jumps from the right card (Attendee 1) to the left card (Attendee 2) and back on each Tab. The registrant enters the first person's name, is thrown to the second person's name, then back to the first person's email, collapsing the per-attendee model; the RTL direction adds a layer because a left-to-right assumption would even misjudge which order counts as logical.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: lang/dir are correct, every input/select has a correct label-for, both cards have visible headings, there is no tabindex, and contrast passes — so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse report a clean, well-localised form. They have no model that email/job/diet belong with the same attendee's name, nor do they reason about RTL logical order. Detecting that Attendee 2's fields are woven into Attendee 1's group requires reading the Arabic content, grouping each attendee, and judging focus order against that grouping in the correct reading direction.

citation.quote: Care should be taken so that the focus order makes sense to both of these sets of users and does not appear to either of them to jump around randomly.

pages.scenario: ATS job application (Talentforge) Background step, single-column layout with two stacked sections — Education (Highest degree, School/university, Graduation year) wholly above Work experience (Most recent job title, Most recent company, Years in role). The DOM interleaves the two sections row-by-row (education-degree, work-title, education-school, work-company, ...) and CSS grid pins each field into its section block, so with no tabindex keyboard focus jumps ~300px down to Work and back up to Education on alternate Tabs while a sighted user sees two clean stacked blocks.
pages.mechanism: Two semantic groups (Education vs. Work experience) are interleaved by raw DOM order in a single-column layout, so focus alternates between the two CV sections instead of completing each. The applicant starts describing their degree, is yanked down past the 'Work experience' heading into their job history, then back up to their school — the two distinct parts of a résumé are woven together, making it easy to type a university into the company field or a job title where the degree belongs.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: No tabindex; every input/select has a correct label-for and is operable; both sections have visible headings; contrast passes — so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse see a valid form. They have no model that School/university and Graduation year belong with Highest degree (Education) and that the job fields are a separate section, so they cannot detect that the Work fields are woven into the Education section. Recognising the two CV sections as distinct groups, and that focus crosses between them on every Tab, requires understanding the content.

citation.quote: Most noticeable when focus order does not follow the logical order of operation (normally top to bottom, left to right).

aspects.title: Revealed non-modal dialog/menu is not next in the navigation order (F85, open branch)
aspects.plain: Clicking a button opens an in-page dialog or menu, but pressing Tab next lands on unrelated page content instead of inside the thing that just appeared.
aspects.description: F85's core failure: a trigger button reveals an in-page dialog or menu, but the revealed widget is NOT focus-managed AND is not next in the sequential navigation order — typically because the dialog markup sits at the end of the DOM. After activating the trigger, the keyboard user's focus stays on (or just after) the trigger, so to reach the visually-overlaid dialog they must tab through the entire rest of the page. On a self-contained HTML page this is testable with a tiny script that only toggles visibility (no focus move). It requires multi-state interaction judgment: you must activate the control, then evaluate where focus lands relative to where it visually/logically should be. This is the TT 4.F step 2b 'reveal hidden content... check the focus order to, from, and within the revealed content' manual step.
aspects.scLimb: Revealed/hidden-content traversal limb (TT 4.F step 2b) + F85 open branch — focus to/within revealed content not adjacent to its trigger.
aspects.whyUncovered: 0 ACT cases for 2.4.3, and F85 is explicitly a manual procedure ('Activate the trigger control via the keyboard'). Static analysis cannot know that the visually-overlaid dialog is the user's intended next interaction; it sees a hidden div somewhere in the DOM. No automated tool simulates 'open, then check the next Tab stop is in the dialog.'

references.quote: If focus is not set to the dialog or menu, or a logical focusable descendent of these widgets, and the widget or a focusable descendent is not next in the sequential navigation order, it will be difficult for the keyboard user to operate the dialog or menu.

Since the dialog is found at the end of the DOM, it is at the end of the keyboard navigation order. Because a user's focus isn't managed... the user will need to tab through the rest of the web page before they can interact with the dialog.

It may be necessary to use the keyboard to activate trigger controls that reveal hidden content with focusable elements (menus, dialogs, modal dialog boxes, expandable tree list) to check the focus order to, from, and within the revealed content.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: Municipal government portal: a 'Subscribe to alerts' button in a top announcement bar reveals a centered non-modal newsletter dialog whose markup is the last block before </body>; the open handler only toggles a CSS .open class and never moves focus, so after keyboard activation focus stays on the trigger and the next Tab lands on the first nav/content link, not the dialog.
pages.mechanism: F85 open branch: dialog is at the end of the DOM (after the footer) and openDialog() performs no .focus(); both F85 step-1 checks are false (focus not set into dialog AND next Tab does not enter it), so the keyboard user must traverse the whole page to reach the visually-centered email field.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Markup is well-formed: role=dialog, resolving aria-labelledby/aria-describedby, label[for] on the email input, fine contrast — axe/WAVE/Lighthouse all pass. The defect is purely positional+behavioral (dialog DOM position far from trigger AND no focus move on open), only observable by activating the trigger and watching where the next Tab lands relative to where the dialog visually appears; static single-snapshot scanners just see a hidden div somewhere in the DOM.

citation.quote: A non-native HTML dialog is created, with it being marked up at the end of the DOM (Document Object Model). Script was created to reveal the dialog, but no script was added to move focus to it. The dialog is visually positioned above the content of the page and the user's focus isn't moved to the dialog. Since the dialog is found at the end of the DOM, it is at the end of the keyboard navigation order. Because a user's focus isn't managed, or a keyboard mechanism isn't provided to allow them to immediately move to the invoked dialog, the user will need to tab through the rest of the web page before they can interact with the dialog.

pages.scenario: Restaurant ordering site: a top-bar 'Menu ▾' button reveals a navigation flyout (role=menu) that appears visually directly under the button but whose markup is the last element in <body>; the click handler flips .open and aria-expanded only, with no focus move, so the next Tab from the button goes to the first page link ('Start your order'), not the menu items.
pages.mechanism: F85 open branch / TT 4.F step 2b: the revealed role=menu sits at the end of the DOM and the handler never focuses a menuitem; aria-expanded='true' even announces 'expanded' reinforcing the illusion, yet both F85 step-1 checks are false so the six menu items are unreachable until the end of the tab order.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The flyout is more correct on paper than most (real role=menu/menuitem, working aria-haspopup, aria-expanded that updates) so nothing is missing or empty and scanners pass; aria-expanded='true' would even nudge a naive heuristic toward 'fine.' The failure that activating the trigger strands focus and the menu is at the end of the tab order rather than adjacent is a runtime multi-state keyboard behavior no DOM scan exercises.

citation.quote: It may be necessary to use the keyboard to **activate trigger controls that reveal hidden content** with focusable elements (menus, dialogs, modal dialog boxes, expandable tree list) to check the focus order to, from, and within the revealed content.

pages.scenario: Boundary PASS counter-example: a coffee-roaster wholesale page where the 'Get the wholesale price list' button reveals a non-modal dialog whose markup is placed immediately after the trigger, so the dialog's email field is the very next node in source order; the visibility-only toggle is correct here and dismissal returns focus to the trigger.
pages.mechanism: WCAG Understanding non-modal PASS pattern: because the dialog's interactive elements come immediately after the button in source order, F85 step-1's second check is TRUE (moving focus forward once enters the dialog) even with no focus script, and btn.focus() on dismiss satisfies F85 step 2 — focus order goes trigger -> dialog fields -> following content, preserving meaning and operability.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Statically, case-03 and case-01 are indistinguishable (both a role=dialog with a labelled email field and a visibility toggle), so tools return identical 'no issues' on both. Only by activating the trigger and observing the next Tab land inside the panel (here) versus skipping to unrelated content (case-01) can a human confirm the PASS verdict, which depends on DOM adjacency plus observed tab order that static analysis does not evaluate.

citation.quote: A web page implements non-modal dialogs. When the trigger button is activated, a dialog opens. The interactive elements in the dialog are inserted in the focus order immediately after the button. When the dialog is open, the focus order goes from the button to the elements of the dialog, then to the interactive element following the button. When the dialog is closed, the focus order goes from the button to the following element.

pages.scenario: Real-estate listings results page: a toolbar 'Filters' button reveals a filter form (price/bedrooms/type) that is position:fixed to appear right beside the button on the left, but whose markup is the last element in the document after every listing and the footer; the toggle adds .open only, with no focus move, so the next Tab goes to 'Sort: Newest' and then through eight listing links before reaching the filter controls.
pages.mechanism: F85 open branch with geometry-vs-source mismatch: CSS position:fixed;left:26px renders the panel beside the button while its DOM index is dead last; no .focus() on open, so both F85 step-1 checks are false. Screen-magnifier users are hit hardest — they see the magnified filter controls beside the button, Tab expecting to land there, and their focus ring vanishes off into the results grid outside their viewport.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The filter form is exemplary static markup (fieldset/legend grouping, labelled radios/checkboxes, aria-label on the form, working aria-expanded) so scanners find nothing. A static tool cannot compute that position:fixed;left:26px renders the panel beside the button while its DOM position is last, nor know the panel should be the next Tab stop once opened; confirming the failure requires opening it, seeing where it renders, and tabbing to find focus goes elsewhere.

citation.quote: The dialog is visually positioned above the content of the page and the user's focus isn't moved to the dialog. Since the dialog is found at the end of the DOM, it is at the end of the keyboard navigation order.

pages.scenario: University admissions page: an 'Explore Northgate ▾' mega-menu button in the header partial reveals a disclosure panel — a labelled <nav aria-label='Explore Northgate'> of plain <a> links (no role=menu/menuitem) — emitted by the footer theme partial, so its markup sits near the end of the DOM while position:absolute;top:96px floats it under the header to look attached; opening it only toggles .open/aria-expanded with no focus move, so the next Tab from the trigger goes to header/main-content links, not into the panel.
pages.mechanism: F85 open branch via include-file split: the trigger (header partial) and the revealed disclosure panel (footer theme partial) are far apart in the flattened DOM, and the open handler performs no focus move (zero .focus() calls), so both F85 step-1 checks are false and the eight program links are reachable only after tabbing the whole page and footer.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Static analysis sees a syntactically clean mega-menu (menu button with aria-haspopup/aria-expanded, role=menu with labelled menuitems, real headings, working Escape) and cannot know the page was assembled from two include files; it sees one flattened DOM where the panel happens to be near the bottom. The runtime relationship between a header trigger and a footer-rendered menu floated to look adjacent is only revealed by opening it and observing the next Tab leave the menu.

citation.quote: This describes the failure condition that results when a web page opens a dialog or menu interface component embedded on the page in a way that makes it difficult for a keyboard user to operate because of its position in the sequential navigation order.

pages.scenario: Arabic RTL developer forum thread: each comment has a 'رد' (Reply) button; activating Reply on the first comment reveals a reply form whose markup is appended at the very end of the thread DOM (after every other post and the footer) by a framework rendering one shared form per thread; the toggle flips .open/aria-expanded only with no focus move, so the next Tab goes to 'إعجاب' (Like) and through the rest of the thread before reaching the textarea.
pages.mechanism: F85 open branch in an RTL context: the per-comment Reply trigger and the singleton end-of-thread form are far apart in source order, and no .focus() targets the textarea on open; crucially dir=rtl mirrors visual layout but the sequential focus order still follows DOM order, so the end-of-DOM form is dead last and both F85 step-1 checks are false.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The page is well-formed and even careful (correct lang=ar/dir=rtl, aria-label naming which comment the form replies to, label[for] on the textarea, updating aria-expanded) so scanners pass and may be reassured by the RTL correctness. Static tools commonly conflate dir=rtl with reversed tab order; here a human must know Tab follows DOM order, then actually open the form and observe focus land elsewhere — none of which is in a single-snapshot scan.

citation.quote: Activate the trigger control via the keyboard. — Check whether focus has been set to the menu, dialog, or a logical focusable descendent of the widget. — If not, check whether moving the focus forward once in the sequential navigation order puts focus in the menu or dialog.

aspects.title: Focus not returned (or returned illogically) after a dialog/menu is dismissed (F85, close branch + modal return)
aspects.plain: After closing a dialog, focus is dumped at the top of the page instead of returning to the button that opened it, stranding keyboard users.
aspects.description: F85's second failure branch and the Understanding's modal example: after the user dismisses an in-page menu or dialog, focus is dumped on document.body (or scrolls to top), forcing the user to tab from the very start of the page back to where they were. The pass condition is nuanced: focus should return to the trigger control, OR — if the trigger was removed by the action — to a logical neighboring element (F85's tag-delete note). Evaluating this requires understanding what the 'logical' return point is given what the action did: deleting an item should move focus to the next item, not the top of the page; cancelling should return to the trigger. This is a state-transition reasoning task.
aspects.scLimb: Revealed/hidden-content traversal limb (focus FROM revealed content, TT 4.F step 2b) + F85 close branch + Understanding modal 'focus returns to the button or the element following the button'.
aspects.whyUncovered: 0 ACT cases. The 'where should focus go after close' decision depends on the semantics of the action that closed the widget (cancel vs delete vs save), which no static tool models. F85 marks it manual ('Check whether keyboard focus is put back on the trigger control'). The 'logical neighbor' exception means even a tool that naively checked 'focus == trigger' would mis-fire on the legitimate delete-then-move-to-next case.

references.quote: When a menu is dismissed, it is removed or hidden from the web page and focus is set to the document. The user must tab from the beginning of the navigation sequence to reach the point from which the menu was opened.

If the trigger control itself was removed as a result of the activation, check if the focus has been put on the interactive element immediately preceding or following the removed trigger control, or wherever is logical.
When the dialog is dismissed, focus returns to the button or the element following the button.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: SaaS analytics dashboard (Metrico) 'Dashboard settings' modal. On open, focus correctly moves into the dialog; on close (via ×, Cancel, Save, or Escape — all routed through one closeDialog()), focus is dropped to document.body instead of returning to the 'Dashboard settings' trigger, so the next Tab restarts at the top-of-page header nav.
pages.mechanism: closeDialog() hides the overlay and explicitly blurs/sets focus to document.body without calling openBtn.focus(); F85 'focus is set to the document' close-branch failure — verified by Puppeteer: after Escape, document.activeElement === body and the next Tab lands on the first header nav link (Overview), forcing the keyboard user to tab from the page top back to the toolbar.
pages.primarySelector: #open-settings (trigger that should regain focus); defect in #settings-dialog closeDialog() handler
pages.selectorNote: Settings trigger that should regain focus when #settings-dialog closeDialog runs; defect drops focus to body
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The dialog passes every static check (valid role=dialog/aria-modal, aria-labelledby resolves to a real heading, close button has aria-label, fields labeled, focus correctly moved INTO the dialog on open). axe/WAVE/Lighthouse audit one DOM snapshot and never open then dismiss the dialog to observe focus landing on document.body; detecting the lost focus return is a runtime close-then-Tab observation requiring a human or AT.

citation.quote: When a menu is dismissed, it is removed or hidden from the web page and focus is set to the document. The user must tab from the beginning of the navigation sequence to reach the point from which the menu was opened.

pages.scenario: Healthcare patient portal (Riverbend) medication list with per-row Remove and an alertdialog confirm. Cancel ('Keep it') correctly returns focus to the Remove trigger, but Confirm ('Remove') deletes the row, calls window.scrollTo(0,0), and focuses the first header nav link instead of the next/previous medication's controls — the logical neighbor F85 requires when the trigger is removed.
pages.mechanism: confirmRemove() removes li[data-med] (detaching the focused Remove button) then focuses .topbar nav a; F85 trigger-removed sub-case demands focus move to the preceding/following item 'or wherever is logical'. Verified by Puppeteer: after confirming Metformin's deletion, row is removed and activeElement is the top nav link 'Appointments'; the cancel path correctly returns to the Remove button.
pages.primarySelector: #c-confirm handler (confirmRemove); should target the adjacent li in #med-list
pages.selectorNote: First Remove trigger; on confirmRemove the deleted row's logical neighbour should get focus but page scrolls to top
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Where focus should go depends on action semantics: cancel must return to trigger, but a delete that removes the trigger must move to the adjacent item. A naive 'focus must equal the trigger after close' rule would be wrong on any correct delete (trigger no longer exists), so tools cannot encode it without modeling the action's meaning. Markup is clean (role=alertdialog, aria-modal, labelled/described, even a correct cancel path), so static scanners report nothing.

citation.quote: If the trigger control itself was removed as a result of the activation, check if the focus has been put on the interactive element immediately preceding or following the removed trigger control, or wherever is logical.

pages.scenario: Developer issue tracker (Forge) label-chip list. Each chip's × opens an alertdialog confirm; confirming deletes the chip and moves focus to the NEXT chip's × (falling back to the previous chip when the deleted one was last, and to '+ Add label' when none remain). This is the F85 tag-delete exception that must NOT be flagged. Cancel returns to the chip's × (chip survives).
pages.mechanism: confirmRemove() resolves a logical neighbor (nextElementSibling.x || previousElementSibling.x || .addlabel) and focuses it after removing li.chip; satisfies F85 step 2's removed-trigger branch. Verified by Puppeteer: deleting the middle 'payments' chip lands focus on 'needs-repro' remove button; deleting the last 'p1' chip lands focus on the now-last chip's remove button.
pages.selectorNote: First label remove button; confirmRemove correctly routes focus to neighbouring chip .x (PASS path)
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: This case exposes automation's false-positive mode: any simple rule a tool could encode — 'after a dialog closes, focus must return to the element that opened it' — would WRONGLY flag this correct page because the opening element no longer exists after a delete. Static scans report nothing (ARIA/labelling clean). Judging it a PASS requires reasoning that a deletion legitimately removes the trigger and the chosen neighbor is the meaningful landing point.

citation.quote: On confirming the deletion, the tag is deleted, the modal dialog closes, and focus is placed on the next tag in the list of tags. Placing focus onto a different, but logical, control is not a failure of Success Criterion 2.4.3.

pages.scenario: News/editorial site (The Meridian) full-screen search overlay opened from the masthead. On open it sets aria-hidden=false and moves focus into the search input; on Escape/Close it re-applies aria-hidden=true and hides the overlay but never restores focus to the Search trigger, leaving focus stranded on the now-hidden input so the next Tab restarts from the top of the page.
pages.mechanism: closeSearch() toggles aria-hidden=true + the open class (display:none) without openBtn.focus(); focus lingers on #q inside a hidden subtree. Verified by Puppeteer: after Escape, activeElement is #q with a 0x0 box inside a display:none container, and the next Tab moves to #open-search (the first focusable control at the page top), confirming the restart-from-top failure.
pages.primarySelector: #open-search (trigger that should regain focus); defect in #search-overlay closeSearch() handler
pages.selectorNote: Search trigger that should regain focus when #search-overlay closeSearch runs; defect leaves focus on hidden overlay
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: In the overlay's resting (closed) state — the only state a page-load scan sees — aria-hidden=true sits on a display:none container, which is valid, so the axe 'aria-hidden must not contain focusable elements' rule does not fire (display:none removes descendants from the focus order). The defect is purely temporal: focus is only stranded AFTER a keyboard open-then-Escape, a transition static snapshots never exercise.

citation.quote: When a menu is dismissed, it is removed or hidden from the web page and focus is set to the document. The user must tab from the beginning of the navigation sequence to reach the point from which the menu was opened.

pages.scenario: E-commerce seller console (Looma) orders table where every row has an identical Actions menu button (aria-haspopup/aria-expanded, role=menu/menuitem, accessible names, correct on-open focus). Three menus (rows 1,3,4) return focus to their trigger on close; the visually-identical twin on row 2 (#LG-90411) calls document.activeElement.blur() on close, dropping focus to document.body so the next Tab restarts from the sidebar nav. The page fails because of that one broken menu.
pages.mechanism: Row-2 close() runs document.activeElement.blur() (focus -> body) instead of trg.focus(); F85 step 2 'keyboard focus is put back on the trigger control' is violated for that menu only. Verified by Puppeteer: closing row-1 menu lands focus on #trg-1 (PASS), while closing the markup-identical row-2 menu lands on document.body (FAIL).
pages.selectorNote: Row 2 Actions trigger; #menu-2 close blurs activeElement to body instead of returning focus to #trg-2 (FAIL)
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: All four menus are structurally identical and structurally valid; nothing in any DOM snapshot distinguishes the broken one — the only difference is a single line in a JS close handler that runs at dismissal time. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse never open each menu, select an item, and observe focus, and could not infer that a sibling with identical markup behaves differently at runtime. Catching the broken twin requires operating each menu by keyboard.

citation.quote: Check whether keyboard focus is put back on the trigger control

pages.scenario: Job board / ATS profile (Hirelane) with an 'Edit profile' button opening a three-step modal wizard (Basics → Availability → Summary). Each step moves focus to its first field; the final step swaps Next for Done. Pressing Done commits the edited values, closes the wizard, and returns focus to the originating 'Edit profile' trigger — the same return as Cancel and Escape — the affirmative PASS for terminal-confirm dismissal.
pages.mechanism: All exits (Cancel, Escape, Done) route through closeWizard() which calls editBtn.focus(); commitAndClose() writes values back then returns focus to the trigger, satisfying F85 step 2 and the Understanding modal example. Verified by Puppeteer: stepping to Done lands focus back on #edit-profile and the committed headline value is written into the profile card.
pages.selectorNote: Edit-profile trigger; wizard Done (commitAndClose->closeWizard) correctly returns focus to #edit-profile (PASS)
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: This is a PASS automation can neither confirm nor refute from a snapshot: per-step focus moves, the aria-live step announcement, and the final focus-return are all runtime behaviors. A static scan sees a valid role=dialog with labeled fields and reports nothing — it cannot demonstrate the criterion is MET, which depends on operating the wizard to Done and observing focus land on #edit-profile.

citation.quote: When the dialog is dismissed, focus returns to the button or the element following the button.

aspects.title: Modal dialog focus is not contained — forward Tab or backward Shift+Tab escapes behind the inert backdrop
aspects.plain: A popup dialog looks like it blocks the page, but pressing Shift+Tab or Tab at its edge lets focus slip out to the hidden content behind it.
aspects.description: The Understanding modal example and TT 4.F step 3 require that for a modal, keyboard focus navigating BOTH forward and backward remains within the dialog until it closes, with outside content inert. The subtle, human-judgment failure: a 'modal' that looks modal (dim backdrop, centered card) and may even trap forward Tab, but Shift+Tab (backward) escapes to the page behind it, or the last element's forward Tab leaks to page content. Because TT says backward order need not mirror forward but must still preserve operability, evaluating containment requires testing BOTH directions and judging whether escaped focus lands the user somewhere that destroys the modal's operability. This is distinct from a 2.1.2 keyboard trap (inability to leave); here the failure is leaving when the user should be contained.
aspects.scLimb: Modal-dialog containment limb (TT 4.F step 3: 'keyboard focus navigating both forward and backward should remain within the modal dialog box until it is closed') + backward-focus-order limb (TT 4.F step 2d).
aspects.whyUncovered: 0 ACT cases. Containment is a runtime, bidirectional interaction property: a static rule cannot determine that a div with role=dialog actually keeps focus inside under Shift+Tab, nor that the backdrop content was made inert. The forward-vs-backward asymmetry (forward trapped, backward leaking) is precisely the manual both-directions check TT calls out and no automated checker performs.

references.quote: For modal dialog boxes, keyboard focus navigating both forward and backward should remain within the modal dialog box until it is closed.
As long as the dialog is open, all web page content outside the dialog becomes inert and cannot receive focus
Backward focus order does not have to mirror the forward focus order. However, it must preserve the meaning and operability of the page.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: Northbridge Bank 'Confirm transfer' modal (dim backdrop + centered card). A hand-rolled focus trap wraps only the FORWARD direction; the Shift+Tab branch was never written. Forward Tab is perfectly trapped, but Shift+Tab from the first control (the amount field) falls through to the browser default and lands on the page header's 'Log out' link behind the non-inert backdrop.
pages.mechanism: Asymmetric modal containment: the keydown handler on #modal implements only the `!e.shiftKey && activeElement===last` forward wrap and has no backward branch, and the background (header/main) is never made inert/aria-hidden. So backward Shift+Tab from the first control escapes the open modal onto an operable destructive control ('Log out') behind the backdrop, violating TT 4.F step 3's both-directions containment.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: role=dialog, aria-modal=true, aria-labelledby to a visible title, labelled fields and named buttons are all present, and contrast is fine — axe reports zero violations. aria-modal is treated as a declaration, not verified. Detecting the leak requires a human to press Shift+Tab specifically from the first control and observe focus land behind the backdrop, plus the judgment that a modal must contain focus in BOTH directions; no static checker drives bidirectional Tab or infers from the keydown source that the backward branch is missing while the forward branch is present.

citation.quote: For modal dialog boxes, keyboard focus navigating both forward and backward should remain within the modal dialog box until it is closed.

pages.scenario: Hexagon Arena box-office 'Have a promo code?' jQuery-UI-style dialog. The developer moved initial focus in and restored it on close but never added a Tab wrap on the last control. Pressing Tab on the 'Apply code' button (the dialog's last control) follows DOM order to the page's first focusable element — a visually-hidden 'Skip to footer' skip-link — instead of cycling back to the first dialog control.
pages.mechanism: Forward containment breaks at the dialog's trailing boundary: there is no keydown wrap handler at all, so Tab on #dlg-apply moves to the next focusable in document order (#skip-footer at the top of the page), and the background is not inert. Forward focus escapes the open modal onto page chrome, violating TT 4.F step 3 (focus must remain within the modal in both directions).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every static signal is healthy — role=dialog, aria-modal=true, aria-labelledby to the visible title, labelled inputs, named buttons, and a textbook visible-on-focus skip-link that scanners actively reward — so axe reports no issue. The failure is the ABSENCE of a wrap (no containment handler), which a linter cannot flag. Catching it requires a human to Tab to the LAST dialog control and press Tab once more, then recognise that focus landing on a page-level skip-link while a modal is open violates containment; no tool drives Tab to a widget boundary or reasons about modal containment.

citation.doc: Trusted Tester v5.1.3 — Test 4.F Focus Order, How to Test step 3 (refs/trusted-tester/sc-2.4.3-focus-order.md)
citation.quote: For modal dialog boxes, keyboard focus navigating both forward and backward should remain within the modal dialog box until it is closed.

pages.scenario: The Tideline Review newsletter-signup promo (Privy/Mailchimp-style) appears over a dark scrim as a centered card. It looks modal and the developer moved initial focus into the email field, but there is NO focus trap and the background was never made inert/aria-hidden. Tabbing forward from the email field walks past Subscribe onto the article's 'Search the archive' input and button, hidden under the scrim; Shift+Tab leaks too.
pages.mechanism: Visual-only modality: a position:fixed z-index scrim dims the page but does not remove background content from the tab sequence or accessibility tree. The promo is a non-dialog <section aria-label> with no role=dialog/aria-modal, no trap, and no inert, so both forward Tab and backward Shift+Tab reach the background search controls (#q, #q-go) hidden beneath the scrim, violating modal containment in both directions.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: There is deliberately no role=dialog/aria-modal — the promo is a plain styled landmark section, exactly as many marketing widgets ship — so a containment rule has nothing to key on; a scanner just sees two ordinary well-labelled forms in valid landmarks (axe is clean, region rule satisfied). Recognising the failure requires the human judgment that the scrim communicates modality visually, plus driving Tab to observe focus sliding under the scrim onto the search field; static tools do neither.

citation.quote: As long as the dialog is open, all web page content outside the dialog becomes inert and cannot receive focus (though, depending on implementation, the focus cycle might still include user agent controls).

pages.scenario: Calverton DMV 'Confirm renewal & payment' modal. The developer used the modern recommended technique — set the page wrapper's inert=true and rely on inert (no JS trap) to contain focus. But a OneTrust-style cookie-consent banner was injected by the tag manager as a direct child of <body>, OUTSIDE the inerted #page wrapper, so its 'Accept all cookies' / 'Manage' buttons stay focusable. Tab off the dialog's last control and Shift+Tab off its first control both land on the cookie buttons.
pages.mechanism: Scoping mismatch between the inerted subtree and the set of background focusables: page.inert=true neutralises only #page, but #cookie is a body-level sibling, so #cookie-accept/#cookie-manage remain in the tab order. With #page inert, the live focusables are the dialog's controls plus the two banner buttons, so forward Tab from #pay and backward Shift+Tab from #card both escape the open modal onto an operable, site-wide consent control behind the backdrop.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: This is the hardest variant: inert IS applied (a tool that checks for inert sees the good pattern), role=dialog/aria-modal/aria-labelledby/labels are all present, and the cookie banner is valid named landmark markup — axe is clean. The failure is a scoping error (inerted subtree does not match where every focusable lives because a sibling was injected outside it). Detecting it requires knowing the DOM topology (banner is a body sibling, not inside #page) and Tabbing off both dialog edges; no tool reasons about which subtree was inerted versus where focusables are, nor drives the keyboard.

citation.doc: WCAG 2.2 Understanding SC 2.4.3 — Examples of Focus Order, modal example (wcag-understanding/focus-order.html)
citation.quote: As long as the dialog is open, all web page content outside the dialog becomes inert and cannot receive focus (though, depending on implementation, the focus cycle might still include user agent controls).

pages.scenario: Brightpath LMS 'Submit Lab Report 3' modal opened with native dialog.showModal() (UA-managed inert + containment). Inside, the formatting toolbar is an APG roving-tabindex group (one Tab stop, arrow-key navigation), so the FORWARD Tab order and the BACKWARD Shift+Tab order are intentionally NOT mirror images — yet focus never leaves the dialog and every control stays reachable and operable. PASS counter-example for the 'backward need not mirror forward' limb (TT 4.F step 2d).
pages.mechanism: Native showModal() makes content outside <dialog> inert, so neither Tab nor Shift+Tab can leave the dialog (verified: 0 page-content focus hits over 20 Tabs; the background trigger is non-focusable while open). The roving-tabindex toolbar is a single tab stop, so the forward and backward sequences differ by design, but every control remains reachable (arrows within the toolbar) and operable. TT 4.F step 2d permits a non-mirrored backward order as long as meaning and operability are preserved, so this conforms.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: This case exists to catch FALSE POSITIVES. A naive checker or over-eager heuristic might compute the forward and backward Tab sequences, notice they are not exact reverses (because of the roving toolbar), and wrongly flag a focus-order problem. A correct verdict requires applying TT 4.F step 2d (backward need not mirror forward) and confirming by keyboard that focus never leaves the dialog and every control is reachable — judgments a static tool cannot make, since it cannot drive showModal() containment or arrow-key roving navigation.
