citation.quote: Backward focus order does not have to mirror the forward focus order. However, it must preserve the meaning and operability of the page.

pages.scenario: Al-Nakheel Clinic (Arabic, lang=ar dir=rtl) 'Confirm appointment' modal. The developer hand-rolled the dialog (no native <dialog>) but did containment correctly: on open they set the background wrapper inert AND aria-hidden=true, and installed a keydown handler that wraps BOTH directions (Tab on last -> first, Shift+Tab on first -> last). In RTL the visual left/right is mirrored but Tab semantics are unchanged. Focus never escapes the modal in either direction. PASS boundary that directly contrasts case-01.
pages.mechanism: Correct bidirectional containment with defence in depth (verified: 0 escapes forward or backward): the keydown trap on #modal implements both the `e.shiftKey && activeElement===first -> last` backward wrap and the `!e.shiftKey && activeElement===last -> first` forward wrap, and #page is set inert + aria-hidden=true while the modal is open, so even a missed wrap would not reach the background. RTL does not change Tab/Shift+Tab semantics and the author introduced no direction bug, so focus stays within the open modal both ways and all controls remain operable.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Automated tools cannot confirm this PASS for the same reason they miss the failing cases: they do not drive the keyboard, so they cannot prove that BOTH Tab and Shift+Tab wrap inside. The page is included so the corpus rewards a verdict reached by bidirectional keyboard testing rather than pattern-matching: a model that sees 'hand-rolled trap' or 'RTL' and assumes a direction bug would wrongly fail it. The correct PASS depends on a human/agent observing the present backward branch and confirming containment in both directions.

citation.doc: Trusted Tester v5.1.3 — Test 4.F Focus Order, How to Test step 3 (refs/trusted-tester/sc-2.4.3-focus-order.md)
citation.quote: For modal dialog boxes, keyboard focus navigating both forward and backward should remain within the modal dialog box until it is closed.

aspects.title: Multiple valid orders — row-wise vs column-wise grid/table traversal must NOT be flagged
aspects.plain: A grid or table of controls can legitimately be tabbed either row-by-row or column-by-column, so flagging the column-wise order as broken would be a false alarm.
aspects.description: The false-positive trap built into the SC: when content has two-dimensional structure (a table of interactive controls, a grid of cards), EITHER row-by-row OR column-by-column focus order can satisfy the SC because both 'reflect the logical relationships in the content.' An evaluator must recognize that a column-wise tab order through a data-entry table is NOT a violation just because it isn't the more common row-wise order — provided meaning/operation are preserved. The hard judgment is distinguishing 'a different-but-valid logical order' from 'an order that destroys meaning.' The SC explicitly says only one valid order need be provided. This aspect exists to measure whether a judge OVER-flags valid alternatives.
aspects.scLimb: Multiple-valid-orders limb: 'There may be different orders that reflect logical relationships... Either order may satisfy this success criterion' and 'If there is more than one order that preserves meaning and operability, only one of them needs to be provided.'
aspects.whyUncovered: 0 ACT cases. An automated tool has no concept of 'this alternative order still reflects a logical relationship'; it would either ignore order entirely or naively flag any non-source/non-left-to-right order. The spec demands the evaluator simultaneously hold several acceptable orders — a reasoning task, not a pattern match.

references.quote: moving through components in a table one row at a time or one column at a time both reflect the logical relationships in the content. Either order may satisfy this success criterion.
If there is more than one order that preserves meaning and operability, only one of them needs to be provided.
Focus order does not necessarily need to be top to bottom, left to right.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: B2B wholesale coffee order grid: 3x3 matrix of quantity inputs (rows=pack sizes, columns=blends). Visual layout is row-major but Tab walks column-by-column (all sizes of one blend before the next), achieved purely by column-major DOM source order + CSS Grid placement (no tabindex). Completing one product's full size-ladder at a time is a logical purchasing workflow.
pages.mechanism: Focus order is column-major by blend (Morning-6,12,24 -> Decaf -> Espresso). Every input has an explicit <label>, so each stop is unambiguous; the per-blend run preserves meaning (a product size-ladder) and operability (each cell reachable once). The SC explicitly blesses one-column-at-a-time as a valid alternative and requires only one valid order, so this must NOT be flagged for being non-row-major. Verified in Chromium: real Tab order = morning_6,morning_12,morning_24,decaf_6,decaf_12,decaf_24,espresso_6,espresso_12,espresso_24.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The page has no detectable defect (labels present, headers/scope fine, contrast fine, nothing hidden) so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse stay silent. The aspect tests OVER-flagging: a naive heuristic that flagged any non-visual/non-LTR tab order would false-positive here. Deciding that column-major 'still reflects a logical relationship in the content' requires understanding the purchasing workflow — a reasoning task no static tool performs.

citation.quote: There may be different orders that reflect logical relationships in the content. For example, moving through components in a table one row at a time or one column at a time both reflect the logical relationships in the content. Either order may satisfy this success criterion.

pages.scenario: University seminar-availability picker: a weekly timetable <table> of checkboxes (rows=time slots, columns=weekdays). Students plan one day at a time, so focus is driven column-major (by day) using contiguous, day-grouped positive tabindex values (Mon=10-13, Tue=14-17, ... Fri=26-29). The day-grouping means the order follows a content relationship, so it is a valid alternative, not an F44 scramble.
pages.mechanism: Tab order ascends tabindex 10->29, traversing the grid column-major by weekday. Each checkbox has a unique wrapped <label> ('Mon 13:00, A3, checkbox'), so the by-day run is coherent and operability/meaning are preserved. Positive tabindex is present (a generic automated red-flag) but the order it produces is logical. Verified in Chromium: real Tab order = mon_0800,mon_1000,mon_1300,mon_1500,tue_0800,...,fri_1500.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse have no rule that fails 2.4.3 on order; at most they emit a generic 'avoid positive tabindex' best-practice advisory (often suppressed), which is not a conformance failure and fires identically on a valid OR invalid order. They cannot determine that the tabindex sequence groups by day. A checker that failed 2.4.3 on any positive tabindex would false-positive on this legitimate page.

citation.quote: If there is more than one order that preserves meaning and operability, only one of them needs to be provided.

pages.scenario: Public-library FY budget worksheet (rows=expense categories, columns=quarters). A 2-D budget grid has two valid orders (row-major = one category's full year; column-major = one quarter across all categories), but this page provides NEITHER: positive tabindex (1-16) snakes diagonally so each Tab jumps to a cell sharing neither a category nor a quarter with the previous one. The meaning-destroying near-twin of the valid column grids.
pages.mechanism: Tab order follows tabindex 1->16 along a diagonal (sal_q1 -> trv_q2 -> eqp_q3 -> sft_q4 -> trv_q1 -> ...). Each input is named, but the SEQUENCE conveys no relationship: the user cannot complete one category's year nor one quarter, and to enter 'all of Q1' must hunt non-adjacent stops (positions 1,5,9,13). This impedes both the meaning (two intersecting groupings) and operability (coherent data entry) = F44. Verified in Chromium: real Tab order matches the documented diagonal scatter exactly.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every cell has a real accessible name (aria-label), headers/scope correct, contrast passes, and tabindex values are syntactically valid integers — so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse report no 2.4.3 failure (at most the generic positive-tabindex advisory, which fires identically on the VALID case-02 and so cannot distinguish them). No static tool models whether a tab sequence follows a row or column relationship; detecting that this diagonal walk breaks both 2-D relationships is a human reasoning judgment.

citation.quote: When the values of the tabindex attribute are assigned in a different order than the relationships and sequences in the content, the tab order no longer follows the relationships and sequences in the content.

pages.scenario: HR 360-degree competency review: a 4x4 matrix where each cell is its own <input type=range> slider (rows=competencies, columns=rater perspectives Self/Manager/Peer/Direct report). Not a radio-group matrix, so focus order is governed by DOM source order. Visual layout is row-major but Tab walks column-major by rater (all four Self sliders, then Manager, ...) via column-major source order + CSS Grid (no tabindex). Assessing from one perspective at a time is exactly how a 360 instrument is completed.
pages.mechanism: Tab order is column-major by rater (self_comm,self_own,self_coll,self_adapt,mgr_comm,...). Every slider has an explicit <label> giving a unique rater+competency name, so each stop is unambiguous and the per-rater run preserves meaning (a per-rater assessment column) and operability (each slider reachable once, arrow-key adjustable). Column-at-a-time is an accepted alternative and only one valid order is required. Verified in Chromium: real Tab order matches the documented per-rater column order exactly.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: No detectable defect (all sliders labeled, real headers, contrast passes, nothing hidden) so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse stay silent. The aspect tests over-flagging: a heuristic insisting on row-major or visual-order tab flow would false-positive. Judging that 'one rater column at a time' reflects a logical relationship requires understanding the 360-review workflow, which no static tool models.

citation.quote: moving through components in a table one row at a time or one column at a time both reflect the logical relationships in the content. Either order may satisfy this success criterion.

pages.scenario: RTL Arabic mosque iqamah-time editor (dir=rtl): a weekly grid of <input type=time> controls (rows=five prayers, columns=seven days, Saturday is the right-most visual column). The admin completes one full day before the next, so a script assigns contiguous per-day tabindex producing column-major-by-day focus that, because of RTL, runs right-to-left. A valid column alternative compounded by an RTL locale where LTR top-to-bottom-left-to-right assumptions do not apply.
pages.mechanism: After the inline script runs, tabIndex 1-35 walks column-major by day (Saturday block 1-5, Sunday 6-10, ...). Focus visits sat_fajr,sat_dhuhr,...,sat_isha,sun_fajr,... starting from the right-most (Saturday) column and moving leftward. Each time input has a bilingual aria-label, so every stop is unambiguous and the per-day run preserves meaning (a per-day prayer-schedule column read right-to-left) and operability. The SC accepts column-at-a-time and explicitly does not require top-to-bottom-left-to-right. Verified in Chromium: real Tab order = full sat->fri per-day column order (time-widget hour/minute segments consume extra Tab presses but the inter-control order is exactly as documented).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: No detectable defect (every input labeled, <table> scope correct, dir/lang set, contrast passes) so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse stay silent. They cannot evaluate whether a right-to-left, column-major-by-day path reflects a logical relationship in an RTL prayer schedule, nor correct an LTR-anchored intuition. Recognizing this as a valid alternative (not a scramble) is a human, locale-aware reasoning judgment.

citation.quote: Focus order does not necessarily need to be top to bottom, left to right.

pages.scenario: Theatre seat-selection map: 4x6 grid of toggle buttons (role=checkbox) where rows are seat rows A-D and columns are seat numbers 1-6. Both row-by-row and column-by-column would be valid (either reflects the auditorium's spatial layout), but the seat buttons are emitted in a RANDOM SCATTER DOM source order (the drag order from a visual layout tool: B3,A6,D1,A2,C5,...) with CSS Grid pinning each to its true (row,seat) coordinate, so the map LOOKS correct while Tab teleports the focus ring around the auditorium.
pages.mechanism: Focus order follows the scattered source order (B3 -> A6 -> D1 -> A2 -> C5 -> ...); consecutive stops share no row, no seat number, and no adjacency. A keyboard user cannot track their position or pick adjacent seats; a screen-reader user hears seats announced in an order that conveys no spatial structure ('Row B Seat 3','Row A Seat 6','Row D Seat 1'). This impedes both the meaning (the auditorium's spatial layout) and operability = an illogical/confusing focus order. Verified in Chromium: first Tab lands on B3 (mid-grid, not top-left A1) and the full Tab order matches the documented scatter exactly.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every seat button has a correct accessible name (aria-label), valid role=checkbox + aria-checked, sufficient contrast, and a visible focus ring — axe/WAVE/Lighthouse report nothing. No static tool reconstructs the seat grid's spatial relationship to test whether the DOM/focus sequence follows it. Distinguishing this random scatter from a valid column-major seat order requires a human to understand the map's spatial meaning and watch where the focus ring actually travels.

citation.quote: Care should be taken so that the focus order makes sense to both of these sets of users and does not appear to either of them to jump around randomly.

aspects.title: Confusing/illogical focus stops from nested focusable wrappers or focusable static content
aspects.plain: Making a wrapper div or plain text focusable adds pointless or duplicate Tab stops, so keyboard users land on the same control twice or pause on dead content.
aspects.description:
The Understanding note: the SC 'does not prohibit making non-operable content (e.g., static text) focusable,' BUT 'it is a failure of Focus Order if items receive focus in an order that impedes the meaning or operation of content, or creates confusing or illogical focus orders — for example, a control appearing to receive focus multiple times due to the use of nested focusable elements' (e.g. `
`). The judgment is whether the extra/duplicate/odd focus stops impede meaning or operability: a control that appears to receive focus twice, a tabindex=0 on a non-interactive wrapper that injects a meaningless stop mid-sequence, or static text that grabs focus between two related controls and breaks the flow. Whether such stops merely add tedium (best-practice, not a failure) or actually 'impede meaning/operation' (a failure) is exactly the human line the note draws.
aspects.scLimb: Static/non-interactive-focusable + nested-focusable limb (Understanding note): non-operable focusable content is allowed unless it 'impedes meaning/operation' or creates 'confusing or illogical focus orders... a control appearing to receive focus multiple times due to the use of nested focusable elements.'
aspects.whyUncovered: 0 ACT cases. A tool can mechanically count tabindex=0 attributes but cannot judge whether a focus stop is 'confusing or illogical' or whether a double-focus (wrapper + child) 'impedes meaning'. The note explicitly permits focusable static content; only the meaning-impeding subset fails, which is a contextual human judgment, not a static pattern.

references.quote: it is a failure of Focus Order if items receive focus in an order that impedes the meaning or operation of content, or creates confusing or illogical focus orders — for example, a control appearing to receive focus multiple times due to the use of nested focusable elements.
This success criterion does not prohibit making non-operable content (e.g., static text) focusable, or programmatically moving focus to such content.
Static/non-interactive elements can receive focus, as long as they don't impede operation of the content, or result in confusing or illogical focus order.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: Artisan pottery e-commerce product page where a focusable div[tabindex=0][role=button] wraps a real <button> 'Add to basket', so Tab stops on the wrapper then the button — the same control appears to receive focus twice (the exact div[tabindex=0]><button> shape pictured in the Understanding note).
pages.mechanism: A focusable wrapper around a single focusable child produces a redundant/duplicate focus stop: AT announces 'Add to basket, button' on the wrapper, then 'Add to basket, button' again on the inner native button. One physical control reads as two identical back-to-back buttons, making a single action ambiguous (did I add two mugs? did the first press fail?) — impeding operation.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: tabindex=0 on a div is valid, role=button is a real correctly-spelled role, and the inner element is a genuine <button> with a non-empty accessible name; nothing is aria-hidden or empty. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse have no rule for 'a focusable wrapper immediately around a single focusable child.' Catching it requires tabbing the page, observing focus lands on the SAME control twice, and judging the duplicate stop impedes operation rather than being harmlessly tedious — human reasoning. Verified live: tab stops 5 and 6 both resolve to 'Add to basket'.

citation.quote: it is a failure of Focus Order if items receive focus in an order that impedes the meaning or operation of content, or creates confusing or illogical focus orders — for example, a control appearing to receive focus multiple times due to the use of nested focusable elements.

pages.scenario: Ticketing checkout where a decorative 'Payment details' text divider was made tabindex=0 (for a reveal-on-focus animation) and sits in source between the Card number input and the Expiry input, injecting a meaningless focus stop into the middle of the card-entry sequence.
pages.mechanism: A non-interactive focusable element wedged between two coupled payment fields breaks the data-entry flow: a keyboard user typing their card number presses Tab expecting Expiry but lands on a non-operable text node (a screen reader announces 'Payment details' with nothing to act on), then must Tab again to reach Expiry. The dead mid-sequence stop impedes operation of a rapid field-to-field entry chain.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The divider is a valid <div> with a legal tabindex=0; it is not a control, so there is no missing label/role to flag, and no rule fires on 'focusable non-interactive element placed mid-form.' Recognising that the stop lands BETWEEN two related payment fields and therefore breaks the entry flow requires understanding the form's meaning/sequence and tabbing through it. Verified live: tab order is Card number (#cardnum) -> .accent 'Payment details' -> Expiry (#exp).

citation.quote: Static/non-interactive elements can receive focus, as long as they don't impede operation of the content, or result in confusing or illogical focus order.

pages.scenario: Recipe 'Cook mode' page (Hearthline, slow-braised short ribs): each step's 'Start 30 min / 8 min / 3 hr timer' <button> is nested inside a focusable static badge span (tabindex="0") that hosts a coachmark on focus, so tabbing each timed step lands first on the badge (whose text already reads out the timer action) and then on the timer button — a doubled focus stop on the same control.
pages.mechanism: Each timed step's real 'Start … timer' <button> is nested INSIDE a focusable static badge (<span class="badge focusable" tabindex="0">) whose own accessible text already includes the nested button's wording, so Tab stops on the badge (announcing the timer action) and then again on the button itself — the same timer control appears to receive focus twice in a row. This is the Understanding note's named failure ('a control appearing to receive focus multiple times due to the use of nested focusable elements'); the doubled, confusing stop impedes operation.
pages.selectorNote: Focusable step badge wrapping a real timer button, causing a doubled stop; orig div.convert matched nothing
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The read-out is valid markup (tabindex=0 legal on a div, carries text, lang/dir correctly matched so no i18n rule fires) and is not a form control, so there is no missing-label finding. Tools cannot determine that a focusable non-operable block sits between two sequential transfer steps, nor that the interruption impedes operation. Judging it requires reading the RTL flow, understanding step dependency, and tabbing through. Verified live: tab order is amount (#amount) -> .convert read-out -> delivery method (#method).

citation.quote: This success criterion does not prohibit making non-operable content (e.g., static text) focusable, or programmatically moving focus to such content. However, it is a failure of Focus Order if items receive focus in an order that impedes the meaning or operation of content, or creates confusing or illogical focus orders

pages.scenario: Public-radio episode list (Tidewater FM) where each li.episode contains an absolutely-positioned a.cover link filling the card AND a visible a.listen 'Listen now' link, both pointing to the same #ep- anchor, so Tab stops twice per episode across the four-episode list (card-title link, then 'Listen now' to the identical destination).
pages.mechanism: Two focusable links per card — an absolutely-positioned 'stretched' card-cover <a> filling the whole card plus a visible 'Listen now' <a> — both resolve to the same episode destination, producing a redundant duplicate focus stop for every item.
pages.selectorNote: Stretched card-cover link sharing destination with sibling Listen-now link; orig article.card[role=link] matched nothing
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Each card is a valid linkified element (legal tabindex=0, real role=link, aria-label) wrapping a real <a> with href and visible text; nothing is empty, hidden, or mis-roled. No rule exists for 'a focusable wrapper and a focusable descendant resolving to the same destination.' Detecting the doubled stop requires tabbing the grid, noticing each story is reached twice, and judging the nested-focusable duplication confusing. Verified live: tab order alternates card -> 'Read more' -> card -> 'Read more' (8 stops for 4 destinations).

citation.quote: a control appearing to receive focus multiple times due to the use of nested focusable elements.

pages.scenario: PASS boundary: a clinical 'add a patient allergy' form containing two focusable non-interactive elements placed where they do NOT impede operation — a role=status region (tabindex=-1) after the Save button that focus moves to on save, and a focusable end-of-form review summary placed AFTER all inputs and the submit button.
pages.mechanism: Focusable static content is explicitly permitted by the note when it does not impede operation. The review summary is reached only after the user passes the submit button, so it never breaks the entry chain; on save, focus is programmatically moved to the status region (a logical, permitted focus move that also announces via aria-live). No control receives focus twice and no non-operable stop is wedged between two related controls, so focus order preserves meaning and operability.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: This is the inverse trap: a naive heuristic that flags ANY focusable non-interactive element (counting tabindex=0 on non-controls, or focus moved to static text) would WRONGLY fail this conforming page. The elements are valid AND well-placed; confirming the page passes requires tabbing it and verifying the focusable static content sits at logical points and impedes nothing — the same human judgment that catches the failures, applied to correctly distinguish 'allowed' from 'failure.' Verified live: tab order is allergen -> reaction -> severity -> notes -> Save -> summary (summary last; status region correctly out of the tab order at tabindex=-1).

citation.quote: This success criterion does not prohibit making non-operable content (e.g., static text) focusable, or programmatically moving focus to such content.

pages.scenario: PASS boundary (hardest 'tedious vs impedes operation' line): a developer API reference sidebar where each category section header (Getting started / Core / Advanced) is a focusable static span[tabindex=0], adding an extra Tab stop per category. The stops are merely tedious — each label heads its OWN group, no link is duplicated, and no stop is wedged between two coupled controls.
pages.mechanism: Extra-but-orderly focus stops are best-practice/tedium territory the note frames as advice, not a failure. Tabbing the sidebar goes label -> its links -> next label -> its links; a screen reader announces each header as static text then the group's links in order. The order preserves meaning (each header introduces the group beneath it) and operability (every link reached exactly once, in logical order); nothing receives focus twice and no dead stop interrupts a coupled sequence.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A naive heuristic that flags 'many tabindex=0 on non-interactive elements = extra focus stops' would WRONGLY fail this page, and a tool cannot make the note's required distinction. The labels are valid focusable spans. Deciding the stops are merely TEDIOUS (allowed) rather than CONFUSING/ILLOGICAL (a failure) — by confirming none duplicate a control and none interrupt a coupled sequence — is the precise human judgment that separates this PASS from the FAIL cases. Verified live: tab order is 'Getting started' header -> its 2 links -> 'Core' header -> its 3 links -> 'Advanced' header -> its 3 links -> next-page button (orderly grouping, no doubled control).

citation.quote: As a best practice, avoid having focusable elements which cannot be operated or actioned, as these are likely to make operation tedious for keyboard users.

aspects.title: Positive tabindex creates a tab order that does not preserve meaning (F44), with the meaning-judgment a human must make
aspects.plain: Hand-numbered tabindex values force Tab to visit controls in an order that contradicts the content's logical sequence, scrambling the experience for keyboard users.
aspects.description: F44: positive tabindex values impose an explicit tab order that does not follow the content's logical relationships and sequences (the <ol> example tabbing Homepage, chapter 3, chapter 2, chapter 1). While a static tool can DETECT the presence of positive tabindex (axe flags it as best-practice), the actual 2.4.3 failure requires judging that the resulting order breaks meaning — a positive-tabindex page whose order happens to match the content sequence is NOT a failure, and a positive tabindex that re-establishes the correct order after a CSS reflow can even be the fix. So the human contribution is deciding whether the imposed numeric order preserves or destroys meaning/operability, and recognizing the common edit-drift case (a new field without tabindex gets pushed to the end).
aspects.scLimb: tabindex-misuse failure (F44): positive tabindex creating a tab order that does not follow content sequence/relationships.
aspects.whyUncovered: 0 ACT rules cover F44. Automated tools can surface 'positive tabindex present' as a best-practice warning but cannot decide whether the specific numeric order preserves or breaks meaning — they would either flag every positive tabindex (false positives on correctly-ordered ones, and on the legitimate 'tabindex used to repair CSS reflow' case) or none. The meaning-preservation judgment is human; that is why this is kept but at lower priority than the no-tabindex aspects.

references.quote: When the values of the tabindex attribute are assigned in a different order than the relationships and sequences in the content, the tab order no longer follows the relationships and sequences in the content.
If this list is navigated by the tab key, the list is navigated in the order Homepage, chapter 3, chapter 2, chapter 1, which does not follow the sequence in the content.
the page is modified to add a new field in the middle of the page, but the author forgets to add a tabindex attribute to the new field. As a result, the new field is at the end of the tab order.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: Self-paced LMS course outline (ordered list of Start + Module 1-4). Links carry positive tabindex 1,5,4,3,2, so Tab visits Start then Module 4,3,2,1 - reversing the visible, content-meaningful study sequence the page explicitly says must be done in order. Canonical F44 reversed-list pattern in a real course page.
pages.mechanism: Positive tabindex (1,5,4,3,2) imposes a numeric focus order that reverses the modules against their visible 1->4 sequence; verified empirically via puppeteer (traversal: Start -> Module 4 -> Module 3 -> Module 2 -> Module 1) and by focused screenshot (2nd Tab stop = Module 4 capstone). Keyboard/SR users tabbing 'to the next module' are steered backwards through prerequisites.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe fires only its best-practice 'tabindex' note for the PRESENCE of positive tabindex (confirmed: tabindex:5, the same flag it emits on the PASS case-03 and inapplicable case-06). No tool reads the visible module labels, infers the intended study sequence, and compares it to the 1->5->4->3->2 traversal to decide the order is reversed relative to meaning - that is a reading-comprehension and visual-sequence judgment.

citation.quote: When the values of the tabindex attribute are assigned in a different order than the relationships and sequences in the content, the tab order no longer follows the relationships and sequences in the content.

pages.scenario: Government benefits-enrollment form (Step 2 of 4) where every field has explicit positive tabindex 1-8, but a later-added required 'Daytime phone' field was dropped in with NO tabindex. Because positive-tabindex elements are visited first, the un-indexed phone field is tabbed dead last, after the Submit button. The F44 edit-drift variant the technique itself describes.
pages.mechanism: The single tabindex-less control (#phone) is excluded from the positive-tabindex pass and traversed last in DOM order; verified traversal: First->Last->Email->Address->City->ZIP->Continue(Submit)->Save->Phone. A required contact field is skipped in the natural top-to-bottom pass and reachable only AFTER the submit control, breaking both meaning and operability.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every control is labelled, valid, well-contrasted with correct autocomplete - naive checks pass. axe emits only the best-practice positive-tabindex note (tabindex:8) and has no rule that detects a single control OMITTED from an otherwise-explicit numbering, nor that the omission strands a required field after Submit. Recognising that a data field reached only post-submit is effectively unreachable is a human form-flow/operability judgment.

citation.quote: Later, the page is modified to add a new field in the middle of the page, but the author forgets to add a tabindex attribute to the new field. As a result, the new field is at the end of the tab order.

pages.scenario: PASS counter-example: a nonprofit donation form laid out with CSS flexbox 'order' so the amount block sits visually on top while it is authored SECOND in the DOM. Positive tabindex 1-5 is used DELIBERATELY to restore the visually-meaningful entry order (amount -> custom -> name -> email -> Donate). Uses positive tabindex but PRESERVES meaning, so it must not be flagged.
pages.mechanism: CSS order (.block-amount:1, .block-contact:2, .block-actions:3) makes visual order != DOM order; positive tabindex realigns focus with the VISUAL order. Verified traversal (amount preset -> custom -> name -> email -> Donate) matches the on-screen top-to-bottom sequence exactly - nothing jumps, nothing stranded, Donate last. Focus order preserves the meaning implied by the visual presentation.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Hard negative: axe emits the IDENTICAL best-practice positive-tabindex note here (tabindex:7) as on the failing pages. A tool or judge keyed on positive-tabindex presence would raise a false positive on this legitimate reflow repair. Confirming it passes requires computing the rendered visual order (driven by CSS order) and verifying it AGREES with the focus traversal - a visual-plus-semantic comparison no scanner performs.

citation.quote: Focus order does not necessarily need to follow the visual layout of the web page, as long as the order in which elements receive focus is logical, and the hierarchy and relationship of content implied by the visual presentation is preserved.

pages.scenario: Mortgage 'configure & compare rate locks' tool with two side-by-side columns (Plan A 30-yr, Plan B 15-yr), each stacking Loan amount / Down payment / Points. Positive tabindex row-interleaves the columns (A.amt=1,B.amt=2,A.down=3,B.down=4,A.pts=5,B.pts=6), so Tab ping-pongs left-right across the gutter, breaking each plan's must-be-completed-as-a-unit field group.
pages.mechanism: tabindex interleaves the two interdependent column units; verified traversal: A.amt->B.amt->A.down->B.down->A.pts->B.pts->Compare. The user is thrown out of Plan A mid-configuration into Plan B and back; at 300% magnification only one column is in the viewport, so each Tab yanks focus off-screen and back, destroying the 'these three fields belong to Plan A' relationship.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Markup is valid (labelled inputs, aria-labelledby sections, good contrast); axe emits only the best-practice positive-tabindex note (tabindex:7). The SAME row-interleaved order would be perfectly valid for an INDEPENDENT read-only data table navigated row-by-row (the Understanding doc allows either row- or column-major). The verdict flips only because these columns are interdependent CONFIGURATION units - a task-semantics + magnifier-viewport judgment no scanner models.

citation.quote: However, if the two columns are independent of each other, and meaning/operation are not affected, it is not a failure if elements in the right-hand column receive focus first, followed by the elements in the left-hand column.

pages.scenario: Arabic-language (dir=rtl) clinic appointment form localized from an English template. In RTL the rightmost box is visually first (given name; day), but positive tabindex was numbered left-to-right (1,2,3...) for the original LTR layout and never updated. Tab thus visits family->father->given and year->month->day - the exact reverse of the right-to-left reading order.
pages.mechanism: LTR-ascending tabindex under an RTL visual flip reverses meaning; verified traversal: name row family(1)->father(2)->given(3) and DOB row year(4)->month(5)->day(6), each the reverse of the right-to-left reading the Arabic user follows. Focus contradicts the meaning implied by the RTL presentation (lowest tabindex lands on the visually-last leftmost field).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: lang=ar/dir=rtl are correct, every field has an Arabic label, DOB is a grouped role=group; axe emits only the best-practice positive-tabindex note (tabindex:8) and has NO model of RTL reading order - it cannot tell that under dir=rtl the lowest tabindex lands on the visually-last field. Catching the reversal requires reading Arabic, knowing RTL direction, and comparing it to the numeric traversal: a bilingual, directional, visual judgment.

citation.quote: Determine if the focus order impacts the page meaning (e.g., form fields for a mailing address are presented in the expected sequence).

pages.scenario: BOUNDARY counter-example: an engineering-blog post footer with a row of five social-share buttons (X, Facebook, LinkedIn, Email, Copy link) carrying SCRAMBLED positive tabindex 3,1,4,2,5. Despite positive tabindex present AND in a scrambled order, the five actions are mutually independent so their order carries no meaning - the canonical 'row of social-media icons' Does-Not-Apply example.
pages.mechanism: tabindex scrambles the share-button order (verified traversal: Facebook->Email->X->LinkedIn->Copy link), but each button is a complete independent action with no sequence/dependency, and the rest of the page (article + related links, no tabindex) tabs in normal DOM order. The navigation sequence does not affect meaning or operability, so SC 2.4.3 does not apply.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Statically indistinguishable from a failing page: positive tabindex present and numeric order differs from source - the same signals as case-01, and axe emits the identical best-practice note (tabindex:5). A tool or judge keyed on 'positive tabindex' or even 'tab order != source order' would FALSE-POSITIVE. The only thing making it pass is the semantic fact that five share actions are independent so order carries no meaning - a judgment about whether sequence affects meaning that no scanner can make.

citation.quote: When focus order does not affect meaning or operability, this test Does Not Apply (e.g., a row of icons linking to social media may not need to be navigated in a particular order).

aspects.title: Generic/boilerplate link text with a non-empty name but no purpose, and no context that rescues it (G91/H30 substantive failure)
aspects.plain: A link reads only 'click here' or 'read more' (or a raw URL) with no nearby explaining text, so a screen-reader user listing links can't tell where any goes.
aspects.description: A link whose accessible name exists and is non-empty but is generic boilerplate ('click here', 'read more', 'more', 'here', 'details', 'learn more', 'link', 'continue', '>>') or is just the bare URL, AND for which no programmatically determined link context (the same sentence, paragraph, list item, table cell, or associated table-header cell, or aria-label/labelledby/describedby) supplies the missing purpose. The name passes the only APPROVED rule (c487ae) trivially because it is a pure name-presence gate. The judgment is irreducibly semantic: read the link text plus its containing block and decide whether a user can infer the destination's purpose without leaving the link. Includes the bare-URL case, where the Understanding/G91 say the URI is 'generally not sufficiently descriptive'. The borderline case — where context ALMOST but not-quite rescues a generic name — is the hardest and the most valuable.
aspects.scLimb: Tests the substantive limb of 2.4.4: whether the link text, alone or with its programmatically determined link context, actually conveys the link's PURPOSE — not merely that a non-empty name exists (the c487ae floor).
aspects.whyUncovered: The only APPROVED rule (c487ae) is a pure name-PRESENCE gate; 'click here' passes it. The substantive limb lives only in PROPOSED, unapproved rule 5effbb, whose failed examples use stilted single-word names ('More', 'Workshop', 'Go') on otherwise-empty pages, never the real-world boilerplate a person actually meets, and never the borderline case where residual context nearly rescues a generic name. A fully-automated checker can flag a hard-coded blocklist of phrases but cannot decide whether the surrounding prose makes the purpose inferable — that is a meaning judgment a human must make.

references.quote: Whenever possible, provide link text that identifies the purpose of the link without needing additional context.
The description lets a user distinguish this link from links in the web page that lead to other destinations and helps the user determine whether to follow the link.
Note that simply providing the URI of the destination is generally not sufficiently descriptive.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: Local-newspaper front page: a lead story ends with a paragraph whose entire content is a single link reading 'Read more'. The only descriptive text (the headline) is in a different block (the <h2>), which is not programmatically determined link context.
pages.mechanism:
The link's programmatically determined context is its own

, which contains only the generic phrase 'Read more' with no purpose words; the descriptive headline sits in a separate block and is not same-sentence/paragraph/list-item/cell nor aria-linked, so a screen-reader user on the Links List hears only 'Read more, link' and cannot determine the destination (the F63 adjacent-block condition).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The <a> has a non-empty computable accessible name ('Read more') confirmed via the Chrome AX tree, so axe link-name, WAVE, Lighthouse, and ACT c487ae all pass; there is only one such link so identical-text heuristics never fire. Deciding that the link's OWN block supplies no purpose, and that the headline in a separate block does not count as programmatic context, is an irreducible human semantic judgment.

citation.quote: A news service lists the first few sentences of an article in a paragraph. The next paragraph contains the link "Read More...". Because the link is not in the same paragraph as the lead sentence, the user cannot easily discover what the link will let the user read more about.

pages.scenario: SaaS pricing page: a paragraph reads '...for full pricing details, click here.' where the generic phrase 'click here' is the link but the purpose words ('full pricing details') precede it in the SAME sentence — the boundary near-PASS that is identical boilerplate to a failing page, rescued only by its enclosing sentence (G53).
pages.mechanism: The link's same-sentence programmatically determined context names the destination's purpose ('full pricing details') BEFORE the generic phrase, so a screen-reader user reading the paragraph hears the purpose first and can identify the link without leaving it; 2.4.4 is satisfied by link text combined with programmatic context per technique G53.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: This is a false-positive trap: phrase-blocklist heuristics flag the literal string 'click here' (accessible name confirmed as 'click here' via the AX tree) and report a violation, which is WRONG because the enclosing sentence rescues it under G53. No tool can parse the sentence, locate the purpose words, confirm they precede the link, and judge they describe the destination — that is the human in-context judgment.

citation.quote: A web page contains the sentence "To advertise on this page, click here." ... Although the link phrase 'click here' is not sufficient to understand the link, the information needed precedes the link in the same sentence.

pages.scenario: Restaurant site footer 'More' column: three list items, each containing only a link named 'Details', going to three different pages (menu, private events, gift cards). No text inside any <li> distinguishes them.
pages.mechanism: Each link's programmatically determined context is its own <li>, whose entire content is the word 'Details' — no same-list-item text, no aria-label/labelledby/describedby — so a screen-reader user hears 'Details, Details, Details' on the Links List and cannot tell which leads where; the visual 'More' heading is in a sibling element and is not programmatic link context.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: All three links have the non-empty accessible name 'Details' (confirmed via AX tree), so c487ae and axe link-name pass. A 'same text, different href' heuristic may warn but is neither necessary nor sufficient for 2.4.4 — WCAG explicitly permits repeated link text when context disambiguates (the PDF/mp3 book-list example). Whether each link's OWN list item supplies purpose requires a human reading the in-context text.

citation.quote: "Programmatically determined link context" is limited to same sentence/paragraph/list-item/table-cell or associated table header — not arbitrary nearby text.

pages.scenario: Investor-relations 'Quarterly Disclosures' page: a link whose entire accessible name is the bare raw URL 'https://example.com/products/2024/q3-report.pdf', surrounded only by the words 'Document available at:' which name nothing.
pages.mechanism: The accessible name is the raw URL itself (confirmed via AX tree); a screen reader spells it out or reads it as an opaque token, and the user must mentally parse path segments to guess 'q3-report' is a Q3 report with no certainty of year/entity/type. The containing block adds only 'Document available at:', which names nothing — and WCAG G91/G53/H30 state the URI is 'generally not sufficiently descriptive'.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The accessible name is a long, non-empty, UNIQUE string, so c487ae and axe link-name pass and duplicate-text heuristics never fire. A tool would have to recognize the name is a URL, parse its path, and judge whether the segments adequately convey purpose to a human — which WCAG frames as 'generally' insufficient, i.e. a case-by-case human judgment, and which no static check performs reliably.

citation.quote: The objective of this technique is to describe the purpose of a link in the text of the link. ... The URI of the destination is generally not sufficiently descriptive.

pages.scenario: Electronics shop: the SAME '>>' (raquo) chevron glyph link appears twice. In 'Editor's pick' it sits in the same sentence as a named product ('iPhone 15 Pro >>') and also carries an aria-label — that link PASSES. In 'Also trending' the identical glyph sits alone in its own paragraph with no product name in the block — that link FAILS. One page, opposite verdicts decided only by context.
pages.mechanism: The PASS link's accessible name is 'iPhone 15 Pro details' (aria-label) and is reinforced by the same-sentence product name (G53). The FAIL link's accessible name computes to the bare glyph '»' (confirmed via AX tree — non-empty), and its programmatic context (its own paragraph) contains no product name, heading, or ARIA association, so a user cannot determine it leads to the Aurora Bluetooth speaker. Identical glyph, opposite outcomes, decided purely by surrounding meaning.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Both links have non-empty accessible names ('iPhone 15 Pro details' and the glyph '»'), so c487ae and axe link-name pass for both — critically the failing link is NOT an empty-name linter hit. A glyph like '>>'/'»' is not on phrase blocklists, so heuristic ambiguous-text checkers flag neither. Separating the rescued glyph from the orphaned one requires reading each enclosing sentence for a product name — a pure human meaning judgment.

citation.quote: The sentence enclosing the link provides context for an otherwise unclear link. The description lets a user distinguish this link from links in the web page that lead to other destinations and helps the user determine whether to follow the link.

pages.scenario: Public-health dashboard: a bar chart of childhood MMR coverage with a <figcaption> ending in a 'learn more' link. The caption sentence names the destination subject ('the methodology and clinic-level breakdown behind this 2025 dip in MMR coverage') immediately before the generic phrase, and the link lives INSIDE the figcaption — the hardest borderline PASS.
pages.mechanism: The link is a descendant of the <figcaption>, which is the link's containing block (and the figure's accessible name via aria-labelledby); the caption sentence names the subject BEFORE 'learn more', so a screen-reader user reading the caption hears the purpose first and can identify the link in context (2.4.4 same-block rule + G53). Accessible name confirmed as 'learn more' via AX tree.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: False-positive trap: 'learn more' is on phrase blocklists so heuristic tools flag a violation — incorrectly, because the figcaption rescues it. A name-presence tool passes it but for the wrong reason (it never reads context). Reaching the correct PASS requires a human to read the caption, locate the subject words ('2025 dip in MMR coverage'), confirm they sit in the link's containing block and precede the link, and judge they convey purpose; the chart data is an aria-label on role=img, opaque to text analysis.

citation.quote: This can be achieved by putting the description of the link in the same sentence, paragraph, list item, or table cell as the link, or in the table header cell for a link in a data table, because these are directly associated with the link itself.

aspects.title: Purpose visible on the page but located OUTSIDE the programmatic link context (F63 — wrong container, including context that follows the link)
aspects.plain: The text explaining a vague link exists on the page but sits in a separate paragraph or cell, so a screen reader never connects it to the link.
aspects.description: The information needed to understand a vague link IS present and visible — a sighted reader can find it — but it sits in content that is NOT programmatically associated with the link: a different paragraph, an adjacent (non-header) table cell, a different list item, a layout-table row above, or text that FOLLOWS the link in the same visual region. The page LOOKS fine, which is exactly the trap. The judgment requires reasoning about DOM container boundaries (sentence/paragraph/list-item/table-cell/associated <th>) AND about reading-order direction: Understanding and G53 warn that context which follows the link is confusing for screen-reader users reading top to bottom. This is distinct from the generic-text aspect: here the purpose words exist but the question is association and ordering, not absence.
aspects.scLimb: Tests the 'programmatically determined link context' clause of 2.4.4: purpose must come from the link text plus context that is directly associated with the link, not from arbitrary nearby text a user would have to leave the link to find.
aspects.whyUncovered:
5effbb has a few canonical F63-flavoured failures (the W3C 'Workshop'-in-a-different-

, Gutenberg-list, and table 'Download' examples), but they are the exact W3C fixtures and all use the same 'context-in-the-wrong-block' shape. The corpus does NOT exercise context that FOLLOWS the link in the same region (the explicit ordering hazard), context split across a layout-table row, dt/dd associations, or visually-adjacent siblings a person would assume are associated. Deciding whether nearby text is in the same sentence/paragraph/cell requires parsing prose-sentence boundaries and judging programmatic association — and the residual-context sufficiency is semantic; an automated tool cannot do this reliably.

references.quote: This describes a failure condition when the context needed for understanding the purpose of a link is located in content that is not programmatically determined link context.
Because the link is not in the same paragraph as the lead sentence, the user cannot easily discover what the link will let the user read more about.
If the description follows the link, there can be confusion and difficulty for screen reader users who are reading through the page in order (top to bottom).
"Programmatically determined link context" is limited to same sentence/paragraph/list-item/table-cell or associated table header — not arbitrary nearby text.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario:
Local-news teaser where the stand-alone 'Read the full document' link sits in its own

, and the clause that names the document ('the proposed fee schedule…') is a separate following

. An em-dash makes the two blocks read as one sentence visually, but the description is outside the link's paragraph AND follows it in reading order — two identical links open two different documents.
pages.mechanism:
The link's accessible name is 'Read the full document' and its containing

holds only the link; the disambiguating clause is in the next sibling

, which is not the link's sentence/paragraph/list-item/table-cell and is not an ARIA-associated description. The describing text also follows the link in DOM/reading order, so a screen-reader user reading top-to-bottom (or on the Links list) hears 'Read the full document' with no destination, and must leave the link to find the context — the F63 wrong-container failure plus the G53/Understanding ordering hazard.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss:
Both links have non-empty human-readable text, valid hrefs, and good contrast, so axe-core/WAVE/Lighthouse pass. No tool parses prose to notice that the only words distinguishing two identical 'Read the full document' links live in a different

that follows the link; judging paragraph-container boundaries and reading-order direction is semantic reasoning a static scanner cannot do.

citation.quote: If the description follows the link, there can be confusion and difficulty for screen reader users who are reading through the page in order (top to bottom).

pages.scenario: A transactional HTML-email layout table (credit-union statement notice). Each document is a bold label row ('June 2025 Account Statement', '2024 Year-End Tax Form (1099-INT)') followed two rows later by a separate <td> holding only a blue 'View' button link. The describing label is in a different row/cell than the link, in a role='presentation' layout table that exposes no structure.
pages.mechanism: The table is role='presentation', so AT exposes no rows/columns/headers — it is pure layout. Each link's accessible name is 'View'; the document name is in an earlier sibling tr>td.label-cell, which (in a presentation table) is not the link's table cell and not an associated <th>, and no aria-label/labelledby ties the button to the label. A screen-reader user on the Links list hears 'View, link' / 'View, link' with no way to tell a statement from a tax form — the canonical F63 adjacent-cell-in-a-layout-table failure.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Both links have non-empty names and good contrast, and the table is correctly marked role='presentation' so no 'layout-table-as-data-table' heuristic fires. No tool can know that 'View' is under-descriptive AND that the only disambiguating text sits in a non-associated row above; recognizing that a presentation table provides zero programmatic association requires human judgment.

citation.quote: An audio site provides links to where its player can be downloaded. The information about what would be downloaded by the link is in the preceding row of the layout table, which is not programmatically determined context for the link.

pages.scenario: An investor-relations 'Events & Presentations' page using a definition list: each <dt> holds a recording title ('Q1 FY2025 earnings call', '2025 Investor Day keynote', 'Q4 FY2024 earnings call') and the matching <dd> holds only a pill-shaped 'Listen' link. Three different recordings, three identical 'Listen' links; the title-to-link relationship is dt/dd, which WCAG's closed list of associated contexts does not include.
pages.mechanism: The link lives in the <dd> with accessible name 'Listen' (the play SVG is aria-hidden) and has no aria-label/aria-labelledby. The describing title is in the sibling <dt>. WCAG enumerates programmatic link context as same sentence/paragraph/list-item/table-cell or associated <th> (or an ARIA property) — a <dt> is none of these, and screen readers do not announce the matching <dt> when focus lands on the <dd> link. The user must leave the link to find the title: F63 via a dt/dd association that is not in the enumerated set.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The <dl>/<dt>/<dd> markup is valid, each 'Listen' link has a non-empty name, the SVG is correctly aria-hidden, and contrast passes. There is no automated rule asserting 'a <dt> does not count as a <dd> link's programmatic context' — that is a fine semantic distinction about which DOM relationships WCAG enumerates as associated, requiring a human to read the closed list and judge that 'Listen' alone is under-descriptive.

citation.quote: "Programmatically determined link context" is **limited** to same sentence/paragraph/list-item/table-cell or associated table header — not arbitrary nearby text.

pages.scenario: A county procurement data table listing solicitations, each with two 'Download' links (Specifications packet vs. Bid Form). The two document columns are distinguished ONLY by a second header-looking sub-row whose cells are <td> styled bold/centered to mimic headers — not real <th> and with no scope — so nothing programmatically associates 'Specifications'/'Bid Form' with the link cells. Six identical 'Download' links.
pages.mechanism: This is a genuine data table (first header row is real <th scope="col">), so AT announces header associations as it navigates cells — but only for actual headers. The 'Specifications'/'Bid Form' labels are tr.subhead > td with no scope and nothing pointing to them via headers, so AT treats them as ordinary data, not the column header for the download cells. On a 'Download' link the announced context is at best the merged real header 'Documents' for BOTH columns, so a spec packet and a bid form are indistinguishable; the disambiguating words exist visually but are not the link's associated header cell — F63. (A real <th scope="col"> sub-row would have passed, which is the boundary.)
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The table is well-formed (real <thead>, real <th scope='col'>, valid colspan, every link with a non-empty name and href, good contrast). axe-core/WAVE/Lighthouse have no rule flagging 'a styled <td> that looks like a header but isn't'. Catching it needs noticing the second header line is <td> not <th>, knowing only an associated header counts as context, and judging 'Download' + 'Documents' still cannot distinguish spec from bid form.

citation.quote: …or in the table header cell for a link in a data table, because these are directly associated with the link itself.

pages.scenario: An outdoor-gear e-commerce category grid. Each product card is a flex column with an .info <div> (product name, blurb, price) and a separate sibling .action <div> holding a green 'View' button link. Visually the card reads as one unit, but the product name and the link are in two different sibling <div>s; every link's accessible name is just 'View'.
pages.mechanism: Each link is in <div class="action"> with accessible name 'View'; the product name is in a separate sibling <div class="info">. The card is a plain <div> with no list semantics, no heading inside the link, and no aria-labelledby pointing the <a> at the name — verified at runtime that the link does not share a container with the name. The link's programmatic context is therefore empty ('View'); the visually-adjacent name is programmatically unrelated, so a screen-reader user on the Links list hears 'View / View / View' and must leave the link to learn the product — the visually-adjacent-sibling F63 trap.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Each link has a non-empty name ('View'), a valid unique href, good contrast, and well-formed markup, so axe-core/WAVE/Lighthouse pass. No tool reasons that the visually-adjacent product name is in a different <div> and thus not the link's programmatic context; recognizing that visual proximity is not programmatic association and that 'View' alone is non-descriptive is human visual/semantic judgment.

citation.quote: This describes a failure condition when the context needed for understanding the purpose of a link is located in content that is not programmatically determined link context.

pages.scenario: A university LMS course-readings list (BIO 201). Each reading is emitted as TWO separate <li> elements — first an <li class="open"> with only the 'Open' link, then an <li class="desc"> with the chapter title — and a CSS grid positions the title cell on the left and the link cell on the right of the same visual row. On screen it reads 'Chapter 4 … Open' (looks compliant); in DOM/reading order it is 'Open' then 'Chapter 4 …', i.e. the description is a different list item that follows the link.
pages.mechanism: The link's own list item (li.open) contains only 'Open'; the chapter title is in the following sibling li.desc — a different list item, with no ARIA association. Screen readers and the Links list follow DOM order, not the CSS-grid visual order, so the title both sits outside the link's list-item context AND follows the link in reading order. Verified at runtime: per reading the <li> sequence is [open]'Open' then [desc]'Chapter…', and all three links expose the name 'Open'. F63 (wrong container = different list item) compounded by the ordering hazard, with CSS deliberately making the visual snapshot look correct.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The visual snapshot looks fully compliant (title beside its link); each link has a non-empty name, valid href, good contrast, and valid <ul>/<li> markup, so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse pass — a left-to-right visual reader would even 'see' the title before the link. Detecting it requires comparing CSS-grid visual order against DOM/reading order, knowing the title is in a different <li>, and judging 'Open' is non-descriptive — three layers of reasoning no scanner performs.

citation.quote: If the additional information follows the link, there can be confusion and difficulty for screen reader users who are reading through the page in order (top to bottom).

aspects.title: Image/icon/SVG-only links with a non-empty name that misdescribes or fails to convey the rendered glyph's purpose (F89 semantic-mismatch variant)
aspects.plain: An icon-only link has a label, but it misdescribes the icon or is useless (a search icon labeled 'image'), so screen-reader users are misled about it.
aspects.description: A link contains only an image, SVG, or icon-font glyph and DOES have a non-empty accessible name (alt, aria-label, title, or aria-labelledby), so F89's empty-name failure and c487ae both PASS — but the name does not match what the glyph depicts or where the link goes. Examples: a magnifying-glass icon labelled 'image' / 'icon1' / the filename 'search.png'; a social brand glyph labelled the generic 'social'; a printer icon whose alt says 'document'; a hamburger menu whose aria-label says 'logo'; an icon-font link whose accessible name is a literal private-use codepoint that conveys nothing; a back-arrow whose alt says 'forward'. The string exists and looks plausible, so it survives every name-presence check, but a person looking at the rendered icon sees the label is wrong or uselessly generic for the link's purpose. Requires VISUAL judgment of the rendered glyph against the name.
aspects.scLimb: Tests whether the accessible name carried by a non-text-only link actually DESCRIBES the link's purpose, beyond the c487ae/F89 floor of merely having some non-empty name.
aspects.whyUncovered: c487ae's image-link cases only test name presence vs absence on a single stock logo or planets imagemap; a 'wrong but present' alt passes every one. 5effbb's icon examples are always correctly-labelled passes or empty-text fails — never a non-empty-but-wrong label. F89 itself only fires on the empty case. Detecting the mismatch requires looking at the rendered icon and comparing it to the accessible name (and destination) — an automated tool has no notion of what a glyph depicts, so this is irreducibly visual/semantic and human-only.

references.quote: This failure condition occurs when a link contains only non-text content, such as an image, and that link cannot be identified by an accessible name.
The text of, or associated with, the link is intended to describe the purpose of the link.
The img has a text alternative which is the name used for the icon in the site help, which describes clicking the home page icon.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: SaaS CRM header toolbar of three icon-only links — magnifying glass (aria-label="img_2031", the sprite export id), gear (aria-label="settings.svg", the source filename), envelope (aria-label="link", a scaffold placeholder). Every link has a non-empty, mutually-distinct accessible name so c487ae/F89 pass and axe reports discernible text, but none describes the search/settings/inbox purpose the glyph depicts.
pages.mechanism: Each <a> is in the a11y tree with role=link and a non-empty accessible name from aria-label (inner SVG is aria-hidden). The name is an asset filename / sprite id / placeholder, not the link's purpose, so the purpose cannot be determined from the link text and there is no programmatic context. Name-presence floor met; descriptive limb of 2.4.4 fails.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse only test that an interactive element has a non-empty accessible name; "img_2031", "settings.svg", "link" are all non-empty and distinct (verified: axe link-name = 7 passes, 0 violations). No tool renders the inline SVG to recognise a magnifying glass/gear/envelope or judge that a filename fails to convey search/settings/mail. The glyph-vs-name comparison is irreducibly visual and human-only.

citation.quote: When an image is the only content of a link, the text alternative for the image describes the unique function of the link.

pages.scenario: Local-news article breadcrumb: an icon link back to the Transit section index renders a LEFT-pointing chevron-plus-shaft (the universal back/previous glyph) via a data-URI SVG, destination /transit/index (where the reader came from). Its img alt is the non-empty word "forward" (copied from a paginator's next-arrow sprite); the visible "Transit desk" caption is aria-hidden, so the link's whole accessible name contradicts the glyph and the destination.
pages.mechanism: The <a> is exposed as role=link with accessible name "forward" (only the img alt contributes; the SVG is via src and the caption span is removed by aria-hidden — confirmed via CDP). A screen-reader user hears "forward" and expects to advance, but the link moves them backward to the index. Present, programmatically-determined name that misdescribes both the arrow's direction and the link purpose: F89's present-but-wrong sibling.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The link has a non-empty accessible name ("forward"), so axe passes it (verified: 2 passes, 0 violations). No checker decodes the data-URI SVG polyline to see the chevron points left, nor correlates that with a destination that is the page's previous location. Recognising "forward" is the opposite of a back-arrow's meaning needs a human to view the rendered icon and reason about direction and destination.

citation.quote: The text of, or associated with, the link is intended to describe the purpose of the link.

pages.scenario: Nonprofit food-bank donation footer with a social row of four icon-only brand links (Facebook, X/Twitter, Instagram, YouTube) pointing to four different platform profiles, but every link carries the identical non-empty aria-label "social media" (a themed CMS social-block applied one global label to every network).
pages.mechanism: All four <a> are role=link with the same accessible name "social media" (each SVG is aria-hidden — confirmed via CDP: four identical names). A screen-reader user listing links hears "social media" four times; the platform each opens lives only in the visual logo, absent from name and programmatic context. Each passes the non-empty floor but cannot have its purpose determined; 2.4.4 fails for the set.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Each link has a non-empty accessible name, so axe passes the link-name rule (verified: 4 passes, 0 violations). A same-name heuristic cannot fire as a failure because, per fd3a94, identical-named links are only wrong when they serve different purposes — and a tool cannot know facebook.com/x.com/instagram.com/youtube.com are distinct destinations, nor read the rendered logos. Telling the brand glyphs apart and judging "social media" describes none specifically requires seeing each logo.

citation.quote: It is also a best practice for links with different purposes and destinations to have different link text.

pages.scenario: Developer console API-keys data table with per-row pencil (edit) and trash (revoke) icon links. The custom icon set assigned each glyph a Unicode Private Use Area codepoint and auto-emitted the literal PUA character as the aria-label, so each link's accessible name is a single private-use character (U+E801 for edit, U+E803 for delete) — non-empty but semantically meaningless.
pages.mechanism: Each <a> is role=link with a non-empty accessible name of one PUA character (SVG is aria-hidden — confirmed via CDP: name.value codepoints are U+E801/U+E803). PUA codepoints carry no assigned Unicode meaning, so AT announces nothing useful (silence / "private use area E801" / fallback symbol), yet the link IS named. The trash action is destructive (revoke a key) with no spoken warning. Floor met; purpose undeterminable; 2.4.4 fails.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The accname computation returns a non-empty string (one PUA character) for each link, so axe reports discernible text — VERIFIED: axe link-name = 6 passes, 0 violations even though Chrome's AX display shows name="" because the PUA glyph has no printable form. No tool resolves the PUA codepoint back to the pencil/trash glyph it was minted for, renders it, and judges the name fails to convey edit/revoke; that mapping lives only in the private font and the rendering.

citation.quote: This failure condition occurs when a link contains only non-text content, such as an image, and that link cannot be identified by an accessible name.

pages.scenario: RTL Arabic recipe site (lang=ar dir=rtl). In a chicken-kabsa recipe card header, an icon-only link renders a download glyph (downward arrow into a tray) pointing to kabsa.pdf — purpose: save the recipe as PDF. But the CMS template bound the aria-label to the article-title variable, so the link is named "كبسة الدجاج بالخطوات" (the recipe's own name), well-formed meaningful Arabic that describes the article rather than the download action.
pages.mechanism: The <a> is role=link with accessible name "كبسة الدجاج بالخطوات" (confirmed via CDP). A screen-reader user hears the recipe title spoken twice (once as h1, once as this link) with no indication the second is a download control; they cannot tell it saves a PDF. Name present, programmatically determined, linguistically valid, but does not convey the link's purpose (the download action); 2.4.4 fails.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The accessible name is a non-empty, correctly-scripted Arabic string with proper lang/dir, so axe passes the discernible-text rule (verified: 3 passes, 0 violations) and no language/empty-name finding fires. No tool renders the SVG to recognise a download glyph, reads that the href is a .pdf, or knows that naming a control after the surrounding article (not its action) misdescribes its purpose — requiring reading Arabic plus visual+semantic judgment.

citation.quote: In cases where the link takes one to a document or a web application, the name of the document or web application would be sufficient to describe the purpose of the link (which is to take you to the document or web application).

pages.scenario: Boundary PASS control: a municipal transit (Route 12 schedule) utility bar of three icon-only links — house (aria-label="Metro Transit home"), printer (aria-label="Print this schedule"), telephone (aria-label="Call rider services: 311", a tel: link). Each has a non-empty name AND the name correctly describes the rendered glyph and the link's purpose, so the page satisfies 2.4.4.
pages.mechanism: Each <a> is role=link with a non-empty accessible name from aria-label that matches its glyph and destination (confirmed via CDP: "Metro Transit home" / "Print this schedule" / "Call rider services: 311"; SVGs aria-hidden). A screen-reader user can determine each link's purpose from the link text alone. Both the name-presence floor (c487ae/F89) and the descriptive limb of 2.4.4 are met.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: This is a true PASS, so there is no failure to miss — its role is to show the discriminator is glyph-vs-name AGREEMENT, not name presence. Crucially, the SAME automated signal ("has a non-empty name") is reported identically here and on failing cases 01-05 (verified: axe link-name = 3 passes, 0 violations, indistinguishable from the FAILs), which is exactly why tools cannot separate this PASS from those FAILs — only a human comparing each rendered glyph to its name can.

citation.quote: The intent of this success criterion is to help users understand the purpose of each link so they can decide whether they want to follow the link.

aspects.title: Identical accessible name AND identical context, but the links resolve to genuinely different purposes (fd3a94 equivalence judgment)
aspects.plain: Several links share the same text and surroundings yet lead to genuinely different places, so a user picking from them can't tell which one does what they want.
aspects.description: Two or more links on the page share the same accessible name AND the same programmatically determined context, yet lead to different resources serving different purposes — the classic 'three Read more / three Download / two Contact us' problem. The judgment is doubly semantic: (a) are the contexts truly identical, and (b) do the destinations serve EQUIVALENT purposes or genuinely different ones? Equivalent (e.g. the same data offered as PDF/XLSX/CSV) can PASS; genuinely different destinations (chat page vs phone page; sales@ vs support@) FAIL. On a self-contained page this is testable using same-page #fragment anchors and mailto:/tel: targets whose differing purposes are determinable from the page. The disambiguation can also be visual-only (alignment with an image or price block above), which a tool cannot read.
aspects.scLimb: Reflects the 2.4.4 best-practice that links with different purposes have different text; when names AND context are identical but purposes differ, at least one link fails to let the user determine its purpose.
aspects.whyUncovered: fd3a94 is PROPOSED/unapproved and explicitly notFullyAutomatable; its examples are fixed W3C 'About us / Contact us' pairs that require fetching external W3C test-asset URLs to resolve, so they are unusable as self-contained single-page fixtures and never cover same-page #fragments or mailto/tel disambiguation. No APPROVED corpus test exercises duplicate-name disambiguation at all. Resolving 'equivalent purpose' is irreducibly a meaning judgment, and visual-only disambiguation cannot be read by an automated tool.

references.quote: It is also a best practice for links with different purposes and destinations to have different link text.
if two or more links have the same accessible name but resolve to different resources, at least one of them does not accurately describe its purpose.

pages.scenario:
Bakery ordering page: one lead sentence (one

) contains two inline links both named 'order form', one targeting #cake-form (a bespoke priced celebration-cake quote) and one targeting #bread-form (a recurring Saturday bread subscription). Identical accessible name, identical same-DOM-node context, genuinely different on-page purposes resolvable via fragment anchors.
pages.mechanism: Two <a> in the same paragraph have identical accessible name 'order form' and therefore identical programmatically determined link context, but resolve to two #fragment sections that serve non-equivalent purposes (one-off priced cake quote vs recurring bread subscription). The disambiguating words ('for celebration cakes' / 'for sourdough and bread boxes') trail each link and are not part of, nor programmatically associated with, it — so a screen-reader links list yields 'order form / order form' with no way to choose.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Both links have non-empty identical accessible names and valid in-page hrefs, so link-name/discernible-text rules pass. The two links share the SAME DOM node as context, so any tool comparing 'programmatically determined context' sees them as identical and cannot tell the identity is the problem rather than evidence of equivalence. Deciding whether #cake-form and #bread-form serve equivalent or genuinely different purposes requires reading both sections and judging their meaning — an irreducible semantic judgment.

citation.quote: It is a best practice for links with the same destination to have consistent text (and this is a requirement per Success Criterion 3.2.4 Consistent Identification for pages in a set). It is also a best practice for links with different purposes and destinations to have different link text.

pages.scenario:
Charity grant-spending page: one sentence (one

) offers the SAME four-row dataset in three takeaway formats, each behind an identical link named 'Download this data' — a PDF, an XLSX and a CSV delivered via self-contained data: URIs. Identical name, identical same-DOM-node context, but the destinations are equivalent (same data, different format). PASS boundary control where the discriminator is purpose-equivalence.
pages.mechanism: Three <a download> with identical accessible name 'Download this data' in one paragraph resolve to three encodings (PDF/XLSX/CSV) of one identical dataset (the CSV data: URI literally encodes the same Food/Fuel/Children/Rent figures shown in the table). Per fd3a94's expectation, links sharing name+context PASS when they resolve to equivalent resources; 'same data, different file format' is the canonical equivalence (mirrored by the Understanding's HTML/PDF/mp3 'list of book titles' example). Every user gets the same content from any link, so each link's purpose — obtain this dataset — is determinable.
pages.primarySelector: p > a[download$=".pdf"], p > a[download$=".xlsx"], p > a[download$=".csv"]
pages.selectorNote: First 'download the form' link (consent); same name/cell as medical-history.txt link, different purpose; orig used .pdf/.xlsx/.csv > p which don't exist
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A naive duplicate-link heuristic would FALSELY flag three same-named links as a likely ambiguity failure; the tool cannot open the PDF/XLSX/CSV, parse them, and discover identical content. Conversely no name/role/href defect exists, so strict linters say nothing. Either way pass/fail hinges on the human-only judgment 'are these destinations the same data?' — exactly the equivalence call fd3a94 marks not fully automatable.
