pages.scenario:
Developer-tools SaaS contact card: one sentence (one

) has two inline links both named 'Email us', the first opening mailto:sales@latchkey.dev (pricing/seats/trial), the second mailto:support@latchkey.dev (production incidents/on-call). Identical name, identical same-DOM-node context, non-equivalent mailto destinations routed to different teams; picking the wrong one sends an outage to the sales queue.
pages.mechanism: Two <a> in one paragraph have identical accessible name 'Email us' (hence identical programmatic context) but resolve to two different mailto recipients (sales@ vs support@) serving different functions. Per fd3a94's assumptions the mailto target (a URL) is not counted as disambiguating context, and the distinguishing clauses ('to talk pricing' / 'if something is broken') trail each link without being associated with it — so a links-list view gives 'Email us / Email us' and the user cannot pick the right inbox.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Both links have non-empty identical names and valid mailto: hrefs, so link-name rules pass; sharing the same DOM-node context, a context comparison sees no difference. A tool would have to know that sales@ and support@ are different PURPOSES (not two aliases for one inbox) and that the surrounding prose makes the distinction available only to sighted readers — an organisational/semantic judgment beyond static analysis.

citation.quote: This rule assumes that reading the URL, such as from the status bar when the link is focused, is not considered part of the context, and therefore, it does not disambiguate links.

pages.scenario: Plant-care app pricing table laid out as a CSS Grid: two plans (Sprout $9/mo, Greenhouse $99/mo) side by side, each column ending in an identical 'Buy now' link. Each link sits in its own bare grid cell with NO plan name or price; the $9 / $99 price blocks are in separate grid cells positioned visually above their buttons. Disambiguation is conveyed purely by visual column alignment (verified: buy x-centers 123/549 align under price columns 237/663).
pages.mechanism: Two <a> named 'Buy now' resolve to non-equivalent destinations (#checkout-sprout $9 vs #checkout-greenhouse $99), but each link's programmatically determined link context (its own .buyrow cell) is equally bare — neither cell carries the plan or price, which lives in a sibling .price grid cell (the F63 'context not in the link's sentence/paragraph/cell' trap). Sighted users disambiguate by visual alignment under the price column; AT users get two identical 'Buy now' contexts. Because the page DOES convey the difference visually but not programmatically, fd3a94's 'no visual information' exemption does not apply and it fails.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Both links have valid hrefs and identical non-empty names, so link-name passes; the price and plan exist in the DOM so no 'missing text' rule fires. A tool cannot tell the price is VISUALLY but not PROGRAMMATICALLY associated with each button (the association is grid geometry). Recognising that link-to-price-block alignment is the ONLY disambiguator requires rendering the layout and reasoning about spatial relationships, which the accessibility tree and static analysis do not capture.

Spanish-language (lang=es) public health-centre contact page (i18n long-tail): one sentence (one

A tool would need to read Spanish prose to learn one link is for appointments and one for emergencies, AND know that tel:112 is the emergency number whose purpose differs categorically from a switchboard — locale-specific semantic reasoning beyond any static check.

pages.scenario: Volunteer-run tech conference page (negative control): one paragraph contains two inline links both named 'contact us' in the same sentence-pair, one framed around accessibility needs and one around invoices/VAT receipts. Per fd3a94 this PASSES because 'both links resolve to the same resource' — the strongest equivalence. The surrounding clauses describe two topics (access vs finance) but both are served by one team at one address, so whichever link the user picks, the purpose (reach the organisers) is satisfied identically and no user is misled.

aspects.title: Sufficiency of preceding-heading / list-grouping context as the purpose carrier (H80 judgment, including when the heading is NOT the link's context)
aspects.plain: A vague link like 'Map' or 'Book now' only makes sense from the heading above it, raising whether that heading is really tied to the link well enough.
aspects.description: A vague link ('Map', 'Book now', 'PDF', 'Read more') is rescued — or not — by a preceding heading or by the grouping structure it sits in (a section heading above a nav of links, a hotel-block heading, a document offered in three formats under one heading, a card whose <h2> headline is the appended 'Read more' link's group). The H80 judgment is whether the link text combined with that preceding heading describes the purpose, AND whether the heading is genuinely the link's context versus merely visually-above content. This is distinct from F63 (which is about context in the WRONG container) and from generic-text-alone: here the heading/grouping mechanism is the intended carrier, and the call is whether it sufficiently and correctly associates. Repeated identical link sets under different headings ('Map'/'Photos'/'Book now' for two hotels) are the canonical case where context is the only differentiator.
aspects.scLimb: Tests the 'link text together with its programmatically determined link context' clause where the carrier is a preceding heading or grouping structure — whether that combination conveys purpose and whether the heading is actually the link's context.
aspects.whyUncovered: H80 is an advisory technique with no ACT rule of its own; the approved c487ae corpus ignores context entirely, and 5effbb's context cases do not exercise preceding-heading or grouped-nav sufficiency, nor the repeated-link-set-under-different-headings pattern where the heading is the sole differentiator. Judging whether 'Map' under a hotel heading conveys 'map of THIS hotel' — and whether the heading is the link's actual context rather than coincidentally-above text — requires reading the heading and the grouping and making a meaning call no automated checker can make.

references.quote: The preceding heading provides context for an otherwise unclear link. The description lets a user distinguish this link from links in the web page that lead to other destinations and helps the user determine whether to follow the link.

This can be achieved by putting the description of the link in the same sentence, paragraph, list item, or table cell as the link, or in the table header cell for a link in a data table, because these are directly associated with the link itself.
This context will be most usable if it precedes the link.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: Two conference hotels (Royal Palm, Three Rivers). The H80 hotel-block shape is broken: instead of each hotel heading being followed by its own nav, both descriptions sit on top and ALL booking links are pooled into one shared 'Quick links' bar as a flat <ul>, with two byte-identical 'Map / Photos / Book now' triads separated only by plain-text <li> sub-labels. Repeated identical link sets where context is the sole differentiator — and that differentiator has been severed.
pages.mechanism: The hotel <h2> names are no longer the preceding grouping heading of the links; the links' nearest grouping heading is the generic 'Quick links'. The 'Royal Palm'/'Three Rivers' labels are in separate <li> elements, not the link's list item, so they are not programmatically determined link context. AT enumerates 'Map, Photos, Book now, Map, Photos, Book now' with no way to tie any 'Map' to a hotel.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every link has non-empty descriptive-looking text (c487ae/axe link-name passes); the <ul> has a valid aria-labelledby to a real heading so no unlabeled-region warning fires; two 'Map' links going to two different URLs is legitimate (different maps), so a same-name/different-URL heuristic cannot decide it is a failure. Judging that the two triads are mutually indistinguishable and that the hotel name in an adjacent <li> is not the link's context requires reading the page's meaning and the H80 grouping rule.

The correct verdict (pass) is unreachable by automation in either direction.

pages.scenario: A real-estate site lists two properties (14 Maple Court, 8 Birch Lane). Both cards use the H80 grouping correctly in form — an <h2> names the property and the per-listing <nav> is aria-labelledby that heading — but the second card was copy-pasted and its nav still references id='listing-maple' (the FIRST listing). When a screen-reader user enters that region the group is announced as Maple Court even though the links go to Birch Lane URLs and the visible <h2> reads '8 Birch Lane'. aspects.title: A specific, well-formed link name that contradicts its actual on-page destination (deceptive but descriptive name)
aspects.plain: A link has a clear, specific label that is wrong about its target (a 'Privacy Policy' link jumping to the Terms section), deceiving users about where it goes.
aspects.description: The link has a clear, descriptive, non-empty accessible name that reads as 'good' in isolation, but it is WRONG about where the link goes. On a self-contained page this is testable when the destination is a same-page #fragment anchor (or a labelled on-page section) whose actual content is verifiable: a 'Read our Privacy Policy' link whose href is '#terms' (a Terms section that exists on the page); a 'Skip to main content' link pointing to '#footer' instead of '#main'; a table-of-contents entry 'Chapter 3: Results' whose anchor actually holds Chapter 5; a 'Basic — $0/mo : Get started' link jumping to an '#enterprise-checkout' section. The name passes every presence and descriptiveness heuristic; the failure is that the name does not describe the link's ACTUAL purpose. This is the inverse of generic text — the text is specific but false — and requires a human to cross-check the claimed purpose against the on-page target.
aspects.scLimb: Tests the core intent of 2.4.4 — that the link's name lets the user understand its purpose and decide whether to follow it — by exposing names that misrepresent the actual (on-page-verifiable) destination.
aspects.whyUncovered: Every ACT fixture (approved and proposed) assumes the name honestly reflects the destination; 5effbb's whole premise is 'does the name describe the purpose' under the implicit assumption the author is not lying. There is NO test where a high-quality descriptive name points to a contradictory target. An automated tool would have to semantically understand the destination and compare it to the link text's claim — a meaning-level cross-check only a human can perform, here scoped to same-page anchors so the destination is verifiable on the single page.

pages.scenario: County parking-permit application page with a canonical skip link 'Skip to main content'. The page has a real <main id="main"> (the application form) and a real <footer id="site-footer"> (contact/hours). The skip link's href is '#site-footer', so it sends keyboard users to the page bottom, skipping the entire form, instead of '#main'.
pages.mechanism: The exemplary skip-link name 'Skip to main content' targets '#site-footer' (the footer) rather than '#main' (the form). Activating it moves focus past/below all main content to the footer — the destination is the opposite of what the name promises, defeating the bypass-block purpose.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: 'Skip to main content' is the recommended skip-link wording, so name-quality heuristics treat it as ideal and tools reward the mere presence of a skip link; '#site-footer' resolves to a real element and both <main> and <footer> are valid landmarks, so anchor and landmark checks pass. Catching it requires knowing 'main content' should target the <main> form, not the <footer> — resolving the fragment and judging the destination contradicts the name.

pages.scenario: Single-page final technical report with a table of contents (Chapter 1..5) and on-page chapters #ch1..#ch5. The TOC entry 'Chapter 3: Results' has href='#ch5' (the 'Chapter 5: Conclusions' heading). The real Results chapter is #ch3. Selecting Results lands the reader on Conclusions — a different, real chapter.
pages.mechanism: TOC link 'Chapter 3: Results' resolves to '#ch5' (the Chapter 5: Conclusions heading) instead of '#ch3' (Results); the descriptive name announces a destination that does not match the actual on-page chapter it scrolls to, so the link misrepresents its purpose.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every TOC label is non-empty, specific, and unique (ideal link text), '#ch5' resolves to a present heading, and both the Results (#ch3) and Conclusions (#ch5) chapters exist with proper headings — so name and anchor-validity checks pass. The only way to detect it is to follow 'Chapter 3: Results', read that the heading reached is 'Chapter 5: Conclusions', and recognise the numeric/topic contradiction — a semantic comparison requiring a human reader.

citation.quote: Check that text of the link describes the purpose of the link

pages.scenario: SaaS pricing page with three tier cards (Basic free, Pro, Enterprise) and three on-page sign-up sections (#basic-signup, #pro-signup, #enterprise-checkout). The Basic card's CTA reads 'Basic plan — $0/mo: Get started free' but its href is '#enterprise-checkout', the paid Enterprise purchase flow ($1,200/mo, annual contract). Honest target is #basic-signup.
pages.mechanism: The free-plan CTA's specific name 'Basic plan — $0/mo: Get started free' resolves to '#enterprise-checkout' — the paid Enterprise checkout section — instead of '#basic-signup'; the link's name describes a free signup while its actual destination is a high-commitment paid purchase flow, so the name does not describe the real purpose.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The name is non-empty, highly specific, and unique (passes c487ae and generic/duplicate heuristics), '#enterprise-checkout' resolves to a real section, and all three sign-up sections are well-formed. The contradiction is only visible by following the link, reading that the destination is the paid Enterprise checkout, and comparing it to the link's 'free Basic' promise — a semantic price/plan judgement no scanner makes.

citation.quote: The combination of the programmatically determined link context and the ANDI Output provide adequate description of the link's purpose.

pages.scenario: Arabic RTL (lang=ar, dir=rtl) municipal transit page for bus route 12 with two on-page schedule sections (#northbound-schedule, #southbound-schedule), each a distinct departures table. The quick-links 'الجدول الزمني للخط الشمالي' (Northbound timetable) link has href='#southbound-schedule' (the southbound section). Honest target is #northbound-schedule.
pages.mechanism: The link's Arabic accessible name says 'northbound' (الشمالي) but resolves to '#southbound-schedule', whose heading is 'southbound' (الجنوبي) — the opposite direction; the descriptive name misrepresents the link's actual on-page destination, the most safety-relevant fact on a transit page.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Both link names are non-empty, specific, and unique, lang='ar'/dir='rtl' are set correctly, '#southbound-schedule' resolves to a real element, and both schedule sections use valid <table> markup — so name, language, and anchor checks pass. Detecting it requires reading Arabic, following the 'northbound' link, and recognising the destination heading says 'southbound' — a cross-language, meaning-level comparison no automated checker performs.

citation.quote: Determine whether the ANDI Output, in combination with the programmatically determined link context

pages.scenario: PASS control: a healthcare patient-portal information hub with the SAME structure as the failing cases (skip link, in-page jump list, footer document links, labelled #fragment sections) but where every descriptive name correctly matches its destination: 'Read our Privacy Policy'→#privacy (the Privacy Policy), 'Skip to your message inbox'→#inbox, 'Jump to: Booking a flu vaccine'→#flu, 'Read our Notice of Patient Rights'→#rights.
pages.mechanism: Each link's accessible name resolves to the on-page section whose heading matches that name (e.g. 'Read our Privacy Policy'→#privacy headed 'Privacy Policy'), so the name reliably describes the link's actual purpose/destination — the intent of 2.4.4 is met. Exact same-text contrast with case-01 ('Read our Privacy Policy', href '#terms').
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Automated tools cannot adjudicate this either way: they see non-empty, descriptive, unique names and resolvable fragments and report 'no issue', which here is correct only because a human can confirm the name-to-destination match. The tools never perform that confirmation, so the PASS verdict (like the FAIL verdicts) rests entirely on human semantic cross-checking the scanner is blind to.

citation.quote:
The intent of this success criterion is to help users understand the purpose of each
         link so they can decide whether they want to follow the link.

aspects.title: Headings and labels that are present and topically true but too generic/boilerplate to orient (Information, Section 2, Value, Details)
aspects.plain: A heading or field label is technically accurate but so generic ('Information', 'Details', 'Value') that users can't predict what the section contains or what to type.
aspects.description: The hardest real-world 2.4.6 calls are headings and labels that are not WRONG but are uselessly generic and therefore non-orienting: section headings like 'Information', 'More', 'Details', 'Section 2', 'Content', 'Misc', or field labels like 'Field', 'Input', 'Value', 'Setting 1'. Each one technically relates to the content beneath/within it, so a naive topic-match passes, yet it defeats the Understanding intent that a user can 'find the information they seek more easily' and 'predict what each section contains'. A heading 'Information' over a refund-policy section is true-but-not-descriptive; a label 'Value' over an email input is true-but-not-descriptive. This is a graded human judgment (two reviewers can disagree on where 'generic' tips into 'inadequate') that no checker has a semantic notion of. It is the borderline tier the entire ACT corpus deliberately omits.
aspects.scLimb: Both limbs — 'Headings and labels describe topic or purpose.' Covers the descriptiveness/adequacy of heading text (b49b2e limb) AND of form-control/button labels (cc0f0a limb) when the text is technically relevant but too generic to be descriptive.
aspects.whyUncovered: ACT fails are deliberate absurd mismatches ('Weather' over opening hours, 'Menu' over a name field) — a 100% topic mismatch. The corpus has NO 'technically-relevant-but-vague' case; the SC's own coverage summary admits there are 'no SUBTLE/borderline cases (e.g. a heading that is vague, overly generic like Information, technically-true-but-unhelpful, or only partially relevant) which is where real-world 2.4.6 judgment is hard.' Generic-ness is exactly the graded judgment the binary pass/fail fixtures hide, and a fully-automated checker cannot judge whether a real word is 'too generic to orient'.

references.quote: When headings are clear and descriptive, users can find the information they seek more easily, and they can understand the relationships between different parts of the content more easily.
These people benefit when section titles make it possible to predict what each section contains.
Authors may also want to consider putting the most important information at the beginning of each heading. This helps users "skim" the headings to locate the specific content they need
Each visual form label is sufficiently clear and descriptive, so users know what input data is expected

aspects.ttWhy: Cites generic section headings and generic field labels alike.

pages.scenario: E-commerce 'Orders & Returns' help page whose three sections (refund policy, delivery times, two-year warranty) are all headed 'Information', 'More Information', 'Additional Information' — each heading topically true of the substantive, distinct content beneath it but giving no predictive cue about which section holds what.
pages.mechanism: Heading limb (b49b2e): correctly-nested, non-empty <h2> headings that are topically related but non-descriptive. A screen-reader heading-list / in-page ToC collapses to 'Information / More Information / Additional Information', conveying nothing about refund-vs-delivery-vs-warranty, so the user cannot find or predict section content (fails TT 10.A: heading must describe topic/purpose of its content).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe-core empty-heading/heading-order/page-has-heading-one all satisfied (verified 0 violations); 'Information' is a real, correctly-spelled word genuinely related to the content so even a topic-overlap heuristic passes. No checker has a semantic model of whether a true word is too generic to predict section contents — a graded human judgment where reviewers can disagree on where 'generic' tips into 'inadequate'.

citation.quote: Descriptive headings are especially helpful for users who have disabilities that make reading slow and for people with limited short-term memory. These people benefit when section titles make it possible to predict what each section contains.

pages.scenario: CRM 'Notification preferences' settings form whose four real controls (digest-frequency select, theme select, language select, quiet-hours time input) carry properly-associated visible labels reading 'Value', 'Setting 1', 'Setting 2', 'Setting 3' — present and bound but conveying nothing about what each field controls.
pages.mechanism: Label limb (cc0f0a): native <label for> correctly associated with each <select>/<input>, so the control is named (4.1.2) and labelled (3.3.2), but the label text does not make the control's purpose clear. A user tabbing the form hears 'Value, combobox' / 'Setting 1' with no way to know it sets email frequency, theme, language, or quiet-hours start (fails TT 5.B: label must be descriptive of expected input).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every control has a non-empty <label for> correctly bound to it, so axe-core label/select-name pass (verified 0 violations) — the tools' entire model of this SC is presence+association. 'Value'/'Setting 1' are non-empty real strings so no empty-label rule fires. Whether 'Value' adequately describes a digest-frequency control is a meaning judgment comparing each label to what its control actually does, which no checker performs.

citation.quote: This success criterion does not require the use of labels; however, it does require that if labels are present, they must be accurate and sufficiently clear or descriptive.

pages.scenario:
Coffee-roastery FAQ page with a single section heading 'Details' above a block that actually answers three unrelated questions — subscription billing dates, how to pause/skip a box, and what to do about a damaged delivery; the three questions are visually bold

, not headings.
pages.mechanism:
Heading limb (b49b2e): the page's only

('Details') is loosely true (the block does give details) but under-describes a three-topic block and provides no navigational landmark to reach billing vs. pausing vs. damaged-delivery. The bolded questions are plain

so they are not in the heading list at all; a screen-reader heading list shows one useless entry (fails TT 10.A).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: One non-empty <h2> in valid order, so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse pass (verified 0 violations after fixing incidental contrast/landmark noise). 'Details' is a real on-topic word so no keyword heuristic flags it. Recognising one heading is too few for three topics, and that 'Details' fails to name or separate them, requires a human to read the whole block and judge structural/semantic under-description.

citation.quote: The intent of this success criterion is to help users understand what information is contained in web pages and how that information is organized. When headings are clear and descriptive, users can find the information they seek more easily.

pages.scenario: Internal SaaS operations dashboard with four metric cards: three are descriptively titled ('Active subscriptions', 'Support backlog', 'Churn rate') and the fourth is headed 'Stuff' over an inline-SVG bar chart that is actually monthly recurring revenue. The SVG carries a correct aria-label, so the descriptive truth lives on the image, not the heading.
pages.mechanism: Heading limb (b49b2e): the <h2> 'Stuff' is generic to the point of useless yet not an outright mismatch (a chart is 'stuff' on the dashboard). The card landmark named 'Stuff' gives no clue it holds revenue; the only descriptive text is the SVG's aria-label, which the heading SC does not govern. The three descriptive sibling headings sharpen the contrast (fails TT 10.A while 1.1.1/4.1.2 on the chart pass).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The <h2> is non-empty and in valid order and the SVG has a correct accessible name, so there is literally nothing empty or missing — axe passes (verified 0 violations after raising card titles to h2 to fix heading-order and wrapping the top bar in a landmark). A tool cannot tell that 'Stuff' under-describes a revenue chart, nor that the descriptive text lives in the image label rather than the heading; that requires a human reading the heading against the chart content.

citation.quote: Goal: A page's content is described in headings and labels

pages.scenario: GOV.UK-style council-tax-reduction benefits wizard (step 3 of 5) with multiple <button>s: three are labelled 'Submit' but perform different functions (add a household member to a list, upload the chosen evidence file, save the whole application and advance to step 4) and a fourth is labelled 'Action'.
pages.mechanism: Button-label sub-limb of cc0f0a (TT 5.B second condition): each <button>'s visible text is its accessible name, so all are named (4.1.2) and labelled (3.3.2), but 'Submit' x3 and 'Action' are not sufficiently descriptive of each button's distinct function. A screen-reader / voice-control user hears three indistinguishable 'Submit, button' targets and a meaningless 'Action, button'.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every <button> has a non-empty accessible name so axe button-name passes (verified 0 violations after wrapping the gov bar in a header landmark). Duplicate-name heuristics target links in lists, not buttons that legitimately repeat, and cannot tell whether repetition is appropriate (three 'Add to cart' in a grid) or confusing (three 'Submit' doing different things). Deciding the labels fail to convey each function requires a human to map each button to the action it performs.

citation.doc: WCAG Techniques — G131: Providing descriptive labels
citation.quote: The objective of this technique is to ensure that the label for any interactive component within web content makes the component's purpose clear.

pages.scenario: PASS control that mirrors the structure of case-01 (three-section help article) and case-02 (preferences form) on one page, but re-headed descriptively ('Refund policy', 'Delivery times & costs', 'Two-year warranty', 'Notification preferences') and re-labelled descriptively ('Email digest frequency', 'Colour theme', 'Interface language', 'Quiet-hours start time') so a reviewer can see exactly where generic tips into orienting.
pages.mechanism: Both limbs satisfied: headings describe the topic/purpose of their sections (TT 10.A) and labels make each control's purpose clear (TT 5.B). Same DOM shape and body content as the failing cases — only the heading/label text changed — so a screen-reader heading list now yields a meaningful outline and each control announces a name that tells the user what it does.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Automated tools also pass this page, but for the wrong reason — they only verified presence/association, exactly as they did for failing cases 01 and 02. The reason this page genuinely passes (the text is descriptive) is invisible to them; only a human comparing each heading/label to its content can confirm descriptiveness. Its value is to show presence-checking cannot distinguish the control from the failing pages.

citation.quote: When headings are clear and descriptive, users can find the information they seek more easily, and they can understand the relationships between different parts of the content more easily. Descriptive labels help users identify specific components within the content.

aspects.title: Repeated or near-identical headings/labels among siblings that fail to differentiate sections (relational/uniqueness facet of G130)
aspects.plain: Several headings or labels on the page are identical or near-identical ('Description, Description, Description'), so a screen-reader user skimming them can't tell the sections apart.
aspects.description: G130 states descriptive headings identify sections 'in relation both to the web page as a whole and to other sections of the same web page', so descriptiveness is partly RELATIONAL: a heading or label can describe its own content yet fail to distinguish it from a sibling, defeating heading-to-heading and skim navigation. Real failures: three accordion panels all headed 'Description'; multiple product cards each headed 'Product'; two form fieldsets both holding inputs labeled 'Name' with no Shipping/Billing qualifier on the field; tabs all labeled 'Details'. Each heading/label is individually plausible but collectively non-orienting — a screen-reader user jumping heading-to-heading or scanning a generated heading list hears 'Description, Description, Description'. This is a cross-element, whole-page semantic judgment, not a per-element topic match.
aspects.scLimb: Both limbs — applies G130's relational requirement to heading text and to form-control labels. A heading or label fails not on its own content match but because it is indistinguishable from its siblings.
aspects.whyUncovered: All b49b2e fixtures are single-heading micro-pages (the coverage summary: 'no multiple headings on a page, so heading-to-section scoping and competing next content situations are never exercised'). The only multi-field ACT fixture (b0b11b83, verified: a Shipping fieldset and a Billing fieldset each with 'Name'/'Street') is a PASS where the section heading disambiguates the repeated labels — there is NO fixture where repeated identical headings/labels are left ambiguous. The relational uniqueness facet of G130 is never failed, and an automated checker cannot judge whether sibling sections are confusable.

references.quote: Descriptive headings identify sections of the content in relation both to the web page as a whole and to other sections of the same web page.
Note that the level 2 headings have the distinguishing information at the beginning (i.e., instead of "Preparation for floods", "Preparation for fires", etc).

helps people who use screen readers by ensuring that labels and headings are clearer when presented in a different format — for example, in an automatically generated list of headings, a table of contents, or when jumping from heading to heading within a page.
they can understand the relationships between different parts of the content more easily.

aspects.ttWhy: Non-distinct sibling headings and repeated form-field labels both fail relationally.

pages.scenario: E-commerce houseplant listing: a 3-column grid of six product cards where every card's <h3> heading reads the single word 'Product'; the distinguishing species name (Monstera, Snake plant, ZZ plant, etc.) lives in a non-heading span in the card body. The generated heading list reads 'Product, Product, Product, Product, Product, Product'.
pages.mechanism: Heading limb of G130 (relational/uniqueness): each <h3> is individually plausible (each card IS a product) but the six sibling headings are identical, so a screen-reader user jumping H3-to-H3 or opening the headings rotor gets no differentiation between products. The species name is in span.name, which is not part of the heading text and so never appears in the heading list. Confirmed via Chrome accessibility tree: heading list = 'Product' x6.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: All six headings are present, non-empty, sequentially nested (h1>h2>h3), and validly marked up, so axe-core empty-heading / heading-order / page-has-heading-one, WAVE, and Lighthouse all pass. 'Product' is a real word that accurately describes the card. No automated checker performs the cross-element comparison of whether six sibling headings are mutually distinguishing or whether the generated heading list would orient a user — that is a whole-page semantic judgment.

citation.quote: Descriptive headings identify sections of the content in relation both to the web page as a whole and to other sections of the same web page.

pages.scenario: A product-detail page uses a fully correct WAI-ARIA APG tabs widget (arrow-key nav, roving tabindex, aria-selected, aria-controls/aria-labelledby) to switch between a spec table, customer reviews, and shipping info — but all three tab buttons are labeled 'Details'. A tab label is the label of the section it reveals, and the three sibling tab labels are identical.
pages.mechanism: Label limb of SC 2.4.6 (TT 5.B), relational/uniqueness: a screen-reader user arrowing the tablist hears 'Details, tab 1 of 3 ... Details, tab 2 of 3 ... Details, tab 3 of 3'. Because only the selected panel is exposed (others are hidden), the tab label is the sole orientation cue and it is identical for all three, so the user cannot tell which tab leads to specs vs reviews vs shipping. Confirmed via Chrome a11y tree: tab list = 'Details' x3.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The widget is ARIA-perfect: each tab has a valid role, a non-empty accessible name ('Details'), correct aria-selected, and valid aria-controls. axe-core (aria-roles, aria-required-attr, aria-valid-attr-value, button-name) and Lighthouse pass, and 4.1.2 Name/Role/Value is satisfied because a name is present. No rule compares sibling tab labels for distinctiveness; recognizing that one repeated word cannot differentiate three sections requires reading each panel's content — human judgment.

citation.quote: 1. Each visual form label is sufficiently clear and descriptive, so users know what input data is expected, AND 2. Each visual button label is sufficiently clear and descriptive, so users know its function.

pages.scenario: An online-banking 'Your accounts overview' page lists three accounts — Everyday Checking, High-Yield Savings, and a Platinum Rewards credit card — each in its own labelled <section> opened by an <h2> reading 'Account Summary'. The distinguishing nickname/number sits in a non-heading div below each heading; each section is also aria-labelledby its own 'Account Summary' h2.
pages.mechanism: Heading limb of G130 (relational): 'Account Summary' accurately names each block in isolation but the three sibling headings are identical, so a user opening the headings list to jump to 'my savings account' hears three indistinguishable 'Account Summary' entries; region navigation is equally undifferentiated because each section's accessible name is also 'Account Summary'. Confirmed via Chrome a11y tree: heading list = 'Account Summary' x3.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Headings are present, non-empty, sequential (one h1 then three h2), and validly marked up, so axe-core, WAVE, and Lighthouse pass. 'Account Summary' is a legitimate, accurate phrase a linter cannot flag. Detecting the failure requires recognizing the page holds three different accounts, that the true differentiator (Checking/Savings/Credit) was demoted out of the heading, and that the heading list cannot orient a user — a whole-page semantic comparison.

citation.quote: Authors may also want to consider putting the most important information at the beginning of each heading. This helps users "skim" the headings to locate the specific content they need, and is especially helpful when browsers or assistive technology allow navigation from heading to heading.

pages.scenario:
A hospital patient-portal prescription-refill form lists four medications (Lisinopril, Metformin, Atorvastatin, Levothyroxine), each in a
whose reads 'Medication', with a checkbox labeled 'Refill' and a quantity
pages.mechanism: Label limb of SC 2.4.6 (TT 5.B), relational: every control has a present, correctly for/id-associated, non-empty label, but the legend ('Medication') and labels ('Refill','Quantity') are identical across the four sibling medications. A screen-reader user tabbing the form hears 'Medication, Refill, checkbox' four times and cannot tell which 'Refill' refills the Lisinopril vs the Levothyroxine — a medication-safety ambiguity. Confirmed via Chrome a11y tree: controls = 'Refill'/'Quantity' x4, with no drug name in any accessible name.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every control has a programmatically associated, non-empty label/legend, so axe-core (label, select-name, form-field-multiple-labels), WAVE, and Lighthouse pass — those rules check presence/association (3.3.2, 4.1.2), which is satisfied. No rule reads the four fieldsets, notices they concern four different drugs, and judges that the repeated labels fail to distinguish them; that cross-control semantic comparison (and noticing the differentiator was placed outside the label) is human judgment.

citation.quote: It is possible for controls and inputs to have an appropriate accessible name (e.g. using aria-label="…") and therefore pass Success Criterion 4.1.2, but to still fail this success criterion (if the label is inaccurate or insufficiently clear or descriptive).

pages.scenario:
An Arabic-language (RTL) university LMS course page splits a data-science course into five weekly modules, each a labelled
opened by an

reading the single word 'الوحدة' ('the module'). The distinct weekly topic (Intro to Python, Probability, Data cleaning, Visualization, Intro to ML) is rendered in a non-heading

below each heading. An Arabic screen reader navigating by heading hears 'الوحدة' five times.
pages.mechanism: Heading limb of G130 (relational), in Arabic: each 'الوحدة' heading is individually plausible but the five sibling headings are identical, so a heading list / H2-to-H2 jump gives no orientation among five distinct topics; each section is aria-labelledby its own 'الوحدة' h2 so region nav is equally undifferentiated. Confirmed via Chrome a11y tree: heading list = 'الوحدة' x5. lang=ar/dir=rtl are correct, so this is purely the relational-uniqueness defect, not a markup error.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Headings are present, non-empty, sequential (one h1 then five h2), validly marked up, with correct lang/dir, so axe-core, WAVE, and Lighthouse pass. Two layers defeat heuristics: 'الوحدة' is a legitimate Arabic word no rule can flag, and any tool leaning on an English bad-string list ('Untitled','Heading','Section') sees nothing because the text is non-Latin script. Detecting the failure requires reading and understanding Arabic, recognizing five distinct topics, and judging that the repeated heading collapses the distinction — language-aware semantic judgment.

citation.quote: Descriptive headings identify sections of the content in relation both to the web page as a whole and to other sections of the same web page.

pages.scenario: PASS control: a checkout+FAQ page that is the structural twin of the failing cases but correctly disambiguated. The FAQ accordion's four <h3> headings each lead with the actual question; the form's Shipping and Billing <fieldset>s each have a section <legend> AND every field label leads with its qualifier ('Shipping — Full name', 'Billing — Full name', 'Shipping — Street address', 'Billing — Street address'), so both the heading list and a flat form-controls list orient the user. Mirrors G130's flood/fire example and the ACT cc0f0a b0b11b83 PASS.
pages.mechanism: Both limbs satisfied: the four <h3> are mutually distinct questions (TT 10.A), and the four form labels are mutually distinct and lead with the distinguishing word so they orient the user even in a flat list that strips group context (TT 5.B, G130 'distinguishing information at the beginning'). Confirmed via Chrome a11y tree: heading list = four distinct questions; controls = four distinct 'Shipping — …'/'Billing — …' labels. The disambiguation is genuinely in the DOM, not faked.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Automated tools also report no violation here — but so does a human, for the right reason: the sibling headings/labels are genuinely distinct. The control's value is that it is the near-twin of case-04 (same fieldset/legend/repeated-label hazard) yet passes; a tool cannot tell case-04 (fail) from case-06 (pass) because both have present, associated, non-empty labels. Only the human relational judgment separates them, which is exactly why the failing cases need human review.

citation.quote: Note that the level 2 headings have the distinguishing information at the beginning (i.e., instead of "Preparation for floods", "Preparation for fires", etc).

aspects.title: Graphical/icon-only labels whose glyph is misleading or context-dependent for the control's real function
aspects.plain: An icon labeling a control is misleading for its real function, like a floppy-disk icon on a 'Send' button or a magnifying glass on a filter button.
aspects.description: The Understanding text devotes three paragraphs to icon labels: an image can BE a descriptive label, but 'the same image can be interpreted differently in different contexts' — a magnifying-glass icon next to a text field reads as 'Search', the same icon on a picture reads as 'zoom/magnify'. 2.4.6's label limb and TT 5.B ('The label or instruction can be graphical or textual') therefore require a human visual judgment: is THIS glyph, in THIS placement, a commonly-understood cue for the control's actual function? Failures are present-but-misleading icons: a floppy-disk icon labeling a 'Send' button; a magnifying glass on a button that actually filters rather than searches; a funnel glyph on a control accessibly named 'Search'; a gear icon used as the label for a 'Log out' control; or an icon whose accessible name names the GLYPH ('magnifier') rather than the FUNCTION ('Search'). A checker can confirm an accessible name exists; it cannot judge whether the chosen glyph is the commonly-understood cue for the function in that spot.
aspects.scLimb: Labels limb — the descriptiveness of a control's label when the label is graphical (icon) rather than textual. TT 5.B explicitly admits graphical labels into this limb.
aspects.whyUncovered: No cc0f0a fixture uses a graphical label at all — every label is literal text ('First name:', 'Menu', 'Info:'). The icon-as-label scenario, despite being the single most-elaborated example in the Understanding doc (the entire loupe/magnifier discussion), has ZERO fixtures. Context-dependence (same icon, two meanings) and glyph/function disagreement are inherently semantic+visual judgments the rule never instantiates, and an automated tool that only checks for a non-empty accessible name will pass every one of these.

references.quote: Note that the same image can be interpreted differently in different contexts. However, it can still be considered descriptive if its use is commonly understood in each context.
when accompanying a text field, a loupe or magnifying glass icon with text alternative of "Search" is commonly interpreted as indicating the field is for entering and submitting a search query.
Placed on or near another image, a loupe or magnifying glass icon is commonly interpreted as a means to view a magnified version of the image
The label or instruction can be graphical or textual.

aspects.ttWhy: Graphical/icon labels on form controls and buttons; 5.B allows graphical labels.

pages.scenario: Document/PDF viewer toolbar: a magnifying-glass icon button with accessible name "Search" actually opens a print-preview dialog. The loupe glyph and the accessible name agree with each other (loupe=Search) but both misdescribe the control's real function (print preview); the page has no search feature at all.
pages.mechanism: Button exposed as role=button, accessible name "Search" computed from aria-label (inner loupe SVG is aria-hidden). A SR user hears "Search, button" and a sighted user reads the universally-understood loupe, both led to expect text search; activating instead opens a print-preview <dialog>. The graphical label is not a commonly-understood cue for the actual function, failing the 2.4.6 label limb (TT 5.B) though name presence (4.1.2) is met.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe-core button-name, WAVE, and Lighthouse only verify a non-empty accessible name; "Search" qualifies and all pass (verified: accessibility tree resolves the control to role=button name="Search"). No tool rasterises the inline SVG to identify the loupe, and none executes the onclick to learn it opens print preview rather than searching. Judging that a loupe+"Search" pairing misdescribes a print action is an inherently visual + behavioural + semantic human judgment.

citation.quote: Note that the same image can be interpreted differently in different contexts. However, it can still be considered descriptive if its use is commonly understood in each context. For example, when accompanying a text field, a loupe or magnifying glass icon with text alternative of "Search" is commonly interpreted as indicating the field is for entering and submitting a search query.

pages.scenario: Webmail compose action bar: the primary submit button carries accessible name "Send message" and sends the email, but its only visible label is a floppy-disk SVG — the near-universal "Save"/"Save draft" glyph. A user scanning by icon reads the floppy disk as "save a draft" and may click expecting to save, only to dispatch the message.
pages.mechanism: type=submit button exposed as role=button, accessible name "Send message" (floppy SVG aria-hidden). The SR-announced name is correct, but the sole visible label for sighted/low-vision/magnifier users is a floppy disk, the commonly-understood cue for save, not send (whose convention is a paper plane/arrow). The graphical label is not a commonly-understood cue for the control's true function, failing the 2.4.6 label limb (TT 5.B); name presence (4.1.2) passes.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe-core button-name, WAVE, and Lighthouse confirm only a non-empty accessible name on the submit button — "Send message" satisfies that (verified via accessibility tree). None render the inline SVG to recognise a floppy disk, and none encode the convention "floppy disk means save, not send." The defect is a visual-semantic mismatch between a commonly-understood glyph and the action it labels, catchable only by a human who sees the icon and knows the convention.

citation.quote: The label or instruction can be graphical or textual.

pages.scenario: Real-estate listings search: inside a role=search landmark, the trailing submit button correctly submits the typed query and is accessibly named "Search", but its rendered glyph is a funnel — the universal filter icon — sitting exactly where a loupe (commonly understood as Search) belongs. A user scanning by icon expects it to open filter facets, not run the text search.
pages.mechanism: Button exposed as role=button, accessible name "Search" (funnel SVG aria-hidden), inside a correctly identified search landmark; programmatically everything reads as a valid search submit. Visually the only label is a funnel, the commonly-understood cue for filtering, not searching, so the graphical label is not a commonly-understood cue for the control's actual function — the 2.4.6 label limb fails even though name/role/landmark are all correct.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Engineered to defeat heuristics: the button has a non-empty name ("Search", verified via accessibility tree), a valid role=search landmark wraps it, and it really submits the query, so axe-core/WAVE/Lighthouse have every readable signal pointing to "correct search button" and pass it. The sole defect is the rendered funnel glyph, which no tool rasterises or classifies, and none encode "funnel=filter vs loupe=search." Recognising the glyph contradicts the function is a visual + conventional human judgment.

citation.quote: Note that the same image can be interpreted differently in different contexts. However, it can still be considered descriptive if its use is commonly understood in each context. For example, when accompanying a text field, a loupe or magnifying glass icon with text alternative of "Search" is commonly interpreted as indicating the field is for entering and submitting a search query.

pages.scenario: Online-banking dashboard: the only session-end control is a top-bar icon button rendering a gear/cog glyph (universally "Settings") with accessible name literally "gear" (the name names the glyph, not the function); clicking it ends the secure session (log out). Both the glyph (gear=settings) and the literal name ("gear") point away from the real function, with real consequences in a banking context.
pages.mechanism: Button exposed as role=button, accessible name "gear" (from aria-label; cog SVG aria-hidden). A SR user hears "gear, button" — a description of the picture giving no clue it logs them out; a sighted user sees a cog, the commonly-understood cue for settings, and likewise will not expect session termination. The label fails on both channels: programmatically it names the glyph not the purpose, and visually the glyph is the wrong commonly-understood cue for "log out" — failing the 2.4.6 label limb (TT 5.B).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe-core button-name, WAVE, and Lighthouse pass any button with a non-empty accessible name; "gear" qualifies (verified via accessibility tree). No tool reasons that "gear" describes the glyph rather than the action, none rasterise the SVG to recognise a cog, and none encode "cog conventionally means settings, not log out." Catching that the name names the picture and the glyph is the wrong cue for the function requires a human who reads the announced string and knows the icon convention.

citation.quote: It is possible for controls and inputs to have an appropriate accessible name (e.g. using aria-label="…") and therefore pass Success Criterion 4.1.2, but to still fail this success criterion (if the label is inaccurate or insufficiently clear or descriptive).

pages.scenario: Recipe page action bar with two visually identical heart toggle buttons side by side: one saves the recipe privately to the user's own cookbook, the other posts a public like attributed to the user. Both render the same heart glyph and both carry accessible name "heart", so neither icon nor name disambiguates the two consequential actions — and one carries a privacy implication the other does not.
pages.mechanism: Both buttons expose role=button, the identical accessible name "heart" (heart SVGs aria-hidden), and aria-pressed state. A SR user navigating by control hears "heart, toggle button" twice with nothing to distinguish a private save from a public like; adjacent count text is in a separate element and not part of either name. The same glyph in the same context is reused for two different functions without each use being commonly understood, failing the 2.4.6 label limb (TT 5.B); duplicate names and name presence (4.1.2) are legal/met.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe-core, WAVE, and Lighthouse pass both buttons (non-empty button-name, valid aria-pressed; verified via accessibility tree showing two role=button name="heart"). Duplicate accessible names are not an error and there is no label-in-name mismatch. No tool rasterises the heart glyph, and none reasons that one heart means private-save while the other means public-like, or that the shared name "heart" describes the picture rather than either purpose. Detecting the ambiguity — including the privacy-relevant action — requires a human comparing both controls' real behaviours.

citation.quote: Note that the same image can be interpreted differently in different contexts. However, it can still be considered descriptive if its use is commonly understood in each context.

pages.scenario: E-commerce product page (PASS control): the same magnifying-glass glyph is used in two places, each correctly. In the header a loupe trails a text field named "Search" and submits a product query; on the product photo the same loupe (with a small +) is named "Zoom image" and opens an enlarged lightbox. This is the canonical context-appropriate reuse described verbatim in the SC 2.4.6 Understanding doc, so the graphical labels are descriptive and the page passes; included to contrast appropriate reuse against the misuse in case-01..05.
pages.mechanism: Both buttons expose role=button with a non-empty accessible name (loupe SVGs aria-hidden). The first, accompanying a text field and named "Search", is the commonly-understood query affordance; the second, placed on an image and named "Zoom image", is the commonly-understood magnify affordance. In each placement the glyph's conventional meaning matches the context and the name names the function (not the glyph), and each control does what its label says — so both graphical labels are descriptive, satisfying the 2.4.6 label limb.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Automated tools also pass this page (both buttons have non-empty names; verified via accessibility tree showing role=button name="Search" and name="Zoom image") — but here the pass verdict is correct, and that is the point. A tool cannot tell that this is the appropriate reuse the Understanding doc endorses while case-01..05 are inappropriate misuse, because that distinction is a human judgment about whether each glyph's conventional meaning fits its context. The aspect requires a human to ratify good reuse as confidently as flagging bad reuse.

citation.quote: Placed on or near another image, a loupe or magnifying glass icon is commonly interpreted as a means to view a magnified version of the image (for instance, acting as a mechanism to zoom into the image, or opening a full-sized image in a new window).

aspects.title: Labels that name the field's topic but omit required data-format / data-requirement cues (format, required, data type)
aspects.plain: A field's label names its topic but hides the format it secretly demands (a 'Date' box requiring MM/DD/YYYY), so users can't tell what input is accepted.
aspects.description: 2.4.6's label limb is not satisfied merely by a label that names the field's topic; per TT 5.B and G131 the label must make the field's purpose AND its applicable data requirements clear. A label like 'Date of birth:' on a native date picker is the ACT canonical pass, but real failures are subtler: a free-text field labeled only 'Date' that silently demands MM/DD/YYYY; an 'Amount' field that secretly rejects a currency symbol; a 'Card number' field that only accepts un-spaced digits; a required field whose label gives no required indicator while siblings do. The label is present, grammatically describes the topic, and passes axe — yet a user cannot tell what input is expected, which is exactly the descriptiveness shortfall TT 5.B calls out (and an error-after-submit message is explicitly insufficient).
aspects.scLimb: Labels limb — descriptiveness of a form-control label, specifically the 'applicable data requirements' dimension (format, required-status, data type) that the ACT cc0f0a expectation reduces away to a pure topic-match.
aspects.whyUncovered: Every cc0f0a fixture pairs a single bare input with a one-or-two-word label and judges only topic match ('First name:' pass vs 'Menu' fail). No fixture has a field with a non-obvious data format, a required field, or a constrained data type, or a label that is topically right but requirement-blind. The data-requirement dimension that TT 5.B explicitly enumerates is entirely absent, and a checker that only verifies a label is associated and non-empty cannot judge whether the expected format is communicated.

references.quote: Determine whether labels and/or instructions for form components sufficiently describe the purpose and applicable data requirements (date formats, required fields, data type, etc.).
An error message is not sufficient to communicate the expected format to pass this test.
The label may also be used to include text or a text symbol indicating that input is required.
Descriptive labels help users identify specific components within the content.

aspects.ttWhy: Form-field labels missing data-format/required cues; directly invokes TT 5.B/G131.

pages.scenario: UK borough council 'Report a missed bin collection' form: a plain text input (not type=date, so no native picker hints at order) labelled only 'Date' whose JS validator silently accepts only day-first DD-MM-YYYY and rejects 11/06/2026, 2026-11-06, '6 November 2026'. The DD-MM-YYYY format is disclosed for the first time only in the post-submit error.
pages.mechanism: Label names the topic ('Date') correctly and is associated + non-empty, but communicates none of the applicable data requirement (day-first DD-MM-YYYY). The format constraint lives only in the submit-handler regex /^(0[1-9]|[12]\d|3[01])-(0[1-9]|1[0-2])-\d{4}$/ and the after-submit error, which TT 5.B's Note says is insufficient. A screen-reader user hears 'Date, edit text' and cannot know the field rejects reasonable inputs.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The <label> is present, associated via for/id, and non-empty, and the input has valid attributes, so axe-core/WAVE/Lighthouse report a correctly labelled field. No static scanner parses the submit-handler regex to learn the field demands day-first DD-MM-YYYY, and none can judge that 'Date' alone fails to tell a user what format is expected; recognising that the label is topically right but requirement-blind needs human reasoning.

citation.quote: An error message is not sufficient to communicate the expected format to pass this test.

pages.scenario: Nonprofit donation form with a legend 'Fields marked (required) must be completed.' Two fields are labelled 'First name (required)' and 'Gift amount (required)'; a third field that is ALSO required (has the required attribute, blocks submit, receives the receipt) is labelled only 'Email' with no '(required)' word, silently breaking the page's own stated convention.
pages.mechanism: The label 'Email' names the topic correctly and the field carries a real required attribute, but the visible label omits the required-status cue that the page taught the user marks mandatory fields and that sibling labels carry. The descriptiveness shortfall is that the label fails to convey the required data requirement TT 5.B enumerates and G131 says a label may carry.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The label is associated and non-empty and the field has a valid required attribute, so axe-core sees a correctly labelled, required input and may even read 'required' as a positive signal. No checker compares the visible '(required)' convention used on sibling labels against this one to spot the inconsistency, nor judges that given the page's own legend the omission makes the label non-descriptive of its requirement — a contextual human reading.

citation.quote: The label may also be used to include text or a text symbol indicating that input is required.

pages.scenario: E-commerce bike-shop checkout. Sibling fields carry their format inline ('Expiry (MM/YY)', 'Security code (3 digits)') but the card-number field is labelled merely 'Card number'. Its validator is /^\d{16}$/ — it accepts only 16 bare digits and rejects the grouped form '4111 1111 1111 1111' that is printed on the card and that nearly everyone types. No mask, no inline cue; the format appears only in the post-submit error.
pages.mechanism: Label states the topic ('Card number') but not the applicable data type/format (exactly 16 digits, no spaces). The constraint lives only in the /^\d{16}$/ submit handler and the error message. The contrast with sibling labels that DO show their format sharpens the shortfall — the field with the strictest, least-obvious constraint is the one missing its cue.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The label is present, associated, and non-empty and the input has valid attributes (inputmode, autocomplete=cc-number), so axe-core/WAVE/Lighthouse report a correctly labelled field. No scanner executes or parses the /^\d{16}$/ regex to discover spaces are rejected, and none can judge that 'Card number' alone fails to communicate the accepted format — especially when its own siblings show theirs.

citation.quote: Each visual form label is sufficiently clear and descriptive, so users know what input data is expected

pages.scenario: SaaS workspace signup. The password-creation field is labelled 'Password' with a visible help line that only says 'Choose something memorable' — friendly but misleading. The real complexity rules (at least 12 characters AND at least one symbol) are enforced only by the submit handler and disclosed only in the error after a rejected submit: error-as-format.
pages.mechanism: Neither the label ('Password') nor its associated instruction ('Choose something memorable') communicates the applicable data requirements (>=12 chars, a symbol); the rule lives only in the validator (v.length>=12 && /[^A-Za-z0-9]/.test(v)) and the post-submit error. Presence of a label and an instruction satisfies 3.3.2/4.1.2, but the descriptiveness limb fails because the requirement surfaces only on error — which TT 5.B forbids.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The label is associated and non-empty AND there is a visible instruction paragraph, so axe-core/WAVE/Lighthouse see a generously labelled field; the presence of some help text can even read as a positive signal. No scanner evaluates whether that instruction states the enforced policy or reads the validator to learn the 12-char/symbol rule. Judging that 'Choose something memorable' fails to convey the real requirement is a semantic comparison only a human can make.

citation.quote: An error message is not sufficient to communicate the expected format to pass this test.

pages.scenario: German statutory health-insurer portal (lang=de) reimbursement claim. The amount field is labelled with the correct topic noun 'Betrag' (Amount). Its validator /^\d+,\d{2}$/ accepts only a comma decimal with exactly two fraction digits and NO currency symbol and NO thousands separator (e.g. '85,00'); the natural German entry '85,00 €' is rejected solely for the euro sign, as are '85.00' and '1.250,00'. A sibling field 'IBAN (DE, 22 Stellen)' DOES carry its format; the required shape for Betrag appears only in the post-submit error.
pages.mechanism: Label 'Betrag' states the topic but omits the locale-specific data requirement: comma decimal, two fraction digits, no € symbol, no thousands dot. A German user typing '85,00 €' as on paper is rejected with no way to anticipate it from the label; the format is disclosed only in the after-submit error. Pure missing-requirement limb, not a topic mismatch.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The label is present, associated, and non-empty in the document's declared language, so axe-core/WAVE/Lighthouse report a properly labelled field. No scanner reads the /^\d+,\d{2}$/ validator to learn the euro symbol and thousands separator are rejected, and none has the locale knowledge to judge that a German amount label should state 'no € symbol, comma decimal' — requiring a human who understands German number conventions.

citation.quote: Determine whether labels and/or instructions for form components sufficiently describe the purpose and applicable data requirements (date formats, required fields, data type, etc.).

pages.scenario: PASS / boundary control: a term-life insurance quote form that reuses the exact failing fields from case-01 (free-text date) and case-02 (required email) but now carries each requirement cue inline: 'Date of birth (MM/DD/YYYY)', 'Email (required)' (consistent with the '*' legend), and 'ZIP code (5 digits)'. The input attributes (placeholder/pattern) agree with the labelled format, so a user knows what input is expected before submitting and no requirement is hidden behind an error.
pages.mechanism: Each label now conveys both topic and applicable data requirement: the date format up front (no error reliance), the required-status consistent with the legend, the ZIP data type/length. The accessible name includes the requirement, so a screen-reader user hears 'Date of birth (MM/DD/YYYY), required, edit text' and can satisfy the field before submission — the canonical-pass shape G131 describes.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Automated tools would also pass this page, but only for the shallow reason that the labels are present, associated, and non-empty — the SAME signal they emit for the failing cases 01-05. The genuine pass/fail difference (requirement cue present vs absent) is exactly the dimension no checker evaluates; confirming this page truly passes the descriptiveness limb requires a human to read the label and judge the format/required cue is present and accurate.

citation.quote: The objective of this technique is to ensure that the label for any interactive component within web content makes the component's purpose clear.

aspects.title: Button/control labels (text) that do not make the control's function clear — generic, ambiguous, or mismatched action verbs
aspects.plain: A button's text is too vague to reveal what it does, like several 'OK'/'Go' buttons that each behave differently or a 'Continue' button that actually deletes your draft.
aspects.description: TT 5.B has a second explicit prong: 'Each visual button label is sufficiently clear and descriptive, so users know its function', and G131's whole objective is that 'the label for any interactive component makes the component's purpose clear.' A textual button label can be present and grammatical yet fail to convey the action: a row of 'Submit'/'OK'/'Go' buttons that each do different things; a 'Continue' button that actually deletes a draft; multiple 'Edit' / 'Remove' buttons in a list where the label alone does not say WHAT is edited/removed; a primary button labeled 'Click here'. This is a function-descriptiveness judgment over interactive controls, distinct from the topic-descriptiveness of input field labels and distinct from icon labels — it is the button-label half of the labels limb, judged on its action verb and specificity.
aspects.scLimb: Labels limb — specifically the button/control 'function' prong of TT 5.B (parallel to the input 'expected data' prong), applied to text-labeled actionable controls.
aspects.whyUncovered: The cc0f0a corpus tests only single bare INPUT fields with topic-noun labels; it contains no button/control whose label must convey an ACTION, and no case where a generic or mismatched verb leaves the function unclear. TT 5.B's button-function prong is therefore never exercised, and an automated checker that confirms a button has a non-empty accessible name cannot judge whether 'Submit'/'Continue'/'Click here' actually tells the user what the control does in context.

references.quote: Each visual button label is sufficiently clear and descriptive, so users know its function.
The objective of this technique is to ensure that the label for any interactive component within web content makes the component's purpose clear.
Descriptive labels help users identify specific components within the content.
The controls are labeled "Zoom in (Ctrl + Shift + L)" And "Zoom out (Ctrl + Shift + R)."

aspects.ttWhy: Button/control labels not conveying function; 5.B's explicit button-label prong.

pages.scenario: A SaaS analytics dashboard editor raises an unsaved-changes alertdialog whose three action buttons are ALL labeled 'OK'; they respectively save (persist edits), discard (revert), and export (.json), and are even rendered in a different order than the prose lists them. The visible button label alone never says which 'OK' does which.
pages.mechanism: Three sibling controls perform three distinct consequential functions (save/discard/export) yet share the generic, verb-less accessible name 'OK'. The label conveys only 'this is a confirm button', not WHICH function; the disambiguating prose is present but not associated with any button, and DOM order does not match prose order. A screen-reader user tabbing the dialog hears 'OK, OK, OK' and cannot tell save from discard from export — failing TT 5.B's button-function prong (G131: label must make the component's purpose clear).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every button has a non-empty accessible name ('OK') and valid role, so axe button-name, WAVE, and Lighthouse pass; duplicate accessible names across siblings are not a flagged violation. Judging that 'OK' fails to convey FUNCTION — and that three identical 'OK's on save/discard/export is dangerous — requires reading the dialog prose, mapping it to the buttons, and reasoning about each action's consequence: an irreducible human semantic judgment no static rule models.

citation.quote: Each visual button label is sufficiently clear and descriptive, so users know its function.

pages.scenario: A four-step pet-insurance quote wizard showing 'Review' as step 3 (with 'Done' still ahead) has a primary button labeled 'Continue'. The label implies advancing to the next step, but the control actually BINDS the policy and charges the saved card immediately with no further confirmation; step 4 is only a receipt.
pages.mechanism: Mismatched action verb: a generic progression verb ('Continue'), reinforced by a step indicator that makes the user expect another step, labels a consequential, irreversible commit-and-charge action. The accessible name affirmatively signals navigation, not commitment, so neither sighted nor screen-reader users are warned by the label that activating it spends money. TT 5.B requires the visible button label to make the function clear; here it actively misrepresents the function.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: 'Continue' is a non-empty, conventional, well-formed accessible name that every name/role checker rates as a GOOD label — there is nothing wrong with the string in isolation. The failure lives entirely in the gap between the label's implied action and the click handler's real effect (bind + charge), discoverable only by reading the step indicator and fine print and reasoning that 'Done' is merely a receipt. No automated tool reasons about whether a verb matches what the handler does.

citation.quote: Conversely, it is also possible for content to pass Success Criterion 1.3.1 (with headings or labels correctly marked up or identified), while failing this success criterion (if those headings or labels are inaccurate or insufficiently clear).

pages.scenario: A newsroom CMS 'My drafts' screen lists five unpublished stories, each row carrying a single 'Remove' button (removal is permanent). Every button is the bare word 'Remove' — the label never names WHICH story it removes; the disambiguating title sits in a sibling span, not in the button and not programmatically associated.
pages.mechanism: Action label with no object: the verb ('Remove') is apt but the button never names the object it acts on. The row title lives in a separate node and is not chained into the accessible name via aria-labelledby, so it does not reach AT. A screen-reader user navigating by button hears 'Remove, Remove, Remove, Remove, Remove' and cannot tell which permanent deletion each triggers — in a repeated list, knowing the function means knowing which object, which the label omits (fails TT 5.B / G131).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Each button has a non-empty accessible name and valid role, so button-name, WAVE, and Lighthouse pass; repeated identical names are not flagged. A tool cannot decide 'Remove' is insufficient BECAUSE the object is missing — that requires understanding the list is a set of distinct drafts and that the per-row title (a sibling node, not associated) is the object the button should name. Whether the adjacent title rescues the label is a programmatic-association plus semantic judgment only a human reading the DOM relationships can confirm.

citation.quote: Each visual button label is sufficiently clear and descriptive, so users know its function.

pages.scenario: An official county Department of Revenue page for 'Form RT-1: Annual Resident Tax Return' has a single primary call-to-action button labeled 'Click here'. The label is a pure interaction instruction with no function cue; the function (download the RT-1 PDF) appears only in surrounding prose and the file row, never in the button.
pages.mechanism: Generic interaction-instruction label ('Click here') that conveys no action and no object. The accessible name tells AT only 'this is a button' — nothing about downloading a 412 KB tax-return PDF. The prose that supplies the function is not part of the button's name, so a screen-reader user listing controls hears 'Click here, button' and learns nothing. 'Click here' is the canonical label that names no function, failing TT 5.B's button-function prong.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The button has a non-empty accessible name and valid role, so button-name, WAVE, and Lighthouse pass; 'Click here' is grammatical, so no empty-label rule trips. Some tools heuristically warn on literal 'click here' for LINKS, but this is a button, and even when warned a tool cannot judge whether the surrounding heading/file-row makes the function clear — only that the string is generic. Deciding it fails to convey the download-the-RT-1 function versus an adequate 'Download Form RT-1 (PDF)' is a label-vs-purpose reading no static check performs.

citation.quote: This success criterion does not require the use of labels; however, it does require that if labels are present, they must be accurate and sufficiently clear or descriptive.

pages.scenario: A municipal transit trip planner has an ARIA toolbar with two stop fields and three text buttons ALL labeled 'Go': the first runs the trip search, the second clears the From/To fields, and the third opens the rider settings panel. Each 'Go' is plausible beside a search field in isolation, but the single word never says which of three distinct functions it triggers.
pages.mechanism: Generic action verb ('Go') repeated on three controls with three different functions. 'Go' implies execute-the-search, so a screen-reader user moving through the toolbar hears 'Go, Go, Go' and reasonably activates one expecting departures, instead erasing entered stops or being taken to settings. The label conveys neither the differing functions nor any warning of the destructive/navigational ones; for two of the three the verb is outright misleading (fails TT 5.B / G131).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Each button has a non-empty accessible name and valid role inside a labelled toolbar, so button-name, WAVE, and Lighthouse pass; repeated identical names are not flagged. A tool cannot know that one 'Go' searches, one clears, and one opens settings — the functions live in the click handlers and page behaviour, not in any attribute. Recognising that one verb cannot distinguish three functions, and that 'Go' actively misdescribes the clear and settings actions, is a semantic, behavioural reading no static check performs.

citation.quote: Check that each label makes the component's purpose clear.

pages.scenario: PASS control: a meal-planner app reusing the two failing component families (a repeated list of row-action buttons and a three-choice confirmation) but with every button re-labeled to name BOTH action and specific object — 'Remove "Lemon & thyme roast chicken" from this week', 'Save changes to recipe', 'Discard changes', 'Export recipe as PDF'. No control relies on a generic verb, omitted object, or mismatched verb.
pages.mechanism: Every visible button label names its action verb AND its specific object or function, so each control's purpose is determinable from its label alone. A screen-reader user navigating by button hears five distinct, function-clear names and never encounters an ambiguous 'OK', 'Remove', 'Go', 'Continue', or 'Click here' — satisfying TT 5.B's button-function prong. This is the deliberate contrast control isolating the aspect (label quality) from label presence.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Automated tools also PASS this page, but only for the trivial reason that all accessible names are non-empty — the same (wrong) conclusion they reach for the failing cases case-01..case-05. The value of this control is that a HUMAN applying the function-descriptiveness judgment ALSO passes it, confirming the aspect is about label quality, not presence — exactly the distinction automated checks cannot draw.

citation.quote: Each visual button label is sufficiently clear and descriptive, so users know its function.

aspects.title: Heading/label descriptiveness that holds in source order but breaks under visual reading order, or for collapsed/dynamic content
aspects.plain: A heading matches the content right after it in the code, but once CSS reorders the layout or a panel collapses, it ends up over unrelated content.
aspects.description: The b49b2e rule's own Assumptions name two hard cases it never instantiates: (a) divergence between flat-tree order and visual reading order via CSS positioning/grid/flex order, and (b) headings for expandable/collapsed (hidden) content. A heading can be descriptive of the content that follows it in the DOM but sit visually above unrelated content (CSS order reorders columns/cards), so a sighted user sees 'Pricing' over the FAQ block; or a heading describes content that is only correct once a panel is expanded, while the collapsed default exposes a different (mismatched) summary. Judging these requires rendering the page and reading it visually AND interacting with disclosure state — neither of which a static automated checker or a flat-tree-only rule performs. TT pointedly judges the VISIBLE heading-to-content relationship, which is exactly what diverges here.
aspects.scLimb: Headings limb primarily (descriptiveness of a heading relative to the content a user actually perceives under it), with the labels limb implicated when a control's label changes on interaction. Tests the rendered/interacted descriptiveness the flat-tree rule and static checkers miss.
aspects.whyUncovered: The coverage summary states the rule's own hard cases — 'flat-tree vs visual reading order divergence via CSS positioning/grid/flex order, and headings for expandable/collapsed (hidden) content — are called out in the Assumptions but have NO test fixtures here.' Every b49b2e fixture is heading-then-single-paragraph in trivial DOM order. A static checker reads source order, not rendered visual order or post-interaction state, so it cannot detect a heading that is descriptive in the DOM but mis-orienting on screen or after a disclosure toggles. TT explicitly judges the visible heading-to-content relationship and includes interaction-driven label changes.

references.quote: For each visually identified heading, compare the heading text to the content beneath the heading.
Any changes to form labels that occur automatically or as a result of interaction should be included.
When headings are clear and descriptive, users can find the information they seek more easily, and they can understand the relationships between different parts of the content more easily.
Descriptive headings help users find specific content and orient themselves within the web page.
