aspects.ttWhy: Heading-to-content adequacy under visual reading order and collapsed disclosure state.

pages.scenario: E-commerce product page: a CSS grid-template-areas layout places the DOM-adjacent 'Shipping & returns' <h2> into the top-right grid cell, so it renders visually directly above the unrelated customer-reviews block. The heading is descriptive in flat-tree order but mis-orienting on screen.
pages.mechanism: A heading describes the content following it in the flat tree (shipping text) but CSS grid-area places its rendered cell directly above the customer-reviews panel; a sighted/low-vision/magnifier user perceives the 'Shipping & returns' heading over five-star reviews — the visible heading-to-content relationship is wrong (TT 10.A), while the screen-reader flat-tree order is correct.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse and ACT rule b49b2e judge the flat tree, where the heading is immediately followed by matching shipping text (a clean pass); they do not compute rendered grid geometry or judge whether a heading describes the content perceived beneath it. b49b2e's Assumptions explicitly note the rule breaks when positioning renders an order differing from tree order. Requires rendering + visual semantic judgment.

citation.doc: ACT Rule b49b2e — Heading is descriptive (Assumptions)
citation.quote: This rule assumes that the flat tree order is close to the reading order as elements are rendered on the page. Due to positioning, it is possible to render a document in an order that greatly differs from the tree order, in which case the content which is visually associated with a heading might not be the content following it in tree order and this rule might fail while Success Criterion 2.4.6 Headings and Label is still satisfied.

pages.scenario: Arabic (RTL) retail-banking dashboard as a single vertical flex column: CSS `order` on sibling flex items pushes the fee table down and pulls the contact block up, so the rendered column reads 'Service fees' heading → contact block → 'Contact your branch' heading → fee table. Each heading visually sits over content it does not describe, though DOM-adjacent to its matching content.
pages.mechanism: `order` reorders flex items independently of DOM order (verified by bounding-box tops: feesHead 117 → contactBody 154 → contactHead 366 → feesBody 403), so the 'رسوم الخدمة / Service fees' heading renders over the branch address/phone/hours and 'Contact your branch' over the fee table. Screen-reader flat-tree order keeps each heading glued to its matching content, so this is purely a rendered visual-order failure (TT 10.A).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A checker walks the DOM, where each heading is immediately followed by its matching content (passes). Tools do not resolve flex `order` into a rendered reading sequence, and RTL writing mode further decouples DOM from on-screen order; the Arabic text defeats English-keyword lexical shortcuts. Detecting it requires rendering, reading the visible column order, and comparing meaning per heading.

citation.doc: ACT Rule b49b2e — Heading is descriptive (Expectation & Assumptions)
citation.quote: Each target element describes the topic or purpose of the first perceivable content after the test target that is not decorative. The order of elements is determined by the flat tree.

pages.scenario: Healthcare patient-portal visit summary with native <details>/<summary> disclosures. The first summary (collapsed default heading) reads 'Estimated cost for today's visit' but the panel body, revealed only on expansion, is the practice's missed-appointment / cancellation policy. The heading mis-orients in the default visual state; two sibling disclosures are apt.
pages.mechanism: The <summary> acts as the section heading and is what every user lands on in the collapsed state. 'Estimated cost for today's visit' promises pricing but expands to a no-show/cancellation fee policy — the heading describes a different section. The body is display:none while collapsed, so the heading-to-content mismatch is gated on disclosure state; the summary has a valid non-empty accessible name so name/role checks are green.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The <details>/<summary> markup is valid with a non-empty accessible name and structurally the summary precedes its body in the flat tree (a tool sees a heading-then-content pair). While collapsed the policy text is display:none and not perceivable; b49b2e's Assumptions explicitly exclude hidden/expandable content. No tool reads 'Estimated cost', expands the disclosure, reads 'cancellation policy', and reasons the two do not match — that is human semantic judgment over interacted content.

citation.doc: ACT Rule b49b2e — Heading is descriptive (Assumptions)
citation.quote: This rule also assumes that the content the heading is intended to describe is visible and not hidden from assistive technologies. Otherwise, cases such as expandable content using a heading might fail this rule while Success Criterion 2.4.6 Headings and Label is still satisfied.

pages.scenario: Meridian Bank 'Send money' multi-step transfer wizard whose single primary <button id="primary"> is labelled 'Continue' in every step; the label is apt while it advances steps 1->2->3, but in the final 'Confirm and send' step the button's function becomes 'irreversibly send $1,250.00' and the still-generic 'Continue' no longer describes that consequential action.
pages.mechanism: A single primary <button id="primary"> drives a multi-step money-transfer wizard; its visible label stays the generic 'Continue' in every step. On steps 1-2 'Continue' aptly describes 'advance to the next step', but in the interacted-into final step (Confirm and send) the same control's function becomes 'irreversibly send the money', and 'Continue' no longer describes that consequential, non-reversible action — descriptiveness that holds in the early state breaks in the dynamic state the user navigates into (TT 5.B Notes: adequacy must be judged in the interacted-into state). #secondary relabels too ('Cancel' -> 'Back') but stays adequate, isolating the failure to the final 'Continue'.
pages.selectorNote: Wizard primary button whose 'Continue' label under-describes irreversible send at step 3; orig #t1 absent
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The triggers are well-formed buttons with non-empty accessible names, correct aria-controls, and accurate aria-expanded — no rule flags a generic-but-present name. The descriptive topic text is inside [hidden] collapsed panels (not perceivable; b49b2e excludes expandable/hidden content). Recognizing that 'Read article →' is too generic to describe a specific FAQ, and that the real topic is buried in collapsed content, is a semantic judgment no tool performs.

citation.doc: WCAG Techniques G130 — Providing descriptive headings (Tests / Procedure)
citation.quote: Determine if the web page contains headings. Check that each heading identifies its section of the content.

pages.scenario: SaaS CRM lead card: a button labeled 'Show details' (descriptive of its toggle function) relabels to 'Submit' after the user clicks it, while the control still only expands/collapses a panel and submits nothing. The post-interaction label misdescribes the function. A sibling 'Show notes' button relabels to 'Hide notes' (a pass control whose new label stays descriptive).
pages.mechanism: TT 5.B requires that label changes occurring as a result of interaction be judged. After the click handler runs (verified at runtime: textContent becomes 'Submit') the visible label tells every user — sighted, screen-reader, voice-control — the control will submit the record, but it only toggles #detailsPanel. Visible text equals accessible name in both states, so label-in-name passes; only the post-interaction label adequacy fails.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A static scan of the initial DOM sees the descriptive 'Show details' and passes; accessible name matches visible text in both states so label-in-name is green throughout. No tool clicks the button, observes the relabel to 'Submit', and reasons a panel-toggle must not be labeled 'Submit'. The pass control (notes button relabeling to 'Hide notes') shows 'label changed on click' alone is not a violation, so even a mutation-watcher would over-flag without semantic judgment.

citation.quote: Any changes to form labels that occur automatically or as a result of interaction should be included.

pages.scenario: PASS boundary: an analytics dashboard using the SAME risky techniques as the failing cases — CSS grid-template-areas board + a <details>/<summary> disclosure — but applied correctly. The grid area string mirrors DOM order (no order overrides, no area swaps) so each heading renders over its own content; the disclosure summary 'Methodology & data sources' expands to a methodology explanation.
pages.mechanism: Grid areas are declared in DOM order with no order/positioning override, so rendered top-to-bottom/left-to-right reading order matches the flat tree: each <h2> sits visually directly above the content it describes, and the disclosure summary accurately predicts its expanded body in both states. Every visible heading describes the content perceived beneath it (TT 10.A) for sighted, low-vision, magnifier, and screen-reader users alike.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Included to sharpen the aspect: a tool that flags 'uses CSS grid areas' or 'has a <details>' would wrongly fail it. A correct evaluator must return passed here while failing case-01..05 — and the only way to distinguish them is to render the page, read the visible heading-to-content relationships, exercise the disclosure, and judge meaning. The techniques are identical to the failing cases; only the divergence (absent here) is the defect, which automated tools cannot assess.

citation.quote: The heading describes the topic or purpose of its content.

aspects.title: Visible label/heading and accessible name diverge in descriptiveness — one surface is descriptive, the other is not
aspects.plain: The on-screen label and the label a screen reader actually announces disagree (shown as 'First name' but announced as 'field1'), so sighted and screen-reader users get different labels.
aspects.description: 2.4.6 is judged differently by the two methodologies: ACT/b49b2e judges the ACCESSIBLE NAME, while TT 5.B/10.A judge the VISIBLE label/heading. The untested gap is when the visible text and the accessible name DIVERGE in descriptiveness. A field visibly labeled 'First name' but given aria-label='field1' (sighted user fine, screen-reader user stranded); or the reverse, a visibly cryptic 'X' button whose aria-label='Close dialog' is the descriptive one; or a heading visibly reading 'Quarterly Earnings' whose aria-labelledby points at a stray 'Q' so AT announces just 'Q'. The Understanding doc warns 2.4.6 is independent of 4.1.2 — a control 'can have an appropriate accessible name and therefore pass 4.1.2, but still fail this success criterion if the label is inaccurate or insufficiently clear.' Deciding which surface to judge, and whether the divergent name is descriptive, is a human call: the name exists (so 4.1.2 / axe pass) but the two surfaces carry different meanings against the field's true purpose.
aspects.scLimb: Both limbs — applies to form-control labels and to headings whose accessible name is computed from an override (aria-label / aria-labelledby) that differs in descriptiveness from the visible text.
aspects.whyUncovered:
The coverage summary notes accessible-name computation is exercised 'only trivially (literal text, one img alt, one role=heading); no aria-label/aria-labelledby overrides, no name composed from multiple sources, no name that differs from visible text.' The cc0f0a aria-labelledby fixtures keep visible and programmatic text identical — verified: fixture fa5104f9 sets both the visible

and the labelledby source to the same word 'Menu', so there is no descriptiveness DIVERGENCE between eye and AT. A checker confirms a non-empty accessible name (passing 4.1.2) and cannot weigh the visible-vs-announced surfaces against the control's purpose, which is the explicitly-separate 2.4.6 judgment.

references.quote: It is possible for controls and inputs to have an appropriate accessible name (e.g. using aria-label="…") and therefore pass Success Criterion 4.1.2, but to still fail this success criterion (if the label is inaccurate or insufficiently clear or descriptive).
Review the visual labels and/or instructions provided for each form component/control.
For each visually identified heading, compare the heading text to the content beneath the heading.

this success criterion does not take into consideration whether or not alternative methods of providing an accessible name for form controls and inputs have been used — that aspect is covered separately by

aspects.ttWhy: Divergence affects both visible form labels and visible headings.

pages.scenario: Healthcare patient-registration date-of-birth field: visible associated <label> reads 'Date of birth (MM/DD/YYYY)' (descriptive + carries the data-format requirement) but aria-label='dob_1' wins the name computation, so AT announces the bare slug 'dob_1'. Visible-descriptive / announced-vague.
pages.mechanism: aria-label overrides the associated <label for> in the accessible-name computation; computed accName='dob_1' (verified role=textbox), discarding both the purpose and the MM/DD/YYYY format the visible label conveys.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Field has a non-empty accessible name and a correctly associated <label>, so axe 4.1.2/label-presence pass (verified full axe.run + label-content-name-mismatch = 0 violations). No rule judges whether 'dob_1' is descriptive of the field's purpose; there is no visible text node, so no contained-text mismatch to detect. Descriptiveness is a human semantic call.

citation.quote: It is possible for controls and inputs to have an appropriate accessible name (e.g. using aria-label="…") and therefore pass Success Criterion 4.1.2, but to still fail this success criterion (if the label is inaccurate or insufficiently clear or descriptive).

pages.scenario: Online-banking close-account confirmation: destructive button visibly reads 'Delete account' (permanent account closure) but aria-labelledby composes the accessible name 'Delete account draft', misleadingly implying a recoverable draft deletion. Visible-accurate / announced-misleading (different function).
pages.mechanism: aria-labelledby concatenates two hidden spans ('Delete account' + 'draft') -> accName='Delete account draft' (verified role=button). The extra 'draft' qualifier describes a different, far less destructive function than the control performs.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Deliberately defeats axe's label-content-name-mismatch (ACT 2ee8b8): the visible 'Delete account' IS a substring of the accessible name, so the subset check is satisfied (verified full axe.run + that rule enabled = 0 violations). Both IDREFs resolve and the name is fluent, so no dangling/empty heuristic fires. Judging that the extra word makes the announced function wrong requires understanding the panel's real consequence.

citation.quote: Each visual button label is sufficiently clear and descriptive, so users know its function.

pages.scenario:
Investor-relations results page: an

visibly reads 'Quarterly Earnings' (with a superscript 'Q' footnote marker) but its aria-labelledby points at the stray Q, so the computed heading name is just 'Q'. Screen-reader heading navigation announces 'Q, heading level 2'.
pages.mechanism: aria-labelledby points at a tiny marker sub-element instead of the heading text; it takes absolute precedence over the element's own content, so accName='Q' (verified role=heading) while the visible heading is 'Quarterly Earnings'.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The <h2> has a non-empty accessible name and the IDREF resolves to a present element, so no empty-heading / missing-name / dangling-reference rule fires (verified full axe.run = 0 violations after wrapping body in <main>). Tools cannot read the section prose and judge that 'Q' fails to describe quarterly-earnings content — the topic-vs-heading comparison TT 10.A requires.

citation.quote: Conversely, it is also possible for content to pass Success Criterion 1.3.1 (with headings or labels correctly marked up or identified), while failing this success criterion (if those headings or labels are inaccurate or insufficiently clear).

pages.scenario: Web email client toolbar (REVERSE / verdict-flip): the close control is a bare cryptic 'X' glyph with no text, while aria-label='Close conversation' is the descriptive surface. ACT/axe judge the (good) accessible name -> pass; TT 5.B judges the (cryptic) visible button label -> fail. The judge must decide which surface governs.
pages.mechanism: Visible label is the lone glyph '✕' (accName='Close conversation' verified role=button). 2.4.6 TT 5.B judges the visible button label, which is not self-describing to a sighted user in a mail toolbar (could mean delete/dismiss/close); the descriptive text exists only in aria-label.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The button has a correct role and a descriptive non-empty accessible name, so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse pass it outright (verified full axe.run + label-content-name-mismatch = 0 violations); 2.5.3 is N/A (no visible text label). No tool evaluates whether the visible glyph is self-describing to a sighted user — that is the TT 5.B manual judgment, and name-keyed tools will actively pass it, masking the visible-surface failure.

citation.quote: Each visual button label is sufficiently clear and descriptive, so users know its function.

pages.scenario: Arabic RTL government residence-permit portal (i18n long-tail): national-ID field has a descriptive associated Arabic <label> 'رقم الهوية الوطنية' (National ID number) but aria-label='field2' (leftover English scaffold slug) wins, so the accessible name is 'field2'. Divergence in both descriptiveness AND language.
pages.mechanism: aria-label overrides the translated <label for> -> accName='field2' (verified role=textbox). An Arabic screen reader announces the meaningless Latin slug instead of the Arabic label, and voice-control users speaking the visible Arabic cannot target the field; mixed-language compounds the divergence.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Field has a non-empty accessible name and an associated <label>, so 4.1.2/label-presence pass (verified full axe.run + label-content-name-mismatch = 0 violations). Tools do not judge whether 'field2' is descriptive, nor flag that the accessible name is in a different language than lang='ar' and the visible label — both are human semantic/linguistic judgments.

citation.quote: Form input controls with labels that clearly and accurately describe the content that is expected to be entered helps users know how to successfully complete the form.

pages.scenario: PASS boundary (newsletter signup): a search field labelled by a magnifying-glass icon button whose accessible name is 'Search' (the Understanding doc's own descriptive-graphical-label example), plus an email field whose visible <label> 'Email address' and redundant aria-label='Email address' agree exactly. Both surfaces agree and are descriptive — no divergence.
pages.mechanism: Loupe icon button accName='Search' (verified role=button) — visible icon and announced name agree per the Understanding convention; email field visible <label> == aria-label = 'Email address' (verified accName matches visible label). No eye/AT divergence to judge.
pages.selectorNote: Roman gallery heading whose aria-labelledby misnames it 'Anglo-Saxon Treasures'; orig button selector absent
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: This is the control / true negative: tools correctly find no violation (verified full axe.run + label-content-name-mismatch = 0 violations) and so does a human — but tools pass it for the wrong reason (a name is present) while a human passes it for the right reason (the two surfaces agree and are descriptive). It shares the same structural ingredients as the failing cases so a judge must reason rather than pattern-match aria-label presence to 'fail'.

citation.quote: For example, when accompanying a text field, a loupe or magnifying glass icon with text alternative of "Search" is commonly interpreted as indicating the field is for entering and submitting a search query.

aspects.title: Focus indicator renders but is perceptually indistinguishable — resting style mimics the ring, or a thick same-color border swallows it (F78 modes 2 & 3)
aspects.plain: Every control already has a border that looks just like the focus outline, so when one gets keyboard focus the highlight blends in invisibly.
aspects.description: F78 documents two failures where the focus indicator IS drawn (pixels change on focus) yet a sighted keyboard user still cannot tell which element is focused. Mode 2: the author gives every link/control a permanent static outline that looks identical to the browser focus ring (e.g. a {outline: thin dotted black}); when one element focuses, the UA overlays its own dotted ring, but because all elements already look dotted/outlined, the focused one is not distinguishable from its neighbours. Mode 3: the element has a thick border in the same color as the focus ring (e.g. a {border: medium solid black}); the UA draws its black ring just outside the border, but as both are black and the border is thicker, the ring 'no longer meets the definition of visible' against it. In both, the pixel diff is non-zero so the rule passes, yet the SC purpose — 'help a person know which element has the keyboard focus' — is defeated. Catching this requires a human to compare the focused appearance against the resting appearance of ALL elements (mode 2) or against the adjacent colors (mode 3) and judge whether the difference is genuinely distinguishing, not merely non-zero.
aspects.scLimb: The distinguishability/perceptibility limb of 'the keyboard focus indicator is visible': an indicator must let the user know WHICH element has focus, not merely cause some pixel to change. F78 explicitly carves out these 'present but not visible' cases as failures of 2.4.7.
aspects.whyUncovered: oj04fd is a pure focused-vs-unfocused pixel diff on a SINGLE element that 'does not care how large it is' or whether it is perceptible, and it never compares the focused element against the resting look of OTHER elements or against its own adjacent colors. The ACT fail fixture is only the blatant outline:none case; there is no fixture pairing a focus-ring-mimicking resting outline or a thick same-color border with the default ring. A fully-automated tool registers the non-zero edge-pixel diff and passes; only human visual judgment about distinguishability/perceptual contrast against context can catch it.

references.quote: The following CSS example will create an outline around links that looks the same as the focus indicator. This makes it impossible for users to determine which one in fact has the focus, even though the user agent does draw the focus indicator.
the focus indicator is drawn just outside the border, but as both are black and the border is thicker than the focus indicator, it no longer meets the definition of "visible".
The purpose of this success criterion is to help a person know which element has the keyboard focus.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: Government civic-portal primary nav of 6 links, each given a permanent outline:1px dotted #000; the UA keyboard-focus ring (itself a 1px dotted black line) is left intact, so the focused link is visually identical to its five permanently-dotted neighbours (F78 mode 2).
pages.mechanism: Every nav link has a resting outline:1px dotted #000 identical in style/weight/colour to the UA focus ring; on Tab the UA dotted ring is drawn but blends into the already-dotted siblings, so a sighted keyboard user cannot tell which link has focus though the pixel diff is non-zero.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: No outline:none is set and the UA focus ring demonstrably appears, so a single-element focused-vs-unfocused pixel diff (ACT oj04fd's mechanism) is non-zero and axe/WAVE/Lighthouse pass. No tool compares the focused link against the RESTING appearance of its neighbours to judge that a dotted ring over an already-dotted box is not distinguishing — that distinguishability comparison requires human visual judgment.

citation.quote: The following CSS example will create an outline around links that looks the same as the focus indicator. This makes it impossible for users to determine which one in fact has the focus, even though the user agent does draw the focus indicator.

pages.scenario: Healthcare patient-portal medication-refill form where every control has a resting 2px solid #1a73e8 border AND a matching 2px solid blue outline; the :focus rule re-applies the same blue outline with only a 1px offset nudge, so tabbing produces a tiny edge-pixel change but no perceptible difference (F78 mode 2).
pages.mechanism: Resting outline matches the focus ring in colour and weight (both 2px solid #1a73e8); :focus only shifts outline-offset by 1px, so the focused field looks the same blue-bordered control it was at rest and the keyboard user cannot tell which of the seven controls is active.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A :focus style exists, no control uses outline:none, and the 1px offset shift makes a focused/unfocused diff non-zero — so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse register a focus indicator and pass. They do not measure whether the focused appearance is perceptibly different from the same-colour, same-weight resting appearance; judging zero human-perceptible change requires visual comparison.

citation.quote: Other styling may make it difficult to see the focus indicator even though it is present, such as outlines that look the same as the focus outline, or thick borders that are the same color as the focus indicator so it cannot be seen against them.

pages.scenario: Legal Master Services Agreement page listing related-clause links as boxed chips, each with border:4px solid #000 on a near-white page; the black UA focus ring drawn just outside the box is absorbed by the thick black frame (F78 mode 3).
pages.mechanism: Each clause link has a resting border:4px solid #000; the UA focus ring is a thinner black line drawn just outside that thicker black border, so it 'no longer meets the definition of visible' and the focused boxed link looks identical to every other boxed link.
pages.selectorNote: API endpoint chip links with 4px black border + black 2px ring; orig .clause-refs a absent
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: No outline:none, the UA ring is present, and an edge-pixel diff on the focused link is non-zero — so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse pass. None compares the ring colour to the ADJACENT border colour to decide perceptual distinguishability; concluding a 1px black ring against a 4px black border is absorbed requires a human to weigh contrast in context, not the binary did-any-pixel-change an automated rule computes.

citation.quote: In this case the focus indicator is drawn just outside the border, but as both are black and the border is thicker than the focus indicator, it no longer meets the definition of "visible".

pages.scenario: SaaS analytics dashboard chart toolbar of buttons, each with a permanent 5px solid navy (#1b2a4a) border; the team supplied a CUSTOM focus ring (outline:2px solid #1b2a4a) in the same navy, so the author ring is buried in the button's own thick navy resting border (F78 mode 3 applied to a custom ring).
pages.mechanism: Resting border:5px solid #1b2a4a and the author :focus outline are the identical navy; the 2px navy ring drawn 2px outside the 5px navy border blends into the thicker same-hue frame, so the focused toolbar button is not distinguishable from its neighbours.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The hardest variant for tooling: a genuine author-supplied :focus rule exists (so even a missing-focus-style heuristic finds one), outline:none never appears, and a single-button diff is non-zero — axe/WAVE/Lighthouse all pass. Determining the navy ring is the same hue as the navy border it sits against, and therefore not distinguishing, requires a human to read the colours in context.

citation.quote: Other styling may make it difficult to see the focus indicator even though it is present, such as outlines that look the same as the focus outline, or thick borders that are the same color as the focus indicator so it cannot be seen against them.

pages.scenario: RTL Arabic (lang=ar dir=rtl) municipal transit-pass booking form where every field and the submit button carry border:3px solid #1a1a1a; the near-black UA focus ring is swallowed by the matching near-black 3px frame (F78 mode 3), broadening the corpus beyond LTR link-only fixtures.
pages.mechanism: All controls have a resting border:3px solid #1a1a1a; the UA near-black focus ring drawn just outside is a thinner near-black line against the thicker near-black border, failing the 'visible' definition. RTL direction does not change the verdict — labels/roles/order are correct, only the visible focus is camouflaged.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: No outline:none anywhere, the UA ring is present, and an edge-pixel diff is non-zero — axe/WAVE/Lighthouse pass. None compares ring colour to the adjacent border colour or reasons that RTL is irrelevant; concluding the near-black ring is lost against the near-black 3px border requires human visual judgment in context.

citation.quote: In this case the focus indicator is drawn just outside the border, but as both are black and the border is thicker than the focus indicator, it no longer meets the definition of "visible".

pages.scenario: PASSED boundary: restaurant menu category tabs that use the SAME tempting dotted resting outline as the failing pages, but whose :focus-visible state swaps the dotted box for a thick 3px solid amber ring with offset plus a background/colour shift — an appearance no resting tab shows — so the focused tab is genuinely distinguishable.
pages.mechanism: Resting outline:1px dotted #6b4f2a on every tab (the mode-2 temptation), but :focus-visible repaints the focused tab with outline:3px solid #d98300; outline-offset:3px; background:#fff3df; color change — a combination unlike any resting tab, so a keyboard user can tell at a glance which tab has focus. Indicator is present AND distinguishing, satisfying 2.4.7.
pages.selectorNote: PASS boundary: menu tabs whose focus swaps dotted box for thick amber ring
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Automated tools also pass this page, but only for the shallow reason that an indicator is present; they cannot distinguish this page (focus state genuinely distinct from the resting dotted look) from case-01 (focus state identical to the resting dotted look) — both have a non-zero focus diff and neither uses outline:none. Only a human comparing focused vs resting sibling appearance separates this pass from the fails.

citation.quote: The purpose of this success criterion is to help a person know which element has the keyboard focus.

aspects.title: Focus indicator present but near the perception threshold — too thin, too low-contrast, or too small to be genuinely seen
aspects.plain: The focus highlight technically appears but is so thin, faint, or low-contrast that a keyboard user can't actually see which element has focus.
aspects.description: An indicator can satisfy the pixel-diff rule while remaining effectively invisible to a human. G195 sets concrete guidance for a genuinely visible author indicator: an area at least a 1 CSS px border around the component (or at least 4 CSS px along the shortest side), and a contrast change of 3:1 or more between focused and unfocused states (or, failing 3:1, at least 2px thick). A page can change SOME pixels with a 1px outline whose color barely differs from the background, a faint sub-3:1 box-shadow, or a fractional letter-spacing nudge that only shifts a few antialiased edge pixels — so the diff is non-zero but no human can reliably perceive the focus. The SC's own purpose ('help a person know which element has focus', 'without a focus indicator sighted keyboard users cannot operate the page') implies the change must actually be noticeable; deciding whether a given magnitude/contrast/size crosses the perceptible line is a visual judgment, distinct from camouflage-against-neighbours.
aspects.scLimb: The 'is the indicator actually visible' magnitude limb — the SC's admitted loophole that ANY pixel change passes oj04fd even when the change is below human perceptibility. This sits within 2.4.7's purpose rather than borrowing the precise 2.4.11/2.4.13 numbers; G195 is the technique that articulates the threshold.
aspects.whyUncovered: oj04fd 'does not care WHAT indicator appears... how large it is' and passes on ANY magnitude of HSL change; the corpus uses only high-contrast navy-on-white or strong default outlines and never stresses the HSL-difference test near its detection boundary. There is no near-threshold fixture. A fully-automated 'did a pixel change' checker cannot decide whether a ~1px, ~1.2:1 indicator is noticeable to a human eye in context — that is exactly the human visual judgment the SC purpose requires.

references.quote: Check that the focus indicator area is at least the size of a 1 CSS px border around the component.
Check that the change of contrast of the indicator between focused and unfocused states has a ratio of 3:1 or more for the minimum focus indicator area.
Without a focus indicator, sighted keyboard users cannot operate the page.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: Newspaper article/section-nav links whose only keyboard-focus change is the link text color shifting from #000000 to #0a0a0a on a white page (default outline removed). A real but sub-perceptual ink shift.
pages.mechanism: The sole :focus change is a text-color move #000->#0a0a0a on #ffffff = a contrast CHANGE of ~1.06:1 (verified rendered maxChannelDelta=10/255). No outline/border/underline/weight change and no indicator area. Far below G195's 3:1 contrast guidance; the focus position is effectively invisible to a sighted keyboard user, defeating the SC's purpose, yet the pixel diff is non-zero so oj04fd passes.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A :focus rule exists and changes a real property, so 'missing focus style / outline:none without replacement' heuristics do not fire (outline:0 + author-supplied alternative is the legal pattern). axe/WAVE/Lighthouse have no check that measures the contrast delta between focused and unfocused states against G195's 3:1; oj04fd passes on ANY HSL change. Judging a ~1.06:1 ink shift below human perception needs rendering both states and a visual noticeability judgment.

citation.quote: The purpose of this success criterion is to help a person know which element has the keyboard focus.

pages.scenario: E-commerce checkout action buttons (Back to cart / Place order) given an author-supplied focus outline, but in the design system's 'subtle border' token #f4f4f4 at 1px, drawn on a white card so it is a near-white hairline on white.
pages.mechanism: .btn:focus-visible draws a 1px outline in #f4f4f4 offset 2px from a white button on a white card. Indicator contrast ~1.08:1 (#f4f4f4 vs #ffffff = 1.10:1; verified maxChannelDelta=11/255), below G195's 3:1, AND only 1px so the '>=2px if under 3:1' fallback also fails. Outline paints real pixels (oj04fd passes) but a near-white hairline on white is imperceptible, so the user cannot tell which button has focus at the moment of payment.
pages.selectorNote: Checkout action buttons given a 1px near-white (#f4f4f4) outline on white
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A :focus-visible rule is present and sets a real outline, so absence heuristics stay quiet. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse do not compute the contrast of a focus outline against the colors behind/around it nor compare its thickness to G195's 2px fallback; a pixel diff only sees the 1px band change value. Concluding a #f4f4f4 hairline on white is imperceptible requires rendering the focused state and human visual judgment.

citation.quote: If the focus indicator does not have 3:1 contrast ratio with its adjacent colors, check that it is at least 2px thick.

pages.scenario: Bank online-banking login: the credential inputs' only focus change is a 1px box-shadow ring at rgba(0,0,0,0.06) over white, and the native text caret is globally suppressed (caret-color:transparent) so the faint ring is the sole cue.
pages.mechanism: input:focus applies box-shadow 0 0 0 1px rgba(0,0,0,.06) which composites to ~#f0f0f0 over the white field = ~1.14:1 change (verified ring-band maxChannelDelta=15/255). Visible band ~1 CSS px so G195's 4-CSS-px-shortest-side and 2px-thick fallbacks both fail. caret-color:transparent removes the native field cue the Understanding doc accepts ('a vertical bar is displayed in the field'). Shadow paints real pixels (oj04fd passes) but nothing perceptible remains.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A :focus rule applies a box-shadow (absence heuristics quiet) and outline:none has a documented replacement. No checker composites the rgba ring against the field, computes the resulting contrast delta, compares band width to G195's 4px/2px thresholds, or flags caret-color:transparent as removing a cue. A pixel diff confirms 'ring band changed.' Judging the ring imperceptible and recognizing the caret was removed is human visual judgment.

citation.quote: When text fields receive focus, a vertical bar is displayed in the field, indicating that the user can insert text, OR all of the text is highlighted, indicating that the user can type over the text.

pages.scenario: SaaS settings page with tiny 8px x 8px custom checkboxes (span role=checkbox). On focus each gets a 1px #f7f7f7 outline offset 1px outside the box on the white page - below the 4 CSS px shortest-side area guidance.
pages.mechanism: .tick:focus draws a 1px ring in #f7f7f7 1px outside an 8px control on #ffffff = ~1.07:1 (verified maxChannelDelta=8/255). Two G195 conditions fail: AREA (1px on each side of an 8px control is not a perceptible 1px border and, lacking 3:1, is neither >=4 CSS px on the shortest side nor >=2px thick) and CONTRAST (~1.07:1 vs 3:1). Ring is offset onto the page so it stays sub-perceptual on both checked-purple and unchecked-grey boxes. Outline paints faint pixels (oj04fd passes) but no human can tell which 8px square is focused.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The widget passes name/role/state checks (4.1.2 linters quiet) and has a :focus rule changing outline (absence heuristics quiet). axe/WAVE/Lighthouse do not measure the rendered indicator's AREA against G195's 4-CSS-px shortest-side rule, nor its contrast delta, nor relate either to the control's 8px size; a pixel diff just sees the 1px ring change. Deciding a 1px #f7f7f7 ring on an 8px control is imperceptible is a combined size-and-contrast visual judgment.

citation.quote: If the focus indicator area is not at least equal to the area of a 1 CSS pixel border, check that it has an area of at least 4 CSS pixels along the shortest side of the component.

pages.scenario: Restaurant menu-section nav links whose only focus change is a fractional letter-spacing nudge (.12em -> .132em, ~0.17px per gap), default outline removed - a sub-pixel reflow that shifts only a handful of antialiased glyph-edge pixels.
pages.mechanism: nav.cats a:focus increases letter-spacing by 0.012em (~0.2px/gap at 17px). Measured live, the focused 'Antipasti' link grows 81.98px->83.36px total (1.38px across 8 gaps); the word does not visibly move. No color/outline/border/size/weight change - nothing a human can point to. The sub-pixel reflow flips a few antialiased edge pixels (per-pixel maxChannelDelta=173 but only on fringe pixels, so a pixel diff records change and oj04fd passes) while remaining below human perception as a focus indicator.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A :focus rule changes a real layout property (letter-spacing) so no 'missing focus style' heuristic fires and outline:0 has an author-supplied (useless) replacement. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse cannot rasterize the two focus states, diff them, and decide the sub-pixel reflow is below perception; a pixel diff only confirms 'some edge pixels changed.' Whether a ~0.17px-per-gap letter-spacing shift is a perceptible focus indicator is a pure human visual judgment.

citation.quote: This success criterion helps anyone who relies on the keyboard to operate the page, by letting them visually determine the component on which keyboard operations will interact at any point in time.

pages.scenario: Government DMV registration wizard whose native selects/inputs/buttons get a 2px solid #1763b5 :focus-visible outline offset 2px on the white form - a genuinely perceptible indicator JUST above the threshold. The passing boundary anchor for the aspect.
pages.mechanism: select/input/.btn:focus-visible draw a 2px #1763b5 ring offset 2px on #ffffff. Contrast change ~6.0:1 (#1763b5 vs #ffffff = 6.02:1; verified maxChannelDelta=232/255 over 1344 changed pixels) - well above G195's 3:1. The band is 2px thick (meets the >=2px fallback) and forms a full border around the component (meets the 1px-border area requirement). The change is large, surrounds the control, and is immediately noticeable, so focus is visibly indicated - a genuine PASS on the perceptible side of the threshold.
pages.selectorNote: PASS boundary: native field sharing the perceptible 2px blue ring; representative input
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Symmetry point of the aspect: a pixel diff confirms 'pixels changed' here exactly as for the invisible failing cases, so it cannot on its own CONFIRM this passes for the right reason (sufficient magnitude) versus passing trivially. The correct passed verdict rests on the same human magnitude/contrast judgment used to fail the others, only resolved on the visible side; automated tools cannot make that call.

citation.quote: Check that the change of contrast of the indicator between focused and unfocused states has a ratio of 3:1 or more for the minimum focus indicator area.

aspects.title: Script removes or steals focus the instant an element receives it (F55: onfocus blur / programmatic focus theft)
aspects.plain: JavaScript yanks focus away the instant a control receives it, so the focus highlight never appears and keyboard users can't tell where they are on the page.
aspects.description: F55 is a failure where script removes focus the moment an element receives it (onfocus="this.blur()", or a handler that immediately moves focus elsewhere). Because focus never settles, no focus indicator is ever shown for that element, and the control becomes pointer-only. This is a temporal/behavioral failure: a single focused snapshot may even render as unfocused because focus has already been stolen. F55's test requires confirming that 'when focus is placed on each element, focus remains there until user moves it' — a property over time, not a single render. The brief notes the corpus is static, single-state, with no asynchronous focus changes and no JS that moves focus then immediately blurs.
aspects.scLimb: The 'focus must remain / be shown when received' temporal limb: the Understanding text states the focus indicator must not be time-limited — 'when the keyboard focus is shown it must remain.' F55 lists 2.4.7 among the SCs it fails. Catching it requires reasoning about the script's effect on focus over time.
aspects.whyUncovered: oj04fd diffs a single focused snapshot vs an unfocused snapshot of an element it has programmatically focused; if a script blurs immediately, the rule's own focus attempt fails to settle, putting the case outside its clean pass/fail model, and no ACT fixture exercises blur-on-focus. A static pixel-diff cannot model 'focus is removed when received'; F55 explicitly requires a temporal/behavioral check (focus remains until the user moves it) that needs human or dynamic testing.

references.quote: Content that normally receives focus when the content is accessed by keyboard may have this focus removed by scripting. This is sometimes done when designer considers the system focus indicator to be unsightly.
Check that when focus is placed on each element, focus remains there until user moves it.
The focus indicator must not be time limited, when the keyboard focus is shown it must remain.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: Online-banking 'Move money' form whose 'Review transfer' submit button carries onfocus="this.blur()" (canonical F55 Example 1). Tabbing from the Memo field to the submit button lands focus and instantly removes it; the valid :focus outline never paints and the button is mouse-only. Junior dev pasted a Stack Overflow 'remove ugly focus ring' snippet.
pages.mechanism: Inline onfocus="this.blur()" on input[type=submit]: the focus event fires and the handler calls .blur() in the same tick, so the declared .btn-primary:focus outline never renders. Verified by Puppeteer Tab traversal — focus moves Memo -> body -> Clear, never settling on 'Review transfer'.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: No automated 2.4.7 indicator rule exists; axe/WAVE/Lighthouse see a named submit button with a valid :focus outline declared in CSS and pass it. The defect is purely temporal — focus is granted then revoked within one event-loop tick — so any single rendered/snapshot state shows the button unfocused, indistinguishable from 'not yet tabbed to.' Only driving Tab and observing over time that the indicator never settles (the F55 procedure) reveals it.

citation.doc: WCAG Techniques — F55: Failure of Success Criteria 2.1.1, 2.4.7, 2.4.13, and 3.2.1 due to using script to remove focus when focus is received
citation.quote: Content that normally receives focus when the content is accessed by keyboard may have this focus removed by scripting. This is sometimes done when designer considers the system focus indicator to be unsightly. However, the system focus indicator is an important part of accessibility for keyboard users. In addition, this practice removes focus from the content entirely, which means that the content can only be operated by a pointing device such as a mouse.

pages.scenario: Newspaper paywall 'Continue reading — subscribe for $1' text link with onfocus="if(this.blur)this.blur();" (canonical F55 Example 3), injected site-wide by a legacy buildSubscribeLink() template helper. Tabbing to the only path past the paywall drops focus instantly; the :focus-visible yellow ring never paints.
pages.mechanism: Inline onfocus="if(this.blur)this.blur();" on the a.cta anchor removes focus the instant it is received; the a.cta:focus-visible style never renders. Puppeteer Tab traversal shows focus moving from the nav links to body, skipping the subscribe link.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The link is a real <a href> with descriptive visible text and a valid :focus-visible indicator — every static name/role/markup check passes and there is no automated 2.4.7 rule. The guarded blur expression only has effect in time (focus granted then revoked in one tick), so a single snapshot shows the link with no ring, identical to an un-tabbed state. Detecting it requires executing the Tab sequence and confirming the indicator never persists.

citation.quote: Content that normally receives focus when the content is accessed by keyboard may have this focus removed by scripting... this practice removes focus from the content entirely, which means that the content can only be operated by a pointing device such as a mouse.

pages.scenario: Boutique ceramics shop whose header brand/logo is an image link (canonical F55 Example 2) and is the page's first tab stop. The instant a keyboard user Tabs into the page, the logo link gains and loses focus, so the very first interactive element never shows an indicator.
pages.mechanism: onfocus="this.blur()" on a.brand removes focus on receipt; the a.brand:focus outline never paints. Puppeteer Tab traversal shows Tab 1 landing on body (logo skipped), then on the nav links — the logo link never holds focus. Image alt and aria-label are correct, so only the behavioral theft is wrong.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every static signal is healthy: the has descriptive alt, the has href and aria-label, and a valid :focus outline is declared — alt-text/link-name/contrast scanners pass and no 2.4.7 rule runs. The fault is behavioral (focus granted then revoked in one tick), so a single DOM snapshot or pixel diff of the focused state shows the logo with no ring, indistinguishable from 'not focused yet.' Only running the keyboard sequence reveals focus refuses to land.

citation.quote: Use the keyboard to verify that you can get to all interactive elements using the keyboard. Check that when focus is placed on each element, focus remains there until user moves it.

pages.scenario: Job-board posting whose primary action is a custom div[role=button][tabindex=0] 'Apply now' widget (correct name, valid :focus style). A page-level delegated focusin listener matching [data-action="apply"] calls document.body.focus() (body has tabindex=-1, outline suppressed), bouncing focus off the widget every time it is received — the F55 'moves focus elsewhere on receipt' variant, distinct from this.blur().
pages.mechanism: A document-level focusin listener relocates focus to body[tabindex=-1] whenever the apply widget gains focus; the .apply-btn:focus ring never paints. Puppeteer Tab traversal shows focus parked on body across every Tab — the widget never settles. Mouse clicks still navigate (separate click handler), masking the keyboard defect.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The widget is textbook-clean in the static DOM (role=button, tabindex=0, correct aria-label, valid :focus outline) so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse flag nothing and none implement a 2.4.7 indicator check. The failure lives in runtime event flow — a focusin listener that fires after focus lands and moves it to <body>. A scanner does not execute the Tab sequence or model focusin bubbling, and a single focused snapshot would appear to show the body focused, not the button.

citation.quote: Content that normally receives focus when the content is accessed by keyboard may have this focus removed by scripting... this practice removes focus from the content entirely, which means that the content can only be operated by a pointing device such as a mouse.

pages.scenario: Municipal 311 services search box whose onfocus calls .focus() on a visually-hidden, focusable role=status span (a misguided attempt to 'announce results early'). The moment a keyboard user tabs into the search input, focus is yanked off-screen onto the hidden span; the input's :focus ring never paints and focus disappears to an invisible element.
pages.mechanism: input[type=search]#q onfocus relocates focus to #srch-status (a .visually-hidden [tabindex=-1] span) in the same tick; the input:focus outline never renders. Puppeteer Tab traversal shows Tab 1 landing directly on span#srch-status.visually-hidden — the search box never holds focus.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Statically the form is exemplary: programmatic <label for=q>, real input[type=search], role=search form, valid :focus outline — label/name/form/ARIA scanners pass and no 2.4.7 rule exists; the role=status span is a legitimate live-region pattern. The failure is the runtime onfocus redirect (focus granted then moved off within a tick), so any single snapshot shows the box unfocused and the clipped span shows no ring. Only tabbing in and observing focus silently leave the screen reveals it.

citation.quote: Test Condition: A visible indication of focus is provided when focus is on the interface component. ... Evaluate Results (PASS if): When each interface element receives focus, there is a visible indication of focus.

pages.scenario: PASS boundary: a SaaS settings panel with three role=switch toggles that each run a script handler ON FOCUS — superficially identical to the F55 pages — but the handler ADDS a high-contrast focus-ring class (SCR31) and removes it on blur, never calling blur() and never moving focus. Focus genuinely settles and a strong indicator persists, drawing the line between 'script styles the focused element' (valid) and 'script removes focus on receipt' (F55).
pages.mechanism: An addEventListener('focus') handler adds .kbd-focus (a two-layer box-shadow ring, SCR31) while the element stays focused; native :focus outline also applies; no blur()/relocation. Puppeteer Tab traversal confirms focus settles on button.switch.kbd-focus[role=switch] and persists across all three switches before moving on — the temporal limb 'when shown it must remain' is satisfied.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: No automated 2.4.7 rule can confirm a pass, and a heuristic that flagged 'scripted focus handlers' would WRONGLY flag this valid SCR31 implementation as F55 — the static signature (a focus listener on each control) is identical to focus theft. Distinguishing them requires running the keyboard sequence and judging the temporal outcome: does focus remain with a persistent indicator (SCR31, pass) or get removed/moved (F55, fail)? That is human/dynamic judgment a scanner cannot make.

citation.doc: WCAG Techniques — SCR31: Using script to change the background color or border of the element with focus (sufficient technique for 2.4.7)
citation.quote: Using script to change the background color or border of the element with focus

aspects.title: Visual feedback exists only for pointer interaction (:hover/:active) or is suppressed for keyboard (:focus-visible mismatch), leaving keyboard focus bare
aspects.plain: Controls only light up on mouse hover and the keyboard outline is stripped, so a keyboard user tabbing through sees no sign of which element is focused.
aspects.description: C15 and C45 stress that the visible feedback must apply to the KEYBOARD focus state, not only pointer interaction. A common real-world failure: authors write ':hover {…}' and ':active {…}' (or rely on JS mouseenter/mouseleave) but never ':focus'/':focus-visible', while also stripping the UA outline. A mouse user sees rich feedback; a keyboard user tabbing through gets nothing. The subtle, judgment-requiring variants are where this matters: :focus-visible heuristics that the UA suppresses for certain elements, :focus reused for both states but styled with mouse-targeted changes, or focus-within applied to a non-focusable wrapper while the real target has outline:none. Distinguishing 'this feedback is pointer-only / modality-mismatched' from 'this is a real keyboard focus indicator' requires understanding the selectors' modality semantics — which input actually triggers the change a keyboard user receives.
aspects.scLimb: The 'mode of operation where the KEYBOARD focus indicator is visible' limb — the indicator must be present specifically for keyboard navigation, not just on pointer hover/active. C45 explains :focus-visible is shown for keyboard but generally not for pointer, making the modality distinction central.
aspects.whyUncovered: The ACT corpus includes only :focus / UA-outline cases and the single outline:none fail; it has no fixture where feedback lives solely on :hover/:active or on a UA-suppressed :focus-visible path. A blatant hover-only-with-outline:none page would fail oj04fd (zero diff under programmatic focus), but the SUBTLE variants — :focus-visible suppressed for a given element type, mouse-driven JS toggles, or focus-within on the wrong node — require a human to reason about which modality actually drives the visible change; a pixel diff cannot attribute a change to input modality.

references.quote: browsers always show these styles when a user is navigating using the keyboard, but will generally not show them as a result of a mouse/pointer interaction
Providing visual feedback may be possible through more than one mode. Usually, it is attained through using a mouse to hover over the element or a keyboard to tab to the element.
Ensure each item receiving focus has a visible indicator.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: Farm-to-table bistro primary navigation. Links light up with a pale-mint pill (#dcffff) on :hover/:active; the UA focus ring is removed via nav.primary a:focus{outline:none} with no replacement. A mouse user sees the pill; a keyboard user tabbing through the menu sees nothing change on the focused link. HEAD case (website-builder/marketing-template default).
pages.mechanism: Visible feedback is bound exclusively to pointer-modality pseudo-classes (:hover and :active). Tab fires :focus, whose only declared rule is outline:none, so the keyboard-focused link is pixel-identical to its idle state. The link is still announced to screen readers, but the sighted keyboard user — the population 2.4.7 protects — has no indication of focus position.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: outline:none is legal CSS and a valid focus indicator could plausibly live on :hover/:focus/box-shadow/a class; there is no reliable automated oracle for SC 2.4.7. A scanner cannot reason that the only state carrying a perceptible change (:hover) is pointer-triggered and never responds to keyboard focus. Verified in Chromium: focusDelta=0 visual properties on every nav link.

citation.quote: Styles defined with the regular :focus pseudo-class are applied whenever an element has focus, regardless of how it received focus. In contrast, user agents apply additional heuristics and logic to decide when to show :focus-visible styles – in particular, browsers always show these styles when a user is navigating using the keyboard, but will generally not show them as a result of a mouse/pointer interaction (with the exception of elements that also support keyboard input, such as <input> elements).

pages.scenario: Credit-union personal-loan application form (step 2 of 4). Text/email/number inputs and a native <select> grow a vivid blue border + glow on :hover; input:focus,select:focus is reset to outline:none with no border/box-shadow change. Tabbing field-to-field gives no focus cue. MID case (premium-form tutorial snippet mis-applied).
pages.mechanism: The author-supplied indicator (border-color:#1a73e8 + box-shadow glow) is gated behind :hover, a pointer-only state. The UA outline was explicitly removed and the :focus rule contains only outline:none. Per C45 browsers normally show :focus-visible for <input> even on mouse, but here no :focus/:focus-visible indicator exists at all — only the pointer :hover one — so a keyboard user cannot track which field (especially the caret-less <select>) holds focus.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every control has a programmatic <label for>, markup is valid, and outline:none is legal; tools reward the labelling and have no SC 2.4.7 check. A scanner cannot determine that the perceptible state change (:hover) is pointer-only while the focus state is inert. Verified in Chromium: focusDelta=0 on every input.

citation.quote: Using a keyboard, tab to the component.

pages.scenario: Real-estate listings card grid. Each card (<article>) has a lift+shadow bound to .card:hover and .card:focus-within; the real focusable address <a> has outline:none. Tabbing onto a listing DOES lift the wrapper card, but the lift is on the wrong node, is pixel-identical to hover, and the focused link itself is bare. LONG-TAIL case (designer wired the interaction to the whole tile).
pages.mechanism: Subtle present-but-wrong-node failure. On Tab, :focus-within fires and the wrapper lifts (transform:translateY(-3px) + shadow), so something visibly changes — but it marks the entire tile rather than the focused control (the link's own outline was removed), so with multiple cards visible the user cannot tell which element holds focus, and the change is indistinguishable from hover. A naive 'did anything change under programmatic focus?' pixel-diff (like oj04fd) would be fooled into passing.
pages.selectorNote: Real focusable address link with outline:none; lift fires on wrapper .card:focus-within instead
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Because a perceptible change occurs on focus, any heuristic that only asks whether the page looks different under programmatic focus passes — including diff-based checks. Judging that the change is on the wrong node, is identical to hover, and leaves the real target bare requires human reasoning about which element focus is on versus where the feedback appears. Verified in Chromium: wrapper transform none -> matrix(1,0,0,1,0,-3) and shadow appear on keyboard focus, yet the focused link's outline stays none.

citation.quote:
The purpose of this success criterion is to help a person know which element has the
         keyboard focus.

pages.scenario: University course-catalog subject filter chips (<button>s). CSS contains a decoy .chip:hover,.chip:focus rule that only nudges the border one near-identical lavender step (#c9c2da -> #c4bdd6); the conspicuous filled-purple .is-hot state is applied by JavaScript bound to mouseenter/mouseleave. Keyboard focus fires neither, so the Tab-focused chip gets an imperceptible border change and nothing else. LONG-TAIL case (legacy jQuery hover-preview ported verbatim).
pages.mechanism: Two-layer deception. The :focus CSS rule exists but its only effect is a sub-perceptible 1-step border shift. The visible 'this chip' state (.is-hot: background:#3b1d6e; color:#fff) is toggled solely by mouseenter/mouseleave — pointer-only DOM events. Pressing Tab dispatches focus, never mouseenter, so .is-hot is never added for keyboard users, leaving effectively no focus indicator (UA outline also reset to none).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A CSS scan finds a :focus rule and assumes focus is styled — it cannot judge that a 1-step border shift is below perceptible threshold; and the real indicator is produced by JS bound to mouse events, which static analysis does not model as an input modality. No tool ties the conspicuous highlight to pointer-only listeners. Verified in Chromium: keyboard focus produced no perceptible change while dispatched pointer events flipped the chip to background:#3b1d6e/color:#fff.

citation.quote:
the
         system focus indicator is an important part of accessibility for keyboard users.

pages.scenario: E-commerce checkout shipping-country field built as an ARIA combobox with aria-activedescendant. The blue option highlight (.opt.hot) is toggled only by mousemove/mouseleave; the ArrowUp/ArrowDown handler updates aria-activedescendant (so screen readers announce the active country) but never paints the active option, and no CSS targets the active descendant. A sighted keyboard user arrowing the list sees nothing move. LONG-TAIL case (mouse-era autocomplete ported to ARIA).
pages.mechanism: In an aria-activedescendant widget DOM focus stays on the input, so the visually-indicated active option IS the focus indicator the keyboard user needs. Here the highlight (.opt.hot) is bound to mousemove, a pointer event keyboard navigation cannot fire; the keydown handler moves aria-activedescendant but applies no class, and there is no [aria-activedescendant]-correlated CSS rule. The screen-reader user hears the active option; the sighted keyboard user sees the highlight frozen on whatever the mouse last touched, or nothing.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The ARIA plumbing is textbook-correct (valid roles, accessible name via aria-labelledby, aria-activedescendant references a real option and updates on arrow keys) — axe actively rewards this. No scanner correlates 'the keyboard moves the active descendant' with 'no CSS ever makes that descendant look different' because the highlight is gated behind pointer-only JS. Verified in Chromium: two ArrowDown presses moved aria-activedescendant to opt-it (Italy) with zero options highlighted; a pointer mousemove over Spain painted opt-es rgb(37,99,235).

citation.quote: Verify that once the component has received focus, a focus indicator is visible

pages.scenario: SaaS pricing page (Solo/Team/Business) with one CTA <button> per tier. The buttons define exactly one styled interactive state: .cta:active{transform:scale(.97)} (a press animation); .cta:focus is reset to outline:none with no replacement. Tabbing onto a CTA and pausing shows no change, because :active only fires while the button is held and springs back on release. MID case (Tailwind/utility-class mindset: focus:outline-none + active:scale-95).
pages.mechanism: :active is the 'currently being activated' state, not a focus state. It fires for a mouse press and for keyboard Space/Enter activation but lasts only while the control is held and reverts instantly on release. With :focus reset to outline:none and no persistent replacement, a keyboard user who Tabs to a CTA and stops sees the button exactly as idle and cannot tell which of the three CTAs holds focus — violating the requirement that the indicator remain while focus is shown.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: There IS interactive-state styling present (:active), outline:none is legal, and a programmatic-focus pixel diff captures the resting focused state — which is unchanged, but tools have no SC 2.4.7 oracle to call that a failure rather than a design choice. Distinguishing transient, modality-agnostic press feedback (:active) from persistent focus feedback (:focus/:focus-visible) is a semantic judgment about which state a Tab-and-stop produces. Verified in Chromium: resting focusDelta=0 on every CTA.

citation.quote: The focus indicator must not be time limited, when the keyboard focus is shown it must remain.

aspects.title: Custom-drawn indicator that vanishes in forced-colors mode or that AT cannot track (G165 / C40 caveats)
aspects.plain: A custom focus highlight (a box-shadow or painted square) looks fine normally but vanishes in Windows high-contrast mode or can't be located by screen-reader users.
aspects.description: G165 warns that if you draw your OWN focus indicator (e.g. coloring sections of the page in response to user action) rather than using the native indicator, user/AT system-wide focus customizations 'will not carry over, and AT will not usually be able to find your focus indicator.' C40 adds the forced-colors caveat: relying on box-shadow alone fails because 'user agents commonly suppress the box-shadow property in forced-color modes.' So an indicator can look fine in the single default render oj04fd snapshots, yet disappear (box-shadow / background-image / gradient suppressed) or become orphaned from the real focus position (detached painted square, overlay) for users in Windows High Contrast / forced-colors mode or for AT users relying on the native ring. Judging whether the chosen technique is robust across forced colors and tracks the actual focus is a semantic/contextual judgment about the indicator mechanism, not a default-mode pixel count.
aspects.scLimb: The robustness / 'mode of operation' limb under real user rendering conditions — the Understanding text frames 2.4.7 as ensuring at least one mode where focus is visible; G165/C40 show that a default-render-only indicator can fail to be that mode for forced-colors and AT users.
aspects.whyUncovered: oj04fd renders one default-mode snapshot and accepts a box-shadow-only, gradient, or JS-painted indicator as a pass because pixels change; it does not simulate forced-colors mode and the corpus has no dark-mode / system-color (Highlight) dependency. The corpus's Passed Examples 3/4 even use the exact 'drawn, detached' indicators G165 warns about, but never test them under forced colors or for focus-tracking robustness. Recognizing that a box-shadow-only / background-image / JS-painted indicator will be suppressed or orphaned for these users requires a human (or a deliberate forced-colors/AT mode toggle) — a default-render checker cannot.

references.quote: If you draw your own focus indicator, for example by coloring sections of the page in response to user action, these settings will not carry over, and AT will not usually be able to find your focus indicator.
User agents commonly suppress the box-shadow property in forced-color modes, so authors should avoid relying on box-shadow alone to implement focus indicators.
If you use the native focus indicator, any system-wide settings for its visibility will carry over to the web page.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: Public-library 'Current loans' page whose primary 'Renew' buttons get their only focus indicator from a box-shadow glow applied after outline:none. HEAD case (Bootstrap/Tailwind-style 'remove ugly ring, add a nice glow' reset). Looks correct in the default render so oj04fd passes, but forced-colors/Windows High Contrast suppresses box-shadow, leaving no focus cue.
pages.mechanism: `.btn:focus { outline: none; box-shadow: 0 0 0 3px #fff, 0 0 0 6px #1a73e8 }` with no outline/border fallback. Default render shows a blue+white halo (pixels change -> oj04fd pass). In forced-colors mode the UA suppresses the box-shadow property while outline:none still applies, so the focused button renders identically to unfocused ones — no focus indicator survives for forced-colors keyboard users before an irreversible 'Renew' action.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: outline:none is legal CSS when a replacement exists (box-shadow does exist), so no linter fires; the default render genuinely changes pixels so oj04fd/screenshot-diff pass; axe/WAVE/Lighthouse evaluate one default-theme render and never simulate forced-colors mode or reason about WHICH css property carries the indicator. Knowing box-shadow is dropped in forced colors (and nothing else remains) is the human/spec knowledge C40 encodes.

citation.quote: Avoid setting outline: none to use box-shadow on its own. User agents commonly suppress the box-shadow property in forced-color modes, so authors should avoid relying on box-shadow alone to implement focus indicators. If box-shadow only styling is required, consider combining it with an outline: 2px transparent solid property to ensure compatibility with forced-color modes.

pages.scenario: German alpine-hotel ('Alpenhof Resort') primary nav whose links sit on a flat teal panel and convey focus only by swapping in a CSS linear-gradient (teal->green wash) on :focus after outline:none. MID case (marketing-theme gradient highlights). Default render shows the gradient on focus (oj04fd passes); forced-colors mode flattens gradients/background-images to the system Canvas, so focused and unfocused links become identical.
pages.mechanism: `nav.primary a:focus { outline: none; background: linear-gradient(180deg,#7fd6c4,#38a08c); color:#062a29 }` over a flat base `background:#d9efe9`. The gradient is the entire indicator. In forced-colors mode the UA treats author background-image (incl. CSS gradients) as none and paints system Canvas, and overrides the small color change, so the focused nav link is visually identical to its neighbours — the difference that signalled focus is eliminated.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: outline:none plus a real background change is valid and produces a genuine pixel difference, so oj04fd/screenshot-diff pass; axe/WAVE/Lighthouse render one light-mode snapshot and have no concept that a gradient/background-image is treated as 'none' in forced colors. Recognizing the gradient is the ONLY cue and that it disappears in forced colors is the semantic judgment C40's forced-colors caveat and G165 demand of a human.

citation.quote: If you draw your own focus indicator, for example by coloring sections of the page in response to user action, these settings will not carry over, and AT will not usually be able to find your focus indicator.

pages.scenario: Coastliner rail booking seat picker whose custom div[role=button] seats signal focus only by a background-COLOR swap (#f3f5f9 -> #ffe08a) after outline:none; in forced-colors the tint collapses to system Canvas and, being a non-native widget, the seat gets no UA fallback ring, so the focused seat is pixel-identical to its neighbours.
pages.mechanism: Each delivery seat is a custom div[tabindex="0"][role="button"].seat whose only focus cue is a background-color swap on :focus (#f3f5f9 resting -> #ffe08a focused) after outline:none, with no border/box-shadow/outline change. In forced-colors mode the UA overrides author background-color with the system Canvas, so the amber tint collapses to the same colour as the unfocused seats; and because the seats are non-native div[tabindex] widgets, Chromium does not re-apply a UA forced-colors focus ring (it only does so for native input/select/button), leaving no fallback indicator.
pages.selectorNote: Seat picker is custom div[tabindex][role=button]; orig input/select/button.save absent on this page
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: outline:none + a real background-image change is valid CSS with a true pixel difference, so oj04fd/focus screenshot-diff pass; the image is a self-contained data: URI so there is no broken-resource signal to catch; axe/WAVE/Lighthouse render once in the default theme and neither simulate forced colors nor reason that a background-image indicator vanishes there — that inference is the human judgment C40's forced-colors caveat requires.

citation.quote: User agents commonly suppress the box-shadow property in forced-color modes, so authors should avoid relying on box-shadow alone to implement focus indicators.

pages.scenario: Interactive astronomy module: the seven stars of the Big Dipper are scattered absolutely-positioned <a> links. On focus the star's outline is removed and NOTHING changes on the star; JS instead slides a single shared yellow marker square over the matching star NAME in a fixed corner legend. LONG-TAIL case — the indicator is positionally detached/orphaned from the real focus position (the core G165 'drawn, detached' failure).
pages.mechanism: `a.star:focus { outline: none }` (no on-element cue) + JS that repositions a shared `#focus-marker` <span> over `ul#legend li[data-for]` in an aria-hidden corner <aside>. The focused star shows no change; the cue is a detached square elsewhere. For magnifier users zoomed into the map the corner marker is off-screen; for screen-reader users the legend is aria-hidden and the marker is bare markup so AT cannot find/announce it; for forced-colors users the author-drawn box is divorced from the focused element — the indicator never tracks the focus position.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: outline:none is legal because a 'replacement' indicator exists somewhere — a scanner cannot judge it is in the wrong PLACE; a default-render screenshot diff detects a pixel change on the page but cannot reason whether that change is co-located with the focused element (a spatial/semantic judgment a human makes by watching focus move); the markup is well-formed (real links, labelled legend rows) so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse find nothing.

citation.quote: If you draw your own focus indicator, for example by coloring sections of the page in response to user action, these settings will not carry over, and AT will not usually be able to find your focus indicator.

pages.scenario: Grocery checkout custom role='listbox' of delivery time-slots. Real keyboard focus stays on the container (tabindex=0, outline:none); arrow keys do NOT move focus but JS toggles an .is-active class (pale-green background-color) on a sibling option <div>, and the container has no aria-activedescendant. MID case (hand-rolled APG listbox anti-pattern). Default render moves the green tint (oj04fd passes); AT cannot track it and forced-colors flattens the tint.
pages.mechanism: Container `.listbox:focus { outline: none }` (real focus, ring removed) + `.opt.is-active { background-color:#e3f3e7 }` toggled on sibling role='option' divs with NO aria-activedescendant. Sighted keyboard users see the tint move; screen-reader users get only 'listbox' because focus never leaves the container and there is no activedescendant association (G165 'color sections in response to user action'); forced-colors users lose the pale background tint as it collapses to system Canvas, and the container's ring is gone — no robust trackable indicator.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: roles (listbox/option/aria-selected) are present, tabindex=0 is valid, and outline:none is legal given a 'replacement' cue exists, so axe/WAVE find nothing; a default-render pixel diff sees the green tint move and passes — it cannot reason that focus NEVER moved and AT has nothing to announce (requires understanding the widget focus model: aria-activedescendant vs roving tabindex); no tool simulates forced colors to notice the pale tint collapses.

citation.quote: If you draw your own focus indicator, for example by coloring sections of the page in response to user action, these settings will not carry over, and AT will not usually be able to find your focus indicator.

pages.scenario: Food-bank volunteer-shift sign-up page (PASS boundary twin of case-01). The 'Sign up' buttons use the SAME box-shadow glow as case-01 but follow the C40 note exactly: the focus rule pairs the box-shadow with outline:2px solid transparent + outline-offset. The transparent outline is invisible by default (glow does the work) but is forced to a system color in forced-colors mode, producing a real focus-tracking ring. Included to sharpen the aspect: a default-render checker cannot distinguish this from case-01, yet only this one is robust.
pages.mechanism: `.btn:focus-visible { outline: 2px solid transparent; outline-offset: 2px; box-shadow: 0 0 0 3px #fff, 0 0 0 6px #1f6feb }`. Default render: box-shadow glow appears, transparent outline harmless. Forced-colors: UA drops box-shadow but replaces the transparent outline with a system color -> real 2px ring that tracks the focused button. Using :focus-visible keeps it tied to keyboard focus and the ring is on the focused element itself (not detached), so focus is visible in both modes.
pages.selectorNote: PASS boundary: native Sign-up buttons whose transparent-outline ring survives forced colors
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: To a default-render pixel checker (oj04fd, axe focus heuristics) this page is INDISTINGUISHABLE from failing case-01 — both remove the conventional ring and show a box-shadow glow, both 'pass'. The tool cannot see that only this one keeps a forced-colors fallback. Correctly judging this as a pass (and case-01 as a fail) requires the same human/forced-colors reasoning about the mechanism; the load-bearing `outline: 2px solid transparent` is exactly what a default-mode checker is blind to.

citation.quote: If box-shadow only styling is required, consider combining it with an outline: 2px transparent solid property to ensure compatibility with forced-color modes.

aspects.title: Focus indicator drawn but clipped by overflow or pushed outside the visible viewport so the user never sees it
aspects.plain: The focus outline is drawn but gets clipped by an overflow container, hidden behind a sticky header, or scrolled off-screen, so the keyboard user never sees it.
aspects.description: The SC requires a perceptible focus indication for the focused element. A real-world failure: the element receives focus and an indicator IS drawn, but it is clipped by an ancestor's overflow:hidden, hidden behind a sticky/fixed header or off-canvas panel, or the focused element sits scrolled out of the visible viewport, so the changed pixels are never actually seen by the user. Because oj04fd counts a pixel change 'inside the scrolling area of the viewport' and never requires the user to be able to see it without manual scrolling — and the corpus places every indicator immediately adjacent in an otherwise empty body — these clipping/scroll cases are untested.
