Whether the indicator is actually visible to the user (vs technically painted but clipped/offscreen) is a layout/perception judgment; note this partially overlaps WCAG 2.2's 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured, but the bare 'I cannot see any focus indicator at all' outcome still implicates 2.4.7.
aspects.scLimb: The 'the indicator is actually visible to the user' limb — the indicator must be perceivable in the viewport, not merely rendered somewhere in the layout. Overlaps 2.4.12/2.4.11 (Focus Not Obscured) at the edge, but a fully-clipped/offscreen indicator means no visible focus at all, squarely 2.4.7.
aspects.whyUncovered: oj04fd accepts ANY changed pixel anywhere in the scrolling area and the corpus's single bare element in an empty body never has to deal with clipping containers, sticky overlays, or scroll position; there is no fixture where the indicator is painted but clipped/offscreen. A pixel-diff that scans the whole render surface (or auto-scrolls the element into view) reports a change and passes; judging whether a real user navigating by keyboard would actually SEE the indicator given overflow/sticky/scroll context is a layout-aware human visual judgment.

references.quote: Why it's important: Without a focus indicator, sighted keyboard users cannot operate the page.
Ensure each item receiving focus has a visible indicator.

It can be difficult to see the line when it is around a form element which already has an outline, when the focused element is inside a table cell, when the focused element is very small, or when the background of the page is a dark color.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: Online-banking 'Recent transactions' card with overflow:hidden; each row's round details button is pinned flush to (and slightly past) the card's right edge via transform:translateX(13px), so its focus ring is a circle whose right half is clipped off the card by the ancestor's overflow:hidden — only a meaningless left crescent survives.
pages.mechanism: Focus ring is drawn (3px outline + 3px offset) but the focusable .row .go button straddles the .card{overflow:hidden} boundary, so the right half of the ring is painted outside the clip box and removed; verified in Chromium with ring-visible fraction ~0.55 and the right rail clipped.
pages.selectorNote: Round details button flush past .card overflow:hidden edge; right half of ring clipped
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: oj04fd is satisfied because focusing the button changes pixels (tint + surviving crescent) inside the scrolling area, and axe/WAVE/Lighthouse see a valid high-contrast :focus-visible rule plus a real color change. Recognizing that the visible fragment is a meaningless crescent — that the ring is cut at the clip boundary — needs a rendered-state, layout-aware visual judgment scanners do not perform.

citation.quote: For each target element, there is at least one device pixel inside the scrolling area of the viewport whose HSL color value is different when the element is focused from when it is not.

pages.scenario: Long-form news article with an in-article 'In this article' TOC; the two-deck masthead is position:sticky top:0 (~135px). Activating a TOC link via keyboard scrolls the target <h2> to y=0, which lands under the opaque sticky bar, so the heading's :target/focus ring (and subsequent focused controls) are hidden behind the masthead. No scroll-padding-top/scroll-margin-top offset is set.
pages.mechanism: Fragment navigation scrolls the target heading top to viewport y=0; the author's :target/:focus-visible ring is painted there but covered by the opaque position:sticky masthead. Verified in Chromium: after activating the policy TOC link, targetTop=0 while stickyBottom=135, so headingHiddenUnderSticky=true.
pages.selectorNote: First invalid input focused via 'Go to first error' below fold; orig #policy:target absent
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The focus/target style is present and high-contrast and oj04fd passes (activating a link changes many pixels in the scrolling area). The failure is purely positional and emerges only from the keyboard journey; a static DOM/CSS snapshot cannot reason about where a scrolled element ends up relative to a position:sticky overlay — only a scroll-then-look viewport-aware check sees the ring is covered.

citation.quote: Thus it is possible to pass this rule and Success Criterion 2.4.7 Focus Visible with barely perceptible changes at the other end of the page. That would however still be an accessibility issue.

pages.scenario: RTL (dir=rtl, lang=ar) Arabic e-commerce CMS product-description toolbar with overflow:hidden and an overflow fade + '⋯ more' affordance; the inner track is pulled flush with margin-inline-start:-52px, so the first tool in tab order (right-most, 'غامق'/Bold) overhangs the inline-start (right) clip edge and the right rail of its focus ring is clipped off the visible track.
pages.mechanism: On Tab the first .tool gets the author's 3px ring, but margin-inline-start:-52px pushes the button across the .toolbar{overflow:hidden} inline-start (right) boundary, so the ring's right rail and corners are clipped; verified in Chromium with over half the button label cut at the right edge. RTL flips inline-start to the right, where tab-order index 1 lives.
pages.selectorNote: First RTL toolbar button pushed past .toolbar overflow:hidden start edge; ring rail clipped
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every button has a valid high-contrast :focus-visible ring and a tint, so oj04fd passes and axe/WAVE/Lighthouse report nothing. The defect is layout- and writing-mode-aware: in RTL the first tab-order button is the right-most one pinned against the overflow:hidden boundary, so the rail facing the edge is clipped. Whether a keyboard user can actually see the ring given the clip box, RTL inline-start edge, and overflow fade is a human visual judgment.

citation.quote: Other styling may make it difficult to see the focus indicator even though it is present, such as outlines that look the same as the focus outline, or thick borders that are the same color as the focus indicator so it cannot be seen against them.

pages.scenario: Outdoor-gear cookie/privacy consent dialog built from a design-system Surface token that bundles border-radius:18px, overflow:hidden, and contain:paint. The primary action buttons ('Reject all'/'Save choices') are a full-bleed footer flush to the surface's rounded bottom corners, so their outward-offset focus ring is painted into the rounded-corner region that both overflow:hidden and contain:paint remove.
pages.mechanism: Tab reaches a full-bleed footer button; the 3px ring (2px offset) is painted at the surface's bottom corner, where .surface{overflow:hidden; contain:paint; border-radius:18px} clips the ring's bottom rail and corner. Verified in Chromium: with 'Reject all' focused, the bottom and left rails fall outside the clip box and the rounded bottom-left corner cuts the ring.
pages.selectorNote: Full-bleed footer button in rounded corner clipped by overflow:hidden + contain:paint
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every control has a real high-contrast :focus-visible ring and tabbing changes pixels, so oj04fd passes. The surface stacks overflow:hidden AND contain:paint on an 18px-rounded box; full-bleed corner buttons get their ring nibbled away by the clip box and corner radius. contain:paint in particular is a performance property invisible to a focus-style linter, and judging perceivability past two stacked clipping containers is a layout/visual judgment automated tools do not make.

citation.quote: This describes a failure condition that occurs when the user agent's default visual indication of keyboard focus is turned off or rendered non-visible by other styling on the page without providing an author-supplied visual focus indicator.

pages.scenario: Healthcare patient-portal dashboard with an off-canvas navigation drawer closed via transform:translateX(-110%) (chosen over display:none so it can animate). The closed drawer's links remain rendered, focusable, and in the tab order; tabbing from the hamburger button moves focus to the first drawer link, whose focus ring is painted ~300px off the left edge of the viewport while the browser does not scroll to it.
pages.mechanism: Tab from the menu button focuses the first .drawer a; the browser paints the 3px ring but the drawer is translated off-screen by transform:translateX(-110%). Focus/scrollIntoView uses the element's layout box (left:0, on-screen) so the browser does not scroll; a transform moves only the paint. Verified in Chromium: the focused link's box is at x ~ -294..-42, paintedInViewport=false, no ring visible.
pages.selectorNote: Off-canvas drawer link still focusable; ring painted ~300px off-screen via translateX(-110%)
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The drawer links have a valid high-contrast ring and focusing one changes pixels, so oj04fd (which asks only for a changed pixel inside the scrolling area, and the drawer's layout box IS at left:0) is satisfied. Because the drawer is hidden with transform (not display:none/visibility:hidden/inert) its links stay focusable while painted off-screen; judging that the indicator is painted outside the visible region requires running the keyboard sequence and reasoning about transform geometry, which scanners do not do.

citation.quote: For each target element, there is at least one device pixel inside the scrolling area of the viewport whose HSL color value is different when the element is focused from when it is not.

pages.scenario: E-commerce checkout with a position:fixed order-summary footer overlapping the bottom ~76px of the viewport — the same risky pattern that usually clips a focus ring — but the author reserved space with scroll-padding-bottom:96px on the scroll container and scroll-margin-bottom:96px on every field/button, so a field scrolled into view by Tab always stops in the clear band above the fixed footer and its 3px ring stays fully visible. Boundary PASS variant.
pages.mechanism: On Tab to a low field, the browser's scroll-into-view honors scroll-padding-bottom/scroll-margin-bottom and stops the field above the fixed footer, where its 3px :focus-visible ring is fully painted and perceivable. Verified in Chromium: focusing #cvc puts its bottom+ring at y~397 while the fixed footer top is at y~644, so ringClearOfFooter=true.
pages.selectorNote: PASS boundary: low field whose ring clears fixed footer via scroll-padding/margin-bottom
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: This is the flip side of the aspect: just as tools cannot detect the clipped/occluded failures (they only see a conformant :focus-visible rule and a pixel change), they also cannot distinguish this safe layout from the failing ones — to axe/WAVE/Lighthouse this page and the clipped pages look identical, because the distinguishing factor is the runtime scroll position of the focused element relative to a fixed overlay. Only a viewport-aware reviewer who tabs through and watches the ring can tell it stays visible here.

citation.quote: When each interface element receives focus, there is a visible indication of focus.

methodology.enNote: Section Headings — WCAG 2.0 AAA, out of Section 508 A/AA scope; no Trusted Tester test.

aspects.title: A genuine content section in a multi-section page has no heading while sibling sections are headed
aspects.plain: A page split into topical sections gives most of them real headings, but one substantial section is left un-headed, so a screen-reader user can't find or label it.
aspects.description: The heart of 2.4.10 is providing a heading for EACH section when a page is organized into sections, not merely 'the document has a heading somewhere.' The realistic violation is a page divided into several topical content sections where most carry headings but one substantive, topically-distinct section is left un-headed (e.g. a headed 'Abstract', 'Introduction', 'Results', 'Discussion' with a 500-word 'Methods' block of new subject matter wedged between two headed sections carrying only a bold first sentence and no heading). Recognizing that the un-headed prose is a distinct section that 'introduces' new subject matter — and therefore needs its own heading — requires reading the body and topically segmenting it, which is semantic human judgment.
aspects.scLimb: CORE: 'headings for sections of a web page, when the page is organized into sections... When such sections exist, they need to have headings that introduce them' — the per-section obligation, not the binary document-has-a-heading proxy.
aspects.whyUncovered: Every ACT failure (7505d/81d501/929079/4e34ca) removes or hides the ONE heading of the ONE non-repeated #main block, so the corpus encodes only the binary 'document has a heading at all.' There is NO case with 3+ sibling content sections where one mid-document section is missing its heading while others are headed, so the actual 'heading for EACH section' obligation is untested. Automated checkers (axe/WAVE/Lighthouse) cannot detect this: the page contains valid headings and valid HTML; deciding that a particular un-headed prose block is a separate section needing its own heading requires reading and topically segmenting the content.

references.quote: The intent of this success criterion is to provide headings for sections of a web page, when the page is organized into sections. For instance, long documents are often divided into a variety of chapters, chapters have subtopics, etc. When such sections exist, they need to have headings that introduce them.
Check that the content is divided into separate sections. Check that each section on the page starts with a heading.
Examine a page with content organized into sections. Check that a heading for each section exists.

pages.scenario: Ecology research article organised as Abstract / Introduction / Methods / Results / Discussion. Four sections carry native <h2>; the 480-word Methods section (study site, paired-plot design, coring/assays, mixed-effects stats) is pasted between Introduction and Results with only a bold lead paragraph and NO heading. Position = MIDDLE. Verified via Puppeteer: the AT heading outline is Abstract, Introduction, Results, Discussion — Methods is absent.
pages.mechanism:
The Methods block is a substantive, topically-distinct section (per-section obligation of 2.4.10) but its only marker is a font-weight:700

carrying no heading role or level. AT exposes it as ordinary body text, so a screen-reader user navigating by heading jumps straight from Introduction to Results and never lands on a Methods boundary — the methodology, the most-jumped-to part of a paper, is unreachable by heading navigation.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The document has one <h1> and four valid, sequentially nested <h2> elements, so axe-core (page-has-heading-one, empty-heading, heading-order), WAVE and Lighthouse all pass — confirmed zero axe violations. There is simply no element where the Methods heading should be; to flag it a tool would have to read 480 words, recognise they form a self-contained methodological section distinct from the prose before and after, and conclude it needs its own heading — semantic content-segmentation no checker performs.

citation.doc: WCAG 2.2 Understanding 2.4.10 — Intent of Section Headings
citation.quote: The intent of this success criterion is to provide headings for sections of a web page, when the page is organized into sections. For instance, long documents are often divided into a variety of chapters, chapters have subtopics, etc. When such sections exist, they need to have headings that introduce them. … Other page elements may complement headings to improve presentation (e.g., horizontal rules and boxes), but visual presentation is not sufficient to identify document sections.

pages.scenario:
The canonical Understanding example (Appetizers/Salad/Soup/Entree/Dessert) rendered as a real prix-fixe restaurant menu. Four courses use native

; the Salads course (between Appetizers and Soups) is introduced by a

styled with identical font-size, weight, letter-spacing and decorative rule. Position = MIDDLE. Screenshot confirms 'Salads' is visually indistinguishable from the real course headings; Puppeteer confirms the AT outline is Appetizers, Soups, Entrées, Desserts — Salads absent.
pages.mechanism:
Font-size/font-weight alone conveys 'Salads' as a course heading (visual-only conveyance / ARIA anti-pattern: heading-ness chosen for visual size). The styled

has no heading role, so a blind diner pulling up the heading list hears only four courses and, arrowing linearly, finds three salad dishes adrift with no announced course boundary — exactly the 'visual presentation is not sufficient to identify document sections' failure.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss:
All four real

course headings are non-empty and in order under one

, and the styled 'Salads' is a perfectly valid

— axe/WAVE/Lighthouse find no heading defect (no skipped level, no empty heading, no missing h1; confirmed zero axe violations). A tool cannot infer that a

SHOULD be a heading: there is no role to test against and font-size/weight are not reliable heading signals. Recognising 'Salads' is a course on a par with the other four is a human reading + visual-prominence judgment.

citation.doc: WCAG 2.2 Understanding 2.4.10 — Examples of Section Headings
citation.quote: A menu contains different sections for different courses. Each section has a heading: Appetizers, Salad, Soup, Entree, Dessert.

pages.scenario:
Plumbing how-to whose five-step procedure puts each step under an

. Steps 1, 2, 3 and 5 carry

; Step 4 (re-tighten to correct torque, plus a stripped-thread callout) is a bare

bold lead because the Markdown source line lost its leading '### ' and was wrapped in '**…**', emitting -in-paragraph instead of

. Position = MIDDLE of a heading sequence. Puppeteer confirms outline has Step 1, 2, 3, 5 — Step 4 absent.
pages.mechanism: A procedural sub-section equal in rank to its four <h3> siblings has no heading role/level. A blind reader arrowing heading-to-heading from Step 3 lands on Step 5 and silently skips the entire re-tightening step — the one carrying the critical 'no more than three-quarters of a turn' warning. Because the visible numbers run 1-2-3-4-5, a sighted user assumes five equivalent headings, but the AT outline has only four.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The heading levels present run h1 > h2 > h3 with NO skipped level — the Step 4 heading is simply absent, leaving a legal 3,3,3,3 run — so axe-core's heading-order, empty-heading and page-has-heading-one all pass (confirmed zero axe violations) and there is no malformed token to catch. Flagging it requires reading the procedure, noticing 'Step 4' names a step at the same level as Steps 1-3 and 5, and concluding a heading dropped out of the numbered sequence — a content-segmentation judgment.

citation.doc: WCAG Techniques — H69: Providing heading elements at the beginning of each section of content (Tests)
citation.quote: Check that the content is divided into separate sections. Check that each section on the page starts with a heading.

pages.scenario:
City parking-permit guidance page organised into Who can apply / What you'll need / Fees / How to appeal a refusal. The first three are
introduced by visible

; the final appeals section (eligibility, 21-day window, evidence, review process, escalation) is ALSO a
with aria-label="Appeals" but has NO heading element — its visible title is a styled

. Position = LAST. Puppeteer confirms outline = Who can apply, What you'll need, Fees — the appeals section is absent.
pages.mechanism: An aria-label on a region names the LANDMARK but is not a heading — it produces no entry in the heading outline and no in-content heading boundary. The appeals block appears in the landmarks list (terse name 'Appeals') but not the headings list, so a blind resident skimming heading-by-heading for 'how do I challenge this?' finds no appeals heading and may conclude the page does not cover appeals; the landmark name also diverges from the visible 'How to appeal a refusal'.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The page has one <h1> and three valid <h2>s (no empty heading, no skipped level), and the appeals region is a well-formed landmark with a non-empty accessible name — so axe-core flags nothing under any landmark or heading rule (a region with an aria-label is considered correctly named; confirmed zero axe violations). No tool has a rule that a landmark must additionally contain a heading, and the role+aria-label actively masks the gap. Distinguishing a landmark name from a required section heading, and judging the appeals prose is a substantive section needing its own heading, is human reasoning.

citation.doc: WCAG 2.2 Understanding 2.4.10 — Benefits of Section Headings
citation.quote: People who are blind will know when they have moved from one section of a web page to another and will know the purpose of each section.

pages.scenario:
SaaS Terms of Service of six numbered clause sections, pasted from Microsoft Word into a CMS WYSIWYG. Clauses 2-6 used Word 'Heading 2' style and became

; clause 1 (Acceptable Use, a substantive opening clause) was Word body text whose title run was merely bolded, so the CMS emitted

1. Acceptable Use

instead of an

. Position = FIRST. Puppeteer confirms the AT heading outline opens at clause 2 — clause 1 is absent entirely.
pages.mechanism: The opening clause section has no heading role; the document's heading outline begins at clause 2, so a blind user reviewing the contract by heading list sees the agreement apparently start at '2.' with no clause 1 — disorienting in a legal document where clause completeness matters and 'Acceptable Use' is the clause most likely to be searched for. Navigating heading-to-heading skips the binding acceptable-use obligations entirely; the leading section has no programmatic boundary at all.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss:
Clauses 2-6 are five non-empty

s in correct order under one

, so axe-core's page-has-heading-one, empty-heading and heading-order all pass (confirmed zero axe violations): there is no SKIPPED level (the headings merely start at the second clause), no empty heading, and inside

is valid HTML. The Mso class and bold run are exactly what survives a Word paste and are invisible to a structure checker, which has no concept of 'fake heading.' Flagging it requires reading the contract and concluding the FIRST section lacks the heading its siblings have.

citation.quote: Where content is organized in sections, provide section headings.

pages.scenario: BOUNDARY PASS variant. Recipe organised into Ingredients / Instructions / Tips & Variations (a genuinely distinct topic). Ingredients and Instructions use native <h2>; the appended Tips & Variations section is introduced by <div role="heading" aria-level="2"> — a valid programmatic heading, just not a native <h> element, sharing the same visual style. Screenshot confirms uniform appearance; Puppeteer confirms the AT outline exposes all three at level 2: Ingredients, Instructions, Tips & Variations.
pages.mechanism: The ARIA heading is computed into the accessibility tree identically to a native <h2> (role heading, level 2), so it forms a section boundary, appears in the heading list, and AT heading navigation lands on it. Every section, including the last, has a heading that introduces it — the per-section obligation of 2.4.10 is satisfied. This isolates 'does each section have a heading the AT exposes?' from the naive proxy 'does each section start with an <h> tag?'.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A simplistic checker that only COUNTS native <h1>-<h6> elements would see two headings for three visually distinct sections and could mis-report the Tips section as un-headed — a false positive in the opposite direction. axe-core correctly does not flag it (a role=heading with a valid aria-level is an accepted heading; confirmed zero axe violations). Deciding the page is conformant still requires a human to read the prose, confirm three distinct sections exist, AND verify the ARIA heading is genuinely exposed with a valid level — the same semantic segmentation that exposes the failures, here returning 'passed'. Tools cannot perform the segmentation step at all.

citation.doc: WCAG Techniques — G141: Organizing a page using headings (Description)
citation.quote: The objective of this technique is to ensure that sections have headings that identify them. … In HTML, this could be done using the HTML heading elements (h1, h2, h3, h4, h5, and h6). … Other technologies use other techniques for identifying headers.

aspects.title: Visually-demarcated sections (cards, columns, bands, rules, big gaps) with no programmatic heading for each
aspects.plain: Sections are shown only through visual styling like cards, columns, colour bands or whitespace, with no heading markup, so a screen-reader user perceives one undifferentiated blob.
aspects.description: The Understanding explicitly warns that 'visual presentation is not sufficient to identify document sections,' yet a very common pattern lays a page out as visually obvious sections — boxed cards, color-banded rows, multi-column blocks, large whitespace gaps, horizontal rules, or tab panels — where each visual block is plainly a distinct section to a sighted user but NONE carries a programmatic heading. The page may have a single page-level h1 (so 047fe0's non-repeated-block check passes) while the several visually-demarcated content sections beneath it use only styled bold leading text, a CSS border, or color to signal a new section. A human must perceive that the layout communicates multiple sections to sighted users and confirm those sections lack the headings that would convey the same structure to AT users.
aspects.scLimb: 'Other page elements may complement headings to improve presentation (e.g., horizontal rules and boxes), but visual presentation is not sufficient to identify document sections' — applied across MULTIPLE visually-implied sections, not the single-block template.
aspects.whyUncovered: ACT exercises the 'visual not sufficient' limb only inside the single-heading template: 7505d (one big bold strong = visual-only, FAIL) and 33fcbd (one <hr> alongside one real heading, PASS). It never builds a multi-section page where visual layout alone (cards/columns/bands/gaps/tabs) implies several sections without a programmatic heading for each. Automated tools cannot infer from CSS layout, whitespace, borders, or background color that a sighted user perceives several headed-looking sections — perceiving a visual section boundary and judging that it lacks a programmatic heading is inherently a visual + semantic human judgment.

references.quote: Other page elements may complement headings to improve presentation (e.g., horizontal rules and boxes), but visual presentation is not sufficient to identify document sections.
People who are blind will know when they have moved from one section of a web page to another and will know the purpose of each section.
Examine a page with content organized into sections. Check that a heading for each section exists.

pages.scenario: SaaS admin 'Workspace settings' page laid out as four bordered cards (Account, Billing, Notifications, Security). Each card is an unmistakable visual section (box border + tinted header strip + colored dot + 19px/700 bold title), but every card title is a styled <div class="card-title">, not a heading. Section grouping is via <section aria-label> regions only. The single <h1> 'Workspace settings' keeps 047fe0 passing.
pages.mechanism: Four visually-distinct card sections each lack a programmatic heading; the page exposes exactly one heading (the page h1). Screen-reader heading navigation finds only the h1 and cannot jump to the four settings groups. <section aria-label> creates named regions, but regions are a separate mechanism from the section headings 2.4.10 requires.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Nothing is missing or empty: valid h1, labelled controls, good contrast, well-formed markup; a default axe.run reports zero violations and 047fe0 passes. No checker can infer from a 1px border + tinted strip + bold type that the four cards are content sections each needing a heading. Confirmed via Chromium heading extraction: only 1 programmatic heading present.

citation.quote: Other page elements may complement headings to improve presentation (e.g., horizontal rules and boxes), but visual presentation is not sufficient to identify document sections.

and titled in a 23px uppercase serif display face — but every course title is

Cantina del Faro

is a heading.

Decorative <hr> separators are aria-hidden ornaments conveying nothing programmatically. A blind diner using heading navigation hears only the restaurant name and must read the whole menu linearly.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Valid h1, valid <hr> separators (an hr is not an error; ACT 33fcbd allows hr alongside a real heading), semantic <ul> dish lists, good contrast — axe/WAVE/Lighthouse report no violation and 047fe0 passes. No tool can read the four course names, recognize them as the menu's course sections, and conclude each should be a heading. Chromium extraction: only 1 programmatic heading.

pages.scenario: The 'web version' of a club's monthly email (The Trailhead Dispatch), pasted from an email tool into a CMS. A 640px presentation-table laid out as five full-width color bands (intro/white, trail report/green, gear pick/tan, member spotlight/blue, events/white). Each band is a distinct topical section signalled by an eyebrow label + 22px bold band title, but each title is a bold inline-styled <span class="band-title">, not a heading. Only the masthead wordmark is an <h1>.
pages.mechanism: Email clients strip h1-h6, so the designer faked headings with bold spans; background color is presentational and conveys nothing to AT. The five sections the colored bands create visually do not exist programmatically. A screen-reader user reads a flat run of cells, heading navigation lands only on the masthead, and the five topics cannot be skimmed or skipped to.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A role=presentation table is explicitly NOT flagged (correct role for layout), inline contrast passes, the page has one h1 — axe/WAVE/Lighthouse report no violation and 047fe0 passes. No tool can deduce that each colored band is a content section needing a heading; it sees bold table cells, which are not an error. Chromium extraction: only 1 programmatic heading.

RTL Arabic municipal e-services portal whose service catalogue is laid out as four alternating color bands: Identity & civil registry, Traffic & vehicles, Property & building, Water & electricity. Chromium extraction: only 1 programmatic heading.

citation.quote:
The intent of this success criterion is to provide headings for sections of a web
         page, when the page is organized into sections.

pages.scenario: Boundary PASS variant: a hosting pricing page (Northwind Hosting) using the SAME visual idiom as the failing cases — three boxed plan sections (Starter/Pro/Enterprise) plus a 'What's included' comparison, with decorative <hr> separators and a featured colored band on Pro. The difference: every visually-implied section carries a programmatic heading — plan titles via role=heading aria-level=2, comparison via native <h2>, under one page <h1>. Mirrors ACT 33fcbd (hr + real heading passes).
pages.mechanism: Each visual section maps to a real heading: heading navigation yields the page h1 then a level-2 heading for each plan and for the comparison table, mirroring the four sections a sighted user sees. The decorative aria-hidden <hr> and Pro highlight band add nothing programmatic, which is fine because the headings already convey the structure — exactly the SC's permitted 'complement headings' use.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Tools cannot AUTOMATICALLY certify a 2.4.10 pass either: they cannot enumerate the page's visually-implied sections, so cannot confirm EVERY one has a heading. A heuristic pattern-matching on bands/bold lead text would wrongly fail this page; one merely counting heading elements could be fooled the other way. A human must confirm the section-to-heading mapping. Chromium extraction: 5 programmatic headings (h1 + four level-2), one per visual section — confirmation succeeds.

citation.quote: Other page elements may complement headings to improve presentation (e.g., horizontal rules and boxes), but visual presentation is not sufficient to identify document sections.

aspects.title: Heading element present but its text does not name/introduce its section (wrong, copy-pasted, placeholder, or generic)
aspects.plain: A section's heading text is wrong, copy-pasted, or a vague placeholder like 'More', so it doesn't actually name the section and gives a screen-reader user no orientation.
aspects.description: The SC requires headings that 'introduce' their sections and 'clearly indicate the organization of the content' and let users 'know the purpose of each section' — a heading must actually NAME the section it sits above. A page can satisfy the binary presence test while a heading's text is functionally wrong: it describes a DIFFERENT section, was copy-pasted from a template and never updated ('Section Heading', 'Lorem Ipsum'), names the wrong topic (an h2 'Shipping Information' actually heading the returns policy), or is a content-free generic placeholder ('More', 'Stuff', 'Other', 'Untitled') that gives a screen-reader user no orientation. Judging whether a heading's text fits the section body it introduces requires reading both — pure semantic human judgment.
aspects.scLimb: 'they need to have headings that introduce them. This clearly indicates the organization of the content' + Benefit 'will know the purpose of each section' — the heading's TEXT must describe its own section (F2-style meaning failure at section level).
aspects.whyUncovered: Every heading in the ACT corpus carries text that genuinely matches its block ('Three Heroes Swear Brotherhood...', 'Content' for nav). No case has a heading whose text is mismatched to, copied across, or generic for its section. Automated tools only verify a heading element exists and is non-empty and exposed; they have no model of a section's meaning and cannot tell that 'Shipping Information' is the wrong name for a returns-policy block, or that 'Section Heading' is a leftover placeholder. Heading-to-content fit is inherently semantic and beyond axe/WAVE/Lighthouse.

references.quote: When such sections exist, they need to have headings that introduce them. This clearly indicates the organization of the content, facilitates navigation within the content, and provides mental "handles" that aid in comprehension of the content.
People who are blind will know when they have moved from one section of a web page to another and will know the purpose of each section.
Goal: Users understand how content is organized in sections.

pages.scenario: Civic 'Apply for a Residential Parking Permit' page split into three finished, distinct sections (eligibility rules, a fee table, a how-to-apply step list), but all three section h2 read the literal Drupal/CMS template default 'Section Heading' the author never replaced.
pages.mechanism: Mechanism (a) literal CMS placeholder: each section's h2 text is the un-replaced template default 'Section Heading', so the rotor/heading-list reads 'Section Heading' x3 and names none of the sections; the heading is present but introduces no section.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: 'Section Heading' is a non-empty h2 in valid order, so empty-heading / heading-order / page-has-heading-one all pass. Duplicate heading text is not a flagged violation. Recognising the string as a leftover template placeholder that fits none of the eligibility/fees/apply bodies requires reading body+heading together — semantic judgment no checker has.

citation.quote: When such sections exist, they need to have headings that introduce them. This clearly indicates the organization of the content, facilitates navigation within the content, and provides mental "handles" that aid in comprehension of the content.

pages.scenario: UK retailer help article (Shipping / Tracking / Refund policy / Contact). The refund-policy section's body is unambiguously about refunds, but its h2 reads 'Shipping & Delivery' — copied verbatim from the first section and never edited; the in-page TOC correctly says 'Refund policy', so heading and nav silently disagree.
pages.mechanism: Mechanism (b) copied heading: 'Shipping & Delivery' is duplicated from the section above onto the refund-policy section, so the heading names the previous topic; the section's aria-labelledby accessible name is therefore 'Shipping & Delivery' over refund prose.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The outline is a clean h1 -> four non-empty ordered h2; duplicate heading text ('Shipping & Delivery' twice) is not a violation any tool reports. Detecting that the heading names a different topic than the refund body requires reading both and comparing meaning — and tools do not cross-check a hand-authored TOC label against the section's accessible name.

citation.quote: Since headings indicate the start of important sections of content, it is possible for users with assistive technology to jump directly to the appropriate heading and begin reading the content.

pages.scenario: DIY mechanical-keyboard blog post whose middle three section headings are content-free generic words — h2 'More' over the parts list, h2 'Stuff' over the soldering walkthrough, h2 'Other' over the firmware/QMK flashing guide — while the first and last headings are descriptive.
pages.mechanism: Mechanism (c) generic content-free words: 'More' / 'Stuff' / 'Other' are non-empty valid English but carry no topic, so they fail to introduce or identify the substantive, specific bodies beneath them; the heading exists but conveys no purpose.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The words are non-empty h2 in valid order (axe/WAVE/Lighthouse pass) and are correctly-spelled real words, so empty-text and spell heuristics find nothing. No tool can tell that 'Stuff' fails to name a soldering procedure — that the heading conveys none of the section's purpose is a graded semantic judgment.

citation.quote: People who are blind will know when they have moved from one section of a web page to another and will know the purpose of each section.

pages.scenario: SaaS settings screen with two grouped fieldsets: the group headed 'Privacy' contains exclusively notification controls (email digest, push alerts, quiet hours), and the group headed 'Notifications' contains exclusively privacy controls (profile visibility, data sharing, export). The two section headings are swapped relative to their bodies.
pages.mechanism: Mechanism (d) swapped headings: each h2 is the aria-labelledby accessible name of a fieldset whose controls belong to the OTHER heading, so the section name actively mislabels the form controls beneath it.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Outline is h1 -> two non-empty ordered h2; aria-labelledby resolves and fieldsets are named, so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse pass. 'Privacy' and 'Notifications' are both valid settings vocabulary, so nothing reads as anomalous. Detecting the swap requires reading the controls under each heading and recognising they belong to the other heading — semantic comparison no tool performs.

citation.quote: A web application contains a settings page that is divided into groups of related settings. Each section contains a heading describing the class of settings.

pages.scenario: Real-estate listing detail page where a template data-binding bug wired each section's h2 to the wrong listing field: the description is headed 'MLS #CP-2261148', the spec sheet is headed '2,940 sq ft', the agent bio is headed '$849,000', and the neighborhood section is headed '6 days on market'. Correct facts appear only in the sidebar card.
pages.mechanism: Novel beyond-seed mechanism (crossed data binding): every section h2 is a real, non-empty string from the wrong field token, so each heading is genuine text that names a different section than the body it introduces; the rotor reads bare data values, not section names.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: All four h2 are non-empty and ordered and the aria-labelledby refs resolve, so heading rules pass. The strings are real values ('$849,000', '2,940 sq ft'), so nothing reads as empty/placeholder/malformed. No tool models which field a section's heading should carry, so it cannot detect that the price is sitting where the agent name belongs — requires reading each body.

citation.quote: When such sections exist, they need to have headings that introduce them. This clearly indicates the organization of the content, facilitates navigation within the content, and provides mental "handles" that aid in comprehension of the content.

pages.scenario: Local-news 'Tuesday Roundup' with four short single-word section headings — h2 'Weather' over the forecast, h2 'Sports' over the scores, h2 'Markets' over the finance roundup, h2 'Traffic' over the commute report — each terse word genuinely and unambiguously naming its own section. PASS boundary twin of the swap/generic failures.
pages.mechanism: No defect: each one-word heading correctly introduces and identifies the section it sits above (Weather=forecast, Sports=scores, etc.), demonstrating that brevity/genericness of a word is not the 2.4.10 trigger — heading-to-body FIT is. Sharpens that short single-word headings pass when they name the section.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Automated tools pass this for the same shallow reason they pass the failing cases (non-empty, ordered headings), but here the PASS is the CORRECT verdict — and a tool cannot itself VERIFY that 'Weather' truly introduces a forecast. Only a human reading each body can confirm the fit, which is the judgment this aspect tests.

citation.quote: A menu contains different sections for different courses. Each section has a heading: Appetizers, Salad, Soup, Entree, Dessert.

aspects.title: Multiple distinct navigation/landmark regions, none demarcated by a heading (H69 nav demarcation sub-limb)
aspects.plain: A page has several distinct navigation areas (top nav, sidebar, footer links) but none has a heading, so a screen-reader user can't tell them apart when jumping by heading.
aspects.description: H69 calls for heading markup 'to demarcate different navigational sections like top or main navigation, left or secondary navigation and footer navigation.' Real pages frequently carry several distinct navigation regions — a primary top nav, a secondary/left sidebar nav, in-page section nav, and a footer link nav — yet provide a heading for none of them, so a screen-reader user navigating by heading cannot distinguish 'main navigation' from 'footer navigation' from 'related links.' A human must recognize that the page contains several functionally distinct navigation/grouping regions and judge that each needs a section heading to be told apart by AT.
aspects.scLimb: H69 sub-limb: 'demarcate different navigational sections like top or main navigation, left or secondary navigation and footer navigation' — multiple grouping regions each needing a heading.
aspects.whyUncovered: The corpus contains only a single <nav> block (its heading text is 'Content'); there is no footer nav, no secondary/left nav, and no page with multiple navigation regions each requiring its own heading. Automated tools detect landmark roles but cannot judge that two functionally distinct navigation regions are genuinely separate sections that each warrant a distinguishing section heading — that is a semantic/structural judgment about the page's organization. (Visually-identical link lists may be different navigation purposes; only meaning distinguishes them.)

references.quote: to demarcate different navigational sections like top or main navigation, left or secondary navigation and footer navigation;
People who are blind will know when they have moved from one section of a web page to another and will know the purpose of each section.
The objective of this technique is to use section headings to convey the structure of the content.

pages.scenario: Corporate B2B automation marketing site (Northwind Robotics) with three functionally distinct navigation regions — a top/primary site nav, a left/secondary product sub-category nav, and a footer legal/utility nav — none of which carries a heading; the only heading is the main article h1.
pages.mechanism: Three <nav> landmarks (header.top nav, aside.side nav, footer.foot nav) each begin a functionally distinct navigation section, but none is preceded/labelled by a heading element. A screen-reader user navigating by heading (H key) finds only the single content h1 and cannot distinguish main navigation from product navigation from footer navigation — violating H69's nav-demarcation sub-limb and SC 2.4.10's requirement that each section start with a heading.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every nav is a valid landmark with non-empty links, the page has exactly one h1, no empty headings, no skipped levels, and no missing attributes, so axe (page-has-heading-one, empty-heading, heading-order, landmark-unique), WAVE, Lighthouse and ACT 047fe0 all pass. No static rule can judge that three landmark navigation regions are genuinely distinct sections that each warrant a demarcating section heading; that requires reading the link contents and recognizing three different navigational purposes — whole-page semantic judgment.

citation.quote: to demarcate different navigational sections like top or main navigation, left or secondary navigation and footer navigation;

pages.scenario: Developer API-reference docs page (Orbit Payments, Pagination article) with two navigation regions of different purpose — a left site-section docs-tree nav (moves between documents) and a right 'On this page' in-page TOC nav (moves within the current article) — neither demarcated by a heading; only the article's own content h1/h2 headings exist, and the left nav's category sub-labels are styled divs, not headings.
pages.mechanism: Two <nav> landmarks (nav.docnav between-docs, nav.toc within-doc) each begin a distinct navigation section but carry no heading. The styled div.group-label items ('Getting started', 'Core resources') look like structure but have no heading role (F2-style presentation-not-semantics). By heading navigation the user reaches only article content headings (Pagination, Overview, Cursor parameters), never a heading that announces either navigation region.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: One h1, sequential h1->h2 outline, two valid nav landmarks, no empty headings, no missing attributes — axe/WAVE/Lighthouse and ACT 047fe0 pass. A tool cannot tell that a between-documents nav and a within-document nav are two distinct navigation purposes each needing a demarcating heading, nor that the styled group-label divs are pseudo-headings; that is a human reading judgment about what the links do.

citation.quote: to demarcate different navigational sections like top or main navigation, left or secondary navigation and footer navigation;

pages.scenario: SaaS analytics dashboard (Pulse Analytics, Acme Marketing workspace, Overview panel) with a global top nav that switches product areas and a workspace-specific left nav scoped to the current workspace — two operationally different navigations, neither demarcated by a heading; the workspace name is rendered as a styled brand div, not a heading.
pages.mechanism: header.global nav.product (global product-area switcher) and nav.workspace (within-workspace navigation) are distinct navigation sections with no heading; div.wsname 'Acme Marketing' is a styled brand label with no heading role. By heading navigation the user finds only the panel h1 'Overview' and cannot distinguish 'switch product area' from 'navigate within this workspace' — failing H69's top/left navigation demarcation.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: One h1, valid nav landmarks, no empty headings, no missing attributes — axe/WAVE/Lighthouse and ACT 047fe0 pass. No checker can decide that the global top bar and the workspace left rail are two distinct sections each needing a demarcating heading, nor that the styled workspace-name div is a brand label rather than a navigation heading; that is contextual product-comprehension judgment.

citation.quote: to demarcate different navigational sections like top or main navigation, left or secondary navigation and footer navigation;

pages.scenario: Government civic services portal (Clearwater County, Renew a vehicle registration) with three distinct navigation regions, each a <nav> given a correct distinct aria-label (Main / In this section / Footer) so LANDMARK navigation works perfectly — but none has a heading. The sharp boundary case that defeats the 'but the navs have aria-labels' rebuttal.
pages.mechanism: nav.primary[aria-label=Main], nav.section[aria-label='In this section'], nav.footer[aria-label=Footer] are uniquely labelled landmarks (landmark navigation succeeds), but aria-label names a landmark and is NOT a heading and does not appear in the headings list. A user navigating by heading still finds only the content h1 and cannot reach or distinguish the three navigation sections by heading — H69 specifically requires HEADING demarcation, which labelled landmarks do not provide.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Giving each nav a unique aria-label makes axe's landmark-unique/region checks pass MORE cleanly; with one h1, no empty headings and valid markup, WAVE/Lighthouse/ACT 047fe0 also pass. A tool cannot distinguish 'navigation demarcated by section headings' from 'navigation landmarks that merely have aria-labels' — it has no way to know H69 wants heading markup specifically, or that heading-navigation users are unserved by landmark labels. Reading the technique's intent is human judgment.

citation.quote: Check that the content is divided into separate sections.

pages.scenario: Right-to-left Arabic municipal transit website (Oasis City Transit Authority, Bus schedules) with a top primary services nav, a sidebar quick-links utility cluster, and a footer legal nav — three distinct navigation sections, none demarcated by a heading. lang='ar' and dir='rtl' are correctly set (deliberate red herrings); the functional distinctness is only legible by reading the Arabic link text.
pages.mechanism: header.top nav (services), aside.rail nav (quick-links), footer.foot nav (legal) each begin a distinct navigation section with no heading; the only heading is the content h1 'مواعيد الحافلات'. A screen-reader user (e.g. VoiceOver in Arabic) navigating by heading hears only that content heading and cannot distinguish primary, secondary/utility and footer navigation — the H69 spread of nav sections, all undemarcated.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Correct lang/dir, one h1, valid nav landmarks, a properly captioned table, no empty headings, no missing attributes — axe/WAVE/Lighthouse and ACT 047fe0 pass. To detect this a checker would have to read the Arabic link text and recognize that services / quick-links / legal are three different navigational purposes each warranting a demarcating heading — a multilingual semantic reading task far outside any static rule.

citation.quote: to demarcate different navigational sections like top or main navigation, left or secondary navigation and footer navigation;

pages.scenario: PASS / boundary variant: news portal (The Meridian Courier) with the SAME three-region structure (top section nav + 'Related coverage' sidebar nav + footer site-map nav) but where every navigation region IS demarcated by a real visible <h2> ('Sections', 'Related coverage', 'Browse the Courier'), each also naming its landmark via aria-labelledby. Sharpens what 'demarcated by a heading' means — exactly what cases 01-05 lack.
pages.mechanism: Each <nav> begins with a real visible <h2> (nav.sections>h2#secnav-h, aside.related nav>h2#related-h, footer.foot nav>h2#footnav-h) that appears in the headings list AND names the landmark via aria-labelledby. A heading-navigating user hears 'Sections', 'Related coverage', 'Browse the Courier' alongside the article h1/h2s and can jump to and distinguish every navigation region — H69's 'each section starts with a heading' is satisfied for all three nav sections.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Automated tools pass this page — but they would ALSO have passed cases 01-05 which fail, because in both the markup is valid, there is one h1, and the landmarks are present. Tools cannot tell the conformant version from the non-conformant ones; only a human reading the page can confirm a real heading introduces each navigation section here whereas none does in 01-05. The boundary demonstrates the exact judgment the failing cases require.

citation.quote: In this example, heading markup is used to make the navigation and main content sections perceivable.

aspects.title: Heading levels contradict the true content hierarchy (a subsection marked as a sibling, or peers given different levels)
aspects.plain: Heading levels don't match the real content hierarchy, so a sub-topic reads as a sibling or two equal sections read as parent-and-child, confusing how a screen-reader user understands structure.
aspects.description: H69 and G141 require headings 'properly nested' so the level structure conveys the logical hierarchy: a subsection should be one level below its parent, and the level numbers should match the topical containment relationships. A page can pass presence and even level-consistency checks while its heading LEVELS misdescribe the actual nesting — e.g. a sub-topic that is logically inside a chapter is marked h2 (sibling of the chapter) instead of h3, or two co-equal major sections are marked h2 and h3 so the second falsely reads as a subsection of the first. Whether a given block is conceptually a subsection of the one above it (and so demands a deeper level) is a content-meaning judgment, NOT the syntactic numeric-skip check that tools perform.
aspects.scLimb: H69/G141 'properly nested' / 'subsections are given subsequent logical levels (h2 is a subsection of h1)' — the LEVEL must reflect the topical containment, applied where the markup is level-consistent but semantically wrong.
aspects.whyUncovered: The corpus has exactly one nested case (9b25d8: h1 page title + h2 section) and that nesting is correct; there is NO case where the level assignment contradicts the content's true hierarchy. Crucially, axe-core/Lighthouse flag only empty headings or a RAW NUMERIC skip (e.g. h1 then h4) — they cannot tell whether a block is SEMANTICALLY a subsection of the preceding one, so an h2 that should be h3 (or peers arbitrarily given h2/h3) over level-consistent-looking markup passes automation. Deciding the correct level requires understanding the topical containment between sections. NOTE: scope test pages to the semantic-mismatch case (avoid bare numeric h1->h4 skips, which automation already catches).

references.quote: When headings are nested hierarchically, the most important information is given the highest logical level, and subsections are given subsequent logical levels.(i.e., h2 is a subsection of h1).

To facilitate navigation and understanding of overall document structure, authors should use headings that are properly nested (e.g., h1 followed by h2, h2 followed by h2 or h3, h3 followed by h3 or h4, etc.).

Skipping levels in the sequence of headings may create the impression that the structure of the document has not been properly thought through or that specific headings have been chosen for their visual rendering rather than their meaning.

pages.scenario: University course reader 'Chapter 3: Cellular Respiration' (h1) with three sub-topic sections correctly h2 (Glycolysis, Citric Acid Cycle, Oxidative Phosphorylation). A point '3.2.1 Fate of the Reduced Carriers' that elaborates ONLY section 3.2 is tagged h2 (sibling) instead of h3 (child), flattening the hierarchy. Sequence h1,h2,h2,h2,h2 — no numeric skip.
pages.mechanism: H69/G141 'properly nested': a subsection must be given a subsequent logical level (h3 under h2). The fourth heading is logically contained in section 3.2 (it traces where the NADH/FADH2 produced BY the citric acid cycle go next) but is leveled as a peer, so the AT heading outline lists it as a top-level chapter division alongside the three respiration stages — a child presented as a sibling.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The sequence is monotonic and non-skipping (h1->h2->h2->h2->h2), so axe-core heading-order/empty-heading/page-has-heading-one, Lighthouse and WAVE all pass; every heading is non-empty and descriptive. Deciding that '3.2.1 Fate of the Reduced Carriers' is topically contained in '3.2 The Citric Acid Cycle' requires reading and understanding the biochemistry in the prose; no tool models topical containment, and all four h2s render at identical 20px so there is no size cue either.

citation.quote: When headings are nested hierarchically, the most important information is given the highest logical level, and subsections are given subsequent logical levels.(i.e., h2 is a subsection of h1).

pages.scenario: Food-blog recipe 'Browned Butter Banana Bread' (h1). The two canonical co-equal halves of a recipe — 'Ingredients' (h2) and 'Instructions' (h3) — are given different levels, so the cooking steps falsely read as a subsection of the ingredient list. Sequence h1,h2,h3 — no numeric skip; both headings styled identically at 1.3rem.
pages.mechanism: H69/G141 'properly nested': co-equal peer sections must share a level. 'Instructions' is a top-level part of the recipe (peer of 'Ingredients', so h2) but is tagged h3, placing it as a child of the Ingredients h2 in the accessibility tree; the rotor outline announces 'Ingredients level 2 > Instructions level 3', telling the user the steps are a detail of the ingredient list.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: h1->h2->h3 is strictly non-skipping so axe heading-order, Lighthouse and WAVE pass; both headings are non-empty and descriptive. Knowing that Ingredients and Instructions are co-equal top-level parts of a recipe (siblings, both h2) rather than parent/child is document-structure common sense no linter encodes, and the two headings render at the same font size so there is no visual tell.

citation.quote: To facilitate navigation and understanding of overall document structure, authors should use headings that are properly nested (e.g., h1 followed by h2, h2 followed by h2 or h3, h3 followed by h3 or h4, etc.).

pages.scenario: Developer API reference 'Webhooks API — Endpoints' (h1) documenting two co-equal endpoints on the same /v2/webhooks collection. The intro states 'there are two endpoints ... neither is a sub-operation of the other', yet 'POST Create a webhook' is h2 and 'DELETE Delete a webhook' is h3, making the AT outline read DELETE as a child operation of POST. A later peer 'Verifying deliveries' is correctly h2. Sequence h1,h2,h3,h2 — no numeric skip.
pages.mechanism: H69/G141 'properly nested': peer endpoints must share a level. DELETE and POST are sibling operations on one collection (both should be h2) but DELETE is demoted to h3, asserting a parent/child containment the REST semantics — and the explicit intro sentence — deny; a developer scanning the heading list for the delete endpoint as a top-level operation finds it filed one tier down under POST.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: h1->h2->h3->h2 is non-skipping so axe heading-order, Lighthouse and WAVE report a clean outline; all headings are non-empty and descriptive. Recognising POST and DELETE as sibling operations (not parent/child) requires understanding REST semantics and reading the 'there are two endpoints ... neither is a sub-operation of the other' sentence; the theme renders h2 and h3 at the identical 18.4px (verified by screenshot), so there is no visual cue.

citation.quote: When headings are nested hierarchically, the most important information is given the highest logical level, and subsections are given subsequent logical levels.(i.e., h2 is a subsection of h1). Providing this type of structure will help users understand the overall organization of the content more easily.

pages.scenario: County government benefits page 'Help with Heating & Cooling Costs' (h1) describing two separate, independently funded programs. LIHEAP is h2 with two correct h3 sub-sections (qualify/apply). The second program, 'Weatherization Assistance Program (WAP)', begins a NEW top-level program but is tagged h3 — the same level as LIHEAP's sub-sections — so WAP and its own sub-sections read as further children of LIHEAP. Sequence h1,h2,h3,h3,h3,h3,h3 — no numeric skip.
pages.mechanism: H69/G141 'properly nested': a new top-level section must not be given a subsection level. WAP is a sibling of LIHEAP (should be h2) but sits at h3, so everything from 'Weatherization' onward sounds in the heading outline like more sub-detail of LIHEAP; a user eligible only for WAP, skimming for a second top-level program, never hears a second top-level entry and may conclude the page covers only LIHEAP — an entire benefit is hidden.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The sequence is monotonic with no skipped level, so axe heading-order, Lighthouse and WAVE pass; every heading is non-empty and descriptive. Whether 'Weatherization Assistance Program' continues LIHEAP or starts a new independent program is a meaning judgment that depends on reading the prose ('two separate ... programs ... funded differently'); the numeric pattern and the identical blue heading style give automation nothing to flag.

citation.quote: To facilitate navigation and understanding of overall document structure, authors should use headings that are properly nested (e.g., h1 followed by h2, h2 followed by h2 or h3, h3 followed by h3 or h4, etc.).

pages.scenario: RTL Arabic community-pharmacy page 'Home Medication Safety Guidelines' (h1, lang=ar dir=rtl) covering two explicitly independent, equal topics: storing medicines (h2) and safe disposal of expired medicines (h3). The intro states the two topics are 'independent and equal' and that 'neither is part of the other', yet disposal is demoted to h3 so it reads as a subsection of storage. A later peer 'When to contact the pharmacist' is correctly h2. Sequence h1,h2,h3,h2 — no numeric skip; lang/dir correct.
pages.mechanism: H69/G141 'properly nested': co-equal topics must share a level. Safe disposal is a peer of storage (should be h2) but is tagged h3, so an Arabic screen-reader user hears storage at level 2 and disposal at level 3 — i.e. that disposal is a sub-part of storage — contradicting the prose that declares the two topics independent and equal. RTL direction does not change the semantics: level still encodes containment.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: h1->h2->h3->h2 is non-skipping so axe heading-order, Lighthouse and WAVE pass; lang and dir are correct so no i18n rule fires; all headings are non-empty and descriptive. Deciding disposal is a peer of storage requires reading the Arabic prose — specifically the sentence declaring the two topics independent and equal — which no checker parses; direction (RTL) is irrelevant to the purely semantic defect, and the two headings render at identical size/colour.

citation.quote: When such sections exist, they need to have headings that introduce them. This clearly indicates the organization of the content, facilitates navigation within the content, and provides mental "handles" that aid in comprehension of the content.

pages.scenario: SaaS Terms of Service 'Lumen Cloud Storage' (h1) — the deliberate PASS control. Three top-level articles (Your Account, Acceptable Use, Termination) are all h2; the first article has two genuine sub-clauses (Eligibility, Account Security) correctly nested as h3. The level numbers match the topical containment exactly. Sequence h1,h2,h3,h3,h2,h2 — nesting present but semantically correct.
pages.mechanism: H69/G141 'properly nested' is SATISFIED: subsection levels (h3) are used only for genuine sub-clauses of the 'Your Account' article, and peer articles share level h2. The heading outline ('Your Account h2 > Eligibility h3 > Account Security h3 > Acceptable Use h2 > Termination h2') is an accurate model of the document, so a human applying H69/G141 finds no contradiction between the levels and the content hierarchy.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Automated tools also pass this page (clean non-skipping heading-order; non-empty headings) — but here the human verdict agrees with them. The control matters because the five failing cases are likewise green to automation: a model that learned 'nested headings present => flag' would wrongly fail this page. Distinguishing this correct nesting from the contradictory nesting in case-01..05 requires the same human semantic judgment about topical containment that the aspect tests.

aspects.title: Heading element present and exposed but conveying no section name (whitespace-only, decorative-image-only, CSS-image, or dingbat-only)
aspects.plain: A heading element exists but holds only whitespace, a decorative image, or ornamental glyphs, so a screen-reader user hears 'heading' with no name and gains no orientation.
aspects.description: A heading can satisfy the structural presence requirement — an h2 or role=heading element exists, is visible, and is exposed to AT — yet carry no meaningful accessible name for its section: it holds only whitespace / a non-breaking space, only a decorative , only a CSS background-image of the title text with empty real text, or only ornamental glyphs/dingbats. The screen-reader user hears 'heading, level 2' with no label and gains no orientation; the 'mental handle' the SC promises is absent. Whether the rendered heading actually names the section (versus being functionally empty) is something a human reading the page must judge.
aspects.scLimb: 'headings that introduce them... provides mental "handles"' + Benefit 'will know the purpose of each section' — a present-but-nameless heading provides no section name, a failure mode distinct from a fully-absent heading.
aspects.whyUncovered:
Every ACT heading carries meaningful text. The corpus tests a fully ABSENT heading (4e34ca) and HIDDEN headings (81d501 off-screen, 929079 aria-hidden), but never a heading element that is PRESENT-and-exposed-but-nameless — a distinct failure mode. While a strictly empty

is flagged by axe-core, the human-judgment variants are NOT: an h2 holding only a non-breaking space, only a decorative , only a CSS background-image with empty real text (image-of-text-as-heading without a text alternative — F2/H69 sub-limb), or only dingbat glyphs all look like 'a heading exists' to a tool but provide no section name. Scope test pages to these non-empty-but-meaningless variants, not bare

.

People who are blind will know when they have moved from one section of a web page to another and will know the purpose of each section.

pages.scenario: Vegetable recipe page (Ember & Root, 'Slow-roast harissa carrots'). The About/Ingredients/Method sections carry text h2s (with the icon as an aria-hidden accent); the final nutrition section's h2#h-nutri holds only the bar-chart icon-font glyph U+F080 with no text, so it appears in the heading list as a nameless level-2 heading.
pages.mechanism: The fourth section's heading (h2#h-nutri) contains only an icon-font glyph at the Private Use Area codepoint U+F080, painted as a bar-chart icon. The codepoint is non-whitespace so empty-heading does not fire, but U+F080 has no Unicode/CLDR name, so the heading's accessible name is an unpronounceable glyph that conveys no section name. The visible 'Nutrition' meaning lives only in the icon, which AT cannot name.
pages.selectorNote: Nutrition heading whose only content is a wordless PUA icon glyph; orig #sec-fees absent
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe-core's empty-heading does not fire because the <h2> is not literally empty: U+00A0 counts as text content, so the accessible name is the non-empty string " ". WAVE/Lighthouse see 'a heading with content'. No tool can decide a technically-non-empty name (lone whitespace) is semantically vacuous — that is a human reading judgment.

citation.doc: WCAG 2.2 Understanding — Intent of Section Headings
citation.quote: When such sections exist, they need to have headings that introduce them. This clearly indicates the organization of the content, facilitates navigation within the content, and provides mental "handles" that aid in comprehension of the content.

pages.scenario: Fashion lookbook ('Maison Lune — Spring 2026', Shopify Editorial theme) with three sections; the middle 'The Edit' section's title is rendered as a CSS background-image (inline SVG of the script wordmark 'The Edit') while the real <h2 class="art"> contains only a   spacer. The other two sections use plain text headings.
pages.mechanism: Heading is role=heading, level 2, visible, ignored=false, accessible name " ". The visible title 'The Edit' exists only as background-image pixels, which AT never reads (image-of-text heading with no text alternative, F2/H69 sub-limb). Screen-reader heading list reads 'New In … heading level 2 … Care' — the middle section is nameless.
pages.selectorNote: FAQ group heading reading placeholder 'Untitled section'; orig #h-edit absent
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The heading has a non-empty text node ( ) so empty-heading does not fire, and the title lives in a CSS background-image — axe/WAVE/Lighthouse do not OCR background images, so they cannot know the section name is painted into the heading with no text equivalent. Recognising the title is an un-alt'd picture is a human visual judgment.

citation.doc: WCAG Techniques — F2 (Failure due to using changes in text presentation to convey information without appropriate markup or text)
citation.quote: This failure also applies to images of text that are not enclosed in the appropriate semantic markup.

pages.scenario: Recipe page (The Weeknight Larder, 'Slow-Braised Short Rib Ragu'). Before-you-start / Ingredients / To serve sections use text h2s; the Method section's h2#h-method holds only a decorative dashed-rule divider whose alt is the file name, so the heading exposes a junk filename instead of 'Method'.
pages.mechanism: The Method section's heading (h2#h-method) contains only a decorative dashed-rule divider image whose alt was auto-filled with the uploaded file name ('divider-line-ornament-2x.png'). Because the alt is non-empty, empty-heading and image-alt both pass, but the computed accessible name is a meaningless asset filename, not a section name, so the cooking-instructions section is announced by a filename and conveys no purpose.
pages.selectorNote: Method heading named by image filename alt 'divider-line-ornament-2x.png'; orig #h-travel absent
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The markup is correct in isolation: image-alt is satisfied (a decorative image legitimately has alt=""), and empty-heading does not reliably fire because the heading has an element child (), not literally nothing. Flagging this would force flagging every decorative image. Deciding the swirl was meant to be a section title and isn't requires reading the page and judging intent.

citation.doc: WCAG 2.2 Understanding — Benefits of Section Headings
citation.quote: People who are blind will know when they have moved from one section of a web page to another and will know the purpose of each section.

pages.scenario:
SaaS analytics dashboard ('Pulse — Acquisition Overview') with three panels; the geographic-breakdown panel's heading is a design-system divider component rendered as
———
(three em-dashes). The other two panels use text

headings.
pages.mechanism: Element is role=heading, aria-level 2, visible, ignored=false, accessible name '———' (em dash em dash em dash). Screen readers announce the punctuation ('em dash em dash em dash, heading level 2'); a keyboard+SR user jumping panel to panel cannot tell it introduces the country table. Structural presence is satisfied but a punctuation run is not a section name.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The element has a valid role=heading + aria-level and a non-empty text node ('———'), so empty-heading does not fire and WAVE/Lighthouse see a structurally valid ARIA heading with content. No checker has a lexicon to decide a string of em-dashes is decorative punctuation rather than a section title — a human semantic judgment of the rendered string.

citation.doc: WCAG Techniques — G141: Organizing a page using headings
citation.quote: The objective of this technique is to ensure that sections have headings that identify them.

pages.scenario:
Developer SDK release notes ('Quanta SDK v4.7', exported from a Notion-style editor) with four changelog sections; three headings pair an emoji with words (e.g. '⚡ Performance'), but the 'Packaging & distribution' section's heading is only the box emoji:

📦

— the words were never typed.
pages.mechanism: Heading is role=heading, level 2, visible, ignored=false, accessible name '📦'. Screen readers announce the emoji's CLDR label ('package'/'shipping box'), not the section's name. The heading list reads '… package, heading level 2 …' so the developer cannot tell whether the section is about packaging, bundle formats, or npm distribution. Emoji-as-accent (siblings) is fine; emoji-as-whole-name is nameless.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The <h2> has a non-empty text node (the emoji) so empty-heading does not fire, and the accessible-name computation yields a non-empty string, so WAVE/Lighthouse see a named heading. Tools cannot judge that the emoji's label 'package' is an inadequate name for a 'Packaging & distribution' section, nor that emoji-only differs from acceptable emoji-plus-text siblings — a human reading of meaning.

citation.doc: WCAG 2.2 Understanding — Benefits of Section Headings
citation.quote: People who are blind will know when they have moved from one section of a web page to another and will know the purpose of each section.

pages.scenario: BOUNDARY PASS — restaurant dinner menu ('Olive & Ember') whose three course headings are hand-lettered calligraphy IMAGES (looks like the failing decorative-image cases), but each <h2> also carries a visually-hidden <span class="sr-only"> with the real course name and the image is correctly alt="". Image-as-title is acceptable when a text alternative names the section.
pages.mechanism: Each heading is role=heading, level 2, visible, ignored=false, and computes a real accessible name ('Small Plates', 'From the Hearth', 'Sweet') from the sr-only span while the calligraphy image is correctly decorative. The screen-reader heading list reads the real course names, so 2.4.10's 'mental handles' are present.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A tool cannot tell this PASS apart from the failing decorative-image cases (02/03): in all of them the visible title is an image, axe sees a non-empty heading, and no checker reads the calligraphy pixels. Only by computing the accessible name and judging it is a real section name ('Small Plates', not '') can the pass be confirmed — tools neither reward the correct sr-only pattern nor reliably penalise its absence.

citation.quote: Heading markup can be used: … to mark up images of text that are used as headings;

aspects.title: Genuinely unsectioned prose (letter / pre-existing document / continuous narrative) correctly NOT requiring headings
aspects.plain: A page is genuinely one continuous document like a letter or narrative with no real sections, so it correctly needs no section headings and should not be flagged as a failure.
aspects.description: 2.4.10 is Level AAA precisely because 'it cannot be applied to all types of content and it may not always be possible to insert headings' — posting a pre-existing document whose author included no headings, or a long letter covering several topics where 'putting headings into a letter would be very strange.' Correctly judging that such a page is NOT in scope (the content is genuinely a single flowing document, not 'organized into sections') versus a page that IS sectioned and merely lacks headings requires reading the prose and deciding whether it has the topical structure the SC targets. This is a content-genre judgment and a false-positive guard: the verdict should be PASS / not-applicable, not a violation.
aspects.scLimb: Applicability gate + AAA inapplicability: 'when posting a pre-existing document... headings that an author did not include in the original document cannot be inserted' and 'a long letter would often cover different topics, but putting headings into a letter would be very strange.'
aspects.whyUncovered: The corpus models inapplicability with one degenerate artefact (ecc29b: a bare SVG with only a <title>, no HTML document) and one single-paragraph stub (4f112d). Neither models the realistic AAA inapplicability scenario: a multi-paragraph, multi-topic but legitimately heading-less prose document (letter / pre-existing reproduction / continuous narrative) that a human must recognize as out of scope. Automation cannot make this call — it cannot distinguish 'a long letter that legitimately has no headings' from 'a sectioned page missing its headings'; both are just paragraphs with no heading elements. The distinction is entirely about content genre and authorial intent, so this also guards against false-positive flagging.

references.quote: This provision is included at Level AAA because it cannot be applied to all types of content and it may not always be possible to insert headings. For example, when posting a pre-existing document to the web, headings that an author did not include in the original document cannot be inserted.
Or, a long letter would often cover different topics, but putting headings into a letter would be very strange.
What to do: Where content is organized in sections, provide section headings.

pages.scenario: Family-archive verbatim reproduction of a personal WWII letter (salutation, several topic-shifting paragraphs — crossing, weather, money, brother Tom, food — sign-off, P.S.). The only heading is the archive's catalogue <h1> for the artefact; the letter body has no internal headings. Genre = personal letter, the canonical AAA-inapplicability case.
pages.mechanism: Content is a single continuous personal communication, not 'organized into sections', so 2.4.10's applicability precondition is unmet. Per the Understanding text, 'a long letter would often cover different topics, but putting headings into a letter would be very strange'; and as a pre-existing document, headings the author never wrote 'cannot be inserted'. A screen reader hears one heading (the archive label) and reads the letter as one continuous voice — which is correct. Flagging it for no section headings would be a false positive.
