citation.doc: WCAG Techniques — H69: Providing heading elements at the beginning of each section of content (Tests)
citation.quote: Check that the content is divided into separate sections. Check that each section on the page starts with a heading.

pages.scenario: Public-domain speech library reproduces Chief Joseph's 1877 surrender speech verbatim as a continuous <blockquote> of three flowing paragraphs. A speech is a spoken performance never 'organized into sections' and the speaker authored no headings. The page DOES have headings, but only as the library's editorial apparatus: the catalogue <h1> and a clearly-separate 'About this text' <h2> curator's note — neither is a heading inside the speech.
pages.mechanism: The reproduced oration is a pre-existing document into which headings 'cannot be inserted'; it is not 'organized into sections', so 2.4.10's precondition is unmet for the speech and it passes. A screen reader hears two headings (catalogue title + 'About this text') and reads the speech as one continuous utterance. The curator's note IS a genuine authored section and correctly carries its own heading — demonstrating that 'sections' must be scoped to the actual content, not the whole DOM. Flagging the heading-less speech body would be a false positive against a pre-existing document.

pages.scenario: A smart-thermostat 'Getting Started' help article reads as chatty continuous prose but is genuinely organized into five distinct procedural topics walked through in order — (1) unboxing & wiring, (2) connecting to Wi-Fi, (3) creating a schedule, (4) using geofencing, (5) troubleshooting won't-connect. Each is a self-contained help topic a reader would jump to, but none has a heading. The conversational tone disguises the section structure. FAIL twin of the unsectioned-prose PASS cases.
pages.mechanism:
The five

blocks are five distinct procedural sections ('organized into sections'), so 2.4.10 requires a heading per topic; their absence fails. A screen-reader user wanting only the troubleshooting steps pulls up the heading list, finds one entry (the

), and must arrow through wiring, Wi-Fi, scheduling, and geofencing first — exactly the navigation loss 2.4.10 prevents ('jump the focus from heading to heading... to find quickly content of interest').
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss:
The body is five clean

elements, the single

satisfies page-has-heading-one, and there are no empty or out-of-order headings (no sub-headings at all), so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse report nothing. The structure that makes it a failure — that the five paragraphs are five distinct procedural topics — exists only in the meaning of the prose, and the conversational tone (an author writing naturally) actively reads as one flow. Recognising the five sections requires comprehending all five paragraphs and knowing the genre is a multi-topic how-to guide.

citation.quote: The intent of this success criterion is to provide headings for sections of a web page, when the page is organized into sections. For instance, long documents are often divided into a variety of chapters, chapters have subtopics, etc. When such sections exist, they need to have headings that introduce them.

pages.scenario: Court public-records portal reproduces a verbatim sworn witness statement. Legal convention numbers every paragraph consecutively (1..9) as a citation device — but the numbers are NOT topical sections. The statement is one continuous first-person chronological account of a single evening's events (leaving the bakery, the lorry reversing, the impact, staying with the injured plaintiff, the jurat). Long-tail boundary: numbered paragraphs that look like 'sections needing headings' but are not.
pages.mechanism: Consecutive paragraph numbering is a legal-citation/reference device, not topical sectioning; the statement is one continuous chronological narrative, so it is not 'organized into sections' and 2.4.10's precondition is unmet — it passes. As a pre-existing sworn filing, headings cannot be inserted. A screen reader hears one heading (the registry filing label) and reads nine numbered evidentiary paragraphs as one account, with no topical sections to jump between (para 5's lorry and para 7's impact are consecutive beats of one event). Mistaking numbering for sectioning would be a false positive.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: An <ol> of <li>s with no <h2>..<h6> is structurally identical whether the items are topical sections or sequential evidentiary paragraphs. axe has no rule that fires (valid single <h1>, no empty/disordered headings, well-formed list). A heuristic flagging 'numbered blocks without headings' would wrongly fail every affidavit, contract recital, and statute section-list — all of which number for citation. Only reading the nine paragraphs reveals one continuous chronological account, and only knowing the genre (a sworn statement) explains the numbering — human semantic + domain judgment.

citation.quote: The intent of this success criterion is to provide headings for sections of a web page, when the page is organized into sections.

pages.scenario: A journaling app's single-entry view shows one day (Day 47, '21 March') of a solo sailor's field journal: a continuous stream of consciousness drifting across several topics in one flow — the wind shift and sea state, a windvane repair, a remembered argument with the writer's father, what they ate, a pod of dolphins, the dusk doubt about going on. The date is the entry's <h1>; the body has no internal headings. Diary genre = the 'long letter' the AAA note exempts.
pages.mechanism: A free-associating dated journal entry is genuinely unsectioned personal prose — the topic shifts are the natural wandering of one daily reflection, not separable sections a reader navigates to in isolation. Per the AAA note, headings in such personal writing 'would be very strange'; the content is not 'organized into sections', so 2.4.10's precondition is unmet and it passes. A screen reader hears the date heading and the body as one continuous voice. Flagging it for lacking section headings would be a false positive.

document with no empty/disordered headings and report nothing; a naive heuristic would wrongly flag it. aspects.title: Error text is fluent and field-identifying but factually wrong for the value entered / constraint violated (boilerplate mismatch)
aspects.plain: A form shows a fluent, field-specific error message, but it describes the wrong problem for the value you actually typed, so you can't tell what's really wrong.
aspects.description: A page shows a non-empty, grammatically descriptive, field-identifying error message that satisfies rule 36b590's 'describes the cause or how to resolve it' check at the string level, but the described cause is factually wrong for the value the user actually entered or the constraint that was actually violated. The text reads as a competent error description in isolation, so it passes every programmatic facet of the rule, but it misidentifies the nature of the error and so defeats the SC's core intent that the user 'can determine what is wrong'. Examples: a phone field that says 'Remove letters and parentheses' against an all-digit value; a date-of-birth field that says 'Please use MM/DD/YYYY format' against a value that already IS in MM/DD/YYYY (the real, undescribed error is a future date); a password field that says 'must be at least 8 characters' against a 12-character value. Detecting this requires reading the field's stated constraints, the entered value, and the error text TOGETHER and judging semantic agreement — a contextual judgment no checker performs.
aspects.scLimb: 'the error is described to the user' / Intent: 'users ... can determine what is wrong' — the description must match the actual error, not merely be fluent.
aspects.whyUncovered: Rule 36b590 only asks whether at least one indicator describes the cause or fix as a self-contained string; it never compares the message against the actual invalid value or the field's real constraint. Every ACT pass case uses a message that is correct for the contrived value (Age=0 -> 'must be at least 1'), and every ACT fail case fails for a STRUCTURAL reason (generic text, hidden, ambiguous label), never for a message that is fluent-but-wrong. The corpus narrowness 'static hardcoded errors not from real validation' means a plausible message is never pitted against a mismatched value. No automated checker reads the value+constraint+message for semantic agreement.

references.quote: The intent of this success criterion is to ensure that users are aware that an error has occurred and can determine what is wrong.
the user enters alphabetic characters or parentheses into their phone number field that only accepts numbers;
information about the nature and location of the input error is provided in text to enable the users to identify the problem

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: Telecom line-activation wizard, post-submit error state. Phone field is digits-only; the retained value is the all-digit string '12025550143'. The visible, aria-describedby-associated error reads 'Mobile number is invalid. Remove letters and parentheses from your phone number, then try again.' — describing a cause (letters/parentheses) that is factually absent from the value. The real defect (an 11-digit string for a 10-digit field) is never described.
pages.mechanism: Boilerplate mismatch: a fluent, field-identifying error asserts a cause that did not occur for THIS value. The value (all digits) does not exhibit the named defect (letters/parentheses), so the error misidentifies the nature of the error and the user cannot determine what is actually wrong.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: ACT 36b590 Expectation 2 is satisfied — a visible, in-tree indicator names the field and 'describes the cause or how to resolve it' as a self-contained string. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse confirm label, resolved aria-describedby, contrast, textbox role. No checker reads the entered value ('12025550143'), compares it to the field's stated 'digits only' constraint, and judges that the message names a cause the value does not exhibit. That value-vs-message agreement is a contextual semantic judgment.

citation.quote: The intent of this success criterion is to ensure that users are aware that an error has occurred and can determine what is wrong.

pages.scenario: Healthcare new-patient intake, post-submit error state. Date-of-birth field retains '03/14/2027', which already conforms exactly to MM/DD/YYYY. The visible associated error reads 'Date of birth is invalid. Please use the MM/DD/YYYY format.' — naming a constraint that is already satisfied. The actual error (a birth date set in the future) is never described, so the only guidance is a no-op fix.
pages.mechanism: Boilerplate mismatch: message names an already-satisfied constraint (format) while the truly-violated constraint (date must be in the past for a DOB) goes undescribed. Following the stated fix re-enters the same well-formatted date and is rejected again.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: 36b590 passes: a visible, field-identifying indicator describes 'how to resolve it' and is in the accessibility tree. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse see a labelled field, resolved describedby, fine contrast. No tool parses '03/14/2027', recognizes it already matches the demanded MM/DD/YYYY pattern, and reasons that the real defect (future DOB) is the undescribed one. Requires reading value + stated format + semantic domain ('date of birth' implies past) + message together.

citation.quote: the user enters a birth date 2 years in the future;

pages.scenario: SaaS 'set your password' screen, post-submit error state. Password field holds the 14-character value 'riverstonelake' (shown as 14 bullets); the visible aria-describedby error #pw-err reads 'Password must be at least 8 characters.' while the page's own requirements list marks 'At least 8 characters' as MET and 'At least one number' as the only UNMET rule.
pages.mechanism: Boilerplate mismatch: the message asserts a rule already satisfied (>=8 characters on a 14-character password value 'riverstonelake') instead of the rule actually failing (missing digit). The error line ('Password must be at least 8 characters.') and the requirements checklist directly contradict each other, since the checklist marks 'At least 8 characters' MET (green) and 'At least one number' UNMET (red).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: 36b590 passes: a visible field-identifying indicator describes a cause/fix and is in-tree. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse see labelled password field, resolved aria-describedby (to error + requirements list), fine contrast. No tool counts the value's 12 characters, compares to the 'at least 8' claim to see the rule is met, and cross-references the checklist to find the real unmet rule. Multi-element semantic reasoning over value + claim + checklist.

citation.quote: This SC requires that users be provided with information about the nature of the error, including the identity of the item in error.

pages.scenario: German-language (lang=de, de-DE) nonprofit donation page, post-submit error state. Amount field retains '1.234,56' — a perfectly valid de-DE currency string (dot = thousands sep, comma = decimal sep). The visible associated German error reads 'Der Betrag ist ungültig. Bitte geben Sie einen gültigen Betrag im Format 1234.56 ein.' demanding an en-US decimal format that is wrong for a German user and unnecessary for a value already valid in the page's declared locale.
pages.mechanism: Locale-aware boilerplate mismatch: the validation library is configured en-US, so it rejects a value that is valid in the page's declared de-DE locale, and the translated message prescribes a foreign-locale format exemplar ('1234.56'). The message asserts a false format defect; no real error exists.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: 36b590 passes (visible, in-tree indicator names the field and states a format). axe/WAVE/Lighthouse pass: lang='de' is a valid BCP-47 tag, label associated, describedby resolves, contrast fine. No tool parses locale-specific number grammar to see '1.234,56' is already valid de-DE and that the message prescribes en-US format. Judging value-vs-locale-vs-message agreement requires knowing German number formatting.

citation.quote: information that is provided by the user but that falls outside the required data format or allowed values.

pages.scenario: Hotel booking review, post-submit error state. Check-in '2026-08-01', check-out '2026-09-25' (55 nights — check-out IS after check-in). The check-out field's visible associated error reads 'Check-out date must be after your check-in date.' — a relation that already holds. The form's own visible policy states 'Maximum stay: 30 nights'; the real, undescribed error is that a 55-night stay exceeds that cap.
pages.mechanism: Relational boilerplate mismatch: message asserts an ordering constraint already satisfied (out > in) while the actually-violated threshold constraint (stay <= 30 nights, stated separately in the policy) goes undescribed. Acting on the false guidance makes the real problem worse.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: 36b590 passes: a visible field-identifying indicator describes a cause and is in-tree. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse see two labelled date inputs in fieldset/legend, resolved aria-describedby, fine contrast. No tool compares the two date VALUES to confirm out>in (making the message false), then cross-references the separately-stated 30-night policy to find the real violation. Multi-field relational + policy reasoning over values and prose.

citation.quote: the user enters a bid that is below the previous bid or the minimum bid increment.

pages.scenario: E-commerce checkout shipping step, post-submit error state. ZIP field retains the value the user typed, '9021' (four digits). The visible associated server error reads 'ZIP code 90210 not found in our database. Please check the code and try again.' — quoting '90210', a five-digit value the user never entered (a normalizer padded a trailing zero before lookup). The real defect (ZIP too short) is never described and the quoted value contradicts the field's own retained value.
pages.mechanism: Phantom-value boilerplate mismatch: the message quotes a value (90210) different from what the user typed and what the field shows (9021), and never describes the actual defect (incomplete 4-digit ZIP). The announced field value and the value named in the error differ, which the user cannot reconcile.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: 36b590 passes — and the message is, if anything, MORE descriptive than the pass examples because it quotes a code. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse see labelled field, resolved aria-describedby, fine contrast. No tool extracts the ZIP quoted inside the message (90210), compares it to the field's retained value (9021), and concludes the message names a phantom value while omitting the real (too-short) defect. A value-inside-message vs field-value comparison.

citation.quote: the user enters a non existent zip or postal code;

pages.scenario: CONTROL / discrimination foil (PASS). Event-ticketing phone field, post-submit error state — near-identical component to case-01. The retained value is '(202) 555-CALL', which genuinely contains parentheses, a space, a dash, and the letters C-A-L-L. The field is digits-only and the visible associated error reads 'Phone number must contain only digits. Remove the letters, spaces, and parentheses (for example, enter 2025550143).' — a cause that DID occur and correctly describes this value's actual defect.
pages.mechanism: No defect: the described cause matches the entered value's actual error (non-digit characters in a digits-only field) and gives a concrete corrected example, so the user can determine what is wrong and fix it. SC 3.3.1 satisfied. Included to force value-vs-message discrimination rather than a blanket 'phone-digit error = fail' heuristic.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Automated tools cannot make the value-vs-message discrimination at all — they never read the value against the message — so they pass case-01 and case-07 identically. Here that absence happens to coincide with the correct human verdict (pass), which is exactly why a foil is needed: only a human reasoning about value-constraint-message agreement can tell that case-01's message is false for its value while case-07's is true for its value.

aspects.title: Post-submit page suppresses the error: form silently re-displayed (or shows a neutral/success banner) after a real validation failure — trigger-and-observe failure of NO indicator
aspects.plain: After a failed submission the form just reappears with your bad input (or even a success banner) and no error message, so you don't know the submission failed or why.
aspects.description: The SC's most-emphasized procedural limb is trigger-and-observe: submit invalid input, then check whether an error is conveyed in text. The failure the Understanding calls out FIRST is re-displaying the form 'without providing any hint that the submission failed'. On a self-contained page this is staged as the post-submit STATE: the page representing 'the user submitted invalid input and the server bounced it' shows the form again with the bad value retained but NO error message — or worse, shows a neutral/green confirmation that does not mention the failure. A tool inspecting this page finds a form, finds no error indicator, and returns inapplicable/vacuous-pass (like ACT Passed Example 3), while a human who understands the page is the RESULT of a failed submission sees the violation. Distinguishing 'a benign blank form' from 'a post-failure page that suppressed the error' is a contextual judgment driven by page-state cues (retained bad value, submitted indicator, mismatched success banner).
aspects.scLimb: 'If an input error is automatically detected ...' (the trigger) and Intent: 'it is not sufficient to only re-display the form without providing any hint that the submission failed.'
aspects.whyUncovered: Every ACT page is the already-errored state with a hard-coded span; none represents a submission RESULT, and the 'no indicator -> vacuous pass' branch (Passed Example 3) is treated as legitimately passing. There is no case where the ABSENCE of an indicator is itself the failure because an error genuinely occurred. The corpus is 100% static with type='button', so it never submits, validates, or detects an error dynamically — the entire trigger-and-observe limb is unexercised. An automated checker cannot infer that a no-error page is the aftermath of a failed submission; only a human reading the page-state context can.

references.quote: In the case of an unsuccessful form submission, it is not sufficient to only re-display the form without providing any hint that the submission failed.
This is a trigger-and-observe test — the tester must actively cause an error (submit invalid input) and then check whether the resulting error is conveyed in text. It is not a static inspection.
Attempt to submit the form and/or move to the next page. Determine whether the error is identified and described in text.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: City of Glenmore facility-booking confirmation page shown after the server rejected the request (Event date '2019-03-02' breaks the printed 'at least 14 days in advance' rule); the form is silently re-displayed under the success-sounding heading 'Request logged' with the past date retained and no error message anywhere.
pages.mechanism: Post-submit state: the server bounced the booking because Event date '2019-03-02' violates the printed 'at least 14 days in advance' rule, but re-displayed the form under the result-sounding heading 'Request logged' with the out-of-range date retained and ZERO error text anywhere. No field carries required/min/max/pattern, so nothing is computed :invalid and AT announces every field as a normal text box; the 'Request logged' heading actively implies success (G83), so the silent re-display gives no hint the submission failed.
pages.selectorNote: Event-date input holding past 2019-03-02; redisplayed form, no error element (orig prose mismatch)
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The form is flawless to a static scanner — every input has a programmatic label, markup is valid, contrast passes, and there is NO error element to evaluate. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse have no model of 'this page is the aftermath of a failed submission'; with no error indicator present they treat 3.3.1 as inapplicable / a vacuous pass (ACT Passed Example 3). Catching it requires reading page-state context (success-styled heading contradicted by retained out-of-range Age and empty required Email) and inferring a suppressed error — human judgment.

citation.quote: In the case of an unsuccessful form submission, it is not sufficient to only re-display the form without providing any hint that the submission failed. The error must be indicated in text.

pages.scenario: Folio & Thread e-commerce checkout (Step 3 of 3, Payment) bounced after the gateway rejected a 13-digit card number ('4716 1234 5678 9', too short) and empty CVC; the theme injected a green role=status banner 'Thank you — your order is being processed' above the re-displayed payment form with the invalid card retained. Variant B (mismatched success banner). HEAD-prevalence; content-domain e-commerce/checkout, Shopify-Dawn-style theme.
pages.mechanism: An input error was automatically detected (the gateway rejected the card) but the only status text on the page is a role=status banner that announces SUCCESS; a screen-reader user hears 'your order is being processed', concludes the purchase completed, and leaves. The retained 13-digit card and empty CVC are the only failure evidence and neither is described as an error — the error is not merely omitted but overwritten with a false success message.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The banner is a valid div role=status with high-contrast green text; the card input has a proper label, valid markup, and an accessible name. Nothing is structurally wrong and there is no error element to lint. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse cannot read 'your order is being processed' and judge it false, cannot compute that a 13-digit string is too short to be a card, and cannot know the payment was declined. Distinguishing a legitimate confirmation page from a failure dressed as success requires semantic + visual judgment.

citation.quote: Fill out a form, deliberately enter user input that falls outside the required format or values

pages.scenario: Northvale Health patient-portal sign-in re-displayed after a rejected credential check: the username is retained, the password field is correctly cleared, the page title is just 'Sign in', and there is no message that the previous attempt failed. The post-failure page is indistinguishable from a first, fresh visit. HEAD-prevalence; content-domain healthcare/patient portal, authentication form, security-checklist persona.
pages.mechanism: An input error was automatically detected (credentials rejected) but conveyed in zero text. A screen-reader user re-lands on a page announced 'Sign in' with a filled username and empty password and has no cue anything was rejected — no role=alert, no error in the title, no status text — so they may re-press the button or assume the page is broken. A generic 'Incorrect username or password' would satisfy both security and 3.3.1; total silence does not.
pages.selectorNote: Retained username after failed login; password cleared, no failure message anywhere
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The login form is exemplary — labelled inputs, masked password, valid markup, a real submit button — and there is no error markup to evaluate. A scanner cannot tell this render is the aftermath of a failed authentication rather than a first visit; the only machine-visible tell ('username retained + password blank') is also a normal initial-state pattern. Inferring that a real error occurred and was left undescribed requires reasoning about page state.

citation.quote:
This is a **trigger-and-observe** test — the tester must actively *cause* an error
> (submit invalid input) and then check whether the resulting error is conveyed in text. It is not a static
> inspection.

pages.scenario: Brightwater Rivers Trust donation page bounced after the amount was submitted as $0.00 (below the stated $5 minimum) AND the required 'How often?' frequency radio group was left unselected; a warm 'Thank you for your generosity' banner sits above the re-displayed form with the bad amount retained and the radio group still empty and unflagged. Variant B with a second omitted required field. MID/long-tail; content-domain nonprofit/donation, fieldset radio group + currency input, fundraising-CMS persona.
pages.mechanism: Two input errors were automatically detected (amount below minimum; required frequency omitted) but described in zero error text; the only status message is 'Thank you for your generosity', which AT hears as confirmation the gift went through. Tabbing the form, AT meets a required radio group with no selection and no announcement that leaving it empty was an error, and an amount of '0.00' with no out-of-range indication.
pages.primarySelector: div.thanks (false success) over fieldset > input[name="freq"] (none checked) + input#amount[value="0.00"]
pages.selectorNote: Amount 0.00 below $5 minimum, retained unflagged; false thanks banner above
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The amount field has a real label and a valid value; the frequency choices are a textbook fieldset/legend radio group with labelled radios, so axe sees a correctly grouped, correctly named control, and 'no radio checked' is a legal state, not a lint error. The thank-you banner is valid visible text and there is no error markup. A scanner cannot know the gift was declined, that $0.00 is below the stated minimum, or that the empty required group is an error in this post-submit context.

citation.quote: An "input error" includes:

pages.scenario: Cedar Mutual Auto 3-step quote wizard silently advanced to 'Step 3 of 3, Review & buy' after an invalid ZIP ('0', too short) on Step 1 was swallowed — Step 2 (coverage options) was skipped because the rating engine had no usable ZIP. The review summary freezes the invalid ZIP '0' as read-only text and shows a placeholder premium '$—'; no error text appears. Cross-page silent-advance variant. LONG-TAIL; content-domain insurance quote wizard, APG stepper + dl review, lazy-validation persona.
pages.mechanism: An input error was automatically detected (the ZIP was unusable, which is why Step 2 was skipped and the premium could not be computed) but conveyed in zero text; AT is told 'Step 3 of 3, Review & buy', reads a clean-sounding summary, and reaches a 'Confirm & buy' button with no announcement that the ZIP is invalid or that a step was skipped. The erroring field is not even on the current page (shown read-only), so even sighted users can miss it.
pages.selectorNote: Review summary freezing invalid ZIP '0'; wizard jumped to Step 3 with no error
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every element is well formed — the stepper is a labelled ol with aria-current, the summary is a semantic dl, the email field has a real label, and the values are plain text — and there is no error markup to lint. A scanner cannot know this is the wrong step to be on (Step 2 was skipped), that the displayed ZIP '0' is invalid, or that an error on a prior step was swallowed; those are stateful, cross-page facts requiring reconstruction of the wizard flow.

citation.quote: Attempt to **submit** the form and/or move to the next page.

pages.scenario: CONTROL (discrimination boundary): the same Riverbend Library membership flow as case-01, but the genuine SUCCESS result after VALID input (Age 34, a real email). The server accepted the data and rendered a true confirmation — a read-only summary of the accepted values, a real membership number (RVB-2026-08831), and next steps — with no editable form re-displayed and legitimately no error message. Must be judged passed while case-01..05 are failed.
pages.mechanism: 3.3.1 applies only when an input error is automatically detected; here none was — the submission succeeded — so the absence of an error message is correct, required behaviour (ACT Passed Example 3). The page-state cues all point to genuine success: valid accepted values, a real reference number, no editable form to re-submit, and honest success copy conveyed in text. This is the legitimate counterpart that separates a benign result page from a suppressed-failure page.
pages.selectorNote: Read-only accepted values (Age 34) on genuine success control page; correctly no error
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: This case tests discrimination, not detection: it has the same 'no error indicator on a post-submit page' surface that automated tools read as a pass. The risk is the opposite — a context-blind heuristic that flags 'post-submit page + no error' would wrongly fail it. A correct human/LLM judgment uses the page-state cues (valid accepted values, real reference number, no re-displayed editable form, honest success copy) to confirm legitimate success and PASS it, while still failing case-01..05 where the same cue-types point to a hidden failure.

citation.quote: The objective of this technique is to reduce the effort required for users to confirm that an action, such as submitting a web form, was completed successfully. This can be accomplished by providing consistently presented feedback that explicitly indicates success of an action, rather than requiring a user to navigate through content to discover if the action was successful.

aspects.title: Inline error message is visually placed next to the WRONG field, with no programmatic association to check
aspects.plain: An error message sits visually next to the wrong field with no programmatic link, so you read it against the field it appears to belong to and get misled about what's in error.
aspects.description: A self-contained page renders a descriptive error message physically below / next to a field, but the message's text refers to a DIFFERENT field than the one it visually sits under, and there is no aria-describedby tying it to any control (so no programmatic association exists to evaluate). A sighted user reads the message against the field it appears to annotate and is misled about which item is in error. Because identification by visual proximity ('errors inline ... next to the specific fields') is an explicitly sufficient method under the SC, the message passes every programmatic facet of 36b590 — non-empty, descriptive, visible, in the tree, identification 'through presentation'. The only way to detect the violation is to read the message text, read the label of the field it visually adjoins, and notice they disagree — a visual-spatial + semantic judgment.
aspects.scLimb: 'the item that is in error is identified' — identification via presentation/proximity must point at the field actually in error.
aspects.whyUncovered: ACT Failed Example 5 fails only because two fields share IDENTICAL labels (a name-collision the rule reasons about via label text); it never tests a message whose text clearly names field A while being positioned next to field B. Rule 36b590 treats 'through presentation' (proximity) as a valid identification path but never builds a case where presentation actively points at the wrong target, and it has no spatial model of which field a message visually adjoins. The corpus narrowness 'contrived id failures no wrong field' explicitly excludes this. Automated checkers cannot judge visual adjacency vs. message semantics.

references.quote: it may be more appropriate to show errors inline, with error messages next to the specific fields that are in error

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: E-commerce checkout payment row (Card number / Expiry / CVV) in a flex row. The CVV value '12' is the truly-invalid input, but the error 'CVV must be exactly 3 digits.' is rendered in the message slot under the Card number field, and the Card number input carries the red invalid border. No aria-describedby anywhere.
pages.mechanism: Identification rests solely on presentation (proximity) because no aria-describedby/for-id linkage exists. The error span sits in the Card-number field block while its text names CVV, so by visual proximity the message identifies the wrong field; the field actually in error (CVV) appears unflagged. SC 3.3.1 'the item that is in error is identified' fails because presentation points at Card number, not CVV.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The error is non-empty, visible, in the accessibility tree, and descriptive, so every facet axe/WAVE/Lighthouse can check passes; with no aria-describedby there is no association to flag and 36b590 allows identification 'through presentation'. Detecting the fault requires reading the message to learn it names CVV, computing which field the span visually adjoins (Card number), and noticing they disagree — a visual-spatial + semantic judgment no scanner performs.

pages.scenario: Government SNAP-benefits two-column grid form. Row 1 has First name (left, filled 'Maria') and Last name (right, filled). After a failed submit the error 'First name is required.' is placed in the right-column cell directly under the Last name input, and Last name (not First name) gets aria-invalid=true. No aria-describedby links the message to any control.
pages.mechanism: No programmatic association exists, so identification depends on presentation. The error span occupies the Last-name grid cell (and the wrong input carries aria-invalid), so its column position points at Last name while its text names First name — which is filled and valid. Neither the position nor the misplaced aria-invalid matches the field the text names, so the item in error is not identified.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The error text is present, visible, descriptive; the form has proper labels and a role=alert summary, so structural scans pass. Tools have no spatial model of the two-column grid, cannot read the message to learn it names First name, and cannot tell that its column position (and the misplaced aria-invalid) point at a different field. Catching it needs human reading plus spatial reasoning.

pages.scenario: Aerolinks round-trip itinerary (PDX <=> DEN): two legs (Outbound / Return) each labelled 'Travel date' with no aria-describedby, where the generic error 'Travel date is invalid.' is painted under the valid Outbound input (2026-07-14, red-bordered) while the genuinely-invalid Return date (2025-03-02, in the past) gets an empty message slot.
pages.mechanism: Two legs each use the IDENTICAL visible label 'Travel date' and an identical empty .msg slot, with no aria-describedby. The generic error 'Travel date is invalid.' is rendered into the FIRST .msg slot (under the OUTBOUND input, whose date 2026-07-14 is valid and which carries the red .flagged border), while the leg actually in error (Return, 2025-03-02, a past date) shows no message. Identification rests on presentation/proximity, which points at the wrong (valid) leg; the duplicate labels mean the text alone cannot disambiguate either, so the item in error is not identified.
pages.selectorNote: Return-leg input (real error, 2025-03-02) whose message slot is empty; error misplaced under outbound
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The error is non-empty, visible, accessible-tree-present and descriptive; there is no aria-describedby to flag; and in the DOM the error is correctly adjacent to its field, so source-order checks pass. The fault exists only after CSS grid layout, in pixel geometry. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse do not compute post-layout bounding-box adjacency of grid-placed items against message semantics, so the DOM-vs-visual divergence is invisible.

pages.scenario: RTL Arabic (lang=ar dir=rtl) membership address form. A 2-column x 3-row CSS grid holds Postal code (column 1, value 11564, flagged red) and City (column 2, empty). The postal-code error is placed by explicit coordinates into grid-column 2 row 3 — the City column's message slot — so on screen it sits under the empty City input. No aria-describedby.
pages.mechanism: No programmatic association, so identification depends on presentation. In the DOM the error is authored right after the postal input (source-order pairing correct), but explicit grid-column:2 placement plus the RTL column flip render it beneath the City field. A sighted Arabic reader reads a postal-code message against the City field; the City field is empty while the flagged postal field holds a valid 5-digit value. Rendered presentation identifies the wrong field.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The message is non-empty, visible, accessible-tree-present, descriptive, and lang is valid BCP-47; with no aria-describedby there is nothing to flag and DOM order keeps the error adjacent to its field. The fault appears only after grid layout and the bidi/RTL column flip, in rendered geometry. Scanners do not compute post-layout/post-bidi bounding boxes nor read the Arabic text to learn which field it names.

pages.scenario: Healthcare patient-portal blood-pressure intake. Side-by-side Systolic (value 118, normal) and Diastolic (value 135, out of range) number inputs. The error 'Diastolic must be between 40 and 120 mmHg.' is placed in the Systolic column under the Systolic input, and the Systolic input carries the red alert border; the out-of-range Diastolic has no message. No aria-describedby.
pages.mechanism: No programmatic association, so identification rests on presentation. The error sits in the Systolic column (and the wrong input is reddened) while its text names Diastolic; the genuinely out-of-range value is the Diastolic. A clinician reads a diastolic-range message against the normal systolic field and could correct the wrong number — presentation identifies the wrong vital sign, so the item in error is not identified.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The message is present, visible, accessible-tree-present, and even states the valid range; there is no aria-describedby to flag. A scanner cannot read 'Diastolic' and compare it to the column the span sits in, nor know that 135 (not 118) is out of range. Determining that the message's position points at a different vital than its text and data is a semantic + spatial + domain judgment.

pages.scenario: BOUNDARY PASS. Community-garden waitlist form with stacked Full name (valid), Email (value 'priya.nair@', invalid), Phone (valid). The error 'Email address is incomplete — add the part after the @.' is rendered inside the Email field's own block directly under the Email input, which carries the red invalid border. There is NO aria-describedby — identification rests entirely on presentation, done correctly.
pages.mechanism: Structurally identical to the failing siblings (distinct stacked fields, inline red error, no aria-describedby), but proximity is correct: the message's rendered position and its text both name the Email field, and Email is the field actually in error. Visual adjacency and message semantics agree and point at the correct field, satisfying identification 'through presentation'. Programmatic association is not required by SC 3.3.1.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A static scan sees the same thing on every page in this aspect: present, visible, descriptive error text and no aria-describedby to flag. The only thing that flips pass vs fail is whether the message's rendered position points at the field its text names and that is actually in error — a human visual-spatial + semantic judgment. This passing boundary proves the discriminator is the spatial/semantic match, not 'missing ARIA' and not 'inline errors are bad'.

aspects.title: Top-of-form error summary lists fields/causes/counts that do not correspond to the page's actually-flagged fields (summary-vs-state incoherence)
aspects.plain: A top-of-form error summary lists fields, counts, or links that don't match the fields actually flagged on the page, so you can't reliably tell what needs fixing.
aspects.description: Following G83/G84/G85's 'text description at the top of the page', a self-contained page shows a top-of-form error summary block — descriptive, visible, in the tree — but the summary's CONTENT is inconsistent with the rest of the page: it lists a field that is not present, omits a field that is visibly flagged, states a count ('2 errors') that disagrees with the number of flagged fields, names a different field than the one displaying an inline error, or contains anchor links that point to the wrong control. Each individual statement may be a fluent error description (passing 36b590 at the message level), but the summary as a whole misidentifies the items in error, so the user cannot reliably 'determine what is wrong'. Judging this requires cross-referencing the summary list against the actual form fields and their flagged states — a holistic reconciliation no rule performs.
aspects.scLimb: 'the item that is in error is identified' applied to the summary method — the aggregate text-at-top description must agree with the page's actual error state.
aspects.whyUncovered: ACT has exactly one top-of-form-list pass (Passed Example 2) where the summary is perfectly coherent, and one shared-message fail (Failed Example 1) that fails only for genericness. The corpus never builds a summary that is internally detailed yet INCONSISTENT with the flagged state — its narrowness 'single form one error pages no multi error summaries' captures that multi-error reconciliation is absent. 36b590 evaluates each indicator's describing text independently and has no notion of summary/field agreement. A checker can verify an anchor target exists but cannot judge whether the summary's claims match which fields are truly in error.

references.quote: indicates clearly in text at the top of the page that there were input errors. The text describes the nature of the error(s) and clearly indicates which field had the problem so the user can easily navigate to it
A single form field error indicator can be related to multiple test targets. For example, an error message at the top of a form can list all the form fields that are required and are empty.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: GOV.UK council-tax reduction form: top-of-form red error summary announces 'We found 2 errors' and lists Full name + Email, but both render filled and unflagged; the only field actually in error (Telephone, value 'ring me weekdays') has a red border, inline message and aria-invalid=true and is never named. Wrong count AND wrong fields named.
pages.mechanism: The role=alert summary enumerates two fields (Full name, Email) that carry no error state, and omits the single field that bears aria-invalid=true (Telephone). The summary's stated count (2) and named set disagree with the page's actual flagged set (1 / Telephone), so the aggregate text-at-top fails to identify the item that is in error even though each sentence is individually fluent.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse confirm the summary is a valid visible live region, each list item is a fluent specific message tied to a real label (36b590 passes per message), and the genuinely-flagged input is correctly wired. No rule builds the set of fields bearing aria-invalid/red borders and reconciles it against the set the summary enumerates, so the count-and-membership mismatch needs a human cross-reference.

pages.scenario: Restaurant catering-enquiry form: red role=alert summary lists three errors (Event date, City, Number of guests). Event date and Number of guests are genuinely flagged below, but the middle line 'City is required' names a field that does not exist anywhere on the form — the page collects a single free-text 'Venue name & full address' textarea with no City input, label, or control.
pages.mechanism: A summary line asserts an input error for a 'City' field that is absent from the DOM. There is no element whose accessible name is City, so the user cannot locate or correct the claimed error; the phantom line gives a false 'identity of the item in error' and erodes trust in the valid lines.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The phantom line is plain prose with no broken for/id pairing, no empty attribute, no orphan reference; the summary is a valid live region and the two real errors are correctly wired. Detecting that a natural-language summary claim refers to a form field that does not exist in the DOM requires parsing the claim and confirming no corresponding control is present — a semantic judgment outside any static rule.

pages.scenario: Healthcare new-patient registration: red role=alert summary declares 'There is 1 error in this form' and lists only Date of birth, but three fields render red with inline messages and aria-invalid=true — Date of birth (invalid date), Mobile number (too short), and Postcode (invalid). The summary undercounts the real error state by two and omits two flagged fields.

A user trusting the count fixes one field and resubmits, blindsided by the two never surfaced; the aggregate description misrepresents the number and identity of items in error.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every flagged field passes 36b590 (aria-invalid + associated descriptive message) and the summary is a valid visible live region — no malformed markup. No checker tallies the aria-invalid/inline-flagged fields and compares that count and membership to the summary's asserted count; that cross-tabulation is a human reconciliation.

pages.scenario: University admissions application wizard, step 3 Contact details: red role=alert summary lists two G139-style jump links. Both fields (Email holding 'amara.k(at)mail', empty Telephone) are genuinely flagged, but the link labelled 'Fix your email address' has href=#phone, so activating it lands focus on the Telephone field instead of email; both links in fact point to #phone.
pages.mechanism: A summary jump link whose text identifies the email error navigates (via href=#phone) to the Telephone control. The link target does not match the control the link's text describes, so the G139 error-jump mechanism misdirects a keyboard/screen-reader user to the wrong field.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A fragment/anchor checker confirms #phone resolves to a real element — no broken link to flag; both flagged fields are correctly wired and 36b590 passes; the link text is fluent. The failure is a target-vs-purpose mismatch: a link labelled for the email error navigates to the telephone control. Judging whether each link points to the right control requires matching link text to the field its href reaches.

pages.scenario: Credit-union online-banking enrolment: red role=alert summary states 'Password must be at least 10 characters and include a number', but the Password field is valid (green, aria-invalid=false, meets the rule). The only flagged field is its sibling Confirm password (aria-invalid=true, red, 'does not match the password you entered'). The summary blames the wrong sibling and describes a different cause.
pages.mechanism: The summary names and describes Password (which is valid and aria-invalid=false) while the field truly in error is Confirm password (aria-invalid=true) with a mismatch cause. The aggregate identifies the wrong member of a near-identical field pair and the wrong cause, so the user is sent to a field the page itself says is fine.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: 'Password' and 'Confirm password' are both valid distinct labels (no duplicate-label or malformed-markup signal); the summary is a valid live region with a fluent message; the flagged Confirm field has aria-invalid + associated message so 36b590 passes. Recognising the summary points at the valid sibling rather than the flagged one requires reading both near-identical labels and each field's actual validity state.

pages.scenario: Home-insurance quote wizard, step 2 Property: red role=alert summary says 'Please fix 2 things: Country must be selected. Year the property was built must be a 4-digit year'. Year built is genuinely flagged (value 'nineteen eighty'), but the Country control is a disabled <select> pre-set to 'United Kingdom' (locked because the product is UK-only) — greyed, non-focusable, no aria-invalid — and could not have produced input nor be corrected.
pages.mechanism: The summary attributes an input error to a disabled, pre-set control. A disabled control is not submitted by the browser and cannot be edited by the user, so it could not have produced a wrong value and cannot be fixed; labelling it 'in error' misidentifies the item and demands an impossible action, defeating the top-of-form description.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A disabled <select> with a label and a pre-selected option is entirely valid markup; the summary is a valid visible live region; the real error field is correctly wired so 36b590 passes. No structural rule encodes that a summary should not attribute an input error to a disabled, non-editable control — recognising the contradiction requires knowing disabled controls are not submitted and cannot be user-corrected, then matching that against the summary's demand.

pages.scenario: CONTROL (passing): flight-booking Passenger details step. Red role=alert summary states 'There are 2 problems' and lists exactly two G139 jump links — Email (→#email) and Date of birth (→#dob). The page flags exactly those two fields with matching aria-invalid, anchors, and inline message wording; the two valid fields (Given names, Passport number) are correctly not mentioned. Count, membership, link targets, and wording all reconcile.
pages.mechanism: Every item the summary names is genuinely in error, every item in error is named, each jump link reaches the control its text describes, and each line's wording matches that field's inline programmatically-associated message. The aggregate description agrees with the page's actual state, so the items in error are identified and described in text.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Automated tools have no model of summary↔state agreement, so they cannot confirm coherence any more than detect incoherence — they would treat this page identically to the failing cases (no finding). Its correctness is only verifiable by the same human reconciliation: build the flagged set, compare it to what the summary enumerates and links to, and check the wording matches.

citation.quote: the form is re-displayed with a text description at the top informing which mandatory fields were omitted. Each omitted mandatory field is also identified using a text label so that the user does not have to return to the list at the top of the form to find the omitted fields.

aspects.title: Error is signalled ONLY by visual styling (red border / colour / icon glyph) with no error meaning in text anywhere on the page
aspects.plain: A field is flagged as wrong using only colour, a red border, or an icon, with no words anywhere saying an error occurred, so a screen-reader user never learns there's a problem.
aspects.description: A field is clearly flagged as in error by purely visual means — a red border, a red/yellow background, a red exclamation-triangle icon, a red CSS glyph, a reddened label with a trailing asterisk — but there is no text anywhere stating that an error occurred or what it is (no message string, no alt/aria-label conveying error, no visually-hidden text). The SC explicitly allows colour/icon IN ADDITION to text but forbids it as the SOLE indicator: 'The error must be indicated in text.' Detecting this requires a human to look at the rendered page, recognise that the ONLY conveyance of the error is visual styling, and confirm the error meaning is absent from text. A CSS-only red border or a decorative icon with empty alt typically does not register to tools as an 'error indicator' at all, so the page passes vacuously while a sighted user is plainly being signalled an error that is never stated in words.
aspects.scLimb: identification/description must be 'in text' — the SOLE-cue-is-visual prohibition: colour/image is acceptable only in addition to a text description.
aspects.whyUncovered: The entire ACT corpus delivers errors as plain text spans; there is NO case with an icon-only or colour-only indicator, and the narrowness 'no color only cue' confirms it. 36b590's Applicability is triggered by 'form field error indicators' and its expectations check the DESCRIBING text — a page whose only error signal is a red border may surface no textual indicator for the rule to evaluate, so it passes vacuously, masking the real violation. Automated colour-only detection (F81) is unreliable and cannot judge whether the field's error meaning is conveyed in text elsewhere; the rendered-vs-text reconciliation needs human visual judgment.

references.quote: It is perfectly acceptable to indicate the error in other ways such as through the use of an image, color, or other visual indicator, in addition to the text description.
it is not sufficient simply to indicate that a field has an error by putting an asterisk on its label or turning the label red. A text description of the problem should be provided.
the form field that caused the error is indicated by red text only, without an additional non-color indication that the field caused an error.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: Riverside Adult Learning course-enrolment form re-rendered after a failed submit; the 'Number of places to reserve' field input#seats holds value '6', which the server rejected as over the class cap of 4, and wears a 2px red border + red-tinted background (class 'flagged') as the SOLE error cue. No message, no aria-invalid, no hidden text anywhere conveys that an error occurred.
pages.mechanism: Error conveyed only by CSS border (2px solid red) + red-tinted background (input.flagged), which are not part of the accessible name and are never announced; the field is plain type=text with no aria-invalid and no constraint, so a screen reader hears 'Number of places to reserve, edit, 6' identically to a valid field, and the error is not 'in text' as SC 3.3.1 requires.
pages.selectorNote: Errored seats field; .flagged is rendered statically at load (red border, no text)
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A red border + tint is one of the most common decorative styles on the web; axe/WAVE/Lighthouse have no rule that treats it as an error indicator, so there is nothing to flag. ACT 36b590 is triggered by error TEXT and finds none, passing vacuously. Recognising the red box as the sole error signal and confirming the meaning is absent from text requires human rendered-visual judgment.

citation.quote: it is not sufficient to only re-display the form without providing any hint that the submission failed. The error must be indicated in text.

pages.scenario: Healthcare patient-intake form (step 1 of 3); an impossible date of birth (31/02/1991) is flagged ONLY by a red exclamation-triangle SVG image with alt='' beside the field. No nearby/hidden text, aria-label, or aria-invalid conveys the error.
pages.mechanism: The error-bearing icon is marked decorative (alt=''), so AT skips it entirely; the impossible date is announced with nothing wrong. The error meaning lives solely in a picture whose text alternative was emptied, so it is neither in text nor in the accessibility tree.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: alt='' is exactly what linters want for non-informative images, so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse REWARD it and would only flag a missing alt. Tools cannot tell that THIS icon is informative (the error indicator) rather than decorative, nor confirm the error meaning is absent from all other text. The distinction is inherently visual-semantic.

citation.quote: It is perfectly acceptable to indicate the error in other ways such as through the use of an image, color, or other visual indicator, in addition to the text description.

pages.scenario: Pennine Mutual car-insurance quote form re-rendered after the server rejected the postcode 'SW1A 9ZZ XX'; the input#postcode.flagged shows ONLY a red border + a red error glyph rendered as a CSS background-image (inline SVG), with no message, no asterisk, no aria-invalid, and no error text anywhere.
pages.mechanism: On the bounced submit the server adds class='flagged' to the postcode input, which paints ONLY a 2px red border plus a red round error glyph drawn as a CSS background-image (inline-SVG data URI) at the field's right edge. There is no message, no asterisk, no pseudo-element, no aria-invalid, and no text of any kind. A CSS background-image never enters the accessibility tree, so a screen reader announces 'Postcode, edit, SW1A 9ZZ XX' identically to a valid field — the error is conveyed by visual styling alone, not in text as SC 3.3.1 requires.
pages.selectorNote: Errored postcode field; .flagged present at load paints red border + SVG glyph only
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every control has a properly associated label and contrast is fine, so structural scans pass. A label colour change is not an error signal any tool recognises, and ::after content is invisible to most accessibility-tree inspection. No tool infers 'this red asterisk means required AND in error, stated nowhere in text.' ACT 36b590 sees no error text and does not fire.

citation.quote: When users fail to provide input for any mandatory form fields, information is provided in text to enable the users to identify which fields were omitted.

pages.scenario: Bank reset-password screen redisplayed after rejecting a reused password; the field shows a red outline + a red CSS ::before key glyph and carries aria-invalid='true', but emits NO error text, aria-errormessage, or aria-describedby — nothing in words states what is wrong or why.
pages.mechanism: aria-invalid='true' conveys only THAT the field is invalid, not WHAT the error is; SC 3.3.1 requires the error be described in text. There is no message and no aria-errormessage/aria-describedby to read, and the red ::before key is CSS generated content outside the accessibility tree, so a non-visual user learns at most 'invalid' with no reason.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Because aria-invalid='true' is present, a checker sees a programmatically-exposed error state and considers error handling 'present' — it does not complain that handling is missing. No automated rule verifies a textual DESCRIPTION of the error exists and is tied to the field; that is a semantic judgment of meaning. The red key (::before) is invisible to accessibility-tree scans.

citation.quote: This SC requires that users be provided with information about the nature of the error, including the identity of the item in error.

pages.scenario: French bistro reservation form re-rendered after no seating choice was made; the required radio group is flagged ONLY by reddening its <legend> ('Préférence de salle'). No text says a choice is required or that the group errored; no aria-required/aria-invalid.
pages.mechanism: The legend's red color is not announced and is not part of any accessible name; a screen reader entering the group hears 'Préférence de salle, Terrasse radio button not checked 1 of 3' exactly as an optional non-errored group would sound. The error/requirement is conveyed by colour alone, never in text.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The group is correctly built (real fieldset/legend, labelled radios, keyboard operable) so structural scans pass. Colour-only detection (F81) is unreliable, and even noticing the red legend cannot tell whether red MEANS error/required or is brand theming. No required attribute or message exists for a rule to read, so ACT 36b590 passes vacuously.

citation.quote: A user submits an online form and leaves a required field blank, resulting in an error. The form field that caused the error is indicated by red text only, without an additional non-color indication that the field caused an error.

pages.scenario: Corporate intranet expense-claim editor; a £139 meal line breaching the £75 cap is flagged ONLY by a yellow-highlighted <fieldset> (the firm's 'highlight in yellow' convention) with the intended descriptive text omitted. No message, hidden text, or aria state.
pages.mechanism: The fieldset's yellow background is never announced and is not part of any accessible name; a screen reader reads Line 2 identically to the valid lines ('Line 2 Meals, Amount GBP, 139.00'), so a non-visual reviewer cannot learn the line breached the cap. The error meaning is carried by a background colour alone, never in text.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The markup is exemplary (real fieldsets/legends/labels, good contrast on the yellow) and a container background colour is never treated as an error indicator. No tool reads the amounts, applies the £75 business rule, notices the yellow fieldset, and infers a cap breach stated nowhere in text. ACT 36b590 finds no error text and does not fire.

citation.quote: In addition to describing the error and providing a unique character to make it easy to search for the fields, the fields are highlighted in yellow to make it easier to visually search for them as well.

pages.scenario: CONTROL (discrimination boundary): auction 'place a bid' form with the IDENTICAL red border + tint on the email field, but the error is also identified and described in text ('Email address is not valid.') tied via aria-describedby, with aria-invalid='true' and the decorative icon aria-hidden. Should pass.
pages.mechanism: The aria-describedby association surfaces the message and aria-invalid surfaces the state, so a screen reader hears 'Email address, invalid entry, ..., Email address is not valid.' The error is identified and described IN TEXT; the red styling/icon are now acceptable ADDITIONAL cues (icon aria-hidden so it is not double-announced).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Tools cannot reliably distinguish this passing page from the failing ones because they never recognised the red styling as an error indicator at all; case-01 and case-07 look structurally similar to a scanner. The discriminating signal — whether a conforming text description tied to the field exists and actually describes the error — is a semantic check requiring human judgment.

citation.quote: It is perfectly acceptable to indicate the error in other ways such as through the use of an image, color, or other visual indicator, in addition to the text description.

aspects.title: Error is conveyed via an icon/image that HAS a text alternative, but the alt/name misstates, genericises, or mislocates the error
aspects.plain: An error icon has alt text, but the text is wrong, generic, or describes the icon's appearance instead of the actual error, so it doesn't tell a screen-reader user what's wrong.
aspects.description: An error is delivered through an image/icon, which the SC permits provided the meaning is conveyed 'in text or a text alternative'. The page DOES give the icon a non-empty text alternative, so a tool finds the alt/aria-label present and is satisfied — but the alternative is wrong or uselessly generic relative to the actual error: an icon beside a malformed-email field has alt='error' or alt='red triangle' (describes appearance, not the error) or alt='This field is required' (wrong cause — the field was filled but mis-formatted), or two error icons share one generic title 'Invalid input' (cannot identify which field/what error), or the alt is the correct cause for a DIFFERENT field than the one it sits beside. The image exists, the alt exists, the role/name machinery is intact — only a human comparing the alternative's MEANING against the field's actual error state can tell the text alternative fails to identify or describe the error.
aspects.scLimb: 'in text or a text alternative' — when the indicator is non-text, the text alternative itself must identify and describe the actual error, not merely exist.
aspects.whyUncovered: No ACT case uses an image as the error indicator at all, so the text-alternative delivery path the SC explicitly blesses is wholly unexercised, and the specific failure of an icon with present-but-misleading alt is impossible in a corpus of plain text spans. 36b590 would see a named non-text indicator and treat Expectation 1 (identification 'through non-text content') as satisfied, never judging whether the alt's semantics match the error. Automated checkers verify alt PRESENCE, not whether the alt correctly describes the field's actual error — that is a semantic comparison only a human (or judging model) can make.

references.quote: the only requirement is for errors  to be presented to users in text or a text alternative.
at least one of the form field error indicators allows the identification of the related test target, through text , or through non-text content , or through presentation
users be provided with information about the nature of the error, including the identity of the item in error

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: Retail account signup re-displayed after a failed submit; the email field holds a malformed address (jane.summit.example.com, no @) and the sole per-field error indicator is an error icon carrying a non-empty but uselessly generic alt="error".
pages.mechanism: The icon exposes role=img with accessible name "error" (CDP-confirmed), correctly associated via aria-describedby. A screen-reader user hears only "error" — the alternative restates that something is wrong but does not identify the email-format problem (missing @) the SC requires to be described in text or a text alternative.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse verify the image HAS a non-empty alt — alt="error" satisfies the alt-present rule; aria wiring and contrast are valid. No rule compares the alt's meaning to the field's actual error state. Recognising that "error" fails to describe the malformed email is a semantic judgment only a human/judging model can make.

citation.quote: This SC requires that users be provided with information about the nature of the error, including the identity of the item in error.

pages.scenario: Workforce SaaS password reset; the user supplied a 7-char password (policy requires 10) so the field is filled-but-too-short, yet the error icon emitted by a validation-plugin template carries alt="This field is required" — the wrong cause.
pages.mechanism: The icon exposes role=img name="This field is required" (CDP-confirmed), tied to the field via aria-errormessage. The field is not empty (value summer7); the announced cause (required/omitted) contradicts the true error (outside required values — too short), so the user re-types content that is already present and never learns the real rule.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The image has a non-empty alt, aria-errormessage is correctly wired, and contrast is fine — every structural rule passes. Tools cannot read the field value and the 10-char policy to know the password was supplied but too short, nor judge that "required" is the wrong cause; identifying a wrong-cause alternative requires reasoning about the field's actual state.

citation.quote: An "input error" includes: information that is required by the web page but omitted by the user, or information that is provided by the user but that falls outside the required data format or allowed values.

pages.scenario: Nonprofit one-time-gift form; the donor entered 25000 (over the stated $10,000 online maximum) and the error is conveyed by a Material-Icons-style icon-font glyph whose aria-label is the literal ligature key "error_outline" — describing the picture, not the error.
pages.mechanism: The glyph exposes role=img name="error_outline" (CDP-confirmed), associated via aria-describedby. A screen-reader user hears a glyph identifier that conveys neither the cause (amount exceeds the $10,000 cap) nor that this concerns the amount field; it is an appearance/identity token, not an error description.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The element has role=img and a non-empty accessible name, so it is treated as a properly-labelled graphic — no empty-name or missing-role finding. Tools cannot know "error_outline" is an icon-set token rather than a meaningful description, nor that 25000 is out of range; distinguishing a describes-the-picture alternative from a describes-the-error one is semantic.

citation.quote: The "in text" portion of the success criterion underscores that it is not sufficient simply to indicate that a field has an error by putting an asterisk on its label or turning the label red. A text description of the problem should be provided.

pages.scenario: Homeware ecommerce checkout (en-GB); shipping postcode 9021 is too short and billing postcode SW1A 0AA! has an illegal character, but both reuse one SVG sprite and both <svg role=img> wrappers carry the identical hardcoded aria-label="Invalid input".
pages.mechanism: Both icons compute role=img name="Invalid input" (CDP-confirmed for both), each associated via aria-describedby. A screen-reader user hears the same generic phrase at two different fields with two different errors; nothing identifies which postcode or what is wrong (too short vs. illegal character), so the distinct errors are indistinguishable.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Each icon has role=img and a non-empty accessible name with valid aria associations — no unlabeled-graphic or empty-name finding. Tools have no notion that two correctly-labelled icons both saying "Invalid input" fail to distinguish two field errors; judging that the shared generic name cannot identify the field or describe the specific error requires human reasoning about context.

citation.quote: The form field with the error is identified in text (e.g., "Error: Password field.").

pages.scenario: Alumni reunion RSVP (en-GB); email ravi@@pembury.ac.uk (double @) and date 2024-07-18 (in the past) are both invalid, but a refactor cut-and-pasted the date row's error icon above the email row without updating it, so the email field sits beside an SVG whose aria-label="Date is in the past" — correct cause for the wrong field.
pages.mechanism: The email icon exposes role=img name="Date is in the past" (CDP-confirmed) via aria-describedby on the email input. The description is specific and well-formed but describes the date field's error, not the email's (double @) — it is actively misleading; meanwhile the genuinely-past date field has no surviving indicator and is silent.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The icon has role=img, a non-empty (even descriptive) accessible name, and valid aria wiring — nothing for a linter to flag, and the alt is neither empty nor generic. No rule checks whether "Date is in the past" matches the email field it adjoins, nor that the date field lost its indicator; detecting a correctly-worded but mislocated alternative requires matching each alternative's meaning to its actual field.

citation.quote:
Determine whether the error is identified and described in text.
   - a. The form field with the error is identified in text (e.g., "Error: Password field.").

pages.scenario: Online-banking add-payee; the German IBAN DE89 3704 0044 0532 0130 0X ends in an illegal X and is invalid (red border), but a Vue state-merge bug left the field's status SVG at its initial success state: a green check with <title>Looks good!</title> — an inverted text alternative.
pages.mechanism: The SVG exposes role=img name="Looks good!" from its <title> child (CDP-confirmed), associated via aria-describedby. A screen-reader user on the invalid IBAN hears a positive assertion that denies any error exists; the alternative does not identify or describe the error — it contradicts it, the worst form of the aspect.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The SVG has role=img and a non-empty accessible name from a valid <title>, contrast and aria wiring intact — no structural finding. Tools cannot validate the IBAN checksum, cannot know the field is invalid, and cannot detect that "Looks good!" contradicts the real state; catching an inverted/stale alternative requires comparing meaning against the actual error condition.

citation.quote: In the case of an unsuccessful form submission, it is not sufficient to only re-display the form without providing any hint that the submission failed.

pages.scenario: CONTROL (passes): government heating-assistance application; the email carla.mendes#state.gov uses # instead of @ and the error icon carries a correct, specific alt="Email address must contain an @ symbol — for example, name@example.com", echoed by a linked error summary.
pages.mechanism: The icon exposes role=img with the full descriptive accessible name (CDP-confirmed) via aria-describedby. A screen-reader user hears the field identified and the actual error (missing @) described in a text alternative, with a matching summary — satisfying the SC's "in text or a text alternative" limb.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Automated tools would pass this page — but they would equally have passed the failing siblings, since they only check that the alt is PRESENT, never that it correctly describes the error. This control is statically near-identical to the failures (img + non-empty alt + aria wiring) yet is the only one a human marks conforming, proving the aspect is decided by the alternative's meaning, which checkers do not evaluate.

citation.quote: It is perfectly acceptable to indicate the error in other ways such as through the use of an image, color, or other visual indicator, in addition to the text description.

aspects.title: Instruction promised on focus does not actually become perceivable when the field is focused
aspects.plain: A field's only instruction is meant to appear when you focus it, but it never shows, is clipped off-screen, vanishes too fast, or needs a mouse hover instead of keyboard focus.
aspects.description: WCAG explicitly blesses the pattern of withholding a long/verbose instruction until the field receives focus, and Trusted Tester makes 'visible when the form field has focus' a normative requirement. The conformance question is therefore behavioral: when the field is focused, does the promised instruction (password-complexity rule, date-format hint, character rules) actually become visible? The failure is a field whose only instruction is wired to appear on focus but in fact (a) never appears, (b) appears empty/placeholder-only, (c) appears off-screen / clipped / behind another element, (d) auto-dismisses before the user can read or act on it, or (e) requires hover (not keyboard focus) so keyboard users never get it. The static DOM looks fine; only driving the focus state and visually judging the rendered result reveals whether the instruction is honored. This is the entire 'available only when the individual control has focus' limb operationalized as a failure.
aspects.scLimb: Understanding intent para 1 — instructions may be made available only when the individual control has focus (especially when long/verbose); TT note — the label or instruction must be visible when the form field has focus.
aspects.whyUncovered: There are zero ACT rules and zero test-case pages for 3.3.2, so nothing exercises any dynamic state. All 8 technique docs show static, always-visible labels; none demonstrates a focus-revealed instruction, let alone one that fails to appear, time out, or trigger on hover instead of focus. The 8-pattern seed file is entirely about placeholder/required/grouping in the static DOM. A linter inspecting static HTML sees the instruction node (or a :focus CSS rule) present and reports a label exists; it cannot drive focus, observe what actually renders, time the appearance/disappearance, distinguish a :hover trigger from a :focus trigger, or judge whether the focused instruction is genuinely perceivable. This requires interacting with the page and visually judging the focused state.

references.quote: Content authors may also choose to make such instructions available to users only when the individual control has focus especially when instructions are long and verbose.
The label or instruction must be visible when the form field has focus.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: Fintech (Tellard) wallet signup. The password field's only instruction is its complexity rules ('12+ chars, 1 number, 1 symbol') in #pw-hint. The password's focus handler was copied from the email field and still targets #email-hint, so focusing the password reveals the email-domain hint; #pw-hint is display:none + aria-hidden and never un-hides, so the actual rules reach no one.
pages.mechanism: The password field's focus handler was copy-pasted from the email field and never re-targeted: it adds .show to #email-hint, so focusing #pw reveals the EMAIL field's domain hint, not the password rules. The password's own complexity-rules node (#pw-hint) is class='hint' (display:none), carries aria-hidden='true', has no aria-describedby pointing at it, and nothing ever adds .show — so it is pruned from the AX tree and never shown to anyone. Both populations lose the password field's only instruction.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The input has a correct programmatic <label> ('Create password') and the rules node exists in the static DOM with real text plus an aria-describedby reference, so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse report a label-and-description present and pass it. No static checker drives focus, executes the handler to observe that classList.remove('hide') is a no-op leaving display:none in place, or judges that the only instruction never becomes perceivable.
