A scanner that merely confirms a hidden describedby node or a :focus rule exists would wrongly treat the instruction as provided — distinguishing 'instruction node exists' from 'instruction actually renders on focus' requires driving focus and visually judging the focused state.

citation.quote: Content authors may also choose to make such instructions available to users only when the individual control has focus especially when instructions are long and verbose.

pages.scenario: Brightleaf Coffee Co. checkout payment step. The promo-code field accepts only format 'ABC-1234' (three letters, dash, four digits) — the field's only instruction. The hint is revealed by a CSS '.promo-wrap:hover .promo-hint' rule ONLY; there is no :focus / :focus-within rule. A mouse user who hovers sees the format; a keyboard user who tabs to the field gets nothing.
pages.mechanism: Reveal is gated purely on :hover of the wrapper. On keyboard focus the hint stays opacity:0; max-height:0; overflow:hidden (collapsed, imperceptible). Verified headless: after page.focus(#promo) the hint reports opacity 0 / height 18 collapsed; only after page.hover(#promo) does it reach opacity 1 / height 50. Keyboard and most screen-reader users (who reach the field by focus, not hover) never receive the format instruction.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The input has a correct associated <label> ('Promo code'), so the form-label check passes, and the hint text plus a :hover reveal rule exist in the static stylesheet, so a static scan sees an instruction node and a reveal rule. Automated checkers do not distinguish a :hover trigger from a :focus trigger, do not drive keyboard focus to observe nothing reveals, and cannot judge that keyboard users never receive the instruction. Telling :hover apart from :focus and confirming the instruction is absent for keyboard users requires interaction (tabbing) and human judgment.

citation.quote: The label or instruction must be visible when the form field has focus.

pages.scenario: Aerolink flight-booking date step. The travel-date field requires day-first format 'DD/MM/YYYY' — its only instruction. The hint is a 'floating help bar' (position:fixed; bottom:0) revealed on focus, but a booking-summary footer is ALSO position:fixed; bottom:0 with a higher z-index and opaque background. Both pin to the viewport bottom, so on focus the revealed hint paints directly behind the opaque footer and is fully occluded in every viewport.
pages.mechanism: #travel:focus ~ .date-hint sets display:block and the hint is visibility:visible/opacity:1 on focus, but .date-hint (position:fixed; bottom:0; z-index:10) and .summary-bar (position:fixed; bottom:0; z-index:50, opaque) share the bottom band, so the footer paints over the hint. Verified headless: after driving keyboard focus, document.elementFromPoint at the hint's center returns .summary-bar (not the hint) at viewports 800x600, 1024x768, 1280x900 and 1440x1024 — occlusion is deterministic across heights.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The input has a correct associated <label> ('Travel date'), so the form-label check passes; the hint node exists, transitions display:none->display:block on focus, and is wired via aria-describedby, so a static scan sees an instruction that 'appears on focus.' Automated checkers do not compute the painted stacking order of two competing position:fixed bottom bars, do not drive focus to render the focused state, and do not visually judge that the revealed instruction is hidden behind another element. Detecting the occlusion requires rendering the focused state and looking.

citation.quote: Instructions or labels may also specify data formats for data entry fields, especially if they are out of the customary formats or if there are specific rules for correct input.

pages.scenario: Thornwood Makers community-forum signup. The username rules ('3-20 chars; letters/numbers/hyphens/underscores; must start with a letter') are the field's only instruction. On focus the tooltip fades in correctly, but a setTimeout(...,1500) then fades it out and sets aria-hidden while the field still has focus — it auto-dismisses before a slow reader finishes and does not return unless the field is blurred and re-focused.
pages.mechanism: The focus handler adds class 'show' then, 1500ms later, runs tip.classList.remove('show'); tip.setAttribute('aria-hidden','true') — dismissing the instruction during the same focus session, with no re-show on later interaction. Verified headless: after focus the tooltip is opacity:1 with real text; after waiting past 1.5s (field still focused) it is opacity:0 and aria-hidden. The aria-describedby target becomes hidden, so a re-querying screen reader finds nothing and a slow/magnifier user loses it mid-read.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The input has a correct associated <label> ('Choose a username'), so the form-label check passes; the instruction node exists, is shown on focus, and is wired via aria-describedby, so a DOM snapshot may even capture it visible. No automated checker measures how long an instruction stays perceivable, drives focus and waits 1.5s to watch it disappear, or judges that a timed auto-dismiss with no recovery path leaves the instruction effectively unavailable. Timing the appearance/disappearance and judging the window is too short requires interacting over time and human judgment.

citation.quote: The goal is to make certain that enough information is provided for the user to accomplish the task without undue confusion or navigation.

pages.scenario: Faktura cross-border invoicing billing setup. The Tax-ID field requires a jurisdiction-specific format — its only instruction — delivered by a focus-revealed callout populated from the i18n string 'hint.taxid.format'. That key is missing from the en catalog and the templating layer's missing-key fallback is a single non-breaking space, so on focus a styled bordered box flicks into view but its entire content is U+00A0, conveying nothing.
pages.mechanism: #taxid:focus ~ .taxid-hint sets display:block and the box renders with padding/border on focus, but its only text node is a non-breaking space (the missing-i18n-key fallback). Verified headless: after focus the hint is display:block, in viewport, 450x38, but meaningfulChars=0 (text is only U+00A0). Screen readers following aria-describedby reach a node whose only content is a non-breaking space (announced 'blank'/a space); sighted users see a box that implies an instruction but states none.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The input has a correct associated <label> ('VAT / Tax identification number'), so this is not a missing-accessible-name case and the form-label check passes. The hint is not an empty element a linter would flag: its content is a non-breaking space (U+00A0), a non-empty text node, so whitespace-only/zero-length emptiness heuristics do not fire — many tools and AT explicitly count   as content. No automated checker reads the focus-revealed callout, recognizes that a non-breaking space carries no instruction, or judges the field's only instruction is meaningless; that requires reading the rendered focused state and a human judgment that U+00A0 is not an instruction.

citation.quote:
On this website additional instructions 
would need to accompany the field to prevent users from encountering unnecessary errors.

pages.scenario: Harbour Mutual insurance policy-verification page (PASSING boundary variant). The policy-reference field requires format 'two letters, a hyphen, eight digits' (GB-49120753) — its only instruction. The focus-revealed-instruction pattern is implemented correctly: the hint un-hides on keyboard focus (:focus-within and :focus, not only hover), renders fully on-screen in normal flow, persists for the whole focus session (no timer), and contains real meaningful text. Included to sharpen the aspect: the discriminator is behavioral, not structural.
pages.mechanism: Reveal fires on keyboard focus via .policy-field:focus-within .policy-hint and #policy:focus ~ .policy-hint (also on hover and while the field holds a value). On focus the hint is display:block, fully visible, in normal flow with nothing painting over it, and persistent; the aria-describedby='policy-hint' target is now a visible populated node so the real format guidance is announced. Verified headless: after driving keyboard focus the hint is display:block, in viewport at top=354, with 140 meaningful characters and no occluder.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A static scan cannot confirm this PASS any more than it can catch the failing cases: it sees the identical shape — a real <label>, a hidden instruction node, a :focus reveal rule, aria-describedby — and has no signal distinguishing an honored focus-reveal from a broken one (it passes the label check on all six). Confirming this page genuinely passes requires driving keyboard focus and visually judging that the promised instruction truly appears, is fully on-screen, persists, and reads meaningfully — the same human/behavioral judgment the failing cases need, applied to a correct implementation.

citation.quote: The label or instruction must be visible when the form field has focus.

aspects.title: Instruction is present and well-formatted but semantically wrong, stale, or contradicts the field's actual rule
aspects.plain: A field shows a clear instruction that's actually wrong for what it accepts (says MM/DD/YYYY but wants DD/MM/YYYY), so following it guarantees an error.
aspects.description: 3.3.2 requires instructions that identify the controls so users know what input data is expected and that specify data formats, especially out-of-customary formats or specific input rules. A field can DISPLAY a confident, perfectly-marked-up instruction that is simply incorrect or stale relative to what the field accepts: the visible hint says 'MM/DD/YYYY' but the field enforces DD/MM/YYYY; 'Max 20 characters' while it truncates at 10; 'Enter your 5-digit ZIP' next to a field requiring ZIP+4; or copied boilerplate naming the wrong purpose entirely ('Enter your member ID' on a promo-code field). The user is actively misled — following the instruction guarantees an error — which the Understanding warns is as harmful as too little. The label/instruction is structurally perfect; the defect is purely the correspondence between the words and the field's real behavior.
aspects.scLimb: Understanding intent para 1 — instructions/labels may specify data formats, especially out-of-customary formats or specific rules for correct input; intent para 2 — too much information or instruction can be just as harmful as too little.
aspects.whyUncovered: No ACT rule/test exists; the technique examples only show instructions correct by construction (the date-format example, the username-rules example). There is no failure technique for a wrong/stale instruction and no seed pattern covers content that is present-but-false (the seeds are all about missing/placeholder/color-only labels). Automated tools verify the existence and association of label text; they have no model of what the field actually accepts (the pattern/maxlength/validation logic vs. the prose) to compare against, so they cannot detect a contradiction between a hint and the field's behavior. Catching this requires reading the instruction, inferring the rule, and noticing the conflict.

references.quote: Instructions or labels may also specify data formats for data entry fields, especially if they are out of the customary formats or if there are specific rules for correct input.

Too much information or instruction can be just as harmful as too little. The goal is to make certain that enough information is provided for the user to accomplish the task without undue confusion or navigation.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: GOV.UK-style driving-licence renewal: the date-of-birth field's visible, programmatically associated hint reads 'Format: MM/DD/YYYY — for example 03/27/1986' but the field's pattern, maxlength, and JS validator enforce DD/MM/YYYY. A user who follows the printed month-first instruction (03/27/1986) is rejected; the day-first format the field actually wants is never stated up front. The licence-number field is an always-correct contrast control.
pages.mechanism: A format instruction specifying the data-entry order is present and correctly associated, but it states MM/DD while the field enforces DD/MM — opposite day/month order. The instruction the SC governs actively directs the user to a guaranteed validation error; the corrective rule appears only post-submit.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse and TT 5.A verify only that a visible instruction is present and associated (both true). No tool parses the prose 'MM/DD/YYYY', parses the pattern regex, and reasons that the two specify opposite field orders; there is no automated model of what the field accepts to compare against the words.

citation.quote: Instructions or labels may also specify data formats for data entry fields, especially if they are out of the customary formats or if there are specific rules for correct input.

pages.scenario: Bank two-step verification: the visible helper text, associated with the OTP group via aria-labelledby/aria-describedby, says 'Enter the 6-digit code we sent to your phone', but the field is built from exactly four single-character boxes (each maxlength=1) and the inline validator requires exactly four digits. A user who waits for/enters a six-digit code can physically only enter four; the stated count contradicts the field's real capacity.
pages.mechanism: The instruction states a digit count (6) that exceeds the field's enforced length (4 boxes, validator /^\d{4}$/). Following the stated count cannot succeed; auto-advance even ejects the user after the 4th keystroke with two digits unentered.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The instruction exists, is non-empty, and is associated, so TT 5.A and ACT pass it. No scanner extracts the integer '6' from prose, counts the four maxlength=1 boxes (or reads the \d{4} validator), and reasons 6 != 4 — there is no automated model of a composite field's accepted length to check the words against.

citation.quote: The goal is to make certain that enough information is provided for the user to accomplish the task without undue confusion or navigation.

pages.scenario: SaaS workspace signup: the password field shows a visible, associated requirements list whose first bullet says 'At least 8 characters', but the field enforces twelve — minlength=12, pattern requiring .{12,}, strength meter and submit validator both reject under 12. An instruction-compliant 8-character password (e.g. Passw0rdX) is rejected. The work-email field is an always-correct contrast control.
pages.mechanism: The stated minimum length (8) is below the enforced minimum (12). A user who satisfies every announced rule still fails; the real threshold is announced only post-submit via role=alert. The up-front instruction the SC governs understates the rule for correct input.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The requirements list is present, associated, and readable, so TT 5.A and axe/WAVE/Lighthouse pass it. No tool extracts '8' from the bullet, reads minlength=12/the pattern quantifier, and reasons 8 < 12; there is no automated comparison between a prose threshold and an enforced numeric constraint.

citation.quote:
Providing labels and instructions (including examples of expected
            data formats) helps all users — but particularly those with cognitive, language, and learning
            disabilities — to enter information correctly.

pages.scenario: E-commerce checkout phone control built as the H71 fieldset/legend pattern: legend reads 'Phone number (US, 10 digits)', but an unmentioned leading country-code box exists and the submit validator requires 11 digits total (/^\d{11}$/) with the country-code box filled. A US shopper who follows the legend and enters their familiar 10-digit number into the three labelled boxes is rejected; the group instruction understates the real requirement.
pages.mechanism: The group-level legend (the sanctioned instruction for a split control) states a digit count (10) one short of the enforced count (11) and omits the required country-code field. Following the legend cannot produce an accepted value.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The fieldset has a non-empty legend and every sub-field has an accessible name, so H71, TT 5.A, and axe/WAVE/Lighthouse pass. No scanner parses '10 digits' from the legend, counts the four boxes (or reads the \d{11} validator and the required country-code check), and reasons the enforced total exceeds the stated count.

citation.quote:
The single "Phone number" label also cannot label all three fields. To address this, the
            three fields are grouped in a fieldset with the legend "Phone number".

pages.scenario: Nonprofit food-bank donation form: the custom-amount field's visible, associated instruction gives a worked example — 'Enter an amount in US dollars — for example 25.00' — but the field rejects decimals (step=1, pattern=\d+, validator /^\d+$/ accepts whole dollars only). The very example the instruction offers, 25.00, is itself an invalid value; a donor who copies it verbatim is rejected.
pages.mechanism: The instruction's own worked example violates the field's enforced rule (integers only). The aid that should help users enter correct data demonstrates a forbidden format; the real rule (no cents) surfaces only post-submit.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The instruction is present, associated, and gives an example, so TT 5.A and axe/WAVE/Lighthouse pass. No tool extracts the literal example '25.00' from prose, reads step=1/pattern=\d+, and tests the example against the field's own constraint to discover it fails — there is no 'does the instruction's example validate' check.

citation.quote:
Providing labels and instructions (including examples of expected
            data formats) helps all users — but particularly those with cognitive, language, and learning
            disabilities — to enter information correctly.

pages.scenario: Film-festival ticket checkout: the field labelled 'Discount code' is in fact a promo-code box (validator accepts codes like LUMIERE25, placeholder 'PROMO CODE'), but its visible, associated instruction is leftover boilerplate naming a different purpose entirely — 'Enter your member ID (8 digits) to apply your membership benefit'. Following it (hunting for a member ID or typing 8 digits) is rejected. The sibling membership-tier select is a passed contrast control whose instruction matches its field exactly.
pages.mechanism: Copied boilerplate names the wrong purpose (member ID vs promo code) and states a rule (8 numeric digits) incompatible with the field's alphanumeric promo pattern; the instruction misidentifies the control so the user does not know what input is expected. Mechanism is wrong-purpose naming, distinct from the numeric/format mismatches in the other cases.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The instruction is present, non-empty, associated, and readable, so TT 5.A and axe/WAVE/Lighthouse pass. No scanner reads 'member ID (8 digits)', reads the alphanumeric promo pattern and 'PROMO CODE' placeholder, and reasons that the instruction names a different purpose and incompatible rule — there is no automated model of what the field is actually for.

citation.quote:
The intent of this success criterion is to have content authors present instructions
         or labels that identify the controls in a form so that users know what input data
         is expected.

aspects.title: Image-only / icon-only label that is not 'widely understood by the intended target audience'
aspects.plain: A data-entry field's only visible cue is an ambiguous icon or symbol that doesn't make clear what to type, so a sighted user can't tell what input is expected.
aspects.description: The Understanding accepts images as labels but adds the explicit caveat that authors must ensure the images are widely understood by the intended target audience, recommending supplementary tooltips/text for clarity. G167's happy path uses near-universal icons (magnify glass, paper-airplane send). The uncovered failure is a data-entry field whose ONLY visible cue is an ambiguous, decorative, or domain-obscure glyph — a lone '#' next to a field secretly meaning 'enter quantity', a generic gear/sliders icon as the only cue for a 'budget' field, two adjacent fields each cued by indistinguishable icons. A sighted user cannot tell what to type. This is a 3.3.2 visible-cue-adequacy failure even if the icon carries correct alt text giving it an accessible name (which would pass 4.1.2) — the visible cue still fails to communicate purpose to everyone.
aspects.scLimb: Understanding intent para 3 — using images as labels meets the criterion only if the images are widely understood by the intended target audience; TT note — the label or instruction can be graphical or textual.
aspects.whyUncovered: No ACT rule/test exists, and G167 only documents well-understood icons; there is no failure technique for an obscure icon and no seed pattern covers image-label adequacy (seeds are all text/placeholder/color cases). Tools can confirm an icon has alt text / an accessible name, but they have no notion of whether the rendered GLYPH is interpretable by a human looking at it. 'Widely understood by the intended target audience' is an irreducibly human, audience-relative semantic judgment that requires actually viewing the icon and reasoning about what a typical user would infer.

references.quote: Using images as labels meets the requirements of the criterion, but care should be taken to ensure that the images are widely understood by the intended target audience. Authors may consider providing additional hints, such as text-based tooltips or supplementary text, to support clarity when using image-based labels.
The label or instruction can be graphical or textual.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: Messio profile editor: the only visible cue for a username/handle field is a lone '#' (octothorpe) glyph in a leading affordance tile; no text, placeholder, or tooltip. A magnifying-glass search box on the same page is the deliberate passing contrast. A sighted user cannot tell whether '#' means enter a number, a topic tag, or a handle.
pages.mechanism: Input exposes accessible name 'Username handle' via aria-label (4.1.2 passes) while the glyph SVG is aria-hidden; the ONLY visible label is a '#' glyph that is not widely understood as 'type your username', so the 3.3.2 visible-cue-adequacy limb for image labels fails for sighted users.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe-core/WAVE/Lighthouse only confirm a non-empty accessible name (aria-label satisfies this); none rasterise the inline SVG to see it renders as '#', and none can reason that a sighted user reading '#' cannot infer the field wants a handle. 'Widely understood by the intended target audience' is an irreducibly human, audience-relative visual-semantic judgment.

citation.quote: Using images as labels meets the requirements of the criterion, but care should be taken to ensure that the images are widely understood by the intended target audience. Authors may consider providing additional hints, such as text-based tooltips or supplementary text, to support clarity when using image-based labels.

pages.scenario: Pulsegrid Analytics workspace settings: a 'Data pipeline' fieldset has two stacked inputs, each cued only by a small cog/gear glyph that renders visually indistinguishable (the second is the same cog rotated ~22 degrees). One field wants a refresh interval in seconds, the other a retention window in days; the generic 'gear' cue does not differentiate them.
pages.mechanism: Both inputs carry distinct aria-labels (4.1.2 passes) and both cog SVGs are aria-hidden; the only per-field visible cue is an indistinguishable gear glyph, and the legend 'Data pipeline' names neither field, so a sighted user has no visible way to tell the two fields apart — a 3.3.2 visible-cue-adequacy failure.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe-core's label rule is satisfied by the aria-labels and both glyphs are aria-hidden; no tool renders the two cog SVGs to discover they are visually indistinguishable, nor can reason that a sighted user therefore cannot distinguish the 'refresh interval' field from the 'retention window' field. Glyph distinguishability and per-field meaning are human visual judgments.

citation.quote: The intent of this success criterion is to have content authors present instructions or labels that identify the controls in a form so that users know what input data is expected.

pages.scenario: Northvale Invest robo-advisor onboarding (Step 2 of 4): a field's only visible cue is a three-horizontal-slider 'equalizer/mixer' glyph in a round badge (with a trailing '/ 10'). The field silently expects the investor's risk-tolerance score 1-10, but an equalizer is a sound-mixing / generic-settings metaphor not conventionally associated with risk tolerance.
pages.mechanism: Input has accessible name 'Risk tolerance score from 1 to 10' via aria-label (4.1.2 passes); the SVG is aria-hidden. No visible text states the field is about risk tolerance — the only visible cue is a domain-obscure equalizer glyph not widely understood for that purpose, failing the 3.3.2 image-label limb.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe-core/Lighthouse confirm an accessible name via aria-label and the glyph is aria-hidden; no tool renders the equalizer glyph or carries any model of which symbols mean 'risk tolerance' to a financial-services audience. Deciding a mixer glyph is not 'widely understood by the intended target audience' is an audience-relative human semantic judgment.

citation.quote: Using images as labels meets the requirements of the criterion, but care should be taken to ensure that the images are widely understood by the intended target audience.

pages.scenario: Quillbeck accounts-payable 'Add a vendor' form: the first two fields have proper visible text labels (Vendor name, Billing email), but a third full-width field has NO text label — its only visible cue is the Quillbeck company brand mark (a decorative quill nib, the same logo from the top bar) repurposed as the field's icon. The field expects the internal vendor account ID.
pages.mechanism: Input has accessible name 'Quillbeck vendor account ID' via aria-label (4.1.2 passes); the brand SVG is aria-hidden and there is no <label>. The only visible cue is a decorative brand mark that conveys no field-purpose meaning, so the visible-cue limb of 3.3.2 fails (a brand mark is, by construction, not a widely-understood symbol for 'vendor account ID').
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe-core/WAVE confirm the input has an accessible name and the brand SVG is aria-hidden, so no label violation. No tool can recognise the rendered glyph is merely the company logo reused as decoration, nor reason that a brand mark conveys no field-purpose meaning to a sighted user — a human visual-semantic judgment about whether the glyph is 'widely understood' for the field.

citation.quote: It is possible for controls and inputs to have an appropriate accessible name or description (e.g. using aria-label="...") and therefore pass Success Criterion 4.1.2, but to still fail this success criterion (if the labels or instructions aren't presented to all users, not just those using assistive technologies).

pages.scenario: Trattoria Lume 'Reserve a table' form: it has text-labeled Date and Time rows (Time is a select), then a third row whose only visible cue is a clock-face glyph with no text. A clock universally reads as 'time', and a Time field already exists above it, so a sighted user reads this as another time input — but it actually expects the number of guests. The glyph's conventional meaning contradicts the field's real purpose.
pages.mechanism: Input has accessible name 'Number of guests' via aria-label (4.1.2 passes); the clock SVG is aria-hidden. The only visible cue is a clock glyph that conventionally means 'time' and actively misleads a sighted user (compounded by the real 'Time' select directly above), so the 3.3.2 image-label limb fails despite the correct programmatic name.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe-core/Lighthouse confirm an accessible name and the clock SVG is aria-hidden, so no label violation. No scanner rasterises the glyph to recognise a clock face, knows a clock conventionally signals 'time', or notices a real 'Time' select sits directly above making the glyph misleading. Detecting that the visible cue misleads a sighted user is an irreducibly human visual + contextual judgment.

citation.quote: The goal is to make certain that enough information is provided for the user to accomplish the task without undue confusion or navigation.

pages.scenario: Portbridge Logistics 'International shipping label' form — the correctly-built PASS boundary: a magnifying-glass icon-only search box uses the universal loupe, and both data-entry fields (Destination country code, Parcel weight) pair a glyph (globe; weight scale) with a VISIBLE text label and a format instruction. The glyph is garnish; the visible text is the real cue, so no field relies on a glyph alone.
pages.mechanism: Every input has both a visible text label (read by sighted users) and a programmatic association via <label for> (read by AT), plus a visible instruction; the leading SVGs are decorative (aria-hidden). The only icon-only control is a search field cued by the Understanding/G167-endorsed universal magnifying glass, so the 3.3.2 visible-cue limb is satisfied — nothing relies on a non-understood glyph alone.
pages.selectorNote: Household-count field whose only visible cue is an opaque pilcrow glyph (orig label[for=ccode] mismatch)
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: This is the case where tools and human judgment AGREE: automated checkers report no violation (labels present and associated), and a human inspecting the rendered glyphs also finds no 'not widely understood' problem because no field depends on a glyph alone. Included as a clean contrast so the aspect is not read as 'any leading icon on a field fails' — icons garnishing real visible text labels, and the universal loupe for search, are acceptable.

citation.quote: A website provides a global search field in the header of the site. Any term can be entered, so there are no instructions needed, but the field needs a cue to communicate its purpose. Commonly, such search field will be paired with a "loupe" or "magnify glass" search icon, serving as its visible label, if not also doubling as the visual identifier for the button that submits the search query.

aspects.title: Group-level (legend/heading) label is needed where individual labels are insufficient, but is absent or only visual — F82 generalized beyond phone numbers
aspects.plain: Several related fields each have labels too vague alone (Street, City, Zip), and the group has no overall heading, so you can't tell what the set is for, like billing versus shipping.
aspects.description: F82 is the one documented failure technique but is narrowly framed around US phone-number fields. The underlying failure generalizes: any set of fields where each field's individual label, read alone, is insufficient and a GROUP-level description is required (H71's core rationale) but the group description is absent or present only as visual proximity/styling, not as a real label. H71 names the test: where a group of controls within a larger form requires an additional heading to provide a description specific to that group. The failure is judging that a particular set DOES need a group label and that the visible page fails to provide one. Examples beyond phone: billing vs shipping address blocks with identical inner labels (Street/City/Zip) and no group heading; a split Given/Family name where neither field alone says 'Name'; date-as-three-selects (Day/Month/Year) with no 'Date of birth' grouping.
aspects.scLimb: Understanding intent para 1 + examples — options/groups must be labeled so users know what they are selecting; the phone-number and Given/Family-name examples; failure F82 generalized; H71 'an additional heading to provide a description specific to that particular group'.
aspects.whyUncovered: No ACT rule/test page exists. F82 is technique prose limited to phone numbers. The seed file's only grouping pattern is custom radios with broken radiogroup semantics — a different, partly programmatic defect that axe-adjacent tooling and the seed already cover, so this aspect must be constructed with otherwise-correctly-labeled native inputs to avoid duplicating it. Recognizing that a set of fields NEEDS a group label, and that visual proximity is doing work the textual labeling does not, is a contextual semantic judgment about whether the per-field labels are sufficient standalone. Tools can detect a missing fieldset/legend, but presence of fieldset/legend is neither necessary (a visible group heading can suffice) nor a reliable signal of the actual failure (two identical address blocks can each have labeled inputs and pass every linter while being genuinely ambiguous). The 'is a group label needed here?' decision is human.

references.quote: where a group of controls within a larger form requires an additional heading to provide a description specific to that particular group, the use of fieldset and legend elements is appropriate.
even if all the fields have programmatically determined names, a text label must also identify the set of fields as a phone number.
Rather than having a single label "Name" (which would appear to leave the second text field unlabelled), each field is given an explicit label — "Given Name" and "Family Name".

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: E-commerce checkout (Maple & Birch Home Goods) collects billing AND shipping as two structurally identical address blocks side by side; every native input is correctly labelled 'Full name / Street address / City / State / ZIP' but the labels are identical across both blocks and there is NO visible 'Billing' / 'Shipping' heading — only column position distinguishes them, and that cue is itself unlabelled.
pages.mechanism: Two field sets that collect DIFFERENT data (b_* vs s_*) are disambiguated only by horizontal position; a group-level description ('Billing'/'Shipping') required per H71's rule-of-thumb is absent. A screen-reader/Braille user reading linearly hears two identical 'Full name…ZIP' groups with no group description and cannot tell which address they fill.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every input has a programmatically associated, non-empty, visible <label>, so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse report 'form elements have labels' and pass. No rule requires a fieldset (H71 allows a visible heading), and legend presence is neither necessary nor a reliable signal — two fully-labelled address blocks pass every linter while being genuinely ambiguous. Detecting it needs human reasoning that the page collects two different addresses and that 'Street/City/ZIP' alone cannot say which.

citation.quote: For instance, several fields that collect a user's address might be grouped together with a legend of "Address", thus providing a group level description for these controls. As a rule of thumb, it can be said that where a group of controls within a larger form requires an additional heading to provide a description specific to that particular group, the use of fieldset and legend elements is appropriate.

pages.scenario: Municipal resident-parking-permit application (City of Hartwell) captures the applicant's date of birth as three native <select> elements labelled only 'Day', 'Month', 'Year', sitting between a correctly-grouped name fieldset and a license-plate field; nowhere — no legend, heading, or text — does the page state that the trio composes a 'Date of birth'.
pages.mechanism: The three selects collect ONE value (a birth date) but the collective purpose is never stated. 'Day/Month/Year' read alone are ambiguous (day/month/year of what?). Correct bday-* autocomplete tokens satisfy 1.3.5 but are invisible to users and not what 3.3.2 evaluates; a screen-reader user hears three combo boxes with no indication they form a birth date.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: All three selects have associated, visible, non-empty labels and valid autocomplete tokens, so scanners pass them. No rule requires a fieldset, and tools cannot infer that 'Day/Month/Year' alone is semantically insufficient or that the set's purpose (date of birth) is unstated — recognizing the trio needs a group description is human judgment.

citation.quote: In the case of radio buttons, checkboxes, comboboxes, or similar controls that provide users with options, each option must have an appropriate label so that users know what they are actually selecting.

pages.scenario: Insurance underwriting wildfire-risk survey (Cascade Mutual) collects the insured structure's latitude/longitude as two adjacent native inputs, each labelled only with its UNIT ('Decimal degrees'); the left is the latitude (name=lat), the right the longitude (name=lng), but neither field alone says 'latitude'/'longitude' and nothing labels the two as a coordinate — role and order are conveyed only by left-to-right position and the invisible name attribute.
pages.mechanism: 'Decimal degrees' labels the unit, not the field's role. The lat/lng pair needs a group/role description; without it a typed-entry user must guess the order, and swapping the two silently relocates the pin. A screen-reader user hears two identical 'Decimal degrees, edit' fields with no group meaning.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Both inputs are programmatically labelled with non-empty visible text and the map carries a valid aria-label, so scanners pass everything. No tool can know two fields both labelled 'Decimal degrees' are an ordered latitude/longitude pair, that the unit is not the role, or that a coordinate-group description is missing — that requires domain knowledge and visual reasoning.

citation.quote: However, even if all the fields have programmatically determined names, a text label must also identify the set of fields as a phone number.

pages.scenario: Bank 'Add a payment card' form (Solstice Bank) splits the 16-digit card number into four maxlength=4 boxes separated by literal dash glyphs; each box carries a programmatic aria-label ('First/Next/Last four digits') so it passes label checks, but the only VISIBLE label is a placeholder of four dashes ('----') and there is NO visible 'Card number' text labelling the set — the four-part grouping is conveyed solely by visual dashed formatting.
pages.mechanism: Boxes have a programmatic name (4.1.2 passes) but no VISIBLE label presented to all users — the dash placeholder is not a label and vanishes on input, and no visible 'Card number' text labels the set. The grouping/meaning is conveyed only by the F82-style visual formatting; even the aria-labels never say 'card number', so the set's purpose is stated to no one.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every input has a non-empty aria-label, so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse pass the missing-label rule; the failure is the absence of a VISIBLE label/instruction (3.3.2's 'presented to all users' limb) and of any group description — which tools cannot evaluate. Judging that a four-dash placeholder is not a real label, and that the dashed four-box layout silently encodes 'card number', requires human visual-semantic reasoning.

citation.quote: It is possible for controls and inputs to have an appropriate accessible name or description (e.g. using aria-label="...") and therefore pass Success Criterion 4.1.2, but to still fail this success criterion (if the labels or instructions aren't presented to all users, not just those using assistive technologies).

pages.scenario: DevNorth 2026 conference-ticket checkout collects two attendees in two structurally identical cards with byte-identical inner labels (Full name / Email for the ticket / T-shirt size); the only thing naming each block — the 'Attendee 1' / 'Attendee 2' bar — is a decorative <div>, not a legend/heading and not bound to the group via aria, so the required group description is present visually but presented to no one as a label.
pages.mechanism: Two structurally identical attendee blocks have byte-identical inner labels (Full name / Email for the ticket / T-shirt size). The only disambiguator is the title 'Attendee 1' / 'Attendee 2', which is REAL DOM text inside a styled <div class='ticket-bar'> — but it is not a <legend>, not a heading, and is not referenced by the <section> or any control via aria-labelledby. So it is part of no accessible name; an AT user in forms mode hears two identical 'Full name…' groups with no group boundary announced.
pages.selectorNote: Decorative title-bar div ('Attendee 1/2'), the only group disambiguator but not a real label
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: All inputs have associated visible labels, the form has an aria-label, and nothing is empty in the DOM, so scanners pass the label rules. Tools do not compare a visible CSS-generated group label against what AT actually receives, nor reason that two identical blocks NEED a group label the generated content fails to provide accessibly.

citation.quote: It is possible for controls and inputs to have an appropriate accessible name or description (e.g. using aria-label="...") and therefore pass Success Criterion 4.1.2, but to still fail this success criterion (if the labels or instructions aren't presented to all users, not just those using assistive technologies).

pages.scenario: PASSING contrast: university graduate-housing application (Thornfield University) collects current AND permanent addresses in two structurally identical groups with byte-identical inner labels, but each group is preceded by a visible <h3> 'Current address' / 'Permanent address' and each <section> is programmatically tied to its heading via aria-labelledby — deliberately NOT a fieldset, to show H71's 'additional heading' can suffice.
pages.mechanism: The group-level description the failing cases lack is supplied as real, visible, all-users text and programmatically associated: a sighted user reads the headings, and a screen-reader user entering a field hears the group name (e.g. 'Current address, Street address, edit') via aria-labelledby, disambiguating the identical inner labels.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Automated tools pass BOTH this page and the failing case-01 for the same reason — every input has an associated label and nothing is empty — so they cannot tell the conformant page from the ambiguous one. They do not evaluate whether a visible group heading is present and sufficient (fieldset presence is neither necessary nor checked). A human must judge that the visible <h3> headings here genuinely resolve the ambiguity whereas bare column position does not.

citation.quote: As a rule of thumb, it can be said that where a group of controls within a larger form requires an additional heading to provide a description specific to that particular group, the use of fieldset and legend elements is appropriate.

aspects.title: Format/required instruction exists but is positioned or styled so it is not perceivable as belonging to the field (visually orphaned instruction)
aspects.plain: A field's instruction text exists but sits far away, in a collapsed panel, or is tiny and low-contrast, so a sighted user doesn't connect it to the field or can't read it.
aspects.description: 3.3.2 is about whether the instruction is PRESENTED to all users for that control. A subtle failure: the instruction text genuinely exists and is visible somewhere on the page, but is visually disconnected from the field it governs — placed far above the form, after the submit button, in a collapsed/closed-by-default help panel, in a footnote, or styled so small/low-contrast/greyed that a sighted user does not associate it with (or cannot read) the field. The Understanding warns the goal is to provide enough information to accomplish the task without undue confusion or navigation; an orphaned instruction forces exactly that navigation. The static text node exists, so a 'does instruction text exist?' check passes; whether a real user perceives it as the field's instruction is a layout/visual judgment.
aspects.scLimb: Understanding 4.1.2-distinction para — labels/instructions must be presented to all users, not just AT users; intent para 2 — enough information without undue confusion or navigation.
aspects.whyUncovered: No ACT rule/test exists. Technique examples always place the instruction adjacent to or programmatically tied to the field; there is no failure technique for an orphaned instruction, and the seed patterns center on missing/placeholder/color-only labels, not mispositioned-but-present ones. An automated tool searching the DOM for instruction text would FIND it and not flag a problem; tools cannot reason about spatial proximity, reading-order distance, collapsed-disclosure state, contrast-as-it-relates-to-association, or whether a human would visually bind the instruction to the field. This is a perception/layout judgment requiring a rendered view.

references.quote: It is possible for controls and inputs to have an appropriate accessible name or description (e.g. using aria-label="...") and therefore pass Success Criterion 4.1.2, but to still fail this success criterion (if the labels or instructions aren't presented to all users, not just those using assistive technologies).
The goal is to make certain that enough information is provided for the user to accomplish the task without undue confusion or navigation.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: GOV.UK-style HMRC Self Assessment registration form. The only statement of the required DD/MM/YYYY date format sits in a single high-contrast notice at the very top of the form; the governed Date of birth field (a Day/Month/Year group with a proper label but no inline hint) is rendered ~1262px below it, after two full sections and two dividers, off the first viewport. The cue is not perceivable at the point of entry.
pages.mechanism: Format instruction (a non-customary date format) is stated once at top-of-form inside role=note and is orphaned from its field by reading-order/pixel distance; the date group has no aria-describedby to the note and no adjacent hint, so at the point of input neither sighted nor screen-reader users are presented the instruction for that control.
pages.selectorNote: Top-of-form DD/MM/YYYY notice orphaned far above the governed dob field
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The instruction text exists, is high-contrast, and sits in a role=note, and the DOB field has a visible label and labelled group, so every 'instruction exists?' / 'field labelled?' check passes. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse have no model of reading-order or pixel DISTANCE between an instruction and the control it governs, nor whether a user reaching the field still perceives a top-of-page note as that field's instruction — a rendered point-of-entry perception judgment. Verified: notice bottom y=256, DOB top y=1518 (1262px apart, below first viewport), no own inline hint.

citation.quote: The goal is to make certain that enough information is provided for the user to accomplish the task without undue confusion or navigation.

pages.scenario: Tidewater Federal Credit Union 'Reset your security answer' page. The security-answer field has a strict case-sensitive, space-significant matching rule (#answer-rule). The rule is wired via aria-describedby but rendered .sr-only, so it is announced to AT yet never shown to sighted users, who type the answer however they remember it and are rejected.
pages.mechanism: The security-answer field's matching rule (case-sensitive, spaces significant) lives in #answer-rule, correctly associated via aria-describedby, but the span is class='sr-only' (1px clipped box; NOT display:none, NOT aria-hidden). It stays in the accessibility tree so screen readers announce it, yet it is invisible on screen — a sighted user sees the 'Your answer' field with no cue that case and spaces matter. Orphaned from sighted users by visually-hidden styling.
pages.primarySelector: details.help (open=false) wrapping #po-help, the help body for #po
pages.selectorNote: sr-only matching-rule instruction served only to AT, invisible to sighted users (orig details.help mismatch)
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The instruction is non-empty, present in the DOM, and aria-describedby correctly references an existing id, so 'instruction exists?' and 'programmatic association?' both pass; a closed <details> is valid, intentional markup that no linter flags. Tools do not evaluate a disclosure's open/closed state as a failure and cannot judge that the hidden content is a mandatory format rule sighted users need before typing. Screenshot confirmed: rendered page shows only the toggle, no format text.

citation.quote: It is possible for controls and inputs to have an appropriate accessible name or description (e.g. using aria-label="...") and therefore pass Success Criterion 4.1.2, but to still fail this success criterion (if the labels or instructions aren't presented to all users, not just those using assistive technologies).

pages.scenario: Healthcare patient portal (Cedar Park Health — Add your insurance). The Member ID field needs a non-obvious format (3-letter carrier prefix + 9 digits, no spaces). The format instruction is present in the DOM, complete, sits directly beneath the field, and is wired with aria-describedby, but it is styled font-size:9px in #cdd4da on white (~1.5:1) — far below readable size/contrast. The neighboring Group number hint is normal-sized and readable, proving the orphaning is styling, not a missing node.
pages.mechanism: The required-format instruction is present and adjacent but rendered too small and too low-contrast to be perceived as the field's instruction by a typical sighted user; effectively the field has no usable format guidance even though the text exists and is announced to AT via aria-describedby. Orphaned by sub-legible styling.
pages.selectorNote: Member-ID format hint rendered 9px in #cdd4da, unreadable as the field's instruction
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The instruction is a complete sentence present in the DOM and associated via aria-describedby, so 'instruction exists/associated' passes. A contrast scanner may emit only a generic low-contrast note (1.4.3 has size carve-outs and tools key on computed style, not meaning) and cannot infer that the unreadable text is the field's required-format instruction and that 3.3.2 is consequently failed. Verified computed font-size=9px, contrast 1.5:1; screenshot shows a near-invisible smudge while the adjacent Group hint is legible.

citation.quote: Providing labels and instructions (including examples of expected data formats) helps all users — but particularly those with cognitive, language, and learning disabilities — to enter information correctly.

pages.scenario: University graduate financial-aid form (Lakemont State University — Taxpayer information). The Taxpayer identification number field requires exactly 9 digits with no dashes or spaces. That readable, high-contrast format rule is collected into a 'Notes' block placed AFTER the 'Save and continue' submit button, so in both visual and DOM reading order it follows the action rather than informing the field; a user who fills the fields and clicks submit never sees it.
pages.mechanism: The field's format instruction is positioned after the submit action (and below the field it governs) in both visual and reading order, so it cannot inform the control at the point of entry; the user is forced into back-tracking the SC warns against. Orphaned by post-action placement.
pages.primarySelector: .post-notes (the <ul> after button[type=submit]) — TIN '9 digits with no dashes or spaces' item; governs #tin which has no adjacent hint
pages.selectorNote: Notes block placed after submit button; TIN format rule never informs the field
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The instruction is non-empty, high-contrast, readable, present in the DOM, and the TIN field has a proper visible label, so 'instruction exists?' and 'field labelled?' pass. Tools have no notion of whether an instruction is positioned before or after the control/action it governs, nor that a trailing Notes list explains a field rendered far above. Verified: notes block follows the button in DOM order, is visually below the button, and is below the TIN field; TIN has no own adjacent hint.

citation.quote: Providing labels and instructions (including identification of required fields) can prevent users from making incomplete or incorrect form submissions, which prevents users from having to navigate once more through a page/form in order to fix submission errors.

pages.scenario: Northwind Tickets checkout payment step. The Security code (#cvc) field's only cue about digit count and location is #cvc-note, which is absolutely positioned to the lower-left of the payment row and so renders beneath the full-width Card number field rather than beside the Security code input it actually governs; proximity attaches it to the wrong field.
pages.mechanism: The Security-code (CVC) format note (#cvc-note: 3 digits on the back, 4 on the front for Amex) is correctly tied to #cvc via aria-describedby and follows it in source order, but .cvc-note is position:absolute; left:0; bottom:0 within the payment row, so it paints in the empty band beneath the full-width 'Card number' field above — visually reading as the Card number's instruction, while the Security code box (upper-right) appears to have none. Orphaned by wrong-position rendering.
pages.primarySelector: .hint paragraph 'Enter the 9-digit number printed in the bottom-left of your check…' — the instruction for #routing, rendered in the grid cell beside #nickname
pages.selectorNote: Absolutely-positioned CVC instruction paints under Card number, not the Security code it governs
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every field has a proper visible label and the instruction text is present, readable, and high-contrast, so 'field labelled?' and 'instruction exists?' pass. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse reason about DOM order and programmatic association, not the rendered 2-D position of an instruction relative to multiple candidate fields in a CSS grid; they cannot compute which field a hint visually belongs to. Verified: routing hint top y=245 sits ~10px below the nickname field bottom (y=235) — same row band, beside a different field.

citation.quote: The intent of this success criterion is to have content authors present instructions or labels that identify the controls in a form so that users know what input data is expected.

pages.scenario: Events/community ticketing form (Harborfront Film Festival — Reserve your screening pass). PASS boundary: the Screening date field uses the same non-customary date format (DD-MMM-YYYY, e.g. 14-SEP-2026) that the failing cases orphan, but the instruction is rendered as normal-sized, high-contrast text immediately beneath the field, visible to all users at the point of entry, and additionally associated via aria-describedby. Nothing is distant, collapsed, sub-legible, post-action, or in the wrong column.
pages.mechanism: The format instruction is present AND perceivably presented as this field's instruction: adjacent, legible (13px full contrast), in the same column directly below the input, and announced to AT via aria-describedby on focus — exactly the adjacent, presented-to-all pattern SC 3.3.2 requires. No orphaning mechanism present.
pages.primarySelector: #date-hint (the inline format instruction for #show-date, immediately below it, same column, aria-describedby=date-hint)
pages.selectorNote: Inline legible date-format hint directly below its field (PASS boundary; instruction properly bound)
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Automated tools would also pass this page, but for the shallow reason that instruction text exists — they cannot distinguish this genuinely-bound instruction from the orphaned ones in case-01..05 where the same kind of text exists but is not perceivably presented. Included so the aspect is judged on perceivable binding to the control, not the mere presence of instruction text. Verified: hint 13.12px, immediately below, same column, aria-describedby present.

citation.quote: A field for entering a date has text instructions to indicate the correct format for the date.

aspects.title: False-positive guard: links and non-data-entry controls correctly out of scope (do not require labels/instructions)
aspects.plain: Buttons, links, and toggles aren't data-entry fields, so they correctly need no input instructions and shouldn't be flagged for lacking them.
aspects.description: 3.3.2 explicitly does NOT apply to links or other interactive controls that are not associated with data entry (expand/collapse widgets, menu toggles, tabs, pagination links, accordions, dialog-open buttons). The uncovered situation is the INAPPLICABLE / correct-pass case that prevents false positives: a page rich in buttons, links, and disclosure widgets that legitimately have NO field-style instructions because they are not data-entry controls. An evaluator (human or model) must recognize the scope boundary and NOT demand a '3.3.2 instruction' for a non-input control, while still correctly flagging any genuine data-entry field on the same page that lacks instruction. This guards against over-flagging and tests whether the evaluator has internalized the scope clause rather than treating every interactive element as needing input instructions.
aspects.scLimb: Understanding intent — applies only to controls associated with data entry; explicit scope clause excluding links and non-data-entry interactive components.
aspects.whyUncovered: No ACT rule/test exists, and there is no inapplicable/pass fixture in the corpus at all (testCaseCount 0). The techniques only demonstrate data-entry controls; nothing operationalizes the scope boundary that links/disclosure widgets are out of scope. The seed file is entirely failing data-entry patterns. Recognizing that a control is NOT a data-entry control — and therefore needs no 3.3.2 instruction — is a semantic/contextual judgment about each control's role and purpose that a naive checker (or an over-eager model) can get wrong by demanding labels everywhere. This is a precision/over-flagging guard that requires reasoning about what each control does.

references.quote: This success criterion does not apply to links or other controls (such as an expand/collapse widget, or similar interactive components) that are not associated with data entry.

The use of "requires" in this criterion's normative wording does not mean that the criterion only applies to required form fields... The criterion applies to all form fields, whether they're required or optional.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: Developer-docs 'Webhooks' page dense with non-data-entry controls (9 sidebar nav links, 5 expand/collapse FAQ disclosures, 3 anchor jumps, Copy + Theme buttons) plus exactly ONE genuine data-entry control — the docs search field — which is correctly given both a visible <label> and a visible usage instruction. Overall page passes 3.3.2; the disclosures/links/action buttons are out of scope.
pages.mechanism: Only one control is associated with data entry (input[type=search] #q, AX role searchbox 'Search the developer docs'); it carries label[for=q] + #q-hint instruction via aria-describedby. The 17 links and 7 buttons are navigation/disclosure/action controls to which 3.3.2 does not apply, so they correctly owe no field instruction.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse emit no 3.3.2 finding, but only by confirming each control merely HAS an accessible name — they cannot perform the real judgment that the non-input controls are correctly EXEMPT (disclosures/links not associated with data entry) while the one input is correctly instructed. Distinguishing a data-entry control from a disclosure/link/action button is a semantic role/purpose judgment, not an attribute lint; the fixture exposes evaluators that over-apply 3.3.2 to every interactive element.

citation.quote: This success criterion does not apply to links or other controls (such as an expand/collapse widget, or similar interactive components) that are not associated with data entry.

pages.scenario: Long-form news article whose entire interactive surface is navigation/action controls — breadcrumb links, a 'Share' menu-button opening a menu of share links, a Print action button, prev/next + numbered pagination links, related-reading links, topic tags — with ZERO data-entry fields (no form, no input, no editable element). The correct disposition is inapplicable.
pages.mechanism: SC 3.3.2 applies only 'when content requires user input.' The accessibility tree confirms data-entry-role nodes: NONE (17 links, 3 buttons, no input/textbox/combobox/checkbox). With no form-element population, there is nothing for 3.3.2 to test (Trusted Tester DNA; EN 'does not contain content relevant').
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Tools emit no 3.3.2 finding simply because there are no inputs to label, but 'no rule fired' is not the affirmative judgment 'inapplicable because nothing here is a data-entry control.' A checker cannot tell whether silence means passed, no-inputs, or skipped. Recognising that the share menu-button, pagination, and breadcrumbs are navigation (not data entry) and therefore neither owe nor lack a 3.3.2 instruction is a scope judgment that requires reasoning about each control's purpose.

citation.quote: DNA if the page does not have form elements or all form elements are disabled.

pages.scenario: Banking 'Statement summary' trap page: a <div contenteditable=false> is styled to look exactly like a filled text input (read-only balance '$2,418.05'), and a <button> is styled to look like a select/combobox ('Jun 2026') but opens a dialog of statement links. Both LOOK like fields but are not data entry. The one real data-entry control (Search transactions) is correctly labelled + instructed. Page passes 3.3.2.
pages.mechanism: By role/behaviour the input-looking controls are not data entry: AX confirms the balance div is StaticText (contenteditable=false, aria-readonly=true, not a textbox, not a tab stop) and the period control is a button (aria-haspopup=dialog). Only #txn is a searchbox, satisfied by label[for=txn] + #txn-hint. 3.3.2 owes the read-only display and dialog-opener no instruction despite their input-like styling.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A contenteditable=false div is not an <input>, so no 'missing label' rule fires; the period control is a named button — automated tools flag nothing. The inverse risk they cannot adjudicate is a human/model OVER-flagging these because they visually resemble text boxes. Deciding that an input-looking element is in fact read-only output (or a dialog-opener) requires reasoning about editability, role, and behaviour, not reading an attribute.

citation.quote: This success criterion does not apply to links or other controls (such as an expand/collapse widget, or similar interactive components) that are not associated with data entry.

pages.scenario: City parking-permits page full of out-of-scope controls (4 jump links, 5 policy accordions, breadcrumb, language menu-button, back-to-top) plus EXACTLY ONE genuine data-entry control: a feedback <textarea> that has aria-label='Feedback' (so 4.1.2/axe pass) but NO visible label and NO visible instruction — only a placeholder that vanishes on input. That single field is the sole 3.3.2 failure.
pages.mechanism: The textarea has a programmatic accessible name (aria-label, AX textbox 'Feedback') but no label/instruction presented to ALL users; the placeholder is not a visible label because it disappears on input. 3.3.2 requires the cue be presented to everyone, not just AT users (it explicitly distinguishes this from 4.1.2). The accordions/links are disclosures/navigation and out of scope, so the failure is confined to this one field.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The textarea HAS an accessible name via aria-label, so axe's 'form elements must have labels' and 4.1.2 checks PASS — no tool flags it. Catching the 3.3.2 failure needs two human judgments no checker makes: (1) a placeholder-only cue is not a visible label/instruction because it vanishes on input; and (2) the failure is isolated to this one data-entry control while the surrounding accordions and links are out of scope and must not be over-flagged.

citation.quote: It is possible for controls and inputs to have an appropriate accessible name or description (e.g. using aria-label="...") and therefore pass Success Criterion 4.1.2, but to still fail this success criterion (if the labels or instructions aren't presented to all users, not just those using assistive technologies).

pages.scenario: Recipe page where out-of-scope controls (Recipe-actions menu-button, 4 step disclosures, scale toggle buttons, tag/jump links) coexist with a genuine data-entry selection control: an ingredient shopping checklist of real <input type=checkbox>. Each checkbox's label is a quantity-only fragment ('2 fillets','1 tbsp','to taste') and the ingredient noun is in an aria-hidden adjacent column, so per-option labels don't say WHAT is selected. The checkbox group fails 3.3.2; the menu/disclosures/toggles do not.
pages.mechanism: Checkboxes are in scope per the Intent ('checkboxes... each option must have an appropriate label so that users know what they are actually selecting'). AX confirms each checkbox's accessible name is the bare quantity ('2 fillets', etc.) because the meaningful noun column is aria-hidden and there is no fieldset/legend or group name. A screen-reader user cannot tell what they are selecting → fail, on the checkbox group only.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every checkbox HAS an associated <label> (the quantity), so axe's 'form elements must have labels' PASSES — no tool flags it. Judging that a present, correctly-associated label nonetheless fails 'so that users know what they are actually selecting' — because the ingredient noun is excluded from the accessible name — is a semantic judgment about the option's meaning. Tools also cannot tell the surrounding menu-button/disclosures/toggles are correctly out of scope.

citation.quote: In the case of radio buttons, checkboxes, comboboxes, or similar controls that provide users with options, each option must have an appropriate label so that users know what they are actually selecting.

pages.scenario: CRM analytics dashboard dense with non-data-entry controls — a 4-tab tablist, 'Open settings' dialog-trigger, 'Refresh' action button, 'Export' menu-button, Day/Week/Month aria-pressed toggle group, and custom <span role=button> chart 'player' controls — plus exactly ONE data-entry control, the 'Filter deals' combobox, correctly given a visible <label> and a visible instruction. Page passes 3.3.2.
pages.mechanism: AX confirms one data-entry role (combobox 'Filter deals'), satisfied by label[for=dealFilter] + #filter-hint; the 9 buttons, 4 tabs, and 5 links (incl. custom span role=button player controls) are actions/navigation/toggles to which 3.3.2 does not apply. Adding field instructions to action/tab/toggle controls would be the unnecessary clutter the Intent warns against.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Tools raise no 3.3.2 issue only because every control happens to have an accessible name and the filter has a <label>. They cannot perform the discriminating scope judgment this fixture is about: which of a dozen dense, partly-custom controls are associated with data entry (exactly one) versus actions/navigation/toggles (the rest). A scope-blind evaluator is liable to over-flag the Refresh button or the custom span role=button player controls as 'missing input instructions.'

citation.quote: The intent of this success criterion is not to clutter the page with unnecessary information but to provide important cues and instructions that will benefit people with disabilities. Too much information or instruction can be just as harmful as too little.

aspects.title: Error identified in text but no correction suggestion given, though the fix is clearly knowable
aspects.plain: A form says what's wrong ('Invalid date') but never tells you how to fix it, even though the correct format or rule is clearly knowable.
aspects.description: This is the central, distinctive obligation of 3.3.3 versus 3.3.1: the page DOES identify the error in text (so 3.3.1 passes and any 'is there an error message' heuristic is satisfied), but the message stops at naming the problem and never tells the user HOW TO FIX it, even though the correction is plainly knowable from the field's constraints. Examples: 'Invalid date' with no format given, 'Password not strong enough' with no rules listed, 'Invalid entry' for a field that accepts exactly one of a small enumerated set. The required human judgment is twofold: (1) is a correction knowable here, and (2) does the present text actually convey it, or merely restate that something is wrong. A self-contained HTML page can be pre-rendered in its post-submit error state so no interaction is needed.
aspects.scLimb: Core PASS/FAIL obligation: 'the suggestions are provided to the user' (the harder follow-up to 3.3.1's 'is the error identified') when suggestions for correction are known.
aspects.whyUncovered: The ACT corpus for 3.3.3 is entirely empty (0 rules, 0 test cases), so there is no executable case for the pass/fail obligation at all. Automated tools at best detect that error TEXT exists (the 3.3.1 limb); they cannot judge whether that text contains an actionable suggestion versus a bare restatement, because both are valid non-empty strings. Distinguishing 'Invalid date' from 'Invalid date — use MM/DD/YYYY' requires semantic reading of whether a correction is present.

references.quote: 3.3.1 asks *"is the error identified & described?"*; 3.3.3 asks the harder follow-up *"does it tell you how to fix it?"*.
Suggestions for corrected input are provided, OR The description contains adequate information for the user to know what is required to fix the error.
persons with cognitive limitations may find it difficult to understand how to correct the errors. People with visual disabilities may not be able to figure out exactly how to correct the error.
Provide examples of the correct data entry for the field, Describe the correct data entry for the field, Show values of the correct data entry that are similar to the user's data entry

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: Travis County homestead-exemption form, post-submit error state. Date-of-birth field holds a real but misshapen value (3-7-1965); server accepts only MM/DD/YYYY. The associated error reads only 'Invalid date.' with no format, example, or hint anywhere on the page, though the correction is trivially knowable.
pages.mechanism: Bare restatement of a format error: the message names the error in text (3.3.1 passes) but omits the knowable fixed accepted format (MM/DD/YYYY), so a screen-reader/cognitive user is told THAT it is wrong but never HOW to fix it.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every structural facet passes (label resolves, aria-describedby resolves to a non-empty string, aria-invalid=true, role=alert summary, ~7:1 contrast). 'Invalid date.' and 'Invalid date — use MM/DD/YYYY' are both valid non-empty strings correctly wired to the field; no checker reads the value + the field's fixed accepted format + the message together to judge that a correction is knowable yet absent. That is semantic judgment, not a linter rule.

citation.quote: Provide examples of the correct data entry for the field, Describe the correct data entry for the field, Show values of the correct data entry that are similar to the user's data entry

pages.scenario: Lumen Hall box-office reservation card (the deliberate PASS twin of case-01), post-submit error state. The performance-date field (value 7/4/2025, missing leading zero) accepts only MM/DD/YYYY, but the error SUPPLIES the knowable correction in text: 'Use a two-digit month and day with a four-digit year — MM/DD/YYYY (for example, 07/04/2025).'
pages.mechanism: The error message both describes the required format AND gives a worked example matching the user's intent, so the suggestion of corrected input is provided to the user — satisfying the 3.3.3 obligation that case-01 violates.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: This is the crux of the aspect: an automated checker scores case-01 (fail) and case-02 (pass) IDENTICALLY because every structural facet is the same (label, resolved aria-describedby, aria-invalid, contrast). The only thing separating pass from fail is whether the non-empty string contains an actionable correction versus a restatement — meaning no axe/WAVE/Lighthouse rule reads.

citation.quote: Where errors are detected, suggest known ways to correct them.

pages.scenario: Cadence HR workspace-creation form, post-submit error state. The chosen password 'summertime' violates 3 of 4 rules that are literally encoded in the page's own RULES array in the inline <script> (>=12 chars, uppercase, digit, symbol). The validator computes the failed-rule set but the visible error reads only 'Password does not meet requirements.' — no rule is surfaced and no policy hint appears anywhere in the UI.
pages.mechanism: Bare restatement where the system already knows the specific failed rules: the message names the failure category but withholds the knowable, safe-to-state new-password requirements (the security carve-out does not apply to creation rules).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The password policy lives in JavaScript, not in any attribute; checkers confirm label + resolved aria-describedby + aria-invalid + contrast (3.3.1 passes) but cannot read the RULES array, determine which knowable rules the value breaks, and judge that the visible string surfaces none of them. 'does not meet requirements' vs an enumerated rule list are both valid strings — only semantic reading distinguishes them.

citation.quote: Providing information about how to correct the error would jeopardize the security or purpose of the content (e.g., details about an incorrect password).

pages.scenario: Beacon Mutual auto-insurance quote wizard, post-submit error state. The free-text 'State' field accepts only the fixed enumeration of 50 USPS two-letter codes; the user typed 'Calif.' (one edit from CA). The error reads only 'Please enter a valid state.' — no list of allowed values, no format hint, no nearest-match 'Did you mean CA?'.
pages.mechanism: Bare restatement on a limited-allowed-values field: the correction is doubly knowable (the allowed set is a fixed list AND the entry maps to exactly one valid value), yet neither the list nor the nearest match is suggested.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Checkers confirm label + resolved aria-describedby + aria-invalid + contrast (3.3.1 passes) but have no way to know this free-text field's true domain is a 50-value enumeration, nor that 'Calif.' is one edit from 'CA'; they cannot judge that the message lists none of the allowed values and suggests no match. Distinguishing 'Please enter a valid state.' from 'Enter the two-letter code, e.g. CA' requires knowing the allowed-value set.

citation.quote: When input must be one of a set of allowed values, the text description should indicate this fact. It should include the list of values if possible, or suggest the allowed value that is most similar to the entered value.

pages.scenario: Ferndale Roastery B2B wholesale reorder line, post-submit error state. A custom role=spinbutton 'Cases per order' control with aria-valuemin=1/aria-valuemax=10 holds the value 24. The human-readable error reads only 'Value not allowed.' and never states the permitted 1–10 range, even though that range is the entire knowable correction and is declared on the same element.
pages.mechanism: Bare restatement where the range bound (aria-valuemin/valuemax) is programmatic control metadata, NOT a corrected-input suggestion after a failed submit; the error text surfaced post-submit carries no range, so the suggestion the SC requires is not provided.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse see an exemplary spinbutton (role, accessible name, valuemin/valuemax/valuenow, associated message, contrast) and could even be MISLED by the presence of valuemin/max into assuming the user is guided. No checker judges that the human-readable error omits the range, or that range metadata on a control is not the same as a corrected-input suggestion. 'Value not allowed.' vs 'Enter a quantity from 1 to 10.' are both valid strings.

citation.quote: Goal: Users get suggestions on how to resolve errors.

pages.scenario: Orbit Developer Hub 'claim your handles' step, post-submit error state, built as a controlled comparison. The Username field error reads only 'Username unavailable.' (no suggestion), while the sibling Project-slug field on the same page offers computed alternatives ('Taken. Try one of: orbit-telemetry-2, orbit-telemetry-io, or telemetry-by-mira.') — proving the alternative-suggestion engine exists and runs here, so the missing username suggestion is a genuine failure, not a not-knowable DNA.
pages.mechanism: Bare restatement where the correction is provably knowable: the adjacent field uses the same suggestion engine to produce alternatives, defeating any 'suggestions are not known' defense, yet the username error provides no alternatives and no naming-rule hint.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Checkers see two structurally identical, correctly-wired error messages (labels resolve, aria-describedby resolves to non-empty strings, aria-invalid, contrast) — 3.3.1 passes on both. No tool reads the CONTENT of the two messages to notice one carries actionable suggestions and the other is an empty restatement, and none reasons that the suggestion-bearing sibling proves the correction is knowable for the failing field. That cross-field content-comparing inference is pure human judgment.

citation.quote: The objective of this technique is to suggest correct text where the information supplied by the user is not accepted and possible correct text is known. The suggestions may include correct spelling or similar text from a known pool of possible text.

aspects.title: Suggestion text is present but wrong, misleading, or contradicts the actual validation rule
aspects.plain: A form gives a specific fix-it suggestion, but it's factually wrong for the field, so even following it the input still gets rejected.
aspects.description: The page provides a confident, specific correction suggestion, so every 'a suggestion is present' check passes — but the suggestion is factually incorrect for this field: it names the wrong format, the wrong allowed range, a 'did-you-mean' value that is itself invalid, or a fix the validator will still reject. This is the direct analogue of 'alt exists but misrepresents the image.' Per Trusted Tester the obligation is that the guidance provides SUFFICIENT/ADEQUATE detail to fix the error; a misleading suggestion fails that even though text exists. Only a human who knows the field's true rule can detect the mismatch between the suggestion and reality.
aspects.scLimb: Quality/correctness of the provided suggestion: 'adequate information ... to know what is required to fix the error' / 'sufficient details for how to correct the error.'
