aspects.whyUncovered: No ACT case exists, and even a hypothetical one would assert on the presence of suggestion text, not its correctness against the field's true constraint. Automated tools have no model of what the field actually accepts, so they cannot tell that 'Use DD/MM/YYYY' is wrong when the parser only accepts MM/DD/YYYY, or that 'Did you mean January?' was offered for an input that was already valid. Correctness is a semantic, ground-truth judgment.

references.quote: Determine whether guidance provides **sufficient details** for how to correct the error and/or offers suggestions of corrected input.
The description contains adequate information for the user to know what is required to fix the error.
The conversion of the input data interpreted as a different month format, e.g., "Do you mean 'December'?"

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: Credit-union online-banking password setup. A visible policy box states 'at least 12 characters' and the field enforces minlength=12, but the confident, announced error suggestion says 'Use at least 8 characters to continue.' Following the suggestion (an 8-char password) re-fails.
pages.mechanism: On failed submit a role=alert region (aria-describedby-linked) announces a specific corrective threshold of 8 characters, but the field's enforced minimum is 12; the only corrective guidance offered names a value the field rejects, so acting on it loops the user back to the same error.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse confirm a specific, associated, announced suggestion is present (TT 5.G presence check passes). None parse the number '8' from the alert prose, read minlength=12 / the validator / the policy bullets, and judge that 8<12 makes the suggested fix self-defeating. They have no model of the field's true constraint to test the suggestion against.

citation.quote: The description contains adequate information for the user to know what is required to fix the error.

pages.scenario: GOV.UK-styled UK council recycling-centre postcode lookup (lang=en-GB, label 'UK postcode', hint 'SW1A 1AA'). The announced error suggestion says 'Postcodes must be 5 digits. Please enter your 5-digit postcode (for example, 90210).' UK postcodes are alphanumeric; no 5-digit value can ever match the field's pattern.
pages.mechanism: A role=alert suggestion names a US-ZIP 5-digit format for an alphanumeric UK-postcode field; the field's pattern cannot match any all-digit string, so following the announced suggestion produces an infinite re-failure loop for a screen-reader user with no visual access to the contradicting 'SW1A 1AA' hint.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Scanners have no geographic/world knowledge: they cannot know UK postcodes are alphanumeric, that '90210' is a US ZIP, or parse the field's pattern to see no 5-digit value can match. The presence-of-suggestion check passes; judging that the suggested format is wrong for this locale requires human knowledge of what a UK postcode is.

citation.quote: It should include the list of values if possible, or suggest the allowed value that is most similar to the entered value.

pages.scenario: Home-goods checkout promo field. An unknown code triggers a 'did you mean SPRING20? Apply SPRING20' suggestion, but the page's own visible promotions table shows SPRING20 expired 30 Apr 2026 while today is 14 June 2026; clicking Apply re-fails with 'This code has expired.'
pages.mechanism: A role=status live region offers a one-click 'did you mean' correction (canonical G177 sufficient pattern) whose suggested value is itself invalid/expired; the single corrective action the page offers, when activated by a screen-reader user, lands back on an error.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The page exemplifies the sufficient technique on its face (suggestion present, associated, announced, actionable). A scanner cannot know the live set of valid codes, cannot read the expiry from the promotions table, and cannot simulate the Apply click to discover the suggested code is rejected. Judging the suggestion is itself invalid is a semantic ground-truth comparison.

citation.quote: Check that the user is presented with suggestions for the correct text.

pages.scenario: Contents-insurance quote wizard, 'number of high-value items'. Visible help text says 'up to 50 scheduled items' and the field enforces max=50, but the announced error suggestion says 'Please enter a number between 1 and 100.' Any value 51-100 the suggestion invites is rejected.
pages.mechanism: A role=alert suggestion gives an explicit corrective RANGE (1-100) whose upper bound is double the field's true/enforced ceiling (50); a user acting on the announced range re-enters a value (e.g. 75) that is squarely inside the suggested range and squarely rejected by the field.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The suggestion is present, specific, associated, and announced (presence check passes). No scanner parses 'between 1 and 100' from the prose, reads max=50 / the validator / the 'up to 50' help text, and computes that 100 exceeds the true ceiling so the suggested range is partly invalid. It has no model of the field's allowed range.

citation.quote: information that is provided by the user but that falls outside the required data format or allowed values

pages.scenario: Festival 'arrival month as a number 1-12' field. Typing a valid '07' (July) fires a gratuitous 'We read that as the 7th - did you mean December? Use December instead' suggestion that overwrites the field with 12. 07 was already valid and 7 is July, not December.
pages.mechanism: A role=status live region surfaces a confident 'did you mean' correction on input that was ALREADY VALID (no aria-invalid is set, confirming no real error), and the offered substitution is the wrong month (7 maps to July, not December); a screen-reader user trusting the single corrective action silently converts a correct July choice into an unintended December one.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A scanner sees a 'did you mean' suggestion present, associated, announced, and actionable (the sufficient pattern). It cannot know that '07' was already valid (no error to correct), that 7 means July not December, or that the offered substitution is wrong. Recognising both the gratuitousness and the factual error requires human knowledge of the month-number mapping and the field's validity state.

citation.quote: The conversion of the input data interpreted as a different month format, e.g., "Do you mean 'December'?"

pages.scenario: PASS twin. Patient-portal mobile-number field requires exactly 10 digits incl. area code (stated in help text + enforced). A 7-digit entry fires an accurate, actionable suggestion: 'Enter all 10 digits, including your 3-digit area code - for example (415) 555-2671. You entered 7 digits.' Following it (adding the area code) is accepted.
pages.mechanism: On failed submit a role=alert region announces the correct required format, a worked example that is itself a valid value, and the user's actual digit count; the named format matches the validator and acting on it resolves the error, satisfying 'adequate information to know what is required to fix the error.'
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A naive scanner cannot certify a PASS on this limb either: it only confirms suggestion text exists, is associated, and is announced - equally true on the failing pages in this set. Confirming the suggestion is CORRECT (named format matches validator, the example is a valid value, the count is accurate, following it clears the error) requires a human to read it, infer the field's true rule, and verify they agree.

citation.quote: Provide examples of the correct data entry for the field,

aspects.title: Suggestion correctly WITHHELD for a security/purpose-sensitive field (exception that must read as PASS)
aspects.plain: For a security-sensitive field like a password, giving only a generic error and no specific fix is correct to avoid leaking information, so it shouldn't be flagged as a failure.
aspects.description: The SC explicitly carves out 'unless it would jeopardize the security or purpose of the content.' A correct implementation of a security-sensitive field (login password, security-question answer, 2FA code, payment CVV) deliberately gives a generic, non-revealing error and offers no specific correction — and that is the right outcome, a PASS. The hard human judgment is recognizing when withholding a suggestion is correct (and must not be flagged) versus when the same generic message ('Invalid input') on a non-sensitive field is a real failure. This inverts the naive heuristic: here the absence of a suggestion is conformant.
aspects.scLimb: Exception clause: 'unless it would jeopardize the security or purpose of the content' (TT DNA: 'details about an incorrect password').
aspects.whyUncovered: The ACT corpus is empty and, per the survey, no case exercises a security-sensitive field where correctly withholding a suggestion is the right outcome. Automated tools cannot classify a field as security/purpose-sensitive, so they would either never flag missing suggestions at all, or wrongly flag the deliberately-generic login error as a failure. Deciding the field's sensitivity and whether the exception applies is purely contextual.

references.quote: Providing information about how to correct the error would **jeopardize the security or purpose** of the content (e.g., details about an incorrect password).
If an input error is automatically detected and suggestions for correction are known, then the suggestions are provided to the user, unless it would jeopardize the security or purpose of the content.
unless the data is in a security related field where it would be inappropriate to retain the data for re-display (e.g. password)

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: Webmail login in the post-submit failed-login state. A single generic 'Email or password is incorrect. Please try again.' governs the credential pair, deliberately not revealing which half was wrong and offering no field-specific correction. The security exception applies (anti-enumeration), so withholding the suggestion is the correct, conformant outcome.
pages.mechanism: A role=alert error referenced by both email and password inputs via aria-describedby announces a generic credential failure plus the only non-jeopardizing correction ('try again'); a field-specific suggestion would leak whether the email exists or that the password was close, which the SC 3.3.3 security/purpose exception forbids, so the absence of a specific suggestion is required, not a defect.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse see a clean, named, programmatically-associated role=alert and cannot grade message specificity at all; the harder trap is a 'input error detected but no specific correction => fail' heuristic that would wrongly flag this. No tool can classify the inputs as security-sensitive credentials, know the SC 3.3.3 security exception applies, or judge that the deliberately-generic message is the required outcome — a purely contextual human judgment.

citation.quote: Providing information about how to correct the error would **jeopardize the security or purpose** of the content (e.g., details about an incorrect password).

pages.scenario: Bank wire-transfer security verification: the user mis-keys the last four digits of the recipient's account number. The error names the field and gives a non-revealing fix ('re-enter exactly as printed on the recipient's statement') but deliberately does NOT echo the expected digits or show the recipient account number, because the correct value is itself a secret. Withholding the literal correction is correct.
pages.mechanism: A role=alert tied to a labelled group of four single-char inputs via aria-describedby provides field identification and an out-of-band correction path while withholding the literal expected value; a G177-style 'show the suggested correct text' would print part of the recipient's account number, so the security/purpose exception requires withholding it — making the page conformant.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A structural scanner sees a labelled group, an associated role=alert, valid markup and good contrast — no objection. A suggestion-quality heuristic modelled on G177/G85 would actively MISJUDGE it, either flagging the page for not echoing the expected digits or pushing a developer to leak part of the account number. No tool can recognise the expected value is a secret and that withholding it is the conformant choice.

citation.quote: Check that other data previously entered by the user is re-displayed, unless the data is in a security related field where it would be inappropriate to retain the data for re-display (e.g. password).

pages.scenario: E-commerce checkout in post-submit error state shows two near-identical terse errors: 'Invalid security code.' on the CVV (correctly withheld, PASS limb) and 'Invalid.' on the ZIP code (a genuine failure — knowable, non-sensitive value with no description or suggestion). The judge must apply the security exception selectively; the page is overall FAILED because of the ZIP field.
pages.mechanism: #zip-error gives a bare 'Invalid.' on a non-sensitive field whose value (941) is three digits where a knowable 5-digit US ZIP is required; the security exception does not apply, so the missing description/suggestion is a real SC 3.3.3 failure, while the structurally-identical #cvv-error is conformant because the CVV is security-sensitive.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Both errors are structurally identical and well-formed (named, role=alert, aria-describedby-associated, high-contrast); axe/WAVE/Lighthouse object to neither and cannot grade message quality. A 'no suggestion => fail' heuristic would flag BOTH (wrongly faulting the CVV) or pass both (missing the ZIP failure). Distinguishing a security-sensitive field from a non-sensitive one with a knowable fix is exactly the contextual judgment tools cannot perform.

citation.quote: When input must be one of a set of allowed values, the text description should indicate this fact. It should include the list of values if possible, or suggest the allowed value that is most similar to the entered value.

pages.scenario: Patient-portal account-recovery identity check asks for date of birth and last-4 SSN. One factor is wrong; a single generic 'We couldn't verify your identity... try again, or call Member Services' deliberately does not reveal which factor failed or echo any expected value, with an out-of-band recovery path. Per-field disclosure would defeat identity proofing, so withholding is correct.
pages.mechanism: A single form-level role=alert shared by both inputs via aria-describedby announces a generic verification failure plus non-revealing correction paths; saying which knowledge factor matched would let an attacker brute-force the other and confirm a DOB/SSN fragment belongs to a real member, so the per-field suggestion 3.3.3 would normally want is forbidden by the security/purpose exception — the generic message is the conformant outcome.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The error is a clean, named, associated role=alert; axe/WAVE/Lighthouse object to nothing and cannot grade specificity. A heuristic flagging 'error detected but page does not say which field is wrong' would wrongly fault it. No tool can classify DOB + SSN-last-4 as identity-proofing knowledge factors, know per-field confirmation is forbidden, or judge that the generic message is conformant.

citation.quote:
If an input error is automatically detected and suggestions for correction are known, then
the suggestions are provided to the user, unless it would jeopardize the security or purpose of the content.

pages.scenario: Bank 'set a new password' screen. The author tried to be helpful and gave a very specific, well-associated suggestion for the rejected new password that LEAKS secrets, quoting the user's security-question answer ('Hawthorne') and previous password ('Maple2021!') verbatim. The exception should apply but the author violated it by disclosing. Over-disclosure FAIL.
pages.mechanism: #newpw-error (role=alert, tied to the password input via aria-describedby) contains a specific, fluent suggestion whose CONTENT discloses the user's stored security-question answer and previous password; the accessibility tree literally carries the secrets and screen-reader speech broadcasts them, jeopardizing the security the password field protects — the exact disclosure the SC 3.3.3 exception exists to prevent.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The message is grammatical, named, role=alert, programmatically associated, and high-contrast — a structurally model error suggestion that axe/WAVE/Lighthouse would praise and a 'did the page suggest a correction?' heuristic would mark PASS (the opposite of correct). No tool can recognise that the quoted strings are the user's security answer and prior password, nor that printing them jeopardizes security.

citation.quote: Providing information about how to correct the error would **jeopardize the security or purpose** of the content (e.g., details about an incorrect password).

pages.scenario: Two-step verification screen rejects a one-time code. Instead of a generic withheld message, the author gives an over-helpful suggestion that turns the field into a brute-force oracle: 'Almost! Your first 3 digits (4 1 9) are correct, but the code has 6 digits and you entered 5...'. Confirming the correct prefix and exact length collapses the code's entropy. Over-disclosure FAIL, distinct from case-05.
pages.mechanism: #otp-error (role=alert, tied to the six-input one-time-code group via aria-describedby) supplies partial-match feedback that confirms which leading digits matched and the exact expected length; this comparative oracle materially reduces the work to defeat the second factor, jeopardizing the security/purpose of the 2FA code — the disclosure the SC 3.3.3 exception forbids — so a well-formed suggestion still fails.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The message is friendly, named, role=alert, associated, and high-contrast — an exemplary error suggestion that axe/WAVE/Lighthouse would approve and a 'did the page help the user fix the error?' heuristic would mark PASS (exactly wrong). No tool can reason that 'first 3 digits correct + length is 6' is a security leak that collapses a 2FA code's entropy and defeats its purpose.

citation.quote:
If an input error is automatically detected and suggestions for correction are known, then
the suggestions are provided to the user, unless it would jeopardize the security or purpose of the content.

aspects.title: Correction not knowable: no suggestion required and absence must not be penalized (the DNA/precondition gate)
aspects.plain: For a free-text field where the system genuinely can't know the right answer, offering only a generic message is fine and shouldn't be penalized for lacking a suggestion.
aspects.description: 3.3.3 only obliges a suggestion when 'suggestions for correction are known.' For free-form fields where the correct value is genuinely not inferable by the system (a free-text 'Tell us why', an open-ended display name, a one-time human-verified value), no specific suggestion is possible and the page conformantly provides only a generic 'This field is required' or 'We couldn't verify this.' The judge must decide whether the correction is knowable at all before deciding pass/fail — a precondition gate that distinguishes 'no suggestion because none is possible' (PASS/DNA) from 'no suggestion despite one being obvious' (the first aspect's FAIL). This is a semantic call about the nature of the field, not its markup.
aspects.scLimb: Precondition / knowability gate: 'and suggestions for correction are known' (TT DNA: 'suggestions for correction cannot be provided because they are not knowable').
aspects.whyUncovered: Per the survey the knowability gate is uncovered: no ACT rule/test distinguishes a field whose correction is inferable from one where it is not. Automated tools have no concept of whether a correction is computable for a given field; they cannot tell an enumerable 'month' field (suggestion knowable, absence is a fail) from a free-text 'feedback' field (suggestion not knowable, absence is fine). The distinction is entirely about meaning and field semantics.

references.quote: Based on the type of input required, suggestions for correction **cannot be provided** because they are not knowable.
If an input error is automatically detected and suggestions for correction are known, then the suggestions are provided to the user
the intent of this success criterion is to ensure that users receive appropriate suggestions for correction of an input error if it is possible.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: E-commerce returns flow in post-submit error state: a required free-text 'Reason for return' textarea was left empty and shows only 'Please tell us your reason for return — this field is required.' No specific suggestion is offered, and none is possible because the field collects open-ended prose. Canonical knowability-gate PASS.
pages.mechanism: The only knowable rule for an open prose 'reason' field is non-empty, which the associated error states. SC 3.3.3 obliges a suggestion only when one is known; for a free-text reason the correct value is not inferable or enumerable, so the generic required-message is the conformant maximum. AT hears a complete, correct, sufficient message via aria-describedby; there is no missing suggestion to provide.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse confirm the structural facts (label, resolved aria-describedby, aria-invalid, contrast) but have no concept of whether a correction is COMPUTABLE for a field. They cannot tell an open prose field (suggestion not knowable -> absence fine, PASS) from an enumerable field like 'Month' (suggestion knowable -> absence a fail). A tool that flagged 'error present but no suggestion text' would WRONGLY fail this. The gate is a meaning judgment about field nature.

citation.quote: The intent of this success criterion is to ensure that users receive appropriate suggestions for correction of an input error if it is possible.

pages.scenario: Warranty-registration form in post-submit error state. Two fields show structurally identical 'Required' errors: an enumerable 'Purchase month' TEXT input (correct value is one of twelve known months -> suggestion knowable -> FAIL) sits next to a free-text 'Anything else we should know?' textarea (open prose -> no knowable suggestion -> PASS). The judge must split the gate per field; the page fails because the Month field fails.
pages.mechanism: 'Purchase month' has an enumerable correct set (January..December) so a suggestion is knowable ('Choose one of: ...'), but the field is a plain text box showing only 'Required' — the allowed values are nowhere in the accessibility tree, leaving the user to blind-guess. The free-text notes field passes the gate identically-worded. A single failing field fails the SC for the page.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The two errors are byte-for-byte structurally identical (same markup, same aria wiring, same '[label] — Required' string); axe/WAVE/Lighthouse pass both and cannot rank them. No tool models that 'Purchase month' has an enumerable correct set (knowable suggestion) while 'Anything else' is open prose (no knowable suggestion). Deciding which of two identical-looking errors is a failure is a semantic call about field meaning.

citation.quote: An input field requires that a month name be entered. If the user enters "12," suggestions for correction may include: A list of the acceptable values, e.g., "Choose one of: January, February, March, April, May, June, July, August, September, October, November, December."

pages.scenario: Credit-union 2FA sign-in step in post-submit error state: a wrong 6-digit one-time emailed code was entered and the field shows 'That code didn't match. Check the most recent email from us and enter the 6-digit code. Codes expire after 10 minutes.' No suggested correct value is offered. PASS under a DOUBLE DNA gate (un-inferable + security).
pages.mechanism: A random one-time code is not inferable from a wrong guess (not knowable), and echoing the correct code would jeopardize the security/purpose of verification — both are explicit DNA conditions. The associated message gives maximum actionable guidance (where to look, what to enter, the time limit, plus a 'send a new code' action) without revealing the secret, satisfying the SC.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A naive scan sees 'error present, no suggested value' and may flag a 3.3.3 fail. No tool can reason that the correct value is (a) un-inferable from a wrong guess and (b) deliberately withheld for security. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse confirm label, aria-describedby, aria-invalid, contrast but have no model of 'this value is a secret one-time code.' The double gate (knowability + security/purpose) is a semantic and policy judgment, not a markup property.

citation.quote: Providing information about how to correct the error would **jeopardize the security or purpose** of the content (e.g., details about an incorrect password).

pages.scenario: Creator-platform onboarding in post-submit error state: claiming page address 'plinth.co/studio' is rejected with only 'That address is already taken. Please choose another.' — no alternatives suggested. The INVERSION case: a unique-handle field superficially looks un-inferable like a free-form name, but the platform owns the taken/available registry, so concrete available alternatives ARE knowable and are withheld. FAIL.
pages.mechanism: Availability is computable by the system (it just ran the taken/available check), so a suggestion is KNOWN — WCAG's 'name from a known pool' scenario. Returning only 'already taken, choose another' forces the user into a blind trial-and-error resubmit loop with zero guidance toward an accepted value, exactly the burden 3.3.3 exists to remove. The generic message is NOT the conformant maximum because the field is not actually un-inferable.
pages.selectorNote: Errored file-upload field (corrupt PDF); error present at load, no knowable suggestion
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The error is present, visible, and correctly associated, so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse pass it structurally and stop. They cannot know that availability is computable — that the backend holds a registry from which valid alternatives could be generated. The whole judgment is recognizing that this field, despite resembling an un-inferable free-form name, has a KNOWABLE correction, flipping it from DNA/PASS to FAIL. No tool models field semantics or backend computability.

citation.quote: The objective of this technique is to suggest correct text where the information supplied by the user is not accepted and possible correct text is known. The suggestions may include correct spelling or similar text from a known pool of possible text.

pages.scenario: Multilingual community platform 'set your display name' step in post-submit error state: the blank field shows only 'Please enter a display name.' A self-chosen name (any language/script) is open-ended, so no specific suggestion is possible. PASS. i18n decoys (lang=ja note, dir=rtl Arabic example chip) invite over-scrutiny but do not change the verdict.
pages.mechanism: A free-choice display name has no knowable correct value — the system cannot guess or enumerate what a member wants to be called. The only knowable rule is non-empty, which the associated message plus the visible length hint convey. SC 3.3.3 obliges a suggestion only when one is known, so the generic required-message is conformant.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A checker flagging 'error present but no suggested value' would WRONGLY fail this conformant page. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse verify label, aria-describedby, aria-invalid, correct lang/dir on the multilingual passages, and contrast — all pass — but none can decide a self-chosen name is un-inferable and thus exempt from the suggestion obligation. That is a meaning judgment about the field's nature, the uncovered knowability gate.

citation.quote: Based on the type of input required, suggestions for correction **cannot be provided** because they are not knowable.

pages.scenario: County records-office identity-verification step in post-submit error state: the required 'Full legal name (exactly as printed on your photo ID)' field was left blank and shows 'Enter your full legal name exactly as it appears on your photo ID.' No suggested value — and none is possible, because a hand-verified legal name is known only to the applicant and their document. Boundary PASS that sharpens the gate next to the enumerable FAILs.
pages.mechanism: A human-verified legal name is un-inferable to the system (no database to enumerate it from); the only knowable rule is non-empty plus a human-checkable 'match your ID' instruction, which the associated message and visible hint state. Unlike the enumerable month or the computable slug, no correction is knowable here, so the same generic-message SHAPE that fails there PASSES here. A clerk verifies against the uploaded ID later.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A checker mechanically requiring a suggested value for every error would WRONGLY fail this — especially confusing because the same generic-message shape would correctly fail an enumerable field. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse confirm label, aria-describedby, aria-invalid, visible focus style, and contrast but cannot decide that a legal name is un-inferable to the system while a month name is enumerable. Distinguishing this boundary PASS from neighbouring FAILs is a per-field knowability judgment about meaning.

citation.quote: Based on the type of input required, suggestions for correction **cannot be provided** because they are not knowable.

aspects.title: Suggestion technically present but too vague/generic to actually let the user fix the error
aspects.plain: An error message gestures at fixing ('Please check your entry') but is too generic to tell you what to actually change, so you still can't correct the input.
aspects.description: The error message contains language that gestures at a fix but is so generic it does not give the user enough to actually correct the input: 'Please check your entry and try again', 'That doesn't look right — please fix it', 'Enter a valid value', 'Improve your input.' A presence-of-text check passes and even a 'does it mention fixing?' heuristic may pass, yet the user still cannot determine WHAT to change. Trusted Tester requires the description to contain ADEQUATE information for the user to know what is required to fix the error; vague filler fails that bar. The judgment is whether the words, in this field's context, are actionable — distinct from the 'wrong/misleading' aspect (which is confidently specific but false) and from the 'no suggestion' aspect (which has no fix language at all).
aspects.scLimb: Adequacy threshold of the suggestion: 'The description contains adequate information for the user to know what is required to fix the error' / 'sufficient details for how to correct the error.'
aspects.whyUncovered: No ACT case exists. Even a presence heuristic that scans for fix-oriented phrasing ('please correct', 'try again') is satisfied by vague filler. Judging whether the suggestion actually conveys what to change — given the specific field's constraints — is a semantic adequacy call no automated tool can make; 'Enter a valid value' is a syntactically valid suggestion but conveys nothing.

references.quote: The description contains adequate information for the user to know what is required to fix the error.
Determine whether guidance provides **sufficient details** for how to correct the error and/or offers suggestions of corrected input.
Where errors are detected, suggest known ways to correct them.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: Healthcare patient portal re-displays an appointment form after a failed POST. The date-of-birth field is correctly flagged (aria-invalid, aria-describedby error, role=alert summary, focus moved) but the inline error and summary both say only 'Please check your entry and try again.' — content-free filler on a field whose format (MM/DD/YYYY, in the past) is fully knowable. A sibling insurance-member-ID field is a PASS twin whose hint names the exact format.
pages.mechanism: 3.3.1 fully satisfied (error identified, associated, in a live role=alert, focused) but the suggestion is fix-oriented filler that conveys nothing about the knowable required format; SC 3.3.3 requires the description to contain adequate information to fix the error, which 'check your entry and try again' does not.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse confirm the error is present, non-empty, programmatically associated, and live (3.3.1 passes); a fix-phrasing heuristic ('please','try again','check') is satisfied by the string. No tool can judge that the words carry no field-specific content while the field's correct constraint is knowable — a semantic adequacy call.

citation.quote: The description contains adequate information for the user to know what is required to fix the error.

pages.scenario: E-commerce cart with an APG custom spinbutton (role=spinbutton, aria-valuemin=1, aria-valuemax=10) for quantity. A quantity of 14 is correctly flagged and announced in a live region, but the error reads only 'Enter a valid value.' — the valid range (1-10) is literally encoded in aria-valuemax yet never stated. A second product row is a PASS twin spinbutton whose error names the bound ('between 1 and 6').
pages.mechanism: The allowed range is enforced and present in the ARIA value attributes, making a suggestion possible and trivial; the default library validity string 'Enter a valid value' provides neither a suggested value nor the range, failing both TT result limbs.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Structurally a model APG spinbutton: bounded values, associated error, live status, clean roles/contrast — all pass automated checks and 3.3.1. 'Enter a valid value' reads as an instruction so a fix-phrasing heuristic passes. No scanner reasons that the valid range is aria-valuemin..aria-valuemax, that the message omits it, and that omission makes the suggestion inadequate.

citation.quote:
A list of the acceptable values, e.g., "Choose one of: January, February, March, April,
                  May, June, July, August, September, October, November, December."

pages.scenario: SaaS signup (Cobalt Project Tracker) validates a new password live: an aria-live=polite status announces the result, aria-invalid is set, the message is associated. On failure the only feedback is 'Improve your password.' while the enforced policy (>=12 chars, a digit, a symbol) is concrete and never surfaced. This is account creation, so the 3.3.3 security carve-out (incorrect login password) does not apply.
pages.mechanism: The creation policy is determinate and code-defined and stating it does not jeopardize security, so a correction suggestion is possible; 'Improve your password' gives no actionable direction (longer? a number? a symbol?), failing the adequacy bar.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Clean inline-validation widget: labelled input, live role=status, aria-invalid, aria-describedby, good contrast/focus — passes automated checks and 3.3.1. 'Improve your password' is an imperative so a fix-phrasing heuristic passes. No scanner reads the validator to learn the policy is >=12+digit+symbol, sees the message states none of it, and distinguishes a creation policy (must be stated) from a login response (must not) — both human judgments.

citation.quote:
Providing information about how to correct input errors allows users who have learning
            disabilities to fill in a form successfully.

pages.scenario: German state tax portal (lang=de) re-displays a tax-return form after a failed submit. The Steuer-Identifikationsnummer field is correctly flagged (aria-invalid, aria-describedby, role=alert, focus) but the message is the German filler 'Bitte überprüfen Sie Ihre Eingabe und versuchen Sie es erneut.' over a fixed, knowable 11-digit format. A sibling Postleitzahl field is an always-correct contrast control naming its format precisely.
pages.mechanism: The tax-ID format is fixed and publicly documented (exactly 11 digits, enforced by the validator), so a correction is suggestable; the German fix-oriented filler states neither the format nor an example nor a suggestion, failing 3.3.3 — and the adequacy judgment must be made on non-English prose.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: 3.3.1 passes regardless of language (error identified, associated, role=alert, focused). To flag this a tool must understand the German sentence is content-free filler, know the Steuer-ID's canonical 11-digit format, and judge the message withholds it — a cross-lingual semantic-adequacy chain; any error-quality heuristics that exist are English-tuned.

citation.quote: Provide examples of the correct data entry for the field,

pages.scenario: PASS boundary. A checkout shipping form flags the ZIP-code field with the SAME plumbing as the failing pages (aria-invalid, aria-describedby, role=alert, focus moved), but the message is ADEQUATE: 'Enter a 5-digit ZIP code, for example 90210. You entered "9021" — it looks like one digit is missing.' It names the format, gives an example, and suggests a correction from the user's own input. Exists to sharpen the line between 'mentions fixing' (fail) and 'tells you how' (pass).
pages.mechanism: The description contains adequate information for the user to know what is required (a 5-digit number, with an example) AND offers a suggested correction inferred from the input; either TT result limb alone would pass, and both are present.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: To a scanner this PASS is indistinguishable from the FAIL twins: all have present, non-empty, programmatically associated error text in a live role=alert with focus management. The pass/fail distinction is entirely a semantic-adequacy reading of the message contents, which axe/WAVE/Lighthouse cannot perform — making the boundary valuable for a human/LLM judge and invisible to automation.

citation.quote: Suggestions for corrected input are provided, OR

pages.scenario: Online-banking dashboard validates a recipient IBAN asynchronously on blur. The result is announced through a correctly built toast (pre-rendered role=status aria-live=polite container updated on change), with aria-invalid set and aria-describedby association — so 4.1.3 Status Messages genuinely passes. But the announced text is only 'We couldn't process that — please review the details and try again.' over a determinate IBAN rule (GB = 22 chars + mod-97 checksum); the user is one digit short and told nothing actionable.
pages.mechanism: Every dynamic/live-region requirement is met (4.1.3 satisfied: announced without focus change), so the failure is purely 3.3.3 adequacy: the IBAN length/format/checksum make the correct shape knowable but the announced suggestion withholds all of it; the security carve-out does not apply because the public IBAN format is not sensitive.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Engineered to pass every automatable check: pre-rendered polite live region (4.1.3 passes under live-region heuristics), associated error + aria-invalid (3.3.1 passes), dark-theme contrast fine. A fix-phrasing heuristic matches 'please review … and try again.' Flagging it requires reading validIBAN, recognizing the rule is determinate (length+mod-97), judging the announced sentence withholds it, AND ruling out a security carve-out — layered semantic reasoning over correctly-announced dynamic content, beyond static/single-snapshot scanners.

citation.quote:
In the case of an unsuccessful form submission, users may abandon the form
         because they may be unsure of how to correct the error even though they are aware
         that it has occurred.

aspects.title: Suggestion present but stranded far from its field with no proximity, association, or jump mechanism (locatability of the fix)
aspects.plain: A correct fix-it suggestion exists but is placed far from its field with no link or proximity, so you can't find it or connect it to the field that needs fixing.
aspects.description: The page contains a correct, adequate suggestion for the erroring field, but it is placed where the user cannot reasonably connect it to or reach the field: a correct 'Use MM/DD/YYYY' tip buried in a footer while the date field is at the top; a top-of-page error summary that names the fix but offers no working link to jump to the field and no near-field repetition; or a suggestion placed inside the wrong section so it reads as belonging to a different field. G177 and G139 make proximity/locatability part of HOW the suggestion must be provided. Whether the suggestion is close enough, associated with the right field, or reachable is a visual/spatial and contextual judgment about the rendered page, not a property of any single element.
aspects.scLimb: Provision/locatability limb: the suggestion must be 'provided to the user' in a way they can find and connect to the right field (G177 proximity, G139 jump mechanism, G84 'ways to locate the field(s) with a problem easily').
aspects.whyUncovered: No ACT case exists, and the survey notes proximity/locatability is covered only as authoring techniques with manual procedures. Automated tools can confirm the suggestion string exists somewhere in the DOM but cannot judge whether it is positioned close enough, visually/semantically associated with the right field, or reachable via a working jump link — these are layout/relevance judgments. A scanner sees the text and passes; a human sees a suggestion stranded far from its field or pointing at the wrong one.

references.quote: Suggestions or links to the suggestions should be placed close to the form fields they are associated with, such as at the top of the form, preceding the form fields, or next to the form fields requiring correction.
a link to that error is provided so that the user does not have to search for it.
describes the nature of the problem, and provides ways to locate the field(s) with a problem easily.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: Festival performer-registration form: the Preferred performance date field is near the top and shows a bare inline error with no format, while the correct 'Use MM/DD/YYYY (e.g. 06/30/2026)' suggestion is rendered ONLY in the page footer after the submit button, stranded below every other section.
pages.mechanism: Correct, adequate suggestion exists but is physically/reading-order distant from the field that erred; the field's aria-describedby points only to a no-fix message, so the suggestion is not provided at the point of need (G177 proximity).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The suggestion string is present, non-empty, high-contrast, and in a labelled footer; the field has a name and an associated error. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse have no model of the pixel/reading-order distance between a suggestion and the control it governs, so they cannot judge that the correct tip is unreachably far from the date input.

citation.quote: Suggestions or links to the suggestions should be placed close to the form fields they are associated with, such as at the top of the form, preceding the form fields, or next to the form fields requiring correction.

pages.scenario: Cedar County Public Library card-renewal form, post-submit error: the card-number field input#barcode is flagged with an AT-exposed bare error, but the only correct correction (the 14-digit format + example) is in div#barcode-fix, which is aria-hidden='true' and unreferenced — visible on screen yet unreachable to assistive technology.
pages.mechanism: The erroring field input#barcode (value '2134-5000-1234') is identified to AT via aria-invalid='true' + aria-describedby='barcode-status' (bare AT-exposed status 'This card number was not accepted.'), so 3.3.1 passes. The correct, adequate correction — 'Library card numbers are 14 digits ... (for example, 21345000123456). Re-enter the full 14-digit number.' — sits visibly right under the field in div#barcode-fix, but that container carries aria-hidden='true' and is NOT referenced by the input's aria-describedby, so the suggestion is excised from the accessibility tree and never provided to screen-reader users. A decoy 'Need help with your card number?' toggle is AT-exposed but only reveals generic boilerplate, not the 14-digit format.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The suggestion text exists, is correct, and sits in a valid role=alert region with a heading; the email field has a real label. Whether the summary item is a working link to the field and whether the fix is repeated/associated at the field is a locatability/reachability judgment over the rendered page that scanners do not perform.

citation.quote: a text description at the top of the page that indicates the fact that there was an input error, describes the nature of the problem, and provides a link the field(s) with a problem.

pages.scenario: Healthcare provider-credentialing portal: the NPI field in Section 1 erred and shows only a bare 'Please review this entry', while its correct suggestion ('Your NPI must be exactly 10 digits…') is printed inside Section 3's panel directly under the State license number field, where it reads as license guidance.
pages.mechanism: A correct suggestion is mis-associated — placed under a different field in a different section so its spatial and reading-order context ties it to the wrong control (license number), not the NPI field that erred (G177 association).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The suggestion is non-empty, correct, and inside a labelled panel adjacent to a labelled field; nothing is empty or broken. Deciding the suggestion sits under the WRONG field — that a human would read the 10-digit NPI rule as guidance for the license number two sections down — is a semantic-relevance plus spatial-association judgment scanners cannot make.

citation.quote: clearly indicates which field had the problem so the user can easily navigate to it to fix the problem.

pages.scenario: Meridian Banking SEPA-transfer form, post-submit error: the Recipient IBAN field input#iban shows only a bare fix-free error, while the correct IBAN format and worked example live solely in a hover-only title='' tooltip on a non-focusable info glyph — present on the page but reachable only by mouse hover.
pages.mechanism: The erroring field input#iban (value 'DE89 3704 0044 0532 0130') has aria-invalid='true' and aria-describedby='iban-err' pointing to a bare, fix-free error #iban-err 'This entry can't be processed.' The correct, adequate correction (full IBAN format + worked example 'DE89370400440532013000' + the exact deficit) exists only inside the title='' attribute of a non-interactive, non-focusable info <span class="info"> beside the error — a mouse-hover-only native tooltip. It is in no visible text node, not in the field's accessible description, and not surfaced on keyboard focus or touch, so the suggestion is effectively unreachable for keyboard/touch/AT users.
pages.selectorNote: Info glyph whose title holds the only (hover-only, unreachable) IBAN fix suggestion
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Each <a href='#x'> is a syntactically valid in-page link and the suggestion text is correct; the fields have names and associated messages. Scanners do not resolve each fragment href against the DOM to confirm a matching target exists, nor reason that the dangling link strands the only path to the fix.

citation.quote: a text description at the top of the page that indicates the fact that there was an input error, describes the nature of the problem, and provides a link the field(s) with a problem.

pages.scenario: E-commerce checkout shipping step: city/ZIP fail verification; the correct did-you-mean suggestion ('Did you mean Cambridge, MA 02139?' with an apply button) is rendered ONLY inside a collapsed <details> disclosure whose summary just says 'Address options', with no cue the fix is inside and the field messages saying only 'Check your city and ZIP.'
pages.mechanism: A correct suggestion is hidden in a closed disclosure (its content not in the a11y tree while collapsed) behind a non-descriptive label, with nothing telling the user to expand it — so the suggestion is not effectively provided to the user.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The disclosure is a valid, keyboard-operable, correctly-named widget with proper expanded/collapsed semantics, and the suggestion text is present in the DOM. Whether a user would ever discover the fix — whether 'Address options' signals 'your correction is in here' — is a content-discoverability judgment about meaning and likely behavior that scanners cannot evaluate.

citation.quote: Where errors are detected, suggest known ways to correct them.

pages.scenario: PASS twin — state-park campsite reservation: the same Arrival-date MM/DD/YYYY fix is repeated inline immediately beside the date field and associated via aria-describedby, AND the top error-summary item is a working jump link (href='#arrival') that lands on the real field id. Proves proximity/locatability, not mere presence, is what is judged.
pages.mechanism: The correct suggestion is provided locatably: associated with and adjacent to the erroring field (G177) and reachable via a working jump mechanism (G139), satisfying the locatability limb.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: This is the boundary the aspect turns on: a scanner sees 'a suggestion exists' on both this page and the stranded-footer FAIL and would treat them identically — it has no measure of proximity or reachability. Only a human recognizes the fix here sits beside the field and the jump link lands on it, so the page passes.

citation.quote: Suggestions or links to the suggestions should be placed close to the form fields they are associated with, such as at the top of the form, preceding the form fields, or next to the form fields requiring correction.

aspects.title: Color/asterisk/icon-only error indication with no text suggestion — the 'in text' limb
aspects.plain: A field's error and how to fix it are conveyed only by colour, a red asterisk, or an icon, with no text describing the correction, so a screen-reader user gets no guidance.
aspects.description: The page communicates that a field is in error and what to do purely through non-text means: turning the label red, adding a red asterisk, swapping in a warning icon, or showing a red border — with NO text description of the problem or the correction. G84 explicitly states this is insufficient: an asterisk or red label does not satisfy the SC; a text description is required. The judgment is visual and semantic: confirm that the red/icon is the ONLY carrier of the error+fix information and that no equivalent text suggestion accompanies it. The 3.3.3-specific limb is the missing CORRECTION TEXT, distinct from the 1.4.1 'use of color' / 3.3.1 'error identification' framings.
aspects.scLimb: The 'in text' provision: a text description/suggestion is required; non-text indicators (asterisk, red label, icon, border) do not satisfy the SC (G84).
aspects.whyUncovered: No ACT case exists for 3.3.3, and while a generic 1.4.1 'use of color' scanner might flag the red, it cannot determine that the missing element is specifically a TEXT SUGGESTION for correction (the 3.3.3 obligation) rather than just identification. Confirming there is no accompanying correction text anywhere, and that the visual carries the whole job, requires reading the rendered page and judging meaning.

references.quote: it is not sufficient simply to indicate that a field has an error by putting an asterisk on its label or turning the label red. A text description of the problem should be provided.
Users who are blind or have impaired vision understand more easily the nature of the input error and how to correct it.
information about the nature and location of the input error is provided in text to enable the users to identify the problem.

aspects.ttWhy: Sole TT test for this SC.

pages.scenario: Nonprofit one-time donation form, server-rendered after rejecting a £3 gift (£5 processor minimum). The 'Other amount' field is flagged ONLY by a red label + 2px red border + pink fill via a .is-error class. No error summary, no inline message, no aria-invalid, no hidden text, no title — the knowable correction ('enter £5 or more') is stated nowhere.
pages.mechanism: A detected input error whose correction is knowable (the £5 floor) is conveyed solely by colour (red label + red border + pink background). The input is plain type=text with a well-formed value '3', so validity.valid===true and the accessibility tree exposes invalid:false — a screen reader announces the field identically to a valid one and there is no text suggestion of the accepted value anywhere. G84: an asterisk/red label does not satisfy the SC; text is required.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: DOM is valid HTML5 with a programmatic label and nothing empty; type=text + well-formed value means validity.valid===true and AX invalid:false with no aria-invalid to key on. No checker knows an error was detected (the £3<£5 rule is server-side) or the £5 business rule, and none asserts 'a detected error must carry TEXT correction.' A 1.4.1 colour heuristic could note the red but cannot determine the specifically-missing element is the correction text (3.3.3) vs mere identification — needs submitting the form and judging meaning.

citation.quote: The "in text" portion of the success criterion underscores that it is not sufficient simply to indicate that a field has an error by putting an asterisk on its label or turning the label red. A text description of the problem should be provided.

pages.scenario: E-commerce cart re-rendered after 'Update cart' with quantity 8 on an item with only 5 left. A real role=alert banner IDENTIFIES the quantity problem in text (3.3.1 satisfied) and the offending input carries aria-invalid=true, but the knowable correction (remaining stock / 'reduce to 5 or fewer') appears nowhere — the single red-bordered pink input is the only carrier tying the generic banner to the right row.
pages.mechanism: Error identification is fully present (role=alert text + aria-invalid=true), so this isolates the 3.3.3 suggestion limb: the correction value (available stock = 5) is conveyed only by the red input border. A screen reader hears 'quantity ... invalid entry' but never the ceiling, so the user must guess-and-resubmit. The knowable suggestion is provided through colour alone, which G84 says is insufficient.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The page is a model citizen for the checks tools run: a real role=alert with text, aria-invalid=true on the bad input, labels on every field — identification and ARIA heuristics all pass. No tool knows the remaining stock is 5, so none can assert the available number is the missing suggestion; tools cannot distinguish 'a correction suggestion is absent' from 'an error message exists' — both look like text+aria-invalid in a snapshot. Requires reading the banner, noticing it states no fix value, and knowing the fix value is knowable.

citation.quote: When input must be one of a set of allowed values, the text description should indicate this fact. It should include the list of values if possible, or suggest the allowed value that is most similar to the entered value.

pages.scenario: SaaS signup card. The password 'summer24' is classified weak by JS, which lights only the first of four strength-meter segments in red, reddens the field border, and silently blocks submit (preventDefault while weak). The knowable rules (>=8 chars, mixed case, a digit, a symbol, not a common word-stem) are stated nowhere; the red meter + red border are the entire 'guidance'.
pages.mechanism: Input is rejected (submit silently refused) with a fully knowable correction (the rules), conveyed only by the meter colour/fill and red border. The meter is aria-hidden=true so even the visual cue is absent from the AX tree; the gate lives in JS so validity.valid===true, AX invalid:false, no aria-invalid, no live region. A blind user experiences a form that won't submit with zero text guidance about why or how to fix it. G85: a text description of the required format/values is required.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Password field has a real label and valid type; the meter is aria-hidden so no broken-widget rule fires and nothing is empty/malformed. The strength gate is in JS not HTML constraints, so validity.valid===true and AX invalid:false with no aria-invalid; submit is blocked with no DOM change to observe. No tool can read the JS rules or know the meter colour is the only place they're expressed — recognising the missing element is the suggestion text needs typing a weak value, watching the meter, finding submit silently refuses, and reasoning the rules are knowable yet unwritten.

citation.quote: However the text description is provided, it should do one of the following things to assist the user: Provide examples of the correct data entry for the field, Describe the correct data entry for the field, Show values of the correct data entry that are similar to the user's data entry, with instructions to the user as to how to enter one of these correct values should the user choose to do so.

pages.scenario: Healthcare patient-registration wizard (step 2/4), re-rendered after the date of birth was typed '7 Mar 1981' when MM/DD/YYYY is required. The field is flagged by revealing a red warning-triangle SVG beside the label (aria-label empty, aria-hidden=true) plus a red border + pink fill. No format-correction text exists — yet the phone and MRN rows DO keep their format hints, so only the errored row lost its guidance.
pages.mechanism: A detected format error with a knowable correction (MM/DD/YYYY, e.g. 03/07/1981) is signalled only by an AT-silent icon and colour. The triangle is aria-hidden with empty aria-label and the input is plain type=text with a well-formed value, so validity.valid===true, AX invalid:false, no aria-invalid — the field announces identically to a valid one. Even a sighted user gets only a generic 'something wrong' triangle with no statement of the format, although every other field carries a hint. G84: swapping in an icon / reddening the field does not satisfy the SC.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The warning icon is CORRECTLY hidden from AT (aria-hidden=true, empty aria-label, focusable=false) — valid decorative markup with no missing-alt/empty-name defect; flagging it would be a false positive. The input is type=text with a well-formed value, so validity.valid===true, AX invalid:false, no aria-invalid. No tool knows MM/DD/YYYY is required or that the icon/colour is the only carrier; recognising the missing format-correction text needs reading the page, noticing the sibling rows have hints while the errored one does not, and judging meaning.

citation.quote: The "in text" portion of the success criterion underscores that it is not sufficient simply to indicate that a field has an error by putting an asterisk on its label or turning the label red. A text description of the problem should be provided.

pages.scenario: Government transit-authority Arabic (RTL) ticket-refund form, re-rendered after a 9-digit national ID was entered when the ID must be exactly 10 digits and begin with 1 or 2. The .bad class darkens and enlarges the already-present red required asterisk and reddens the input (border + pink fill). No Arabic error text, no aria-invalid, no hidden text — the knowable correction is stated nowhere; the asterisk has no legend, and the ticket/IBAN fields keep their Arabic help.
pages.mechanism: A detected format error with a knowable correction (10 digits, starts with 1 or 2) is signalled only by an asterisk colour/weight shift (#cf3b2c->#8e1a0e, 1.15em) plus a red border. The required asterisk is a CSS ::after pseudo-element most screen readers do not announce, and the input is type=text with a well-formed value so validity.valid===true, AX invalid:false, no aria-invalid — an Arabic SR announces the field identically to a valid one with no statement of the required format. G84: an asterisk/red label does not satisfy the SC.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: lang=ar, dir=rtl, and label for on every input are correct and nothing is empty/malformed, so structural/i18n linters pass. The field is type=text with a well-formed value (validity.valid===true, AX invalid:false, no aria-invalid). The required marker is a CSS ::after pseudo-element — outside the parsed DOM, so invisible to static markup checks. No tool can read Arabic semantics, know the 10-digit/starts-with-1-or-2 rule, or tell the asterisk colour-shift + red border is the only carrier; judging the missing correction text needs reading the page in Arabic and reasoning about the format.

citation.quote: The "in text" portion of the success criterion underscores that it is not sufficient simply to indicate that a field has an error by putting an asterisk on its label or turning the label red. A text description of the problem should be provided.

pages.scenario: PASS twin — higher-ed LMS course-registration confirmation, re-rendered after the term-start date was typed 'Aug 25 2026' when MM/DD/YYYY is required. The field shows the SAME visual treatment as the failing twins (red warning triangle + red border + pink fill) BUT also renders a text correction 'Enter the term start date as MM/DD/YYYY — for example, 08/25/2026.' tied to the input via aria-describedby with aria-invalid=true.
pages.mechanism: An input error is detected and a knowable, useful correction is provided IN TEXT and programmatically associated: aria-invalid=true announces the invalid state and aria-describedby=start-err pulls the format+example into the field's description, so a screen reader hears the error AND the exact fix independent of colour. Satisfies G84/G85/G177; the red icon/border are redundant reinforcement, not the sole carrier. The only meaningful difference from the failing twins is the presence of associated correction text — the 3.3.3 limb.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Even on this PASS page no scanner can confirm success: a tool can see aria-describedby resolves to non-empty text but cannot verify that text is a correct, useful correction rather than e.g. 'Invalid date'. A field could carry aria-invalid + an associated but useless message and still pass every automated check while failing 3.3.3. That 'does the text actually state the fix?' requires human semantic reading is exactly why the icon/colour-only twins evade axe/WAVE/Lighthouse; this twin pins the discriminator as the correction text, not the red treatment.

citation.quote: The objective of this technique is to suggest correct text where the information supplied by the user is not accepted and possible correct text is known. ... Suggestions or links to the suggestions should be placed close to the form fields they are associated with, such as at the top of the form, preceding the form fields, or next to the form fields requiring correction.

aspects.title: Accessible name does not contain the visible label text (F111 / label-in-name overlap, 4.1.2 limb)
aspects.plain: A control's spoken name leaves out the words printed on it, so a voice-control user who says the visible label can't activate the control.
aspects.description: A control has BOTH a visible text label AND a non-empty accessible name, but the accessible name omits, contradicts, or wholly replaces the words a sighted user reads on the control. Every ACT 4.1.2 name rule (97a4e1 Button, e086e5 Form field, c487ae Link, 59796f Image button, m6b1q3 Menuitem, 2t702h Summary) terminates the instant accName !== ""; none compare the computed name STRING against the rendered visible label STRING. F111 maps explicitly to 4.1.2 (its title is 'Failure of Success Criteria 1.3.1, 2.5.3, and 4.1.2 due to a control with visible label text but no accessible name') and demands the third check the rules never perform: the accessible name must CONTAIN the visible label, or speech-input users cannot speak what they see to activate the control. Detection requires rendering the page, reading the visible label off the pixels, computing the accessible name, and judging textual overlap — pure visual+semantic comparison, not present in the corpus where any non-empty name is a uniform PASS.
aspects.scLimb: The 'Name' limb: the name is programmatically determined and non-empty (rules pass) but fails to be programmatically determinable AS the visible label, so the name does not let an AT/speech user identify and operate the component by its rendered text.
aspects.whyUncovered: The six non-empty-name ACT rules stop at accName !== ""; none of 4.1.2's mapped rules compare the accessible-name string against the rendered visible label string. The corpus contains no fixture where a present visible label and a present-but-divergent accessible name coexist, so a non-empty-but-mismatched name is always a PASS. The string-comparison only lives in 2.5.3 (not in this SC's rule set), and no fully-automated checker reliably extracts the 'visible label' from pixels to compare it, so this needs human visual judgment.

references.quote: Failure of Success Criteria 1.3.1, 2.5.3, and 4.1.2 due to a control with visible label text but no accessible name
The accessible name contains the text that appears as the visible label.
If check #1 is true, but checks #2 and/or #3 are false, the content fails the Success Criterion.

aspects.ttWhy: Generic control name/label-in-name; TT tests this via 5.C/6.A/7.x, no isolated test in the 4.1.2 file.

pages.scenario: SaaS document-editor toolbar: the primary action button visibly reads 'Save' but carries aria-label='Persist document to server', so the visible word 'Save' appears nowhere in the accessible name. Verified in Chromium: role=button, accName='Persist document to server'.
pages.mechanism: aria-label on a native <button> overrides and suppresses the child text node 'Save'; the accessible name is non-empty (97a4e1 passes) and role is correct, but it omits the visible label, so a speech-input user saying 'click Save' matches nothing and a screen-reader user gets no anchor to the on-screen word. F111 check #3 (accName must contain the visible label) fails.
pages.selectorNote: Checkbox with copy-pasted aria-labelledby naming a different workshop
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse and ACT rule 97a4e1 terminate at accName !== ''; none of 4.1.2's mapped rules extract the rendered visible label 'Save' from pixels/DOM and compare it to the computed name string (that string-overlap check lives only in 2.5.3). aria-label is well-formed, so no empty/missing-attribute lint fires; catching it needs a human to read 'Save' and judge it absent from the name.

citation.quote: For all controls with a visible label (e.g., link text, button text, programmatically linked label, images in links or buttons with text, etc.), check that: 1. The control has a visible text label. 2. The control has an accessible name. 3. The accessible name contains the text that appears as the visible label.

pages.scenario: Pharmacy search field with a real visible <label for='med-search'>Search medications</label>, but the input also has aria-labelledby pointing to a visually-hidden node containing only the back-end query key 'rx-query'. The explicit aria-labelledby wins over the <label>. Verified in Chromium: role=searchbox, accName='rx-query' (zero word overlap with the visible label).
pages.mechanism: aria-labelledby is consulted before the <label> association in the accessible-name computation, so the visible 'Search medications' is discarded and the name becomes the internal slug 'rx-query'. Name is non-empty (e086e5 passes) and role correct, but it shares no words with the visible label, so voice users cannot speak it and screen-reader users hear a meaningless field name. F111 check #3 fails.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: e086e5 / axe / WAVE / Lighthouse confirm a non-empty name and stop. The aria-labelledby IDREF resolves to a real present element, so the dangling-reference lint does not fire. No checker reads the visible <label> text off the rendered page and diffs it against 'rx-query'; recognizing the name is a telemetry key rather than the on-screen label is a semantic judgment.

citation.quote: If check #1 is true, but checks #2 and/or #3 are false, the content fails the Success Criterion.

pages.scenario: Government fiscal-office page listing property-tax PDFs. The first download link is an <a> containing a PDF icon plus visible text 'Download PDF', but a reusable-component placeholder aria-label='document' was left on the anchor, suppressing the child text. Verified in Chromium: role=link, accName='document' (the other rows, with no aria-label, correctly name themselves by their visible text).
pages.mechanism: aria-label on the anchor wins over its descendant text, so the icon+text child 'Download PDF' is not contributed to the name; the generic 'document' wholly replaces the visible label. Name is non-empty (c487ae passes) and role correct, but in a links list the user cannot distinguish or voice-target it. F111 check #3 fails.
pages.selectorNote: Pay button whose aria-labelledby points at row 3's invoice context span
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: c487ae and axe/WAVE/Lighthouse see a non-empty link name and pass; 'document' is a plausible real word with no empty/dangling attribute to lint. Detecting the failure requires reading the visible 'Download PDF' off the rendered row and recognizing the programmatic name 'document' neither contains nor describes it — a visual+semantic comparison no automated 4.1.2 checker performs.

citation.quote: When speech input users interact with a web page, they usually speak a command followed by the reference to some visible label (like the text in a button or a link, or the text labelling some input). If the control lacks an accessible name, speech users won't be able to activate the control using its visible label.

pages.scenario: Literary-magazine pagination (page 2 of 9). The forward control visibly reads 'Next' plus a decorative chevron, but aria-label='›' (U+203A, single right-pointing angle quotation mark) was set on the anchor, replacing the visible word with a lone unspeakable glyph. Verified in Chromium: role=link, accName='›'.
pages.mechanism: aria-label overrides the child text 'Next', leaving the accessible name as a single punctuation glyph. It is technically non-empty (c487ae passes) and role correct, but a screen reader announces a symbol name or nothing, and a speech-input user has no spoken token for '›', so the control is unreachable by voice and the visible label 'Next' is absent from the name. F111 check #3 fails.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The name is a non-empty string, so c487ae / axe / WAVE / Lighthouse pass; none classify whether the name is a single non-speakable glyph that fails to match the visible word 'Next'. That requires reading the rendered 'Next' and a human visual+linguistic judgment that '›' is neither the visible label nor a speakable name.

citation.quote: Success Criterion 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value requires a programmatically determinable name for all user interface components. Names may be visible or invisible. Occasionally, the name needs to be visible, in which case it is identified as a label.

pages.scenario: Renters-insurance quote wizard (step 3 of 3). The final action is a native <input type='submit' value='Get my quote'> so the button face reads 'Get my quote', but a form-builder integration emitted aria-label='quote-submit-btn-v2' (the component's internal id), which overrides the value. Verified in Chromium: role=button, accName='quote-submit-btn-v2'.
pages.mechanism: For a submit input the value normally becomes the accessible name, but aria-label takes precedence and replaces it with a hyphenated developer slug. Name is non-empty (97a4e1 passes) and role correct, but a screen reader reads an internal identifier and a speech-input user saying 'click Get my quote' cannot activate it. F111 check #3 fails.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: 97a4e1 / axe / WAVE / Lighthouse confirm a non-empty name and pass; 'quote-submit-btn-v2' is a valid string with no empty or dangling attribute to lint. Recognizing the programmatic name is an internal id rather than the rendered 'Get my quote' requires reading the button face and judging the string mismatch — overlap logic that lives only in 2.5.3, not in this SC's rule set.

citation.quote: When standard controls from accessible technologies are used, this process is straightforward. If the user interface elements are used according to specification the conditions of this provision will be met.

pages.scenario: French bistro reservation panel (<html lang='fr'>). The primary button visibly reads 'Réserver une table', but aria-labelledby concatenates two visually-hidden untranslated English nodes ('Confirm' + 'booking'). Verified in Chromium: failing button role=button, accName='Confirm booking'; a co-located passing twin 'Annuler' computes accName='Annuler la réservation' (contains the visible word), included as a boundary contrast.
pages.mechanism: aria-labelledby overrides the button's own French text and concatenates the referenced hidden nodes, so the accessible name is English 'Confirm booking' on a French page — a language switch with zero word overlap with the visible 'Réserver une table'. Name is non-empty (97a4e1 passes) and role correct, but a French voice-control user saying « Réserver une table » activates nothing and a screen reader contradicts the visible label. The passing twin's name is a superset of its visible 'Annuler', satisfying F111 check #3; the primary control fails it.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Both buttons have non-empty names, valid aria-labelledby IDREFs resolving to present elements, and valid roles, so 97a4e1 / axe / WAVE / Lighthouse pass both. No automated 4.1.2 checker reads the visible French label off the rendered button, detects the language switch to English, and diffs it against 'Confirm booking'. Judging the name is in the wrong language and omits the visible label is a human visual+linguistic decision.

citation.quote: For each user interface control element where an aria-labelledby attribute is present: 1. Check that the value of the aria-labelledby attribute is the id of an element or a space separated list of ids on the web page. 2. Check that the text of the referenced element or elements accurately labels the user interface control.

aspects.title: Accessible name is present but uninformative / does not communicate the control's purpose (ARIA14 name-quality)
aspects.plain: A button has a screen-reader name like 'button' or an icon filename, so the user hears something but still has no idea what the control does.
aspects.description: A user-interface control has a non-empty, machine-valid accessible name, but the name does not identify what the control DOES — it is placeholder text, an asset filename, a developer string, or a generic token duplicated across distinct controls. Every ACT 4.1.2 name rule is scoped to non-emptiness only and explicitly does not assess descriptiveness, so a name like 'button', 'icon_search_24px.svg', 'TODO label', or five identical 'star' labels passes uniformly. ARIA14 sets the actual bar: 'users with assistive technologies rely on accessible names that clearly communicate the purpose of components,' and the Understanding doc requires controls to 'provide important and appropriate information to assistive technologies.' Judging adequacy requires inferring the control's function from its icon, position, and behavior, then deciding whether the name conveys that function — semantic judgment no non-emptiness scan performs. (This is distinct from F111: here there may be no visible text label at all; the name is simply meaningless, not mismatched against a visible label.)
aspects.scLimb: The 'Name' limb: the name is programmatically determined and non-empty (rules pass) but does not constitute 'important and appropriate information' identifying the component, so AT users cannot determine its purpose.
aspects.whyUncovered: ACT 4.1.2 name rules check non-emptiness only and per the inventory do NOT assess name quality, descriptiveness, or uniqueness; the synthetic fixtures use either one clean correct name or a degenerate empty/default name, never a non-empty-but-useless name (which by rule definition PASSES). Whether a present name actually communicates purpose depends on the control's visual/behavioral identity, which a fully-automated checker cannot reliably infer — it requires human semantic judgment.
