aspects.ttWhy: Generic accessible-name quality on a control; TT tests this via 5.C/6.A/7.x, no isolated test in the 4.1.2 file.

pages.scenario: Document-editor formatting toolbar of five icon-only buttons (cut, copy, paste, undo, redo), each rendering a distinct SVG glyph and performing a distinct action, but all carrying the identical accessible name aria-label="button". A screen-reader user hears "button, button, button, button, button" and cannot distinguish function.
pages.mechanism: AccName of all five buttons computes to "button" (from aria-label, overriding the aria-hidden SVG). Non-empty and role-correct so the ACT 'Button has non-empty accessible name' rule passes, but the generic token conveys no purpose — verified via Chrome CDP accessibility tree: five buttons all named "button".
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse only test that each interactive element has a NON-EMPTY accessible name; "button" satisfies that. No 4.1.2 automated rule assesses descriptiveness, and the only identical-name uniqueness rule is iframe-scoped, never button-scoped. Judging that "button" fails to identify a cut/paste control requires reading the rendered scissors/clipboard glyphs and inferring purpose — visual-semantic judgment.

citation.quote: While it might be visually clear that the button with the “×” symbol closes the dialog, users with assistive technologies rely on accessible names that clearly communicate the purpose of components, in this case “Close”.

pages.scenario: Online-banking transfer-review screen whose submit control is an <input type="image"> styled as a green 'Confirm transfer' pill. Its alt — and therefore its accessible name — was left as the SVG asset's filename, alt="icon_arrow_forward_24dp.svg". For a control that moves $1,450 irreversibly, AT announces a file path, not the action.
pages.mechanism: For <input type="image"> the accessible name is computed from alt; CDP confirms AccName = "icon_arrow_forward_24dp.svg". The visible 'Confirm transfer' caption is a CSS-painted aria-hidden span that does NOT contribute to the name (verified — it is not an F111 visible-label mismatch, the name is simply a non-descriptive filename). Non-empty, so ACT 'Image button has non-empty accessible name' passes.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Scanners require only a non-empty alt on image inputs; a filename satisfies that. No rule recognizes a ".svg" path as a meaningless name versus a purpose, and none can read the transfer context to know the button confirms a $1,450 transfer. Determining the name is meaningless requires understanding the screen and the arrow glyph — human semantic/visual judgment.

citation.quote: users with assistive technologies rely on accessible names that clearly communicate the purpose of components, in this case “Close”.

pages.scenario: Restaurant-review form whose overall rating is an interactive five-star widget: five <button>s where activating the Nth sets the rating to N stars, each given the identical accessible name aria-label="star". AT users hear "star, star, star, star, star" and cannot choose a specific rating value.
pages.mechanism: AccName of each of the five buttons = "star" (CDP-verified). The distinguishing value lives only in data-value (1-5) and left-to-right position, neither of which reaches the name. aria-pressed state updates correctly, so the NAME — which must encode the value (Rate 1 star...Rate 5 stars) — is the sole defect. The textbox correctly resolves to "Your review", isolating the stars as the failure.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: All five buttons have non-empty names, so every name rule passes. The single ACT rule that flags identical accessible names without equivalent purpose is scoped to <iframe>, not buttons, so it never fires. Detecting the defect requires knowing the widget assigns 1-5 by position and judging that "star" fails to distinguish the five values — behavioral/semantic reasoning beyond static analysis.

pages.scenario: Healthcare patient-portal modal dialog (confirm appointment). The top-right '×' close control was shipped with a leftover developer placeholder as its accessible name: aria-label="TODO label". The dialog's other ARIA wiring (role=dialog, aria-modal, aria-labelledby) is correct, so the close button's name is the sole defect.
pages.mechanism: AccName = "TODO label" (CDP-verified; the explicit aria-label overrides the × text node). A screen reader announces "TODO label, button"; a voice-control user cannot say 'click close'. The role is correct and the dialog is otherwise well-formed, so AT users perceive the dialog but cannot determine how to dismiss it from the control's name. This is precisely ARIA14's named close-button case.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: "TODO label" is a syntactically valid, non-empty string, so name checks pass; no automated rule flags placeholder or to-do text. Recognizing it as an un-replaced developer note — and that the control is the dialog's close button (by the ×/top-right convention) — requires human reading of the string and the visual convention.

citation.quote: An example is the “×” often used in the top-right corner of dialogs to indicate the control for closing the dialog. While it might be visually clear that the button with the “×” symbol closes the dialog, users with assistive technologies rely on accessible names that clearly communicate the purpose of components, in this case “Close”.

pages.scenario: Municipal transit trip-planner map with three floating icon controls. The two zoom buttons' accessible names are raw, un-interpolated i18n message keys (aria-label="map.ctrl.zoomIn" / "map.ctrl.zoomOut") that the translation layer never resolved. The third control ('locate me') is correctly named 'Center map on my location' and is included as a within-page PASS boundary to sharpen the contrast.
pages.mechanism: CDP confirms the two zoom buttons resolve to the literal key strings "map.ctrl.zoomIn"/"map.ctrl.zoomOut" while the locate-me button resolves to "Center map on my location". Same widget, same toolbar: two non-empty-but-meaningless dotted keys (rules pass, purpose not communicated) versus one descriptive name (genuine pass). The page fails 4.1.2 driven by the two zoom buttons.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: All three buttons have non-empty names, so scanners pass every one — including the two leaked keys. No automated rule recognizes "map.ctrl.zoomIn" as an un-resolved i18n key versus "Center map on my location" as a real purpose; both are valid strings to a parser. Distinguishing meaningless keys from a meaningful name requires a human to read the strings and map them to the + / − / crosshair glyphs.

citation.quote: When no clear visible text label is available due to design decisions, the accessible name can be set by using the aria-label attribute instead, provided that the element has an implicit or explicit role that supports naming.

pages.scenario: Real-estate CRM 'edit contact' panel with three contentEditable <div role="textbox"> fields — mailing address, internal notes, follow-up reminder — each with a visible <h3> heading above it, but all sharing the identical accessible name aria-label="editor". AT users hear "editor, edit text" three times and cannot tell address from private notes from reminder.
pages.mechanism: AccName of each editor = "editor" (CDP-verified). Because these are contentEditable divs (not labelable form controls), the adjacent <h3> text does NOT become the accessible name; the explicit aria-label is authoritative and identical across all three. role=textbox + aria-multiline are correct, so users know they are in a multiline editor but not WHICH field. The Cancel/Save buttons resolve to correct names, isolating the editors as the defect.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Each editor has a non-empty name ("editor"), so name checks pass — nothing is empty or missing. The identical-name uniqueness rule is iframe-scoped, never textbox-scoped, so it never fires. A scanner cannot read the three visible <h3> headings and field contents to conclude that "editor" is generic and the fields hold different content — human semantic judgment of each field's purpose is required.

aspects.title: Role is syntactically valid but is the wrong role for the control's appearance/behavior (F15/F59 semantic variant)
aspects.plain: A toggle switch is coded as a checkbox (or a heading, link, etc.), so the screen reader announces the wrong kind of control and the user misjudges how to use it.
aspects.description: An interactive element carries a role that is a real ARIA token (so 674b10 'Role attribute has valid value' passes) and whose required states are present (so 4e8ab6 passes), but the role is WRONG for what the element actually is and does. A sliding toggle switch coded role="checkbox", a control that depresses and fires an in-page action coded role="link", an operable disclosure header marked role="heading", a clickable star coded role="img". F59's literal failure is a div/span with NO role (axe-core flags clickable-with-no-role); the genuinely uncovered, automation-resistant case is a VALID but inappropriate role. Deciding the role is wrong requires seeing the rendered widget, reasoning about its affordance and behavior, and comparing that to the announced role — visual+behavioral judgment, not a token-validity check. The Understanding doc anchors this: when elements 'are programmed... to have a different role and/or function than usual, then additional measures need to be taken.'
aspects.scLimb: The 'Role' limb: the role is programmatically determined and is a valid token (rules pass) but does not correctly convey the component's actual role/function, so AT announces the wrong affordance.
aspects.whyUncovered: 674b10 only checks the role VALUE is a real ARIA token and 4e8ab6 only checks the declared role has its required states present; neither checks the declared role MATCHES the element's visual/behavioral identity. The corpus's role fixtures cover invalid tokens and missing required states, never a valid-but-inappropriate role. A fully-automated checker cannot determine the 'correct' role from rendered appearance and behavior — that is human judgment.

aspects.ttWhy: Generic control role; TT tests this via 5.C/6.A/7.x, no isolated role test in the 4.1.2 file.

pages.scenario: Northwind Postmaster notification settings: sliding pill toggle switches (thumb-on-track, green=on/grey=off, instant effect) coded as div role=checkbox with aria-checked. Visually/behaviourally a switch, announced as a checkbox.
pages.mechanism: The control's rendered/behavioural identity is an on/off SWITCH (correct role=switch, announced 'on/off'), but it is coded role=checkbox (a valid ARIA token with its required aria-checked state present and synced), so AT announces 'checkbox, checked' — a form selection affordance rather than a live setting toggle. The role is valid but inappropriate for the widget.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse confirm role is a valid token (674b10), the checkbox's required aria-checked is present (4e8ab6), the element has an accessible name, and it is focusable/operable — all true. No tool renders the thumb-on-track pill, recognises the switch affordance, and decides 'switch' rather than 'checkbox' is the correct role. That comparison of rendered identity to declared role is human visual judgment.

citation.quote: If custom controls are created, however, or interface elements are programmed (in code or script) to have a different role and/or function than usual, then additional measures need to be taken to ensure that the controls provide important and appropriate information to assistive technologies and allow themselves to be controlled by assistive technologies.

pages.scenario: Cadence pricing page: 'Choose Pro' CTA pill that visibly depresses on press and performs an IN-PAGE action (updates a live order-summary box, no navigation) coded as span role=link.
pages.mechanism: role=link is a valid ARIA token (no extra required states, so nothing for 4e8ab6 to fail) and the accessible name is correct, but the link role signals navigation to a new location/context. The control performs an in-page action and never navigates (no href, no URL change), so the correct role is button. Announcing an in-page action control as a 'link' misleads AT users about what activation will do.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse confirm role=link is valid, the element has a name, and it is focusable/operable; a link without href is a common, legitimate JS-link pattern and not an automatic violation. No tool inspects the handler, observes that activation mutates an on-page region rather than navigating, and concludes the role should be button. Telling navigation apart from an in-page action requires reading behaviour — human judgment.

pages.scenario: Cirro Weather display settings: a joined segmented control for temperature unit (°C / °F) where exactly one is always selected and choosing one deselects the other, but each segment is coded div role=button with aria-pressed.
pages.mechanism: Each segment carries a valid role=button (674b10 passes) with the allowed aria-pressed state (nothing for 4e8ab6 to fail) and a correct name, but coding mutually-exclusive options as independent toggle buttons hides the single-select radiogroup semantics: AT never announces a group, 'x of N' position, or that choosing one cancels the other. The correct semantics are role=radiogroup containing role=radio. The role is valid but inappropriate for a single-select group.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse confirm role=button is valid, aria-pressed is an allowed state, and each segment has a name; a set of toggle buttons is a legitimate pattern, so nothing fires. No tool can look at a joined segmented pill with one-of-two always selected and decide these should be radios in a radiogroup. Recognising 'single-select rendered as a segmented control' is human visual/behavioural judgment.

pages.scenario: Meadowbrook Veterinary Clinic FAQ accordion: operable headers with a rotating disclosure triangle and click/key expand-collapse behaviour coded div role=heading aria-level=3 (with aria-expanded) and no button semantics.
pages.mechanism: role=heading is a valid token (674b10 passes) and its required aria-level is present (4e8ab6 passes), but heading declares a static section title, while the element is an operable disclosure (the APG disclosure pattern is a button, optionally wrapped in a heading). A user navigating by heading lands on an inert-seeming title that surprisingly operates; aria-expanded on a bare heading is poorly surfaced by AT. The role is valid but inappropriate for an operable control.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse confirm role=heading is valid and the required aria-level is present; a focusable heading is unusual but not an automatic violation and aria-expanded is globally allowed. No tool renders the rotating triangle, observes the click-to-expand behaviour, and decides the operable control should be a button rather than a heading. Recognising 'operable disclosure mis-coded as a static heading' requires reasoning about affordance and behaviour — human judgment.

pages.scenario: Tavola restaurant review form: an interactive 5-star rating widget (hover preview, click-to-set, fills gold, populates a submitted hidden input) where each star is coded span role=img aria-label='N stars' with click/key handlers.
pages.mechanism: role=img is a valid token (674b10 passes) with a correct accessible name (no required state for 4e8ab6 to fail), but img declares a NON-interactive graphic — AT presents an image to be described, never operated. The stars respond to clicks/keys and set a form value, so the interactive rating behaviour flatly contradicts the img role; correct semantics are a radiogroup of radio (or a slider). The role is valid but inappropriate for an operable control.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse confirm role=img is valid and each star has a name — indeed an img WITH a name is the canonical lint-passing pattern for an informative image, so checkers actively approve it. tabindex on an img is unusual but not an automatic violation. No tool observes that these 'images' carry click/key/hover handlers that set a submitted value and concludes the role should be radio/slider. Recognising 'interactive rating mis-coded as static images' requires seeing behaviour — human judgment.

citation.quote: If this is not done, then assistive technologies will not be able to understand what the control is or how to operate it or may not even know of its existence.

pages.scenario: Bibliothek (de-DE) settings boundary/PASS counterexample: an icon-only '✕' close that looks like a graphic but is a native button, a sliding night-mode switch correctly coded role=switch, and an operable disclosure correctly coded role=button — every role matches its rendered/behavioural identity.
pages.mechanism: On all three controls the programmatically-determined role is both a valid token AND the correct role for what the control is and does: the icon close exposes as button (dismiss action), the sliding pill as switch (on/off setting), the disclosure as button (expand/collapse). There is no valid-but-inappropriate role; a human comparing each rendered affordance to its announced role finds agreement, so the Role limb is satisfied.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse 'pass' this page for the same shallow facts that are ALSO true on the failing pages (valid roles, present required states aria-checked/aria-expanded, accessible names) — they cannot distinguish it from case-01/04/05 on those facts alone. The reason this page GENUINELY passes is the deeper role-matches-behaviour judgment tools cannot perform; they merely coincide with the human-correct answer here. This boundary case shows the deciding factor is human visual/behavioural judgment, not the machine-checkable facts.

citation.quote: When standard controls from accessible technologies are used, this process is straightforward.

aspects.title: Exposed ARIA state/value is present and valid but contradicts the rendered control state (value correctness, not presence)
aspects.plain: A toggle looks ON but is still coded as 'off' (aria-checked false), so the screen reader tells the user the opposite of what's actually showing on screen.
aspects.description: A custom control exposes a state/value (aria-checked, aria-expanded, aria-selected, aria-pressed, aria-valuenow) that is a permitted, syntactically-valid value (so 4e8ab6, 5c01ea, 6a7281 all pass) but that does not match the control's CURRENT visible state: a toggle rendered ON with aria-checked="false", an accordion visibly expanded with aria-expanded="false", a highlighted active tab while aria-selected stays on the first tab, a slider thumb at max with aria-valuenow="0". SC 4.1.2 requires that states/values 'can be programmatically set' AND that 'notification of changes... is available'; a stale value silently lies to AT. Catching it requires rendering the widget, reading its true visual state, and comparing against the exposed attribute — a visual comparison the static-string ACT rules structurally cannot perform.
aspects.scLimb: The 'Value/State' limb: states and values are programmatically present and valid (rules pass) but do not reflect the component's actual current state, so AT is given an incorrect value and changes are not truthfully reflected.
aspects.whyUncovered: ACT state rules (4e8ab6, 5c01ea, 6a7281, 5f99a7) check presence, permittedness, and value-validity — all static-string checks. None compare the state value against the actual rendered/interactive state of the widget. The corpus has no fixture where a syntactically perfect aria-checked/aria-expanded/aria-valuenow disagrees with the visual state, because asserting that disagreement requires rendering and visual judgment a fully-automated checker cannot supply.

aspects.ttWhy: Initial static state/value mismatch, not an auto-update; TT tests value via 5.C/6.A/7.x, not isolated here.

pages.scenario: A Meridian Bank Security Alerts & Notifications settings screen. The first custom role="switch" toggle ("Sign-in alerts") is rendered unmistakably ON (green track, thumb pushed right via the .is-on class) while its exposed state is hard-coded aria-checked="false"; the other two switches are genuinely off. Browser-confirmed: visual ON, aria-checked=false.
pages.mechanism: Value-correctness contradiction on aria-checked. role=switch, accessible name, and a permitted/valid boolean are all present, so a screen reader announces the visibly-ON switch as 'Sign-in alerts, switch, off' — the exact inverse of the rendered state; a voice-control user toggles it expecting to turn it on and instead turns it off. SC 4.1.2's 'keep up to date on the status' requirement fails because AT receives the wrong value.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: aria-checked="false" is present, permitted, and a syntactically valid boolean, so ACT 4e8ab6/5c01ea/6a7281 and axe/WAVE/Lighthouse all pass. No checker renders the widget and compares the green/thumb-right ON appearance against the exposed aria-checked; that visual-vs-attribute comparison requires a human or vision model to read the rendered state.

citation.quote: The intent of this success criterion is to ensure that Assistive Technologies (AT) can gather appropriate information about, activate (or set) and keep up to date on the status of user interface controls in the content.

pages.scenario: A Riverside Family Health patient-portal FAQ accordion ("Before Your Appointment"). The first item is rendered open by default — wrapper has .open, the disclosure chevron is rotated, and the answer list is visible — but the trigger button exposes aria-expanded="false"; the other two items are genuinely collapsed. Browser-confirmed: panel open, aria-expanded=false.
pages.mechanism: Value-correctness contradiction on aria-expanded. The trigger is a real button with an accessible name and a valid boolean, so a screen reader announces the visibly-open disclosure as 'collapsed'; a user who activates it to 'open' it actually closes the panel and hides the content. The expanded/collapsed status that the Understanding doc explicitly names is reported opposite to reality.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: role=button, accessible name, and aria-expanded="false" (a permitted, valid boolean) all pass ACT 4e8ab6/5c01ea/6a7281 and axe/WAVE/Lighthouse. No static checker knows the controlled panel is visibly expanded (chevron rotated, content showing) while the button says collapsed; detecting it requires rendering the accordion and comparing the open panel to the exposed state.

citation.quote: Other examples of user interface control states are whether or not a checkbox or radio button has been selected, or whether a collapsible tree view or accordion is expanded or collapsed.

pages.scenario: A Quanta Insights SaaS analytics dashboard tab strip (Overview / Audience / Funnel / Revenue). The third tab, Funnel, is the one rendered active (bright text + blue underline) and the only visible tabpanel, but aria-selected="true" sits on the first tab, Overview; Funnel carries aria-selected="false". Browser-confirmed: visually active = Funnel, aria-selected true on Overview.
pages.mechanism: Value-correctness contradiction on aria-selected: the selected state is on the wrong tab. Exactly one tab is marked selected (structurally valid single-selection), but a screen reader announces 'Overview, tab, selected' and 'Funnel, tab' (not selected) — the inverse of the rendered active tab and the displayed panel, so AT's notion of the current tab is wrong.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The tablist is well-formed: four role=tab elements with names, aria-controls, and exactly one aria-selected="true", so ACT 4e8ab6/5c01ea/6a7281 and tab-pattern linters pass. Automated tools have no model of which tab looks active or which panel is visible; they cannot tell the highlighted tab and shown panel are Funnel while aria-selected=true is on Overview.

citation.quote: states, properties, and values that can be set by the user can be programmatically set; and notification of changes to these items is available to user agents, including assistive technologies.

pages.scenario: A Tidewater Radio Now Playing media player with a custom volume slider. The slider renders at maximum — the fill spans the full rail and the thumb sits flush at the far right — while aria-valuenow="0" (aria-valuemin=0, aria-valuemax=100) and no aria-valuetext is present. Browser-confirmed: thumb left:100%, fill width:100%, aria-valuenow=0.
pages.mechanism: Value-correctness contradiction on aria-valuenow. role=slider, accessible name, and the full required range-state set are present and valid, so a screen reader announces 'Volume, slider, 0' for a thumb at maximum; with no aria-valuetext to override, the numeric lie is all AT hears. A user told volume is already 0 cannot lower it / overshoots when raising.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: aria-valuemin/max/now are all present and syntactically valid numbers in range, so ACT 4e8ab6/5c01ea/6a7281 pass and nothing is malformed. No checker computes the thumb's pixel position relative to the rail and compares it to aria-valuenow; recognizing the thumb is at the far-right maximum while the value says 0 is a position-vs-value visual judgment.

pages.scenario: A Metro Transit Open Data 'Weekday Route Punctuality' table. The On-time % column header shows a down arrow (▼) and the rows are sorted clearly descending (96.8% down to 71.2%, caption states 'highest to lowest'), but that header's aria-sort is hard-coded 'ascending'. Browser-confirmed: arrow ▼, first row 96.8%, last row 71.2%, aria-sort=ascending.
pages.mechanism: Value-correctness contradiction on aria-sort. The token is one of the permitted values, so a screen reader announces 'On-time %, sorted ascending' for a visibly descending column; a non-sighted user reasons the worst routes are first and the best route is lowest — the inverse of the truth. aria-sort, the property that communicates current sort direction, misrepresents the component's actual state.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: aria-sort="ascending" is a permitted token on a column header, so ACT 5c01ea and 6a7281 pass and there is no missing-attribute trigger for 4e8ab6. A scanner cannot read the ▼ glyph as 'descending', cannot perceive that rows run high-to-low, and does no rendered-sort-vs-token comparison; determining the token lies needs human/visual judgment.

pages.scenario: PASS BOUNDARY: a TalentPipe ATS 'Filter Candidates' multi-select listbox (Required skills: Go, Python, PostgreSQL, Kubernetes, Rust). Two options — Go and PostgreSQL — are visually highlighted (tint + check mark) and both carry aria-selected="true"; the highlight is CSS-bound to [aria-selected="true"] so the visual and exposed selection cannot drift. Browser-confirmed: selected-true = [Go, PostgreSQL], matching the highlighted set.
pages.mechanism: Control/discriminator: the rendered selection equals the exposed selection because the highlight and check mark are generated from aria-selected itself. A screen reader announces 'Go, selected' and 'PostgreSQL, selected', matching what a sighted user sees and the candidate list. The selected state is present, valid, and truthful — satisfying 4.1.2's keep-state-current requirement. This proves the aspect's defect is value contradiction, not attribute presence.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Symmetry point: a checker passes this for the shallow reason (every option has a permitted, valid aria-selected boolean and the listbox is aria-multiselectable, so ACT 4e8ab6/5c01ea/6a7281 pass) and would ALSO pass an otherwise-identical page where aria-selected=true were on the wrong, non-highlighted options. Only a human/vision comparison confirms the highlighted set and the aria-selected=true set are the same, which is what makes this a true pass.

citation.quote: allow user-settable properties to be directly set, and provide notification of changes

aspects.title: Accessible name/text alternative on a dynamic named component goes stale after the content changes (F20, temporal correctness)
aspects.plain: A button's content changes by script, but its screen-reader name stays frozen on the old content, so the user is told about something that's no longer there.
aspects.description: A named or interactive component whose visual content is swapped by script (a status-icon button, a favorite/star toggle, a refreshable image control, a rotating banner acting as a named region) keeps its accessible name/alt frozen on the OLD content. F20 is explicit: 'the non-text content is updated, but the text alternative is not updated at the same time.' The name was once correct and is non-empty, so every presence rule passes when sampled once; after the state change it describes a different thing than what is rendered. Catching it requires triggering the change on the page, then comparing the NEW visual to the UNCHANGED name — a temporal + visual judgment no one-shot static scan performs. Scope this to named/interactive components (the 4.1.2 limb) rather than purely decorative images (that angle is 1.1.1).
aspects.scLimb: The 'Name/Value' limb over time: 4.1.2 requires AT 'keep up to date on the status of user interface controls'; a frozen name after a content change means the component's name no longer reflects its current state.
aspects.whyUncovered: All ACT 4.1.2 fixtures are static single-state snapshots; none mutate component content via script and re-check the name afterward. The non-emptiness rules sample the name once and pass. There is no temporal/diff dimension in the corpus, and F20's failure is fundamentally name-correct-then-stale, which a one-shot automated scan cannot represent — it needs interaction plus before/after visual judgment.
