A Sales chart is updated to October results, but the text alternative still describes September results.
keep up to date on the status of user interface controls in the content

aspects.ttWhy: Name stale after automatic content change; 2.D checks notification of auto-updating dynamic content changes.

pages.scenario: E-commerce favorite/star toggle (copper kettle product page): clicking the button swaps the from an empty outline star to a filled gold star and shows 'Saved to your favorites.', but the that is the button's entire accessible name stays frozen at 'Add to favorites' (should become 'Remove from favorites').
pages.mechanism: F20: the non-text content (star glyph) is updated on click but its text alternative () is not, so the toggle's accessible name describes the opposite action from the one it now performs. Verified with Puppeteer: icon src fingerprint changed (empty->filled) while computed name stayed 'Add to favorites'.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The always has a non-empty alt, so axe image-alt/button-name and Lighthouse pass on every sample; there is never an empty name to flag. The name is correct at load and only becomes wrong AFTER a click, so a one-shot static scan that reads the DOM once sees a valid named button. Catching it needs triggering the click then comparing the new filled-star pixels against the unchanged name (a visual + temporal judgment).

citation.quote: The objective of this failure condition is to address situations where the non-text content is updated, but the text alternative is not updated at the same time. If the text in the text alternative cannot still be used in place of the non-text content without losing information or function, then it fails because it is no longer a text alternative for the non-text content.

pages.scenario: SaaS support-desk presence toggle: clicking flips Online->Away (status dot recolors green->amber, visible word changes, aria-pressed flips true/false), but the button's accessible name from a static aria-label stays frozen at 'Set status: you are Online' while the agent is visibly Away.
pages.mechanism: F20 over the 4.1.2 name/value-over-time limb: aria-pressed (the boolean state) flips but the human-readable name string ('you are Online') is never rewritten, so the name contradicts the new amber 'Away' state. Also a voice-control hazard: the spoken target ('Online') no longer matches what the control does. Verified with Puppeteer: dot/visible-text fingerprint changed while aria-label stayed 'Set status: you are Online'.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The button always has a non-empty aria-label (button-name passes) and a present, valid aria-pressed (ARIA state/property checks like 4e8ab6 pass). A tool that checks 'does a state change on interaction?' sees aria-pressed flip and is satisfied. No scanner reads the literal word 'Online' inside the name and judges that it contradicts the new amber 'Away' pixels — that cross-modal semantic comparison requires a human.

citation.quote: The intent of this success criterion is to ensure that Assistive Technologies (AT) can gather appropriate information about, activate (or set) and keep up to date on the status of user interface controls in the content.

pages.scenario: Government DMV registration-renewal CAPTCHA: a 'Get a new challenge' button repaints the challenge image with a new code, but the that spells out the characters to type stays frozen describing the first puzzle ('Type the characters shown: 7 K 2 Q F.').
pages.mechanism: F20 Failure Example 3 (script-updated image src, text alternative not updated): the AT/braille user relies entirely on alt to know which characters to type; after refresh the canvas shows a new code but alt still names the old one, so the user is instructed to type the wrong code and is locked out. Verified with Puppeteer: image src fingerprint changed while #captchaImg alt stayed the original puzzle string.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The always has a meaningful non-empty alt, so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse image-alt passes on every sample; descriptive CAPTCHA alt is even recommended practice (H86), making the stale-after-refresh failure especially subtle. Detecting it requires triggering the refresh, OCR-ing the new rendered glyphs, and diffing them against the unchanged alt string — no scanner reconciles drawn pixels with the name text.

citation.quote: The source attribute of images on a page is updated periodically using script, but the text alternatives are not updated at the same time.

pages.scenario: SaaS analytics dashboard revenue chart (div role='img'): a Q1/Q2 segmented control repoints the drawn bars and value labels to Q2 figures and updates the visible figcaption, but the chart's aria-label (its text alternative) stays frozen on the Q1 description ('West $1.20M ... West leads; South trails').
pages.mechanism: F20 Failure Example 1 (sales chart updated, alt still describes prior period): a screen-reader user's only access to the chart is the aria-label; after switching to Q2 the bars show East leading at $1.31M but AT still announces the Q1 numbers and wrong leading region. The numbers in the label are real but STALE. Verified with Puppeteer: value-label fingerprint changed ($0.94M->$1.31M on East) while #chart aria-label stayed the Q1 string.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The chart is role='img' with a long, descriptive, non-empty aria-label — exactly the recommended pattern for a complex graphic — so axe/Lighthouse see a properly named image and pass. The label even contains real figures, so it reads as a correct alternative. Detecting the failure requires reading the bar heights/value labels now rendered and reconciling them with the prose numbers in the frozen name; no scanner extracts data from drawn <rect>s and diffs it against the name string.

citation.quote: A Sales chart is updated to October results, but the text alternative still describes September results.

pages.scenario: Tideline ambient-music player (lang='en'): an icon-only repeat-mode cycle button whose sole accessible name is its <svg><title>. After the second click the glyph and visible caption show 'Repeat one track' but the <svg><title> (the whole name) is still 'Repeat all tracks', so AT announces the previous mode.
pages.mechanism: F20 on the icon-only repeat-MODE cycle button (button#repeatBtn): its entire accessible name is the inline <svg><title id='repeatTitle'>, with no visible text or aria-label to dilute it. Each click cycles off→all→one, morphing the glyph (loop recolor, '1' overlay) and updating the visible caption, but the handler rewrites the <title> only on the first transition (off→all), so from the second click the name is frozen one state behind — e.g. glyph/caption read 'Repeat one track' while the announced name stays 'Repeat all tracks'.
pages.selectorNote: Icon-only repeat-mode button; its svg title is the sole accessible name
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The button always has a non-empty accessible name computed from <svg><title>, so axe button-name passes on every sample. The name source is an SVG <title>, which static linters rarely diff against a rendered fill color or an adjacent badge, so nothing flags that the title is now semantically wrong. The contradiction (red 'reported' glyph + Arabic 'Undo' badge vs. a name saying 'Report this post') is a cross-modal, post-interaction, cross-lingual judgment a scanner cannot make.

citation.quote: The objective of this failure condition is to address situations where the non-text content is updated, but the text alternative is not updated at the same time. If the text in the text alternative cannot still be used in place of the non-text content without losing information or function, then it fails because it is no longer a text alternative for the non-text content.

pages.scenario: BOUNDARY (passed): a field-school video player with two correctly-built toggles of the same component class — a mute/unmute button whose aria-label is rewritten ('Mute audio'<->'Unmute audio') in lockstep with the swapped glyph, and a caption-language refresh button whose flag regenerates alt ('Captions: English'->'Captions: Espanol'->...) together with src.
pages.mechanism: No F20 condition: every handler that swaps visual content also rewrites the accessible name, so the text alternative remains usable in place of the non-text content after each change. Verified with Puppeteer: clicking #muteBtn changed the wave glyph display (inline->none) AND the name (Mute->Unmute); clicking #langBtn changed #flagImg alt (English->Espanol) AND its src together.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A static one-shot scan cannot tell this pass apart from the case-02 fail: at every instant both pages present a non-empty, validly named toggle, so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse report 'pass' for both. The only discriminator is whether the name TRACKED the content across the state change — a temporal comparison that requires triggering the interaction and re-reading the name, which automated tools do not perform. This case proves the aspect is about temporal correctness, not name presence.

citation.quote: If check #1 is true then the text alternative is not up to date with current item, this failure condition applies, and content fails these Success Criteria.

aspects.title: User-settable state/value cannot be programmatically set via AT or its change is not notified (F15, the 'can be set / notification of changes' limb)
aspects.plain: A custom slider or switch only updates its value for mouse users, so a keyboard or screen-reader user can't change it or never hears that it changed.
aspects.description: SC 4.1.2 requires that states/values 'that can be set by the user can be programmatically set; and notification of changes to these items is available' to AT. A custom control can expose a valid role and a valid initial value (so 674b10/4e8ab6/6a7281 pass) yet be uncontrollable or non-reactive for AT: a slider widget that updates aria-valuenow only on mouse drag and never on keyboard/AT activation, a custom switch whose aria-checked never flips when toggled via the accessibility tree, an expander whose aria-expanded never updates when programmatically activated. F15 covers custom controls that 'do so incompletely' — exposing some semantics statically but failing the set/notify contract. Detecting this requires operating the control through the keyboard/AT path and observing whether the exposed value actually changes — interactive behavioral judgment, not a static attribute scan. (Distinct from the stale-value aspect: there the initial value is simply wrong; here the value is initially correct but cannot be changed or its change is never propagated.)
aspects.scLimb: The 'Value can be set + notification of changes' limb: the value is programmatically determinable initially (rules pass) but is not programmatically SETTABLE by the user via AT, and/or changes are not notified to user agents/AT.
aspects.whyUncovered: All ACT 4.1.2 state/value rules inspect static attribute presence/validity at a single snapshot; none operate the control through the keyboard or accessibility API to verify the value can actually be changed and that the change is reflected/notified. The corpus has no interactive set-and-observe fixture, and a fully-automated checker cannot determine settability/notification without driving the control's interaction and observing AT-visible updates.

references.quote: states, properties, and values that can be set by the user can be programmatically set; and notification of changes to these items is available to user agents, including assistive technologies
when custom controls are created, it is up to the control's author to ensure that the control is correctly exposed to users via the platform's accessibility API
allow themselves to be controlled by assistive technologies

aspects.ttWhy: The 'notification of changes' limb; 2.D isolates whether automatic state/value changes are programmatically notified to AT.

pages.scenario: Fintech onboarding 'risk tolerance' custom slider (role=slider) whose drag math updates the visible fill/thumb and a readout, but never reassigns aria-valuenow/aria-valuetext, with no keydown handler at all.
pages.mechanism: role/name/initial aria-valuenow all valid; Arrow keys are inert (no keydown) so value is not settable via AT, and mouse-driven changes never update aria-valuenow (verified: aria stays 30 while visText reaches 80) — set+notify limb broken.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse inspect one static snapshot where the slider has a valid role, name (aria-labelledby) and in-range aria-valuemin/max/now, passing 674b10/4e8ab6/6a7281; no static rule presses Arrow keys or drags the thumb and re-reads aria-valuenow, so none can observe the value is non-settable and unreflected.

citation.quote: states, properties, and values that can be set by the user can be programmatically set; and notification of changes to these items is available to user agents, including assistive technologies.

pages.scenario: Healthcare patient-portal privacy toggles (role=switch) whose green ON visual is driven by a CSS .on class on click, while aria-checked is hard-wired in the HTML and never reassigned.
pages.mechanism: Valid role/name/initial aria-checked; activation toggles only the .on class so aria-checked diverges permanently (verified: click sets .on=true while aria-checked stays false) — change to a user-settable state is never notified to AT.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Each switch has a valid role, name and aria-checked value on the static snapshot (passes 4e8ab6/6a7281); the divergence between the visual .on class and aria-checked only appears after a click, and no scanner activates the switch then re-reads and compares the attribute to the rendered state.

citation.quote: When custom controls are created, it is up to the control's author to ensure that the control is correctly exposed to users via the platform's accessibility API. If this is not done, then assistive technologies will not be able to understand what the control is or how to operate it or may not even know of its existence.

pages.scenario: Municipal transit 'Service Alerts' disclosure accordion whose headers (button, aria-expanded=false, aria-controls) open the panel via an .open class on the wrapper but never update aria-expanded.
pages.mechanism: Valid button role/name/initial aria-expanded; activation flips a CSS class so the panel becomes display:block while aria-expanded stays 'false' (verified) — expanded/collapsed state change is never notified to AT.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The attribute is present and valid on the static snapshot, so there is no 'missing aria-expanded' or invalid-value finding; tools cannot determine the value SHOULD flip on activation, which requires operating each header and checking aria-expanded against the now-visible panel.

citation.quote: Other examples of user interface control states are whether or not a checkbox or radio button has been selected, or whether a collapsible tree view or accordion is expanded or collapsed.

pages.scenario: SaaS analytics sortable table whose th[aria-sort] headers carry a correct initial sort (Spend descending, others none); clicking another header re-sorts the rows and moves a CSS arrow via data-active but never rewrites any aria-sort.
pages.mechanism: Initial aria-sort is exemplary (one descending, rest none); after activating Conversions the rows re-sort and the arrow moves but Conversions stays aria-sort=none and Spend stays descending (verified) — the user-settable current-sort value is not updated or notified.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The static snapshot has valid table semantics and exactly one aria-sort=descending with the rest none, so every static ARIA-value rule passes and there is no invalid/missing state to flag; catching it needs an operate-then-observe step (sort by another column, re-read aria-sort) that no static scanner performs.

citation.quote: However, when custom controls are created, it is up to the control's author to ensure that the control is correctly exposed to users via the platform's accessibility API. If this is not done, then assistive technologies will not be able to understand what the control is or how to operate it or may not even know of its existence.

pages.scenario: Restaurant review star-rating exposed as a role=slider (with aria-hidden star buttons) and a correct initial aria-valuenow=3; clicking a star fills the visual and rewrites a hint but never updates the slider's aria-valuenow, and there is no keydown handler.
pages.mechanism: Valid slider role/name/initial value; clicking the 5th star fills five stars and updates the hint while aria-valuenow stays 3, and Arrow keys are inert (verified) — rating is neither settable via AT nor notified when changed.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The static snapshot is valid (role=slider, aria-label, in-range aria-valuemin/max/now, aria-valuetext) and the aria-hidden stars create no focusable-inside-hidden conflict, so 674b10/4e8ab6/6a7281 pass; no rule clicks a star or presses an Arrow key and re-reads the slider's value to see it never reflects the choice.

citation.quote: The intent of this success criterion is to ensure that Assistive Technologies (AT) can gather appropriate information about, activate (or set) and keep up to date on the status of user interface controls in the content.

pages.scenario: E-commerce checkout delivery-speed chooser built as a custom role=radiogroup of role=radio divs that CORRECTLY reassigns aria-checked on every option on selection, implements APG roving-tabindex + Arrow/Space/Enter, and drives a non-color tick from aria-checked — the PASS boundary of the same control family.
pages.mechanism: Value is programmatically determinable, fully settable via AT (ArrowDown moves aria-checked true to Express; click moves it to Overnight — verified [true,false,false]->[false,true,false]->[false,false,true]) and the change is notified because aria-checked is reassigned on every radio; the visible ✓ is rendered from aria-checked so state cannot diverge.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Not a failure: automated tools correctly report no 4.1.2 violation here, just as they wrongly report none on the failing siblings — the ONLY difference is runtime behavior (whether the handler reassigns the exposed value), which static scanners never exercise, so a correct human/AT judgment requires operating the control.

citation.quote: states, properties, and values that can be set by the user can be programmatically set; and notification of changes to these items is available to user agents, including assistive technologies.

aspects.title: Iframe has a non-empty accessible name that does not describe its actual content (TT 12.D)
aspects.plain: An embedded frame has a vague title like 'iframe' or 'content', so a screen-reader user jumping between frames can't tell what each one actually contains.
aspects.description: An <iframe> has a non-empty title / aria-label (so cae760 'Iframe element has non-empty accessible name' passes), but that name does not describe what the frame actually contains — a payment widget iframe titled 'iframe', an embedded map titled 'content', a video-player frame titled 'frame1', or two distinct frames sharing a generic name. Trusted Tester 12.D's pass condition is that 'the combination of accessible name and description for each <iframe> describes its content' — the tester must look INSIDE the frame and judge whether the name matches. The only iframe rule that goes beyond non-emptiness, 4b1c6c (same-name-must-have-equivalent-purpose), is flagged notFullyAutomatable and covers only the narrow duplicate-name case; nothing covers a single non-empty-but-undescriptive frame name. Judging adequacy requires rendering the frame's content and comparing it to the name — human content judgment.
aspects.scLimb: The 'Name' limb for embedded frames: the iframe's name is programmatically determined and non-empty (rule passes) but does not communicate the frame's purpose/content, so an AT user navigating frames cannot identify what each frame is.
aspects.whyUncovered: cae760 checks iframe-name non-emptiness only; 4b1c6c is notFullyAutomatable and only checks that iframes sharing an identical name have equivalent purpose — neither evaluates whether a single frame's name describes its content. TT 12.D requires looking inside the frame to judge descriptiveness, which a fully-automated checker cannot do; the corpus has no fixture pairing a generic iframe name against meaningfully different embedded content.

references.quote: The combination of accessible name and description for each <iframe> describes its content.
review each frame's corresponding title attribute for a meaningful description of content
the controls provide important and appropriate information to assistive technologies

aspects.ttWhy: Iframe accessible name must describe its content; this is exactly 12.D's pass condition.

pages.scenario: Coffee-shop checkout (step 3 'Payment') embeds the card-entry hosted-fields iframe. The frame renders a full credit/debit card form (card number, expiry, CVC, billing ZIP, 'Pay $42.00') but its title attribute is the literal default 'iframe' — non-empty yet undescriptive of a payment widget.
pages.mechanism: iframe is in sequential focus order and exposed in the accessibility tree as role Iframe with accessible name 'iframe' (verified via CDP). A screen-reader user navigating frames hears only 'iframe' and cannot tell this is the payment step; the name is programmatically determined and non-empty (cae760 passes) but does not communicate the frame's purpose, failing TT 12.D.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse evaluate iframe names only for non-emptiness; 'iframe' is non-empty so cae760 passes. With a single frame, 4b1c6c (identical-name) is inapplicable. No tool can render the frame, recognise a credit-card payment form, and judge 'iframe' fails to describe it — that requires a human to look inside the frame and compare content to name.

citation.quote: Test Condition: *The combination of accessible name and description for each `<iframe>` describes its content.*

pages.scenario: A dental practice 'Visit our practice' page embeds an interactive street map (location pin, named roads, 'Sunset Rec Center' landmark, attribution, zoom +/- controls) next to the address. The iframe's title is the page-builder placeholder 'content'.
pages.mechanism: iframe is in the tab order, exposed as role Iframe with accessible name 'content' (verified via CDP). A screen-reader user navigating frames hears 'content', indistinguishable from any embed, with no hint the frame is an interactive location map. The name is non-empty (cae760 passes) but does not describe the content, failing TT 12.D.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: 'content' is a non-empty accessible name so cae760 passes and scanners report no error; with one iframe 4b1c6c never fires. The map is built from CSS-positioned divs (no /alt to inspect), so no scanner can perceive it is an interactive map and decide 'content' is inadequate — only a human opening the frame and comparing content to name (TT 12.D) catches it.

citation.quote: Each target element has an accessible name that is not empty ( "" ).

pages.scenario: A gardening-blog article has an in-article embed slot captioned 'Newsletter signup', wired as the iframe's accessible name via aria-labelledby. The frame's actual content is a GrowFast plant-food advertisement ('Advertisement — GrowFast Plant Food', 'Bigger leaves in 30 days', 'Shop GrowFast'), so the name describes DIFFERENT content than the frame contains.
pages.mechanism: iframe is in the tab order with role Iframe and a non-empty accessible name computed from aria-labelledby -> #promo-label ('Newsletter signup'; rendered uppercase via text-transform, reference resolves correctly, verified via CDP). A screen-reader user hears 'Newsletter signup', expects an email-capture form, but enters advertising. The name is non-empty (cae760 passes) but actively misdescribes the content — a TT 12.D failure.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The aria-labelledby reference resolves to a real element, so the accessible name is non-empty and the markup is valid — cae760 passes and no ARIA-reference error is raised; single frame means 4b1c6c is inapplicable. Tools cannot render the frame to discover its content is an ad, nor model 'the name describes the wrong content.' Only a human reading the name against the rendered frame (TT 12.D) sees that name and content disagree.

citation.quote: The ANDI Output for each `<iframe>` in the tab order sufficiently describes its content.

pages.scenario: A book-review page lazy-loads a comments thread into an iframe. The script sets aria-label='Loading…' as a placeholder name during fetch; on load it injects the comments markup (three reader comments, reply buttons, a comment box) but never clears the placeholder, so the stale transient string remains the frame's permanent accessible name.
pages.mechanism: After the async injection settles the iframe is in the tab order, role Iframe, accessible name still 'Loading…' (verified via CDP after a 700ms settle while the comments are present). A screen-reader user navigating frames hears 'Loading…' indefinitely — implying the frame is still busy — when it actually holds a populated comments thread. Non-empty name (cae760 passes) but a stale status string that does not describe current content, failing TT 12.D.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A scan after the page settles sees a non-empty name ('Loading…') so cae760 passes; one iframe means 4b1c6c never applies. The defect is a state/timing inconsistency between a transient name and loaded content — invisible to static rules, which have no concept that 'Loading…' is a status string and no way to read the frame's current content. A human must read the name against the loaded comments (TT 12.D).

citation.quote: Review the ANDI Output for each iframe with a non-negative tabindex (or where tabindex is not defined) to determine whether the accessible name and description accurately describe the content of each `<iframe>`.

pages.scenario: A SaaS Support Console places two embedded tools side by side: Panel 1 is a live chat widget (active agent conversation, message box), Panel 2 is a help-doc viewer ('Backup job stuck at 0%' troubleshooting). The dashboard grid auto-names the slots by position: title='Section A' and title='Section B' — non-empty and DISTINCT, yet neither says what its tool is.
pages.mechanism: Both iframes are in the tab order, role Iframe, with accessible names 'Section A' / 'Section B' (verified via CDP). A screen-reader user navigating frames hears two positional labels and cannot tell which is the live chat (where they might type to an agent) and which is static docs. Each name is non-empty (cae760 passes) and distinct, but neither describes its content, failing TT 12.D for each frame.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Two validly named, uniquely named iframes pass cae760; because the names DIFFER, 4b1c6c — whose entire applicability is two-or-more iframes with matching names — never engages. Scanners see two correctly named frames and report nothing. They cannot render the frames to learn one is a chat widget and the other a help-doc viewer, nor judge 'Section A/B' fails to distinguish those purposes — the per-frame content-to-name judgement TT 12.D requires, exactly the gap 4b1c6c leaves by covering only identical names.

citation.quote: This rule applies to any set of any two or more iframe elements which: are in the same web page (HTML) ; and are included in an accessibility tree ; and that have matching accessible names that are not empty ( "" ).

pages.scenario: BOUNDARY (PASS). An e-learning lesson page embeds a video-player iframe and a transcript iframe, each given a title that fully describes its content: 'Video player: Generics — writing reusable, type-safe functions (Lesson 4)' and 'Transcript: Generics — writing reusable, type-safe functions (Lesson 4)'. Both are in the tab order; a human applying TT 12.D finds each name describes its frame, so the page passes — sharpening the aspect by showing what adequate iframe naming looks like.
pages.mechanism: Both iframes are in the tab order, role Iframe, with accessible names that name both the media type and the specific lesson (names match titles verbatim, verified via CDP). A screen-reader user navigating frames can tell exactly what each frame is and how they relate; the combination of accessible name and content describes the content for each frame, satisfying the Name limb of 4.1.2 for embedded frames under TT 12.D.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Automated tools also cannot confirm a PASS of descriptiveness — they only see two non-empty, distinct names (cae760 pass, 4b1c6c inapplicable) and cannot verify the names actually match the frames' content. The pass is established by the same human TT 12.D judgement that flags cases 01–05; this case demonstrates that judgement returning 'passes' when names are genuinely descriptive, anchoring the aspect boundary.

citation.quote: The ANDI Output for each `<iframe>` in the tab order sufficiently describes its content.

aspects.title: Each part of a multi-part field has a present but ambiguous/undifferentiated sub-name (F86 semantic variant)
aspects.plain: A phone or date split into several inputs labels every box the same ('Phone', 'Phone', 'Phone'), so a screen-reader user can't tell which box is which part.
aspects.description: A compound field (US phone as 3 inputs, date as day/month/year, credit card in 4 groups, time as hour/minute/AM-PM) gives EACH sub-input a non-empty accessible name (so e086e5 passes on every part) — but the per-part names fail to convey each part's role within the whole: all three phone parts named 'Phone', a date's three fields all named 'Date', or area-code and prefix both named 'Number'. F86's intent is that without correctly differentiated per-part names users experience 'undefined text fields'; the automation-resistant case is when names exist but are interchangeable/unhelpful. Deciding the sub-names are inadequate requires understanding the compound semantics and the visual grouping (the punctuation/layout that signals 'this is area code, this is prefix') — semantic judgment the per-field non-emptiness rule cannot express.
aspects.scLimb: The 'Name' limb at sub-field granularity: each part's name is programmatically determined and non-empty (rule passes) but does not identify the part's specific role within the multi-part whole, so AT users cannot tell which field is which.
aspects.whyUncovered: e086e5 fires only when a sub-field's accName is empty; it cannot judge whether three present names ('Phone','Phone','Phone') collectively fail to identify area/prefix/suffix. F86's requirement is a multi-part SEMANTIC one (each part named for ITS role in the whole) that a per-field non-emptiness check structurally cannot express, and the corpus has no grouped multi-part fixture with present-but-undifferentiated sub-names. A fully-automated checker cannot infer the intended per-part roles from layout.

references.quote: A user with assistive technology will be led to believe that the first field is for the entire phone number, and will experience the second and third fields as undefined text fields.
Check that the value of the aria-label attribute properly describes the purpose of an element where user input is required
some or all of the parts of multi-part form field do not have names

aspects.ttWhy: Compound form-field sub-names; TT tests this via 5.C, no isolated test in the 4.1.2 file.

pages.scenario: E-commerce checkout (Trailhead Outfitters) mobile-number field built as three boxes laid out '( 402 ) 555 - 0173'. Visual parentheses/dash make the area/prefix/line structure obvious, but all three inputs carry the identical aria-label="Phone".
pages.mechanism: Three split-phone <input>s each have a non-empty accessible name 'Phone' (so e086e5 passes per-field), but the three identical names do not identify which box is the area code, the prefix, or the four-digit line number; the disambiguating '( ) -' punctuation is in aria-hidden spans. Chrome AX tree confirms three textboxes all named exactly 'Phone'.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse implement ACT e086e5, which fails a field only when its accessible name is EMPTY. Here every input's name is the non-empty string 'Phone', so all parts pass and no tool fires. Detecting the defect requires recognizing the three inputs are one compound phone field, reading the visual '( ) -' grouping to infer per-part roles, and judging that three interchangeable 'Phone' names fail to differentiate them — multi-part semantic + visual reasoning a per-field non-emptiness check structurally cannot express.

citation.quote: A user with assistive technology will experience these as three undefined text fields. Some assistive technologies will read the punctuation as identification for the text fields, which can be even more confusing. In the case of a three-field US phone number, some assistive technologies would name the fields "(", ")" and "-", which is not very useful.

pages.scenario: UK council GOV.UK-styled 'Apply for a Blue Badge' form collects date of birth as three boxes laid out DD / MM / YYYY; all three inputs use aria-labelledby pointing at the single group caption #dob-label ('Date of birth'), so each box's computed name is the identical 'Date of birth'.
pages.mechanism: Each of the day/month/year inputs resolves a valid aria-labelledby IDREF to non-empty text 'Date of birth' (e086e5 passes per-field), but the three identical names cannot tell day from month from year; per-part roles (DD/MM/YYYY) live only in aria-hidden caption spans. In en-GB day-first order this causes real transposition errors. Chrome AX tree confirms three textboxes all named 'Date of birth'.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: e086e5 fires only on an empty name; every input resolves through a valid aria-labelledby to non-empty text, so all three pass. Multiple controls legitimately sharing one label reference is valid (e.g. a column header), so axe will not flag the duplicate target either. Catching it requires reading the DD/MM/YYYY visual order, understanding the compound-date roles, and judging that three identical 'Date of birth' names cannot identify day vs month vs year — a semantic+visual inference no static checker performs.

citation.quote: The failure occurs when there is not a name for each of the three fields in the Accessibility API. A user with assistive technology will experience these as three undefined text fields.

pages.scenario: SaaS billing page (Lumen Studio) 'Add a payment method' enters a 16-digit card number as four ordered four-digit boxes rendered '4242 .. 4242 .. 4242 .. 4242', component-library style in a <div role=group>; every box carries aria-label="Card number".
pages.mechanism: Each of the four segment inputs has the non-empty name 'Card number' (e086e5 passes per-field), but the four identical names lose the 'which segment' information a sighted user gets from position and the gaps; the only segment cues are visual order plus aria-hidden .sep spacers. Auto-advance compounds it. Chrome AX tree confirms four textboxes all named 'Card number'.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: e086e5 only checks non-emptiness; 'Card number' is non-empty on every box so all four pass. A tool would need to infer the boxes are ordered segments of one value, that AT users navigate to them out of order, and that identical names therefore drop the positional 'which segment' role — none of which a per-field emptiness check or any static rule can determine. The defensible fix (positional names like 'Card number, digits 1-4') is itself a human judgment about compound semantics.

citation.quote: For each subfield in the multi-part form field: Check that there is a programmatically determined name for the field.

pages.scenario: Holloway & Pike Lettings rental search (lang='en'): a 'Price range (per month)' filter as two boxes '$ ___ – $ ___'. The minimum box (#price-min) is named 'Price range'; the maximum box (#price-max) is labelled only by the en-dash separator, so AT names it '–', failing to identify the maximum-price field.
pages.mechanism: F86 Example 3 (label associated with the first part only). The price-range filter is one 'from–to' value in two boxes: the visible 'Price range' is a <label for='price-min'> naming ONLY the minimum box, while the maximum box's only associated label is the en-dash separator (<label for='price-max'>–</label>), so its computed accessible name is the lone character '–'. The maximum sub-field therefore has no name identifying it as a price field — a multi-part field whose parts are not differentiated.
pages.selectorNote: Maximum-price box whose only associated label is the en-dash separator
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: e086e5 only checks non-emptiness; '郵便番号' is non-empty on both boxes so both pass, and tools do not flag two inputs sharing an aria-label string. Detecting the failure requires language-specific knowledge that a Japanese postal code is a 3+4 split, reading the 〒/hyphen layout, and judging that two identical '郵便番号' names cannot identify the 上3桁 vs 下4桁 blocks — compound semantics plus visual-layout inference no automated checker performs.

citation.quote: Often, forms asking for a telephone number will include three separate fields, but with a single label... The failure occurs when there is not a name for each of the three fields in the Accessibility API.

pages.scenario: Posthaven Courier shipping label (lang='en'): a 'Delivery contact phone' field as three boxes (country code / area code / local number). Each input's only accessible name is its placeholder mask ('+##', '###', '#### ####'); the visible captions are unassociated spans, so AT names the boxes by their digit masks rather than their roles.
pages.mechanism: A compound delivery phone is split into three boxes (country code, area code, local number). Each box has a VISIBLE caption beside it (a plain <span class='cap'>) that is never associated (no for=, aria-label, or aria-labelledby), so the only accessible-name source on each input is its placeholder format mask. The computed names are therefore '+##', '###', and '#### ####' — masks that do not identify which part is the country code, area code, or local number (F86, compounded by F111 since the visible captions are absent from the names).
pages.selectorNote: Country-code box named only by placeholder mask, not the visible caption
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: e086e5 only checks non-emptiness, and title is a valid accessible-name source per the accName computation, so all three controls pass; axe will not warn that three controls share a title-derived name. Detecting it requires knowing a BP reading is a systolic/diastolic/unit compound, reading the 'Systolic / Diastolic / mmHg' layout, and judging that three identical 'Blood pressure' names fail to identify the parts — domain + visual reasoning beyond a per-field emptiness check.

citation.quote: Check that the value of the aria-label attribute properly describes the purpose of an element where user input is required

pages.scenario: B2B account 'Contact preferences' page (Meridian Logistics) collects an international work phone as three boxes '+ 44 20 - 7946 0991', built correctly per the ARIA14 multi-field example: each part has a distinct role-appropriate aria-label (country code / area code / subscriber number) inside a role=group captioned 'Work phone'. PASS boundary contrast.
pages.mechanism: Same multi-part structural shape as the failing cases, but each sub-input has a DISTINCT, role-appropriate accessible name plus matching autocomplete tel token, so a user landing on any single box knows exactly which segment it is. Chrome AX tree confirms three textboxes named 'country code', 'area code', 'subscriber number' respectively. This isolates the aspect: the failure under test is undifferentiated naming, not the presence of a multi-part field.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Automated tools pass this page for the same shallow reason they pass the failing cases — every input has a non-empty name. The difference that makes it genuinely conformant (distinct, role-appropriate per-part names) is invisible to a per-field non-emptiness check. Including this passing contrast forces the annotator/model to make the exact discrimination the aspect is about, since the DOM is near-identical to case-01 and only the per-part name strings differ.

citation.quote: +<input autocomplete="tel-country-code" type="number" aria-label="country code">

methodology.enNote: Status Messages — WCAG 2.1 AA; no Trusted Tester test.

aspects.title: Live-region politeness is semantically wrong for the message's urgency and update frequency
aspects.plain: A live region announces with the wrong urgency, so either a trivial ticking counter rudely interrupts the screen reader constantly, or a critical warning gets queued and arrives too late.
aspects.description: The status message IS in a working, present live region and IS announced, so every automated tool and every seed (which all model the crude 'no live region at all' failure) passes it. The defect is that the chosen politeness is semantically wrong for what the message MEANS and how often it fires. Two opposite failure shapes: (a) a low-value, high-frequency message (a ticking stock/crypto price, a per-keystroke 'N results' count, a 'last saved 3s ago' autosave heartbeat, a 'people viewing this item: 14' badge) is wired role=alert / aria-live=assertive, so it rudely interrupts and clobbers whatever the screen reader was reading every few seconds, making the app intolerably 'chatty'; (b) conversely a genuinely time-critical / blocking message (session-expiry countdown, 'payment declined — do not navigate away', a security warning) is wired only aria-live=polite, so it is queued behind ongoing speech and the user acts before hearing it. Both politeness values are syntactically valid, so there is no markup error; judging the right priority requires understanding what the message means to the user and its cadence — a contextual call no checker can make from static markup.
aspects.scLimb: Chattiness / appropriateness — Understanding 'Other uses of live regions or alerts' + intent 'doesn't unnecessarily interrupt'; advisory SCR14 (toggle non-emergency alerts).
aspects.whyUncovered: ACT corpus is completely empty (actRuleCount:0, testCaseCount:0). All 25 seeds model only the binary 'message not in a live region -> silent' failure; none models a message that IS announced but at the WRONG priority. Automated tools (axe/WAVE/Lighthouse) cannot flag it because polite and assertive are both valid attribute values — correctness depends on the human meaning and update frequency of the message, which a static or single-snapshot scan has no way to weigh.

references.quote: to make users aware of important changes in content that are not given focus, and to do so in a way that doesn't unnecessarily interrupt their work

references.doc: Understanding 4.1.3 (Other uses of live regions or alerts)
references.quote: there is a risk of making an application too "chatty" for a screen reader user. User testing should be carried out to ensure the appropriate level of feedback is achieved
By default, when the stock price changes, the change is announced by screen readers. This could be annoying to some users, so there are buttons to allow users to toggle the announcements on or off.
The aria live region role of status has an implicit aria-live value of polite, which allows a user to be notified via AT (such as a screen reader) when status messages are added.

pages.scenario: E-commerce running-shoe store with an instant search filter: a 'N results' counter beneath the search box updates on every keystroke. The counter is a present, valid live region wired role=alert (assertive), so typing 'shoes' fires five assertive announcements in under a second, each interrupting and clobbering the last. A low-value, high-frequency count should be polite (role=status), not assertive.
pages.mechanism: role=alert maps to an assertive live region: each text change interrupts current speech. The region's text is replaced on every 'input' event, so a per-keystroke result count repeatedly preempts whatever the screen reader was reading and cuts off its own prior announcements. The message is announced (absence-checkers pass) but at a politeness inappropriate for its low value and high cadence — the 'too chatty' failure.
pages.selectorNote: Resting empty banner aria-live=off; saved message written on submit
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A non-empty live region is present at load with role=alert + aria-atomic=true and genuinely announces. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse verify only that a status message CAN be announced; both assertive and polite are legal values, so no rule fires. No static or single-snapshot scan can weigh that a count firing on every keystroke is low-value, high-cadence content that should be polite — that needs human understanding of the message's meaning and frequency.

citation.doc: WCAG 2.2 Understanding SC 4.1.3 Status Messages — 'Other uses of live regions or alerts' (wcag-understanding/status-messages.html)
citation.quote: Live regions and alerts can be usefully applied in many situations where a change of content takes place which does not constitute a status message, as defined in this success criterion. However, there is a risk of making an application too "chatty" for a screen reader user. User testing should be carried out to ensure the appropriate level of feedback is achieved.

pages.scenario: Financial-news long-form article with a sticky 'Watchlist' price ticker in the right rail. The ticker is a present, valid live region wired aria-live=assertive, and a setInterval re-prices NDX/SPX/BTC every 2 seconds. For a screen-reader user reading the article, the price tape assertively interrupts the narration every two seconds, indefinitely. A ticking price board is the textbook low-value, high-frequency status SCR14 says should be polite and toggleable.
pages.mechanism: An aria-atomic=true assertive region re-priced every 2000ms re-announces the entire board on each tick, interrupting current speech each time. The user can never finish reading a paragraph because the AT keeps cutting in to recite fluctuating prices. The markup is valid; the defect is the wrong politeness for the message's value and cadence.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The ticker is a genuine non-empty live region with a valid aria-live=assertive value and aria-atomic=true; it really announces. Tools confirm announcement is possible and stop — assertive is legal. No static or single-snapshot tool observes the 2-second mutation cadence or judges that a fluctuating price is non-essential content that must not interrupt; that depends on the meaning and frequency of the update.

citation.doc: WCAG Techniques — SCR14 'Using scripts to make nonessential alerts optional' (wcag-techniques/client-side-script/SCR14.html)
citation.quote: The objective of this technique is to toggle announcements to screen readers of changes in a stock-price alert component. By default, when the stock price changes, the change is announced by screen readers. This could be annoying to some users, so there are buttons to allow users to toggle the announcements on or off.

pages.scenario: Government unemployment-benefits wizard, 'certify your claim' step. The user must read a long legal certification statement before checking the agree box. A secure-session region (present, valid) is wired aria-live=polite; when the 30-second expiry countdown is injected, polite politeness queues it behind the long statement the screen reader is still narrating, so it is heard only after the session has already ended and the answers are discarded. A blocking, time-critical countdown must be assertive.
pages.mechanism: Polite live regions defer until the AT finishes current and queued speech. The session-expiry countdown is injected while four dense paragraphs of certification text are being narrated, so 'your session expires in 30 seconds' is not voiced until that minute-plus of speech finishes — long after the deadline has passed. The message IS announced (absence-checkers pass) but the politeness defeats its time-critical purpose; the correct value is assertive/role=alert.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: #sessionMsg is a present, non-empty live region with valid aria-live=polite + aria-atomic=true and announces correctly in isolation. Tools test only that a status message can be announced — polite is a legal value, so nothing fails. Determining that THIS message is time-critical and blocking (a session-expiry countdown), and is queued behind a long passage, is a contextual human judgment no static or single-snapshot scan can make.

citation.doc: WCAG 2.2 Understanding SC 4.1.3 Status Messages — Intent (wcag-understanding/status-messages.html)
citation.quote: The intent of this success criterion is to make users aware of important changes in content that are not given focus, and to do so in a way that doesn't unnecessarily interrupt their work.

pages.scenario: Higher-ed LMS essay editor with an autosave indicator in the toolbar. The indicator is a present, valid live region wired role=alert (assertive); a debounced handler flips it 'Saving…' -> 'All changes saved' roughly every two seconds while the student is still typing. Each flip assertively interrupts the screen reader's typing echo, so the student stops hearing their own words. An autosave confirmation is low-value and belongs in a polite region at most.
pages.mechanism: role=alert is assertive: each text change interrupts current speech. While the user composes, the AT echoes their typing; every ~2s the debounced autosave flips the assertive region twice ('Saving…' then 'All changes saved'), each flip preempting the typing echo (verified by MutationObserver capturing both transitions during active typing). The information is low-value, high-cadence — it should be polite (role=status). Valid markup, wrong politeness.
pages.selectorNote: role=status present at load, muted to aria-live=off; failure text on submit
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: #autosave is a present, non-empty live region with valid role=alert + aria-atomic=true (role=alert is even a sufficient technique). Tools confirm the message can be announced and find nothing wrong — assertive is legal. No static or single-snapshot scan detects that the region is rewritten every two seconds during active typing, nor weighs that an autosave confirmation is low-value content that should be polite; that needs understanding of meaning and cadence relative to the user's task.

citation.doc: WCAG 2.2 Understanding SC 4.1.3 Status Messages — 'Other uses of live regions or alerts' (wcag-understanding/status-messages.html)
citation.quote: However, there is a risk of making an application too "chatty" for a screen reader user. User testing should be carried out to ensure the appropriate level of feedback is achieved.

pages.scenario: Coffee-store checkout. Submitting a declined card injects a critical, action-blocking instruction ('Payment declined — do NOT refresh or press Pay again, a second attempt may place a duplicate charge') into a present, valid live region wired aria-live=polite. On submit the screen reader is narrating a long order summary (line items, discount, shipping, tax, total, address, delivery note), so the polite decline is queued behind all of it; the non-visual user, hearing nothing, may refresh/resubmit and be double-charged before the warning is voiced. A blocking payment error must be assertive.
pages.mechanism: Polite live regions defer until current and queued speech finish. The decline instruction is injected while the verbose order summary is being narrated, so the 'do not refresh' warning is voiced too late to prevent the harmful action. The message IS announced (absence-checkers pass) but the politeness defeats its protective purpose; the correct value is assertive/role=alert.
pages.selectorNote: Resting empty role=status; gets bland filler while urgent text goes elsewhere
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: #payMsg is a present live region with valid aria-live=polite + aria-atomic=true; on decline it genuinely announces. Tools verify only that announcement is possible — polite is legal, so no rule fires. No static or single-snapshot tool can know this specific message is a critical, blocking instruction that must interrupt, nor that it is queued behind a long summary; weighing urgency against politeness is a human contextual judgment.

citation.doc: WCAG 2.2 Understanding SC 4.1.3 Status Messages — In brief (wcag-understanding/status-messages.html)
citation.quote: Goal

pages.scenario: PASS boundary: a bank sign-in verification screen with correct urgency-to-politeness mapping in BOTH directions. (A) A 60-second one-time-code expiry that BLOCKS sign-in is correctly wired role=alert (assertive) so the user hears the deadline in time. (B) A trivial 'Devices currently signed in: N' badge updating every few seconds is correctly wired aria-live=polite so it never interrupts, and carries an on/off toggle exactly as SCR14 prescribes for nonessential alerts. Politeness matches meaning and cadence, so the page passes.
pages.mechanism: Assertive on the blocking code-expiry warning is correct: it interrupts to deliver the time-critical deadline immediately. Polite on the low-value device-count badge is correct: updates queue behind speech and never preempt the user, and the SCR14 toggle flips aria-live to off so the user can suppress them. Both messages are announced, each at a politeness appropriate to its meaning and frequency — no defect.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse pass this page — but they would EQUALLY pass it if the politeness values were swapped (urgent message polite, trivial badge assertive), because both assertive and polite are legal and a live region is present either way. The tools cannot distinguish a correct urgency mapping from an incorrect one; only a human reviewer weighing each message's meaning and update frequency can confirm the mapping is right. This control proves the aspect is about human judgment, not markup validity.

citation.doc: WCAG Techniques — SCR14 'Using scripts to make nonessential alerts optional' (wcag-techniques/client-side-script/SCR14.html)
citation.quote: If the user presses the "Turn Announcements Off" button, their screen reader will stop making announcements when the stock value changes; if they press the "Turn Announcements On" button, the announcements will start again.

aspects.title: Partial update without aria-atomic announces only the changed fragment, losing meaning
aspects.plain: Only the changed value is announced without its surrounding label, so the screen reader says a bare 'three' instead of 'three items in cart' and the meaning is lost.
aspects.description: A persistent status region is correctly marked (role=status / aria-live=polite) and DOES announce on change — passing every tool and every seed. But only an inner sub-node holding the volatile value is updated, and the region is not atomic, so the screen reader speaks just the bare changed token in isolation: 'three' instead of 'three items in cart', 'red' instead of 'filtered to red, 24 products', '2' instead of '2 errors on this page', '85' instead of '85 percent complete'. The visible string is perfectly meaningful because the sighted user sees the surrounding static label; the announced fragment is meaningless because the static context was not re-read. Catching this requires judging whether the spoken fragment alone conveys the same information as the visible whole — a semantic equivalence judgment.
aspects.scLimb: Modification of status text — Understanding 'Modification of status text' (re-announce the whole modified string; correct use of aria-atomic); ARIA22.
aspects.whyUncovered: No ACT case exists, and the seeds only cover regions that announce nothing at all — none covers a region that announces the wrong (truncated) thing. Automated tools cannot detect it: aria-atomic defaults differ by role and by AT, the page has valid markup with a present live region, and whether the announced fragment is intelligible on its own depends entirely on the human meaning of the surrounding (un-announced) label. There is no rule for 'announced text is grammatically/semantically incomplete'.

references.quote: where only the number in this string was coded as an updated chunk of content, the resulting experience for screen reader users could be to only hear "three", which may not be sufficient information to provide context for the user. In such situations, marking the entire "3 items" string as the status text would normally be a better solution

The role of status also has a default aria-atomic value of true, so that updates to the container marked with a role of status will result in the AT presenting the entire contents of the container to the user, including any author-defined labels

since role="status" is currently not treated as atomic by default in some environments, it is advisable to add an explicit aria-atomic="true" if the entire contents of the container should be announced

pages.scenario: MyHealth patient-portal prescriptions page: 'You have 3 refills remaining' wrapped in p#refill-region[role=status][aria-atomic=false]; clicking 'Request a refill' rewrites ONLY the inner span.num#refill-count 3->2, so AT announces a bare 'two' instead of 'two refills remaining'.
pages.mechanism: p#refill-region has role="status" but the developer set aria-atomic="false" EXPLICITLY (overriding the role's atomic default), so on update AT presents only the changed subtree. The 'Request a refill' click handler rewrites ONLY the inner span.num#refill-count (3->2), so AT announces the bare number, dropping the surrounding 'You have' / 'refills remaining' text nodes that carry the meaning.
pages.selectorNote: role=status region present at load; aria-atomic=false truncates updates
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse see a valid role=status live region with good contrast and PASS it (they even credit the live region). They cannot determine aria-atomic's effective value across AT, do not fire the click, do not track that only an inner node mutates, and have no rule for 'the spoken fragment is semantically incomplete versus the visible whole'. Catching it needs a human to judge that 'three' alone is not equivalent to 'three items in cart'.

citation.doc: WCAG 2.2 Understanding 4.1.3 — Modification of status text
citation.quote: However, where only the number in this string was coded as an updated chunk of content, the resulting experience for screen reader users could be to only hear "three", which may not be sufficient information to provide context for the user. In such situations, marking the entire "3 items" string as the status text would normally be a better solution. See Sufficient Techniques for more discussion, including the use of aria-atomic.

pages.scenario: Hiking-boot faceted store with a result summary 'Showing 38 products' inside aria-live=polite; toggling a filter rewrites ONLY the inner <b id=count> numeral while the region is non-atomic (aria-atomic defaults to false for explicit aria-live), so AT announces a context-free '24'.
pages.mechanism: An element carrying an explicit aria-live (not role=status) has aria-atomic defaulting to false, so a non-atomic region announces only the mutated subtree; rewriting only #count makes AT speak the lone numeral '24' with no 'Showing ... products' label.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A static scan finds a valid aria-live region, labelled checkbox facets, correct contrast, and real product markup — all green. Tools audit one DOM snapshot, neither firing the filter nor tracking which subtree mutates, and have no model of aria-atomic's effect on what is spoken. There is no rule for 'the announced numeral is meaningless without its label'; separating it from a correct atomic region requires firing the update and judging that '24' alone is not equivalent to 'Showing 24 products'.

citation.doc: WCAG Techniques ARIA22 — Using role=status to present status messages
citation.quote: The role of status also has a default aria-atomic value of true, so that updates to the container marked with a role of status will result in the AT presenting the entire contents of the container to the user, including any author-defined labels (or additional nested elements). Such additional context can be critical where the status message text alone will not provide an equivalent to the visual experience.

pages.scenario: Legal case-management document upload with 'Uploading: 0% complete' in p[role=status][aria-atomic=false]; a timer rewrites ONLY the inner <span id=pct> percentage node, so AT announces a bare '85' (verified live: pct moved to 12 while visible string stayed 'Uploading: 12% complete') with no 'percent complete'.
pages.mechanism: aria-atomic="false" forces AT to present only the changed node when the region mutates; since JS touches only #pct, AT speaks the bare percentage digits with neither 'Uploading' nor 'percent complete', destroying the unit. The dev set false to reduce chattiness — the wrong lever.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: aria-atomic="false" is a perfectly legal boolean value; no linter flags it and the region is a valid role=status, so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse pass and credit the live region. They do not run the upload, do not see that only the inner span mutates, and have no heuristic that a bare percentage is unintelligible. Distinguishing it from acceptable design requires firing the upload and judging that '85' spoken alone is not equivalent to '85 percent complete'.

citation.doc: WCAG 2.2 Understanding 4.1.3 — Modification of status text
citation.quote: Typical methods of writing such changes in the page content result in the entire modified text string being considered a new change, and thus read by assistive technologies. However, where only the number in this string was coded as an updated chunk of content, the resulting experience for screen reader users could be to only hear "three", which may not be sufficient information to provide context for the user.

pages.scenario: Arabic RTL library catalogue with result count 'النتائج: ٠ نتيجة' (Results: 0 result) in p[role=status]; each search rewrites ONLY the inner <b id=n> Eastern-Arabic numeral while the region is non-atomic, so AT announces a bare '٢٤' having dropped both the leading 'results:' label and the trailing 'result(s)' unit.
pages.mechanism: role=status's atomic default is unreliable across AT (ARIA22 advises explicit aria-atomic=true); without it the AT speaks only the mutated numeral. In RTL the meaning depends on both the leading label and the trailing unit, both of which are lost, leaving an orphaned '٢٤'.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Scanners see a valid role=status region, a labelled type=search field, correct contrast, valid lang=ar/dir=rtl, and real catalogue items — all pass. They do not fire the search, do not track which node mutates, and have no model of aria-atomic across AT. There is no rule for 'the announced numeral lacks its label and unit', and the RTL/Eastern-numeral framing is invisible to a structural check; catching it requires judging that '٢٤' alone is not equivalent to '24 results'.

citation.doc: WCAG Techniques ARIA22 — Using role=status to present status messages
citation.quote: Note that since role="status" is currently not treated as atomic by default in some environments, it is advisable to add an explicit aria-atomic="true" if the entire contents of the container should be announced.

pages.scenario: Social-post composer with a character-budget meter '280 characters remaining' in p[role=status]; typing rewrites ONLY the inner <b id=left> count node, so AT announces a bare '267' that loses not just the unit but the polarity (used vs remaining), which lives entirely in the un-announced trailing words.
pages.mechanism: role=status's atomic default is unreliable; without explicit aria-atomic=true a non-atomic region speaks only the mutated #left node. Two layers of meaning are destroyed: the unit ('characters') and the polarity — a bare decrementing '267' gives no hint whether the budget counts down (remaining) or up (used), as that direction is encoded only in the trailing words.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The meter is a valid role=status region with good contrast and a properly off-screen-labelled textarea — every static check passes. Tools do not simulate typing, do not track which node mutates, and have no model of how aria-atomic shapes spoken output; there is certainly no rule for 'the announced number is ambiguous in polarity'. Separating it from an acceptable counter requires typing, listening, and reasoning that '267' alone conveys neither the unit nor the direction.

citation.doc: WCAG Techniques ARIA22 — Using role=status to present status messages
citation.quote: Such additional context can be critical where the status message text alone will not provide an equivalent to the visual experience.

pages.scenario: PASS boundary: ambient web-radio player 'Now playing: Track 1 — Slow Harbor by Elin Brook' in p[role=status][aria-atomic=true]; Skip rewrites ONLY the inner #track/#title/#artist nodes (same partial-update mechanism as the failing cases) but aria-atomic=true makes AT re-announce the WHOLE region (verified live: 'Now playing: Track 4 — Tidal Glass by Marin Vale').
pages.mechanism: aria-atomic="true" instructs AT to present the entire live region whenever any descendant changes, including author-defined labels; mutating only the inner value nodes still triggers a full re-announcement of 'Now playing: Track 4, Tidal Glass by Marin Vale', so the announced whole is equivalent to the visible whole — the correct remediation for the partial-update trap.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: This is the crux: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse treat case-06 IDENTICALLY to the failing cases — all are valid role=status live regions with good contrast and real content — and pass every page the same way. They cannot evaluate that here the announced whole IS semantically equivalent to the visible whole whereas in case-01/03/05 the announced fragment is NOT. Separating this pass from those fails is exactly the human semantic-equivalence judgment no automated rule performs.

citation.doc: WCAG Techniques ARIA22 — Using role=status to present status messages
citation.quote: The role of status also has a default aria-atomic value of true, so that updates to the container marked with a role of status will result in the AT presenting the entire contents of the container to the user, including any author-defined labels (or additional nested elements). Such additional context can be critical where the status message text alone will not provide an equivalent to the visual experience.

aspects.title: Role/aria-live added together with (or after) the content, instead of pre-existing empty
aspects.plain: The live region is created at the same instant its message is, but screen readers only announce changes to regions that already existed, so the message is never spoken.
aspects.description: The FINAL DOM looks perfect: there is a <div role="status" aria-live="polite"> containing the message, with valid markup. A static scan and the seeds (which key on absence of role/aria-live) both pass it. But the region — or its role/aria-live attribute — was created/attached at the same moment the message text was injected, rather than existing as an empty container at page load. Most screen readers only announce mutations to live regions that were already present and registered, so a region born with its content never fires. F103 calls out this timing limb explicitly; ARIA19 requires the empty container at page load; ARIA22's test step 1 requires the role to be present BEFORE the message occurs. Confirming it requires reasoning about the ORDER of DOM operations (and ideally observing AT behavior), not the resting markup.
aspects.scLimb: Failure limb F103 'role or property not set before the dynamic content is added' / empty-container-present-at-load (ARIA19 step 1, ARIA22 step 1).
aspects.whyUncovered: Empty ACT corpus; the seeds detect the static absence of a live region, so a page whose final DOM HAS a correct live region sails through — yet it can still fail because the region was injected with its content. Automated single-snapshot tools see only the end state (a valid live region with text) and have no signal that the container was not present-and-empty at load; the failure is purely temporal/behavioral.

references.quote: Additionally, if the role or property is not set before the dynamic content is added, this also predicts a failure.
Check that the element containing the new content does not have a pre-existing aria role of status, alert, or log, or an aria-live attribute
The error container must be present in the DOM on page load for the error message to be spoken by most screen readers.
Check that the container destined to hold the status message has a role attribute with a value of status before the status message occurs.

pages.scenario:
City recycling-bin request form: on submit the handler does resultArea.innerHTML = '
Your recycling cart request was received…
', so the role=status attribute is born inside the same markup string as the confirmation text. The resting DOM is a textbook-correct live region but no live region existed at page load.
pages.mechanism: F103 timing limb / ARIA19 step 1: a live region must be present-and-empty when the AT registers it so a later content mutation fires. Here the role=status node and its text enter the DOM together via innerHTML, producing no empty-region-then-mutation transition, so NVDA/JAWS/VoiceOver stay silent; the screen-reader user gets no submit confirmation (and the form was hidden).
pages.selectorNote: Resting empty container; confirmation role=status injected on submit
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse evaluate a single post-submit DOM snapshot in which the role=status region with text and good contrast is fully valid, so every rule passes. No static tool records WHEN the role attribute came into existence relative to the text; it cannot distinguish a region empty-at-load-then-filled (announces) from one born-with-its-content (silent). Verified via puppeteer: liveRegionsAtLoad=0, then a role=status born-with-content node appears after click.

citation.quote: The absence of all of these techniques predicts a failure for the status message be announced to the user. Additionally, if the role or property is not set before the dynamic content is added, this also predicts a failure.

pages.scenario: SaaS analytics 'Run now' dashboard with a hand-rolled toast helper: showToast() does document.createElement('div'), setAttribute('role','status') and aria-live='polite', sets two text children, and ONLY THEN appendChild()s the finished element. Region and message arrive in one tick on a node that was detached until connection.
pages.mechanism: Live-region announcements diff the contents of a region the AT is already monitoring. Assembling role/aria-live and the text on a detached element and connecting it as one subtree yields no empty-registered-region → content-added transition, so the 'Pipeline started' toast is not spoken. Auto-dismiss after 6s compounds the loss.
pages.selectorNote: Resting empty toast container; born-with-content toast appended on click
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Once present the toast is a fully valid role=status aria-live=polite element with text — nothing to flag — and it may auto-dismiss before a scan runs. A static tool has no model of the setAttribute→textContent→appendChild ordering and cannot tell attributes-applied-before-connection (silent) from text-into-an-already-connected-empty-region (announced). Verified via puppeteer: liveRegionsAtLoad=0, born-with-content node after click.

citation.quote: The error container must be present in the DOM on page load for the error message to be spoken by most screen readers.

pages.scenario: University library catalog same-page search: #results ships as a plain div with no aria-live; on submit render() calls box.setAttribute('aria-live','polite') and writes the '7 results found' status line + hits into the same element in one synchronous operation, so aria-live is upgraded onto the element at the same tick it is filled.
pages.mechanism: For a polite announcement the element must be registered as a live region and THEN have its contents mutate. Adding aria-live in the same operation that injects the text moves the element straight from 'not a live region, empty' to 'live region, full' with no intermediate empty-registered state, so the '7 results found' status message (an in-scope status per Understanding 4.1.3) is never announced.
pages.selectorNote: Resting plain div; aria-live + results written same tick on search
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The post-search DOM holds a valid aria-live=polite region with a non-empty count message, so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse pass. No static tool records the ORDER in which aria-live and the text were applied — it sees only that both exist in the final snapshot — so 'attribute predated content' (announces) is indistinguishable from 'attribute and content applied together' (silent). Verified via puppeteer: liveRegionsAtLoad=0, aria-live born-with-content after submit.

citation.quote: After a user presses a Search button, the page content is updated to include the results of the search, which are displayed in a section below the Search button. The change to content also includes the message "5 results returned" near the top of this new content. This text is given an appropriate role for a status message. A screen reader announces, "Five results returned".

pages.scenario: Real-time stock-price watchlist (novel long-tail): when a price-alert threshold is crossed the app mounts a custom element <price-alert>, whose connectedCallback createElement('div'), sets role=status and aria-live=assertive, sets textContent to the alert, and appends it — assembling a filled live region as the element enters the DOM via the custom-element lifecycle.
pages.mechanism: connectedCallback runs at insertion; building the role=status child with textContent already set and appending it materializes attribute+text as one connected subtree, with no empty-registered-region → mutation transition. Even aria-live=assertive typically stays silent because the region was never registered while empty, so the screen-reader trader gets no spoken alert.
pages.selectorNote: Resting empty mount; born-with-content price-alert region mounted later
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: After mount the DOM holds a syntactically valid role=status aria-live=assertive region with text, so every rule passes; the element also auto-removes after 8s. The failure lives entirely in the custom-element lifecycle — a tool would have to model that connectedCallback set role and text before the node was ever observable as empty, which no static checker does. Verified via puppeteer: liveRegionsAtLoad=0, born-with-content node appears via connectedCallback.

citation.quote: Check that the container destined to hold the status message has a role attribute with a value of status before the status message occurs.

pages.scenario: RTL Arabic pharmacy refill portal (novel long-tail + i18n): each Renew button clones a <template> whose content node ALREADY carries role=status, aria-live=polite, and the Arabic confirmation copy; cloneNode(true) then appendChild inserts a born-with-content live region. Resting DOM is a valid Arabic role=status region with a full refill confirmation.
pages.mechanism: cloneNode(true) of the template fragment yields a detached subtree where role=status, aria-live, and the Arabic text coexist; appendChild connects the whole subtree at once, so there is no empty-region-then-mutation event and the 'refill received' status is not announced to NVDA/JAWS/VoiceOver/TalkBack reading Arabic.
pages.selectorNote: Resting empty container; cloned born-with-content status appended on renew
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The appended clone is a valid role=status aria-live=polite region with non-empty, well-contrasted Arabic text, so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse report nothing. They cannot see that the role attribute and the text were authored together inside a <template> and cloned as one unit; the snapshot shows only the correct end state. Distinguishing cloned-already-filled (silent) from text-into-pre-existing-empty (announced) needs reasoning about the template-clone-append sequence. Verified via puppeteer: liveRegionsAtLoad=0, born-with-content Arabic node after Renew.

citation.quote: Check that the container destined to hold the status message has a role attribute with a value of status before the status message occurs. Check that when the status message is triggered, it is inside the container.

pages.scenario: Boundary PASS control: a single-origin coffee storefront ships a persistent empty <div id="snackbar" role="status" aria-live="polite"> in the markup AT PAGE LOAD; add-to-cart writes only textContent into that pre-existing, already-registered region ('Yirgacheffe added to your cart. 1 item.'). Same final markup as the failing cases, but the region pre-existed empty.
pages.mechanism: Because the role=status (implicit aria-live=polite) region is in the DOM and empty at load, the browser/AT registers and monitors it up front; a later textContent mutation is observed and announced. Satisfies ARIA19 (empty container at load → content injected) and ARIA22 (role present before the status message occurs) — the exact inverse of the born-with-content failures.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Automated tools also pass this page, but for the wrong reason: they pass because the end-state markup is a valid live region — the very same end state they pass in the failing cases. They cannot tell genuinely-correct (region pre-existed empty) from genuinely-broken (region born with content) because the distinguishing fact is temporal and absent from any single snapshot. This control shows the PASS/FAIL boundary lives entirely in the ORDER of DOM operations. Verified via puppeteer: liveRegionsAtLoad=1 (empty), then text-only mutation with preexisting-empty marker.
